Cons:
_ Lack of monsters and summons variety.
_ Having wrongly skilled your hero is quite unforgiving, it's better to reset the game and start all over.
_ Luck almost always prevails over strategy, which is my biggest negative point. Even with the right skill points allocation, right strategy, you will not win if you don't have a minimum of luck, which can be seriously frustrating at times.
The biggest changes I would like to see in the future are probably:
_ Possibility to respec the skill points.
_ Reducing the impact of luck in the battle, which currently makes things go very random, and that's just not fun. (Note that I say reducing, not remove totally)

Serious Sam The Second Encounter is a game that understand itself in a very deep and meaningful way. Much in the same way the First Encounter did this sequel makes no pretense of having a story or anything of the sort. This is about shooting aliens and looking cool while doing it, nothing more and nothing less.
Right out the gate you will notice the similarities to the First Encounter, not much has changed overall. The graphics has gotten a little sharper, the enemies a little faster, the locales more varied. Although this rehash of the original does pain me somewhat, I would have loved to seen more innovation than this, it does still succeed on the same basic levels as the original did. The Second Encounter is a no frills, full speed ahead first person shooter featuring a badass protagonist spouting off one liners that would have made Duke Nukem proud.
Instead of just the sandy surroundings of the original you now get to slaughter through alien hordes in a variety of different locales, still looking as pretty as ever. The maps are still huge and the number of enemies that gets thrown at you is still preposterous. A bigger emphasis on environmental traps makes for some very intense encounters although the puzzle sections are still highly lacking. In particular the series of jumping puzzles near the start of the game leaves you bored and hoping at that some headless suiciders come crashing through soon.
Some new weapons are introduced, most notably the sniper rifle and although Sam Stone still has a high quality arsenal at his disposal you are as last time around lacking that one iconic gun you will remember for years to come.
The soundtrack is relatively unimpressive but the weapons sounds great, both the firing and the impacting. Sam's one liners are still funny and the ambiance is passable.
All in all Serious Sam The Second Encounter could best be described as a plus one sequel. The developers have taken everything they liked from the first game and simply added a little something extra to every aspect. This creates an experience that is every bit as entertaining but still earns a little disappointment for not innovating more. Like the original, this was a bargain price even on release and as such it is a game that should be in the library of every serious FPS gamer.

Yomawari: Night Alone is a cute horror adventure game where you play as a little girl searching for your big sister and lost dog.
You wander alone in the dark, with only a flashlight to help guide your way. Terrible creatures lurk in the night, and many of them will try to hunt you down.
In this game, you don’t have a health bar to monitor, and you are always one-shotted if you get hit, so expect to die quite a bit. The only resource that you need to monitor is your stamina. While in close proximity to monsters, your stamina drains even faster, and the sound of the heartbeat intensifies; pounding louder and faster, it really makes you feel on edge, especially if you don’t know exactly where the enemies are coming from.
Trial and error definitely plays a role as you venture around the town, and because of this, you will often learn what to do the hard way. Fortunately, death is very forgiving, and it’s more of an inconvenience than anything else. Some people will view this as a pro, while others will view it as a con, depending on what you hope to get from the game. You get to keep any items you found before dying, and you respawn at either your house, or the last shrine that you quick saved at. You quick save using coins that you find around the world, they are plentiful.
There isn’t much reason to want to replay the game, but there are a lot of collectibles you can find. When you finish the story, it’s nice that you can continue collecting items if you want to.
The game took me a bit over 5 hours to complete, but this was with me exploring a fair amount, and dying several times on a few different parts. I enjoyed the game quite a bit, but I admit that there were a couple parts that I found frustrating. Overall, it’s a quality game though, and if you’re looking for decent horror adventure, it’s one worth checking out. I would like to see some improvements made to the resolution settings and performance, but it wasn’t enough to make me not like the game. Keep in mind though, that the game is a bit on the short side for the price, so you might want to wait for a sale.

TL;DR - This is a short puzzle game (even with a bit of exploration on my end it only took a little over 6 hours to complete), and the strategy tag is a mislabel. Still a fun play, but not for $20.
========
Coming on the heels of Firely Diaries, and considering it was a handheld game, I didn't expect a long trip. The overall atmosphere is self-explanatory - a quiet town in the dead of night. No music to intensify or interfere with the experience. Just silence and ambient noises.
Since the game is played top down, it's less of a horror game (cute tag is of notable detriment) and far more of a puzzle adventure. The strategy tag really has no place up top, considering it's pretty basic what you can do: hide, run, and die. There
a tiptoe option for movement, but I never found a use for it. Almost all the enemies are triggered by proximity, and distracting them with objects tended to only work on a few of the basic ones. Knowing when and how to hustle is your best (and later on only) friend.
The difficulty is fairly casual, in that items you pick up are still in your log/inventory even after death. While this means some puzzles can be entirely negated by suicide running them, the intent was to soften the blow when confronted with the larger stretches of the game where save points are infrequent or don't exist. This is worthwhile in several scenarios beginning around the third chapter.

As a fan of classic arcade games, I want to like Titan Attacks. Its polished visuals and basic core gameplay are well executed. However, control and pacing issues outweigh these positives.
To achieve fast movement, you must play with a mouse. And yet, the game does not lock your cursor to its window, nor does it lock in fullscreen mode with multiple monitors. If your mouse leaves the game, your movement is dropped. Players with multi-monitor setups have to disable all but one monitor to reliably play Titan Attacks, which is absurd.
So the mouse controls want you to play in fullscreen, which is cumbersome but manageable. But at least on Linux (haven't tested on Windows), minimizing while in fullscreen mode effectively crashes the game. I lost a couple hour-long sessions to this minimization crash, which is the biggest reason for my non-recommendation.
After each level, you are placed in a shop menu for purchasing tank upgrades. Given the brevity of levels, this menu seriously disrupts the flow. You can max out your ship quite quickly, rendering the shop nothing more than a health/bomb restore option, or more frequently, a "continue" button you must click before proceeding. I like the shop system, but wish it were integrated in a non-invasive manner.
Titan Attacks has clean, basic, and enjoyable gameplay. I just find it difficult to appreciate that action against these issues.

Everyone praises Morrowind because it was a childhood memory of theirs, thus they hold it in greater light. The reality is, Morrowind is an archaic game with broken mechanics and hardly any voice acting. The rules and mechanics are meant for a D&D-esque boardgame, not a video game. 95% of your attacks will miss, regardless of how accurate your shot or how close you are. That's not a quality feature, that's a f*cking annoyance with little to no purpose. If realism is what they were aiming for, they should have had the occasional attack miss. Not the occasional attack hit.
Furthermore, I never did like Morrowind's quest system. It was blocky and confusing. Same goes for the directions. Yes, I get that broad directions are sometimes good for a game (like in Mount & Blade games), but the way they did it didn't work.
The only thing I can commend Morrowind for is the graphics, which are WAY better than Oblivion's graphics for some reason.
1: No fast travel or sprinting. To get anywhere in Morrowind, you have to either slowly walk or buy a stiltstrider ride (AKA a taxi) to the location you want. Not to mention every-♥♥♥♥ing-thing in Morrowind is coloured grey, so stiltstriders just sorta blend into the background and it's very hard to find them.
2: The map is not interactive. You can't drag it to see points of the world you want. No, the map only shows you a very small portion of the area you're currently in. And y'know the best part? Nothing's labelled! :D
3: All NPCs are basically walking encyclopedias. They all have way more information than a run-of-the-mill citizen would generally have, but none of them have anything new to say. You can ask 100 NPCs the same question, and they'll all give the exact same answer.
4: The animations. Yeah, I know it's old, but we've had WAY better games during Morrowind's release. See, I don't care about graphics all that much (I honestly think newer games like Fallout 4 should accommodate older computers like mine with a "♥♥♥♥♥♥ visuals" option), but you gotta be in an ACCEPTABLE RANGE. You can't have XCOM 2 come out, then have Pong come out the same year and expect me to leave Pong's (lack-of) graphics alone. The animations for everyone make you look like you♥♥♥♥♥♥yourself. It looks awful.
5: THE COMBAT. Everything works on a dice system. Every attack has a very high possibility to miss, because your "accuracy" or what-the-♥♥♥♥-ever isn't high enough. However, even low-level NPCs will almost never miss. This makes progressing in this game NEARLY IMPOSSIBLE BECAUSE YOU CAN'T LEVEL UP. YOU CAN'T LEVEL UP BECAUSE YOU CAN'T FIGHT. YOU CAN'T FIGHT BECAUSE YOU CAN'T LEVEL UP. ETC.
6: Every single NPC, regardless of story importance, is mortal. Meaning, your game can be ruined by accident.
7: If you're a khajiit or an argonian in Morrowind, guess what? Because of your snout and elongated feet, you're not allowed to wear ANY boots or full-faced helmets! These humanoid items would indeed not fit them. However, ARGONIANS AND KHAJIITS HAVE BEEN A THING FOR THOUSANDS OF YEARS, WOULDN'T ARGONIAN AND KHAJIIT-DESIGNED ITEMS EXIST?!
When mods are necessary to play your♥♥♥♥♥♥properly, your game is bad. I'm so ♥♥♥♥ing tired of explaining that to Morrowind ♥♥♥♥ers. And when I say that, I mean they actually have sex with the box/disc of Morrowind because they love it so much. You love it because you grew up with it. If you played it for the first time today, you'd hate it. It's a bad game.

The best way to describe this game, in my mind, would be this: Think if Elder Scrolls and Command and Conquer decided to have a kid that was really into mideval days. Then the child meets Stewey Griffin and he is brainwashed with images of total world domination.
The Result: An overwhelmingly addictive offline/online strategy game that not only makes you worry about whether you can repel a seige against a kingdom's 1000 Nord Huscarls with only your 80 men and a giant battle axe, but this game allows you to become more familiar with the real-life aspects within the game itself.
For example, if you raid villages, the economy of the nearby town will decay. If you flood a market with the... uuh... "randomly obtained" resources from a village, prices of goods will drop/raise in other parts of the land.
Another great aspect of the game is the social interactions with other lords within the realm.
You fight a lord, they lose because youre Archer Army KILLS EVERYTHING before they even reach over the crest of the hill, the captured lord has a chance to be brought to their knees and beg for freedom. Youre choices will bring good reputation from some lords, and bad rep from others. Youll begin to see the personalities in each lord/vassal based on how they speak to you. Many games arent even able to give characters a catch phrase to say; let alone an entire story of their lives within each and every character in this game.
Tired of the seeing all these pesky kingdoms fightign over who has the bigger............ Castle?
THEN MAKE YOURE OWN KINGDOM AND CLAIM TO HAVE THE BIGGEST YOURSELF!
Attempt to recruit lords from other factions, capture castles without trying to♥♥♥♥♥♥off the other kingdoms to have a World War 0.9, and figure out the perfect army composition using your preference of spearmen, crossbow sharpshooters, Knights in shiny red blood-soaked armor, or a 300 peasant army of doom.
Hate the kingdoms and just want to make a S*** ton of money? Then, become a mercenary! Buy land in cities to make Businesses, tax caravans, work for other kingdoms to fight their enemies and run when you get your money.
Overall, this game is VERY easy to run on any computer due to the age of the game, the possibilities in this game are endless, and your 300 peasant army can wipe out any cow herd that stands in your way.
WORTH. EVERY. PENNY.

It’s time to relaunch Indie Game of the Week with a boom, of dynamite that is!
Cave Coaster is an addictive new Indie Game which sees yourself as a gem hungry miner who loves to ride the rails with his miner buddies and risk it all to claim as many jewels as possible before they fall from the tracks.
We’ve been taking our cart for a ride and here are our thoughts on the game.
Well paced action keeps you playing at a speed that’s balanced enough for you to decide your next move but fast enough to keep you on your toes. As you progress so does the game, making it more challenging and adding more objects for you to understand.
Common in most casual Indie Games are Power Ups as they offer the player a goal to aim for that helps to improve their game.
First up we have the Magnet power-up, this one is designed to suck in all the gems around and help the miner collect more.
Top Tip – Make sure to use the magnet when you’re in a section that is almost completely filled with gems as you’ll collect a lot more!
The Rocket is a big blaster, designed to help speed sections and progress at pace.
Finally the Shield is used to defend your cart against damage, at first this will seem like a un-needed power up but what you quickly come to learn once the game develops is this is one of the most important.
The best ways to keep riding the rails for longer and progress more within a single run is by picking up friends along the way. Each miner in your cart can be compared to a life in terms of when you crash into a barrier you’ll lose one but be able to recover. Keep your cart full so when it starts getting hairy you’re prepared. As well as having a full cart of miners it’s important to keep an eye on your Shield power up and make sure it’s charged just in case. Using both these solutions will give you a much better chance at survival.
Want to boost for longer, feel stronger or collect more? Then you’ll want to upgrade your power-ups. Using the gems you’ve won and collected you can earn enough to level up and improve your arsenal of powers. Bored of your mine cart? Don’t worry they are unlockable too so keep hitting the caves and you’ll be riding in all sorts of vehicles.
Vibrant, full of colour and well crafted. Although when we played it didn’t display in a full screen we were still able to enjoy the rich environments of the caves.

World's Dawn is a game I found annoying until I got the hang of it. BUT. That is only because I had never played a Harvest Moon-esque game before . Once I got the hang of it, it became very fun and addicting, though there were some times where I wanted to take a break or got a little bored. Despite that, I found myself returning to the game again and again until I got to the play time I'm at now.
The graphics of World's Dawn are really cute, and the characters are pretty interesting to get to know. The music is also excellent, and fits the overall style and setting of the game. The quest for the Feral Shades, while it may be tough if you don't know what you're doing, I think is rewarding in the whole 'story complete' way. Others may disagree, though. Once that is done, however, there's so much more to complete for completionists out there. And I like the idea of having that replayability. More so because the gameplay really isn't all that bad when you get used to how things work in Sugar Blossom Village. It's simple, but has some variety in things to do. Not to mention all of the festivals that will certainly keep you busy preparing for! A lot of it, really, has to do with time management.
All in all, this is a pretty fun game! And I am very happy to say that I don't regret purchasing it to try out of curiosity nearly as much as I did in the beginning. If you can get the hang of the gameplay as I did, or if you're a fan of games like Harvest Moon, I definitely recommend this one!
P.S. My only problem is that Steam achievements may be glitched for some, and I really don't want to replay through a part or a bunch of parts just to get it. But have no fear! The marks, at least, should still record themselves just fine in your Collection Journal.

This game is a nice throwback to Space Invaders in a few areas, but overall I wouldn’t recommend this game to anyone at its price for the following reasons.
- Smart Bombs keep rising in price throughout the game. This wouldn’t be an issue if it weren’t for...
- ...The fact that Smart Bombs are hard to come by in the rounds, and a good deal of rounds are along the lines of “burn smart bombs or die” kind, making this worse!
- Carpel tunnel is going to be an issue. Weapons do not fire rapidly unless you continue to tap the button, and secondary weapons do not proc unless you tap. It gets annoy fast.
- Capturing Titans...this is annoying, especially with the first point. If you shot them, nothing happens. If you capture them you get money. Fail to do so, and you lose cash equal to what you would have earned. You could easily find yourself in a bind where you’ll end up debating if losing the cash is worth it, or if you should risk having lives eaten into trying to save a bit more cash for smart bombs.
- Barely any mercy invincibility is the worse offender. All too easily you can lose a full stock of shields in under five seconds, ESPECIALLY in later levels.
Overall, I’d say skip it unless its in a bundle or on sale for no less than 50%. Otherwise keep away. Keep FAR away.
Also I bet it in 115 minutes, a bit under two hours. So if that’s too short for 100 waves, that’s another reason to wait for a sale.

I do rather love this game, but I won't recommend it.
I remember back when it was still in development and little by little sneak peeks were shown and it looked amazingly awesome... and then when it came out it (like so many other games) had been significantly dumbed down for a less complex more mainstream gameplay. Even so there was (and still is) a huge amount of delight to be had in raising your creatures from single celled organisms, chosing their skills by rewriting their DNA from generation to generation until they become civilized and then developing them into the endgame (space exploration) via technological advances.
So why no recommendation?
Well for a start the game is just outright unstable. The general instability just doesn't seem to be fixable. Everywhere I looked I found it was just an accepted side effect of running the game. So it will crash. And it doesn't autosave. So you must save often. And if you screw up and save after it's begun breaking it will destroy that save game and make it forever unloadable. It's also been ditched by EA so it won't be being fixed.
The actual evolutionary stages (barring the last) are just too plain short. I wanted to spend hours on each stage but you zoom forwards, even if you go the completionist route and stick around until you've done every last thing you can. The combat is not great, the social minigame is read a cue and then press one of four buttons (creature stage) three buttons (tribal stage) oh we got rid of the buttons just click on it already (civ stage)
The final space stage is huge and is where you will will either spend most of your time, or where you will get quickly fed up and return to the start to create more creatures. There is literally an entire galaxy to take over including a race of extremely unfriendly borg *cough* sorry, I mean Grox towards to the centre. Your creature, that you poured so much time and attention into is replaced by a spaceship and it all gets a bit meh.... Galactic Adventures does try to address this but not well... (I'll deal with that on it's own though).
Initially you will ooooh over the creature creator. Eventually you will be frustrated by it's limitations and the relatively restrictive set of main parts. The inability to set a gender/voice for your creature is most evidenced when you create something female looking and it talks like a brawny guy or something cute and sounds like it's just waiting to eat you for breakfast. There are a huge number of really minor fixes that could have been added to this that would have provided some huge quality of life improvements for this game... but despite them being suggested over and over again when the game's developers were still active, they were unfortunately never addressed.
I still love Spore. It holds a very special place in my heart, but I can't recommend it. If you still fancy it despite its issues then you'll probably have a great time with it. I'd love to see a sequel - some of the things that were cutting edge when this came out are much more developed now and it could be awesome... unlikely, but still...

P.B. winterbottem is not a game for the faint of heart, nor one which should be delved into without the full understanding of its message. Naturally the "pie"; the object of P.B.s never ending pursuit represents wealth and stature which will never be achieved by those born into poverty. The fact that the glorious pie will never be attained highlights the tragic situation many of the working class find themselves in. Forced to work in mundane tedium until death, how many people have only their pensions to think of keeping them going? These messages may only be attained form a game this complex or even cerebral as PB.

Star Trek Online has improved steadily since its uneven launch.  Space is bigger and more interesting now.  Duty Officers are fun, and they add flavor to the game.  There are now many "episodes" to play, and some "Trek" stars lend their voice-acting skills.  The "Foundry" features lots of memorable (and not-so-memborable) content created by the player base.  Recent patches have improved the planet-based crafting system that shipped at launch; crafting is more interesting now.  The game is still stronger in space than on land, but the gap has narrowed.
The game isn't perfect.  It's got that MMO grind going on, which cyclically grabs me and then loses me.  I find myself drifting in and out periodically.  I still find the UI hotkey to be awkward.  It's gotten better, but it's still not as easy to use as, say, World of Warcraft's.  And for whatever reason, I find I tend to play this game solo.  Even when I was in a "fleet" (a guild), I played alone-together -- adventuring by myself while chatting occasionally.
If you like Star Trek, then I'd suggest you give this game a try.

Vermintide is a Multi-player PvE game similar to Left for Dead, but with a melee centric focus. Immediately I thought this would make for an inferior game. How much skill is there left-clicking a sword around and whacking things? In L4D at least you have to aim your guns.
Well I couldn't be more wrong. Combat is chiefly melee. A simple left-click will do a quick strike. But holding it down releases a more powerful charged strike, but leaves you open to attack. Right click will block, but you can only sustain so many strikes before your guard fails. Lastly, you can push enemies around you knocking them down, but this too exhausts your guard.
The game's biggest strengths is how you as a player get better. You will quickly learn how the many different weapons play, but also learn how rats will behave. Starting off at Normal difficulty will be just right, but once you progress to Hard, the jump is noticeable. But soon enough you will learn to avoid damage and move on to Nightmare which seem will seem impossible. But after more hours of getting a feel for things, you will then find it easy and move on to Catacylsm, where even veterans will occasionally wipe.
This is not a game of luck. A highly skilled player can beat maps, even alone, on the highest difficulty, with the worst weapons in the game, simply by using in game knowledge and mechanics. It's this rewarding type of gameplay that distinguishes Vermintide and keeps you coming back.
The other big thing that'll keep you coming back is the reward system. At the end of every match you will randomly be given loot. The better you did on the map, and the higher the difficulty, the better the reward. The best weapons in the game will drop ~5% of the time at the end of a Nightmare map, which is just enough to make it possible, but not so frequent to feel simple.
Graphics, voice acting, setting, and optimization are all good here. But it's the gameplay that keeps you coming back.

I've spent 11 hours in game since I got it and I've already finished the story mode, built everything that can be built, collected all the food I can etc. Although I enjoyed the 11 hours in game, I feel that is about it for the content.
The gameplay itself was quite pleasing, with an interesting take on the resource/base building genre and delicious graphics to go along with it maintained itself well on my poor spec machine.
With it's current level, I would give it the following ratings:
Audio: 7/10 - OST was great however encountered a few bugs with the leaks in bases and with sound around 250m-350m
Visual: 7/10 - For what the game is and how well it ran on my low spec machine, the graphic content was sound.
Gameplay and Content: 5/10 - Good, but see below for my suggestions.
Replayability: 3/10 - Not enough content to keep me coming back. The gold for the sandbox version is a good idea, however it should be permanent total, that is increased by collecting more in the story and survival modes. Having to go back into the game and replay to play another sandbox game is just enforcing replayability to get the best out of the game.
What I personally would like to see, would be the following:
1. Caves that can be explored with air pockets that only give so much air before they disappear.
2. A shark frenzy, as in late game gameplay, I found that I spent a fair bit of time hunting sharks for food as opposed to being fearful.
3. A possible crafting set up so we can use the materials that we harvest or a crafting guide written somewhere, like what does fertilizer do in game and how do I use it?
4. The idea of multiplayer mode would be good, 2-4 player co-op would be good, any more than that and resources might become a little thin.
With these things in mind, I would be reluctant to suggest this game to people on the basis that there doesn't really feel very much value for money. Comparing the game to others in the same genre of sandbox/resource gathering/base-building/survival - The other games have a LOT more content and replayability for the same price. If the suggestions that I myself have made and the other players that have written the details in the review section are considered and possibly implemented, then I would definately suggest this game. At the moment, it still feels like it's in beta stage and a lot more content could be added.
I'll definately be keeping a close eye on this game though, as with any future content updates could only make this gem better.

I originally picked this game up after spending hundreds of hours playing Stardew Valley.  I'm sure there are more out there like me so I'll say this, if you are buying this game to scratch the itch, take a moment to consider what you like about Stardew. If you're like me and love socializing and getting to know the town, you will LOVE this game.  This game encourages you to make friends, it encourages you to get to know the little details about everyone in town and it does it WELL.  There were so many social interactions that were done so much better and things that I wished I'd gotten out of playing Stardew.  Particularly with the marriage aspect.  I haven't delved much into the married life itself yet, in fact, I literally just got married in game, but everything from the proposal to the towns reaction to the wedding itself is absolutely wonderful.  I was on an absolute cute overload.  10/10 absolutely perfect and that's an aspect I'll see myself replaying the game to see again.
However, this game does have downsides.  Farming takes a backseat.  I mentioned before if what you like about Stardew was the socializing, then you will love this.  If you prefer making tons of cash, min/maxing, designing your farm, and disregarding relationships, you might still be able to enjoy this game, but you need to keep in mind that that isn't the focus of this game where having 8000 coins is considered rich.
That said, I loved playing through this game, and I will likely replay it a few more times before I've had enough.  Absolutely wonderful.

First off, we might as well get this out of the way; this isn't as good as Stardew Valley. While the game is fundamentally similar, there are too many little things here that just irk me, which is a shame. This game seems to put much greater emphasis on establishing relationships with townsfolk, and I like that. Unfortunately, it seems to do so at the cost of everything else. You only have two 5x5 farm plots (though I admit, perhaps I simply couldn't find someone in game who could potentially expand the field), which seriously puts a limit on how profitable farming is in game. The alternatives are fishing and mining, both of which are done better on Stardew Valley.
That said, I did enjoy my time with this game. While I feel the map is overly cluttered with obtrusive plantlife (I'm reminded of the last time I loaded up my old GC ANimal Crossing village), I did enjoy the characters in this a bit more than Stardew Valley. I also liked the idea of having an overall goal (and no, gramps is coming in a few years to judge me isn't really a goal); the town is failing, and you have to find the spirits to reinvigorate the land. This game also has a fair amount of secrets, and stumbling upon one is always enjoyable.
There are even a few things in this game I would like to see in Stardew Valley; the option of resting on benches to recover stamina, the ability to save without having to go to the next in-game day, the whole lockball game, and THE DOG HAVING A PURPOSE. Okay, it's just to help find buried stuff, but hey; it does something. I also found a bug that let me duplicate bottles. That's really not part of my review or anything; I'm just tickled to have found a game bug on my own.
Despite it's faults, I do recommend it, especially for people who have already finished Stardew. The developer is still working on updates, which is always a plus in my book, and the game does have a lot of charm. If the developer is for some reason reading this, I have three suggestions; 1. hire someone to clear out the excessive topiary in the village. 2. BIGGER FIELDS! (apologies again if I simply missed the expansion option). 3. Remove the stamina drain caused by running. I thought it was a neat idea at first, but by the end of my playtime, I was heartily sick of it.

I have to say that I really wanted to like this game. I loved Stardew Valley, and I bet I could love this game just as much - story and content wise. The issue is the gameplay. The best word for it is "Clunky". There isn't a single aspect of the game that didn't seem under developed, glitchy, or over simplified OR over complicated. The fishing game is frustrating and pointless, the backpack is badly organized, growing crops is also fairly pointless, animals are super simplified which makes them boring, etc.
The focus of this game, as opposed to Stardew or the Harvest Moon games, is clearly on the townsfolk and socializing. I have no problem with this, but there isn't enough incentive in the other aspects of the game to encourage me to keep playing.

Things I have learnt:
Do not underestimate Paxel the old nutter. He's a lockball beast and I broke out in cold sweat playing against him.

I think that World's Dawn really suffered from being released so soon before Stardew Valley, a much larger and more complex game - which is a shame, because World's Dawn provided exactly the experience I was looking for. It's simple, relaxing, and charming. It made me feel nostalgic, like I was playing one of the Harvest Moon games for the first time as a kid.
World's Dawn doesn't include very many items, or very many crops, or very much space in which to do your farming. There's no crafting system. There are only a few potential upgrades for your tools and your farm. But those were positive points for me: I was happy with a game where I could focus on straightforward goals and developing relationships with other characters without getting bogged down by the sheer number of options and features. And I really DO like all of the characters and the ambiance of the world they live in. Some of my very favorite moments of the game involved finding letters that fleshed out the relationships between various townspeople. The sense of affinity and community between the characters is really touching at times.
The game isn't stressful (...except for the final match of the LockBall tournament...), but it's not boringly easy, either. Since there's a very limited amount of space for crops--and you probably need to save some of your crops for cooking and presents--you really have to budget your money and time carefully during the first couple of seasons. It DID make me feel like a brand new farmer: just barely scraping by, trying to prioritize the things I needed the most. I didn't even have my own calendar to start! And the town comes with a few extra mysteries and secrets that may not be immediately apparent.
Due to the relatively limited scope of the game features, there isn't much reason to play more than 1-2 in-game years, but even a single year amounted to about 40 hours of play time, which I found perfectly satisfactory. A single year still gives you plenty to do between trying to improve your farm, revive the town, building friendships, and perhaps getting married. The developer is apparently working on additional romance routes, too, and I'd be very glad to re-play the game for the sake of exploring other routes.
I'd love to have more character customization available (particularly options for skin tones) and for there to be be more cutscenes on the romance paths, but I've thoroughly enjoyed my experience with the game and hope that it gains greater attention.

This game gave me a really pleasant nostalgic, old Harvest Moon type feeling. The world itself is cute, the music is sweet, and there's a nice small town community vibe to the whole game. There are a few minor graphical blips (ex: characters standing on benches, there's no sprite for riding your horse around so you just become your horse to cruise the town) but nothing that causes a real issue to the game.

As an avid gamer old enough to have played such classics as Galaga and Astrosmash when they were still relatively new I'll be the first to point out that not all things retro are necessarily positive additions to modern gaming or more specifically the wave of neo-retro titles we've been seeing of late.  In consistent Puppy Games fashion Titan Attacks flaunts its retro styling mixed with modern shader effects indicative of an old meets new formula which seeks to be more than the sum of its parts. However like their other titles the decidedly more modern features of Titan Attacks are severely undermined by the cartoonishly exaggerated retro grade difficulty . Upgrades to the player controlled tank which are admittedly cool on paper are immediately rendered underwhelming as the game rapidly devolves into near bullet-hell nonsense. For those who fondly recollect their quarters being crunched as though it were one of the finer aspects of the golden era of arcade gaming maybe you should dig a little deeper and remember that there was more to retro gaming than punishment and frustration. It was the game mechanics that really shined. Some gamers prefer to no-life every game they play until satisfied that they are superior to said games in every conceivable way possible and take an arguably dubious pride in astronomically high scores, full achievements, difficulty levels mastered, etc. Some of us value our time and money just a touch more than that. Therein lies the biggest problem with Titan attacks: With crushing difficulty scaling and no special features conveying any sort of replay value the average player is likely to get little more than a couple hours worth of game play out of this title. So if the hippsterific  devs over at Puppy Games are so excruciatingly retro why is this the case? I seem to recall getting loads more play time out of my Intellivision and NES cartridges back in the day. Let's make a 'retro' comparison shall we? Used to be that you'd rent a game for about 3 bucks at your local video rental outlet and proceed to play that game all weekend. Go a bit further back and you may recal spending less than $3 worth of quarters to get several hours of game play from your favorite cabinet at the local arcade. Puppy Games has carved out a comfy little niche for themselves charging around 11 bucks for a few measly hours of so-so game play per title. I'm not one to shout down rehashes and remakes or blindly endorse retro games in their purest original form just to remind people that I played them. I believe that many new games are better simply because they benefit directly from being new and all that it entails. In this case however players really would be better served by dusting off their old games and playing those instead. I can honestly say without any pretensions that you will play them longer and have more fun. In the end (which I promise will come rather quickly if you decide to pick it up anyway) Titan Attacks is a soulless experience that leaves you feeling like your cash has been grabbed. If you absolutely must see for yourself than try to grab it while it's on sale.

About 41 hours clocked in this game at the time of this review and I have to say I am impressed with the game.
Even though it might be in a completely different sport, the feel of the game reminds me of old football manager games. And I don't mean the game Football Manager, because the ones I've played have in my opinion not been good enough - but I am talking about the old Championship Manager games.
In this game, you try to stay ahead of the other teams - in the races as well as talking car/part development. It is all about prioritizing where to put your money. Spending more money on the car (in pre-season), developing new car parts during the season, the HQ (building and upgrading) and/or the drivers. Upgrading the HQ will make your drivers stay fit easier, will enable you to develope and build better parts for the cars, have better/more information about weather (so that you can have an edge when it comes to choosing the right tyres) etc etc.
Finding that balance is what this game is about - that and when to pit and how.
The content is great and the game is very stable - even on low spec PC's. Can't recommend this enough for someone looking for a really good manager sim. You don't have to have a lot of information of, or a huge interest in, motorsports to understand this game.

Do you like large scale battles? That's the game for you!
Do you like (small scale) politics? That's the game for you!
Do you like beating the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your enemies with a giant stick in various historic settings (thanks to free total conversions in the workshop)? Guess what? That's the game for you!
Whether you like to be a fierce warrior for your lord or try to become a warlord yourself, this game will satisfy your needs.
This game it's an action / sandbox / rpg, as in there's a huge map with more than a faction that will ally or wage war with each other.
You can choose your destiny: you can become a criminal stealing from farmers and caravans, a justice warrior that hunts down bandits and looters, a vassal to your lord, or the lord of a faction itself.
You still have to manage your character (classic Strength - Agility - Intelligence - Charisma primary stats + related abilities) and your army (you can train peasants willing to join you and make them fierce warriors under your command, if they manage not to die too early) and your villages (once you earn them).
Mount&Blade it's a game you play in the long run. It will beat you up, drag you into dirt, beat your children and wife in front of you. You will lose your army. You will see your possessions attacked and looted.
But it'll also let you stand up again, buy some peasants some equipment and have your vengeance. If you are careful and smart you can become rich and powerful, seizing the whole land for yourself.
The combat system is pretty advanced, whereas you have to decide which direction you want to attack and defend.
So if your enemy is attacking on your left and you don't move your mouse to your left you are gonna get hit, if you attack your enemy will parry from time to time, so don't expect an hack'n'slash, they will drop you in a few hits.
You may tweak the difficulty to receive less damage (if you just want to enjoy the scenery), so whether you like it hard or not, you can have what you want.

Do you want to go on an adventure with boundless possibilties and seemingly endless quests? Then you've come to the right place, outlander. Unlike Skyrim, Morrowind is an investigative game. No quest marker, no mindlessly fast-travelling to where ever you want to go. No, Morrowind is all about figuring it out yourself. With detailed entries in your journal and multiple dialogue options for quests there is always a solution, though it may seem as though there isn't.
As well as investigating, you will make various choices. Say a man wants you to find a thief, and through investigation you locate and approach said thief. But the thief offers to put in a good word in for you for House Redoran, as he is a high ranking member in that house. You have a choice. One that may require even more investigation to decide upon.
The combat in Morrowind takes getting used to (you can miss if your agility/stamina is low). You will find yourself having to run from some enemies because they are simply too powerful for you, which adds a sense of realism to the game unlike Skyrim or Oblivion where most enemies level with your character. Of course, like most RPGs, the combat could be improved. But there are many mods out there that are easy to get and install that make changes to the combat (such as disabling the hit-or-miss system, adding more weapons, adding more spells, etc.). As well as serious investigations and decisive combat, there are hilariously funny moments in the game. So, if you like taking your clothes off in order to have a House Hlaalu member sponsor you, you will very much enjoy this game.
There are many downfalls to Morrowind that, to make my review fair, must be brought to attention. The graphics are pretty low-end, I mean, it's a pretty old game. There are mods like "Morrowind Overhaul" but they typically slow the game down pretty bad and the installation takes some time. As well as bad graphics, movement around NPCs is a bit clunky. If you find yourself on a skinny and railed bridge with some NPCs walking towards you, you'd be better off jumping off or just killing them because there's no way you will be able to walk past them. Or, if your acrobatics are very high you might be able to jump over them. Fortunately, there aren't too many bridges or paths like that, and the likelyhood of NPCs walking along it aren't too high. Also, when you start out the game you are probably the slowest person to ever exist. It doesn't take too long you get your speed stat up, but it must be mentioned. The economy system is pretty good. Gold (also known as drakes, septims, or gp) is the currency and it's not hard to get if you know where to go. Character creation is very in depth, thus making it difficult to start the game off good without reading a proper tutorial on how to make a good character. If you make, say, a High-Elf warrior you are not going to have a fun first playthrough. So, if you buy this game I recommend at least glancing at a character creation guide. I recommend a Dark Elf Archer for a first playthrough as Dunmer are a good starter race and archery allows you to kill enemies from far away without taking much damage. Another problem with the game (if you buy the GotY version) is that (WARNING: SPOILER)

Overall, I really recommend this game for RPG lovers. If you're used to playing games where you're spoon fed everything, just have patience, you will learn to love this game. The lore is amazing and the gameplay is phenominal. Completely worth the $20.

It's a great game, but you should be warned about it's minor cons.

First of all, it's more of an experience than anything else. The story mode could easily be beaten very quickly if you were to rush through and find all the objectives. But if you explore a bit, the game is very worth it.
Second, Don't pay attention to people calling this game "minecraft, but underwater". The only thing you can build and customize right now is your base, and even so, there isn't much point in doing so, except to allow for more room for chests. The game also tells you what materials you need to craft items, so it's not much of a mystery, and you don't need a wiki to figure it out.
Third, gathering materials is very easy. You are given an item that will collect whatever you place it on, for as long as you want it to. Not to mention they don't cost much to build, I found that I had an excess of almost every mineral, and had the best set of equipment, about 40 minutes into the game.

Yes I've only played 40 minutes, but that was enough... that was enough.
This is quite possibly the worst game of this genre I have ever played.
First off, the movement. There is no option to run in this game, meaning you kind of quick walk everywhere. This makes the pacing very lackadaisical and is very annoying when your spawn is quite a way away from the action.
Well, I say action, every animation in this game seems to be about half the speed it should be, kicking takes about three seconds and jumping seems to give you some strange t-pose animation which looks really stupid when you're near other objects.
Things in the game are illogical, you can go under water and literally just walk. You can even fire your gun or jump around, and when you die from submersion with little warning, you just fall to the floor.
The HUD is very underdeveloped, with a font that just looks comical and out of place. There's no real sense of injury or health being lost unless you pay careful attention to the small health meter at the bottom of the screen. This makes it hard to tell when you're close to death, although most the time you die in one hit anyway meaning you have to repeat the whole process of getting to the combat all over again.
The maps have a very small combat area with badly positioned invisible walls, this isn't good for a game which is designed for so many people to play at one time and can make the areas feel crowded and hard to navigate, but I guess that's fine as the movement speeds are so slow that by the time you'd made a strategic move up instead of charging in and getting killed instantly the timer would be up.
As for the combat itself, it's very lacking. You can be killed from long range without any warning and if you actually get into a combat area it is almost impossible to kill someone with some classes. I've seen people chasing each other to try and get a kill and I've just walked away from attackers before and survived.
The music accompanying the game is very off-putting, featuring songs such as 'Hallelujah Chorus' - yeah...
In all fairness, this game does have some good points, although textures are awful when you're close up, from a distance (which is probably where you'll be most the time) they look good. The water effects are really good in the game and the muzzle flashes are very cool.
Having the ability to switch between first and third person is welcome as it allows for a range of different play styles and the camera is well positioned when you're in third person allowing for a good field of view.
The character creation is a very cool addition with a wide range of customisable areas for your character meaning each player looks different in the game. It's great to have a feature like this, it makes the game feel a bit more interactive and personal.
In summary, I don't think I'll go above 40 minutes on this game. It just doesn't match up to games I'm used to playing of this genre like Chivalry. It's features are lacking and the multiplayer is simply boring.

is a retro, arcade, 2-D shooter where the nameless
fends off the
invasion with his trusty pixelated tank.
The game commences on Earth then progresses to new zones. Zone progression occurs when its boss is defeated. There are a total of five zones, each containing twenty levels, with their own unique design. Once all five have been defeated, it loops back to Earth, albeit with a slightly higher difficulty.
The game mechanics are fairly straightforward; aim & kill. Fortunately, that doesn’t do
the justice it deserves. The mechanics conspire in such a way to exude a simple & fun experience. There are a number of boosts & improvements that can be purchased between levels to mitigate your success. For example, there are powerful area-of-effect bombs, weapon add-ons, additional shielding & more. Currency is derived from killing enemies & also capturing them. Capturing enemies adds a unique dimension to some situations, as doing so can be lethally dangerous, but extremely profitable. The Titans have a wide arsenal of ships & weapons that change in function & attitude from zone to zone, which can easily lead to your undoing if not cautious. There are bonus rounds that gauge your accuracy & reward you accordingly so keep nimble. These rounds occur between levels, after every seventh level.
There isn’t really any story, beyond what’s presented visually but that’s really to be expected with an arcade shooter. The sound is also quite typical of the genre, with generally the same music repeated throughout. The graphics while pixelated, are visually appealing, with colors & art that mesh together nicely.
For high score hunters, your high score is saved onto online leaderboards. So you can show off your skills or lack of them to your friends.

OK... to be honest, this is probably a great game. And I really do think people could actually get to like this.
Things that I liked:
- The weapons sway, even when prone. Proning reduces the sway, but it's still there. Weapons don't always hit their targets, even rifles. Because in the real world, firearms don't always hit their mark. If anyone has shot a rifle and/or handgun before, they know what I'm talking about.
- There are all kinds rifles, CQC weapons, and even explosives! Even some of the guns that alot of World War II games keep ignoring. Such as the M3 Grease Gun for example. You'll find the M1 Garand, the B.A.R. Machine Gun, the MP34 and an MG34, the whole works! Yes, there's an MP40, M1A1 Thompson, and PPSh-41. So, don't worry.
- Also, there is something unique about this game that makes it diffferent from most multiplayer games. Stealth is possible and the environment is enough to make guys wary of their surroundings! Yes, there is stealth in this multiplayer! Making your targets harder to pinpoint unlike Assassin's Creed multiplayer. Even with brightness turned up to max, you need a sharp eye to search for any hidden targets. Yes, even those big hulking tanks are so hard to spot! So, good luck finding them. It's not so easy now, is it?
- The Anti-Tank weapons such as the Panzerfaust 60s and the M1A1 Bazookas HAVE TO, I repeat, HAVE TO hit the tanks at the right angle, or those rockets will just bounce off and not do any damage!! Tanks are also not possible to kill in one hit with Anti-Tank firearms. Including Tanks vs. Tanks.
- So... many... tanks!! Yes, SO MUCH TANKS! There are alot of different tanks in this game! No more worrying about being limited to only one type of tank to choose from unlike Battlefield! Also, it takes more than one tank round to destroy a tank.
- Weapons need to be repaired after some uses out on the battlefield. Yes, EVERYTHING! Including ammo, firearms, and even vehicles! Except certain vehicles like the American jeeps and German jeeps with the machine guns mounted on them and weapons such as melee weapons and wrenches for example does not need to be repaired. Don't panic if the MGs are used alot. But for everything else, make sure to keep your equipment in top condition!
WARNING! Upgraded weapons will consume more cash if you equip them as well as excessive uses of explosives. Yes, including grenades. So, pick carefully on which you want to repair and what not to. You can set it to where you can Auto-Repair them with In-Game currency or Gold(Which you can get by playing daily to get 4 gold per day or buying gold with real money) after every match.
That's all I can say about this game that I like... However, now I'm gonna draw the downsides to this game...
Things I dislike about this game:
- The things you need to buy in the store(with in-game currency not real money. Real money is optional) is not exactly cheap... take the Jeep for example. It costs about 46000. When you spend alot of time out in the field, you get up to about... 1000 to 2000 per match. Results mary vary depending on the match.
- The things done on this game is very offputting, such as grenade spamming which results in Teamkilling.
- This is my personal opinion, but I think the damage upgrades on the Bolt-Actions need to be removed. But that's just me, cause I hate One-Hit Kill weapons. AKA: Sniper rifles on Call of Duty...
- No voice chats... then again, we don't have to listen to the things we usually hear on the mics, for ex: 8 year old children screaming on the microphones. So, this is debatable.
- One last thing... the game is pretty buggy. And the models of the soldiers used on the game are very... well... not so good. Though, you can drive in First-Person and/or Third-Person, so that's cool.
- The game still is not out of BETA... it's been almost 4 years since it's release and it's still in BETA.
That's all I have to say. If you are willing to risk the things I've listed on here, then knock yourself out. Other than that, this game is nothing like Call of Duty, and/or Battlefield. Brace yourself if you wish to attempt this game, because the usual things you always do on Call of Duty and Battlefield will be thrown out the window once you step in the game. Good luck, and have fun!

Over time the genre of games based on a single block has expanded to be among the biggest - and among those with the highest amount of early-access indie games.
Now this game certainly fits both descriptions, does however bring quite the unique twist to it: mechanics. It sounds boring, I will admit that. But let me explain:
Being creative by building a house is one thing, it is an entirely different thing to make the house then grow legs and walk away. Which you can do in this game. Since rotating and expanding parts play a huge role in this game blocks actually make a lot of sense as a basic unit - they are all the same length and allow to easily fit things into each other without having to worry about size constraints.
The game brings a lot to the table - rotating bearings, engines, controler units, thrusters, sensors and even basic logic gates. It doesn't, however, offer any kind of story or survival mode.
While I personally enjoy this as it allows you to simply focus on mechanical engineering some people might find it detering, so be warned. A survival experience is already in the making at the time of writing, so this might have changed.
Performance is quite good on my rig (i7 4790 and a GTX 770) until you start throwing huge projects into the world. This is possible due to amazingly integrated steam workshop support which allows you to share all your creations and check out those of other people.
The physics could be just a tad better but are fine as they are now.

If you like Harvest Moon, especially the ones on the GameBoy/DS, then I personally think you'll really like this game. However, a big issue I have is pacing. Theoretically, you could finish the main story in one in game year, (which is about a day, in real time.) I guess that you could say that the point of the story is too finish in one year. However, I feel like if you're going to make a Harvest Moon, you need to make the story last a bit longer. It's not just my issues with the story, it's the fact that plants seem to grow pretty fast too, and they don't grow back. I get really burnt out on replanting them all the time. Again, if you like Harvest Moon, go for it! Besides my pacing issue, I love the game to pieces and hope that others enjoy it too!

Initially, I thought that this game was going to be a flop. This in part to the fact that it looked like it had a bunch messy graphics, hundreds of achievements (which some would say is meant to be a way to basically charge for achievements that you don't have to actually put any effort into) and small number of reviews.
I've always been a fan of DDR, and Slash it ultimate reminded me of it as well. So after playing it for about 30 minutes and figuring everything out, I've gotta say that I'm amazed and ultimately hooked.
The most notable surprises to me, were for example: how in the arrow mode, you could consider it easy, but you basically have to watch all rows, because there is no one row that the arrow keys are specifically set on and this was a very subtle and easy way to trick the player into accidentally pressing something else.
Another example would have to be the typing mode, where you type out the words in a certain amount of time (this is what I had been doing at first), but I had come to learned that in addition to meeting the time constraints for each word, that you had to keep the rhythm of the song AND pay attention to the outter lines of where other words were starting to float in.
Pair these surprises with the fact that there is a TON of content to unlock with the game, and you get a very reasonably priced and well polished game. Thank you Just1337.

I'm giving this one a thumbs up but just barely.   You're basically dropped into a underwater survival sandbox.  The atmosphere is nice with a suitably moody setting and good sound effects.  You go about your business as you would in most other survival games by building a base, crafting better weapons and tools,  avoiding starvation,  O2 depreviation or best of all,  thrashed about in a sharks mouth.   All these survival aspects play out more or less well and the random map generation helps a lot.
And thus, nothing is perfect.  There's a nice game here but after the first play,  it becomes more or less a speedplay routine.  Content is lacking.  That said,  the store page says it's a finished game, not a early access,  which may sound like an outrage but I actually think it's more honest in a way:  it's not pretending to ever evolve into something it's not some day.   That said, it's still a shame because there is so much potential for more content.  The graphics are decent enough overall yet somewhat dated looking,  in need of more work which is also a big shame.
Last, what almost pushes this game over the edge,  is stability problems.  Luckily I was able to fix mine right away,  but many others have had issues and literally the only people around is the small community on the forum,  who are a nice helpful bunch.
6/10  A slider of a game:  A delicious few bites and it's over.  Wait for a big sale and don't plan more than a day on it,  and don't get your hopes up for an update.

FarSky is one of the most paradoxically tense and soothing games I've played in recent years.
On the one hand, the deep sea theme is beautiful and calming. The graphics are a bit chunky and aren't anything to write home about, but they get the point across without feeling cluttered and there are lots of pretty sea creatures and seascapes to look at.
At the same time, the constant pressure of the depleting air tank, Nathan the Diving Man's stomach, and all of the pretty sea creature who want to murder the heck out of you keep the game from being a walk in the park.
This is not a long game, nor is it a particularly difficult one. Taking even basic precautions should keep you from getting eaten and skilled survivor gamers will probably be able to beat both Adventure AND the more difficult Survivor mode in just a few hours. That said, if you have the money so spare and a few hours to kill, the game it definitely worth it.

Whether you like to be a fierce warrior for your lord or try to become a warlord yourself, this game will satisfy your needs.

Mount&Blade it's a game you play in the long run. It will beat you up, drag you into dirt, beat your children and wife in front of you. You will lose your army. You will see your possessions attacked and looted.

So if your enemy is attacking on your left and you don't move your mouse to your left you are gonna get hit, if you attack your enemy will parry from time to time, so don't expect an hack'n'slash, they will drop you in a few hits.
You may tweak the difficulty to receive less damage (if you just want to enjoy the scenery), so whether you like it hard or not, you can have what you want.

Can I just say, if you really love Star Trek, and you really love  MMORPGs, you will love this game. I am a huge fan of anything science fiction. When i discovered this game and found out that you can captain your own ship, I nearly exploded from excitment. The game did not disapoint. In the following paragraphs I will state things I enjoy about this game, and the very few cons that I have.
Pros- This game lets you captain a starship and fight any enemy the federation has ever faced. You fight Klingons, Romulans, Borg, Gorn, Cardassians, and even more! The stories do an extremely good job of putting you in the shoes of a captain and the space combat is fantastic. This game is extremely customizable and hundreds of different abilities for space comabt, and ground combat are available making each players build unique! Some people complain that once you reach level 60, the game is a cash grab. For people that aren't patient, yes it is. They complain that in order to receive tier 6 ships, you need to spend money. This is not entirely true becasue every year there are two or three events that give you the opportunity to win t6 starships. Sure, its a long process to win them but in the long run it's worth it! Or, if you've been a veteran for a decent amount of time, you may receive a free t6 ship from arc games thanking you for playing their game. Thats how I got mine! Also, going back to the campaign, the Iconian War story is fanominal! Also you can captain Klingon and Romulan ships. Nuff said.
Cons- I don't have many issues with this game except for a couple small issues. I think the ground combat could be a little better improved. Unless you're extremely duked out in shields and weapons at level 60, you will die alot. That being said, I do agree with some of the issues that many people have about the game being a cash grab. Yes, you can get free t6 ships, but if you want a t6 ship without waiting, it will cost 30$ of real money. Thats way too much to spend for just a decent ship in an MMO. For people that may not be as patient, this game is such a cash grab.
Overall, I have enjoyed this game alot. There is so much to do in it and its space combat is extremely engaging and addictive. If you aren't the most patient person out there, this game could potentially become a cash grab but if you have the patience at level 60, you will receive a t6 ship in time. All in all, get this game. Its so much fun!

So I bought this game after watching Markiplier play it on YouTube and had to try it for myself. For $9.99 this game is actually pretty solid. There is tons of content for the meager price tag and is seriously addictive. Of course, I do see through the facade of making it a hentai game in order to sell a puzzle game. With Bejeweled and Candy Crush Saga-esque knock-offs flooding the market, it makes sense to sell this game the only way developers know how, with sex. Ever hear the phrase: "Sex sells"? Well, in this case it does. I'm disappointed of course by the Steam enforced censoring policy, but even with that, it's still a VERY enjoyable game from start to... well, whenever you get bored I suppose. There are a total of twelve girls to romance, flirt, and date with (not to mention have the strangest instance of a sex scene I have ever seen) and literally hours worth of gameplay to be had. I also like how each of the girls are fully voiced by extremely talented and well-placed actors. The soundtrack is aweswome and easy to vibe to, the puzzle game is easy to learn but challenging to strategize through later in the game, and the sheer number of facts to remember about each girl is staggering, but I'll bet you'll remember everything about these girls for a long time. And finally, the artwork that is given to you for going on a successful date is, in a word, gorgeous. There was obviously a lot of care and hard work put into this game, and I love it. In the end, I'd give it 8 out of 10. It's an enjoyable game, but if you don't enjoy puzzle games, this probably won't be for you.

The Ship is definitely not your usual first-person shooter, where you just shoot anything that looks at you funny - although there is a game mode for that.
It feeds on your cleverness and paranoia. Each game round, you have to kill on specific person onboard one of several ocean liners - the titular Ships - and at the same time, someone is hunting you. Both you and your target - or 'quarry' - can take cover under the watchful eye of a Security Guard or Camera, but your hunter will likely be quite happy to bribe the Security to ignore their crimes while they bring that big ol' bat of theirs and beat your♥♥♥♥♥to death with it.
Each other player you meet is a potential threat, and whether they come right at you wielding axe or gun, or sneak around and try to whack you from behind or lure you into a trap is up to them.
But, again, it's not just that simple - the winner of the match is decided by who has earned the most money for their kills at the end, and each weapon has a randomized and steadily increasing price for its use, be it Frying Pan, Revolver, Flare Gun, Umbrella or Wallet Bomb. Once the weapon is used, its price drops down to a measely $100. Thankfully, you have access to a list that shows which weapons are paying out the highest. It's up to you to find them, mind.
While all of this is going on, your character has needs of their own - hunger, exhaustion, hygiene and growing loneliness all play a factor, and the longer you're alive, the harder it becomes to stay that way.
The environments are beautifully stylized. Each map has a different theme while sticking to a creepy, paranoia-fuelling atmosphere. The larger ships are a little dark and foreboding, while the smaller ones are much more colorful and fun. As the amount of people out for your blood increases, the atmosphere and your sanity darkens.
Every ship is laid out completely differently, from the very simple to the aggressively complex. Learning the maps and where to find hiding spots and secrets is the key to success.
The character design is quite cartoony, something between TF2 and TellTale characters. It fits the tone very well, being neither silly nor realistic.
The sound design is just marvellous. Every weapon impact on your quarry is satisfying, my personal favorite being the 'THWANG' of the Frying Pan or Cooking Pot. Old timey music plays through every radio and in every bar and restaurant, footsteps getting louder behind you make your heart jump, the wind, splashing water and airhorn blasts outside make you chill, and... well, let's say your character's visit to the bathroom is... descriptive.
If I have to criticize it, I will say the AI bots are very thick, more concerned with wandering about like cattle, more grazing, sleeping and pooping than hunting, only engaging in combat when they happen upon their quarry by chance.
All in all, I love this game. An exciting, fast-paced murdery romp on the high seas, combining regular first-person combat skills with strategy, planning and lunatic paranoia. There is a bit of a learning curve, but once you get the hang of it, you'll be totally enthralled.

-The Security is my absolute biggest beef. The passengers seem to count as Security as well, and they're everywhere. Security works if you bring out a weapon, a simple
will get you fined. 0.1 seconds is literally all it takes for a weapon to be seen. And your Quarry absolutely loves to hang out where the Camera's and Security are. I thought that the crew knew this was going on and was paid to make sure no one was going against it!
-Everyone in the game has Asthma. If you thought the Running in Half-Life 2
or Skyward Sword was bad, then wait till' you just tap the Shift key. In just four seconds you're out of Stamina and it takes about half a minute or more to refill unless you sit down, leaving yourself very vulnerable to a Griefer or your Hunter.
-The AI is absolutely stupid. X-ray vision security guards, and the Passengers/Quarry that don't get out of the way, making you run in place, have to kill them in order for them to get out of the way, which costs $250-$2000 if you have to get through a bunch of them because they won't stop blocking you, in which you lose your Quarry.

-You have a lot of needs, Sleep, hunger, thirst, social activity, bladder, taking a dump, showering, etc. Most of these go down very, very fast. Especially Sleep, hunger and thirst. What can I say about World's Dawn?
Overall, it's a game that draws inspiration from the Harvest Moon series, a series of games I personally enjoy. You take on the role of a young farmer new to town who has dreams of running a successful farm. Gameplay is much like the Harvest Moon games. You plant crops, socialize with townsfolk, forage, and fish, among other things. The artwork is cute enough, and the soundtrack is charming. Like with Harvest Moon, the characters possess some personality, though it's limited to small bits of dialogue that are repeated every time you speak to them. That said, with all of the other features the game has, I'm not really complaining that the characters do not each have huge, sweeping backstories.
If you're a fan of the Harvest Moon series, I suggest giving World's Dawn a try.

I'm going to go ahead and give you my unbiased opinion on this one as typing/rhythm games are personally not my thing. Though there is no denying that this game excels in what it is trying to do & is a huge improvement on it's predecessors. As Slash It 1 & 2 are quick cash grabs geared only towards your run of the mill achievement sl*t (example: ME!). Except "Just 1337" have gone & made an ACTUAL game this time!
You have the previous alphabet, number, & word modes. This time around you also have a single button/space bar mode, arrow keys mode (a bit like DDR on the keyboard), a cube mode (which involves you navigating a virtual cube along a track jumping & dodging obstacles), & mouse mode. A library of music instead of the same repetitive track! Leaderboards, a multitude of languages, the ability to switch between normal & hard difficulties, a money system (giving you incentive to play better for more money) & some crisp new visuals with a fancy new HUD to go with as well.
It's like this is what Slash It wanted to be all along except got scared & went with the safe option of cashing in on those easy achievement games... None the less we got here eventually!

This game is a lot of fun, particularly for a long-suffering fan of racing strategy games (most of which have been horrible to maybe just okay to play).  Could this game be more detailed and complex, like FM has grown to be?  Sure, and I hope the devs continue to add things for the Manager to worry about, when not trying to control the actual race.
Since the game launched, the race AI has gotten better, to the point where it will beat you if you're not doing a good job developing your team and car.  Devs have been good about fixing bugs as well.
At this point, though, the devs should start looking at attacking the boredom that can creep in (and not simply by adding RNG impacts).  Each race weekend is pretty similar -- I think the tracks should have more of an influence based on their characteristics.  The track conditions and weather do impact the racing, but I think the tracks could do so more dramatically.  The mechanics are there to deal with high and low tire wear, or high and low downforce impacts, but the teams and cars all mostly perform the same way (relative to each other).  I think this could be tweaked so that in developing the car, some additional trade-offs would need to be made.
Still, I'm thoroughly enjoying the game and expect to play many more hours.  Refreshing to see this topic execute well enough to make good game.  Now let's hope the devs build on this base.

I don't really review games on Steam. About 5 or 6 years ago I wrote a few reviews for about 5 games or so on here, but I quickly decided to stop because I didn't feel like my word held any kind of importance. But after playing this game, I felt a strong urge to write down my thoughts and opinions on it so at least one other person would see it. The world needs to know.
I need to break this game down and explain what it does wrong piece by piece. Thinking about it now, the number of things that this game does wrong is honestly overwhelming, but I'm going to try anyway. This is important.
This game has over 500 achievements. Why? WHY?? You spend the whole game just getting flooded with countless achievement notifications every waking second you're playing. You can turn off the achievements in settings, but why would anyone ever include this many achievements? 500? There are only 15 songs! It's insane. Simply insane. I can't stand it.
The game didn't save multiple times. I played the game for about 40 minutes, closed it, then opened it again and all the progress I made, all the songs and game modes I purchased and unlocked, all my high scores in each song were just wiped. I played a couple songs and closed the game and re-opened it to see if it saved, and it did. I shrugged it off, assuming it was a glitch, then when I opened it a third time I saw that yet again everything was wiped. It's like the game is trying to anger me.
15 songs, none of which are that good in all honesty, 7 game modes, all of them failing in the worst ways, practically 80% of the game not even feeling like it has any connection to being a rhythm game, just typing games with music in the background, all for $5.00.
Don't buy this game. It's terrible. It's a waste of time and money and even if it was free I'd implore you to not get it. It's a slap in the face to rhythm gaming as a whole. It's worse than some free flash rhythm games online. It's the worst rhythm game I've ever played. I don't know what else to say.

The only downside to this game at this current time is the fact that it has no multiplayer. With multiplayer would come a whole range of different ideas and would allow for people to play with friends and survive with other people.

Great game for those who like to run explore, stack resources, grind and fight your way to being master of the ocean. I got instantly addicted and im NOT a huge minecraft fan. This game has an alure all its own.
Graphics are great for the large scale of the underwater world. Extreamly immersive. Game play is very smooth and responsive, even on highest gfx setting (I5/GTX650ti). Game play mechanics are great, i have yet to get stuck anywhere on the map, unable to reach objects or get into a situation i need to reload a save point. Evolution is not super complex, you can't advance most your gear or buildings more then 3x levels if that makes sense but like i said, its very well developed so everything works graphically and mechanically.
Few things - Minor anoying stuff that doesn't really detract from the actual gameplay; Resolution doesn't stick after setting it. Must be reset each restart. I have yet to figure how to split stacks in the game but not everything in the game is overtly obvious like most games that force you to sit through a boring tutorial. For the most part everything is straight forward, they figure you're smart enough to read mini descriptions and test and interact with your enviroment. No autosave, manual and requires you to quit to main menu each time(but resets daylight and fish/predator locations).
Had i purchased this for 25+ bucks, id probably not be so happy but i would still play it out in an addictive manor. Considering the quality and content id say the 14 dollar price tag is exactly what its worth and is an excellent game for its genre. Hats off to the developers!
Also sweet sound track.
