I bought FarSky on a whim. I had some extra cash to spare and the concept of the game looked compelling enough for me. Since I've finished the initial "campaign mission"/"adventure mode". I think I'm qualified to review the game.
GRAPHICS (9/10):
I was hooked by the graphics in FarSky. I'm serious, the game looks great. It doesn't sink into the "box/block aesthetic" that most voxel-based sandbox survival games like to fall into. For a game built on Java, it looks pretty fantastic. If there's anything that this game does great it's the graphics. It's appropriately minimalistic when it needs to and appropriately detailed when it needs to. No two landscapes look the same, and while there are certain patterns as to where things appear—these patterns never look too obvious.
While textures might fade in and out sometimes—the game's still in a early dev stage and it's probably a problem that will be fixed later in a patch or something.
SOUNDTRACK/SOUND EFFECTS (7/10):
The music does a good job in setting a tone for the game. A good word to describe the soundtrack for the majority of the game is "melancholic". It's peaceful and it's never too distracting.  I would however, hope for more suspenseful tunes for the game during moments where the player is in trouble.
Sound effect wise, the game is pretty quiet. Whilst the game itself is understandably quiet (it's set underwater...and sound doesn't travel well), the lack of sound effects make the game sometimes feel boring. I'm not saying that the game should be a smorgashboard of sounds—but it would be nice if we heard the occaisional whale call or maybe the periodical breathing of our main character. Or maybe even a low and steady hum of the drill you use.
CONTROLS (8/10):
FarSky's your bog-standard survival/voxel-based game. It handles a lot like MineCraft. I'd say that it does a pretty good job at what it's supposed to do—only for a few issues.
1) In other games of similar nature, you're usually allowed to right click on resources or to split resources the way you want them. In FarSky, you can only fill a certain resource up to the maximum amount and that's it. There are no "resource distribution" controls built in the game and that can be quite frustrating.
2) The swimming mechanics are kind of clunky. And for some reason—you can't crouch! I'm hoping that the "no crouching" problem could be fixed later in DLC.
GAMEPLAY (7/10):
For what it has so far, it's pretty good. I mean, it's fun. And it will definitely kill six hours (that's how long it took me to beat the first "adventure mode") and the game has everything that it's advertised to have. You can build bases underwater, you can mine for resources underwater, you can hunt for fishes...et, cetera. There's nothing missing!
But while it's everything it's advertised to be, there aren't enough features! I'm hoping that the devs release periodic updates a la Minecraft and allow for modding support, because this game needs more content to kill more than six hours! I'll probably revisit the game sometime later, but the lack of content is kind-of a turnoff. You'd think that a game that focuses heavily on underwater exploration would have more stuff to explore right?
OVERALL (7.5/10):
I don't regret purchasing FarSky. But I just want more content. I don't care if the devs don't fix the "no crouching" problem, I just want more music, more sound effects and more gameplay elements.
As of the time I'm writing this review, this game is on sale—and it's worth the buy right now. That's if the devs add stuff. If they don't add any new features within the next few months following the posting of this review. Don't buy the game. But if you're going to buy the game now, buy it—it's worth it. And at the very least, it will kill 6 hours of your time.

Yes I've only played 40 minutes, but that was enough... that was enough.
This is quite possibly the worst game of this genre I have ever played.
First off, the movement. There is no option to run in this game, meaning you kind of quick walk everywhere. This makes the pacing very lackadaisical and is very annoying when your spawn is quite a way away from the action.
Well, I say action, every animation in this game seems to be about half the speed it should be, kicking takes about three seconds and jumping seems to give you some strange t-pose animation which looks really stupid when you're near other objects.
Things in the game are illogical, you can go under water and literally just walk. You can even fire your gun or jump around, and when you die from submersion with little warning, you just fall to the floor.
The HUD is very underdeveloped, with a font that just looks comical and out of place. There's no real sense of injury or health being lost unless you pay careful attention to the small health meter at the bottom of the screen. This makes it hard to tell when you're close to death, although most the time you die in one hit anyway meaning you have to repeat the whole process of getting to the combat all over again.
The maps have a very small combat area with badly positioned invisible walls, this isn't good for a game which is designed for so many people to play at one time and can make the areas feel crowded and hard to navigate, but I guess that's fine as the movement speeds are so slow that by the time you'd made a strategic move up instead of charging in and getting killed instantly the timer would be up.
As for the combat itself, it's very lacking. You can be killed from long range without any warning and if you actually get into a combat area it is almost impossible to kill someone with some classes. I've seen people chasing each other to try and get a kill and I've just walked away from attackers before and survived.
The music accompanying the game is very off-putting, featuring songs such as 'Hallelujah Chorus' - yeah...
In all fairness, this game does have some good points, although textures are awful when you're close up, from a distance (which is probably where you'll be most the time) they look good. The water effects are really good in the game and the muzzle flashes are very cool.
Having the ability to switch between first and third person is welcome as it allows for a range of different play styles and the camera is well positioned when you're in third person allowing for a good field of view.
The character creation is a very cool addition with a wide range of customisable areas for your character meaning each player looks different in the game. It's great to have a feature like this, it makes the game feel a bit more interactive and personal.
In summary, I don't think I'll go above 40 minutes on this game. It just doesn't match up to games I'm used to playing of this genre like Chivalry. It's features are lacking and the multiplayer is simply boring.

I have played this game off and on for several years. Although there are a few aspects of Star Trek life that it still has not yet gotten to I find it very enjoyable.

So, I decided to finally write up a review for this game. I figure that around 370 hours of play is enough to be able to know what I'm writing about.
So, the first question you have to ask of Star Trek Online: Does it feel like Star Trek? The short answer is kind of. The long answer is yes and no. Whilst it has familiar staples of the franchise, it is also lacking in some elements. For example, more exploration that DIDN'T invariably lead into combat encounters wouldn't go amiss. I won't say it doesn't feel like Star Trek, but it feels almost exclusively like seasons six and seven of DS9 and season three of Enterprise. It has some Trek aspects, but it feels more like a Trek skin for a generic Space MMO and action based MMO. It does, however, have some nice fan service in appearances by existing characters, with several, including Spock, Worf, Sela, Tom Paris, Harry Kim, Seven of Nine, Neelix, the Doctor and Miral Paris, being voiced by their actors from the shows. An opening narration by Leonard Nimoy and an EMH voiced by Zachary Quinto are also both nice touches.
What's worth considering on the lack of Trek feel to this game, is that it is somewhat remedied by the foundry; the user generated content is, in my experience, of great quality more often than not. In fact, there have been occassions where I've felt the foundry content had come out better than the content released by Cryptic / Perfect World / Whatever they want to call themselves now. A prime example is the Breen missions; whilst a fun little arc, some of the missions involved in it can be awkward to play. That's not to say all user created content is amazing and infinitely better than the stuff the studio puts out, just that it often has a more Star Trek feel to it.
My next point is in regards to the playable classes. At the start of the game, you pick one of three factions, between Federation, Klingons and Romulans. It's worth noting that, while playing as a Romulan, you play as a member of the new Romulan Republic faction, NOT a member of the Romulan Star Empire, so if you're hoping to be the bad guy, your bubble's burst, I'm sorry. Each of these factions have their own stories, with the Federation being my favourite, the Romulans proving suitably intriguing but the Klingon story feels somewhat closer to how they have been portrayed in Trek before, so I find myself with a bias towards them over the Romulans.
Once you've chosen your faction, we then get into the actual classes, broken up into the three basic areas of Starfleet; Tactical (i.e. Worf, Tuvok, Reed), Operations (i.e. Scotty, Data, O'Brien) or Science (i.e. Spock, Jadzia Dax, T'pol), with each filling their own role not quite typical of MMO's; Tactical tends to work best with the smaller, faster ships with run and gun tactics, Operations works with the big cruisers and dreadnoughts, and Science works with a sort of intermediary with more buffs. That's not to say you can't play a Tactical character in a Dreadnought (I do!) or a Science character in a light escort, it's just their abilities are more geared towards the ship types mentioned before.
My one gripe with this game is the micro transactions; they aren't micro at all! Zen works out as almost 1p per 1 Zen, so when you see a ship for 3000 Zen, you're looking at about £30.00! Of course, Zen can be farmed via Dilithium mining. However, at the moment, it is 260 odd Dilithium per Zen, with an 8000 per character per day cap on amount you can refine; that translates to a lot of grinding for Dilithium. It doesn't help that the Z-store ships are noticably better than those found in the ship store that you get a free ship from as you go through. Wit hthe introduction of the new T6 ships, this is more noticable than ever, and I hope to see some real F2P T6 ships implemented soon!
Overall, it's a good enough game. It's not a great Star Trek game, but it does pay fan service in the right places at least. My final opinion is; I'd reccomend this, but Trekkies, be patient with it, it'll take roughly as much patience as the Trek reboots do, so if you enjoy them, you'll enjoy this, if you don't, maybe give this one a miss.

This was my favorite game to play on the computer back when it was all in-browser. It was really simple with just 3 weapons, but the maps were really fun and each time I played was a different experience. But one day, I couldn't find the page for it, so I just quit, but eventually, I found it here on steam, and saw how most of it had changed, with better graphics, what looked to be a class system and more weapons, so I bought it. Then when I hopped on a server, the game just didn't feel right, like there was something wrong. What Jagex has done has sort of made the game unnescessarily complicated. The classes just didn't fit, I felt the sniper was too powerful, because in the old version of the game, the rifle was the best all-around weapon and could fit any medium to long range engagement. Now, the class seems to be the most played, and because of that, barely anyone plays the objective and spawn camping is everywhere. Most of the other classes seem unnescessary because the standard soldier in the old version could do anything each class now can (except the rocketeer), just not as good. There is a gamemode called "classic" mode, which only gives you a rifle, shovel, and some blocks, and you play on a ctf type of gamemode, and this is the only part of the game reminiscent of the old game, and it doesn't port it over well. Only 1 weapon from the previous game (the rifle) makes it so no one goes for the flag and they just stay back and snipe. Not to mention the limited maps for the gamemode.
Overall, this game has gone downhill since Jagex took control, and now it just doesn't appeal to me. The new graphics   don't really fit with the blocky/pixelated/retro feel of the game, the classes were unnescessary, and the gameplay in general is pretty bland now.
Gameplay wise, I would rate it 6/10.
But in my personal opinion, I would rate it a 4/10.

Ah ElderScrolls III Morrowind.
For this review I need to point out that I did not play this game when it first came out
so I'm not running on nostalgia goggles here.
At first it didn't seem that I would like this game initally.
Compared to The Elder Scrolls IV Oblivion (the first game of the series I played) it seened so damn Archaic.
I didn't think I would be able to enjoy it. This game seemed so much more difficult to start off and the mechanics are much older.
However once I really sat down and played for real I was hooked. The game even after all this time is still an outstanding game with a refreshing fantasy setting and great story with an even greater lore. If you want a real challenge and a good RPG story this is an excellent game.
However a word of a warning. Although I admit I'm still fairly new to The Elder Scrolls Series (as a someone who had only played on Nintendo platforms for most of their life until recently)  I own Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim on PC via steam.
I have seen the trend many refer to as "dumbing down" and I'm afraid I am in agreement with this term.
This game is much more difficult than skyrim and has almost a completely different method of mechanics in terms of gameplay (Leveling and combat) and functions with quest work (I.E being promoted in factions/directions/Quest orgainzation)
I can only recommend this game to Gamers who have the patience to work with a more complex gameplay and input anymore effort into a character. If you can, outstanding! Play this game and have fun. And you don't then please continue to play other games that you enjoy. Its your loss.

While I enjoyed aspects of this game it is not worth the $15 at full price. Wait until it receives a massive sale, because while the game is enjoyable it is short, linear (despite random levels and sandbox). You harvest a resource to go a little deeper, find some items, and repeat.
The visuals are nice and the idea of exploring a randomly generated world seems good at first, but like everything else in the game it is simplified to the extreme. There are three tiers of depth, not a varied seascape, so you are prompted to upgrade to a certain depth, find resources for the next depth, and repeat. Dangerous depths could have been a fantastic mechanic but you essentially start at the top of an underwater mountain and work your way down, and there is no variation from this from new game to new game.

Mount & Blade: Warband is an action adventure RPG game set in the medieval age in a fictional kingdom of Calradia. There are six different factions, you can join them or rebel against them. All of them has different troops. All of the factions have their pros and cons, so all of them are quite balanced. You can start your character as a nobleman or a commoner. There is a leveling system in this game so you can upgrade your character throughout the game. You can play in first person or third person. Throughout the game, you will recruit people to join your troop. They can be upgraded once they have a certain amount of experience. You can also hire mercenaries too. In combat, you can command your troops to form a certain formation.
Mount & Blade: Warband is one of my favorite RPG game, it is very fun and addicting. The troops are quite balanced. The combat animation looks quite realistic. There are so many mods for this game, so you won't get bored easily. The towns and villages in the game looks beautiful. The soundtrack in the game is great as well.
Despite that, the graphic in this game looks really outdated. There are some minor glitches as well. There is no Steam Cloud feature for this game which is quite needed. Some aspect of the game looks poorly optimized for widescreen resolution.
In conclusion, Mount & Blade: Warband is an outstanding action adventure RPG game. I don't think there are other games like this. I would really recommend this game.

When I first saw the trailer for the game I was blown away by the concept and unique setting presented, and bought it right then. I have been playing crafting/survival games for awhile now am  hooked on the genre. I tend to play horror games a lot also so when they are combined (like in 7 days to die) there is a good formula for a game. But as far as horror games go no amount of zombies or mutilated aliens or jump scares or screaming bloody murder is truly scary. The reason being is that games and movies have been all over those settings for a long time, and they have become a big repetitive. Zombies, aliens, obscene amounts of gore, thats old material.
Now, what isn't old material:deep, dark oceans, drowning, massive sea monsters, and whatever that feeling is that everyone had when they were a kid and they swam in the deep end of the swimming pool, afraid somehow there was a massive shark or octopus underneath you.
FarSky takes advantage of these fears, and combined with it's unique setting makes for a perfect formula of a game that fulfills the void left by the fact that there has not been any kind of game like it. Deep ocean has got to be the best grounds for a survival game there is. I just finished the game and have got to say it was fun, really fun, especially when I was running (swimming) for my life trying to get into my base before a shark ripped my arm off. And the bone chilling feeling of fragile safety being inside of my base looking out the windows at the dark, scary ocean and seeing hordes of dangerous fish really made me feel immersed in the game. Knowing that a piece of glass was all that protected you from an infinite expanse of your worst childhood nightmares was nice feature, and  Jumping off an undersea cliff really gave me a feeling of adventure. Also it got me immediately thinking about all the horrible sea monsters that could be below me, which got me thinking I need to get back to my base and go back to that feeling of safety that felt so good. I give this game a well deserved 10/10.

This is such a wonderfully bizzare game. It's essentially a Left 4 Dead Clone with a much greater focus on melee gameplay, loot, and progression, and somehow it all works. Instead of fighting zombies, you're fighting hordes of literal rat men, called the Skaven. Ordinary Skaven behave just like ordinary infected in L4D, and special Skaven each act just like their special infected counterparts from Left 4 Dead. There are tank rats, smoker rats, hunter rats, you name it.
What makes this game stand out is the level design and progression. As you play the game, you'll gradually unlock more and more loot for your characters that increase their efficiency. Loot can be broken down into crystals that are used to alter, upgrade, or improve loot that you find. You can increase the quality of loot you recieve by playing on higher difficulties and hunting down special items in each level - tomes and grimoires. Once you have these items, you must carry them all the way to the end in order for them to take effect. Tomes don't have a penalty to carry (but take up your healing item slot), but grimoires lower the maximum health of all players by 30%, which means they increase the challenge of a given level in exchange for better loot if you pull it off.
The chaacter variety is decent, but most characters aside from the Pyromancer feel largely the same: Swing your weapon most of the time, shoot your ranged weapon some of the time. Ammo is a precious resource and so it's hard to go full-on ranger. It's just a reality that you'll run out of ammo really quickly, so it's advised to save your ammo for use against the special skaven or for situations where you have to keep the horde at a distance.
The level design is what will win you over. Pretty much every single level in the game is fun to play through. You can also find treasure chests on the map that encourage thorough exploration every time you play a level instead of always beelining the most efficient route, Another nice feature is that if the player who hosts the game owns the DLC, then all players can use those levels regardless of whether or not they own it, and the DLC levels are among the best the game has to offer.
There's also a horde mode where you defend a single point endlessly, but honestly I'm not too big of a fan of that. This game's rgeatest strength is its compelling levels and opting to play a mode without that just doesn't do it for me.
Overall, would recommend. This is a great co-op game and I have no doubt that if you play this with a group of buddies, you'll have a really good time.

Full disclosure: I received a free "Loyalty" copy of the game for having downloaded the game before the kickstarter was announced.
First off, I am NOT a fan of the Harvest Moon games. I never played them when they came out and was never a fan of the farming-style game in general. I have been enoying World's Dawn though, despite a couple of glaring issues that will hopefully be addressed in future updates.
The first issue is the controls. The configuration settings are SUPER confusing. Instead of assigning a key or gamepad button to an action, you're assigning them to arbitrary "A B C X Y Z L and R" buttons that the game uses. The only way to get the buttons assigned to do what you want is trial and error. It's particularly bad when your gamepad only shows up with "button 1" through "Button 10" and you have to guess at BOTH what button is what on your gamepad, and also what button is what in the game. There appears to be NO mouse and keyboard control as well, which is extremely disappointing.
The other issue is that it runs very poorly, though that is likely because the laptop I've been playing it on so far doesn't technically meet the minimum requirements, as it only has a 1.80 GHz CPU. That said, it probably should run on basically anything, given how simple it is. I think the fact that it was made in RPG maker actually holds it back in this regard.
The final - and possibly worst - issue is the lack of content.  Currently there are only 40 spots total on which to plant seeds. It's a small garden - not a farm. You also can only have a handful of livestock that you can raise. There is mining, and fishing, but they're both exceptionally shallow from a mechanical standpoint. There are no skills to upgrade, no buildings to upgrade or purchase that I have found yet, and no real sense of progress.
It's unfortunate, because the game looks pretty good. The art is generally very good. The characters are well designed, the art style is bubbly and cute, and the world itself is well designed. Sadly, it just doesn't make up for the lack of content in the game. I've had the good fortune of being able to see a lot of the obvious competition Stardew Valley, and that game appears to be, in every way, a more complete and entertaining experience. And considering Stardew is only a dollar or two more than World's Dawn, it's hard to recommend this over that.

A staggering quest of epic proportions, you begin as a vision-touched prisoner aboard a boat, sent from the capital of imperial Tamriel to the remote, swamp-and-desert island of Morrowind. An incredible journey of discovery, betrayal, deicide, vengeance, and conquest spreads out from there.
Open world game with heavy RPG elements and storyline.
Very well-polished game with the old "Daggerfall" Kirkbride lore touch, which is to say "you can drown in the world's content".  The plot is sublime, with hours of invested time needed to complete it, with epic proportions matched only by juggernauts of the gaming industry.  The engine allows for an incredible amount of flexibility and freedom - you can spend time to become any kind of character you would desire, and there are multiple paths to get to the final plot.
Detail is given to pretty much everything in the game, and if you are a curious explorer, you can get lost in the environment.  Despite the outdated graphics by today's standards, the sheer level of content is overwhelming, and sets a standard that is sadly unmet since.  The musical score matches the scale of the setting, and fans of the game will instantly recognise the strains of Morrowind's soundtrack - along with the pang of longing that it will bring.
Bethesda kept to it's normal tradition of making the game extremely moddable, and even supported the game well past the three expansions they released for it;
simply to enhance the game that little bit more, and if you wish to mod it further with extra content,

So this is my first review on Steam, and I'm writing it because this is a game that I find really interesting. Firstly - expect to be frustrated at times if you do get it. Racing is massively unpredictable at times, and so is this game. You can apparently nail your setup, have a good car with capable drivers, qualify well, then lose 10 places on lap 1 and put up with a terrible race or have a part fail two laps from victory. There are definitely a few faults with it too, but I would still recommend MM, even at full price.
Cons:
- Race starts are a bit unpredictable, possibly too much so - I've had drivers go from 6th to 2nd then back to 15th on lap 1 before without any mistakes, crashes, etc
- Contract negotiation really needs to be looked at - at the moment you can only sign drivers NOW, not at the end of the season, which is just daft
- Errors at pit stops always used to be reasonable (an extra second or two), but since a patch they've been ridiculous - a highly trained pit crew which can change a tyre in 2 seconds if all goes well will randomly take 11 or 12 seconds because they didn't quite get it right first time, and that just shouldn't happen. To be honest, pit strategy really needs fixed as a whole
- Some of the drivers' comments are redundant or just plain wrong
- Driver ability sometimes means less than it should - I've seen 3 star drivers winning World Championships ahead of much better teammates/rivals
I enjoyed most other aspects of the game, but some of my favourites include:
+ Really varied management styles - corrupt or clean, developmental or cash-splashing, they all get results if you use them right
+ Rule changes make for a dynamic environment (spec engines change everything!)
+ Immersive race weekends - some people think they take too long, but I think they create a more realistic race experience (although 1x speed is far too slow), and you can save and exit for a break whenever you want
+ Good R&D path for components and parts
+ Tongue-in-cheek ripping off of real-life teams and drivers - like the red Italian team with the German and Finnish drivers who *definitely aren't* Ferrari, or mildly corrupt governing body chief "Ernie Hecklerock" - keeps the game realistic while also not taking image rights too seriously
+ Interesting but balanced random events
Overall, while the game has its faults, Motorsport Manager is by far the best racing sim I've seen yet, and it is a genuinely immersive and interesting experience. If you're a racing fan, I'd recommend it at any price; if you're a fan of the genre, then this would be a good buy in a sale.

Way back then, if you got an hour and half into certain quest chains and you had to log out, you had to restart the quest chain all over again.  I didn't like that. Yes I've only played 40 minutes, but that was enough... that was enough.
This is quite possibly the worst game of this genre I have ever played.
First off, the movement. There is no option to run in this game, meaning you kind of quick walk everywhere. This makes the pacing very lackadaisical and is very annoying when your spawn is quite a way away from the action.
Well, I say action, every animation in this game seems to be about half the speed it should be, kicking takes about three seconds and jumping seems to give you some strange t-pose animation which looks really stupid when you're near other objects.
Things in the game are illogical, you can go under water and literally just walk. You can even fire your gun or jump around, and when you die from submersion with little warning, you just fall to the floor.
The HUD is very underdeveloped, with a font that just looks comical and out of place. There's no real sense of injury or health being lost unless you pay careful attention to the small health meter at the bottom of the screen. This makes it hard to tell when you're close to death, although most the time you die in one hit anyway meaning you have to repeat the whole process of getting to the combat all over again.
The maps have a very small combat area with badly positioned invisible walls, this isn't good for a game which is designed for so many people to play at one time and can make the areas feel crowded and hard to navigate, but I guess that's fine as the movement speeds are so slow that by the time you'd made a strategic move up instead of charging in and getting killed instantly the timer would be up.
As for the combat itself, it's very lacking. You can be killed from long range without any warning and if you actually get into a combat area it is almost impossible to kill someone with some classes. I've seen people chasing each other to try and get a kill and I've just walked away from attackers before and survived.
The music accompanying the game is very off-putting, featuring songs such as 'Hallelujah Chorus' - yeah...
In all fairness, this game does have some good points, although textures are awful when you're close up, from a distance (which is probably where you'll be most the time) they look good. The water effects are really good in the game and the muzzle flashes are very cool.
Having the ability to switch between first and third person is welcome as it allows for a range of different play styles and the camera is well positioned when you're in third person allowing for a good field of view.
The character creation is a very cool addition with a wide range of customisable areas for your character meaning each player looks different in the game. It's great to have a feature like this, it makes the game feel a bit more interactive and personal.
In summary, I don't think I'll go above 40 minutes on this game. It just doesn't match up to games I'm used to playing of this genre like Chivalry. It's features are lacking and the multiplayer is simply boring.

Now this is interesting. For all intents and purposes, this is a first-person interpretation of Steve Jackson's "Killer" live action game, but set in a tighter environment and with more weapon variety. With that in mind it even has shades of the excellent pre-murder-mystery game "Kill Doctor Lucky".
Now, you might think that a game that, intentionally or not, reflects these other sources may be a bit derivative, but it really isn't. Indeed it is a particularly refreshing thing to be playing, not quite as frenetic as the FPS games out there, but lacking the long-term sense of digging in that the survival games have. It really does sit nicely in its niche and seems likely to occupy those periods where I need a quick blast of multi-player gaming that requires the use of my rarely deployed sense of deviousness.
Graphically it isn't amazing, but it is still certainly appealing and a good job is done setting the different shipboard environments.
more than anything though, this game is probably going to generate a lot of anecdotal moments and that is increasingly rare these days.
Sure, the graphics aren't top notch, the sound is atmospheric but not rich and the environments are not sprawling (and this is a good thing), but what we have is a great little self-contained game that deserves ongoing attention. Well worth the price of admission.

Alright, but enough complaining, here's what I don't like about it:
1. It's too sensitive. You're all over the screen, it's very hard to get a target on the ball, and it's even harder to navigate it across the field. It's nearly impossible with a fast opponant. 2. The NPCs can do this little thing where they can drag the ball over a space with them as they move. You can't do that, so if you get it stuck next to the wall, you basically have to give it to the opponent, and then, if it's a fast opponent, they get it into the goal pretty easily. You have to go to the other side of the ball to push it left or right on the field, (which with the too sensitive controls makes it even harder) and with that, it takes too long to react, and if you've got a fast opponent, it's stolen from you super quickly.

Normally, survival type games aren't usually my thing. I usually end up having no clue what to do any dying alot. In FarSky, I had no clue what to do and kept dying alot. But in a good way.
FarSky is a fairly simplistic underwater survival game, in which you are tasked with collecting 9 submarine parts to return to the surface. Easy, right? Wrong.
You are dropped in an underwater base with nothing but a diving suit and a drill, and you must get to these nine parts by your own means. Collect resources, make better equipment, and delve deeper into the depths of the ocean. FarSky is a really atmosperic game, and with it's easy game mechanics I can easily see myself diving (see wot I did der) into the game's sandbox mode, and just having a good ol' explore of the ocean floor.
However, the ocean is no calming retreat. FarSky offers a "hunt or be hunted" type deal, in which you need to hunt for your own food, or get eaten by it. It is quite a challenging experience, but after each death I somehow want to go back and fight off the creature and get my dropped supplies.
However, when I found out that this was not an early access game, I was a little dissapointed. The game doesn't offer many game mechanics (for exapmle there are very few things you can craft), much like a game in the beta phase would play like. It's vast ocean playground is it's saving grace, because it's lack of content really does let it down.
+ The game is quite easy to get into after the first half hour or so
+ The ocean is an atomospheric, and scary, place. FarSky shows that perfectly
+ Offers a good central goal from the get-go. You don't feel as if you are wandering aimlessly
- I would expect this amount of content from an Early Access game, not a full release.
- Combat is very shaky. I often died (maybe b/c I suck)
- Expanding the base is tricky and not very well done (again, maybe b/c I suck)

Morrowind is an amazing open-world RPG that is definately worth playing. It is, in my opinion, the greatest of the Elder Scrolls games. You start out as a nobody; a prisoner boarding a ship to the island of Vvardenfell. You don't know why, but you have been sent to Morrowind. You must carefully choose a race, class, and skills to advance through the game as you see fit.
At this point, you can do whatever you want from this point on. You could join one of the Great Houses of Morrowind, join a guild, progress through the main quest, or just wander. You see a ancient burial site, explore it. You see an Ancient Dwemer ruin, go check it out. You see a daedric shine, go loot it. This is where Morrowind shines. There are so many dungeons that have no correlation with questlines. Exploration in this game is amazing.
The game also must be the most realistic of the franchise. It is hard calling a game with magic and giant floating jellyfish realistic, but the skill system is very good. You will hear many gripes about the combat in Morrowind, on how it takes dozens of hits to kill a mudcrab. You must work and hone your skills to become good at them. If you are highly skilled with a long blade, you will kill that mudcrab with ease. However, if you are a skilled mage, and you go stab that mudcrab with a spear, you will never hit it and your spear may break before you even kill the darn thing.
Morrowind's story tells a great tale, and is aided by a true sense of accomplishment that I have never felt in a game before. To avoid spoilers, you start out as a prisoner, like pretty much ever other Elder Scrolls game, and grow into something much, much greater. And the immersive atmosphere helps the story along just fine. It is true that Morrowind isn't the prettiest game out there, but the sound, lighting, and weather effects polish up your sorroundings.
When you progress, you will have to increase skills to level up. Upon leveling up you can approve your attributes (this is similiar to S.P.E.C.I.A.L in the Fallout series) and get a little motivational message. Accomplishment is well rewarded with a powerful weapon or item, and when you receive that weapon, you feel slightly more powerful. For the most part, enemies are not scaled. So when you do get that extremely powerful weapon, you feel extremely powerful. Soon you'll realize that there are stronger weapons to be found and stronger enemies to overcome. This process can repeat many times over.
There you have it, The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind. It is definately one of my favorite games of all time and worth the purchase.

So this is my first review on Steam, and I'm writing it because this is a game that I find really interesting. Firstly - expect to be frustrated at times if you do get it. Racing is massively unpredictable at times, and so is this game. You can apparently nail your setup, have a good car with capable drivers, qualify well, then lose 10 places on lap 1 and put up with a terrible race or have a part fail two laps from victory. There are definitely a few faults with it too, but I would still recommend MM, even at full price.
Cons:
- Race starts are a bit unpredictable, possibly too much so - I've had drivers go from 6th to 2nd then back to 15th on lap 1 before without any mistakes, crashes, etc
- Contract negotiation really needs to be looked at - at the moment you can only sign drivers NOW, not at the end of the season, which is just daft
- Errors at pit stops always used to be reasonable (an extra second or two), but since a patch they've been ridiculous - a highly trained pit crew which can change a tyre in 2 seconds if all goes well will randomly take 11 or 12 seconds because they didn't quite get it right first time, and that just shouldn't happen. To be honest, pit strategy really needs fixed as a whole
- Some of the drivers' comments are redundant or just plain wrong
- Driver ability sometimes means less than it should - I've seen 3 star drivers winning World Championships ahead of much better teammates/rivals
I enjoyed most other aspects of the game, but some of my favourites include:
+ Really varied management styles - corrupt or clean, developmental or cash-splashing, they all get results if you use them right
+ Rule changes make for a dynamic environment (spec engines change everything!)
+ Immersive race weekends - some people think they take too long, but I think they create a more realistic race experience (although 1x speed is far too slow), and you can save and exit for a break whenever you want
+ Good R&D path for components and parts
+ Tongue-in-cheek ripping off of real-life teams and drivers - like the red Italian team with the German and Finnish drivers who *definitely aren't* Ferrari, or mildly corrupt governing body chief "Ernie Hecklerock" - keeps the game realistic while also not taking image rights too seriously
+ Interesting but balanced random events
Overall, while the game has its faults, Motorsport Manager is by far the best racing sim I've seen yet, and it is a genuinely immersive and interesting experience. If you're a racing fan, I'd recommend it at any price; if you're a fan of the genre, then this would be a good buy in a sale.

If you are looking for a deep, complex and difficult managing game, this is not the game for you. Instead, Motorsport Manager is a straightforward managing simulator that does not require any prior knowledge about racing.   However, due to its simplicity, it is easy to figure out a way to play the game that will always work. As a result, replayability in this game is surprisingly low.
Furthermore, the game tends to waste the time of the player often. For instance, at the end of a training session, the player is obliged to watch all the cars driving to their pits, even though there is nothing to do, nothing to gain, and nothing interesting happening on screen. Pointless pre-season testing where you just see some slicers that move; flashy, good looking animations that aren't important for the gameplay. Patience is a virtue, and you'll need it if you want to play this game.
Like the famous football manager, much of the satisfaction of this game comes from reading the messages that you'll receive in your inbox. After your first win, your driver may dedicate the win to you. After doing great in a season, you may be chosen as the manager of the year. You'll be able to participate in a voting system that shapes next season, and its great to see how a vote goes into your favorite direction.
But also on these good points, the game leds down after a while. Many of the messages are repeating, and at some point, you'll skip reading them because of that. The worst of it all, is the media. You'll often be asked whether you'd like to give an interview. You're better off denying the interview, because it frequently results in a morale penalty for one of your teammates. I really do not understand how to developers have implemented this option in the game like this.
However, in the first few seasons that you play, everything will be new, and at that time the game is really entertaining. This is why I would recommend buying the game when its on discount. You'll get some fun out of the game for sure, and when the game turns into a chore-fest, you'll  just lay it down, and gotten your money's worth out of it.

Metal Slug 3 is a game that will push your reflexes to its limits. If you've ever played a run and gun game, you should know what to expect, lots of action packed, adrenaline pumping, brutally unforgiving gameplay that's loads of fun whether by yourself or with a friend. It plays relatively the same, and it looks and sounds absolutely beautiful, but there are some issues that may hinder your experience. At times, the game won't read your movements, causing you to die from something you couldn't avoid, a problem that was never present in other ports, the smooth, tight controls just aren't there. A few audio clips also suffer a bit of a downgrade which is sad seeing that this is a PC Port of a game almost 20 years old. If you're a fan of the game, or just someone looking for something new, fun and challenging, play this game, but not this port. It's fun, with lots of replayability, but for what it's worth, you get what you paid for.

Short answer: Deffinatly give this a try if you like Star Trek or don't want to pay a lot of money for a good mmo, it wont cost you anything other than some download time!
Pros:
-It's actually free! Some people have called this a "pay to win" game which i find very strange, this is the one of the few games where you can have access to the entire game and become as strong as anybody else without spending any money at all. The way it works is mostly a "pay to skip the grinding" or "grind and sell instead of paying" which I find to be a very nice system. It makes it so you don't feel preasured to pay for anything and even if you don't want to pay nor grind, you wont fall way behind everyone else, in fact you can still go from level 1 to 60 (the max level) and experience the whole storyline including new content without a problem.
-Graphics are not spectacular, but you can play this on an older pc or family laptop, or have something else running the background easy.
-Storyline goes very well with all of the Star Trek series, expect to find some familiar characters with their original voice acting. The story takes place a few years after Star Trek Voyager (there will be lots of Star Trek Voyager characters).
-Despite the fact there is lots of bias as to what is the best way to play, I feel like the gameplay is actually fairly well ballenced. It's not perfect; some may be more difficult to get good at, some may suck early on but even out later on, but I feel like this is better than some other mmo's.
-level syncing option makes playing with friends easier, however someone whos high level still might kill everything in a couple seconds in a low level area.
-I personally found the community a bit nicer than most mmo's when it comes to playing in queues. There is not really any tank-healer-dps roles (there can be but it is not neccessary) so you can't blame people for not doing their role, which makes it overall feel nicer.
-Space and Ground gameplay: 2 different ways you can play, if you prefer one over the other you can choose to do one more than the other (at least for most end-game stuff), however your mostly stuck doing both in the storyline.

Cons:
-A bit glichy, however they do eventually fix them which is better than some other mmo's.
-Not much end-game content. While there is some things to do such as increasing reputation and upgrading gear, most of the end game content is pretty much just "increase the difficulty to advanced or elite". They are constantly adding new content however.
-PvP is almost non-existant unless you get some friends together for it.
-Some areas of the game can be dramaticly easier or harder on your pc, I might run a very pretty graphic heavy scene in one of the earlier storylines at 60 fps but then run a patrol in the delta quadrent at 8 fps and it's not even that graphicly heavy. Probably not a problem if you have any kind of gaming pc.
-Some of my friends in Germany said they had strange problems with translation.
-The 3 roles can be rather confusing, there is Tactical, Engineering, and Science. You might think that it is "Tactical = Dps, Engineering = Tank, and Science = Healer" but it's not. In fact there really is no clear cut roles in this game. They are also slightly different for ground and space.
-For Space: Tactical can deal a little more damage, Engineering can take hits better and heal better, Science does exotic things such as crowd control, draining shields, and some exotic damage (they also have strong shields).
-For Ground: Tactical can deal more damage (also has an aggro catcher which I find strange), Engineering can create turrets, have pets, and regenerate shields. Science can debuff and heal.
-All these roles can also be mix-matched a bit when combined with a different ship. Example: a tactical officer can fly a cruiser (a type of ship with high engineering) for a mix of offence and defense, or he/she can fly a science ship for some exotic dps. There is no right or wrong way to play, you can focus on 1 thing and play a role, or be more diverse.

For $80.00, no.
Honestly, I have to put that out there ahead of anything else I'm about to write. The standard price for this is absurdly high, especially given that this came out some time ago, now.
But for $25.00 during a sale, sure. It has its flaws, and among them is that some pretty important battles (Bagration) are somehow in the DLC rather than the base game, and some battles (Citadel, AKA Kursk) don't even appear to be available at all. Also, it's sometimes needlessly complex (once I group together units, do I really need to Shift-Right Click to attack with the group? Just a right click should do if I bothered to group them, after all) while in other areas somehow still watered-down (partisans are a whack-a-mole annoyance rather than a crucial issue, much of the time).
All that said, have you ever played Unity of Command and wanted a bigger scenario with more complexity? Well, this is basically just that: the biggest UoC scenario is about the scale in space of the medium-sized ones in WitE, and about half the scale in turns.
If you don't know what Unity of Command is, here's another take:
Ever played Civilization games and wanted to do nothing but fight battles with the end-game units? This is basically that, sans helicopters and giant death robots. You'll spend countless turns shuffling across hexes, defending hexes, stacking units (up to three in a tile) according to what you plan on happening, and, of course, fighting for cities (as well as victory points). There's a lot more military complexity, too, and none of that stupidly-simple diplomacy that Civilization fans have come to know and occasionally tolerate.
And beyond all that: if you are a war-gamer, this is one of the most detailed titles in PC war-gaming that you'll find.
But it has its flaws.
I already mentioned the pricing, but the price might feel a little less astronomical if certain other flaws didn't also exist.
For one, the music: you get maybe a grand total of 7 minutes of actual music, divided into 2 tracks. And one of the two tracks, while an excellent attempt at a very martial-sounding march, is itself already repetative. While I don't want to compare HoI4 to this, as the two games are actually quite different in many ways, I have to say that HoI4 itself annoyed me musically, as it had maybe 20 minutes of music at launch and you heard the same stuff over and over again over a 5-10 hour campaign. But WitE is far worse... in just the first hour of actual play, I already found myself thinking about putting on my own music.
Another pretty major non-gameplay-related flaw is the lack of useful tool-tips. You get tool-tips, yes, but most are not very useful and are often limited to a single-sentence that doesn't connect the question at hand to the other gameplay elements. This is an issue in other games, sure, but in a game with such a massive amount of text, how is it that tool-tips are so small? This game doesn't hold hands, but maybe some better tool-tips, at least, would be a good idea... especially given that the manual also doesn't always provide a straight-forward answer (or always explain what an acronym means, or what a couple of gameplay mechanics actually do).
Yet another lack-of-polish issue is that the DLC campaign scenarios are intermingled with the base-game scenarios in the menu. This sounds nit-picky, but when you just want to try the base-game prior to deciding on DLC, it only serves to obscure what you really can play. Worse, the tutorial scenario, because it begins with a 'V' for its name (named after the area it occurs in), is buried in the list... fortunately, V is close enough to T (for Tutorial, you know) that I still found it while looking for a tutorial scenario... but really? You know, seperate folders for game content have been around since Doom had the different WAD files for maps. Doom, guys. Doom. A game that was little more than blasting demons had the foresight to use different folders for maps. And here we are twenty years later with a major war-game that lumps every map into the same folder.
And still another non-gameplay-issue: resolution and full-screen. Resolution can be screwy, and I toyed around with mine a little bit (though fortunately I didn't run into any black-screen issues or more major stuff like some on the Steam forums may have). And true full-screen doesn't exist... a major war-game without even the option to go full-screen. Again, Doom, guys. Doom.
So why still recommend it?
Well, if you don't mind getting through a couple of beginner's traps, don't mind a sort of high learning curve, and don't mind putting on some Moody Blues, then you can jump into a far better depiction of the Eastern Front than you saw in CoH2, HoI4, or in almost any other strategy game.
This is as close as you can get to seeing what really was going on in the Eastern Front. If you allow the Soviets to pull back in those early-war scenarios, you may not get another chance to encircle them. The Panzers often must move forward, keeping the Soviets routing, not allowing them to entrench at the rivers, all while realizing that fuel may become an issue and that once the mud appears, that's it. Unlike most games that depict the winter weather being the downfall of the offensive in 1941, this one accurately shows that the *mud* actually was the beginning of the end, as the Panzers couldn't get ahead fast enough at that point to keep the Soviets retreating.
Really, it's those things that make this game what it is. It's the over-all attention to the military realities, acknowledging that ammunition and fuel are two totally seperate things (unlike HoI4 or UoC), acknowledging that you can't simply empty France and Germany to deploy every last unit against the Soviets (an issue many, many WWII games have run into, where you can win on the Eastern Front by taking everyone who should have had to stay in France and using them in the East, all because the human player knows that the scripted invasion of France won't hit until 1944). Not that the Western Front exists in WitE, but enough scenarios force one or both players to leave garrisons in certain cities in the Eastern Theater in order to not lose victory points.
TL;DR -
Very good gameplay, very thread-bare presentation (music is ultra-repetative, some UI elements are poor).
For $25 (and $10 on I-tunes for some better music), it's worth it. Maybe for $40 if you are really into hex-based wargaming.
But for $80, I'd say wait for a sale.
Definitely a game I recommend, but, well, not for $80.00. Hopefully they chop the standard price in half (at least) before long, but that hardly seems likely from what I've seen... and to anyone still trying to defend the current price: the game is way too old now to justify the price. Super Mario Bro's for the NES in the 1980's might be an all-time classic... but they don't still charge the $30 original price (or whatever it was, adjusting for inflation, etc.). In all likelihood, if the price was set to $25.00 (which it is during winter sales), it would probably make *more* money that way, selling two dozen more copies a year, than it does currently probably selling a couple copies a year at $80.00.

At this point in your life, you've probably seen more crates in video games than you have in real life. You've also pushed and arranged more virtual crates than anyone in the history of the world, all for the privilege of arranging yet more crates. It's easy to bag on the ubiquitous boxes of the game industry, but there's still some joy to be found in crate-based puzzling. Enter Wyv and Keep, two smart-mouthed novice treasure hunters with only a vast assortment of crates, switches, and ridiculously challenging puzzles between them and fortune.
Wyv and Keep is a puzzle platformer pitting you against single-screen rooms full of traps and treasure. You control both feisty finders, switching between them with a press of a button (unless you opt for the co-op mode) to unlock and reach the exit of each level. Along the way you'll find riches to collect, secret doors to crack, notes to flesh out the story, and tons of deadly perils to stop you from reaching any of them. After each level you're rated on your performance in terms of speed, attempts, and treasure secured.
Doubtless you've heard this pitch before, but Wyv and Keep manages to transcend the tired genre in a couple ways. The most prominent of these ways, of course, is how incredibly ♥♥♥♥ing hard it is. I've played a fair share of pushing/shoving puzzle games and beaten or come close in most of them, but W&K started kicking my♥♥♥♥♥by World 3. Right away you'll be faced with those insidious puzzles that appear completely impossible at first blush, but begin to reveal themselves after a dozen or more attempts. I guarantee there is no smooth sailing through this game, as you'll soon be spending a good twenty minutes staring at just one of the game's sixty-plus perplexing puzzles.
That's really the big thing you need to be prepared for, the withering difficulty. These aren't the ah-ha moments of Braid, these are brick walls of intricate pitfalls and switches. Every level is going to take careful planning to work out the precise sequence of moves to complete it, thanks to the two-character element. Both Wyv and Keep can push crates and cut ropes, but they can also serve as blocks themselves, giving the other the leg up they need to reach a high ledge or fill a gap for a crate to cross. These basic abilities are used to the fullest extent to tax your brain in ways you may very well have never been challenged.
Your quest for fortune and glory is rendered in a pretty close approximation of SNES graphics, softly pixellated and lovingly detailed. The sound design is equally charming and pleasant, a necessity as you struggle with the brain-teasers in your way. The only place the design really falls down is in the options, because they don't really exist. As long as you don't mind a smallish windowed experience, though, it shouldn't bother you much. The only thing that might bother you is the precipitous difficulty curve, but if you want your puzzle games to challenge then you'll find your match in Wyv and Keep.

Today I will be talking about a Indie game that you might of heard off called Wyv and Keep: The Temple of the Lost Idol, avaiable on Windows, Linux and Mac. Developed and published by A Jolly Corpse on the 8th August 2014, this game is filled with many puzzles for you to solve with the two characters that you play as throughout the game. With 60 levels of pure puzzle and platforming, this is a enjoyable game whether you play it solo or with a friend.
The game starts you off with these two characters called Wyv and Keep, who are treasure hunters, on their adventures to go through an ancient temple. The objective of each of the levels is to try to get to the door in the least amount of deaths/restarts and in the lowest amount of time. The games most useful mechanic is to be able to stand on your partners head to be able to reach your goal. This is the main mechanic that you will have to use throughout the game as you play through each of the levels. It focuses primarly on the trial and error way of playing some of the puzzle levels without having to think through before taking action. This may be a downfall to the game because of the amount of retrying you may have to do the level. Another thing thjat slightly infurated me was the 1 tile gap to be able to jump to the next platform. Sometimes you are under time constrain because some of the enemies throw projectiles at you. So when you are trying to jump a one tile gap and you can’t because your not in perfect position to jump it you don’t actually jump it and therefore get hit by the enemies projectile. The game doesn’t really gain in difficulty until the third world, making you have to think and plan ahead with each move that you make throughout. From then on the game tempts you to sometimes make shady and difficult jumps in order to gain more coins and treasure that you will find along the way of each of the puzzles. On some levels there are secret passages that lead to more treasure that looks unobtainable until you find that area that you can pass through. Later on in the game you will be able to purchase hats with the money and treasure that you have obtained throughout the game. As far as I know, that is the only way you can spend the treasure that you collect over the course of the game.
You will be rated upon each level on the amount of deaths/restarts and how long it takes you to complete each level. For me, I didn’t really care much about this rating system that went along with the game. I felt like some of these puzzles you really had to be able to complete it first and then come back to it to get a better scrore. This means that the game has a rather nice replay ability, for you to try to complete the puzzle in less deaths, and possibly in a better time than before as well.
You can either play as both of them, switching between the two characters or playing with someone else with Local Co-op. The game seems to have a online feature, but it seems that the servers are kinda dead so playing solo, with a friend on Steam or local co-op would be recommened. Although I found that playing local co-op sometimes would destory your friendship with your friend as the simplist mistake could lead to having to restart the puzzle again.
Now lets talk about the audio of the game, the game has a rather atmospheric music throughout of the worlds that you go to. With the soundtrack continously looping in the background, it really sets the mood for the game and the sort of area that you are currently in. There isn’t any voice acting when there is a cut scene or when you read a note, which there doesn’t need to be on every game. That being said, some of the best games haven’t had voice acting in them and have been rather successful on Steam. I think that because the game does well to create a nice atmosphere with the music and sounds that the voice acting wouldn’t be needed throughout this game.
The graphics of the game are rather retro and simplistic that really suits the way the game plays out throughout. The sprites are rather simplistic and well designed, with the simple few frames on animation as you walk and jump throughout the game. The graphics have a sort of charm to it, each of the objects and characters are rather indetifiable. They did the resolutions of the graphics rather nice, it’s not too high resolution but it’s not too low either. It’s a really nice balance between the resolution of the graphivs throughout the game. Although the resolution for the game is nice, there is no option the change the window size or to be able to put the game in full screen. It seems to be locked into a window which might annoy some people.
+ Fun local co-op or single player
+ Challenging and fun
+ High res graphics
+ Music sets a nice atmosphere
+ Trading cards
- Fixed resolution sized window
- Online multiplayer is dead
- Sometimes the game is too difficult
- No Steam achievements
All in all, this game is a very enjoyable yet difficult type of puzzle platformer game. The game supports solo, local co-op or online multiplayer which kinda seems to be dead at the moment. The graphics of this game are retro styled and rather simplistic which makes this game rather nice to play and enjoy. The graphics are also in a high resolution that makes the game look crisp and clean throughout. The music is atmospheric, and there is a nice amount of replay ability throughout the game. Although you may find the game stressful and too difficult at times, completing a level is rather satifying after a lot of trail and error. I have to say that the price of this game is rather expensive for the content and difficulty throughout. Despite the few negative things about this game here and there, I still recommened this game to those of you who like puzzle platforming games

FarSky is a very fun and tense game, however, it feels unfinished. Building up your base seems a bit pointless because there really isn't much you can fill your base with, so most of the rooms you make are just empty.
The fun in this game is the exploration and the tense fear that you experience when you're traveling in the water at night and theres sharks everywhere, and when you hear the sound of something moving behind you in the water and you look behind you to find a shark about to take your head clean off. But once you get about 4 hours into the game, that feeling dissipates because you have enough materials and the highest level weapon you can make to where you can pretty much 1-2 hit any shark that comes your way.
I did have a lot of fun with this game though, and the extra survivor mode (which is like hardcore modes in ARPG's where if you die, thats it game over) you get after beating the game is motivation enough to do a second playthrough. I recommend this game because its still a great game despite the lacking content. This game would really benefit from a steam workshop and local/online coop.

This game is the breaking point when Bethesda escaped the pixels, and was born into 3d amazingness. Though the graphics take some getting used to, once you break the 10 hour point, everything becomes an adventure, and here's why.
1. Unlike its previous games (aka Daggerfall, Arena), Morrowind has a clear storyline for you to follow and make branched desisions off of.
2. Unlike Skyrim, you can kill whoever you want, without them bowing down and regening their health.
3. Unlike Oblivion, you can gain blessings from any shrine, all you have to do is donate some coin. (has a time limit)
4. The island of vvardenfell takes an hour or so to cross, but will take 30 hours due to the amount of caves, ancestral tombs, daedric ruins, dunmer fortresses, and much much more.
5. Unlike other games, you can choose from a plethora of guilds and groups to join.(a.k.a. House Hlaalu, House Redoran, House Telvanni, Blades, East Empire Company, Fighters Guild, Imperial Cult, Imperial Legion, Mages Guild, Thieves Guild, Ashlander Tribes, Morag Tong, and the tribunal temple. You can also join one of three vampire clans such as the Aundae Clan, the Berne Clan, and the Quarra Clan.)
So with all included, this is a pretty amazing game that deserves the awards it got in its day, and still has talking points that Skyrim, Oblivion, Daggerfall, and Arena cannot compete with.

Morrowwind is a fun open world RPG, with a few things to keep in mind for continued fun game play.  One thing this studio does well is emergent game play which adds (in my opinion) immensely to the feeling that you're in an actual world where npc's have lives of their own that may not revolve around your character.
*Do not save over your saves* Seriously.  They get corrupted very easily that way, and I had to restart multiple games that had gone wrong before someone else made that suggestion to me.
Your game RP choices matter to the world, some factions don't like each other, some are neutral, some are friendly.  Don't expect to join them all in one play through (most, if you are careful, but not all).
There is a thing that can happen where you suddenly aren't able to bring your hands into the ready to cast position.  If this happens check to see if the spell slot has emptied itself.  Sometimes this happens when looting or changing gear.  Just select a spell again and it *should* be fixed.
Potion crafting can break the game.  While hilarious, I do not recommend drinking certain potions made when your intellegence was severely over buffed.  Speed, levitate, jump, swim, water walking (to name a few)... If they're over buffed enough to make the game unplayable, they will *also* take forever to wear off.  Its entertaining to mess around with though as long as you save first! :)

Game brings back wonderful memories, when you could actually find unique armour and weapons for exploring;) And getting demolished by NPCs in dungeons because your character wasnt strong enough. Graphice are obiously not up to par with the newer Elder Scrolls games....but Morrowind is still by far the best one, out of the ones I played (III, IV, and V)!

Alright, I really will try to give this a fair review from my stand point. This is not a game that I normally play, I wasn't really expecting much going into this game but I'll admit it did keep me invested for a while.
The game isn't a typically racing game, you don't play as a racer, rather you play as a manager to make sure your racers are good to go. The game didn't have a tutorial so I went in blind as a bat, learning from experience and little hints the game is telling me. The only mode I played was Single Race so this is going to be focused more on what I learned from that.
Basically you choose your track, then you choose what team/region you want to represent, and then choose two of three racers for that given team/region. They all have different stats and that'll ultimately effect their standards for a race car.
For your first race, it'll be a quick practice test for your racers. They'll get a feel of the car you've given then and over time will throw out their own suggestions, such as if the suppression feels off or it feels stiff turning corners. You gotta take these little comments and change the car's specs accordingly to their liking. This will ensure they feel great when they race, the more they drive during this first race, the better understanding they get of the car and feel safe when driving it in the real race.
The second race is the qualifiers, this race is specfically to show you how fast your racers/cars are compared to the other racers. During this race, you can't change that much other than what tires they're using. You must only change the tires during specific weather conditions.  If it's raining, give them intermediate tires, they'll even say they need those tires if it starts raining to the point their slick tires become a problem.
Finally, the real race begins. This is the crucial part of the game where you must pay attention to everything going on with your racers, the weather, and the cars. Every now a then you should check the parts of the cars and make sure they're good to race, if they start turning yellow or red you need to make your racer stop for a pit and repair that part, of course this will make them lose a few positions so it's highly recommended you send your racers out in top performance in the right conditions so that they don't have to pit early. If you don't repair the cars or replace the tires every so often, your racer will crash and will be disqualified from the race. I've only ever gotten as far as 3rd place while my other racer was in 15th.
This is a difficult game to a hang of, you'll need to practice with whatever team you like constantly to get an idea of their standards and what they like and how often you need to send your racers to a pit. It's kinda stragetic in a way or most racing games are just competitive. This game makes you think of what you're gonna do next, think ahead of the next lap and plan your next pit stop carefully.
Of course I missed a few things about this game but again I didn't play that much of it, just Single Race.
If you've been looking for something different then just a normal racer and something they'll actually make you feel like you're making a difference by what moves you make, then this game is for you.
7.8/10, it's a different kind of racing game, but it's definitely something to try out.

After more than 100 hours playing this game, I owe it a review. Blueline developed this digital version of the game, but it was a board game first. I believe it came out last year (2016), and it's from the mind of John Yanni. He also designed the very very fantastic Hive. Blueline also developed the digital version of that game.
I know Tatsu won't appeal to everyone, but I really dig it. It's my come home from work, turn on some music/podcasts, and relax game. As much as I love Hive and other abstract strategy games, they can be very stress inducing at times. Tatsu certainly rewards strategy and skill, but it's much more chill for me.
The first thing to know about this game is that it's kind of like Backgammon. Rolling the dice and moving the pieces works the same way (except there is a limit of two pieces per space), and the opponents are moving in opposite directions. Tatsu has some very clever twists that make it feel unique and modern, but also like something I'll be playing with my grandchildren years from now. There are two ways to win the game: eliminate all of one of your opponent's color or get all of their pieces out of play. Your pieces or *dragons will continue to go around and around the board; they don't leave play like in Backgammon. There are three color dragons, and they each do something different. The green pieces trap your opponents piece underneath (they can free it by using only the lower of the two values rolled), blue pieces wash your opponent’s pieces out of play, and the red pieces eliminate your opponent’s pieces from the game. To bring a new piece into play, simply end your movement on a green, blue or red space and the matching color piece will enter the ready mat. It can be brought into the game on a 1, 2 or 3. There are a few other itty bitty rules, but that's really all there is to it. You can learn everything you need to know in just a minute or two.
The AI isn't that tough (I've won 68% of my games against the hardest AI), but I enjoy playing against it. It tends to make suboptimal moves now and then, and there's a certain tactic that it doesn't seem to know how to handle. When I've created games to play asynchronously, someone always joins. There have been a few bugs here and there, but the developer has been pretty good about updating the game and responding to feedback from the players. The game looks just like it's physical counterpart although I kind of wish it was 3D like Hive is.
*The theme of the game is about dragons and a Japanese legend. I like the dragon patterns on the pieces and "Tatsu" is a pretty cool name, but it has about as much theme as Backgammon. I'm perfectly OK with that; I just thought it was worth mentioning.
OK so if you like Backgammon, definitely give this a try. If you discovered it because you're a fan of Hive or maybe checking out digital versions of board games, this is a very approachable abstract-strategy game that has some real depth but can be played on a chill level because the luck of the dice kind of takes the edge off compared to something like Hive or Chess. But make no mistake, just like in Backgammon, the more skilled player will win most of the time.

Firing with the mouse will make your finger hurt, though.  The cursor doesn't lock to the window, so you will take damage and ruin your multiplier when you accidentally click outside it on your second monitor or just outside the window.
I also have complaints about design aspects.  The gun feels clunky and random. It isn't fun to use, which is kind of important in a game like this.  The addons feel similarly random.  The game is too focused on score rewards instead of money rewards that would allow you to buy more items and get stronger faster by playing well.  The only way skill can improve your power increase speed is by killing saucers, which sometimes drop money (usually it's a score bonus, though) or by catching the falling alien pilots.
Killing the pilots results in no bonus, but allowing them to fall makes you lose money you already have.  This is really stupid.  Sometimes the falling ship is right on top of the pilot, making it impossible to hit it without killing the pilot or to catch the pilot without getting hit.  Sometimes, there's just too much♥♥♥♥♥♥going on to catch or shoot the pilot, meaning you lose all that money.  I don't understand this choice and think it's far too punishing.
Between the technical problems and the weird design choices,  I don't recommend this game. It's fun maybe fifteen minutes at a time, though, if you like centipede-style shooters.  I would save and quit about that often if I continued to play to rest my finger.

I don't normally *cough*ever*cough* write reviews, but this game is worth it, so bear with me on this. As a long-time player, I did receive a free copy, but this has no bearing on the review.
World's Dawn is a wonderful game with a lot of charm. Anyone to ever play a Harvest Moon game has a good idea of what the game is like, but World's Dawn is better in one of the most important aspects – character. The socialization aspect of the game has been far and away my favorite part - meeting and getting to know all the other characters is just so satisfying! Normally in an HM game I'll make friends with a couple people and whoever I decide to marry I'll boost as quickly as possible and kind of ignore the rest unless I happen to run across them a lot. World's Dawn makes you want to go out of your way to talk to people! It's a real choice between, say, fishing all day and running around town talking to people. And the art is so gorgeous! That's not to say the rest of the game is lackluster – quite the opposite! Fishing is a fun little minigame, mining is a great way to while away an evening, and I make sure to water my crops every morning!
In closing, I would like to give a round of applause to Wayward Prophet, who spent around five long years on this masterpiece, who has fixed bug after bug, made change after tweak, to make this game the gem it is today.

This is the Harvest Moon-esque game we need, but not the one we deserve. After all these failed attemps at making domething like Harvest Moon, World's Dawn manages to capture the essentials and make it friendly enough for anyone to step in and play.

Simple, fun and easy. That's how it should be.

Morrowwind is a fun open world RPG, with a few things to keep in mind for continued fun game play.  One thing this studio does well is emergent game play which adds (in my opinion) immensely to the feeling that you're in an actual world where npc's have lives of their own that may not revolve around your character.
*Do not save over your saves* Seriously.  They get corrupted very easily that way, and I had to restart multiple games that had gone wrong before someone else made that suggestion to me.
Your game RP choices matter to the world, some factions don't like each other, some are neutral, some are friendly.  Don't expect to join them all in one play through (most, if you are careful, but not all).
There is a thing that can happen where you suddenly aren't able to bring your hands into the ready to cast position.  If this happens check to see if the spell slot has emptied itself.  Sometimes this happens when looting or changing gear.  Just select a spell again and it *should* be fixed.
Potion crafting can break the game.  While hilarious, I do not recommend drinking certain potions made when your intellegence was severely over buffed.  Speed, levitate, jump, swim, water walking (to name a few)... If they're over buffed enough to make the game unplayable, they will *also* take forever to wear off.  Its entertaining to mess around with though as long as you save first! :)
