Morrowind is a casualized version of Daggerfall. As a seasoned hardcore gamer, I was hugely disappointed that a lot of cool immersive features from Daggerfall are completely missing. For example, in Daggerfall you bought a map with every settlement on it. You could ask quest NPCs to mark locations on it. In Morrowind, you cannot get questgivers to draw on your map. Also, your map is missing almost every town. There are no printing presses, so why would there be a map thats missing important landmarks? Instead of asking people to point out your destination on your map, they give you "directions" like "walk north until you see a tree, then turn left". With my ultra powerful gamer computer, I can see the tree from miles away, and also that there is a path leading directly towards my destination that the questgiver forgot to mention.
If you are a casual scrub, this is the game for you. But, if you are a hardcore gaming veteran like myself, you are better off playing Daggerfall, which is free on bethesda's website.

First of all, let me say that I have over 220 hours of this game on the original Xbox, so I'm a little more qualified to write this review than my current 3.8 hours would imply.
I know it's a little dated. I know the AI isn't spectacular. I know the combat system is less than stellar. And I know that this is one of my all-time favourite games. How many games let you have an almost fully customizable spell system that lets you provide yourself with spells that can drain the life from an entire building and add it to your own, fly for days, or create items that will give you permanent servants. How many games were crafted inch by beautiful inch by hand? Not many, and of the ones that have been, few can match the brilliance that is Morrowind. Never before or since have I seen a game that could make me fall in love with the world the way Morrowind did. Never before have I been able to scour the land for interesting quests/items/NPCs and been able to actually find them at every turn. Whether it's a sword hidden on top of a guard's wardrobe or a lone warrior wandering the mountains, this game just doesn't dissapoint (not to mention the best DLC I've ever played in the Bloodmoon expansion).
Tell you what, if this game were re-released with upgraded graphics, a tweaked combat system, and AI that gave the characters in the world real lives, I'd pay $100 for it without blinking. Do yourself a favour and pick it up.
Still one of my favourite games. The AI may be pretty janky and it looks dated but the setting and story more than makes up for it.

A potentially fun game is marred by bad implementation. If you retry a level more than a few times, you're rewarded with a steaming pile of poo as your rating. Expect to die many times due to bad jumping mechanics, especially when standing in mud/quicksand. You can't jump in this muck, which unfortunately seems to transfer to the patch of ground next to it, causing extra suffering.
You can push blocks but not pull them. You can pick up select items but not jump while carrying them. Too much trial and error for a game that deducts points for the time it takes to solve and number of attempts is just bad. I was expecting Adventures of Lolo gameplay, where restarts were expected but you weren't punished. This game unfortunately falls short, which is a shame as the sounds and animations are pretty decent.

Wyv and Keep is a pretty fun co-op puzzle game. Play it solo, play it with a friend, or play it with a friend online (a rarity these days for indie games). The pixel art is charmingly well done, music is nice to listen to, and the difficulty is challenging. If you have a significant other to play with, you'll find the dialogue between your characters pretty relatable and comedic. Highly recommend the 2-pack for best experience.

This game...the single player's pretty good, but...
It gets *really* good once you get multiplayer in, and you go through puzzles, even ones you've gotten through before, and find new solutions as a result of that one mixup that you try to salvage, or some *other* way to solve the puzzle that you never thought to try. The puzzles have enough leeway that jury rigging solutions out of the combined intended solutions just to get that last bonus piece of gold really takes it further.
Or when you forgot the puzzle and are trying to figure out exactly what the intent from your online ally is for the solution.
Either way, while there appear to be some hanging bugs from what I've seen of friends playing the game on their end while online, it's made quite a bit of progress over the past couple months.
Got this late last year for the GamesMatter event by IndieGamerChick, but since then, I've noticed that the patches that come through seem to be significantly enhancing the game.
If there's an achilles heel to the game, it's probably the mostly gone multiplayer community for the game - if you're going in now, probably wise to get the 2-pack team pack with a friend to join in, as long as you can continually join in consistently.

Who's That Indie? Is a Blind First Impression's series made of indie based and indie developed games. Today's indie game is Wyv And Keep, created by A Jplly Corpse. It is a puzzle platformer with emphasis on the puzzle. Guide two rookie treasure hunters on their quest to claim the legendary lost idol, using quick wits and teamwork to conquer 6 fiendishly puzzling worlds. Dodge deadly traps and angry pygmies as you puzzle your way toward hordes of ancient treasure.
I found this game very fun and quite simpleto pick up and play, if you want a deeper review please check my first impressions video

There is a certain satisfaction in dropping a weighted crate into perfect position to solve a puzzle. It is a basic notion, pioneered long before Wyv and Keep's existence and an idea that will persist long after. It's only fitting that, in a puzzle game as efficiently simple as Wyv and Keep presents it's challenge often in obfuscation usually reserved for more complicated physics puzzles. In addition from the charm of its beautiful spritework, the witty back and forth of the game's playable duo and the awesome sound track, the game accomplishes great challenge that is easy to pick up and enjoy thanks to effective use of its puzzle design that -while a  perfectly awesome single player experience- can be enjoyed by two players on the same computer as well as online. Wyv and Keep: The Temple of the Lost Idol is a fun, comical, co-op, puzzle platformer game. Each puzzle takes place on a single screen and has a kind of Sokoban-style gameplay. If you play in single player mode, you switch between each characters. If you play with a friend either player controls a character. The price might be a little high at the current $15 for the depth of the game play, but there is a lot of content here if you enjoy the puzzles.
I played with a friend, so my experience with this game is from that point of view. I have not tried single player. The game consists of moving around crates to reach new areas, activate buttons, block traps, and eventually open up the exit which both characters must reach. New obstacles are added in each set of levels, such as arrow traps, spikes, enemies, and lava. In addition, there are new objects to play with such as dynamite and crates hanging from ropes that must be cut down. Without giving away any spoilers, if you make it to the end of the game you are in for the quite the surprise, or at least it was for my friend and me.
The platforming part of this puzzler comes in a lot in the later stages. Once you have figured out where the crates need to be moved around in a particular level, there is still a lot of timing and precise jumping involved.
All in all, I think anyone who is a fan of this genre will enjoy this game, even more so if you have a friend to play it with.

Ladders and cliffs are my main negative notes, getting into base can be tedious and mean death depending if it's nighttime (as I found out when a shark attacked me with very little health b/c of hunger) and I very nearly ragequitted at having to swim back up cliffs. After an hour of exploring depths of the ocean around my base it's safe to say that this indeed worth the $14.99 asking price. The randomly generated map is littered with all kinds of treasures and resources to find, from ship wrecks to veins of gold sticking out of the rock, all of which show up clearly on the minimap.
Crafting, in my honest opinion, is a little too simple. Within 10 minutes I had all the crafting stations set up in my tiny starter base, and had already started equipping the next tier of diving gear that allowed me to reach the darker depths of the sea. But thankfully, exploration is limited by the amount of air left for you to breath. While this can be upgraded along with how far below the ocean you can travel and the amount of damage you can resist, the time limit means you need to be careful you don't wander too far from your base. Thankfully additional bases can be build, if you can find the appropriate materials.
So far I've only had two issues. The first being that I can't figure out why I can't use bandages. I'd select them in my inventory, click use and nothing will happen. Both inside and outside of my base. The second issue, though I doubt this will be a common problem, was that a shark somehow managed to attack me inside my base while I was doing some quick crafting. Other than that the game runs smoothly on the highest settings without any graphical lag or screen tearing.
My only criticism is that there appears to be a lack of things to craft. Outside of weapons, diving gear and additional building parts, the only craftable furniture are tables and stools. I would love to fill my base with more than just crafting stations, storage chests and plant pots.

The stuff that needs to be covered:
The controls are good (obviously), it's point and click.
The visuals are pretty, easy on the eyes. I like the theme. The "roll" box looks a tad out of place as just a green box, perhaps a little bit of style on that and the dice, but not a complaint just a suggestion.
The music is good, decent variety.
The game itself:
I'd never heard of this boardgame but it looked pretty fun, so I got this. The "how to play" tells you what you need to know; how to move, what does what, how to win (or lose :P), and it all became clear after a game or two.
Pass and play works fine, haven't tried online multiplayer but I suspect there's a small community at the moment (whatever could tell you that, oh single english review?)
The AI is, from what I can tell, good. I played against the easy AI and lost twice then started beating it and noticing where it could've done better moves and moved on up the chain. You pick this game up pretty quick. I like the probabilistic element, some may not; the dice can screw you or give you the win, you have to play risk management but that's any dice game.
I still, however, despite the dice felt ultimately skill is in control of how the game plays out. A few times I completely missed a really good move. As they say, easy to learn, hard to master.
It doesn't take too long to play a game, certainly well under half an hour.
If you're a fan of different sorts of boardgames, I'd go ahead and give this a shot. It's a tad like backgammon, but it's got a better theme and has more elements to the gameplay, not as dice-dependent. The dragon theme is nice although I personally would make the dice and some of the other elements fit said theme a tad (the board itself and pieces all have an excellent easy on the eyes look though), the visuals feel ever so mildly miicrosoft ships-with-windows-y, but it is early access after all and I would rather they improve the AI (not that it needs it from what I can tell, but the AI can *always* be improved) or something than a silly little thing like that.
Oh one suggestion would be to add a way to undo what you did with your first dice or undo your move or something, I frequently made a rash decision with my first dice and then saw a much better move. I could, alternatively, just learn to take my time so perhaps I shouldn't have that button :P
So yeah, go ahead and try it out. If the only (ever so mild) complaint I have is a knitpicky one about some visuals, that's a good thing. A fun boardgame to add to my list to pass and play with friends for something different or relax with for an hour or so.

The game would be great if it would let you actually play.
Many say that this game is too complicated. It is not. It is just deep. True, learning the game is a pain. Period. But it does not take that much time to get into it, 3-4 hours and you should be good with most mechanics.
So, is it fun? Yes. It is a challenge and the way the mechanics work, the results of actions make sense. E.g. what you expect to happen in certain situations, like storming a city or attacking across a river or encircling an enemy unit, will give you the results you expect. It is a good "military" simulator rather than a tic-tac-toe puzzle system a la panzer general.
HOWEVER:
The larger the game gets (the bigger the scenario and the further in you get), the longer the time the computer takes to calculate its turn. This is because the AI calculates what it wants to do. In the small scenarios, this is basically irrelevant. But I have been playing the big campaign on the soviet side and am now on turn 58.
It takes the computer 45 minutes to calculate its turn!!!! I'm sorry, but what?!
I would really have liked to finish the campaign (standing at mid-1942 at this point) but I am not going to wait for 45 mins for one turn (= 1 in-game week) to pass. This is even more frustrating as, as a Soviet, I'm not doing much in my own turn at this time in the war. So I'm busy for 3-5 minutes and then wait for almost an hour.
If you really want to play the Great Patriotic War, I would suggest War In The East 1. It's an old DOS game that will give you eye cancer and has very odd controls but once you get used to it, it will at least let you finish the game.
Edit: To address arguments that my computer is just too old: I have an i7-5500 CPU with 2,4 GHz and 12GB RAM. If that is not good enough for a hex-based counter game that is on the technological level of 1998, I'd be surprised.

This is a good game, I suppose. The times I take the time to actually play it I do find it enjoyable, and it's challenging in a fun way to try to do better each time I play the incrementally larger scenarios, and the depth, while I feel it's ridiculously overdone, can be cool, too. You don't have to tinker with which divisions get the best commanders or priority for that howitzer battalion, which I really appreciate, but you can spend time on this to give yourself an extra edge should you want to.
It's just a pity the game is so ridiculously micro-intensive. Building rails consists of moving rail units one hex, giving it the relevant order, moving it the next hex, and so on. Every single turn. You can't tell a unit to move to a distant hex over several turns. You can't select units in several hexes and tell them to move towards a single hex, you have to select them one by one.
Someone please correct me if I'm wrong on any of these, but I really wish quality of life improvements were prioritised in future patches.

A textbook example of why arcade games need a win condition or some sort of end point, even when the point is just surviving for as long as possible and beating your last high score. Because without this, one of two things will inevitably happen:
A: If the difficulty of the game is constantly becoming higher through an algorithm rather than for example a large number of hand-crafted enemy waves cycling through harder and harder variants then it will eventually lead to the game becoming literally unsurvivable. For example, imagine a version of Tetris where the downward speed of the tetrominoes eventually reaches a point where it is impossible to reach the edges of the screen before the tetrominoes reach the bottom of the screen.
B: If the game DOES use hand-crafted enemy waves or, say, maybe the algorithm just stops working after a while then we're gonna find ourselves in a game where the difficulty just stops going up after a while. This is what most older versions of Tetris do, meaning the score can easily be counterstopped when then player has reached a certain skill level. (but any later iteration of tetris except TGM is going to be significantly worse for other reasons, even if that got fixed.)
Now, I can SORT OF live with outcome A here. Inevitably dying does become a climax of sorts, even if it means all players of a high enough skill level have almost identical scores. It's obviously not elegant and more often than not reaching this point will take a really long time and that's probably gonna get really boring, but eh.
Outcome B, however? Yeah, we're gonna have a problem, you and I.
Next to "Every Extend Extra Extreme", "Titan Attacks!" is the most extreme example of this problem in, like, any videogame  that is sold for money. That I know of, obviously.
That playtime of around 3 hours? The vast majority of it is my second and final game. The difficulty plateaus almost IMMEDIATELY, leaving only extreme boredom and the existential dread of slowly realizing that the only way out of this madness is deliberately killing yourself just to end it all. Seriously guys, this is NOT fun and i'm almost convinced that people who have reached the kill screen of Donkey Kong or Pac-Man have actual mental illnesses. At that point those games have
been squeezed of all challenge and enjoyement. Congratulations, you have completely and utterly mastered the game. Now for the love of god,
What's special about "Titan Attacks!" is that this special realm of suffering usually reserved for people who cannot let go of their favourite games long after they have completely
them becomes instantly accessible to basically everyone. In a way, it made me understand those people far more than "King of Kong" could ever hope to. This is not a recommendation of any kind, by the way. Explaining it with words is sufficient and doesn't make you feel like a part of you has died, so that's what i'm gonna do now. It's kind of a miniature version of the psychological process MMORPG developers exploit to make their players keep playing and paying their monthly subscription. It was actually kind of hard to stop playing, knowing that my score and progress would vanish the second I stopped playing. It was that same sense of "
" with a second, suppressed voice crying "
"
So there I found myself, spending three freaking hours mindlessly making the numbers go up in a game that makes you feel actual suffering. I got this game for free but it feels more accurate to say that I was
to it. Moral of the story? Don't play this game and more importantly, don't make a game that can be likened to it.
Seriously. You don't even make subscription money from it.

Wyv and Keep is a great puzzle platformer with a few twists. It's important to note that this might look a bit like games such as Spelunky. While the theme is similar, the gameplay isn't. Basically you control the two treasure hunters - either alone or in coop with a friend. You'll have to avoid enemies and traps rather than fighting or destroying them.
The goal sounds simple: Reach the exit door. However, it's typically not that easy. You'll have to avoid pits, traps, and enemies, while also triggering buttons, moving boxes, etc. Some things can only be solved involving team work. For example, one character might have to fill a gap in the ground, while the other pushes a box over. On another map a wall might be too high, so you'll have to move a box, jump on it, and then use your friend as a stepping stone.
I've been playing this game since its initial Desura release and it can be lots and lots of fun. The game's pixel art is well made and tries to emulate late 16 bit era games (i.e. Super Nintendo and other 2D consoles). Some parts of the game are higher resolution though. If you're not a fan of pixelated game and prefer HD graphics, better skip this game.
The game offers replayability through challenges: Beat a level as fast as possible, beat it with as few retries as possible, and try to collect as much money as you can. Also, the old Desura release had its own level editor. Accordin to the devs (see comments under this review) the editor will return once Steamworks integration is working/complete.

and ive got to say,its pretty darn good,and might be better than certain harvest moon games,but thats up for debate
im just gonna list the differences between this and harvest moon
1:you can't feed your animals like you normally do:unlike harvest moon,when you start off with a dog,you NEED to feed it dog food,not just random fruit or failed dishes (remember those days,HM fans?)and a cat needs to eat fish,and barn animals need to eat their respected feeds,you cant just leave your chickens,horses and cows outside like you normally do,i learned that the hard way
2:recipes are needed for cooking:you need to either watch the weekly cooking show or buy the recipes from the seasonal markets,its not one of those trial and error cooking times.plus the cooking appliances may take time to get and the ingrediant list for cooking can be overwhelming for the typical HM fan
3.smaller farms:well,until they patched it,but its still small compared to other farms in the harvest moon franchise,its somewhat close to HM:return to the homeland or HM:hero of the leaf valley
4:you can gather wild substances from trees and plants:these are mostly for making drinks and energy giving *healing items*,but somehow,you can mix plain water from a well and coconut milk to make fresh milk thats almost exactly resembles that from a cow.....game logic,nuff said.that aside,most HM fans will think of this as HM's cooking portion of the game
5:clothes can be mixed and matched and some give bonuses:this is a nicely added feature,you can make your character look different from other poeples,which is nice.while most of the clothes dont give a bonus,some will.plus you can wear a cloak,who doesnt want a cloak?
6.a bunch of minigames that actually rewards you for playing:you even get a energy boost fruit from doing one of them

9:everything is simpler:things like fishing,farming,mining and events are way more simple and easy,this could either be a good thing or a bad thing,but mostly a good thing for me

This game for what I have played in the many hours, is a really good game. It is good because of all the activities you can do on it. If you want to work on the storyline, go right ahead. If you want to work on getting rich, go right ahead. If you want to work on leveling, go right that way. If you want to work on side quests or guild quests, you can do that too! Even just those few things I listed there are still many more things to do. You can go dungeoning in the many many dungeons the game has to offer, you can go into houses and steal items to sell or keep if you don't get caught, you can work on spells so you have a very high chance of being able to cast it, and you can train yourself in the many different types of weapon styles in dungeons or outside of them. There are many things to do in the game which I have not yet listed, but I still know just trying to finish the whole game will take many many hours. The game might not have the best kind of graphics for someone who wants to play very nice clear stuff, but it works well with computers that can't handle too much gaming.

This was the first game in The Elder Scrolls (TES) series that I played back when this game is new. There are major differences between Morrowind and the newer entries in the series. While as I love this game, I want to highlight the differences for people deciding whether or not they want to buy this game.
First of all, since this is an older game by today's sandards, the graphics, controls, and several other elements will look and feel dated. The character customization is nothing compared to newer TES games. The combat is not as fluid as newer TES games. The NPC characters do not interact with each other and the environment as much as the newer TES games, however; I still think the depth of the story line is greater in this game than the newer TES games. There is a lot to explore in this game. The game offers many impactful choices for the player. The game's main plot feels more non-linear than the newer entries in the series, however; it may be harder to find your way around because this game does not let you just instant travel anywhere you desire.
All in all, if you can get past the dated look and feel, this game is a lot of fun.

Some people might toss around the words 'Left 4 Dead clone' when describing this game. While that might be accurate in the sense that it is a four-player co-op that has you beating back hordes of ravenous enemies, this 'clone' has far exceeded the predecessor in a genre that has yet to be overdone. Where ranged weapons were the focus in L4D, with melee being more of an afterthought, that has been reversed when it comes to Vermintide. Dodging, blocking, power hits and melee combos all give much-needed depth to close quarters combat in a way that is absolutely satisfying. Even people not knowledgeable about the Warhammer franchise could still enjoy the feeding of wading through a tide of rats at the side of a friend. I cannot recommend this game enough, and I'm eagerly awaiting it's recently-announced sequel.

I don't really write reviews often so I will try and explain the game as best as I can with a personal yay or nay on whether or not I liked the game.
Short version - like left4dead but there are enough differences to make it it's own unique game and even different from left4dead.  For example, to name a few differences, instead of guns you use melee weapons like swords, axes, ect, instead of zombies there are giant rats and each character has a slightly unique playstyle and weapon kit instead of everybody running around with the same exact weapon.
Longer version - so this is an action horde co-op. This is based off in the Warhammer fantasy universe (before the Age of Sigmar if you are lore familiar). You and 3 others work together to either get from point A to point B or to accomplish a certain task all while fighting off a horde of man sized rats and other special rats.  You get to pick one out of five unique characters and only one person can play one particular character.  All the characters are fairly unique in their own way, not only in the type of weapons they carry but the type of roles that they can fill.  Even though all of the characters are damage dealers some (the dwarf and the human) can be a bit more tanky when carrying a shield around, while others (the elf and the witch hunter) can be more speed oriented in their attack vs heavy hitters, while the wizard can choose a more group based damage or target focused based.  Although some weapons overlap between characters, they each have a varied enough assortment that you will have a a different play style for each one.  About the weapons, you always carry two weapons, a melee one and a ranged one.  Even though you have that choice you will most likely be up close in melee combat for most of the game, there are only 2 characters (the elf and the wizard) who could get away with using ranged weapons most of the time, but even then there will be times where you will have to beat some faces in.  There is also a weapon crafting/collecting system in place.  Due to the variety in weapons you get to "roll" for a weapon at the end of each level.  The amount of symbols you get on the dice corralates the rarity of the weapon.  The difficulty of the level also affects the cap on weapon rarity and certain in game items can help improve your chances of getting the symbols on your dice.  Now since you are bound to get duplicates, this is where the crafting system comes in.  You break down weapons for simple ores (ore color reflect the rarity) which you can then use to attempt to get another weapon of the same rarity.  You can also use them to improve your weapons and change different stats on your weapons.  In regards of the levels, the base game can be fairly short, but the levels are varied enough that they have some replayability value.  They aren't just get from point A to point B, there are some defense levels, collection levels and sometimes a combination of multiple modes.  You can also increase the challange of each level beyond the difficulty.  There are some items, which are also used for the weapon drop at the end of the level, that you have to carry to the end of the level in order to reap the rewards.  They take up a usable item slot and can also affect your health making it more challanging to get to the end.
So overall the game is pretty fun, especially if you liked other horde based games.  The variety of characters and weapons allows you to play with different combat styles, even if you play with the same character repeatedly.  Even though there might be "optimal" loadouts for the different characters, you aren't penalized for trying out other loadouts.  The levels are rich in design and varied enough that you won't get particularly bored and will challange you in accomplishing the different tasks you encounter.  And due to the fact that they added daily and weekly quests to accomplish (for example, kill a certain unit, finish a certain level, or collect certain items), it adds even more to the replayabilty value of the game.

A fun game where  you stealthily off other shipmates while on a pleasant cruise.
Obviously, the game is more fun with friends, but it's fun with or without them. Unfortunately, the main server browser in the game seems to be faulty, so you have to use the Steam Server Browser in order to find any servers to play on.
The Ship is a game about how a relaxing cruise goes wrong when Mr. X, the man in charge, decides to start a deathmatch between everyone on the ship excluding staff. Whether your weapon of choice is a blunderbuss, a katana, or an umbrella, there's a reward in it for you: cash. Cash you can use to win the game or purchase items to keep yourself fashionable or comfortable.
Speaking of which, there's a bit of a downside to all this murder. While you're taking care of shipmates, you need to take care of yourself. You have needs. You need to be entertained, social, well fed, clean, and more. These needs can be met in a variety of ways on the go, for free, or by paying a service. However, these needs can sometimes serve as vulnerabilities. Sometimes when you sleep, you might not wake up. Just as well, if you don't take care of yourself, you might wind up falling asleep wherever you are, or disintegrating on the spot.
Although it is a deathmatch between your friends on the cruise, make sure to enjoy yourself as well, but always keep an eye open, as someone might be watching.

I picked up the Ultrabundle for $3 or so, definitely a good deal even though I already owned Revenge of the Titans. However, I wouldn't recommend this game (or the bundle) at normal price.
Titan Attacks is quite enjoyable. I played through the first 2 worlds a few times, learning the game and practicing, usually getting destroyed on a few key levels. However, by a few hours in, I broke free. See, the difficulty curve is ramped in the early waves, while you are still building upgrades and gaining power. The game seems to break a bit once you hit Mars, when you usually get maxed add-ons and bullets. After that, what was once a strategic shooter with 1 bullet on screen becomes a spammy hellzone. Waves last a few seconds, cash becomes trivial, even bosses and damage cease to inspire tension. By my 5th new game or so, I could beat the game almost twice. There is no ending, just immediate New Game+ and scaling enemies.
It didn't make me feel like a pro, it made me feel like the game was incomplete. 100 simple levels, menu music that loops after 5 seconds, and so much potential.
It's not all bad. The gameplay and shooting is pretty solid, sounds and music are good, and the visuals are solid if a bit murky in some dark red areas. For $3 or so, a solid experience.
Compared to Revenge (even though I HATED that game) this game feels very simple and short, beatable in an hour or less. Once I finish all the achievements, I probably won't mess with the game much. I'd prefer if the game had more strategy developed in the later levels, nothing really changes. The only real source of difficulty is avoiding a screen full of tiny bullets while enemies just gain HP as the waves go on, slowing the game down without adding any challenge beyond "Fire more". It started great, became decent, and ended with a bigger version of the same boss. I guess it's fair, sometimes it's nice to be able to beat a game and move onto something else. Just watch for a great sale. Now to work on Ultratron and Droid Assault...

This game is currently the ultimate computer game available on the topic of the 1941-45 War In The East between Germany and Russia.  It is a typical "Grognard" game in the style of Gary Grigsby's previous War In The Pacific:AE game.  If you liked that, you will like this more since it is more manageable.  This game has received continuing patch support since it was published. I have been playing it since 2013 and can attest to the fact that it has been truly polished and improved over time and is stable, reasonably balanced, loaded with optional "tweaking" adjustments you can tune to taste, and well worth the time that is involved in playing a monster of this depth (which reaches down to the brigade level !)
If you are interested in WW2 history of the "War In The East", you can't go wrong with this game.

Fantastic game for those who have time and patient to learn it.
If you want a strategy game that covers an entire front during WW2; this is the game!
The number of units and the size of the map can be daunting for a new player. BUT as an experienced strategy gamer I did not find GG War in the East harder to learn than for example Hearts of Iron 2/3/4. This is a combat focused game on a strategic level. The production and economy in the game is much simplified. The AI is better than i most other turn based games (looking at you civilization and Total War).
The majority of the game time goes to moving your hundreds of units around. Expect 100+ hours for a full campaign. So the biggest downside with this game is that it takes considerable time. On the other hand my favourite game The Witcher 3 also took me 100+ hours.
The price is high compared to other games and this is not even a new game. So grab it on a sale and I strongly recommend buying the expansions for some really good designed, new player friendly scenarios.

I can't quite put my finger on what it is about this itteration that has me so enthralled, but I am.
Many years ago, to a much younger me, Metal Slug was a slightly scary, overly violent game at an arcade. By the time I grew up a little and got around to playing it I disliked how easily it ate quarters and lost interest within minutes. Many years later a friend gave me a MAME emulator which included Metal Slug. Unforunately with emulation removing any monetary restrictions, and therefor challenge, I lost interest again within only a handflull of attempts.
Then comes a Steam sale last June I decided to give Metal Slug another shot. After all, despite my only short interactions with it, there is a certain nostalgic value. A value I'm willing to indudlge if the entrance fee is only $2.71CAD.
I played around for a bit and discovered a global high-score board, not normally my cup of tea but this time I was enticed. A game built on itteration, designed for short periods of play, suits a high-score board well. This also fits into my life easily. I don't need to dedicate long periods of time in order to have fun or feel like I'm really accomplishing anything. Combine that with the need for a steady flow of quarters removed and I'm even willing to try, try again.
The game is designed well and introduces new weapons, mechanics and enemies fluidly and in a way that neither breaks up the speed of play or is too jarring. Admitely the time between introduction of new things and the need to overcome a challenge using that new information is rather short but I feel like this is all part of the action-packed nature of the game. Even if it takes a death for you to get it, you get it pretty quick.
Visually I love the game. After growing beyond my adolecent fear of the violence I can really admire the hand-drawn animated sprites and backgrounds. Maybe it's the nostalgic nature of it, but I really do think it's still a good looking game.
As well I find the design and themes of the game entertaning in and of themselves. While routed in a very generalized World War II theme it quickly and freely removes itself from that in entertaining ways. While I'm more interested in trying to perfect my runs of the first few levels I watched a friend of mine beat the campaign for the first time witnessing stranger and more outlandish things than I ever thought the arcade game contained.
Why are there ice-breathing yettis in this cave? Why am I driving an elephant with guns on it? What's going on!? Often the answer is to just shoot all the things.
Overall I just really enjoy playing it. The action is quick and challenging. It punishes misteps but lets you get back to where you were quickly. Everything is presented in a very straight forward way with fun little secrets scattered here and there to keep it interesting for multiple play throughs even if you're not going to go for the high scores.
If you're in it for the "story" you're better off spending your money somewhere else unless the game is on sale. But if you think you could get a few hours of fun out of an old arcade game I can see this being worth the, current, $8CAD.

This was the first game in The Elder Scrolls (TES) series that I played back when this game is new. There are major differences between Morrowind and the newer entries in the series. While as I love this game, I want to highlight the differences for people deciding whether or not they want to buy this game.
First of all, since this is an older game by today's sandards, the graphics, controls, and several other elements will look and feel dated. The character customization is nothing compared to newer TES games. The combat is not as fluid as newer TES games. The NPC characters do not interact with each other and the environment as much as the newer TES games, however; I still think the depth of the story line is greater in this game than the newer TES games. There is a lot to explore in this game. The game offers many impactful choices for the player. The game's main plot feels more non-linear than the newer entries in the series, however; it may be harder to find your way around because this game does not let you just instant travel anywhere you desire.
All in all, if you can get past the dated look and feel, this game is a lot of fun.

First, I admit that I completely love this game and can be really biassed in some aspects. I never before had played any games of this kind, since I don't really like farming or any other management games, but this one called out to me with its relationship building system and a small friendly village with cute art style and very nice atmosphere.

'kay, I said my word and I just want to recommend this game for those who loves stories and characters more than gameplay. Have a nice day!

I really want to love Motorsport Manager. With mods, it's fun. However, it focuses almost solely on race management rather than team management. Sure, you can expand your base, but the staff you hire is limited to the drivers, a chief designer and two race engineers - and no matter how good your staff is, you absolutely and categorically cannot make a big step forward from one year to another in outright pace, because your best parts get carried over from the previous season, and the chassis don't seem to matter.
As is befitting of a niche game anno 2017, it does come with a bunch of features that remind you of freemium games, such as the design process for next year's car. Instead of having the chief designer do his thing with a set budget and whatever manpower you can hand spare him, you choose suppliers of parts, which then affect the chassis performance. Going for the best engines and expect your car to have more power than the previous season? No way. Engines only affect fuel efficiency and chassis improvability - the ability to improve your car with new parts the upcoming season. The only thing missing here really is microtransactions to further increase the base stat.
With Sega publishing it, I was kind of hoping for some Sports Interactive knowhow to somehow be funneled into the process - like Football Manager and Eastside Hockey Manager - games where you can spend tens of hours fiddling with your staff and tactics, and then spend tens more going through statistics for the last 10 seasons just because it's fun. Motorsport Manager lacks all of that. It's extremely superficial, and basically only does the racing simulation part well. Even this leaves you dumbfounded at times when the opposition deploys all of its battery power, which somehow magically results in a laptime 3-4 seconds quicker than anything else out there at the time.
When it comes to team and asset management, it's severely outdone by the 1999 Microprose management game Grand Prix World - a game where an engine has ten parameters, not *one* overall stat - and you negotiate deals with fuel suppliers, said engine suppliers and tyre suppliers (because that was back in the days of good tyres in F1). Sponsorship deals were difficult to come by, they didn't come to you, like they do in Motorsport Manager. Hell, you even managed hospitality for the sponsors at each race in GPW. It's even got a modding scene releasing new season packs every now and then. And pay drivers. As if Marcus Ericsson would get paid to drive anywhere in real life (he does in Motorsport Manager.)
In conclusion - it's not a game I'd recommend, since it's lacking the depth not only of SI management games, but it can't even hold a candle to Grand Prix World which is due to celebrate its 20th anniversary in the near future. Motorsport Manager isn't bad, it's just not that great - personally I'd like the proportion of team to race management to be inverse.

Dont get me wrong; if you want to play a Race-Manager this Game might be for you. I had around 60 hrs of Ups (and Downs) with it. Building up your Car, Team, Buildings, Drivers etc. can be a blast. Graphics are okay, the Sounddesign is very good.
When you come from lets say a Football-Manager and are looking for a different Discipline, then you are golden with this Game. The Managementpart is superb!
But i come from the SimRacingside. If you think you can transfer your knowledge of Racing to this Game, be ready to be frustrated. Numberwise all the Things happening on Track might make Sense. But from a Drivers Point of View it feels like pure Luck or Misfortune (emphasis on "feels"!).
The thing that kills it for me is the Driver-communication.
Example: Safetycar comes out; i needed Fuel and the Tires were worn so i Pitstopped. In the exact Moment the Driver is leaving the Pit he (or she) always -repeat- aaalwaaays tells me that the Safetycar is out (eeehm - thank you) and asks if he (or she) should take a Pitstop... while leaving the Pit with fresh Tires and a full Tank...
Another example is Weatherstrategy: again i need Fuel and Tires, go to the Pits and look at the Weatherforecast. I see that in the next Round it will start to Rain and it wont stop for at least for a couple of Rounds. So obviously (from the SimRacer-perspective) i choose Intermediates (or the Wet-Tires).
Back on Track the Driver always complains about the wrong Tires. Yes they are wrong - but only for 0,5 Laps.
Driving these Tires for half a lap in not optimal condtions slows you down much more in most of the cases then taking an additional Pitstop.
As i said: the Numbers calculated in background might make a mathematical Sense. But this is not how its working in Real- or Sim-Life. An unecessary Pitstop would cost waaay more Time.
TLDR: If you are a Mangerplayer and like Motorsports - buy it. If you are a SimRacer looking for a different Racingexperience - stay away. I am a Sim Racer so i cant recommend it - sadly.

Many people are angry at Jagex for the final version of Ace of Spades. However, what not many people understand is Jagex   had a reason in changing the game from the first version. Although very popular, the first version did not receive good reviews. Critics such as MetaCritic gave the game a 49, so Jagex came in to change that. If their game did not exceed sales, they would have been done for. Jagex tried to come up with something new. In the old versions, everyone had the same weapons and role. Jagex added four new classes to mix things up. Now everyone has a different role that will ensure a different experience and cooperative gameplay. The situation is almost like CoD and Battlefield. Everyone in CoD just chooses a loadout and does the same thing: attack the enemy. There is no versatility. However in Battlefield, players can choose from four classes that support the team and create hella fun. CoD is more popular, but Battlefield is more intriguing and exciting, thus people fail to understand Jagex's version of Ace of Spades.

My Goodness this is a complex, complex game. If you are interested in military history and want to know what really happened on the Russian front in World War Two, then buy this game.
And then weep as your puny human brain is unable to comprehend the sheer complexity of reality as it is brilliantly simulated in praiseworthy detail by the genius who made this game. Cry as you realise you don't know the first thing about operational art, organising corps, armies or army groups, and that far from being like Gary Kasparov and thinking 50 moves ahead, you can barely comprehend the next turn or two.
Fear the Russian Winter. Fear the Russian reserves. Fear the total strategic paralysis of invading Russia and realising you bit off waaaay more than you can chew.
Then be thankful you live in an age where a game like this is available. Truly, if there is a more complex, realistic and delightfully frightful simulation of one of the most awful conflicts in human history, I have never seen it. The detail is staggering, it will push you to a whole new level.

I really wanted to give this game a positive rating, but I cannot.
I write this for potential buyers, who, like me are taken aback by the very steep price.
I watched this game for over a year, and in most sales it is 50% off, but never cheaper. And since it is an old game it will probably stay that way.
This is a very serious WW2 simulator, and in the hex based/counter genre the most encompassing game I have played. All units and leaders are historically accurate (as far as I can tell, and I know a thing or two about WW2), and units come with very detailed information and historical photographs.
It is not a dynamic, or graphically appealing game, all fighting is autoresolved, so it is mostly a game of strategic planning, concentrating your troops and building up fronts.
The AI is pretty decent, for example: It detects attempts to encircle and tries to avoid that. But since the German units start off way better (really rather overpowered, as their historical edge lay at least half in communication, coordination, speed and organisation, things that cannot easily be programmed, so to simulate the advantage of the Germans, their troops are very strong compared to Soviet troops), and since the unit values favors defense greatly for both sides, the Soviet Ai hardly ever attacks and is overall rather passive. Basically the AI only attacks where it has calculated that the odds favor them, and if you keep your units stacked and tidy, that is almost never (except the first winter (special rules)).
Nothing really different from most hex/counter based games, just very broad in scope and very detalied in information. It could have been a very enjoyable game.
But.
The AI takes ages to calculate and complete it's turn. In the first few years this is bearable. But I arrived at turn 160 in late '44, and it takes the AI 15-30 minutes complete one turn, often with the only real action being bombing runs (of which there are no less than 100+, each with an autoresolve report, but that is only a fraction of the time). That truelly kills all immersion and gameplay, and really makes this a waiting game, a complete grind. Finishing off 20 partisan units every turn by moving a unit next to it does also not contribute to a vivid experience. (my PC was high end for the time the game came out: quad core i7 3,4, graphic card doesn't matter in this game, but was also high end)
I cannot imagine how you dare to sell a game for this amount of money, that is so severely testing your patience. All my 180+ hours played are from 3/4 of ONE playthrough by one side (admittedly I took much time learning and exploring the game, checking leaders, moving attachments around etc.).
So, if you wonder if you should buy this, buy it only if you have a LOT (and I mean a LOT) of patience and are a die hard WW2 strategic fan, and then only if it is on sale.
Rather sad, because if you are into realistic strategic WW2 games, this is a great game at it's core.

Ever get that random question from an unwashed stranger:  "If you had one, okay, two computer games to take with you to a deserted island, what would they be?"  Now my first response would be:  "Where am I supposed to plug it in ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥?"  But if I humored this nosy lunatic I'd say unquestionably, "Anything by Graviteam Tactics, and Gary Grigsby's War in the (muthafunkin) East."
Here's why folks:  Graviteam Tactics puts out great tactical war stuff but this isn't their review page so forget that for now.  GG's WitE is the quintessential best, end all, beat all, WW2, Eastern Front, computerized operational level simulator ever on the planet.  That's right, I said it.  You can take that Hearts of Iron 4, pants-tightening chub and go sell it and that game to the tourists, skeezix, cuz this right here is what it's all about.  This is the cat's♥♥♥♥♥of Eastern Front, grognard wargamming.  Not sayin' HOI4 doesn't have it's place, but if you're the kinda dude (let's face it, absolutely zero women probably give a rat's hind end about the East Front and if there's one out there, well that's just one more female I've infuriated in my existence) that read "When Titans Clash" or "Enemy at the Gates" back in the day and it wasn't a college assignment , then this, my friend is for YOU.
Yeah, it's a hefty $80 pricetag, but if someone sold you a $20, Christmas Sale Lincoln Navigator, I doubt that SOB would make it off the lot, and there'd probably be a dead hooker buried in the back that you'd have to explain to the cops as well.  WitE will indeed make it off the lot, purring like a V-8 hemi Charger, with zero dead hookers in the trunk.
Why is it so great you ask?  Well, I'll lay it on you like Dolemite.  This monster encompasses the entire WW2 adventure from Germany's Barbarossa "What's the worst that could happen?" heyday to angry, vodka soaked Russkies rolling all up into Adolf's backyard like drunken soccer hooligans to camp out for the next 40 some-odd years at ye olde Reichstag. Unless of course, you're savvy enough to alter history with your mad, wargaming skills and turn Moscow into a Teutonic holiday retreat.  Good luck with all that, because it ain't gonna be easy, Herr Schlecte-Ahnung.
As the Soviets, you're going to get your cossack handed to you in '41.  But like the real deal, your job is to minimize losses, sacrifice units, dodge Commrade Stalin's temper tantrums, make the Krauts pay for every inch of ground, and stop their encirclement shenanigans long enough until mud and winter roll into town.  Those ladies never disappoint.  You'll suffer too, make no mistake, but not as much as Winter-Fritz in '41 who failed to show up in cold weather gear enough to survive a Wisconsin Indian Summer.
I'm mainly talking about the Grand Campaign here, which is the real reason anybody walks the path to WitE.  Sure, you can play some limited scenarios if you want to.  Be sure and help yourself to some Shirley Temple's over there in the pink cooler while your at it, Sally.  Come join the Mensch when you feel up to it, but don't hurt yourself.
This game is unparalleled in it's handling of minute details that you may or may not ever bother to look at.  But you will.  Eventually, we all look.  And half your game memories will consist of, "Yeah, the city was taken...but good Lord we lost a lotta guys doing it."  And, like the real war, you'll wind up writing off numbers of dead due to the sheer complexity of the titanic struggle.
Everything, and I mean EVERYTHING is factored into this Goliath.  Weather, leaders (which you can change in and out with realistic limitations, or y'know, just have shot), supply, unit cohesion, the f'ing railroads and grade change once you get into real Russia, seaports (as Krauts I still can't take stinking Sevastopol due to their sea supply), air cover, air missions, updated gear and how long it takes to actually become available, scorched earth policies, pulling armor and transport out of units just to save on gas, fortifications, Western Front influences (this was a big one for me and is mirrored appropriately), partisans being a pain disrupting supply, SS units, Guards units, Police units (you can steamroll the town but unless military cops are there to hold it, it'll turn into Detroit sans Robocop).  Sickness and normal attrition play a role as well.  Hell, there's probably a graph chart depicting Pvt. Wiener Humpelstein's syphillis advancement and it's effect on his komrades but I just haven't found it yet.
There you go folks, there's my review.  Is it difficult to learn?  A bit, unless you apply yourself with the same gumption you gave towards getting ol' Heather McScrumpalot's bra off in the rear seat of your hand-me-down '78 Plymouth Duster back in high school.  And, not unlike then, you may hafta even take notes before diving in.
Good Wargaming, y'all, and wear a cup on this one.

There are lots of stupid little bugs that make the game fun (grenades sending bodies to space, spontaneously combusting bicycles when going over jumps, epic drifts and fishtails with the sometimes wonky driving physics), but also a few bugs that make the game frustrating (Bodies sometimes stay standing in a combat pose which could get you killed if you don't check to see if it's actually a live person or not, the clunky prone system, keys pressed while typing into chat becoming stickied "on" until you press them again).
Best part? Absolutely nothing is locked behind a permanent paywall anymore, as it used to be. "War Bonds" can actually generate free cash based on an initial investment, if you have the patience to invest some money to get increased return 6 months in the future. Also, the little 4-gold first win of the day bonuses do stack up over a lot of gametime, allowing you to occasionally purchase small stuff without ingame credits or needing to break out the CC.
Given the fact that the devs are still putting in some great work to this game, I'd say it's definitely worth a look.
EDIT: After 1300+ hours of in-game time (the steam timer lies, since the Steam timer keeps running even if you aren't in a match -- I.E. changing your loadout, managing assault teams on the war map, etc), I can say that this game is definitely a solid FPS for those who enjoy WW2-flavored shooters. Certainly more realistic than COD:WW2, it aims toward people who want a cross between the expansive maps and mixed infantry/vehicle combat of Battlefield 1943 without the run-and-gun tendencies of said games. Skilled squadrons dominate the battlefield, so teaming up with someone in voice chat (which the game lacks, unfortunately) is crucial. Never trust teammates to defend a point any more than you would trust a potato, since they'll be just as effective. Credits aren't too hard to farm once you get the hang of the game, and the devs are pretty frequent about showing the community just what they have in mind for the game. They run frequent streams on Twitch to show what's in the works, such as new maps, vehicles, weapons, bugfixes, etc, and open up dev servers with new builds of the game for everyone to test and give feedback on before pushing an update to the live servers.
Overall, it's a solid game with respectable devs and a decent content release schedule despite their smaller team size. Best advice would be to make friends to coordinate with, or you're in for a bad time when you're getting your s**t pushed in by a coordinated squad.

Alphabeats: Master Edition:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Do you have rhythm in your blood? Do you have good reflexes? Are you good at spelling? Well, you had better have these qualities in abundance, because you are up for a challenge!
Alphabeats: Master Edition is a combination of a spelling / rhythm (music) game.  As you launch the game, you will be presented with a comprehensive menu. In the middle of the screen you will be able to select from over 20 tracks to play – or you can upload your own favourite tracks. Also, you will have an option at the top “How to Play” (which is a good tutorial), an online leader board and the words you manage to spell correctly (the longest too).
At first you have to choose a song; it will be a good idea to begin with a slow tune to really get the feel of the game. On the screen you will see 12 vertical lines and the letters will descend from there. At the bottom of these lines, you will control a pointer. The pointer can only move horizontally in order to catch the letter and spell a word, but also to avoid the letters you don’t want. Let me tell you, it will get tricky when you reach a five or six-letter word, even on a slow tune.  The length of the songs can vary from two to four minutes and you have to score the maximum number of points within that time.  There are three power ups available per song: Double the points – If you managed to spell a rare or a long word click on this power up to double the points (I used this on the word “♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥” and scored 4000 points, not bad for a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥) – Shrink – this one will shrink your current longest word on your pointer, so you can try to make a longer one – Bomb – when you activate the bomb all letters on the vertical lines will disappear. Remember, you can only use one of each per song. Now that you a master of Alphabeat, get a song with a little bit more rhythm. . .  Could I suggest Techno?! The faster the rhythm, the faster the letter will descend, and it will be a challenge to spell a long word. Hold on, all of that on the normal difficulty! You could give it a go on the tricky or spellfire difficulties. In the spellfire difficulty, you make three mistakes and its game over!
You can use either the keyboard or a gamepad for controls but I would recommend the gamepad as I find it easier myself. Great soundtrack with a good varieties of tunes.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great soundtrack
-	Ability to load your own tunes
-	Three level of difficulties
-	Fun gameplay & re-playability
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Can be frustrating on the higher difficulty
-	No trading cards
Alphabeats: Master Edition combines is a really fun game to play and it will give you plenty of re-playability, especially with the option of loading your own track into the game.
8/10

Alphabeats is a combined word and rhythm game that was originally released as free game with pay-to-play levels on mobile platforms but was well reworked for PC, there is practically no trace of being a mobile game in the past.
You control a pointer that can horizontally move and collect letters from the board to form a word; those letters appear concurrently with the song rhythm. You have to make the best words you can, leading you to aim for the highest score (leaderboards are synchronised online). That might sound pretty easy but beware, as the song's speed gets higher and as you aim for longer words, you'll also have to keep in mind that you have to dodge the letters you don't want to use in a word which you plan to put together.
There are twenty levels (songs), all in electronic music genre. I'm not a music expert, but my wild genre guess would say to expect something between trance and dubstep. But even if you hate those music genres, you can still play your own songs! Though I feel this great function shares the same problem with all other rhythm games - the software can't recognize the beats from custom songs perfectly.
There are three difficulty levels, two aimed at casual players with low difficulty, and the third, spellfire difficulty, is aimed towards those who seek true word and rhythm challenge, as you'll have limited amount of lives, so you can't afford to do many mistakes.
While you'll be putting words together, there are three abilites that can help you once for each level. You can double up the points for the word you make next time (great for those who want to get as big as they can), you can destroy all the letters on the board and you can reduce the size of your word to one letter (that may sound like a nonsense but there's a column for every letter otherwise, so as you have bigger word, you also take more space from the board).
Alphabeats has a nice and original idea for casual genre mashup, good vocabulary and nice soundtrack. The game design is thought out pretty well and there isn't any element that would feel amateurish. The first Rad Dragon's Steam game is worth recommending.

God, where to start?
First, the gameplay. It's solid. It plays much like Bejeweled, but there is a larger amount of freedom in preparing for dates and moving tokens on the playable board, allowing for more strategic gameplay rather than purely relying on how good a board you start with. Dates will get steadily harder but it does not have any gimmicks introduced, allowing a fairer difficulty curve. Not to say that the later dates get near impossible without the right loadout. All in all, decent gameplay.
The characters themselves are rather one-dimensional however, and the lack of a storyline for any of the characters outside of 'bang every broad in a 5-mile radius' makes it fall rather flat. Don't expect to be feeling very much outside of euphoria from finally beating the final Bejeweled Blitz game (more affectionately known as SANIC BEJEWELED). If you are looking for more emotional and convincing characters, I would suggest looking for Visual Novels instead (Nekopara is a personal favourite of mine). However, the character dialogue is rather hilarious at times, and is the sort of B-movie slop that you will simply get hooked on.
Dating Sim gameplay is rather simple. Give presents, ask and answer questions, and stuff your waifu with food and drink. This is the only way of getting one of the currencies in the game called Hunie, neede for upgrading Traits to make the Bejeweled sections easier. To get Munie you need to sharpen up you match-3 skills.
HOWEVER, there is one other thing.
THE SOUNDTRACK IS AMAZING. I would HIGHLY suggest getting the Digital Soundtrack if you intend on buying this game. The tunes are catchy, yet also soothing. You can see for yourself how good the music is if you get the game yourself.
All in all, I can highly recommend this game. First, you come for the waifus. Second, you stay for the surprisingly good gameplay complexity. Lastly, you get earworms.

I started following World's Dawn at the end of 2014 when I was browsing random RPG Maker games (figured I'd step away from the low-key horror ones for a bit) and absolutely fell in love with it. The creator is a wonderful person who genuinely cares about the game and I'm so happy to see this game finally getting the attention it deserves.
As with any game, however, there are pros and cons, so lets go over them.
+ A nostalgic feeling for simpler Harvest Moon games such as the 64 version.
+ Easy to learn controls and systems.
+ An enjoyable small town life simulator.
+ Lively characters that make you feel like you're home.
+ Six romanceable bachelors and bachelorettes.
+ The ability to pick your gender and sexuality.
+ Some customization options.
- Repeatable gameplay. ...but that's to be expected with this sort of game.
- Simplistic minigames.
- Lock Ball in particular just isn't that fun. [personal opinion]
- Some glitches and bugs here and there. [being worked on actively!]
- Low replayibility.
There is a lot the game offers and it brings you back to an earlier time. For me, when I play this, I'm a little girl again sitting in my old bedroom in front of my television with wide eyes and tons of hope flooding through me. It's nice to be able to revisit that and step away from everything.
Buy this game. Play it. Fall in love with it. Encourage a sequel to it. Do all you can.

Absolutely glorious remaster of the classic Space Invaders game. Innovative, advanced, and scores of fun to be had.
When aliens living on Titan, Saturn's moon, decide to attack, they lay waste to Earth's military forces. Well most of it. You are the last remaining Tank Commander on Earth, and you are one bad mofo. Battle your way across Earth to stop the invasion, and then you take it to the skies as you hit the Titans' outpost on the Moon, and obliterate it. Next stop, the Titans' Martian colony. They wiped out all the little green men also and need to pay. After Mars, you find yourself on Saturn, and the enemy forces are strong. But not as strong as when you reach Titan itself, taking on the nest of the alien scourge to nearly end our way of life... and the poor Martians.
5 levels, 5 mothership bosses, an entire armada of Titan forces, some rogue and oddly light blue asteroids, and 1 lone tank to destroy them all. Fight your way across the Solar System as you upgrade your tank; outfitting it with extra weapons, additional bullets, faster recharge time, more powerful attacks, Shields, and deadly Smart Bombs. You start out small, but by the time you reach Titan, the force of your tank is ridiculous. But that doesn't mean it's easy. Each world you come to is upping the difficulty, more enemies, more styles of fighting, and a tougher Boss.
Not to mention fun bonus Challenge stages after every 7 waves you defeat, where harmless yet swift yellow flying saucers shoot across the sky. Destroy them all with perfect aim and you get bonus prices.
This game is complete with Highscore boards showing the scores of other players across Steam. Compare your best with others and strive to be the best. All the while this game's gloriously beautiful soundtrack playing in the background as you squash Titan scum.
The tank comander from the original Space Invaders would be jealous to see the rig you are in control of now.

It's obvious that one must always be cautious about user reviews due to the reviewer's inherent likes and dislikes. For 30 years I've mostly enjoyed war and turn-based strategy games. I have absolutely no interest in motorsports, just as I have no interest in football (soccer). But I like Football Manager, and I like this game even more.
Main reason is it's much more visceral during the actual race. And I can play the game with some level of competency without reading a manual, guide or watching (ugh) a drawn out youtube video. They've packed so much meaningful decisionmaking into the management and the race portions, I can't see getting bored for a long while. And then there's all those potentially enjoyable mods on tap.
It's one of the few (if any) games I've bought in a long time that is really worth full price in the long run. For example, I quickly refunded Paradox's Steel Division, but would definitely pick it up later on a 50% off sale. This purchase I don't think I'll every regret.
Of course, once I figure out what I'm doing I expect the game to be even more fun. The car set-ups are the least enjoyable thing for me, but it's probably cause I'm too lazy to read up on it. Where did that "perfect set-up" mod go? The only nitpick so far is the writing style for the fans' and media's comments. It's like ya man, I'm so cool. But hopefully, there will be a mod for that, if there isn't already.
No computer crashes, no bugs I've noticed, and it runs all-out on a vanilla i7 3.6 (16 ram) with a lousy GeForce GTX 745. I can't imagine how much "real" racing fans must be enjoying this, and would be surprised if any general strategy gamer would be disappointed with the purchase.

Gary grigsby's war in the east is truly a collossal game. Encompassing the entirety of the eastern front, a prospective player can expect to be micromanaging everything down to brigade/regimental level. complete with a realistic and detailed combat system which models battles down to the individual smallarms possessed by infantrymen it is certaintly worth your money if you admire detail. while the game is excellent it does have several issues. the first of these is an issue inherent to the game genre itself namely the turn based nature of combat. while this does simplify combat to a manageable level it presents serious challenges in that combat is portrayed as a series of assaults against static units rather than being dynamic and fluid as it is in real life. the second major issue lies in casualties and supply. the game consistently underrepresents casualties sustained in engagements to the point that more often than nought both sides wind up with close to 100% strength. All in all this is an excellent game and I would strongly recommend it to anyone interested in the eastern front.  (ps: prospective buyers should be aware that work has begun on war in the east 2 and it is slated for release sometime in 2017)

Yes, I do recommend this masterpiece.
It has a lot of flaws and bug but it is really great, I wish that Arena, Daggerfall, Adventures: Redguard and An Elder Scrolls Legend: Battlespire were on steam too.
But anyway, this game is really great, it does have flaws but can you tell me which Fallout or Elder Scrolls doesn't have flaws? They all have flaws but in the end, they are all great.
Morrowind being one of the greatest for many reasons, there are lot of weapon types such as darts, crossbows (no DLC needed unlike Skyrim), spears, staves, throwing knives, claymores etc etc...
There's not a lot of weapons but for an old game it's pretty good and there are a lot of weapon types unlike Oblivion and Skyrim.
The dungeons feels different from those in Skyrim and Oblivion, some may be really short but they all feel different from each other unlike those In Skyrim and Oblivion.
The map is small and the gameplay can be slow but it's still one of the greatest game ever plus you can always mod it to your liking.
If you're a newcomer, you should really get it, It is not as hard as people say, it is actually pretty easy if you know what you're doing (which isn't the case for most of the players who have played this game).
If you find it too hard, you can always change the difficulty setting, come on, I'm sure you'll love it.
The skills are great, lot of great skills, it's up to you, you actually have to equip the lockpicks and the other things you find in this game, to be able to use them.
You actually have to repair your stuff, unlike in Skyrim, which in my opinion, is a great addition to games like this one, not every games should have that, but the Fallout and the "The Elder Scrolls" titles should all have it.
It's true that not many people like that setting, so they should just add it as an option.
I personally, love having to repair my weapons and armors, I have to think before doing anything stupid since a broken weapon does almost no damages, even if it is a great weapon.
You'll have to use a lot of repair hammers if you want to repair stuff, and to level up your repair skill.
At first, it will take some time, but quick you'll be a master, I find it pretty cool, it's a little bit grindy, but it's nothing bad, it's actually great, it's not the same kind of grind you'll find in most of the MMO games.
Note: I am not hating on Oblivion or Skyrim, I actually love all of them, Oblivion has several great points that Morrowind do not have while Skyrim has great points that neither Morrowind or Oblivion does not have.
I'd totally love if smithing and a more complexe enchanting system would be available in Morrowind and Oblivion, those are the principal things that are not in neither Morrowind or Oblivion.
Honestly, many of the "negative" points that the community says about this game are more personal than anything else.
Most of them are great points to me.
Perhpas two things that should be changed.
The first one is that you cannot really use your shield, it uses a RNG factor depending on your shield skill level.  I'd love to use the shield at any time, and to bash people with it exactly like in Skyrim, something you cannot do in Oblivion nor Morrowind, but at least, you can use your shield at any time in Oblivion.
The second thing doesn't bother me much, but I would have thought of something better, in my own opinion, the magicka regeneration, there is none, I think that there should be one but only for the true mage characters, some kind of unique perk that you would choose at the start of the game, or something like that.
Anyway, other than that, keep in mind, three different maps (seven if you count the other titles, and even 10 if you count the three mobile games, don't know about those two though, never played them, not interested), different weapons, different time, different cultures, different story, different enemies, etc.
So it's totally worth getting all of them except for the three mobile versions, I have never played them so I can't say, if you are interested to look into them, they're called "The Elder Scrolls Travels Dawnstar", "The Elder Scrolls Travels Stormhold", "The Elder Scrolls Travels Shadowkey".
And above all, the game doesn't follows you everywhere like you were a little baby who can do nothing, you have to do things by yourself in this game, you have to find what you have to do by yourself.

God, where to start?
First, the gameplay. It's solid. It plays much like Bejeweled, but there is a larger amount of freedom in preparing for dates and moving tokens on the playable board, allowing for more strategic gameplay rather than purely relying on how good a board you start with. Dates will get steadily harder but it does not have any gimmicks introduced, allowing a fairer difficulty curve. Not to say that the later dates get near impossible without the right loadout. All in all, decent gameplay.
The characters themselves are rather one-dimensional however, and the lack of a storyline for any of the characters outside of 'bang every broad in a 5-mile radius' makes it fall rather flat. Don't expect to be feeling very much outside of euphoria from finally beating the final Bejeweled Blitz game (more affectionately known as SANIC BEJEWELED). If you are looking for more emotional and convincing characters, I would suggest looking for Visual Novels instead (Nekopara is a personal favourite of mine). However, the character dialogue is rather hilarious at times, and is the sort of B-movie slop that you will simply get hooked on.
Dating Sim gameplay is rather simple. Give presents, ask and answer questions, and stuff your waifu with food and drink. This is the only way of getting one of the currencies in the game called Hunie, neede for upgrading Traits to make the Bejeweled sections easier. To get Munie you need to sharpen up you match-3 skills.
HOWEVER, there is one other thing.
THE SOUNDTRACK IS AMAZING. I would HIGHLY suggest getting the Digital Soundtrack if you intend on buying this game. The tunes are catchy, yet also soothing. You can see for yourself how good the music is if you get the game yourself.
All in all, I can highly recommend this game. First, you come for the waifus. Second, you stay for the surprisingly good gameplay complexity. Lastly, you get earworms.
BUY IT.

If one were to sum up Titan Attacks in one word - that word would be "space invaders". Ok, that's two words, but you get my point. If you like these types of games, Titan Attacks will surely quench your thirst.
The basic formula is the same, you're on the ground - you shoot at alien scum coming from the air, sometimes the alien scum are smart enough to eject from the ship and parachute down to the ground - shoot them for extra points. All really simple. The game is strengthened by an upgrade system. Between each level, one can buy; shields (which deteriorate for each hit) and smartbombs, upgrade; gun power, add mode guns, recharge speed and more bullets. It's an alright system that does make you feel like you've grown and become more powerful throughout the levels.
There are extra bonus levels which put some tension to the game as if you pass them successfully, you will be able to upgrade quicker. All in all there are 100 levels with five boss battles in between, difficulty satisfying core fans of the genre and casuals alike.

Titan Attacks is a remake of the classic Space Invaders. On steroids. With upgrades and a big enemy variety, and by the end it gets so intense that it transforms into a bullet hell game. The distortion effects on the screen are very annoying though, but, luckily, you can turn them off. So, all in all, it’s pretty cool. If you were into these classic games, or want to try out a modern (though still fairly faithful) take on said classic games, then you should try it out.
In fact, I think more classic games should get a modern take like Titan Attacks (which seems like what PuppyGames is doing anyway). … Hm. I think I just got inspiration for what kind of game my next side project should be. Thanks, PuppyGames!
Although, on a side-note, I have to say that due to all the upgrades you can get, and how many enemies there can be, the strategic value of having to time your shots well (which was present in Space Invaders and the beginning stages of Titan Attacks) gets diminished, which is somewhat saddening. On the other hand, the curve of starting with the more slow-paced and strategic Space Invaders and then transforming into a hectic bullet hell provides a nice flow and pace to keep you interested throughout all 100 waves (at least on the first playthrough before you start over with all your upgrades intact).
So, yeah. Titan Attacks. Not much more to say, really.
