Game: Titan Attacks
Summary: Space Invaders + Galaga + upgrades
Rating (5/10 = failure): 7.5/10
Multiplayer: No
Completion: 4 hrs
Cards: Yes
Cloud: Yes
Cost: ~1 USD bundled
Is it Space Invaders? Is it Galaga? How about both! Titan Attacks is straight up old school gaming with a fresh coat of paint. It begins innocently enough as a Space Invaders clone with an upgrade system. As the game progresses, it suddenly turns into Galaga (while keeping the same gameplay!), and then finally a strange fusion of the two.
One problem I have with this game, similar to Ultratron, is that there's just too much stuff to keep track of, and too many blinky lights that make it difficult to see what you should actively be avoiding. You can turn off some of the strobe effects, but that doesn't help with the bombs exploding left and right, bullets flying from every direction, enemies flying right in front of you, power ups and cash you need to grab, aliens you need to not-shoot and grab, and so on.
Another problem with the game is that it is on the stingy side when it comes to money. Money is basically your lifeline. It is imperative that you keep your ship up-to-date in weapons or you will find that enemies take far too many hit before you're swamped in swarms. Unfortunately you do not automatically repair between levels and even trying to maintain a modest 3 health per level can become cost prohibitive. The solution, of course, is not to get hit in the first place, but that's kind of difficult with all the nonsense that comes flying at you.
It's a tough, yet fun diversion, and doable to boot. It's a game you can probably beat in a day, and may possibly cause much frustration in doing so. There's no plot or anything, it's just pure arcade action, and to its credit it does it well.
One concept I often talk about is "quarters". Pretend this is an arcade cabinet and you have to pop in quarters to play. How would this game measure up, relative to its price? For the amount of time invested, cost of a few quarters, and return value in entertainment, I'd say this ranks up there. If you need some way to kill time waiting for something, this is a nice, mindless way to do it. I think this game would be a lot of fun with simultaneous multiplayer capability.

A good strategy game needs at least three things
- to be playable quickly, but also deep enough that you keep learning more for hours and hours
- have a decent UI which effectively organises information and commands
- have a competent AI.
War in the East has all these.  I bought it because Hearts of Iron 4 just didn't deliver in terms of realism or complexity, and so far I've been pleased with the purchase.  You can play the game fairly quickly after mastering basic concepts, but there is waaaay more to the game than just pushing units about.  Once you get into the longer scenarios you will start to find out that you really do need to know what's the difference between the equipment your regular and your SS motorized divisions have, you will need to consider how to airdrop fuel, where to cross that river, how you are going to break through and encircle, and, oh my God, winter is coming!
The game covers all the main scenarios of the invasion, as well as grand campaigns.  Combat, supply, leadership and infrastructure are all dealt with in clear but detailed and complex ways, and if you play through the scenarios in increasing complexity, you can slowly learn the mechanics of the game.  As I said, it allows you to get into the game, but after 15 hours I feel like I know know how much I don't know and which directions to learn.  This is a game you could sink hundreds of hours into.  The AI is competent and has caught me out, but with a human player the tension would be mental.  As for the price, I bought it on sale, as it does seem expensive, but the level of detail and historical faithfulness do make this worth the price.

I've heard in the swamps to the south, our tanks have stalled against another Soviet line... the devil take this war...

As many others have mentioned, if you've ever played a Harvest Moon, then you'll be right at home with World's Dawn. There is very little, if any hand-holding... you're dropped into the environment with a couple pointers and a relatively simple 'Find and Talk to Everyone' quest, then you're off exploring. The first couple days may be spent just figuring things out through trial and error, especially if you aren't familiar with games like Harvest Moon, or the standard RPGMaker keybindings (which you can change, but if you already are familiar with them it makes sense to leave them be).
Once you know what you're doing, the farming aspects are extremely straightforward with no deviation. Most of your time will be spent running around finding people to talk to, or preparing for whatever the next upcoming social event is. Like most games with dialogue, eventually you're going to exhaust the conversation options and there is going to be some repeating until you do something noteworthy, or there is a festival, or you've grinded out the next friendship level.
Making money in the game is easy, the hardest thing, interestingly, is the social ladder grind - trying to become friends with everyone. There is much more focus on the social than on the farming / mining / fishing / ranching... so if that's your cup of tea, check it out. All the other activities are there, of course, they are just relatively simple when compared to making friends.
All in all, it is a good game, and I consider the purchase money well spent. I woulnd't go so far as to say I'm totally engrossed with it, but it's definitely keeping me entertained.
Instead of "just one more turn...", with this game it's "just one more day...".

For better or for worse, World's Dawn is a streamlined Harvest Moon- it doesn't seek to improve old Harvest Moon features, just iterate on them. This isn't inherently bad, but it does make liking the game hinge on how much someone enjoys Harvest Moon features and the quirks that come with them.
The dialog feels like a Harvest Moon game- a bit less repetitive, sure, but it still has the same RPG telling-in-dialog feeling. Two specific interactions immediately come to mind. One of the more frequent ones is a character frequently reiterating their relationship to another one in a way that feels forced and unnatural, like a mother constantly referring to "Bloom, my son," even though the relationship was already introduced. Another is the one-off one-liners about a character's past, like the mailwoman commenting she was orphaned. It's a quirk of Harvest Moon writing systems that carries over here, and while it's endearing due to nostalgia, it isn't exactly good.
The characters themselves are endearing if a bit shallow, where their main development is through small dialogs between two different characters, or festival romance events. The romance events do feel very natural, especially compared to most of the game, but aren't very frequent. Characterization for potential spouses is limited due to that, without the standard Harvest Moon heart event fanfare.
Farming is similarly streamlined, with a limited amount of progression available. There's a balance to place between making farming unmanageable or making it too simple, and the game leans heavily toward the latter. You can increased your crop field through a rather lengthy and unintuitive process, but by the time you can unlock that you may not need the extra money. Because farming is so streamlined, progression can feel non-existent. Unfortunately, this is compounded with how easy it is to buy out the store's products by the end of the first year. Raising animals fairs better. You're caped at two cows and four chickens, but since animals are costly and take longer to start producing products, this doesn't suffer from the same feeling of non-progression.
The aspects World's Dawn improves upon the standard Harvest Moon formula are the forging system, the cooking system, and house and character customization. Forging has two main aspects; finding wild produce on the ground, and collecting ingredients in a bottle. The ingredients is new and it works well, especially combined with the much better cooking system. Cooking is split into mixing and dishes. Mixing requires the bottle ingredients, and you have to remember the recipes for those. These mixes only take two ingredients, so experimenting and remembering isn't taxing. Cooking takes more ingredients, but you are required to have a recipe for larger dishes. This balances experimenting and recipes well, and makes cooking much less about finding a guide online with all the recipes and more about experimenting a little and collecting recipes throughout town.
As stated before, house and character customization is charming and done well, if a bit limited. Though most of the outfits aren't available until after marriage, mixing and matching different clothing items works well and looks nice. Housing fairs similarly, though housing items are available earlier in the game. It's small changes, but they work well. The additional mini-games are also fun, if a bit simple at times, but a nice change of pace.
Despite characters having similar or worse development as compared to previous Harvest Moons, the main plot line works much better than Harvest Moon's standard Harvest Goddess fanfare. The progression in the story is paced well, and the unlocks for progression are rewarding.
Overall, the game is still enjoyable- to those looking for a Harvest Moon experience. It can feel pretty barebones due to streamlining, though this does benefit the pacing of the game as it's faster and less reliant on artificial time-wasting unlocks. However, I don't think it quite makes up for it in writing, which is on par to some of the better installments in the Harvest Moon series. It's still a solid game that captures Harvest Moon well, but it unfortunatly doesn't do enough to capture Harvest Moon without its problems.

Ace of Spades is an online only voxel-built FPS with building and destruction of almost the entirety of all maps. It started as a slow paced, thoughtful, and well-mapped free webgame before it was picked up by Jagex and reworked. The original webgame was largely unfinished and somewhat lacking, but full of promise, so I was really excited for the full release by Jagex (a company I didn't know already had a bad rap before this game). I would wind up dissapointed. Ace of Spades: Battlebuilder (a subtitle they somehow added months after release) adds about as many new features as it breaks simple things.
Ace of Spades: Battlebuilder has a handful of different gamemodes, both FPS staples and interesting new modes like a modified Oddball where you have to dig up and hold diamonds, and demolition where the goal is to destroy the enemy team's base while preserving your own. The different modes are welcome, but most go unplayed. Chances are that if you get in a non-TDM/CTF/zombie game, you'll only have 2 to 5 other people in your VIP/territory control/KOTH game.
Beyond that, all the base game maps are either too small for large numbers of players to reasonably have fun and not die every 15 seconds, or they're so big that everyone gives up playing in frustation at being crossmapped by snipers and not finding anything much to do on the map. It's strange that so many maps get the pacing wrong and that the game doesn't have a matchmaking system to get good amounts of people together. Even the map editor doesn't help much because only custom servers run them, and they are often private or also near empty. So finding good maps and servers in this game is really difficult.
So let's say you were to get in a game and start playing. You're presented with 4 classes unless you're in a special game mode such as zombie, VIP, or the half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥classic. Honestly, the classes were never balanced, and every once in a while when I checked in they'd be offbalanced in some other way. The miner is poor at everything except creating holes, tunnels, and collapsing enemy structures. They have no fighting chance except to drop a platform out from somebody high up or shoot 2 blocks in front of them with the shotgun. The commando is an 80's action movie hero who packs a minigun and an RPG, and you are useless for anything except spamming shots everywhere. There is no way to carefully play a commando-you hope for the best as you rush into the fight to probably be picked off. Then there's the engineer. The engineer has a jump pack which allows him to soar all over the map, an SMG which is surprisingly accurate and damaging, a block cannon to build bridges and things from a range, and deployable sentries. The engineer is a popular class because they are fast, manueverable, and surprisingly lethal. I believe they also have a super damaging melee. Then there's the marksman who is also crazy fast, low profile, and lethal. Marksmen can kill in a couple bodyshots, fire rapidly with one rifle, and have no recoil. In addition they are hard to touch because of their good building prefabs and mines. So, most games devolve into COD-like matches where everyone either zooms around on crack with an OP SMG or they hide in corners just racking up kills and freaking out when they're finally successfully found and killed. Team work is so rare in this game, and there usually isn't a good way to help a teammate out besides helping shoot enemies.
If you manage to find a good server and start having fun with a class you're still at risk of the game failing you. There are a lot of bugs and crashes. I remember teams incorrectly balancing, falling through the sky box, being unable to heal at spawn (there's a tent which is supposed to heal you), and fatal crashes to desktop to name a few. I really wish I could recommend this game, but I cannot. Jagex made too many mistakes, and everyone with the game suffers for it. 5/10 because it can be a couple hours of simple fun when the stars align. I suggest finding another FPS.

It has been 12 years since the release of third numerical (fifth overall) Elder Scrolls game and it's still a blast to play to this day. Why? Because Morrowind did so much right when it was released and introduced many of us to The Elder Scrolls for the first time. Morrowind put you in a world that was much smaller than its predecessors but felt much more alive due to the sheer amount of detail and attention to craft. Apart from the main quest was a plethora of side content including hundreds of side quests, over 20 factions, and many ways to customize your character. Morrowind didn't offer a lot of hand-holding or directional arrows like many modern games do. Your journal was far more than a list of assignments, but a story you crafted as you progressed and a wealth of knowledge as you learned more about the world. For navigation, you used keywords, signs and general directions instead of arrows to find your way. The discovery was just as important as the destination.
Granted, Morrowind was not without some faults. Swinging a sword against an enemy wouldn't always mean you'd hit it, some skills were a bit superfluous, and beast races can't wear shoes. But all of the shortcomings of the game cannot outweigh the good of the game, the atmosphere, the story, the hours many of us put into it or just how much of a landmark this was for western RPGs.
What kept a lot of us playing even after slaying Dagoth Ur was slain is the strong native support for mods. MOG*MOD in particular brought a lot of joy for me in playing this game. Even today there is a strong community of players who continue to modify, update, and add to the game in the form of mods. Definitely one of the finest western RPGs ever made.

In many ways, still the best of the Elder Scrolls games.
Despite the dodgy combat and aged graphics it has something that Oblivion and Skyrim miss. Challenge. And I don't mean being chased all over the map by Cliff Racers. I mean the sense of accomplishment when you beat the game and defeat Dagoth Ur. With the later games it feels like you've been ticking boxes, and following a tightly constrained path If you bother to follow the main quest (which many will ignore), with Morrowind it feels like YOU accomplished it. It's hard to explain unless you've played it. Any way you look at it, it's a very clever piece of writing
And then there's the setting. Unique, alien, you feel like a stranger in a strange land. Whereas Oblivion and Skyrim settle for Generic Fantasy Settings 1 and 2, vaugely medieval and vaguely Nordic. Which is so sad. Thew wqay the lore described it, Cyrodiil in Oblivion could have been an exotic jungle with rice paddies and exotic Mayan style temples and palaces, a fusion of Mezo-American and East-Asian influences, with Dragons circling the White-Gold Tower. But Bethesda chickened out and missed a wonderful opportunity.

STO was a great game at one point.  It's a fairly mediocre game as of late.
Many bad/questionable choices have caused major imbalances in the game, frustrated long time players, and shown that PWE/Cryptic is trying to heavily monitize the game at the expense of the players.
However, that being said, there is much good to be said about STO as well.
1) Decent storylines that pick up where the TV episodes and movies left off.  Cryptic has done a great job of revisiting many of the lesser known races in the STO universe, and bringing many unfinished story lines to a close.
2) Ships, ships, and more ships.  All the amazing ships we know and love as well as quite a few retrofits/refits that bring our favoties up to par with the 25th century.  I love taking out my 23rd century Excelcisior class cruiser and wiping the floor with the Borg or even other players.  Nothing is more embarassing then a 200 year old ship tearing your brand new top of the line cruiser to shreds.
3) Decent player base.  Social interaction is recommended, but not required.  You can go a long ways without ever having to say hello to another player.  However, joining a fleet should be one of the first things that you do, so that you can get further, get better gear, etc.
4) Decent selection of real world money ships, costumes, etc.  Some of them are obvious money grabs, but some of them are just plain awesome too.
5) Seasonal events like the Summer event at Risa and Q's Winter Wonderland help break the slowness in 'seasons' (aka expansions).
6) Ground combat is 'okay'.  Its not up to par with the space combat, but it is certainly playable and how you best explore the main story lines.
All in all, if you like Star Trek, then you'd probably like STO.  If you've never played an MMO before, or don't have much experience in the Star Trek universe, you can try this game, but be prepared for a learning curve.

I wish Steam would give me a "meh" for reviews.  I will continue to play this game, so I guess that's a recommendation.  But I will continue to believe it's bad in many respects.  What led me to finally understand how it is bad was attempting to work with the "The Foundry" level designer.  This is a cool feature that does let players create custom missions for others to play which creates a large variety of content for players to enjoy and experience.  But it's also the main problem with this game.  Whereas the devs/level designers apparently have access to a more advanced version of "The Foundry" - whatever they design with isn't much better than the Foundry.
The limits this very poorly thought out level designer puts on a level designer are enormous.  The primary problem being that there's no branching to story lines AT ALL.  Not a single mission lets you make a choice that will result in a variation of what happens during the quest.  Many RPGs are like this - linear quests with one resolution - but even tiny variations in the progress of the mission are nearly impossible with this level designer and, the thing is, this also plays out in the missions.  No branching wouldn't matter that much IF it were possible to deeply customize gameplay - but it's not.  The mobs are all pretty generic in behavior and they're fought generically.  The variation between classes is basically a few abilities but fighting is all done on the ground by mashing  a few buttons for "shoot phaser rifle."  But remember - there's NO BRANCHING - I mean, there's not even branching in quests as simple as "switch this lever and go down the left hall or switch the right lever and go down the right hall and then you'll be in the main room - you can't pick both."   The only branching is in dialogue which is good and necessary, but without branching at all during the story - it feels very boring in many cases.

I thought this game would be bad because I got it for free, so I avoided it for a while. However, Binary Domain is surprisingly enjoyable, and the most fun I had playing a game in a long time. The setting, gameplay, and characters are all well executed.
Binary Domain is a postcyberpunk game that takes place in 2080, after rising sea levels cause cities to build upwards. Many people are killed due to the environmental catastrophe. Robots became prevalent to perform services, especially in Japan. Illegal, advanced robots that are indistinguishable from humans are found and traced back to Japan. The mission is to capture the person who is creating these "hollow children". The intriguing backstory is used to create interesting environments. For a game that was released on the last generation of consoles and not very demanding by today's standards, it sure looks beautiful.
The game is a squad-based cover shooter. While there is an option to use a microphone for speaking to your teammates, responses and commands can be selected from a menu. The teammates respond well to these commands when not using a microphone, and follow the player's instructions when possible. Sometimes teammates suggest a plan that's based on their abilities to take out the enemies, which can be approved.
What makes the gameplay really special are the enemies, robotic combatants. Their limbs can be shot off changing how they fight. The robots never back down, and even when they have lost both of their legs, they crawl towards and cling to the player. Shooting off any robot's head causes it to attack friendlies. This allows the player to come up with different strategies for defeating hordes of robots. There are different types of robots found in the game with different weapons and abilities, mixing up the combat. A downside of the combat system is the key bindings used on the PC; for instance, spacebar activates cover, climbing, running,
selection in the menus. The controls take some time to get used to.
The boss fights are spectacular and lengthy. One downside to these is the occasional use of quick time events, but that is a minor complaint. During these boss fights, and some other battles, the odds seem impossible until the player remembers that they are a walking arsenal. Like the regular robots, bosses must have their limbs disabled until they are unable to fight and explode. The bosses change their strategy as they lose limbs, keeping the fights interesting. With all the bullets flying everywhere and massive battles, the combat is reminiscent of Japanese shooter arcade games.
The characters are cheesy but likable. The banter among the squad members is amusing and changes depending on which team members the players choose to take along for each mission. There is a trust meter for each ally that increases depending on how many missions you bring them along for. The trust meter also increases when the player is performing well, but decreases for accidentally shooting your teammates and taking too long to clear a wave of robots. The trust level changes how the characters respond to the player and has some impact on the story. It is an interesting idea that offers incentive to keep everybody happy. Another squad element are the nanomachine upgrades that can be purchased and applied to the teammates and the player; it's also an interesting idea.
The player is forced to be with certain characters for much of the story, and given its length, not all trust can easily be maxed in a single playthrough. This has some impact on the story. However, some characters are more interesting than others and more fun to tag along with. Love you, Faye, Bo, and Cain.

Cool little tribute to Space Invaders, Megamania, Centipede, Asteriods, and a few others, with some of the better-looking stylistic pixelated graphics I've seen.
It's not the most balanced game, though. Frequently suffers from "How do you expect me to dodge THIS?!" syndrome, and long-term victory is completely determined by how much money you happen to get in the first 30 levels or so (which is mostly a random factor), and whether you can beat the bonus challenges to save money. Expect to restart the game a lot until you can get a run where you beat the first three bonus challenges, and get enough random money drops from hitting saucers, to earn enough upgrades to make progess through the ridiculous levels later.
But I'm still giving this a thumbs-up for looking, sounding, and handling smoothly. I'd dare say the game is charming.
P.S.: Don't sign up for the newsletter. It only gives you full shields for the very next playthrough.

Human beings are complex organisms which require many resources to remain alive. While humans recieve many nutrients from outside sources, such as light from our nearest star, the vast majority of the energy that powers bodily functions required for life is provided by food. Food is a general word for anything consumed via the mouth for energy, which is measured in Calories, a unit consisting of 1000 calories with a lowercase c. When foods are consumed, the body breaks them down into a number of base substances which are melted down via stomach acid and absorbed via the stomach and upper intestinal tract. Over the course of digestion, which is the breaking down and total absorption of all these substances, a bacterially enriched waste is left behind primarily consisting of fiber that we refer to as Ace of Spades. There is no exact indication of when food is rendered as Ace of Spades, however, and this phrase primarily refers to the waste once it has reached the large intestine. The large intestine continues to absorb water from Ace of Spades, leaving a semi-solid brown lump of undigested fiber and other waste moving through the colon. Finally, Ace of Spades passes through a door known to biologists as the sphincter, which signals its exit from the body. There are many ways to dispose of Ace of Spades after it is removed from the body, and different methods with associated health benefits and detriments are also associated with specific global cultures. First review, because reasons.
I started playing STO about a year after its release. Back then the game needed a monthly fee, and frankly, it just wasn't worth it unless you really really liked Star Trek. PVP was terrible, the game has a fairly large line of bugs, and the game engine was dated even when the game came out. Since then, the game has become a lot better. Numerous content expansions, additional features, solid story content for fans and not fans, and the ever present stream of quality player made contnet makes STO worth playing.
This game is best in PVE, and if you're a Roleplayer there's a load of tools in the game to enhance that experience (you can write custom captain's logs and supplamentals in your journal for example). The Foundry has great content, much of it better than what the devs put out and what the devs put out for storyline isn't bad. There's a lot of group content, but most of it goes unplayed due to the lack of rewards to make them worth playing. That might be a deal breaker for some, because very much STO can feel less like an MMO and more like a Single Player game with other people running around.
The game is very imbalanced... Except it's not really going to hinder you outside PVP.  PVP is bad, but I'm not gonna put on rose tinted glasses. PVP has always been bad. I remember no point in time of playing STO that it wasn't bad. If you want a PVP space combat game try Fractured Space or Eve. They're better and you'll get a lot more out of the experience. Cryptic's current business model isn't very endearing. Many of the best ships are hidden in lock boxes, and cost way too much in game currency or real money to actually obtain. Which is why I highly advise new players not to bother. It's honestly going to suck you in and kill the fun chasing that magic dragon.
And yet, despite its flaws it's still worth playing for fans and even not fans. It's FTP, and at its best when you just relax and let yourslef go from one little project to the next (and the game has lots of little projects). Don't worry about being the uber player, or being top tier. There are better games for that in this genre (Eve). Play STO because you want to feel like you're going on an adventure. You'll find that here in spades.

Absolutley fantastic game. My clocked hours is misleading, as i played most of this game during a car ride across the USA, btw. But to the point, this game is beautiful, in many ways. My favorite part is the environment and the atmosphere. Vvardenfel is such a strange place, you feel like your on another planet sometimes. Wandering through the ashlands, trudging through the swamps, or delving into a daedric ruin, there is tons of stuff to explore.  The dark elf culture is so vibrantly displayed, as is their reactions to other cultures. I DO NOT recommend this game! Why? Because there isn't any real progression in this game. All of your progress in developing technology is RESET whenever you step up to better competition. In the game there are several circuits in which you can compete. If you start at the bottom circuit and progress to the next tier then you lose all of the effort in designing a better car as the game resets you to a base value. This is supposed to be a management game. You have very few important decisions outside of the critical tech decisions. So the game takes all of your careful decisions that you made about which techs to focus on and throws them down the drain. There is no progression ouside of hiring drivers/mechanics/designers/buildings, as nothing else carries over.
That's the core of this game. Developing your technology so you can be more competitive is what it's all about. Then the game resets that technology? Kills immersion and the sense of building something from the ground up. For that reason I feel that this game is poor. It's like having an RPG game without a story. Or having a strategy game without competent AI. This is a very poor 'management' game because there is little to manage.
If they were to add some kind of persistent development for your team it would help me to enjoy it. Either in the form of deeper building options and the ability to interact with our buildings OR a technology tree where my team is working on design theories that could eventually be applied to the parts I build in the circuits.

Overall quite fun, a good amount of detail, but I find that sometimes decisions you make seem to have little effect on the driver/result - hard to determine how much of a race result is "random" and how much is due to parts/reliability/tyre wear/etc. I am enjoying it though, and intend on continuing playing.

I had been meaning to play Binary Domain for quite some time now, since the console release back on PS3, so I was really excited to finally get a hold of it during a Steam Sale. While not the greatest thrid person shooter I have ever played I can definitely say that I had a blast with it. From the cheesey dialouge to the intense action set pieces I would be lying if I said it wasn't fun to go through. However I do have a few issues with the game. For starters you and your team are locked to specific weapons. What I mean is the main character always has his assualt rifle or one of the team members always has their shotgun. There's no mixing up loadouts or anything. You can pick up or buy second primary weapons, handguns and grenade types but only you. Even if you could only equip new weapons that are in the same weapon category that would have been far better than just being locked to one specific weapon along with what ever else youd could find. Secondly the game lacks in weapon variety. There's just so little that by chapter 3 it will absolutely feel like you've tried all the guns and grenades out. Thirdlythe game is rather short, only six chapters, it took me 10 hours to complete this game and I was really wanting more. This especially feels like it needed more considering the ending, which I won't spoil, it just begs the question why there wasn't a story expansion chapter or a seqeul. Lastly the level design. I don't know about anyone else but I found it to be rather bland. I'm not sure if that was the intention considering that there are parts in the game that have you go through an old rundown city. This is also something a sequel could fix by looking for ways to make areas not more open but rather more diverse in the ways you could approach things in combat. Most of the levels were very straigh forward and the few times that did make you look up or down or to the left or right were good sections because it wasn't forcing you to really look one direction the entire time. With those gripes out of the way I can say that despite those short comings I would still recommend the game because it does feel like a game that would have some interesting potential with a sequel.

Some people would call this game "hidden gem". And they would be correct. This a good game that for some reason got overlooked.
You are spec ops guy who infiltrated into future Tokyo to find out who is making human like robots which is forbidden by law. The story is surprisingly good and I cared about it and the characters which does not happen often in shooter games. Its very Japanese story with long cutscenes and a lot dialogue. Normally, I hate this kind of bullcrap but this was the first time I actually enjoyed it. It actually makes you think about things like what if robot can think like human, look like human, is it still a robot?
You play with a team of thee comrades throughout most missions. Your team mates are actually good. They help you out a lot and don't get stuck on terrain. They all have distinct characters and are very likeable. One is this French robot with outrageous French accent, another is sassy black guy, there is this Chinese girl who you have gigidy with. They are all well voice acted and have their own personalities. Also, there is this reputation system where if you shoot your mates they will gradually disrespect you but if you manage some crazy head shots they will give you some sweet respect. I really liked this aspect of game.
You kill robots throughout the game. This would be boring but there's the twist: you can disasemble them. You shoot robot’s right hand, it drops its weapon but then picks it up in another hand. Or you shoot robot’s legs and he starts to crawl toward you. Its really fun. Some robots are massive so you have to bazooka them or climb on top of them. These are usually stage bosses and they look really cool. However, some are insane bullet sponges and take ages to kill. Luckily, this does not happen too often.
Things I did not like were controls. Controls are crap on keyboard so play with controller if you have one. But even then controls are very tanky and will even get you killed sometimes. Also, there is this voice control gimmick but its waste of time unless you wan to be yelling at your PC all the time so turn those off.
Overall its a very good game. Shooting is fun, story is good, its not too long (about 10 hours) which I appreciate. Get it from Amazon for £3 new and activate Steam code on your account. You wont regret it.

P.S. "M" means middle mouse button, you can thank me latter

True to the spirit of Harvest Moon, this game take you to a little, beautiful and cozy rural village.
There you can live your life as you seem fit. You can farm in you little lot, buy and take care of cow and chickens, go to the mines to search for precious gems, go to fish in several ponds or the ocean, gather what nature has to offer, cook and brew discovering recipes in lots of places, explore the cute little village, befriend your new neighbors, participate in festivals and even found true love.
There's no time limits so you can take your time and enjoy the simple pleasures of life. Is a very cute and relaxing game, with characters interesting and charming.
So, if you like the genre, what are you waiting for? A cozy wonderful life in a beautiful rural village awaits for you!!
For those that like things more simple:
Pros:
- Charming characters.
- Tons to things to do.
- Nice art.
- Involved developer.
- It's just fun and relaxing to play.
- Your dog can find nice things buried when walking to you.
Cons:
- The initial farming lot is a bit small, 4x5. You can gain an additional lot later.
- You can't romance all the characters. Madison is so cute... I would love to romance her.
- Some bugs, but the dev is working hard to fix them.
Conclusion: Nice, relaxing, cute and cozy game with tons of things to do and enjoy. A wonderful example of Harvest Moon style games.

One great thing about this game that needs to be said is that the developer is very open to criticisms and updates fast. I and many others were complaining about how sprinting took so much EN, and one day later he patched it. That made me feel pretty good about this game.
You probably notice immediately that it's an RPGMaker game, and that RPGMaker games have a sort of reputation. Well, luckily, this is one of the handful of "worthwhile games" made with this engine.
If you've ever played a Bokujou Monogatari (Harvest Moon/Story of Seasons) game and thought, "I wish there was more unique dialogue" or "I wish there was more of a story" then this game is for you. There are "quests" for you to complete such as making a hot stew for the old man with a cold, along with a "trading game" of sorts where you find someone who can use an old item.
The festivals are also much more engaging. You actually *do* something, besides just entering your stuff in a contest, or simply showing up at the right place at the right time.
All of these things kept me coming back for more.

This game is really super cute and can be as long or as short as you want to make it. I strongly recomend War In The East, it is a true War Game! Now I can do it all again with this fantastic PC version. I have 328 hours in already and have a good feel for how most of the systems work.  I have been playing the Russians in a campaign - stalled the Germans short of Lenningrad and Moscow, its late in the summer of 42 and they Will Not be making any more progress. But that is just an FYI/Wish List for WITE v.2 - Keep up the GREAT work Gary Grigsby.

Puppygames seems to specialise in teaching old dogs new tricks. The old dog in this case is Space Invaders, and the new tricks make it well worth playing again. As you progress you earn money which you use to upgrade your tank, turning it into a laser-spitting death machine. But the aliens are upgrading too, getting faster and deadlier with new abilities. There are five worlds, with a boss at the end of each, and challenge stages every seven levels.
At heart it's still a simple game - nothing can change that - but it's addictive and the graphics are distinctive. It's a good game to play as a break from more complex games.

Titan Attacks! is similar to Space Invaders, but better in every possible way.
It has tank upgrades, checkpoints that save your progress, leaderboards, a health bar, bosses, a variety of enemies, a fitting soundtrack, and an appealing graphics style. Your tank's hitbox is also slightly smaller than it appears, so you never feel like you took damage from a shot that didn't hit you.

If you liked space invaders then you have to try this little game.  Wave after wave of enemy ships with enough variety to keep you interested.  The upgrading is fun too as you will need all the firepower you can get.  It has a retro feel and I definitely recommend it as one of those pick up and play games.

If you dug Space Invaders, but always felt like it could be more, then you should really dig this game. The upgrades for your tank and the different movement patterns the "Invaders" have in this game, totally make it!

Spore may not be what I was expecting. It may not be as good as I thought it could be. But once I looked past the dissappointment, I realised that there is still a good game here.
Let me get the things that upset me out of the way. The Creature stage seems to last too long with little variation. You either kill everyone around you, or charm them. And charming is a bit confusing, so it always boils down to me killing off races of animals and watching the progress bar rise ever so slightly each time.
Space stage is practically pointless. I feel that there is no goal in it. Sometimes, there are parts of space you can't  get to because they are just a tiny bit too far away. Cell stage was funner than both of these, which is pretty sad. City Stage is too short. It only lasts an hour and a half, at the most. Which sucks, because it's my favorite stage. You get to command vehicles you created to destroy other cities and conquer them. But the biggest danger in City Stage is turrets, not enemy vehicles.
That's about it for the things I dislike, so on the the praising for Spore's creativity.
CREATING THINGS IS GREAT. They made spinoffs based only on the Spore Creators, and there is a reason for that. You can construct creatures ranging from spiders with dolphin heads to dragons with butterfly wings and a human nose. It's great. The Vehicle Creators are my absolute favorite part of the game. I have created Spaceships of every shape and size, and i am proud of them. You will never see the same ship twice, unless someone actually made a duplicate. I feel like the game would be cooler if more people played and interacted, creating new creatures, buildings (oh yeah, you can create buildings. not my favorite.), and vehicles. But that's just me. Maybe? People, join me, i'm lonely.
Spore is not a bad game, as long as you are creative and can deal with a bit of boring gameplay early on. You can create endless creatures, vehicles, and building with endless variety. The Tribal and City stages are fun, but short. good thing you can repeat them any time. I give Spore a 6/10, and I do recommend this game.

It's a third person shooter, with combat revolving around the use of cover, kind of like the Gears of War series.
Enemies are all machines, and their different body parts all track damage individually, meaning you can shoot their limbs off like the Dead Space series.  Enemies react consistantly and predictably to losing their limbs, so the player can quickly take control of the pace of a firefight with a few well placed shots.  This makes the game more feel more tactical than the usual shoot until everything is dead, and then move to the next arena.  Boss battles are fairly drawn out and entertaining with the player having to strip the armor plating off massive enemies to expose their weak points.
One feature this game has that I haven't seen elsewhere is you command your AI-controlled squad members by shouting into your microphone.  This would be pretty cool if the voice recognition technology had been better.  Sadly, it doesn't work well.  If you disable the right options in the game settings, then you can use keyboard commmands to issue orders, by holding tab.
I've heard some people say they had gamepad issues.  For me, the game worked perfectly with mouse+keyboard and aim assist turned off.
Graphics look great on a modern system with everything set to maximum.
Story is okay, but tries too hard to create drama between the most generic characters imaginable.
One thing that annoyed me about the game is nothing is skippable, or at least I couldn't find the button to skip things.  Not the developer logos on game launch, not the cutscenes, not the dialogue, and not the end credits.  I just wanted to go back to shooting things.
Overall, a well made entry in the third person shooter genre.  I'm surprised I never heard of it until it popped up for about $5 in my Steam queue.  I think it would probably be more popular if it offered co-op during campaign mode.

World's Dawn is a game that your either going to love or hate. It is not a complicated game so if your coming in looking for a deep farming simulation or complex gameplay then you may want to look elsewhere. What the game does have in spades though is charm.
You start off as a new arrival to the town of Sugar Blossom. You have a small plot of farming land (20 tiles) as well as a barn that can hold 2 cows, a horse, and 4 chickens. On top of this you have a dog you start with and it is even possible to get a cat as well.
There is also fishing, gathering plants that grow around town, and mining, and mixing drinks/juice/sauces, and a local sport called lockball that you can partake in as well though it all remains fairly straightfoward and easy to understand.
So again not the most elaborate set up but enough to let you run your small farm and keep you busy as you progress through the seasons and the story while you learn about the history of the village and the spirits that keep it safe.
Beyond this is the social aspect which is easily the largest portion of the game. There are 25+ other people in the town ranging from the local baker, an artist, the town mayor, the rancher, a priest, etc, etc and all of them have their own personality's, likes, and routines throughout the day, and you can develop friendship or even romance with some of them if you so deire.
It really makes you feel like part of a community as you go about your life in your new home.
Aside from all that each season that I've played so far (after 13 hours I've just started Summer) has a couple markets where the townsfolk gather to meet and sell some goods and two festivals such as a horse race, music festival, and a beach festival each with their own mini activity that you can participate in.
Altogether as said the game absolutely nails the feel that you are in this small cheerful country community. It's not complex, it's not buried in deep mechanics for you to manage your life with. But it is a relaxing and enjoyable way to spend time provided your willing to sit back and go with the flow.
If your looking to manage a farm and make a ton of money from it and to see how quickly you can go from rags to riches this is likely not the game for you. However if you want the gaming equivalent of sitting on your front porch with a nice glass of lemonade and just relaxing and enjoying life for a bit, then I would by all means recommend giving this game a shot.

Vermintide has one of the best melee systems in a game I have ever played. Combat is visceral and responsive. Weapons feel like they have real weight and purpose to them. Each melee strike feels good; you strike where the weapon swings across your screen, and the animations are great enough that each swing is both satisfying and believable. The player characters are amazingly voice acted and written. I myself am unfamiliar with the Warhammer setting, but I quickly fell in love with the 5 main playable characters, and the grim world they inhabit.
The main downside I have is the engine is quite intensive on some systems. Some of my friends' PCs had troubles graphically or had CPU issues due to the size of the rat hordes. The majority of connectivity and stability issues at launch have been stamped out at least! Gameplay/Mechanics wise, you have to be aware of what you are getting. Think less RPG and more melee-focused FPS with Left 4 Dead esque map progression. Character progression is tied mainly to the weapon\trinket drops and their traits. While they can make the difference, the majority of player progression is through honing skill and not amassing phat lootz. This appeals to players like me but might turn off people who were expecting a more RPG/PnP style character progression. Replayability hinges on being driven to improve player skills, and not in-game progression. Some people like this, others might feel it lacks replayability due to lack of overt character progression.
Best part of this game is the developers, Fatshark, who continued to support Vermintide with balancing patches, new free content and system, reasonably priced DLC, and an open ear to the community. While I might not be able to find the time to play everyday, I always make sure to keep up to date with the latest news.

First of all, its an early access game so people who are giving it bad reviews saying that its buggy and updates break things...well thats going to happen. Thats the point of an early access game, you push your content out and have the players test it to find whats wrong so they can fix it. The game is far from finished so don't expect it to run perfectly every time you play. Things will go wrong and things will go right. If you aren't ready for some flaws then don't play right now.
On to the review. I played this game a long while back while it was the orgiginal graphics and menu and it was very difficult then. It felt clunky but it was still fun for what it was. Now, there have been quite a few updates and I do enjoy them. The game plays better, I like the new menu, and it runs pretty well on my machine.
As of now, it is a grind it out type of game to get your unlocks. You do not need them but every upgrade helps and makes the game more fun. You do not need to pay for anything. I do like the challenge of this game, you need to be careful or you will get popped. You can't just wander around aimlessly and you need to stick with your team. Aiming is difficult, there is no arcade feel to the game and that is what I like. Battles take time and you have to cover a lot of distance so its important to plan ahead to make the most out of every spawn.
The devs continue to push out content so the game progress looks promising. I am not expecting an early access game to be perfect but so far it is fun and worth of try. I see this game as something you pop in and play for a while every here and there and not something you should be pouring countless hours into. With that being said, give this game a try because you might really like it. Instead of complaining on here, write to the devs what you like and dont like and any bugs you find so they can fix it in the upcoming releases.

Heroes and Generals is a game for those who want something in between CoD and Battlefeild, in terms of gameplay. maps can range from about 1km^2 to over 100 km^2. Purchased WitE back in the day, which makes me old as 2010 isn't really Back in the Day. BitD is actually 1973 with the release of a paper hex map / cardboard counter game by the name of
. The map was about 4' x 5', the counters totaled over 1,500 individual pieces. Add the expansion
(yes, they invented what would become DLC BitD), and the maps got bigger, with thousands more counters. It took hours just to set up, before ever actually playing. And the play... we met every Saturday night for about a year, and only got into 1943 before marriage, college, the military and various nervous disorders most often resemblng German and Russian language Tourette Syndrome broke up the group and brought the endevour to an end.
All of which is only backstory to my purchase of War in the East - technology has granted us the ability to actually play the beast that is The Great Patriotic War at the operational level without renting a hall and losing our minds. It's been done a number of times in recent decades, but Gary Grigsby has done it the best, by a wide margin. If you've read this far and have any idea what I'm talking about. AND are interested in the subject, then buy this game. I'd forgotten how good it is (getting it on Steam has reintroduced me and taken me away from other CCG and FPS for the past weeks), and how easy it is to immerse oneself in it. But back in the saddle it's the only thing I'll be doing for a while.
Like: It's the @#$%&*! East Front done right, for Zhukov's sake!

For the old cardboard gamers out there, GG WiTE will be familiar.  Many may remember Avalon Hill's classic "Russian Campaign."   The manual is an impressive 377 A4 pages.  Despite this, the game can be played with remarkably little knowledge.  So while the learning curve is long, at the introductory level it is not steep.  After the initial interest of movement and combat you will soon find yourself persusing the manual to find out the finer detail and how to get an advantage on your opponent.   There are, thankfully, no boom/flash graphics.  A well laid out "board" with enough graphical detail to give information without being over the top.  Standard wargaming counters give it that classic boardgame feel.  Multiplayer is well catered for with the Matrix server providing the interaction between players.
So if you like classic wargaming, and part of the fun is reading through the manual, GG WiTE could be a good title to add to your collection.

Feared this game since release :D
Really, this huge scale and price feared me out for years, but finally I decided to get it.
Game provides you with dozens of scenarios and campaigns, diffirent by scale and situations on huge and detailed map devided by 10 miles hexes in Operational/Strategic genre.
You can start grand campaign 41-45, starting from full size "Barbarossa" campaign till the gates of Berlin or choose another starting year or you can choose between smaller by scale/front/time scenarios, even by parts(For example: Phase 1 of Fall Blau, Operation Uranus or full sized Fall Blau).
Little advice - Start with "Road to ..." scenarios on German side, they will gently force you in diffirent situations so you can easier understand game mechanics.
Firstly it will look easy - "Aha, Left click here, right click there, pfff...", but then you will start - "Why this happened?", "Why my panzers stopped there on the edge of my pierce attack? What does those 0% near "jars" mean?", "Why my Guards cant advance there!?", "Where are all my planes? Last week they were here, dozens of'em!" and etc. Read the manual and guides. Game provides you with all you need to know information, not overloaded by it, but to understand how to use it correctly you need to be ready to use manual.
If you are into World War 2 and ready to spend 1-3 hours on one turn - get it, cause it deserves every cent.
Hope that soon we'll see War in the West on Steam :)
P.S. Works on touch screen device, but 41-45 campaign will be hard to play.

I would pay $300.00 for this game if I could just get all of the time I wasted trying to get other WWII Barbarossa games to do what this game does so effortlessly, i.e. Unity of Command is a fun game but because it is smaller scale even in the map editor UoC couldn't deliver my craving for a balls deep plunge into wide open Russia during Barbarossa 41.  This game rewards the knowledge you gain from each turn, and you start feeling like those Kraut armies of yours are all your own well disciplined children that are ready to wreak sytematic havoc and destruction on the Russians ahead.  You will feel proud of them as they attack fearlessly, with you knowing Hitler's meddling won't do them in this time.  You are going to show the world what a well organized modern army can do to it's enemies.  (at least this is how I felt after getting comfortable with my personal Russian whoop♥♥♥♥♥mechanism).
Forget Road to Minks, just start with the 224 turn 41-45 Barbarossa map and start going balls deep into Russia.
You will be thinking what a bunch of German generals thought in the first few weeks, Moscow by Labor Day perhaps.
Little by little your respect grows for the enormity of this map, the challenges of supply, an enemy driven by the whims of a brutal dictator, and the wonders of finding yourself balls deep in a vast and mysterious Soviet landscape.  Just start over each time you learn something awesome so by the 3rd or 4th Barbarossa you are feeling much more confident with your boys because you have the needed "trigger time" from 20 or so hours of gameplay.  I like a game where I can say, "ok ♥♥♥♥♥es, hit me with your best shot, let's see what you got!" and still have fun if you fail to get an objective you set for yourself.  After 70ish hours of gameplay, the closest I have been to Moscow is within 15 hexes, and love how the game challenges me to capture that rathole at any cost.
POSITIVES:  I love the actual numbers of soldiers, etc, I love how the armees are set up for complete freedom of movement, I love I finally found a game that does THE ENTIRE EASTERN FRONT. Thank you Gary Grigsby, your photo is getting framed and going up next to Wagner and Nietzsche on the mantle.
NEGATIVES:  Jeez, we are going to need a powerful microscope to find some dirt here, let me think....ok...there are no naked chicks in this game.  After 70+ hours of gameplay, nothing significant is coming to mind.  It appears pretty polished at this point.  I just want to get back to the game.

So I'm not a massive fan of motorsport, but as an engineer I appreciate the technical challenge of getting a car round a track faster than anyone else within the confines of a ruleset. There's a balance and trade-off to be made with many different aspects of the car and driver.
The thing is whilst that is relatively simple to articulate, it's  completely different affair to begin to understand it. I mean, who has spare millions lying around to play around with a real motorsport team? Not many!
I got the game as the premise sounded interesting. Rather than driving the car, you would be in the pit lane directing the action. The question is, would this make an interesting experience. I'd tried Gran Turismo B-Spec mode before, and not really been enamoured with it. Would this be different, or just the same old same old in a slightly fancier outfit?
Diving into the game and just following the tutorial, it quickly became apparent that there was (a) a learning curve to go up and (b) there was more to the game than meets the eye. But it didn't really capture my attention until I started to make a few inspired ('lucky') strategic tyre decisions in a rainy race, and suddenly found myself no longer at the back of the pack but in the lead. All of a sudden it was a nail biting race to the finish as much faster drivers and cars slowly gained on my position... and fuel was getting low... would I even make it to the finish?
Most satisfying second place ever, and a realisation that if a game can draw me emotionally into watching virtual drivers go round a track, it must be doing something right.
This game is not another variation of a tried and tested formula. It's a little different. It will require you to think. It will require you to plan and strategise. It will require you to make some tough decisions.
What a gem.
Look forward to how the game continues to develop.

Motorsport Manager is a very good game as a whole. Managing a team competing in Single Seater racing series' is a lot of fun. You are kept quite busy tending to the needs of the cars, your HQ, and trying to win one of three levels of Single Seater competitions.
If you are even remotely interested in motorsports, and enjoy management games, this will probably appeal to you. Depending on the rules of the series you are in, you have available up to 6 parts of your vehicle that you can design. Parts are treated as a single stat for performance, such as Deceleration for Brakes, Top Speed for Engines, or Acceleration for Gearboxes. You can design new parts one at a time, generally improving the performance and affecting the parts max performance. In between races, you work on reliability and performance. Upgrading facets of your HQs allows you to improve reliability and performance on more parts at a time, but in the first couple seasons, you'll likely find reliability to be your biggest hurdle in the first handful of races. At the beginning of each season, you get to choose the suppliers for your various parts. This effects the rating of 4 different fields of your vehicle, as well as adding to the base stats of your parts. The best of each part adds to the base stat of that part the next year, so getting the best parts out each season benefits you. You also get to design that season's livery. The livery options are super lacking, even with the free DLC, but you can customize your vehicle to your liking, and that is a nice addition. Trying to get the best vehicle you can during pre-season is motivating and I really enjoy that part of the game.
Staff management is my biggest gripe of the game, however. Most sports management games allow you to interact with your staff in some manner to improve morale or train specific stats. In Motorsport Manager, you only get the occasional email asking you to resolve a dilemma that will, occasionally, have a positive effect on morale or driver-mechanic relationship. The majority of the time, you have to choose between missing out on money for a positive boost, or paying a bunch of money to prevent morale loss. There are other dilemmas that aren't directed at staff, and those generally have more beneficial outcomes. Worse still is trying to sign new drivers or staff. In other sports management games, you could interact with people who aren't employed by you in order to improve your chances of employing them. Not so in this game. Occasionally an interview will ask you about a winning driver and you'll have the opportunity to cause a temporary effect on a driver that makes them interested in joining your team. It is somewhat short lived, and you aren't always in the position to break your current driver's contract. Trying to find a driver who will join your team who will actually boost your team's ratings is also very difficult. After building the scouting facility I finally had the opportunity to hire a driver who was worth hiring, but that was 4 seasons in. Prior to that, roughly 80% of the drivers (or mechanics or designers) were uninterested in joining my team. I know I started as one of the worst teams in the game, but to think that I wouldn't be able to wave some money around at these people and get some interest is ridiculous. As for training drivers and staff, it is entirely down to which buildings you shell out the dough for. Some buildings increase the rate at which specific stats increase. While there are far less stats for the drivers than most sports management games, it still seems odd to me that you can't direct some sort of educational resources towards specific areas to shape your staff towards stats that would benefit your team.
Of course, this being a Motorsport management game, there are races. The series consists of somewhere around 10 to 13 races, although voting in the political gatherings of each series allows the addition or subtraction (as well as replacement) of tracks. Race weekends usually have a practice, may or may not have a qualifying, and then race day. Practice is a timed session where you can gain a perk in Race Trim (for race day) or Qualifying Trim (for qualifying) as well as perks in the tyre compounds that you bring to race weekend. You also have to dial in the car's set ups. Downforce, Handling, and Speed Balance are your continuums, and you must strike the perfect balance in each to get the best performance out of your drivers as well as your car. You get to choose two perks during qualifying and race. They grant a performance boost, based on level gained, to your car during each event. If your driver and mechanic gain a high enough relationship then there are 1 or 2 more perks, specific to the mechanic, available to choose. They grant a variety of different effects, such as faster refuelling, faster part fixes, wearing a tyre more slowly, or even decreasing the risk of a fast pit stop.
Managing race day is great. You have the option to attack, push, keep neutral, conserve, or back up your tyres, effecting tyre wear and heating. For fuel, you can select Overtake, High, Medium, or Low, causing significant changes in fuel consumption. Trying to manage your Tyres and Fuel between each pit is difficult, but entertaining. You'll feel the highs of a well-planned strategy succeeding as well as the lows of completely ruining everything as you throw your drivers on the wrong tyre compound hoping to beat the other drivers, only to realize the laps preceding optimal conditions allows your competition to absolutely dominate your lap times.
So, to sum up this review, I'll wrap things up with some pros and cons.
+ Trying to keep up on your parts against other teams is exciting and a big part of the game
+ Managing race day action is a lot of fun. You get to interact with the race the whole time. The tracks look pretty good, although the camera only zooms and spins.
~ At first dialing in your car's Downforce, Handling, and Speed Balance is enjoyable, but then you're several seasons in and you've done it enough already.
- Interacting with people. Why can't you try to butter up racers in your own league, or who aren't employed, to join your team? I could not find a single driver who was interested in joining my team until after I built the scouting centre.
- A severe lack of detail to the world in general. Interview questions begin repeating almost immediately. Driver traits are also lacking, and repeat just as quickly. I have only had 4 drivers, 2 at a time. Two drivers got the exact same traits. I feel that most Sports Management games do a better job of creating a believable environment for you to exist in.

A wonderful game for fans of the Harvest Moon series. World's Dawn is a beautiful game with a very interesting and (so far) likeable cast of characters. As in the HM fashion your character starts out with a farm that hasn't had an owner for a while in a small village, and it's up to you to liven things up again. There are festivals and different random events that happen and while the main plot of the game has yet to reveal all of itself to me, it's safe to say I'm excited to see what will happen.
The mechanics are so far a lot simpler that what you may go in expecting. Take farming for example, instead of a huge field that you have to clear out and will possibly never fill with crops and flowers, you have a small twenty plot field for your crops. There is also a simple mining and refining system, fishing took a few tries to get used to but it is also rather fun as well. The most annoying mechanic of the game would probably be how running reduces your precious endurance meter by a lot. Now, that wouldn't be such an issue if walking didn't feel so slow and the map felt so big. Perhaps walking will not but such a chore later in the game once I learn the map and increase said endurance meter.
Other than that tiny little critism so far, this game is very enjoyable. I would say the price it very fair for the amount of content and potential playtime you are getting. There are different things that make it stand apart from the Harvest Moon series itself, but it definitely feels like a love letter to the good old days of the farming simualtor series.

Though I'm not done my first season yet, I wanted to jot down some general first impressions. Overall I'm enjoying the game, though I have some gripes that I'll be focusing on.
Firstly, with a cast so large, it is difficult to keep track of all the characters. Moreso, their names. You're given a quest to meet and greet, and from there are given a primer booklet on all the Villagers, their likes and dislikes, and their Affection level. But even after that, remembering names is a bit difficult. Having a name tag alongside the text boxes would go a long way to ensuring players quickly begin to associate the names with the characters.
Secondly, the control bindings have NO context. I'm playing with an X-Box 360 Controller, and while it's working just fine, rebinding keys without knowing what each button does is a hassle. A more robust controls menu is a neccessity in my eyes.
Thirdly, I'm playing full screen on a 1920x1080 monitor, and while it upscales alright, I'm noticing what I think is so minor stretching. It may just be me, but I thought it was an important note. Another small note is, with as great as the character portraits are, I wish they weren't so pixelated at my resolution. Again, they seem to upscale decently, but I wish they looked cleaner.
Lastly, I just wanted to address a couple core issues I have with the game.
- The amount of farmland you start will become a bit restrictive. I know some people have probably harped on this already, but I feel it needs to be said that there should be more. I'm inheriting this legendary farmer's land, and this is all the space he's got to plant? Even if I can't use it all at first, I feel there should be more to it.
- The marriage options are a bit weak. Three girls to choose from is a bit shallow a pool, by this genre's standards, and there are a few women that I was surprised to find weren't available. Some of this comes to preference; many of the older women I find more attractive than the choices we currently have. Still, I'd prefer more options. If I had to be specific, the Nurse, Postwoman, and Artist were three women I was shock weren't courtable.
- There's a complete lack of tension throughout interactions. Most characters are more than happy and friendly to interact with, and though some characters claim others to be gruff, they're really not. Beyond that, character scenes so far don't really introduce anything but fluff. I get that the game wants to be very "feel-good", but it feels a bit flat that all characters seem to respond to you and others with a general cheerfulness or friendliness.
- Though for the moment there seems to be a greater plot line, without more sidequest-esque content, I'm worried about having things to do to keep invested in the game. If the sole objective is bonding with everyone to their max level, I'm not interested in doing that solely through a constant barrage of gifts. Or at the very least, without some objectives to do between.
Now despite my criticisms, I'm enjoying milling around the game, taking part in festivals and soaking in all that the game has to offer initially. How long that will last, I can't say. For the current asking price, I'm not sure that, say, 5-10 hours of milling around this pretty, fluffy world is worth it. But if the game finds ways to continue to engage me, I'd be more inclined to call the game worth the price to play.

Kudos to the developer--very receptive to feedback and quick to act upon it. The community had an issue with energy draining too quickly while running and the developer has already fixed it.
World's Dawn is more of a easy-going life sim than a farm sim, so there is virtually no conflict or antagonist, though the goals and quests do have rewarding outcomes and truly allow you to complete them at your own pace.
Even if you've never played a Harvest Moon game, pick this up and give it a shot! Highly recommended.

Spore is an interesting, different take on the classic god-type genre of games. You begin as a single cell organsim, happily eating (plants or other organisms, or both!) and eventaully running away or fighting other organisms. As you eat, you gain DNA, which is used to modify your creature, from eyes to appendages used to attack others or defend yourself, and other some modifications that do not require DNA, such as enlarging or reducing the size and shape of your creature, enlongating or shortening your spine, even individual segments of your spine!
After you consume enough DNA, you will be able to "find a mate" and change anything you like about your creature, including color, color patterns and layers of color and patterns, and anything else you can imagine. Really, the whole point that Spore really drives home is that your creations are only limited by your imagination. Once enough DNA and parts are gathered you can "evolve" to the next stage of evolution, in this case, evolving legs.
Once you crawl out of the primordial soup and make landfall, you will have a nest for your species to stay in, and the real adventure begins. You will meet other species and decide if you want to befriend them through either "Impressing" them through song and dance and whatnot, or kill them into extinction. In the next stage of evolution you have a third option to send them gifts, which they may or may not accept. Each decision you make affects the outcome of your creature. Befriending tribes gives you abilities to make it easier to befriend other species in the future, as does killing them, or gifting, the economic solution. Whenever you successfully befriend, or kill a species, you will be rewarded with new parts to help evolve your creature. Many of these at this stage have actual benefits, such as arms with hands that have sharp claws, which will aid you in taking down some of the tougher species, or other parts that boost your ability to sing, dance and otherwise impress other species. As with the previous stage, once you have collected enough DNA through befriending or conquering species, you will advance to the next stage of evolution, Tribal. (NOTE: When you finish creature stage, before you advance to tribal stage you will be given one last chance to change your creature in any way you see fit. Once you enter tribal stage, NO MORE CHANGES CAN BE MADE TO YOUR CREATURE.)
The tribal stage is arguably the most difficult stage because you really have to begin managing your resources. You have to gather food to feed your tribe, and plenty extra if you plan on gifting to other tribes. You have a village and as with the previous stage, instead of parts, you have buildings in your village that will assist your tribe in your goal. At this point it is a good idea to settle on whether you plan on being a war-mongering military society, a happy-go-lucky religious society (you still sing and dance to befriend other tribes, but in the next stage you basically convert new species to your religion in order to become allies) or an economic powerhouse (in the near future, capable of purchasing entire star systems). Once you have  enough allies or conquor enough tribes, you advance to the next stage, Civilization.
Civilization stage is much like the creature stage, in that it opens up the game into a new level of depth and this time, micro-management. You will discover Spice, the source of all income, and mine the various spice gysers near and far to increase your income (which replaces DNA) and go crazy with creation. Much like your original creature, you can choose from a preset list from Maxis, or if you signed in at the beginning of the game (or at any time for that matter) you can use or modify any creation by any person who has played Spore. Of course, you can also create your own from the ground up, including a Town  Hall, a Factory, Houses, and Entertainment buildings. You can use these in city planning to create a well-balanced city. Too many factories will boost spice processing, but make your city unhappy and easily susceptible to religious attacks, which are much more effective against unhappy cities. Too many entertainment buildings will make your city happy, but your spice production will suffer. You will learn the proper balance with time, experiment and try different things, which is what Spore is all about! Anyway the objective of this stage is to destroy or ally yourself with other rival factions of your species, which has become the single most dominant sentient creature on your planet. Of course you can also establish trade routes with rival cities and eventually be given the option to purchase them, making them as much yours as a city you started with. Again, eventually you will destroy or ally yourself with all the rival factions on your planet, and advance to the final stage, Space.
This is by far and away the most fun stage in the game, and once you reach space stage with one species, you can start a new species at any stage (Cell, Creature, Tribal, Civilization, or Space) any time you wish. Your species has advanced enough to begin space flight! From this point, the universe is your oyster! The same ways you haved allied yourself, purchased, or conquered others until now remain the same, although, remember that at least in the beginning of space stage, your species exists on but one planet, whereas other species you meet will be spread across several planets and even start systems! If you want an accurate scope of just how huge this game is, zoom out from your planet, to your start system, complete with other planets, to your local star system cluster to eventually the entire galaxy. Every start system, every planet you see you can visit! You can establish colonies on new worlds to expand your empire, meet new species and decide how to deal with them, do missions for them, hunt for valuable artifacts, and even terraform planets from T0 (No atmosphere, very difficult to sustain a profitable colony) to a T3 oasis, with several booming colonies, ripe for the picking with all different kinds of Spice! From this point you can do whatever, go wherever, whenever you want!
All in all, if you like creative freedom, an explorative nature, and want to build your own galaxy spanning empire from a single celled organism to the most powerful species in the galaxy, this game is for you! (On a side note, Spore and Spore Creepy and Cute Parts Pack are completely compatible with Windows 8.1)
