is a Third-Person-Shooter with a cover system set in the future after catastrophic events led the world to some major changes.
In 2080, due to climate changes, the world faced the large flood ever existed, and in search for cheap, reliable labor, the humanity turned to robots, in hope for a better future. To lead this revolution is Bergen, a US-based company, responsible for manufacturing robots for all over the world. But Bergen is not the only one in the business. Amada, a Japanse company, sued Bergen for stealing their technology. Bergen won, much because of its influence... They do manufacture over 90% of world robots, and this made the USA more powerful than ever!
Tension between both companies grew, and to appease everyone's peace of mind, the "
" was created; A new set of rules that determines how far both companies can go in terms of investigation regarding Artificial Intelligence. To impose such law, a world team of the best soldiers was united, nicknamed "
". These brave men step in if any law is broken, and of course we wouldn't have a game if everyone played by the rules...
We take the role of Dan Marshall, an American member of the Rust Crew, who together with a group of interesting soldiers, fight against the production of Hallow Children; robots that look exactly like humans, and believe to be humans, mixed in the society!
Without giving away spoilers,
was (at least in my perspective) heavenly influenced by
, but in a fantastic away, managing to keep a story and spirit of its own.
The eternal intellectual argument is still present, but makes it hard to discuss such issues since the Hallow Children do not wish harm naturally, but like any robot, can be hacked to one's will.
The designer
(
series), managed to give authenticity and atmosphere to the game, with a fantastic personality to each character, and to the whole group. The interactions are extremely well made, with decisions to make that affect the outcome of encounters. Depending on the chosen strategy, answer or decision, will result in a positive or negative point towards the team. This method was so well implanted that if the player has a microphone, he can give vocal orders to the partners. Doesn't work flawlessly, but it's a fantastic idea. Manual choices are obviously included, with dozes of possible options and results. Boost team's morale, make them sad or angry, or just complement their work. It's all up to you. Team party builds up is also a possibility, with a special romantic outcome, and a friendship that outlasts any war.
isn't just about shooting, but it's probably what anyone will spend more time doing so. As an action game with a cover system, I must say it takes inspiration from
, and the result is fantastic. The cover system works flawless, (but be careful for weak cover spots), blind fire, and fast shooting when leaving cover is quite stable and perfect for high-paced players like myself. Don't feel like having your partners doing all the work? Go out there and destroy any robots you want with a fantastic selection of weaponry from grenades, pistols, machine guns, and yours and truly; the Assault Rifle with a Shock Burst! A nice feature that bursts a energy impulse that if upgraded enough can cause massive damaged.
Although picking up weapons from enemies is possible, the game also includes these amazing and cute vending machines that sell all sorts of weaponry, and giveaway some bonuses as part of an automatic lottery game that I just find it hilarious.
In this same machine, upgrading weapons and skills for each member is also available. Increasing health, fire rate, reload speed, and all sorts of enhancements to make your party stronger.
The level design is unique and portraits a futuristic Japan, with a wide variety of scenarios, from suburban areas, to Yakuza districts and even Amada building itself. Every area is pretty much a fantastic place for a fight, with covers not disrupting the environments, but instead, taking a part in the fight.
Mechanically,
is a perfect example of how Third Person Shooters with cover should be, but it still has some flaws. Some encounters are frustrating to fight in, due to how impractical they are comparing how much there is to fight against the space of the AI abilities. This reflects in the boss's, as some are fun to do, amazing and leaves you wishing for more, and others are just boring insipid and don't do justice to this amazing game.
Enemies differ from soldiers to heavies, and pretty much any other class you expect in this kind of game. They are all robotic forms, and shooting their body-plates can sometimes peal them, to reveal weak points!
Any action fan can easily relate to this title, as shooting robots become very satisfying very soon, and trying out higher difficulty modes such as No-Mercy will put you to the test. Unfortunately New Game+ doesn't let you keep any upgrades you might have, and that's a shame.
is one of my favorite games, it has everything I love; Great action moments where the player's skills really mater, deep story, characters that are interesting and react differently to each situation and based on the party chosen. An intriguing plot, that just keeps getting your attention with moral questions.
Can we really kill a robot for not being human, when he deeply believes he is? How is that not a murder? What makes us humans? Bones instead of metal? Or emotions, and if so, how we can't tell if Hallow Children doesn't love, fear, or hate?
This game is about human conditions, what they mean, and how far are we ready to go to keep our own condition alive?

This game is actually pretty good, for how short it is. You know what, scratch that, I wish it was longer. That's perfectly okay with me, though. I checked out this game because of it's cool pixel noire art style and general lack of color, making it feel like some old action thriller. Pros:
-Cool art style
-Good, jazzy soundtrack
-Tight controls
-Decent challenge
-Good use of sparing colors
-Simple mechanics and level design
-Easy to complete
Cons:
-Very, very short (which might be a problem for some)
-Only tells you how to switch weapons after level 2
-Unclear story
-A bit lacking in enemy variety
Overall, Rot Gut is a simple, straight forward action platformer that I (and probably you) could beat and complete in less than half an hour. And for $2, I'd say it's a pretty good way to kill some time and have some quick fun.

I can't really recommend this game at all. Everything about it, from its brevity to the lack of controller support to the pointless (so to speak) mouse cursor on screen during gameplay [you can, of course, move the cursor to the corner of the screen to hide it, but WHY IS IT THERE ANYWAY?], screams "attempt to cash in on what was once a free Flash game". There's no enemy AI to speak of: you shoot a guy, jump to dodge his bullets as he turns and shoots you, then he immediately forgets about you and begins to walk away. Repeat until he's a puddle of red pixels. Why can your character, a hardboiled noir badass, do a double jump? There's nothing gritty about that. There are six short levels, and the pause menu allows you to skip every single one of them, as I discovered when I got bored around Act IV. Oh, and you still get the level completion achievements for the levels you skip. I can't tell if there's a story; you just murder everyone and everything you encounter. Vending machines are scattered throughout the levels, because why not. You push up (or W) to spend some of the coins that flow like gibs when blasting barrels and boxes (and the occasional miniboss). The only problem with this is that because of how the keys are bound, jumping also activates the vending machine. In other words, you can't jump in front of a vending machine. You can only spend. It took me probably 70 misspent in-game dollars to finally learn my lesson. In Rot Gut's defense, the gameplay mechanics, while basic, are pretty solid, although my appreciation of this was dampened by having to use the keyboard rather than a gamepad for the controls. The pixel graphics are... better than some pixel graphics, anyway. In the brief time I spent playing this, I encountered only one notable glitch, when a (normally non-jumping) enemy jumped off a ledge and sort of hovered in the air above me for a while before I put him out of his misery. My favorite part of this game, by far, is its cover image on the store page. And of course, it's relatively cheap. All the same, I have a case of the buyer's remorse. If you want a good Noir platformer, try Gunpoint. In fact, I might just re-play that right now. Damn, that was a good game. In conclusion: I think I spent more time writing this review than I did playing Rot Gut, and I definitely had more fun writing this review than I did playing Rot Gut.

The Elder Scrolls III Morrowind can be described in two words, Simply Amazing.  The combat system was absoulutley awful, because it was a system where your weapon had a chance to completely miss your target.  Spells hod a similar system where the spell had a chance not to cast at all.  The main part of the game is exploration.  With no fast travel system other than the Silt Strider you'll find yourself walking almost everywhere, because the Silt Strider costs monry for every use.  The immense number of side quests originated in this entry, and has been every newer entry, including ESO (Elder Scrolls Online).  Morrowind is challenging and downright unforgiving at times, so it could be quite hard to go back to playing, ecpecially after playing Skyrim.  Altogether The Elder Scrols III Morrowind is my favorite in the twenty year old series, and in my opinion earned a 10/10 score in 2002, and even now holds up to the 10/10 score.

This is, in my opinion, the best of the Elder Scrolls series thus far.  The gameplay, other than the combat, is much more immersive and entertaining.  Additionally the possibility of making your own spells and potions with enchantments as powerful as you can imagine to make them make the game hilariously fun once you improve the skill to make them.  Admittedly, the AI in this game is not as "sophisticated" as Oblivion or Skyrim, but I don't think anyone can argue that this game, if it were given the AI of Oblivion or Skyrim, would be way better.  As for the graphics, a quick graphics mod puts Morrowind right up there in the league with Oblivion and Skyrim and runs smoother than the two recent games because of its less demanding graphics engine.  Highly recommended for roleplayers that prefer the old style of games and are frustrated with the newer streamlined RPGs

Possibly the best entry in the series, Metal Slug 3 is a crazy ride that will have you laughing, crying, and sometimes saying WTF?  From start to finish the game can be completed in about an hour, but there are multiple paths to take in the levels with different vehicles to try.  Its all about trying to increase your score and master the gameplay.
The MS series is a fast paced run & gun side scroller thats all about collecting powerups to give you the edge over the enemies and getting the highest score you can.  Along the way you'll encounter a large variety of enemies not found in MS 1 or 2.  The level design this time around is top notch which gives it an edge over other entries in the series.
Metal Slug can certainly be frustrating at times.  It was designed to eat your quarters in the arcade and it aims to kill you repeatedly and quickly.  This can be overcome with practice and learning the layouts of the levels.  The high difficulty can be countered by switching the difficulty down to an easier level (not possible in the original version).
Possibly the best thing in this version of Metal Slug 3 is the inclusion of online multiplayer.  Its very easy to set up a game and invite someone else to play with you.  Its only 2 player, but at least they don't have to be in the same room playing on the same computer with you.
Overall the game is pretty funny and easy to just pick up and play.  The achievements are also a nice addition and something to work for while mastering the game.

I was a child of the Steppes born to a group of nomads. After I grew up, I became a peddler until I was forced out of my new found homeland.
I fled as a refugee to Tulga in the kingdom of the Khergit Khanate, and was quickly placed into slavery after leaving the town on a quest to help a man from the tavern. My early life after that was spent with different masters, switching hands the moment I ran from my captors. Bandits and army men of the Khergit Khanate looked the same to me as both would take me captive. I travelled long distances before I could escape; months passed before my very eyes. Sometimes between masters I would raise a militia, and even found a companion, Rolf, to share my difficulties. However, each time we were defeated and Rolf was taken prisoner in Ichmaur.
Eventually I came to the Sarranid Sultanate near their south-eastern border with the Khergits as a runaway slave. I was terrified of the bandits and army men alike at first, but the army men there let me be. To protect myself from the bandits, I hired and trained a band of men under my command against them until we grew so strong as to be a match for the generals of the Sultante. As my reknown grew with the stories of my adventures by word of my companions, my fellow ladies brought up how I should have been a vassal of the Sultante by now, if not for my being a lady.
So I saught out Sultante Hakim and pledged under his banner. Under oath, he gave me a banner of my own to which I chose one of black and white to harmonize my rough upbringing and start on life to that of a pirate and vigilante. The other vassals came to respect me as my men and myself fought bravely alongside them with swords and bows in place of sticks and knives. Alright...
This is coming from someone who created a few unreleased video games growing up and now mainly work on 3D modeling and design...
The pros I have to say is:
1. Cute little game that could be fun and a little time waster.
2. The music is really nice. First level will be stuck in my head for the day.
3. The idea is there and the concept isn't too bad.
But here comes the cons.... WATCH OUT! (Will just do them point by point and then elaborate completely)
1. Seeing major flaws in some of the layouts of the levels, especially the 3D models and a few incomplete areas.
2. Artificial difficulty.
3. Only in Spanish (It's Spanish, right...? I know it's some form of espanol or maybe Italian)
4. Few hipcups within certain areas
5. Bad beta testing.
The concept like I said is there and isn't too bad... I'm guessing some ETs came from outer space and started to controlling everything and you need to rip off the heads of those they're controlling because they're too far gone to be saved. I think?
The problem though is it's easy to tell that a lot of the stuff was copy and pasted/plastered within the levels and except for certain areas weren't really thought out well in placements.
Like the final level... why felling wooden blocks near the final boss? I know you wanted it to look like a one way only, but you could've added other assests to get that idea. Maybe have a steel/metal bridge that while you're heading to the boss it falls apart and is on fire? Maybe have when that giant burglar come after you is how the bridge gives out?
Oh and the giant burglar... the reason he's big? That didn't really make much sense and might've made more sense if a smaller species that the final boss is should be chasing you.
And then stuff like floating crates you can climb in the final level and other areas or... I think it was th 3rd level where you started going down into a pit or tunnel, but then you go down even more as the level goes on and you see a city pasted in the background just halfway down the chase... so how high up were you as it didn't make much sense to me?
Oh, and in certain parts you can see that there's no bottom to some of the builldings and you can see right through them and see some of the windows and other incomplete textures. Best not let the player come from an angle or area where models are incomplete as it shows as sloppy work... which you don't want seen.
Artificial difficulty... artificial difficulty... where do I begin...
Level 1 seemed fine, but level 2 really started to get a bit stupid. Random knock-off bullet bills popping up out of no where right behind you and just start chasing you. And they usually chasing you down a path of enemies that are literal bullet sponges meaning you can't stop to attack the bullet bill creature or you take a hit, or you keep running and if you're going after coins, you better not screw up or you'll have to start over as there's most times no where to go rather than to actually take a hit.
The final 2 levels did that same thing with those bullet bills and even worse... especially the final level where you have a rain of mini bullet bills the burglar is shooting at you, a ton of drones that takes a million shots to kill, crazy lunatics that throw grenades at you... and sometimes 2 in one spot... and how can I forget that Cheetah/Leopard Cat thing in a suit that moves so fast and takes way way waaay too long to kill in just Normal Mode.
Oh and I did mention normal mode in that last line? Hard Mode is just Normal Mode with a few adde enemies and drones  within the level and now they take like 3x to 4x longer to kill. The level layout is the same... all that was done was upped the HP and a few extra enemies. That's bad.
Oh and the final boss took about 20 minutes to kill and only because of the damn overdone HP boost in hard mode. Just rubbish.
Mi espanol is muy mal. Like mega mal. Failed Spanish in school since as a child and only got out of going back to Spanish class by an.... agreement...
Enough about me that, but I do know half of the time when starting the game I just hit "si" when it asked me things as I had no clue what I was agreeing to (if I agreed to give you my soul... I already sold it for a crate of Godiva chocolate years ago, sorry...), and the achievements I gave up understanding except for the "Vidas" (which I guess is lives) and "Nivel" which I guess is Level. I did achieved all of the achievements, but it's through just playing and dumb luck.
I'm not asking to have a Japanese or an English option, but more than one could help... I know some or one of you know at least English as I saw the discussion board.
There's a few bad sections in certain areas of the game. Sometimes the character would go through the floor... or half of it whether they have the rocket belt on, or maybe going from one platform to another of a different style. The climbing on the crates, I've got stuck on them a few times as well.
I'm not going to hold you against this though as it seems like a game I would've made in my preteens/early teens and just a bit unpolished. I would guess this is one of the first games you guys worked on so it won't be a glorious masterpiece.
The call on bad beta testing is mostly due to all of the above that I've mentioned.
The problem with hard mode, the problem with certain things not working with other things, the problem with clipping or going through what should be solid, the atrocious placement of some of the enemies... just to add some difficulty just for the sake of it..., the final boss itself and how it's done, and much more I've already listed and I won't say again like a broken record... broken record... record...
As for how the game is right now, there is no way I can recommend it. It would need a lot of retouching and testing before I can do so.
3/10 and 3 of those points is mostly due to 1 being for the music and 2 for making me travel down memory lane when I used to make little video games for myself/family/friends back from the early to mid 2000s.
Don't let this bring you down. You just need to do a hell of a lot better next time. Good luck and have a good Sunday/Monday (wherever you live on the planet.... but seeing the ending shows a really bad drawn of what I guess is California.. I say Sunday)

Gobernators could easily been a fantastic game and a must if you're a free game hunter. Has everything we could hope for; It's free, it has a real cause into it, and it's extremely fun to play. A simple 2.5D shooter that isn't pretentious, but fails on one simple aspect; Doesn't respect your time.
I can't and I won't talk about the graphics, because we all know they're simple but very colorful. The gameplay is basic but has a few politicians to play with. No special moves per character though.
The game gives you 9 lives to start with. This means you can die 9 times in a level, but if you have hearts (up to three) you can avoid death. The checkpoints are actually really well placed, but even if you waste all your lives, it means the level start again.
This was very common in the old classic games, but guess what? Video games moved on. We came a  long way in this industry to still be attached to the most frustrating thing ever. Repeating a level must always be an option, this rule is essential to me, in any video-game. Therefore, my review could never be positive.
It is not a matter of difficulty, but of honor. Concepts, stories, and gameplay can be inspired by the past, but to bring back mechanics worthy of an arcade machine is not my ideal of a good time!
With unlimited lives per level, I might have put in the time to finish the game. I'm sure any hardcore fan of arcade games can learn to enjoy Gobernators, and have a great time.

As more and more creatures inhabit the world, and as evolution forms the future, your species will join herds, clans, even civilizations. The more advanced the creatures of the planet grow, the more complex the strife of survival becomes. And while the player can continue gameplay in Spore at any level -- playing as a cell, as a wild creature, or as a civilized and organized society – players can also step even further out and play the game from the planetary or interstellar level, while also going online to connect worlds with other gamers.

Honestly, this isn't worth the money I didn't pay for it. When I first booted up the game, The graphics were, quite literally, pixelated. I tried changing my resolution, toggling settings, and everything I could but it just wouldn't fix the issue. I wouldn't really consider this major for anyone else, because it's entirely possible this is a personal bug.
Second of all, there's the issue that the game is very much pay-to-win. The First 3 games I played, it was nearly impossible for me to survive- Not because of a lack of skill, but because as soon as I left my spawn area I would be killed by someone in an Expensive tank, or Shot by someone with a Paid-for Sniper. Newer players are given a tutorial that really only teaches basic gameplay, like shooting- stuff most people already know- and then are thrown into the action, clueless, and usually dominated by More experienced players with more items.
The Gameplay is relatively boring. The Movement feels jittery and unnatural, and the shooting could be improved greatly. The Hit-Registration seems to be a bit off, with bullets seeming to fly straight through some players, and the teamplay is horrid. Where you'd expect squads of people to be working together to capture an objective, you find people running over others with bicycles. To make it even worse, on most maps, you have to sit there walking for five minutes to even reach a conflict. The game is so buggy it's comparable to Bethesda AI, or a Ubisoft Title, and the Updates and Patches only break the game even further. The Devs seem more intrigued with gathering money from the players rather than actually helping them. The only real Plus side is that Devs are quick with reports. I personally find the menus to be a bit confusing, but I'm not concerned about that since it doesn't seem to be an issue amongst other players.
If it weren't for the fact that this game is free, I'd be asking for my money back.

This was a nice surprise! I did not even read carefully the description....I thought the game was something completely different....some sort of sci-fi exploration game  with a slow pace (my bad) but it's not.
The game is in 1st person view, it uses Unreal Engine 3 and will last about 4 or 5 hours. It is mostly about exploration, with some puzzles and few platforming fast sections.
You begin without knowing anything about yourself, or where you are. There is very little voice acting, you can understand the story only if you carefully find the pieces of lore scattered around the levels (not hard to find at all, and that is good).
Slowly you can put pieces together and understand what is happening. The story is quite nice and I like the narration more than the story and realization of the game.
Some levels are really well done, and it was also quite scary for me (some levels I had to play them without sounds). I am very sensitive when it comes to horror games....I am often scared of my own shadow. Horror elements: there are cheap jumpscare elements but there are also some nice touches. Definitely this game is not about being horror obviously.
Once I began playing, I could not stop, mostly because I had not such high expectations for the game and was definitely surprised. For sure there are much worse walking simulators out there.

I'm not quite finished with this game yet, but feel compelled to review as I'm hopped up with a head swimming in thoughts about it but it's too late in the night to finish.
Master Reboot is short of masterpiece status solely on account of simple graphics and a few non-intuitive puzzles; easy puzzles, but ones in which the solution is achieved by randomly clicking and with no logic between action and solution (here's looking at you, playground).
The pros far outweigh the cons. The puzzles and environments are varied, never repetitive; the story is haunting, pieced together by messages and pictures you get from optional blue ducks, reversed engineered as you progress; the demons(?) are creepy as hell and made me jump every single time, sometimes just in anticipation. The music, environments and atmosphere all combine for a disturbing and horrific reason to stay up until 3am.
I would definitely recommend, and will be getting Wales Interactive's next game Soul Axiom just as soon as it's out of early access.

A fantastic bit of mind-bending, high-concept, hard sci-fi wrapped in a heart-wrending doomed love story wrapped in an actually-kind-of-mediocre horror game.
(Minor spoilers ahead, kind of)
It's not like it has bad atmosphere or anything, it's just not incredibly scary. Part of that is down to the level design. The story kind of mandates that the levels be haphazard jumbles (it'll make sense when you play it), but that means that the gameplay tends to devolve into traipsing around samey environments hunting for various keys for various doors, and monotony kind of spoils the otherwise-excellent atmosphere. Many times, the game would attempt a jump-scare, or the soundtrack would freak out in such a way as to indicate that a jump-scare was supposed to be happening somewhere, but they forgot to do the work of making me look in that direction first. That's not to say it didn't make me jump when the various horror elements
line up, but the design could stand some tightening up.
That's all a shame, because when the game is at its peak, the experience is to die for. Repetetive environments notwithstanding, the visual design is generally gorgeous, presenting a unique and vibrant virtual world that manages to vary respectably while maintaining a coherent art style. From an aesthetic standpoint, it's absolutely fantastic, even if it's really nothing new in terms of horror elements. Little girls with supernatural powers and psychological issues? Seen it. Childrens' toys coming to life? Seen it. Ominous graveyards? Seen it. Deserted fairgrounds? Seen it. Not a deal-breaker, but it just makes the actual points of novelty seem few and far between. I wish it could have been as rich to experience as it is to look at, is my point. There's one plot point (really trying not to spoil here) that crescendos towards the climax in a way that makes it seem like it's going to go somewhere completely insane and mind-blowing...and then it doesn't.
All that criticism aside, I still did play through to the end and I would recommend it for its excellent storytelling regardless of any technical issues.There are several really intense emotional moments, and it's refreshing to see a work all about the digital age and transhumanism that actually has a
it's trying to make. And if you can look past a couple of imperfections in the design, this one will reel you in like few others can.

While the game has a good premise and great atmosphere; it suffers from abstract puzzles and design flaws.
First off - If you don't like jump scares, probably best to stay away. There's several in this game; and while they're not so prevalent that they get annoying; some just seem unnecessary.
Level design felt average; with nothing standing out that made me excited. Some were cool ideas, while some felt tacked on just to add another puzzle.
The dev's have gone with a sort of "abstract art" sheme with polygons and 'blocky' models. While this is all good when done right; sometimes it seems they did it simply to "cut corners". Some models look straight out of a game from the mid-90's (i.e. the airplane). Round objects like pillars and orbs have straight edges; a lot of textures are very low quality or non-existent, and lighting felt very basic. It's as if they went for a cell-shaded game but didn't quite commit.
This doesn't necessarily take away from the game, but it definitely doesn't add to it; and there several times when I was left wondering "why did they do that?"
The puzzles range from your typical "library maze" and "simon says" to some that are so abstract and "outside of the box" that they become frustrating.  Most of the puzzles are "trial and error"; with nothing really explaining what the goal is.
Some are so "out there", that it takes incredibly long to do something that should be simple. This leaves you wandering around trying to find anything that you might have mised; when usually there nothing else and it's just by chance or luck that you figgure it out.
Some puzzles are designed well, but are frustrating because of poor level design i.e. switches that don't work unless you're in the perfect spot; activating switches that are close to others will activate the undesired one; or something hiding in the shadows. It feels very clunky and unintuitive compared to most puzzle games.
The story itself is interesting; but it suffers from the long "pauses" of trying to solve these abstract puzzles that don't relate in any way to the story, and you start to loose interest. There's also no voiceovers for the cutscenes showing the "past"; so you sit in complete silence watching the story unfold.
In a game like this, lighting is key. However, while the "ambient" lighting is fantastic; lighting on objects and models is horrid. There is no dynamic lighting, so you don't get the "shadow play" effect that creeps you out even more.
Static shadows are grainy, murky messes. The flashlight (which is only in a few levels) only lights up a (polygon) cone and doesn't cast shadows and is full of glitches. Most un-lit corners are pitch black while there's a light 2 feet away. This actually takes away from the game as it keeps players from exploring, (or even seeing) most of the level.
All in all, it's an OK game with very few good puzzles, and while the story is presented poorly, it's not a terrible premise. If you get this game I'd recommend getting it during a sale, so if you get frustrated you don't feel so guilty about letting it go.
I can only recommend this game if you get it for cheap, and\or if you REALLY like puzzle games no matter how abstract or obtuse they are.

Hotline Miami 2 : Wrong Number is, of course, the sequel to the game Hotline Miami, created by Dennaton Games, and published by Devolver Digital. Let's waste no time and get right into the game.
The answer to both of those questions is yes. Wrong Number is quite harder compared to the first one, as it also comes with a "Hard Mode" you unlock after beating the game for the first time, which, if you found the first game easy, shouldn't be overly hard, maybe with a few exceptions. But if you found the first game hard? Good luck, buddy. One of the things that makes this game harder than the first one is the level design, sometimes. Some enemies will be in big open areas, or smaller ones that, coupled with the other enemies in the room, can either make the level hell for you, or a breeze. (Unless there's multiple windows in the room.) Again, it boils down to skill. Also with the numerous characters (which I will talk about soon) and different playstyles the come with.
The gameplay is also, in my opinion, slightly improved, compared to the first one. Controls are a little more tight and responsive, and feel pretty solid. The amount of new weapons is also welcoming, with there being even more brutal ways to smash someone's skull or obliterate enemies with gunshots.
The game takes place in multiple time periods, ranging from before the first game, during it, and after it, focusing mostly on the events that take place inbetween October and December of 1991. The story is all over the place, as in one level, you're in the time period in which the first game took place, playing as an operative similar to Jacket, then, you're in Hawaii, fighting off Soviet soldiers in the middle of the war between the USA and the Soviet Union. One thing I love about this game more than the first one is the settings of the levels. You go to a dockyard, a nightclub, a bank, into the sewers below Miami. Hawaii, etc.
You play as a bunch of characters. The Son, who is, well, the son of the leader of the Russian mafia who Jacket killed in the first game, Manny Pardo, a disheveled, rough cop who is looking into the case of a killer known as the "Miami Mutilator", Evan Wright, a writer trying to uncover the truth behind Jacket's story, and who the callers who left the odd messages on his answering machine are, among others. The game does a good job of quickly establishing who these people are and why they're important to the story. They all serve some purpose to the game, and they're not just there to exist and breathe.
This is a question I often can't figure out, because both soundtracks are amazing. I honestly think they're tied equally, as both of them are just equally amazing. While artists from the first game like Perturbator, Scattle, El Huervo, and M.O.O.N. return, new artists have arrived, like Magic Sword, Mega Drive, Carpenter Brut, and Mitch Murder. All of them, as well as the other new artists, are a great addition to the game, as they also come with more variety, music and artist wise.
Well, there's a few reasons. One of them is the Genocide achievement. Literally one of the worst achievements in Steam history. I don't hate grinding at all usually, but this is just simply insane. Another one, an actual flaw, is that some of the levels on Hard Mode are just, often, very unfair. There's really only two levels like this, but still, it's just bad design and enemy placement. Another thing, while it is also a great part of the game, is the level design. Some of the level design is honestly just, uh, below average. Other than that, that's really all that's wrong with it.
Hotline Miami 2 : Wrong Number is a fantastic game, just like the first game in the series, with a killer soundtrack, great gameplay, a really, really good story, and with a bunch of replayability.
Final score : 9.5/10.

Gone Home and Outlast had a baby, they've called it Layers of Fear.
The story is both deep and cryptic (dare I say layered), and will keep pulling you through the next door despite the increasing sense of dread.
There are numerous jumpscares and a general unnerving creepiness, which is a clever reflection of what goes on in the protagonist's mind. No weapons, no chases, no violence to speak of, just a plain old-school atmospheric nightmare.
The game has different endings, which are triggered by how you play it (what teases your curiosity, how you respond to certain events as they happen, etc). The ending I got is the perfect reflection of what appealed to me the most in the game, which was very satisfying.

First of all, I've played this for at least 100 hours on an older and different account. I saw it cheap during the summersale, so I decided to pick it up incase someone else would.
The Ship is a game about killing, or to be killed. The array of weapons is enourmus, not to speak of hidden ways to kill (Locking them into a freezer!). The map designed is amazing, there's secret passages and stashes you can use to fool less knowing players and while some might seem a bit small - the majority are unique and good in their own way. The game has a very special early 1900's theme to it, with fitting music playing in the background and visuals to go along with it. That said, neither the audio or art design is state of the art. (It is pretty old by now.) However, it all goes together in a sort of cartoony' but bloody murder party.
As for the game, it is divided up into three different downloads. Previously The Ship and The Ship Singleplayer have been separate, but now they're two in one. The Ship is the main multiplayer game where the most fun is to be had. The Ship Singleplayer is as it sounds the games singleplayer campaign. The whole story is rather weak however, but it's great to play for variation and to learn the game. (Which I honestly think they had in mind.) The Ship Tutorial is as it sounds - a tutorial.
A.t.m. I am playing this relatively alone. There's in general filled servers you can join (Use the steam server browser, the one IG is broken!) and the community, although small is in general mature and friendly. That said, in order to get the most out of the game you should play it as a Co-Op title with a voice chat program like Skype, mumble, etc.
For its price, especially during sales when it goes as far as 80% off; it's totally worth. Even just playing on public servers alone or with a friend.

is a Platformer with a Noire-themed aesthetic that is minimalistic in gameplay but contains loads of personality in 25 minutes. The theme is black-and-white/grayscale with red highlights. You play as Unnamed Agent Man in the Prohibition Era of the US. Agent Man sees the murder of a man and follows, finding the body to be disposed of into an incinerator. From here the game is played as a 2D-Platformer with 2 guns available at the start. There are nice little details in this game, like how early on you receive a chest placed pretty clearly to teach you how to better use your Double Jump. Also notable is the cigar in mister Agent's mouth. It glows red and smoke comes up from it. Even if it's a small touch like that, a well-put detail is very much appreciated. There are 3 weapons in total, one of which being unlocked after one of the two(yes, two) boss battles. Enemy variety is pretty small, at about 6 enemy-types seen by the end of the game. The more interesting one includes the dog, which adds a small twitch reaction to the game whenever you think the way is clear. The music is very much of the 20's, being made up of jazzy chiptune pieces meant for looping, and is one of the strongsuits of

.
Overall, while the enemy variety is lacking as well as the game being incredibly short,
was incredibly fun with catchy music and nice little details like the cigar and the transitions between levels. However, if 25 minutes doesn't sound like a good amount of time to spend with the game, then I wouldn't recommend buying it, as I'm honestly one of the worst Platformer gamers out there and I still finished this game in the stated timeframe. edit: I recieved the game for free from SEGA's Make War Not Love 3 competition/promotion a while ago, and have just got around to playing it now.
pros:
Very good story with multiple endings
The game lets you shoot specific parts off of the robot enemies you get to face in this game, and it just feels really satisfying. For example, you can shoot the legs off a robot, and it will start crawling towards you, if you shoot the arms off, it will try to charge you and melee attack you, or if you shoot it's head off, it will start attacking other enemies for you.
Runs pretty smooth on a GTX 950 pair with an AMD x4 860k. According to steam's built in fps counter, I got 60 fps in gameplay, with it rarely dropping, and then 30fps in cutscenes only.
neutral:
The game has a voice command system for your squad in game. It is completely possible to complete the game without using this voice command system, and it's what I did when I beat the game, but it's also a very gimmicky system.
cons:
Has some very wierd mouse acceleration when playing with keyboard and mouse (It is very hard to describe how bad it is, but once you play it you'll know)
When playing with kb + mouse, some on screen button prompts are confusing. For example, every time a quick time event or tutorial wants you to use any of the mouse buttons, it just shows an "M" key icon for the action.
AI for your squadmates is a little rough. They can sometimes run right infront of you when you're firing, and when they do that they get angry in game at you.
Overall verdict: Despite the really janky mouse aiming, in the end I really enjoyed playing this game (and I used kb+m controls the entire playthrough). A few bosses aren't very good gameplay-wise, but overall the story was compelling enough that I strongly recommend this game, and I had enough fun shooting arms and legs off of robots that I'd strongly recommend this. Pick it up on sale, if you can't handle the janky aiming then refund it, otherwise you're in for a good time.

The developers got it spot on.  Any racing management game must still come down to the racing.  Motorsport Manger has nailed it !  And it is thrilling.
For example:
Having selected the top team to play, imagine the excitement of being in 4th place a little less that 20 seconds behind 3rd, 2nd and 1st.  My pit stops are done and they still have to come in.  When the do, my drive is directed to burn everything, fuel, tires etc. to catch them in the pits.  Can he do it???  1st place is about to exit the pit when my driver comes sweeeping down the main straight and passes him just as he exits !!!  What fun.  Or another instance when my driver was trailing 1st place by less than 2 seconds, but fuel is running low and the tires are worn.  I need my scheduled pit stop, so I resign to coming in and losing contact with 1st place.  Lo and behold he comes in right in front of me.  My team give me a great pit stop.  When we pull out of our stalls, we are side by side, drag racing down pit road (at 40 MPH pit road max speed) !   Exiting the pit, I edge into first place and the rest is history.  What a thrill !
The racing is intense, but the management and car set up is straigh forward.  Mangement tasks are simplified and not time consuming.  Build new parts for the cars, improve performance or reliability.  Staff management is also easy.  You only have a lead designer and two chief mechanics, one for each driver.  Sponsors for the car, pick which suits your financial needs.  Scout new drivers as needed and also new staff.  Upgrade you HQ is costly, but is also not complex.
The e-mail system is engaging with as sorts of interesting items from interviews from the press to proposed rule changes that you will need to consider.
The race weekend arrives and during practice, you need to get the right setup for the track you are racing on.   I am not a technical geek when it come to racing and things like wing angles, tire pressures, camber, gear ratios and shock tensions are tedious to me.  They are here too, but the beauty of the interface here is that you are looking a only three things that affect performance.  Down force, Handling and Speed Balance.  Your setup is to find the best balance in those 3 catagories.  Yes you have to adjust the technical items, but they show the changes in those 3 performance categories.  Pretty cool and simple.  Take the car out on the track and bring it in to see what the drive says about the performance from very poor to excellent.  Adjust what is not good and go back out to see what the adjustments equal in performance.  Simply brilliant in get the car balanced.
There are some things that I have for a wish list.
1. Segment replay.  When something happens to the car I don't have the camera on, it would be nice to be able to pause and replay a segment on the track.  In that replay segment, it would be really cool to have different camera angles, including in car.
2. Multiplayer would be nice.  I not sure at what level, but I have a friend that plays and it would be nice to set up a season with our two teams in it and see who tops out at the end of the season.
3.  It would be great to be able to customize the paint schemes on the cars, especially the GT version.
Bottom line - if you are a race fan, then Motorsport Manager is a must  ! ! !

I didn't know what to expect out of the game, I had heard good things but generally it takes a lot for a manager game to be great. Motorsport Manager not only exceeds any expectations that I had but is quite possibly the best management game that I have ever played.

Basically everything that I loved about M&B classic, but with a ton of small improvements and a host of new features. The combat feels more polished, I love the added faction and increased faction dynamics. At times the UI and management features of the game feel tedious, but there are a variety of mods that help improve it, and sticking with native still isn't bad.
Battle tactics and commands are somewhat easily managed, though I wish you could group troops into multiple groups at once to provide for some more interesting strategic possibilities. For example, grouping your cavalry into multiple groups to create flanking possibilities, then grouping them together as cavalry to form up after a charge or flank. It's not impossible to manage through the current controls but it's not easy. Multiplayer is great, though it would be nice to have army battle simulations on the open map with multiplayer to have epic battles of several hundred, each friend commanding their own line.
The mid-game through late-game sags a little with things to do. Even as the leader of your own faction you don't have to manage too much. During peace-time you run out of possible courses aside from grinding more rep or a few more troops. Some actions in the game hardly have a pay-off for the effort invested (like running quests for 200 denars) when you compare them to others (like winning a tournament).
Overall the game is fairly well balanced, a ton of fun during battles (especially if you turn up the difficulty so that you have to manage your troops strategically), and the pain points can be mostly overlooked.

Rot Gut was an impulse buy for me. "A black-and-white 1920s film noir action platformer?! Sign me the hell up!" Is what I thought as I impulsively purchased the game on a whim. Turns out that was a mistake. Even with its crazy low $2 asking price, this is not a game you should be paying for. Contrary to what people may believe, a game being short does not necessarily detract from its value in isolation. Many of the greatest old-school platformers could be beaten within an hour-and-a-half if you're a decent gamer, but that’s not the problem. This game represents everything that is misguided about the indie "retro platformer" scene that is glutting Steam right now.
The game seemed promising up until I realized it was made in Flixel, one of the laziest Pixel art design tools known to man. If you like using Flixel, more power to you, but there are scant few Flixel games I'd actually pay for, given that it's mainly a tool used for simple♥♥♥♥♥newgrounds flash games... and Canabalt. Look, Flixel aside, this game is appallingly underdeveloped, as if the developers decided to give birth two months early. The controls are snappy and responsive, but   there are no rebindable keys and there's no controller support. On top of that the game control has no character. Dicky McGumshoe here has all the weight and momentum as a helium balloon, and so the platforming is woefully basic and flat.
"But it’s a shooter! So maybe the shooting is good?" Not at all. Enemies do two things, walk back and forth, and shoot at you, with the only variable being the weapons they carry and the damage they take. You can see the devs were trying to go for a rock-paper-scissors sort of thing where you use your pistol, shotgun, or Tommy gun as the situation demands-shotguns for the smaller guys and dogs and the Tommy gun for the shotgun-toting big dudes- but the enemies are so static and the levels so flat that it becomes redundant by the second level! Not to mention that the unlimited-ammo pistol works just fine with proper jumping, so the other weapons become even more redundant. To top it off, the (two!) bosses are pathetically easy, and the aesthetic, while under-represented in platformers, is utterly squandered on repetitive and simplistic background design.
This game has a hard time stacking up with free Newgrounds flash games I've played from 10 years ago, let alone modern indie games. the fact that it can be beaten in 30 minutes, if not faster, only sours the deal. But the length is not the issue. The game's design is the issue. Indie Retro Platformers are, discounting a few exceptions, a damn crutch. Dev tools like Flixel allow countless indie devs to fall back on pixel art as way to reduce time and money spent on a game's art design and player feedback rather than as a way to convey crisp visuals and fluidity and immediacy in gameplay. Which is why you'll notice that a lot of indie "retro" platformers don't attempt to imitate the graphical limitations or even the general look of any specific retro system, nor do they attempt to use pixel art to its greatest effect and use it to create levels and worlds with rich graphical detail. Most of it is blocky, Atari-esque pixel artwork with small sprites and simple designs.
And this lazy approach to design tends to carry over to the gameplay, as many games have the trappings of retro gameplay, but none of the nuance and clever design that make those older games classics. Rot Gut is no exception. In fact, it exemplifies all of the problems that I feel a lot of indie retro platformers tend to have, especially when you consider the fact that at a baseline level, the game's not horrible. It functions and can be a bit fun for a while, but that only makes its shortcoming more apparent.
In short, don't buy this game, if not more on principal than anything else. But if you would like to see an undistilled example of the misguided design choices that plague indie platformers, this is a fascinating summary, if nothing else.

Rot Gut - a simplistic side-scrolling shoot'em up set in a greyscale pixelated film-noir city - is a game I cannot recommend, even for its low asking price ($1.69 USD was my ticket to entry at the time of writing). It's insultingly brief and unbelievably easy. Usually, I won't bother with writing a review for a game unless I've put a significant amount of time into it (100 or more hours) or have unlocked every achievement, which normally requires a great deal of time and effort. However,
. Twenty minutes. That's it!
The gameplay is generic as it comes. You can jump, double jump, shoot, and switch weapons from a pistol to a shotgun, and a submachine gun earned halfway through the game (10 minutes in). The control is very fluent, although I could find no way to rebind keys, as the game lacks even a basic options menu. Enemies are witless and easy to kill, and health is never a concern. The two bosses the game gives you are pathetic and not challenging in the least. I never even saw the game over screen throughout my entire playthrough. It all just feels unfinished - while the graphics and sound are okay at best, the fact remains that there is no meat whatsoever in this game, nothing to bring you back for another round.
I've picked up games at or below this price point that have given me ten times the value that Rot Gut has, and I honestly don't feel it's worth it. I wouldn't even charge money for a game this sparsely featured - at its sub-half-hour length, it should be a free demo. But it's a ripoff. I spent more time writing this review than I did playing the game. Unless you want nine dead easy achievements for your records, just avoid Rot Gut.
EDIT: It's a shame that I have to do this on yet another review, but I would appreciate if you told me in the comments why you didn't find this review helpful. I believe this game is a waste of money and I did my best to describe why people should avoid purchasing it. To think that so many people are rushing to Rot Gut's defense by marking my review down is completely laughable and totally unbelievable. Let me know where your problem lies and I will do my best to address it, otherwise, keep in mind that marking a review helpful or not should reflect on the quality of the review, not YOUR opinion of the game.

was the first game I decided to complete in my quest to clear out as much of my backlog as possible. While I didn't have high hopes at first and nearly gave up on it, the game did grow on me after a while and I can see why it has earned itself a bit of a cult following. Truthfully, this game was more fun than I was anticipating it to be. But, I wouldn't call it a great game by any means, because there are a lot of annoying quirks that hold the game back in my eyes.
Surprisingly enough, this game still looks pretty nice by today's standards. I really liked the idea of how Tokyo was flooded, and it really shows the contrast between the scavengers living in the slums and the luxurious lifestyles of the people in the upper city. In retrospect, I think the design of the world was probably
strongest aspect, and although the visuals are a bit dated, that's to be expected for a 5 year old game.
The gameplay is massively hit and miss depending on how you look at it. On one hand, the combat is EXTREMELY satisfying. I had a blast gunning down the endless hordes of robots you fight because they react to where you hit them. For example, shooting them in the legs causes them to crawl towards you. The most interesting of these is when you shoot them in the head, where the robot isn't able to distinguish friend from foe. This means they start shooting their allies, which causes the other robots to react and take down the "rogue" one. I thought this was extremely well done and it made the combat feel a lot more fresh and exciting compared to just "shoot it until it's dead". However, sadly, this doesn't apply to bosses. What they have in spectacle, they lack in substance. None of them are all that interesting, mainly because they're all bullet sponges that are either ridiculously annoying to deal with (the
was the most infuriating for me) or they were complete pushovers. It really killed the mood because some of the bosses had great potential. The trust mechanic is great on paper, but pretty underutilized in this game despite being one of the most marketed aspects to it. You spend about 1/3 of the game with a specific group of characters, and those characters' trust levels don't really influence the story compared to the others. This is also annoying because the teammate AI in this game gave me nightmares. Friendly fire causes your trust with someone to go down, and I found myself having to play a hyper aggressive playstyle just so I wouldn't shoot someone by accident. The worst part to the game, in my opinion, was playing through the first chapter of the game. It was tedious, had some really annoying segments, and ended in kind of a weird way. It's a good thing I kept playing, though, because the game gradually got better from there.
I think the best way to describe this game's story is that it has a great deal of potential. The concepts are there, mainly talking about what it means to be human. I like this idea and the "Hollow Children" are a great way of presenting this. I only wish it was talked about more, because personally I wasn't very satisfied with the climax of the game and it felt like it was forced there to add some kind of
moment. As for the trust mechanic, it does make a big difference depending on who you decide to gain trust with. It can be extremely significant in the storyline, and I'm quite happy about that considering how little impact most choices in video games have. The characters are pretty likable for the most part. A tad bit stereotypical, but that isn't a bad thing here because the game is trying to be a western action movie. Cain and Big Bo were both the highlights to the game, though. A robot who talks French and a pornography-loving Bob Sapp!? Sign me up!
I didn't play with voice commands, so I can't comment on how it functions. However, the audio is solid. The voice acting is so cheesy and over-the-top I couldn't help but love it. The soundtrack was also surprisingly good, and I admit there were a few tunes that I started listening to after I finished the game. There isn't much to say here because there's nothing that makes it particularly special, but it's good enough.
Again, not much to say here. The trust mechanic is influential enough that you could get an extra playthrough or two out of it, but that comes down to how tedious you found it.
Maybe typing this at midnight wasn't a particularly smart idea on my end, but I actually had a pretty hard time coming up with a final opinion for this game. Do I recommend it? Yes, definitely. However, choosing between "good" and "satisfactory", I had to go with the latter. While the game did some things incredibly well, there was a lot of missed potential and some really frustrating things that held the experience back. I would recommend waiting for a sale, but if you treat
like a cheesy western action movie rather than something on par with, say,
I don't think you'll be disappointed.

Although I finished the game, I don't reccomend it. Have you ever had an experience where you keep waiting for it to turn the corner? Master Reboot is like that; worse than simply being a bad game, it is an inconsistent game, which robs all the enjoyment you get by implanting a numb sense of deja-vu when the inevitable bug or slapdash scene overtakes you.
The atmosphere is great, which is a big part of why I finished the game. The plot is mediocre, but gets better as you go. The drawn artwork is generic, and the 3D artwork is sometimes very cool (Fairground) and sometimes lacking (graveyard). The sound effects are where you see the quality decline - yes, there is a lot of good here, but there's also a lot of bad. Consider the Circus scene, where the sound of footsteps show up for no reason (no-one is there); you hear Kali thud as she lands in the trees near you, but she never does anything, so you start to ignore them after a while.
Then there's the puzzles. Often, the puzzles exist just to give you something to do and make no sense (like the block puzzle in the Childhood memory). The plot pieces that the puzzles reveal often don't seem to be worth it. The risk/reward just isn't balanced well.
The gameplay suffers as well. For instance, some sections are timed, but the game never tells you this. Some exits are only triggered if you behave the way that the game expects you to, and so if you think different, you will be stuck. Some scenes run on and on and on for no real reason. Worse, the restore points absolutely suck (consider the last scene), and as a result, you often have to repeat scenes again and again until you master some unimportant skill. Also, the achievements never register for Mac OS X.
The theme is a worthy one, but I just don't think Master Reboot really dealt with the theme seriously enough. The characters aren't explored deeply; when the game ends, you feel that you know only one or two of them well. That is a real missed opportunity.
So while I did enjoy the theme and the atmosphere, the gameplay was incredibly frustrating and unnecessarily so. I don't want to be harsh, but I feel like the game could have used more dev time and definitely more QA time. Maybe Soul Axiom will be better, but I won't be hanging around to find out.

This is my first game review, so I hope it sounds decent.
HuniePop is a colorful and interesting game, full of many diverse girls that you can woo in many different ways. The unlockable characters (which I won't spoil) are even more creative, and in all, I think there's pretty much a girl for every time of girl lover. I do believe a couple of sentences- just a couple- out of many were slightly out of line, but compared to the overwhelming joy the game brings, I think I could personally look over it.
The gameplay is smooth, and the only problem I ever had was the very first time I played it, which was actually caused by my laptop, not the game itself. The calibration is perfect, the achievements unlock properly, and the only actual language issues are when you choose to play as a girl instead of a guy. For reference, that's only the accidental use of the wrong pronoun, which only happens a handful of times, if only one or two.
The art is cute, and the anatomy is pretty great, too. The artist really made the characters work with whatever they were wearing, and the colors were great. It makes me glad that there was at least some racial diversity, more than most games I've played, and way less stereotypical. Well, most of the time.
The music is very pleasant to listen to, and it's one of the few games of this type that I don't mute. Sometimes, music can get annoying after a while, especially when it repeats, but the music in this game is very nice. I've never muted it due to the music even once.
When it comes to dating, the format is easy to get into, and much more fun to use than I expected. Going into the game, I was told the dates would be difficult if I didn't set it to easy, and that the night dates would be even worse. However, I had a lot of fun, even in hard mode! It's not kidding when it says hard mode, though. Be prepared.
All in all, I think I'd give this game an 8.5 out of 10. There's very minimal problems that can be generally overlooked (unless looking for lesbian immersion), and the game doesn't get old or tiring after a few dates. It makes me really want to work for all of the achievements and a 100% completion rate.

Although I didn't know what to expect at the beginning, Binary Domain was a pleasant surprise. I had an eye on it since I first saw it on Steam because it was a rather curious case: A game I had never heard of but had very good reviews by the users. I did not get a chance to play it right away and it was a long time before I could. It was thanks to the SEGA promotion "Make War Not Love" in which they gave away several games, including this one. Before starting to talk about the points more thoroughly I would like to mention the technical problems that I personally had when playing. First, I immediately noticed that the game is a port since when I opened it I found a strange launcher, which does not occupy almost anything these days. Second, browsing the menu is strange and uncomfortable. You can use the keyboard or the mouse but it is clear that the menu was not designed or adapted for PC. These two first problems did not bother me so much, but that is not the case with the third point. Third, every time the character you control climbs or lowers slopes on the ground begins to walk faster. It is as if the speed of its animation and displacement is doubled, causing the character to make a rather funny movement and totally breaking the dive. That would be all here, now we begin.
The plot doesn't stand out much, although I liked quite a few elements of the setting. There aren't many video games set in Japan from the perspective of a foreigner. There were areas that even reminded me a bit about Ghost in the Shell because of the topics it touches. The boundary between the human and the machine. I think the pacing was good. Yes, there is a lot of action, but I didn't get tired of it because of the variety of enemies and situations. Speaking of the characters, there is a robot with French accent. That's all I have to say. Out of joking, the characters didn't impress me much. Each one has its stereotypical or cliché personality but it is not something that particularly bothered me. Yes, I'd have preferred something different but I don't complain.
As you can see, gameplay is focused on action and the whole game revolves around that. Take cover, shoot until all enemies in the area are dead and advance. Do that about 40 times and end of the game. But this could describe about 60% of modern games. From my point of view is the execution that matters, and this game is well executed. The controls are well thought and the scenarios are decent, though I can't help feeling that some chapters are quite unfair in terms of the amount of enemies. Maybe it's just a problem of how slow my PC is and not the game, who knows. As I mentioned before, the game has a cover system that's quite useful against the rain of bullets that the player has to face. It can be a bit rough sometimes because the character can take cover in a different way than the player wants, but should work well most of the time. The shooting system is like in all the TPS that are in PC: Hold RMB to point and press LMB to shoot. Simple. There are a variety of weapons and surprisingly most of them feel different. That's because they are distributed among various classes, whether assault rifles, shotguns, sniper rifles, grenade launchers, rocket launchers, etc. The game also has quick time events which surprisingly (again) are fairly well implemented.
Since my PC isn't very powerful I couldn't play with the graphics to the max, so in this aspect I will analyze it through gameplay videos. For the year it came out I think it stays a bit short on this aspect, even though that allowed me to play it in the first place. Despite having been released in 2012, the game is comparable to titles released between 2006 and 2009. This in reference to lighting, shadows, details in the map, animations, textures, etc. Compared with games like Battlefield 3 (released a year earlier) you really notice the difference. Now, that doesn't mean that the game looks bad, at all. In fact, I think the art style of the game is incredible and it's thanks to this that the game has gorgeous views. The designs of the characters are not bad either. Especially the robot with French accent, that is just great.
To be honest I don't remember much about this. The first reason is that I played the game about a year ago. The second reason is that there was no really memorable music. If I'd have liked some music from the game, chances are I would have searched it on YouTube, which didn't happen. I also can't speak of the voice acting because I played the game in another language, so the voices weren't in english. The sound effects were good though. They fit the different environments and were quite unique.
In conclusion, Binary Domain is a real hidden gem. Although not very well known, it has given me a good experience, and I think that all those who have the least interest in this game should try it.

I'm way overdue on this so I'll keep this short and assume everyone have already bought and finished this.
Oddly enough this game is a mixed bag for me. The difficulty is higher than the last game, besides that it's technically the same as Hotline Miami with extra nuances, not that I'm complaining. But alas, the welcomed spike in difficulty is paired with the same dratted bugs from its predecessor. Doorways are still an empty void where hits refuse to connect (it's actually more prevalent in this game), and the door itself can turn on you by eating your attacks be it ranged or the good old melee. The "predictable" AIs can sometimes have lightning fast reflexes. Some pathways are actually narrower than what you see and you might find yourself getting stuck, causing discord to your plan and breaking any momentum (in this case combos) you've gathered. If you're lucky an enemy won't break out of their patrol route and you won't have to press "R" for the umpteenth time. One of the characters have a buggy sidekick that gets stuck too, if you make a sharp turn past a door. The field of vision, oh don't get me started on this. Ever wonder what it's like to get shot from beyond your maximum zoom distance, well with Hotline Miami 2, you're sure in for a
smashing time! This game requires quick action, sometimes even precision, and some of the level designs and bugs littered across the levels will inevitably hinder you from doing so.
The story...I don't play this for the story but if I have to rate what I know, I give it a 5, maybe 6 if I care to know the characters past their name.
Soundtrack. Imagine the final boss battle's theme song, but it's played for half the game. The bangers are intense and all, but you're going to die...a lot...and you may find yourself frustrated listening to them as they fill your ears, disturbing your concentration.
Tl;dr The bugs affect the game, making it a mediocre sequel at best.
6/10 Buy at your own risk.

Now this is something I really enjoy writing a review about. After all the Manager Games I tried, played and actually paid for to try out this is finally one thats worth speaking about.
With or without DLC, with or without Workshop mods, this represents Motorsport really good.
It's fun to create a team with your name, give it logos, colors and an own livery on the car and slowly but steady lead it to the top.
I wouldn't give a 10/10, but it's a solid 8.5/10.
Pros:
- Motorsport from the managers' POV, something rare
- quite "realistic" growth rates when it comes to the acquisition of staff and drivers
- high difficulty, when you create a team without the "Brooks' Bonus"-Mod
- at least some things on the to-do-list between races
- motivating to play more
- some good mods, despite the relatively small playerbase
- good price (when in sale)
- great UI, better than some triple-A games
Cons:
- a small lack of statistics (e.g. you dont have a list of "races won" where you can see which driver gave you a victory)
- when having completed 6 seasons or more, the game runs out of "new" things to discover
- not enough liveries to be actually interested in creating new ones every season
- reaaaally slow growth in the "create a team" mod
- finances are dull to increase, prize money + sponsors, that's it
- even when driver aid systems are disabled by a rule vote, it doesnt feel like the driver is THAT important
- enemy teams create funds (for improving the HQ e.g.) apparently by dark magic and still improve their cars at a pretty fast pace
- races are time-intense even on 3x speed
- in-race decisions beside pit stops are more or less gimmicks
In the end, it's you that counts: Are you interested in motorsport and the formula one? Buy it.
Are you interested in manager games where you need to bring man and machine together in harmony? Buy it.
If neither of these 2 things pick your interest, don't buy it.
AND: 35€ are definetely too much, wait for sale

What's really disarming about Master Reboot is how innocently it starts off. Having seen the trailer I figured it'd eventually get a bit more hectic, but it's hard to say at what point the "cool Tron aesthetic" atmosphere gave way to creeping dread. It really does just creep up on you, probably somewhere between discovering you're not alone and realising that you still have no weapons.
There is the occasional jump scare, but the game earns them, opting mostly for a creepy atmosphere which is backed up by the odd reminder that you can in fact die.
Also I don't think I've been this traumatised by a giant teddy bear since FNAF.
The story is intriguing in that it keeps you second-guessing yourself, especially regarding previously established 'facts'.
Various memories in the form of photos, official papers and cutscenes are intentionally vague, showing you just enough to *think* you know what's going on, only to throw doubt on your story as seemingly contradictory information is revealed. Add to that the fact that these memories are discovered at your pace and depending on where you go and how thoroughly you search. Subsequent visits to the same memories may yield different information and even your doubts will be different to another player's. Su
In my case, it didn't take too long to assume I was playing as a specific character in the narrative, but I soon realised I could not only be mistaken in that assumption, but that 'my' character might actually be the antagonist.
Overall, a great mix of puzzle-solving, creepy atmosphere and just enough action to keep you on your toes.
Highly recommended.
(PS And if this is a "walking simulator", then Amnesia is a walking sim)

Surreal and minimalistic adventure puzzle game. As someone who has played every F.E.A.R. game, I couldn't help but to see how a couple levels in this game drew a bit of horror influence with the ghost-like girl running across the screen into darkness. There are a few jump scares. So if you have a fragile heart, then don't play this game unless you have someone else play this with you.
The game puts you in a hub-like area, where there are 3 groups of doors, each containing 3~4 doors that each lead to a unique environment and puzzle to solve. I won't disclose what the puzzles are, but they are quite intuitive but a little too easy. There's a lot of people concerned about the scariness of the game, so I'll say that the airplane and the hospital levels are the only levels you should really be ready for. My personal favorite level was the airplane. Without revealing too much, the level for me was the spookiest yet also the most memorable, the way the level was designed. It gives a claustrophobic feeling with nowhere to escape, stuck inside with no one but an unknown ghostly figure that tries to eliminate you.
The game will take around 4 hours to complete. I would wait for a sale. $5 makes more sense, but considering how experimental and cleverly-designed this game is, this is an indie game that deserves some recognition. (note: there are sites that sell Steam keys, and sites that look professional, but most of the times they are a scam. and if they do happen to give you a valid Steam key, then your account will be banned from Steam for breaking the ToS.)

I'm only at low-level still with my German soldier (the only one I play) and I have just more of 50 hours on this played at the time of this review, so this one of mine is kinda lacking because I didn't explore a lot of content of the game.
It has potential, but it feels too much reliant on creds and grinding, Korea-style. Of course you can skip every trouble if you pay for trained soldiers or to skip directly to the perk level that unlocks that iron sights you need. I think this is why it's considered by some a P2W game. Since some time ago though, they've added the chance of getting old premium-only content (like camouflages) with credits... but the income is really low, per game. Especially if you're new and die a lot without earning a lot of experience (best tip about this is, focus on capping and stay in groups).
I played solo, but I think this game expresses its best when played with friends or you're in a clan and you're using voice-comms. Still, it's a hard game. If you like to grind for almost everything, for a lot of time, and of course this means it's rewarding - when you unlock that class choice option, paratrooper for example, after hours, days, weeks of playing, you'll feel fantastic.
I'll give it a no, but really it's because it's not for anybody - I really want to have a "maybe/decent" choice when reviewing it.

Does anyone remember when Assassin's Creed announced it would have a multiplayer mode for the first time? I sure do, because at the time, all I thought was that they were ripping off the ship.
I was wrong. AC multi is a lot worse.
The Ship is one of the best multiplayer experiences on the internet. It's a combination Assassin's Creed, The Sims, and a little Madworld mixed in.
Players are stranded together inside one of several large cruise ships as a random skin, populated with a large host of NPCs as well. Each player has a target, who they recieve a face for and nothing else. Their job is to find that player on the ship and kill them. The trick is that you lose points if you kill anyone you're not hunting or being hunted by, including said npcs. There are cameras at various locations around the ship, which will cause you to get arrested and timed out if caught brandishing weapons openly. However, you have a set of needs such as hunger, thirst, hygeine, bladder and sleep, similar to The Sims, which force you to keep moving to meet them, usually away from the cameras. Your goal is to act as much like the unassuming NPCs as possible, both to avoid detection from those hunting you and to disguise yourself from the prey you're tailing, all while managing your meters and picking up the weapons you'll need to secure the kill.
There's a huge host of weapons and environmental hazards with which to do so, and point values for each vary wildly over time. This forces players who want to stay on top to constantly be changing their tactics and style. Certain weapons can only be found in specific locations on each ship, so highly desired gear can become choke points which force players to meet similar to Q3A duels.
The ship is full of more than weapons, though. In addition to portable food items which can restore health or your need meters in a pinch, most guests board with more than the clothes on their backs. By raiding their rooms for garments, you can swap out your clothing if you think you're being followed or after each kill to disguise yourself and throw the other players off your scent. You can't change your face, but someone following to the side or behind may think you're an NPC and move on.
The result of all this craziness is a really clever form of deathmatch that uses true stealth and deception, because you're trying to trick other players instead of AI. Stalking prey feels really rewarding and so does tricking your attacker into revealing themselves under a camera or turning a corner and unexpectedly fighting back. The ticking time from your meters at the bottom, the rapidly changing point structure and high ranking players attracting more hunters make the pressure always on and puts players on their toes.
If all this seems right up your alley, wait unless you're super eager and have nothing better to do. The Ship is getting an HD version in early 2016, though as far as anyone can tell right now, it will be multiplayer only. The Ship also has a singleplayer campaign, though it's not nearly as fun imho. The unique aspect of Ship combat is pvp stealth and sneaking up on Sims in their sleep feels more like a clunky, uglier Hitman Absolution.
