I really want to like this game. The atmosphere, art style, and concept are neat. The music also deserves special mention. However, the game falls completely flat in the gameplay category. Basically, you get to walk slowly around (often excessively large) levels, stopped by frequent puzzles which either make little to no sense, or end up being just "collect these to unlock the door"-variety. I really need to point out how much not-fun I was having due to moving too slowly. Also, that trite jump-scare where the little girl jumps out of a locker or closet and grabs you gets more than boring, but actually predictable the third time it happens. Especially since you have to Button-Mash-To-Save-Your-Life®.
It's plagued by flaws that make it feel like it was made by extremely inexperienced developers. For example: In one level you have a hammer, and see a broken section of wall. You broke similar broken sections with three hammer strikes. So you hit this one three times, and nothing happens. No special sound or particle effect, no change in the wall. Go ahead and hit it three more times, just for luck. Still nothing. You'll be stuck, trapped, respawning over and over (with a cutscene, to boot!) until you discover it inexplicably takes SEVEN hits to break this wall. As well as the next five walls straight behind it in identical-looking rooms. To top it off, after breaking the final wall, I took a look behind me to see if I missed anything. Upon turning around again, for no reason a door had silently closed at the exit, forcing me to redo the section yet again.
As for those "memorable moments", the only things I can remember about the game are needlessly frustrating sequences like the above. I have to recommend against this game. Better luck next time, Wales Interactive. I hope you learn from your mistakes.

Master Reboot is quite thought provoking. The entire game takes place in a virtual world where the soul purpose of this world is to house digital copies of dead loved ones for the living to go visit. The concept is pretty awesome and the game pulls off this idea quite well, despite there being some pretty annoying flaws in the actual gameplay. Even with it's flaws, Master Reboot managed to keep me entertained till the very end, while also bringing out the emotions, which few games are capable of doing. That part alone warrants this game a 7/10. Anywho, here are some pros and cons of Master Reboot
The Pros:
- Style - The game has a unique look/style too it that is well done
- Sound - Makes great use of ambient effects, perfect with headphones
- a variety of different environments keeps the game fresh
- The puzzles were good
- A Good game-length for what kind of game this is
- A Fantastic Story that can get pretty emotional at times, atleast for me it did.
- Very atmospheric

The Cons:
- Pathetic Jump scares
- Not scary at all
- Terrible hit detection
- recycled monster screams.
- clunky platforming
- The Price is a little high, best to get this game when its on sale
In Conclusion, Master Reboot is a very good game despite its short comings. I can def. see this becoming a cult classic. Its one of the most original games I've ever played.

is filled with ambition, yet inconsistent. While its low points aren't the worst in the world, they stand in large contrast to its highs and some problems with base gameplay can make this a slog to go through. Nevertheless, the game is certainly entertaining and worth a try.
features relatively standard crouch-behind-waist-high-walls third person shooter gameplay, but also has an interesting damage localization model. All of the enemies in the game are robots, and using that model you can pick them apart and modify their behavior. It's a bit similar to
in this regard, in that depending on the situation you may want to stop enemies from moving by shooting off legs, or from shooting by quickly removing their gun arm.
also has an interesting mechanic where if you score repeated headshots you essentially convert an enemy robot to your side, providing a, at least in the higher difficulties, much needed decoy. Besides that gameplay is rather simple, with your standard array of rifles, a shotgun, a rocket launcher, etc.. Your allied teammates also vary in mechanic, occupying the typical weak attack/high defense, flanker, and other role types.
Keeping with the allies, the game also has a rather robust conversation system that develops each character's personality in a great way. It's comparable to the companion systems in
, though scaled down and lacking things like loyalty missions. This provides an alright amount of replayability as you can only pick up to a maximum of 2 companions for each mission, leading to situations where you may not see some characters at all outside of cutscenes that force the entire group together.
Overall game design and progression is where
demonstrates its inconsistency. There are a plethora of boss fights, but from about 50%-75% of the way through the game these bosses turn from something that's cinematic and well designed to pure bullet sponges, and they all come back to back. The pacing takes a nose dive during this section, and I can only surmise that there were some development problems during this portion of the game. Furthermore, some novel systems such as voice commands lack a great deal of polish, despite their use being heavily encouraged throughout the game.
Overall,
is fun. Shooting the limbs off of robots and plowing through is a great experience, and the well-composed cinematics combined with the great cast really do make the game feel like an action movie. There might be some rust around the edges, but it's clear the game's crew put a lot of love in.

This is a perfectly fine game. Like, I don't want to disparage the creative effort of several  dudes who have put out infinitely more games than I have and it's not like the game isn't arguably a more satisfying experience than what you can buy in a vending machine for the exact same price. It's just a perfectly fine game that doesn't really motivate you to do anything besides keep walking left and buying shotgun shells.
There's no point in fighting the enemies (all of which take three times longer to kill than they should), there's no point in exploring the levels, and zero point in using any weapon besides the shotgun. You can collect points, but once you top up on health kits and shells, there's (shockingly) no point in doing that either. Just run to the left for twenty-five minutes and periodically blast your shotgun at the giants that refill all your health. Eventually, you'll reach the last boss, who eventually explodes in an infinite shower of dumb useless coins like some sort of metaphor for your dumb useless life until you walk into the final Exit door, no better or worse for wear as a human being. Then you find out there isn't actually an exit button and you have to force close the executible, and that's how you end up writing a review as meandering and pointless as this game.
All that being said, it's a perfectly fine first effort. Better than any of the (zero) games I've actually made! The team very clearly loved what they were doing, as seen in the caring way chunks of viscera bounce along the ground after you commit murder. Plus, you can buy it with the amount of (pointless) steam cards you have clogging up your inventory, and it has at least entertained me as much as the can of Diet Coke I would have bought with those funds anyway. So go for it, I guess. Or don't. Like the intensely apathetic world of Rut Gut, it won't make much of a difference in my life.

Right off the bat: this is a great game, especially for its price.
For the price you pay ($21 CAD) you get a TON of content
TL:DR
This game is great for medival cravings, and leading your own squad and picking them all is very fun. Unlimited storytelling potential allows for multiple playthroughs without boredom. Mods are alive, well, and very fun
LONG VERSION
The Campaign: At the start you create your own character, and you create thier backstory by choosing what they were as a child, as a young adult, etc until you choose WHY you left your home! Your finished character  gets certain stat boosts depending on what you chose beforehand. The campaign gives you a quick little intro to the game and then a little quest, then it throws you into the harsh world of Calradia. It takes a little while to understand the jist of it, but then the game turns into an amazing world. During battles you are able to tell your troops to do certain things (mount,dismount,charge,retreat,follow me,hold fire,fire at will,stand closer, spread out,etc.). You get to choose what your troops do depending on your playstyle. And after you finnaly get a large band of soldiers willing to fight for you and the game is going well for you, you end up getting attacked by a force 2-4 times larger and you are captured and lose ALL of your troops. But its still fun to go get your revenge.
The Multiplayer: You get to create your characters appearance, then you can join whatever game you like. There are so many different gamemodes to play, and some games incorperate Steam workshop maps! I have played a Siege gamemode (attackers VS defenders) on a replica battle field of Helms Deep (LOTR) with 200 people, which turned into an amazing setting with attackers scaling ladders up the sides of the walls and the defenders spewing arrow after arrow off the battlements into my face. Depending on how many people you killed in your last life, you can use the money you gained from killing those people to buy better armor and weapons (or horses).
The Custom Battles: At the start I played lots of custom battles just to get used to the combat system. Choose 2 factions, choose 1-200 people for each side, then change the percentage of each kind of fighter for that army (Foot soldier, archer, calvalry).
Modules: There are enless amounts of user made modules for you to use and change your M&B Warband experience. If Medival battles like the normal ones in M&B Warband are too bland for you, consider finding a new module to spice it up.
Cheating: You are able to enable cheats in the campaign for infinite money, refill health, knock out the entire enemy army, and so on. I have used cheats for one of my accounts, and i actually enjoyed it.The reason being I am not one for grinding hour upon hour for soldiers and money, only to have it wiped away by some jerk with 300 men. I cheat to enjoy large scale battles with 200 people on each side on a random battlefield. To cheat is up to you, but I will not judge if you cheat.
Side note: For the large scale battles, the normal amount of people allowed on the battlefield at once is max 200. I used M&B battlesizer to increase it to 400 people for larger battles. I reccomend this mod for those who want larger battles and have a good quality computor.
Bad things:I really dont have much to say bad about this game. People are deterred from this game because of its "bad graphics".I dont mind the fact that the developers didnt use ultra realistic graphics for it allows for a larger and more in depth game without all the lag an ultra realistic game would bring. Also, more custom battle maps would be nice but im not too bothered.
Thank you for reading through my rant about this amazing game. Please rate fairly and have a good day playing M&B Warband :)

Where is the "meh" button when you need it.
It looked and sounded great on paper. It's a very simple game with unqiue theme around a vague story with incredibly simple mechanics and puzzles while enshrouded in a plethora of glow and blur effects. I'd say the minimalist visuals attracted me the most about the game and little else.
I beat the game quite quickly - you mostly run around [until your virtualized character runs out of breath *shrug*] clicking all of the blue-glowing rubber ducks. And then when you run out of ducks to click it usually meant there are some other, vibrantly glowing thing you are supposed to click instead. I enjoyed the theme and the simple mechanics, but the whole time I had a poor understanding of who I was playing as and what I was doing - by the time I worked out the "who I was" part, the game was nearly over. Even then I still wasn't sure what I was doing or why I was even here in Tron-land aside from the chronology of seemingly unrelated "memories" I was collecting. I would guess that the final-boss character has something to do with the "Soul Cloud" having errors, but that wasn't ever clarified [that I saw]. The creepy, threat messages left by the "Goddess of Death" were never really explained either.
Starting from the beginning, someone dies and you become Tron. Your purpose is to find the exit door (blue cube thing) to each level that you begin for no reason other than having a door that you can enter. When you have gone through all the doors, you will have accumulated enough "memories" to piece together a vague story about some common tragedies and something-something-something that you won't realize has anything to do with you until someone calls you by name for the first time near the end. And then after that you realize, as an audience, that you really didn't care about the story anyways and continue looking for that damn exit door.
Some better character development for the protagonist would have really helped the game.
Actually, the game would have been more interesting from the perspective of Seren [seren.exe], I think.
Speaking of, I'd say that the only real
value in this game is that the glowy-eyed Seren might occasionally try and make you jump in your seat a little. It's a game suitable for most ages, I'd think.
Oh - And I'll give a Recommend to the game only because between a scale of 1 to 10, the game sits at least somewhere over 5.1 - or something. Like I said, where is the "meh" button when you need it.

Initially this game won me over in the first half hour, but sadly soon spiraled into a rabbit hole of disappointment.
There's a lot to like about Master Reboot.  Mainly the atmosphere and the story as you can make it out.  The game itself is broken into many set pieces which initalliy played like a variety of large scale minigames.  This I really liked in the beginning until I started to realize that the variety was thin and it was essentialy the same scavenger hunt just in a different location usually with a gimmick to spice it up....find the three things in an oversized child's room.....find the three things on a plane while hiding from a spooky flight attendant of death.....find the three things in a hospital with a flashlight....find the three things using a metal detector..... you get the point.
That sound design was pretty bad to the point of painful in some instances....kinda laughable in others (shoot some bottles at the carnival and you'll know what I mean.)  The controls however are what ended up killing the entire experience for me.  Movement is clunky which is even more of a negative considering the game relies pretty heavily on first person platforming in several parts.  Now combine this with a rage inducing bug plaguing the game that causes the controls to stick in one direction (usually left for me,) making you to run constantly into walls or off of platforms.  After replaying the finale of the game (a rather long timed platforming bonaza) and failing three times due to the control issues, I flipped off the screen and decided that even though I was seconds from completion, it just wasn't worth the trouble.

So this is what it takes to get me to play a match-three game.
You know, there was a lot more effort in this game than I expected and I didn't have high expectations, but this game is fully voice-acted, pretty decent art, and a pretty wide range of characters to cater to your needs.
You play as an unnamed male or female character who meets a "love fairy" named Kyu who's here to help you get laid. And now that I've put that in writing I don't entirely believe it. You're introduce to eight main girls (plus Kyu and three secret characters) of various personalities, body types, ethnicities, and backgrounds. Kyu does make a few comments that struck me as borderline racist like how she says she likes Asians by saying she has "yellow fever" but in context its such a cheesy line I can't be mad and HuniePop clearly has no ill will. Also that is really just Kyu, the other characters range from Audrey the "mega b*tch" (that is what the game calls her) to Bali the shy and polite girl.
I guess my overall view of HuniePop is surprise. I had no idea what to expect and didn't have high expectations. Bare in mind this isn't a visual novel so it doesn't have a very heavy story (a shame because there is the foundation for a decent story). I would have liked more content, however I feel I got my money's worth.

If you have any doubts about purchasing this game because it might be too sexual - don't. HuniePop is an amazing puzzle adventure that I have become addicted to. I find myself wanting to play more after I wake up. This game has ruined my sleeping schedule, actually... and that's because of how much I really enjoy it.
Of course there will be reviews out there that enjoy the game strictly for aesthetics, but I look past that. If that's what you're into, though, that's fine. But, strictly rating HuniePop on gameplay: it's fantastic. I have 23 hours clocked into the game, 96% completion rate, and I cannot wait to complete my first file. I plan on starting a new file after I have reached 100% on my first file just to get all of the achievements I've missed while on my first playthrough.
As someone who thoroughly enjoys puzzle games, HuniePop never disappointed me. I love Alpha Mode and its ever-increasingly difficulty. I'm the type of person who loves a challenge. Though HuniePop does get quite challenging with the introduction of Alpha Mode, I still find it to be a relaxing game. I feel like it improves my terrible short-term memory, since the girls will quiz you about themselves and other girls later on in the game. I think that the fact that HuniePop seems to help improve my short-term memory is definitely a bit of a bonus.
Outside of the game being relaxing, challenging, and helpful for memory, it has a great soundtrack. The music tends to be very lighthearted and bubbly. The personalities of the girls made it easy for me to laugh. This game is great for those who want to stay in a great mood.
I would like to commend HuniePot on creating such a wonderful game. I am looking forward to HunieCam Studio - and although it is going to be quite different, I hope has as much work put into it (if not more) than HuniePop, because this game is an absolute steal for its price on steam.
To close out this review, I would like to say thanks for providing an addicting, adult game with memorable characters. I understand that the game may not be suitable for a younger audience, but would recommend it to anyone who is able to pick up the game...to get it. No hesitation there, just get the game.  I am also happy that it has over 20 hours of gameplay in it (for completitonists).
I hope that this review might help someone out there, and I hope that readers end up enjoying the game as much as I am enjoying it right now.

This game is great. Basically it is Left 4 Dead 2 adapted for Warhammer Fantasy where a gang of characters fights hordes of ratmen instead of zombies. However, in many ways it is superior to L4D2. Melee combat is a lot more emphasized but it also has ranged weapons like crossbows, steampunk-esque firearms, wizard fireballs, etc.
Most importantly, combat is bloody, desperate, and a lot of fun. It's an absolute bloodbath. Blood splatters all over the place, covering the ground and walls like paint. Most enemies die in just one or two melee strikes or ranged attacks. If this game was like Skyrim and you had to beat on each enemy 10 times it would be total trash. The way it works here is great because you feel like a real hardcore dude as you chop down enemies every time you press the attack button (there are some tougher varieties of enemies that take a bit more work). You can sidestep/dodge attacks and there is parry/blocking system (which is affected by your chosen weapons) that makes things more interesting than just tapping buttons mindlessly.
Instead of all the characters being the same and picking up different weapons throughout the level, Vermintide has distinct characters. Each character (dwarf, witch hunter, wizard, soldier, and elf) has different possible loadouts with different properties. Each character can choose a ranged weapon and a melee weapon from a selection of basic weapons + whatever you have earned by beating levels.
The choices are pretty interesting. For example, the dwarf has a heavy crossbow that can zoom-in like a sniper rifle and take down even the armored rats with one shot. For a melee weapon, the dwarf might take a big axe or hammer that swings very slowly but pierces armor and does lots of damage. On the other hand, the elf warrior dude can be equipped with a shortbow that does very little damage but can be fired super-fast like a semi-automatic rifle and drop hordes of weak rats quickly. For melee, the elf can dual-wield short swords that hack down weak rats quickly, but if you want to be more of a heavy-hitter you can take a longsword instead.
When you beat levels you can get a random chance for new items like weapons and trinkets that give you different abilities.
Atmosphere, art direction and level design is really great. The graphics are excellent.
Here's another cool thing about this game: if your party host has the DLC, everyone else can play those maps even if they don't have the DLC. And the DLC levels are really great. I think in the standard game you get around 10-12 levels (some long and epic journeys, others just short little missions) once you've unlocked them all. The DLC I think adds another seven missions or so.
There is also a "horde mode" style game where you just fight a bunch of waves with no fancy objectives. I believe there are two maps for this mode.
Overall this is a great coop game that shows how you can take the L4D2 model and make it better. You definitely want to have some friends to play it with, but it's so cheap when it's on sale it's worth buying a copy for yourself and a bro. If you have a four-man team that's the best, but if not then you'll have bot allies that kind of suck but not enough to detract from the fun.

From the creators of Revenge Of The Titans, here is a nice tribute to space invaders, with a design style that I can't get enough of. You progress through various stages and planets with a short description of your mission; which is of course to SAVE THE WORLD. As you progress you build a score as well as a bank in which to use for buying upgrades. Upgrades include weapons, armor, screen clearing bombs, and more. Each planet is finished with a boss who may, or may not, be trying to destroy you. It's a great casual experience that you can walk away from and it will be right where you left off when you come back. The best part is if you die, you return to the beginning of the planet you were on! Yes, you do get set back a bit but it's a nice surprise to not having to start entirely over! So if you liked Space Invaders, you should definitively get this game. Shoot those laser bullets, destroy those aliens, capture and/or kill the ones who try to escape, defend those planets, and win!

Hello and welcome to this review of Binary Domain! A game that's sure to convey mixed feelings. Starts off bad, some things stay bad, some things are great, and sometimes things get amazing for a brief moment.
Binary Domain is a squad-based third person shooter that generally consists of corridors and large outside areas or rooms filled with props that allow you to take cover and methodically gun down your opposition.
On the subject, your opposition is robots, and you can destroy specific parts of them for
efficiency! When you hear that satisfying ding while their head goes flying, you can rest easy knowing they're going to attack their allies...or at least be a decoy for a few seconds. You can also shoot off their legs and watch them crawl at you. Etc.
Your comrades have specific loadouts, and you have a main gun, but you can freely take other secondary guns. Want to snipe? Go for it. Lug around a big RPG? You can! So this all sounds great so far, right? Fight hordes of robots with a variety of gun types and you get this neat injury system to boot? Well, it is! Except...well, it's not?
The game starts you off with a terrible tutorial riddled with cutscenes and dialogue that constantly take you out of the action. Also your first teammate is kind of a very stereotypical african american. Also, I mentioned hordes, and the cutscenes will convey that there are hordes, but then there will only be 4-8 robots (max) and usually from all directions with gunfire buzzing past you like annoying flies.
Much of the voice-acting is great. Except when it isn't (ie the clearly Asian characters that speak English but can't speak their native language correctly for the few words required, odd seeing as how there are actual Japanese voiceactors for other characters.) The story starts off as a very generic search and destroy mission but slowly blossoms into something far better.
Humor. In select situations and moments, it's really great. In others it totally falls completely flat on its face.
Last but not least, the boss fights. Almost every miniboss or boss fight in this game is terribly designed, or rather, the idea is good but the execution of the fight is terrible. For reference, enjoy getting pounded by a gorilla 20 times while you're supposed to be safely shooting it with a high calibre mounted gun...shame it can only turn in a half circle.
On the other hand, all the less than great parts serve to make the good parts shine brighter. And, the camp factor is kind of fun. The story actually does get interesting, even the generic characters grew on me by the end, and there's a good bit of variety in the environments. Towards the end, there's a boss fight or two that's actually good, and a few areas where you can actually fight endless hordes of a variety of the robot types and it is so satisfying to mow them down with your fully upgraded gun.
There's a lot to like about Binary Domain, and a lot to hate, so I guess the question of if you want to play it revolves entirely around if you can enjoy things that are fun because they are bad long enough for it to be fun because it is good, or if you hate anything cheesey.
The graphics in Binary Domain are a bit of a mixed bag. Areas and props kind of blend together all in all, but the level design for whole chapters at least has variety. The shaders and attention to detail is nice, yet I could never stop thinking about how bad most of the hair looked. Animations, especially facial, can be quite janky, not that portraying eye and facial movement realistically is easy.
There's actually some very striking cinematography employed, allowing for some reasonly impactful or emotinal scenes, moments, or screenshots to be had.
Be prepared for a lot of grey, and white, and clinical settings. The areas like the slums, outside areas at the start, or the dumping grounds near the end on the other hand are really great, and I think should have been utilized more for that mix of modern vs futuristic feel.
I think I've commented plenty on how the voice acting is at times good and at times terrible, so let me mention the music. Keep your ears alert, it's actually good. There's a lot of great trance, techno, and other electronic music that really adds some flair and gets your blood boiling for the fights, story climaxes, etc.
Also, again, that satisfying ping when you pop a head off. Most of the other sounds in the game are generic gunplay or explosion sounds, unfortunately.
If you're the kind of person who finds themselves enjoying silly straightforward fun, or wants to take a risk on if it is worth getting invested later on, I recommend Binary Domain:
On sale. In the $4-8 range. Its age is showing and it's been deeply discounted or given away a lot at this point, so there's really no point paying a lot for it. Also considering the oft-questionable design. Still, pick it up to enjoy the finer moments or laugh at the worse ones!

I had a lot of fun with this game, and I never paid anything but my time. If you are a Star Trek fan, you have nothing to lose, and you'll probably enjoy what they've done with the franchise and your personal story. I was tempted to buy cosmetic upgrades because I am a nerd ("Ooh they have Kirk's jacket from Wrath of Khan! I want it!"), but I never felt like I had to pay in order to win. You definitely CAN - you can pay real money to buy upgraded ships with special technology - but I never felt pressured to do so.
I really like the crew management element of the game - essentially, the special abilities of your ship are determined by your bridge officers. Bridge officers can be requisitioned from Starfleet or acquired on missions, which I thought was a nice touch. You can customize your bridge officers appearances in a very satisfying way, from their appearance and uniform to their stance. I got a boring Trill medical officer and made him much more interesting by making him twitchy and neurotic. Once you've customized a uniform for yourself or an officer, it's easy to save the outfit and apply it to whoever you want.
The rest of your crew - rank and file - are mostly just pegs you can shuffle around to complete timed tasks and projects, with a variety of little rewards. I enjoyed this 'Starfleet Spreadsheet Simulator' in kind of a perverse way, sending my little dudes to formulate warp bubble theories and whatnot, but it's mostly a time-waster.
The main problem with the gameplay is this: the ship-to-ship combat is much more polished than the away missions, but away missions are where you will spend most of your time. The on-foot sections of the game have very awkward and inconsistent level design. If I could delegate those bits to my redshirts, I would mostly do it, and enjoy the game more.
I put it down when I didn't feel like playing it anymore, and I haven't picked it up again since, but I enjoyed the time I spent playing it. It didn't feel addictive or manipulative.
tl;dr : Try it if you like Star Trek. It's actually free and not fee-to-pay.

A very nice and very faithful MMO based on Star Trek. Perhaps the biggest draw is the company actually got the full Star Trek Intellectual Property. They get the actual actors from the series to do voice overs and use their images. They get the actual models for starships and weapons. And as far as I can tell, their lore is all accurate (as much as the series is consistent within itself, that is). Very much geared towards fans of Star Trek. Quite enjoyable to be able to beam down to Nimbus III from Star Trek V or see Deep Space 9 from the series, or warp into a system just to hear the infamous "Lower your shields and prepare to be assimillated. Resistance is futile!"
The environments are quite exquisite. I find myself constantly taking screenshots they're so gorgeous. Being stuck in a blinding blizzard on the wastes of Rura Penthe or taking in the view from New Romulus are a treat just to name a few.
The gameplay is nice. Very solo-oriented. Technically there are groups and fleets, but they typically don't do much for you (though the fleet holdings are a perk). I personally really like the space combat with shields, beams, and torpedos. But there is ground combat too as your away teams beam down to the unknown.
Also a shout-out to one of the best in-game purchase systems I've seen. You can essentially get the paid currency (Zen) with in-game currency (Dillithium) or vice-versa. You can get everything with enough time.
Complaints:
- The Zen is weak. It seems like anything worthwhile takes $30-100 worth of real money. And that's just one thing. As mentioned, you can get everything by converting Dilithium, but still.
- There are a lot of options for weapons, consoles, abilities, resistances, and on and on. Not a whole lot of explanation for what you want to use where and why. So it all turns into technobabble for me.
- You can walk around the interior of your starship, but nothing ever really seems to happen there. A real let down and a missed opportunity.
- You only have a few hooks to place trophies in your ship. A game like this desevers several hundred hooks around the whole ship where you can display your exploits and achievements,
Those who criticise this game clearly never played it on release.

Master Reboot is an atmospheric game about the singularity-well, that, and one woman's quest to regain her memories and find out what's going on. You are a person who is part of the Soul Cloud, an initiative to preserve memories and souls, essentially, in a digital cloud. Things aren't all that well, though, because there is a mysterious digital girl who is trying to kill you.
How does it play? It's a first-person exploration-type game, something I think a lot of people are familiar with by now. You wield "weapons" in a few instances, but most of the gameplay is exploring, solving puzzles, and doing the occasional other action like sneaking around or doing a QTE-and this is actually where my criticisms of the game begin.
There's a few moments that can be frustrating for players: there's a few puzzles that are confusing as hell or require you to be really good at memorizing things. There was one QTE that took me like four tries because the controls weren't perfectly intuitive. Near the end, I found myself looking up a walkthrough.
This does not make a strong case for the game, so what does it have going for it? Nice atmosphere, interesting level designs, a plot of at least decent quality (with some tear-jerker elements), nice 2D-animated cutscenes here and there, a slight horror element (very slight), and just a general air of creativity. For a game about the singularity, it's a good fit for the concept.
I would recommend this game, but it's not something I'd play through twice. Still, if you find a hankering for digital-soul stuff, do check this out.

Allright World, this is my first review of a game, ever. I usually do not consider it worth the effort to write a review about a game, but this one, deserves an exception.
So, let's start from the beggining....
Ah, the story. Every good game has a decent story to speak of, right? So, who are you, what's your purpose in this world? What dark conspiracy and hideous enemy will you face and save the World and your loved ones?
Well, errr, I don't know. No really, don't look at me, I don't know. Your story, your past, present and future are yours to control.
The game's concept is simple. You start off by picking from a wide variety of choices regarding your family background and personal history. Then you choose one of the five Kingdoms to start in and *poof*, Welcome to Calradia adventurer! Calradia is the continent in which the game is taking place. A continent in which five Kingdoms fight for supremacy over each other. "And what about me?" You ask. Well.... Have you ever played a game where there's a mercenary band that slowly rises to power to overcome a continent? No? Well, what a stroke of luck! This is the game! You start off with nothing but ♥♥♥♥♥♥ armor, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ weapons and a horse. The tutorial, which involves hunting bandits, killing them and saving a merchant's brother and then leading his men to cleanse the city of bandits, is pretty informative and gives you all you need to start your career as a mercenary.... Or a trader.... Or a slaver, a thief and anything else you can imagine. You can join a faction as a mercenary, rise to power as a noble, even start your own Kingdom! The choices are endless.
What's a conquest-based game without decent combat, eh? Well, definitely not Mount and Blade. Though blocking and attacking can be automated, I'd recommend going with manual control.(You'll find those options in the Options menu). Basically, combat goes like this: There's you, third person or first person and the troops you've hired from villages, taverns etc. You basically only control yourself directly. It is however possible to command your army using your keyboard. It's sluggish at first, and you ain't gonna be using any real tactics any time soon, but you'll get used to it... And it'll rock. Really. In short, combat is a bit tougher than most games around, but it's more fun and it gives off a sense of accomplishment. You'll get what I'm talking about after blocking 3-4 hits in a row with a two-handed weapon against a relentless opponent. It's tough, but it feels damn great. Also, AI tends to cope well with your commands, though it lacks severely in the pure tactics sector. My only complaint is how every group will only form one long line when ordered to hold position. No tactics, no depth, nothing. Just a loooong line. Well damn me. Though that can be solved by using more groups, it's a hassle and hey, I have to point out something negative, right?
Overall the game is amazing. It combines RTS, with a decent RPG-like system which involves levels and the such, without focusing too much on either. Graphics are outdated, sure and it might be a bit tough to get used to, but the Combat system is decent and this game has one dominating point over everything else.
You can not only choose your past, but the way you choose to go about the game, the factions you choose to fight for or that you use for your own benefit and the relationship you forge with other nobles and the rest of the world, is your choice. There's nothing writtend in stone, there isn't anything restraining you. So if you seek a game that allows you to go from a one-man party, hunted and beaten by bandits to the King of All Calradia, go for it.

Let me get this straight, you want me to tell you a review about this game? Whoever you are, you might as well go to the curators, because if you've come for a review on this game, you've come to the wrong place. However, if you have come for an outstanding chocolate chip cookie recipe, you've come to the right place.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
1. Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
2. Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
3. Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
4. Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
5. Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
1. Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.

Raptor: Call of the Shadows is one of those games that nearly any gamer who was active in the '90s played the demo at least once. Thanks to an onerous order process and the fact that no store carried it, most of us only ever played the first "sector" and that was it. A cool game, too bad we were never going to do the dubious mail-order process to get it.
Leave it to Steam to fix that problem *and* the $35 price tag. It only took 20 years to do, too!
Raptor is a top-down vertical scroller typical of the '90s. (Galactix or Xevious are other prime examples.) It's you in your hyper-souped-up fighter jet versus the world...or a few worlds, maybe. All gameplay is through the mouse, with a simple control scheme for a fairly simple game. (You *can* use keyboard or even joystick controls, but you're probably not going to like it.)
There are a few things that make Raptor a stand-out game in a crowded field. First of all, its graphics are (for the era) GORGEOUS. Hand-painted sprites and backgrounds with a lot of variety within levels, and then completely different design aesthetics for the different sectors. It really is something of a shame that the game goes so fast, because if you have any interest in '90s-era videogame art, you'll want to take a close look at the work here. Each sector has about 8 waves, so the content adds up. The other interesting bit is that, like Xevious, you're engaging targets in the air and on the ground simultaneously. Some weapons only work on one or the other, forcing swaps, while others work on both but cost a lot - so play style and dexterity count.
Audio is better than average, and Raptor has a pretty snappy soundtrack. Bonus, the soundtrack is in .wav format, so you have it by default.
Now, given that this is a '90s game time-warped up to 2015, there are some...issues that you should know about before buying. First of all, the UI has a serious problem with savegames. Saves cannot be named, aren't timestamped, and are added to a serial list with all your other savegames. Unless you're pretty religious about pruning out your old games or memorize your bank balance every time you quit so that you can pick out your newest save, you're going to mis-load a game plenty of times. Less frustratingly, there are moments where mouse tracking glitches out, stranding your pointer inside an incorrect "screen edge" until you slide away and try again. This usually happens in the hangar between missions, but can also trip you up in a mission from time to time.
However, in my experience, these in-mission glitches are few and far between, and the game has (so far) been pretty stable - only one serious malfunction that ended up being a slow start - so insofar as a resurrected game goes, Raptor is a pretty good port. (Oh, a recommendation: leave the "HQ Filter" option OFF; it makes the game look...melted.)
Overall, if you're looking for a nostalgia trip that isn't too expensive, Raptor is a good way to go. (Get it on sale for even better results.) It's an enjoyable game with some great content.

The Very First shoot-em up game that I've played as a child. This game is similar to Sky Force, Again, not a Bullet Hell game, but definitely a stategic shoot em up, positioning and knowing when/where the enemy is coming next, is defintely an advantage. You earn money by shooting down enemies, blowing up structures, and boats. Bonus money is also earned through special ships that fly through the stage multiple times.
Basically, you go through different "sectors" and each sector has waves that you can progress through each time you play the same sector. You have a shop that you can buy health, (Hard, because whatever health you had prior to finishing the mission, carries with you to the next..) and sometimes the health is not cheap....You can buy missiles, lazers, guidance systems, etc, However...None of  these power ups last through to the next sector with the exception of a few.
For its time, the graphics were good and so was the sound effects and music. If I were to suggest this, it would be for the old school players, and those who enjoy a difficult shoot em up, not because of the amount of bullets, but because of the timing.

This game gets a 8/10. Basically for its conception back in the 90's. If it were to compare to today's Meta of shoot em ups, It may land on a  6/10. Overall, get this if flying shmups is your thing.

Many positive reviews initially got me interested in Layers of Fear. Though outnumbered, the negative reviews convinced me not to purchase. It just so happened a friend gifted it to me. With my 11 year old daughter in tow, we set out to play.
The first few rooms had nothing of interest. Letters found were long and boring. For me, there was zero fright, but my daughter was mesmorized, so I played on.
In short order it became apparent this walking simulator was a repeating loop of the following:
1) Long corridor of locked doors. The one at the end will be unlocked.
2) A short sequence of rooms with many drawers and cabinets that will yield nothing.
3) A jump scare.
4) A room that has no way out, but then...
5) A door somehow appears.
6) Steps 1-5 repeat with a few variations including....
A) The "special effects" hallway, which melts or flashes. A moaning ghost or other "scary" thing makes an appearance.
B) A room with doors that all open to brick walls. But how to get out? After you try them all...
C) The door you came in (which was locked) is now unlocked....leading to an entirely new locataion!
D) The elevator which takes you up or down, no difference.
E) The "loop de loop": you have to go around and around or backwards, or something to break the loop.
Then you get to the "artifact" room where you find something you need, immediately leading to "the painting" which you begin to reveal.
I've completed this sequence five times so far (five "artifacts" found), but I would have quit long ago had my daughter not prodded me on. There was only one time out of the five that there was an interesting theme (fourth go around).
The story...nothing new here. Not convincing. I never cared. Irritating narrator voice with echo.
If you are easily scared, yet like to be scared, but not TOO scared (such as if you are an 11 year old girl who likes PG-13 movies), this may be for you. If you're a hard-core thriller and/or horror fan, give this a pass.

If you want to make a 'walking simulator', be sure that you have a good story behind it - and know how to tell it. Because this will be the only thing that´ll keep players playing, after all.
Moving forward is a pretty dull action. So is opening drawers. And that´s basically all you have in
. That and some cheap scares. It´s not worth the price of admission.
------------
Ever since
became such a staple of adventure games, there´s an increasing amount of titles that require not much more than pressing 'w' and looking around at whatever wonderful things the developers want you to look at (and think that are wonderful). But take
, for instance. You find no one else in the entire game and spend the whole playthrough inside a house, but alas, it feels alive and booming with intricacies. All of this because there´s a superb story giving it leverage. Or take
, a walking simulator that is so well done that gives you genuine creeps and makes you feel emotionally connected to some entity you only have contact with over your walkie-talkie.
is a bare 'walking simulator' meets 'opening drawers simulator' with good graphics, and playing the game results in such a dull activity as you can imagine from these two titles. You get the story pretty fast, you get that your character is demented, you quickly realize what went on in the old house etc etc, no surprises. Uh, something ghastly is behind the man´s madness, but...is that enough to make you keep moving forward? What is there to find at the end of the 100th same-looking corridor you traverse? A somewhat obvious conclusion to an uninteresting story? More cheap scares (I mean, so cheap you need to be very prone to being mindlessly scared just to feel a tingle)? The headache-inducing endless opening and closing of the very same 3D models of drawers, chests and armoires to eventually find some piece of torn document that gives boring details of something you already know? This is not a game.
There is no interaction. There are no puzzles. Nothing in the story that puzzles you - except if you have a somewhat twisted penchant for sadism and hope to see bloody images by the end of the game. No enemies. Just moving forward, looking repeatedly at the same well-done graphics and objects and wondering if there´s something more than old socks inside that bedroom chest. This is hardly an ideal of fun.
When I received an achievement for opening 100 drawers, I knew something was very wrong. When I entered the Canvas Room for the third time and realized that there are dozens more dull letters, pictures and drawings to find (which means - you guessed it! - opening
more drawers), I quit. Let the madman creep around the same rooms over and over again. Maybe this is some kind of fun activity for someone. But there´s definitely nothing for this old adventure games fan to find here. Let´s move on to the next creepy old house rendered in full glory by Unity.

Mild horror game with an interesting, immersive story, setting and protagonist and solid gameplay; well worth your money.
I'm usually not one for horror games, but since Humble gave it away for free, I thought I'd give it a try. And I must say, I'm not disappointed; this game has the right amount of horror / jumpscares for me. Don't expect tons of blood and gore, or the serious♥♥♥♥♥♥your-pants kind of stuff that a title like Resident Evil 7 might give you. What you can expect is more of a historic, atmospheric and even psychedelic kind of horror and suspense.
For those reviewers that commented that this game is nothing more but a walking simulator and you only have to keep pressing the "W": yeah, you *can* play the game like that, but then you're missing out on quite a bit. The charm of this game partially lies in the "maze" that is the protagonist's (if you can consider the main character to be a protagonist, at any rate) home. At times, you're walking down a corridor and get to a dead end. You turn around, but instead of the corridor that you came through, there is now a wall blocking your path. You turn around again, and you're suddenly in a room. You turn again, and the room has completely changed its appearance. You turn once more, and then there's a jumpscare. You won't completely loose your bearings, but it's enough to keep the game interesting and to keep you on your toes. If you're a completionist, like me, then you'll even *have* to explore the entire house like this to find all the collectibles.
Story-wise the game is not overwhelmingly deep, although the context of being a painter who has lost his wife and who is now frantically working on his magnum opus is something I haven't seen in a lot of games. The story is fleshed out through all kinds of notes you find during the game. It's OK-ish, but again, nothing too deep, complicated, nor are there any plot twists. Also, and this might just be my own personal perception, but it seemed to me like in the first half of the game, you find notes on a fairly regular basis, while there seem to be far less notes in the second half of the game.
Graphically, I really like the game and the art style. The game goes from a nice, Victorian art-style into being more and more twisted, psychedelic and... weird (for lack of a better term) as the story progresses. Every chapter has a distinct atmosphere and theme. Rooms are very detailed and certainly don't feel empty at all (unless a room was, by design, actually meant to be empty). And as mentioned earlier, the fact that the room that you're in might be something completely different once you make a 360 is a nice touch.
Gameplay is fluid and the controls are easy. The "puzzles" aren't very complicated, most are movement / position / viewpoint related, with a few "get a certain item and bring it to point X" things thrown in.
+ plays fluidly, easy controls
+ original setting / background
+ good atmosphere (graphics-wise, music-wise and effects-wise)
+ nice jumpscares
+ not "overly" horror-y (which might be a drawback if you're into seriously heavy horror games - this is not one of those)
+/- limited replayability; there's three different endings, but the second and third playthrough are 75-80%-ish the same as the first playthrough
- notes and story background seem to be mostly present in the first half of the game; while the second half *does* contain some, it becomes more of a "push to the end" kind-of-thing
- not very complicated
- some things become a bit repetitive, especially if you're doing more than 1 playthrough
- to get the "Omniscient" award, you need to get the three different endings ON THE SAME SAVE SLOT, i.e. after finishing the game for the first time, you have to do the 2nd and 3rd playthrough with the same savegame; to me, this was very confusing, since the game offers three save slots to begin with, which caused me to be like "Oh, one slot for each playthrough, neat!"...
If a horror game actually manages me to keep playing it, that means two things: 1. There's not a lot of horror in it (I'd really quit playing a game if it has too much, and I have a low threshold) and 2. the game has an interesting enough setting and story. All in all a solid 7 our of 10 for me.

I have to say I loved the graphical style and attention to detail in the environment in this game. The whole creaky Victorian house during a dark and stormy night is a cliche but sometimes it just works. However, that was pretty much the only thing I liked.
The "gameplay" is a monotonous mix of slowly (the protagonist has a limp) walking through the same (yes, the levels are reused) hallways over and over again, looking for the right doo-hickey that will let you move on to the next identical room or hallway, while annoying stock sounds of crying and screaming play in the background. Every now and then you get a pointless jump scare or hallucination sequence (there were a couple of clever ones, I have to admit) accompanied by a loud sound (usually a dramatic/ear-piercing  orchestral hit).
The story might have been ok, if it weren't drawn out for so long by complete filler "puzzles": Why am I collecting these checkers game pieces? Why does clicking a random object in a room unlock the door? I was also taken out of the game by some of the written notes you find in the game where the language seems at odds with the era the game apparently takes place in, but that's a minor complaint. There really wasn't a whole lot of game here and it all just becomes an exercise in tedium. Near the end I was just going through the motions to see the final cutscene.

Good concept. But the execution needs work.
The game emphasizes the importance of trust with your squad mates. Trust goes up or down depending on how you perform in battle, and how you respond to your team mates.
Your team composes of men, women, American, Chinese, French, British, etc
However you dont get to create your custom character. Nor do you even have control of his personality.
He says dumb or hateful things in the cutscenes sometimes which are the opposite of what i want him to say.
Same with your squad. They say hateful and dumb things in cutscenes. The characters are very unlikable during cutscenes.
Game takes place in 2080. But the characters are stereotypical. Your character is referred to as "yankee" many times. They hate each other because of nationality.  And are racist towards AIs because of fear and ignorance.
There is also a forced romance between your character and one of the 2 females. Same female everytime, you dont get a choice.
You choose 2 squadmates to accompany you at different instances. This gives you the opportunity to gain trust. But at some point later the game separates you and your team from the others which means you may lose the opportunity to gain trust with a member. And this has a consequence on the ending.
GAMEPLAY:
The standard and boss enemies are robotic.
Its satisfying to kill them. You can shoot off specific limbs and head. They will crawl on the ground and grab your leg.
The shooting can get tedious at times.
There are forced walking sections where the fov zooms in way too much.
You can hold 2 main weapons. The first weapon you have with you at all times. Its upgradable. You can pick up a sniper rifle, shotgun, assault riffle, rocket launcher as your second main weapon.
You have a pistol with infinite ammo. And can carry grenades.
Upgrading your team's weapons seems useless.
You can upgrade your skills with "nanomachines". Its very limited and useless for the most part.
There are gameplay elements that are introduced early in the game and never used again later.
PORT
The graphics options are very limited. And they cant be changed in game. You must use the game launcher.
The fov is bad. The fov slider is for vertical view not horizontal.
The game doesnt properly detect my controller on launch. I have to unplug and replug the controller and make sure i press the START button and not the A button.
STORY
Story is fine. There are plot twists. I predicted a plot twist from the beginning, but predicted it for the wrong character. But i was close enough.

Perhaps it felt better at release, but this game doesn't have much going for it today. The port is iffy and the character designs are uninspired (at first you think they're only knocking off Vanquish, a game that came out 2 years before this one, then you later realize they're also knocking off Gears of War - from 6 years before).
The game goes all-in around a voice command mechanic that does not work well at all. Attack is just about the only command your squad will identify, so much so that they might identify it at any time. This works especially poorly since (after reading the command list) I've determined that there is no "take cover" command. So once given the go ahead, you better hope the fight goes well because your squad is going for broke.
The level design is uninteresting and while the plot shows promise, the game controls so poorly that it's not worth it. I quickly determined that I'd rather watch a movie of this game than play this one. This isn't some small bad design choices in a forward thinking game, this is a game that tried to emulate some pretty great games (that solved these problems years before) and failed.
Cover, check. Shooting, check. All the other parts that make a cover-shooter fun? Nope.
It's not worth your time.

This is a superb, action-packed 3rd-person shooter that takes place in a future Japan.  You play the role of a member of the "Rust Crew", a multinational team that is tasked to take out rogue robots.  There's more to it than that, of course...
It is filled with a variety of imaginative combat scenarios beyond the usual 3rd-person "hide behind chest-high walls" that keeps the game play moving, but the core action is still very solid.  Big robots, small robots, teeny robots, massive robots -- you will kill many, many robots, and there's a nice variety of upgradable weapons to try out on them.
For a game released many years ago, it still looks very good.  A lot of care was taken in creating the characters and the varied surroundings.  The special effects are also excellent.  The sound effects and english translation are nearly flawless.
The game does have a few other minor gimmicks, such as the "team response system" that (optionally) utilizes a wonky voice-recognition system. The system gives a little personality to your team.
I found only a couple of flaws in the game: first, some of the objects could have been signposted better.  There were a couple of scenarios that really hid their objectives -- not that I want a quest arrow or anything, but some reasonable indication of where to go next.  Second: oh, Japan.  Sigh.  Your black teammember is this hulking dude who talks straight out of some bad early 2000s sitcom, aight? A 15-year-old girl proposes that your character becomes her boyfriend.  You know, the usual.
I only got around to playing this game because I was combing through my backlog, and it was a very, very pleasant surprise.  In fact, BD helped wash some of the badness that Mass Effect: Andromeda left in my mouth.  BD is tight, focused, nice to look at, well-executed, and well-constructed.  Hightly recommened.

If you're like me, you had a lot of fun as a kid pushing toy cars around in  "races," a loose term of course given the results were entirely at your whim. When I first opened this game and the tutorial race kicked in, memories of this came flooding back. I felt like I was 6 years old again watching tiny cars fight it out beneath my omniscient gaze. It's not the prettiest or most physically accurate race simulation created, but that's not the point of the game. In fact chances are, whilst thinking about that, you just missed a key strategy-changing event and cost one of your drivers valuable points. The press will notice this, and you can expect a roasting in the post-race interview should you dare to attend. Be careful what you say, or you'll upset your Team Chairman, and that might cost you your job. And that, in a nutshell, is Motorsport Manager.
Sure, the management mechanics aren't exactly the most detailed we've ever seen, and they're sure as hell not revolutionary, but the R&D system and personnel management are both very satisfying to interact with. That top driver you've eyed up isn't going to join your no-name team without making it worth is while, and that means less money to build parts to train your R&D staff so they can make parts that you would even consider putting into a car.
But your R&D staff can't make stuff from nothing. They need facilities. Bloody expensive facilities at that, and that's yet more money the Chairman isn't going to like to see the back of. Oh, and that crap press interview you gave after the last race? That probably just put off that killer sponsorship you were hoping for, so kiss goodbye to that £1,000,000 cash you were relying on coming in.
Of course, you could skip all this and join one of the pre-existing teams in the top of the ranks.
But where's the fun in that?

Motorsport Manager is REALLY fun at first. Especially the races are fun to watch.
However, after 2-3 seasons, you've seen it all. Very little content, repeats itself pretty fast.
The whole game is pretty shallow, no realism or depth behind anything, no fine-tuning.
The learning curve stops where it should steepen.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
- The interviews and events repeat themselves very quickly. Additionally, their quantity lacks, too.
- There is no real interaction with drivers and staff, however there should be more, since they are the backbone of you
team, obviously. And you should have to check up on them to ensure they're doing fine.
- Generally, not much to do between the races.
- Very narrow selection of drivers and staff, very few unique personal traits.

be
Yes, you COULD mod additional content (interviews etc.) into the game and i know, that MM does everything to support that. The problem being:
The game itself provides little to no base mechanics to build upon.
There is NO REALISM and ZERO DEPTH behind everything. Just take the higher numbers and done. There you go.
The biggest issue here, the most obvious one, is the car development (-progress) and the racing itself.
Instead of being able to fine-tune certain aspects of certain part in a simplyfied, but realistic approach, you just have every part's power defined as one single number (2, counting reliability), that's it.
No actual testing, no fine-tuning, nothing.
Sure, you're the manager, not the mechanic you might think, but in the end, you'd have the final word on how and where to improve the engine and what to change, right? You'd expect you could actively test your brakes or engines on the test track and let your drivers practise there, but no. Nothing.
If you sell a game for that price, you should atleast provide a wide array of basic mechanics. You can't simply rely on the workshop to mod everything for you. Even tho this might legit be the strategy behind this title.
Recommended?
Full price: NO.
-55%+ on sale: YES.

The nostalgia hits home when I hear that classic soundtrack, and see the familiar faces of the four mercs of Metal Slug. If you loved playing this game series, then you will love being able to play it without having to dump your weekly allowance into trying to beat it!

Are you looking for classic arcade action? Are you looking for bullets flying everywhere, everyone trying to kill you and big explosions?? Look no further than Metal Slug 3!
The game is a port of the classic arcade game. You can play alone, with a friend in the room or with a friend online. The game isn't easy but who are we kidding, you don't want easy anyway! You pick one of 4 players to control and shoot your way through 5 action filled levels. Levels contain multiple routes which can influence how the boss fight plays out. As you fight your way through you can save prisoners and be rewarded with points or one of several enemy crippling weapons. Each level features a large bullet sponge of a boss, but we wouldn't want it any other way now would we? The final level is an endurance round, testing your skills and pushing you to the limit. The game gives you 20 credits (continues) with 3 lives each. Sound like a lot? Well that depends on how good you are, because you might be begging for more. If you're having trouble or finding things too easy, the game does feature four difficulty settings (Easy, Medium, Hard and Very Hard).
Now what are you doing still listening to me? Grab yourself a copy, suit up and mash that fire button like there's no tomorrow, you got a world to save.

+ Interesting premise; exploring human memories through a server-based environment is intriguing in and of itself
+ The sci-fi setting and several locales that you visit throughout the game are fairly well-designed
+ While the graphical quality of the game is nothing to boast about, the vivid colour palette prevents the game from looking ugly
+ The puzzles that you solve throughout the majority of the game are relatively creative and simple (possibly too simple at times).
- Some areas of the game are based too much on trial and error, leading to repetition (and at times annoyance), bogging down the whole experience
- The horror elements of the game are very poor: cheap jump scares and weak sound design accompany you throughout the short campaign (just under 3 hours); the game would’ve been much better having focused solely on the puzzle elements rather than trying to unnecessarily frighten the player.
“This is quite a difficult game to recommend. At times it feels unpolished, but for an indie game it’s possible to overlook that simple fact (not to say that just because it’s an indie game that it can get away with it either). If you’re looking for a fairly short and simple puzzle game with a little atmosphere (which was what I expected it to be), and can look past the annoying horror elements, then I’d recommend you get this on the cheap like I did.”

Reboot is a first person puzzle game that has a focus on the philosophy of what makes the “self” or “soul”. The self is apparently a collection of ducks that form your memory by that aside… the impending question over the playthrough is what defines us, and could it be possible to clone ourselves in a way so that we are exactly the same without losing something beyond our memories. You play as a female protagonist piecing together the puzzles of both the story and environments she has to explore within Soul Chamber.
+Central Hub to play memories again and unlock other ones
+Lights show status of the doors (open/complete/closed)
-No backtracking once you reach the final level (train)
-No extras in main menu to visit memories you unlocked
There is a central hub with doors that lead to certain areas marked with images for the theme. Hospitals, schools, highways, and other themes have all their own puzzles and elements of the story to present to you. You are required to do a set amount of puzzles before the other doors will unlock for you. The doors themselves have light indicators to tell you the status of them, along with bookstands in front of them that allow you to revisit memories. Bookstands outside door shows all info you collected from ducks
+Nice Atmosphere and art style
-Sound quality could be better
The atmosphere is very eerie with a general feel of isolation from the world. There is just as many environments as there are puzzles. The environments allow you to freely explore to a degree but the area of which you can do so is very small with linear segments. The areas tend to have their own way of artistically showing you hints, from symbols in graveyards to color coded pieces scattered amongst the playground. There are even segments where you have to listen closely to sounds and repeat them in order to proceed though many deem this the most annoying part of the game.
+Great puzzle diversity (sounds,cryptic,etc)
-Difficulty Inconsistency
The puzzle diversity in this game ranges from replicating sounds, pictures and figuring out how to navigate through mazes to deciphering symbols, messages, and images.  There are some places where you can do them out of order which tends to lead to inconsistent difficulty, most notably near the end of the game there is 4 puzzles that are simply varying difficulties of the same exact puzzle.
+Fun Theory Crafting
-Unsatisfactory Ending
The ducks (memories) give you hints and glimpses into the memory of your character and the events that have unfold. It is fun making a theory of what occurred as the story unfolds from scenario to scenario until the end of the game though due to lack of backtracking its rather hard to revisit the memories you spent time finding and uncovering. The ending however leaves rather open-ended to speculate to what really happened to your character.
Overall, I would say master reboot is a good game for not only for theorycrafting but for the variety of puzzles that makes the experience kept fresh throughout the game. The main complaints I have is that the rushing I did to collect all the ducks (information) made me incapable of backtracking to look through it all. I plan to play the game a second time and take as much time playing the memories as I do the puzzles in order to get the most enjoyment out of the game possible.

You wont ever find a game like this that is in the horror/mystery genre that incorporates a cyber and technology feel while trying to spook you out at the same time. The graphics in this game are amazing. There would be times where I would just postpone solving puzzles just to walk around and take screenshots.
Where it needed some leverage/extra hand:
-The story is good and all but at the end of it , I found myself asking more questions and using a search engine to fill in the holes
-The cutscenes are good but it goes back to my first point that they had more questions raised than answered
-The story sometimes went to dissapointing parts that you hope it would not go to or you're sitting there thinking of a cliche you've already seen.
Other than that. I still recommend this game based upon the gameplay mechanics and definitely the environment/art in this game. Don't focus on the story aspect as much or it'll be mediocre. Just concentrate on the the game and gameplay and graphics itself.

I have to say, this is possibly the best Indie Game I have ever played here on Steam.
It's a horror adventure game, which - funny enough - reminded me a little bit of Super Mario 64, in the way that you navigate through the Soul Village which acts as a kind of overhead map screen, from which you can enter the different levels. Each level is unique and offers a variety of simple or challenging tasks (puzzles, finding items, stealth quests, survival), which makes the game a lot of fun to play.
I really enjoyed the horror elements. The little scary girl may be a clishé, but it's one I like and I think it's very well executed in this game. The abandoned hospital stage is pretty terrifying and when the game wants to be scary, it certainly manages to.
The only thing I found a bit disappointing is how little time they give the story to conclude at the ending. Also, the intro stage didn't seem to be very appealing. But once you're out of the woods (literally), the real entertainment begins. Apart from that, I was absolutely amazed by how terrific the game was and how immersive the story unfolded itself.

Generally speaking, this game had the potential to be a great Star Trek game.  Sadly, the studio that developes and runs it has turned out to be profit centric to the point of ignoring things like constant spamming by asian players in chat asking you to pay them money for in game currency (which you can't block out until they've spammed you), server disconnects that are rampant (7-12 times per day on average), content that either is tempermental or flat out doesn't work, fleet options that seem to get broken after every other update and content push (which defeats the purpose of having a fleet), etc...
Having put nearly 100 hours into the game itself, I'll admit that aspects of it are quite fun but over the years the quality of the game has been declining.  What I find interesting is that again, this game could be fantastic if it was supported and maintained better.  Sadly, it doesn't seem like this is the goal of the developement team.  I suppose when they had the opportunity to do more as a pay to play format, they did what many of the smaller developers do and soaked up profits while neglecting their product.  In the end, what we have is a game that is more of a tease than a pleasure.
I'll continue to play for now simply because the game isn't completely broken, but I would STRONGLY advise any new players to NOT spend any real cash on this game.  If the developement team would be willing to fix outstanding bugs, content and servers, I would consider revisiting this review and possibly stating that paying for it would be worth it, but as it stands I simply can not encourage anyone to spend their money on this game.
I would caution anyone from complaining on the actual cryptic forums as they have been known to ban people for posting negative reviews on their forum.  If you're going to post anything against them, I would recommend doing it here since Steam isn't beholden to Cryptic studios.

Let me get this straight, you want me to tell you a review about this game? Whoever you are, you might as well go to the curators, because if you've come for a review on this game, you've come to the wrong place. However, if you have come for an outstanding chocolate chip cookie recipe, you've come to the right place.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
1. Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
2. Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
3. Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
4. Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
5. Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
1. Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.

This is a spectacular game that is well worth playing. Be sure to download the official, free, DLC from the Bethesda website.
