Raptor: Call of The Shadows was amongst the first games I played on my brothers 386.
It's a timeless space shooter that never really gets old - even tho I wish there would be a modern re-make.
This version adds a few things, like a HD filter and some other stuff, but I would advise playing with that all turned off, and just enjoy the game how it's designed to be played!
There is also an alternative '1994 Classic Edition' on Steam, which is just the old game running in DOSBox but this one has a few upsides in performance on most systems.
Pro's:
- Actually a modernized port, not just the old version running in DOSBox
- Added achievements
- Still as great as the original
- Plays really well, even on low-end hardware
Cons:
- Sometimes its hard to make an achievement trigger, and you may have to redo some
- Could use better controller and mouse support, but I prefer keyboard anyway
- I didn't verify this for myself, but I heard cheatcodes and some soundtracks were removed
- There are sometimes issues with savegames
The developers of the port promised to fix the issues, but so far there haven't been updates yet over the past two and a half years.
Is it still worth getting this game?
In my opinion totally, even if its just for nostalgia - but if you like games like this, this is one of the true classics and a must have!

Very poor port of an old DOS game.
+Classic top-down shooter with currency system and upgrades.
-Some achievements have trouble working correctly. This requires you to do the achievement over and over again before it finally unlocks.
-Mouse function does not work very well at all. In windowed mode the curser can go outside the window and your ship will stop responding. The mouse also gets hung on imaginary objects at times requiring you to move it around real fast to free it.
-Controller support is poor and might require some tweaking to become functionable for some people.
-The save game system creates a new save every time you save. This normally would not be a problem except you are only allowed 10 save slots and gives an error when you try to save after that. Which requires you to go and delete enough saves to be able to save your game again.
-Cheatcodes from the original game were removed.
-Soundtrack from the original game was changed.
-Says it has cloud support but would not redownload my save sometimes.
-The developers were told about the bugs the game has and responded (in 2015) that they are working on it, but nothing has been fixed and the devs never came back.
This game was an extremely poor port. Which is funny considering the original game is also on Steam and works like it is suppose to and is the same price. The only two things it doesn't have over this release is achievements (which do not work right sometimes) and cloud support (which did not work right sometimes).
Get the original version
for the same price without all the headaches this version has.

To me, it doesn't matter what features your game has, procedural enemy damage, weapon customization, "consequence system", or voice recognition (that has a hard time recognizing simple English words unless you put a forced emphasis on certain consonants), if you make a First person or third person shooter, the shooting mechanics have to feel responsive, effective, and not make the player feel like guns don't shoot well or are effective. Mess up the shooting mechanics, and I have no interest in your shooter.
Binary Domain fails this test for me. Never in my life has a third person shooter felt so bad to shoot. I never could get the reticule right where I wanted and when I did, the enemy felt like it moved too fast for me to compensate for the gun's recoil, or guns didn't feel accurate enough to feel effective. Every gunfight I experienced seem like I could only deliver a couple shots to an enemy before I took major damage (granted, I'm playing on the hardest difficulty, but this has never been a problem for me in similar games), where in a game about shooting out parts of humanoid robots to make them lose limbs, makes it really hard to deal with groups of enemies and make it seems like you're mostly reliant on grenades and co-op partners to kill enemies. Worse off, there doesn't seem to be a button to switch the shoulder you're aiming from - which as far as I'm concerned, is a cardinal sin in a third person shooter and invalidates the game for me. One section of the game required me to deal with a group of riot shielded enemies by charging my weapon's alternate fire for a few seconds, but due to the cover system and aiming, it was extremely difficult to fully charge the shot and then effectively aim said shot (which has very limited ammo to begin with) without being nearly slaughtered. More enemies came up behind them and rushed me and my partner. We barely escaped the rushers, but then I had to fight the aiming controls and the fact that I couldn't get in cover behind a pillar to deal with grunt enemies. I was downed, and I could have revived myself, but I lost interest and rage quit.
I've wanted to play Binary Domain after hearing it mentioned from various Youtubers. I love shooters, and i'll player a medicore shooter if the shooting mechanics feel good and I feel satisfied in my skill in using the weapons. Mass Effect 2/3, Uncharted Series, Warframe, Spec Ops: The Line, Gears of War series all feel good with shooting, but here I feel like I should spam bullets and hope for the best. I'm Done.

Awesome space invaders clone. Absolutely fantastic game. The game is designed in a Puppy Games typical "modern-retro" style which makes all of their games looking great. The music and sound effects fit perfectly to the overall game style.
The game itself is very well balanced. It's an absolutely fantastic game. The difficulty rises with every level and the claims the right strategy on which upgrades to buy. The mini games between some levels are a nice addition.
You are looking for a great space invaders clone? Grab Titan Attacks! This is a 10/10 game and should be in every game library :)

Titan Attacks is a modern remake of Space Invaders with a neat retro aesthetic. It's purely an arcade-style experience: start a game and continue until you die, going for the high score. Your score will mostly be determined by how long you can go without taking a single hit; one hit won't kill you, but it will reset your multiplier that increases when you beat a level. You also buy upgrades between levels, which are vital to surviving later in the game.
If this sounds interesting to you, then it's probably worth picking up. The gameplay is solid, the art and sound is pretty cool, it controls pretty well once you get a few powerups, and the replay value is great. There are certainly many worse ways to spend five dollars, and this game is certainly worth it if you can find it cheaper.

As a toddler did you ever have the toy were you have to fit certian shapes in the right holes? That's the most complicated the games puzzles will get.  On top of that some of the puzzles make absolutley no sense. Heres an example:
During the park memories there is a yellow traingle trapped under a jungle gym with no way to retrieve it. How do you think you solve this? Dig under it? Pry the jungle gym open? Nope. There is a triangle shape on the outskirts of the level that you are supposed to fill with a triangle block that is also on near the borders of the level. This items are a decent distance away from the puzzles themselves which in itself makes little sense. So how does placing the yellow triangle in the yellow hole solve the puzzle you ask? The game may have simplistic puzzles by concept but they are made difficult for the player to solve through terrible design. Here is a description of another puzzle:
The first sequence of the airplane memory has you collecting three key cards that open a door and allow you to proceed. Seems easy right? I picked up this game on sale, and I'm glad I did. That statement is twofold. I'm happy I played the game, but I'm also happy I only paid the sale price for it. Overall, it was a positive experience, but there were some sections that were personally frustrating.
The negatives: The most frustrating thing for me was the platforming elements. I imagine if you're a gamer who likes platforming games, that they will probably be easy and no cause for concern. I however am not a platform gamer and there were a couple sequences in the last level that I found rather frustrating. Second, the collection elements of the game slow you down as you go through levels and can remove the tension that this type of horror game wants to create and destroy it. A minor complaint I have was the "bell" puzzle in the last level, this a musical puzzle and I'm basically tone deaf. Again, this may not be a problem for all players but it was for me. Finally, some of the animated 2d art was at a lower quality than the rest of the game, it was very notable in several of the close up shots on hands.
The positives:
The storytelling. Oh, the storytelling. The world setting was personally appealing to me, with fun touches of science-fiction. More importantly though, was the core story itself. I won't say a lot, so as to avoid spoilers, but following the twists and turns of these young women's lives was a very entertaining experience and it made for a fun psychological thriller. The method of story presentation added a lot to the game as well. A lot of the story was told through single still images that you found as “memories” located throughout the game. Stopping to search for these did hurt the ambiance, as I previously mentioned, but it did make for a rewarding experience as you worked to uncover the truth of what had happened. In retrospect, it is rather ironic that one of my personal gripes about the game also contributed to one of the parts I enjoyed the most. The level design was done well and did have a good feel to it when you were moving through it at a reasonable pace. The last pro I want to list is the 2d art that found by viewing the tattoo glyphs (and in the final level, on the walls) was creepy, disturbing, beautiful and technically accomplished.
tldr; The game has flaws, but if you like horror and don’t hate platforming elements, its worth playing. The story is a blast to uncover.

I rarely write reviews, but I feel, that I have to write for this game one. I can't believe the 59/100 Metacritic rating, because this game is a masterpiece, BUT not for 14$, which is actually EUR here. The game sure looks a bit outdated, but it's moral question is a thing, which is worth thinking on. So basically we are playing as an unknown girl, who has to relive a person's memories. The connections will be revealed later in the game, and damn, the story is awesome! Each memory is a little puzzle, but unfortunately a very basic one. Each memory consists of two levels. A real memory level, where you relive the person's memory, sometimes interrupted by Seren, and a Zero level. Zero levels are really twisted maps. They aren't the person's memories, but something different. Okay, okay, but you may ask, who the hell is Seren? Well Seren is the character, who gives a little bit of horror to the game. Don't worry, the game isn't a fully horror one, but some levels give me chills on my back, when I play them. Seren's appearance is really cliché, because mostly she can't hurt you (á la F.E.A.R.), and if there is a dark hallway, you can expect her appearance. I think she can only hurt you in 2 levels, but I'm not so sure. If I were a Journalist I'd give the game an 85/100. Why? Because it's really unique. I've never seen any game like this before, and thanks to this game, I will buy Soul Axiom too. Master Reboot is kind of a visual novel in first person view, and a really well-written one. So I'd suggest EVERYONE to pick it up, when it's on Sale (like right now). For 3.50$ / EUR it's a short, but amazing game!

I'm going to give my honest opinion on this game. I bought it basically because I wanted to have it when Skywind came out (which is probably going to be awhile from now). I gave it a shot and realized that it was nothing like Skyrim. Skyrim was my first elder scrolls game so this was definitely a different experience for me. The first thing that really stood out to me was the dialogue. As I'm sure you already know, the dialogue is text based. The next thing that stood out to me was the lack of fast travel or quest markers. When I first started playing this game I absolutely HATED the lack of map markers and fast travel. However, I kept playing. I kept exploring, doing quests, and learning about this strange new world in Morrowind. Eventually I got used to the fact that you had to really gather information because the game was not going to hold your hand...at all. Graphics were never really a problem for me even without mods, but some people might not be able to tolerate them.
One of the best features of Morrowind is the landscape of the game. It is so unique that I enjoy getting lost because I get to explore the world further. If you are reading this after playing skyrim or oblivion first, think hard about whether or not you want to stick with the game even though it has no fast travel or map markers because I'm positive that this will turn many gamers away. If you can look past these simple things, you will find yourself lost in the beauty of Morrowind battling monsters, joining guilds, and enjoying the little things that this game has to offer. It has quickly become my favorite Elder Scrolls game and I have yet to start the bloodmoon expansion. Overall I would be happy to recommend this game, if you think about it first.

I played the 2015 remake of the game, but only to avoid any difficulties in getting the game running on modern hardware. I played it because I wanted a brainless shooter and I remember liking the soundtrack.
And that's pretty much all I have to say about it. It's a vertical shoot-em-up from the '90s and - beyond its soundtrack - is pretty much forgettable. Raptor's major distinguishing feature is that you buy new power-ups between missions, which lets you tailor the game somewhat to your play-style. It does result in a lot of extra grinding - you play and replay earlier levels to earn the cash for the aforementioned power-ups - and some of the later levels are brutally hard unless you do just that. But assuming you have the necessary arsenal, the game is an adequate shooter. Not exceptional, not bad. Just fine. Average and unremarkable. Fun if you are into the genre or want to waste a few hours, but not memorable or in any way evolutionary. Just... fine.
It's got some rocking music, though.

I have trouble with grading this "game". Yes, "game" because as an old-school gamer I am expecting that a game should require some skill, like reflex, precision, strategic thinking. A game is supposed to give something to solve with these skills: beat an enemy, go through a level, solve a puzzle etc. I have found none of these here. Yes, there is some interaction,  mainly walking and exploration, searching for things, and something puzzle-like - but nothing requiring really using player's brain in a "gaming" way.
The whole thing reminds a big computer art story-driven demo, with the exception that the interactions puts the observer in a middle of the environment, with immersion much stronger than a typical horror movie. This is the second similarity - horror movie-like tricks (sounds, effects) indeed thrills strongly in some moments (although nothing really unexpected for a person that saw large numbers of such movies over the years...).
Do not get me wrong - there is plenty of good work here - artwork, effects, music etc. - all 1st class. But somehow I cannot get used to current "games" which are in fact such big demos where all the "challenge" is to find the trigger for another thrilling effect. Probably just wrong choice for me - I tried this one out of curiosity and after enthusiastic opinions. So definitely I do not want to discourage people who like such walking/thrilling experiences. But beware that there is not much beyond that. Even the story - which is not bad - but it is not that original: kind of a mixture of "Dorian Gray" (clearly one of the main inpirations,
) with surrealistic crazy visions (
).
Pros:
- artwork, graphics, music, effects
- horror movie-like (but stronger) thrilling experience
- a dramatic story that can be considered interesting
Cons:
- more an experience than a game - too few traditional game challenges
- some of the thrills do not work that well (
)
- becomes boring after a while of nothing new or really interesting to do (fortunately the game is not very long, impression would be much worse then...)
I should put "neutral" - I recommend it to people liking such "experiences".  But cannot recommend it for old-school gamers (like myself ;-)...

TLDR at bottom:
Vermintide is quite similar to Left 4 Dead in the sense that you and 3 buddies have to make your way through maps to get to a "safe room" area, all the while being molested by zombies, er uhm rat-men, and you accomplish this goal by using med kits, potions (pills and adrenaline), bombs and fire bombs (pipes and molotovs).  Some of the special rats include a hunter, a smoker, a tank, a spitter/boomer combo...  OK so it basically IS L4D but in a completely different universe.
Regardless, it's very fun.  one thing Vermintide has that L4D (and a lot of games...) doesn't have is a unique loot system.  Each character can have a variety of custom loadouts, each having its own melee weapon, ranged weapon, and even clothing!  It doesn't shower you in loot like Dead Effect 2, it makes you work for higher level loot.  In order to get this loot, you have to play on the harder difficulties; in order to play the harder difficulties you have to have better
It's a bit of a catch 22.  Luckily this is offset by...
The most friendly community I've ever seen in a game!  About 10 hours in, I got bored and started playing the Nightmare mode.  In most other games, a level 100+ would see my level 12 and immediately votekick.  Not Vermintide.  The community not only allowed me to play, but they taught me the ins-and-outs of the game, allowing me to obtain precious needed equipment to further push the difficulties.  The several games I've played with players who are 200+ higher than me have been a blast.
My biggest regret is that the DLC's are still so expensive.  I got the base game for a few bucks - maybe the DLC's will be cheaper over the xmas sale...
TLDR - It's L4D but with rats and a fun loot system and an awesome community!
Edit:  Playing DLC's with a buddy.  They're equally as impressive.  GG

Dynomite Deluxe is a bubble game. If you don't like your basic facebook bubble games, this game is probably not for you. However, it has options for gameplay that are far different from the average bubble game.
I played this game a ton as a child, so I'm biased to like this game, however I have played 22 hours of it on steam, so I can explain reasons other than nostalgia that you might also love it.
Dynomite Deluxe follows your basic bubble game mechanics. You have a shooter at the bottom of the puzzle, and you toss different colored eggs to try and match pairs of 3 or more. Simple. Your different gamemodes include endless, puzzle, fossil, and time trial, each with a different goal in mind.
Let's go over endless first. In endless mode, your goal is to get a high score, plain and simple. In this mode, the puzzle creeps down towards the warning rope line, if an egg touches said line then an extremely loud warning noise plays (I'm not joking, the sound that plays is actually atrociously loud) and you have a short time to clear the eggs to a point above the warning line before the momma dino gets angry and crushes the puzzle. I'm not joking. That's part of the game. You start off with only a few colors, the number of colors you start with changes depending on the overall difficulty, and after a period of time a lizard on the right side of the screen will say "Doiii Whirley's coming!" After which a purple pterodactyl will quickly move in a zig-zag upwards from the bottom of the screen holding a new color of egg to the current puzzle. If you don't break the egg whirley is holding, that color of egg gets added to the pool of egg colors. However, if you do break the egg, the puzzle starts to move down faster.
Puzzle mode is exactly what it sounds like, you clear puzzles to 0 eggs remaining on screen. Every few egg placements, the puzzle drops lower, a similar mechanic to existing bubble games. Nothing particularly new.
Time trial: You clear x amount of lines with y amount of colors, both variables depending on difficulty. You clear 60 lines on easy, 30 on medium, and 15 on hard. You can take as long as you want, but the goal is to get the fastest time.
Fossil mode: The goal for this gamemode is interesting. You have a fossil fragment in the middle of your puzzle. Your goal is to clear the eggs above the fossil, by ricocheting eggs around it, to make the fossil drop, and that's the basis of it. You can choose to make the puzzle drop down a large amount in intervals (called "strategic" mode), or have it creep very slowly downward from the get-go, and on the same intervals as strategic mode, have the puzzle speed up (Called "Action" mode). For the most part, the former is the easier method, but no matter which one you choose you're probably not reaching the end without save scumming because of the sheer number of fossils you'd have to clear to reach the end.
Pros:
*Fun for all ages
*Great music
*Cheap for its quality
*Multiple game modes, each with unique mechanics that are in no way gimmicky (Only exception being puzzle mode bricks)
*Gameplay suited to 3 sensible difficulty levels
*Cute dinosaur graphics
*Simple, gameplay is exactly what you see
Cons:
-Fossil mode becomes nearly impossible without save-scumming
-Puzzle mode is similarly difficult for similar reasons
-Default high scores aren't easy to beat
-Runs at a very low resolution
--OBNOXIOUSLY LOUD SOUND IF AN EGG REACHES THE WARNING LINE
I definitely recommend the game, I got way more out of this game than the hour-per-dollar ratio I normally look for in a video game, and for its age I think it's still very good, and well worth its price. If you're skeptical, the game does go on sale from time to time, and you can get it then if you're even remotely interested.

I'm pretty disappointed in Spore, which really says something since I bought this with a pretty low exception.
The game is broken up into several stages so, let me break it down.
The Cell Stage: This stage is a fun little minigame. Something similar to Osmos. Not bad, but it's a pretty short section of the game.
The Creature Stage: In this stage, you move around the map, allying with other creatures or attacking them. This boils down to a series of button matching events. I had fun with this stage.
The Tribal Stage: This is a RTS stage. You train tribe members into various roles (healer, heavy damage, lite damage) and attack or ally other tribes. This is where the game started to sour for me. The game world felt very scripted for something to could have been more dynamic.
The Civilization Stage: The is another RTS style stage. My problem with this stage was the tech trees were very shallow. It felt like Maxis did the bare minimum and called it a day for this stage. Very disappointing.
The Space Stage: This is the last stage, and clearly Maxis meant for this to be the bread and butter of the game, which makes it all the worse when you realize that it's not fun. You can fly to other planets, make alliances, fight enemies, and take quests. Although your given teraforming tools, their poorly explained, and I never found much use for them. The bulk of this section is taking quests, going to a planet, picking something up, and dropping it off back at the quest giver. This gets monotonous very fast.
All and all, I think you can find better games than this for what your looking for. This wont really scratch your Sim or Sim City itch. If your just curious, pick it up when it's on sale, but be prepared to give up on it when it becomes boring.

This game can't make up its mind on what it wants to be. Part survival horror, part exploration, part...mini games? The problem is that it doesn't do any of them very well, and on the larger levels the slow plodding along of your character is just frustratingly slow. The survival horror parts quickly lose their luster when you figure out that sounds are scripted at certain locations and can be repeated over and over, or that you can meander along in one of the few "chase" scenes without actually having any worry of being caught.
The story is largely told through finding rubber duckies scattered throughout memories. Some of these, the important ones, thankfully, are easy to find with the briefest bit of looking around. Others are incredibly frustrating due to nearly pixel-perfect jumps and long backtracking times. The end of each memory also has a brief animation revealing some storyline, and I honestly have nothing complimentary to say about them.
The story itself is rather poorly told, with many of the important plot points feeling forced, and much of the rest of it as completely unrealistic. As an example, being inside the "Soul cloud" for more than a certain time causes your physical body to die, and you become trapped there. You find a company memo stating how they've lost several employees to this, and I can't help but wonder how the company hasn't been sued out of existence.
There are some interesting bits scattered here and there, but unfortunately that's all there is - interesting bits. The gameplay is dull for the most part, the puzzles simple, the mini games frustrating or unfun at best, the horror isn't frightening - basically, they tried for everything and succeeded at nothing.

Titan Attacks! is a modern reimagining of the fixed shooters of the coin-op era, combining elements from Space Invaders, Galaga, and those of modern games such as persistent ship upgrades, fast mouse control, and collectable temporary buffs like those seen in contemporary scrolling shoot-em-ups. Anyone who has played either of the aforementioned titles will feel right at home with this game, and find its faster pace, increased variety, and greater sense of progression to be a perfect cocktail of old and new, resulting in a unique experience that is difficult to walk away from. Puppy Games clearly have a love for the genre, and understand exaclty what made it so popular. This shows in everything from the mechanics all the way to the beautiful art design. Fan of the classics or not, Titan Attacks! is a labor of love, and a game you can't afford to miss.

I'm going to give my honest opinion on this game. I bought it basically because I wanted to have it when Skywind came out (which is probably going to be awhile from now). I gave it a shot and realized that it was nothing like Skyrim. Skyrim was my first elder scrolls game so this was definitely a different experience for me. The first thing that really stood out to me was the dialogue. As I'm sure you already know, the dialogue is text based. The next thing that stood out to me was the lack of fast travel or quest markers. When I first started playing this game I absolutely HATED the lack of map markers and fast travel. However, I kept playing. I kept exploring, doing quests, and learning about this strange new world in Morrowind. Eventually I got used to the fact that you had to really gather information because the game was not going to hold your hand...at all. Graphics were never really a problem for me even without mods, but some people might not be able to tolerate them.
One of the best features of Morrowind is the landscape of the game. It is so unique that I enjoy getting lost because I get to explore the world further. If you are reading this after playing skyrim or oblivion first, think hard about whether or not you want to stick with the game even though it has no fast travel or map markers because I'm positive that this will turn many gamers away. If you can look past these simple things, you will find yourself lost in the beauty of Morrowind battling monsters, joining guilds, and enjoying the little things that this game has to offer. It has quickly become my favorite Elder Scrolls game and I have yet to start the bloodmoon expansion. Overall I would be happy to recommend this game, if you think about it first.

Binary Domain is a Science Fiction Third Person Shooter thriller set in a dystopian future, where an army of robots assumes authority over the nation of Japan. Essentially, without spoiling anything; you are a team leader of a small squad of special forces soldiers tasked with infiltrating Japan and stopping the menace.
The gameplay in general feels somewhat similar to Mass Effect. For some reason, I couldn't help but think that the protagonist Dan, feels a lot like Commander Shepard. You know, you are a dashing soldier with an assault rifle blasting futuristic robots to bits and pieces, while being given the ability to communicate with your team and have trust/distrust with them similar to Sherpard's loyalty from his team. The game is a third person shooter, and the guns all feel similar to what Mass Effect had. Of course, I am not suggesting the game is a clone of Mass Effect; the typical gameplay scenarios differ for sure.
The story is pretty interesting, and without going too much into it; it has some depth and does attract you to it. We can all argue that, the depiction of robot armies in the future probably won't look anything like what you see in the game, and as a matter of a fact, the robots would probably 1-hit kill every human resistance from miles away in a fraction of a second.. Of course, that would make the heroics you fulfill in this game impossible, so the robots do shoot somewhat inaccurate half the time. This allows you to not die instantly, and makes them seem like humans in terms of combat prowess.
The voice command system is interesting, it reminds me of an older PS2 game called SOCOM; where you could use your microphone to issue orders to squad members. In this game, the voice commands are rigid and require you to refrain yourself to only certain words that fit the context of the topic/event/scenario. It can be obnoxious at times, because it doesn't always pick up what you said; which is why I just ditched the mic system altogether and opted for using the classic "A B X Y" selections. It is possible though, that my microphone just isn't good enough for this, though it is also possible the game is just not amazing with voice detection. Others may differ and say it worked perfect or was flawed as all hell.
The boss fights are pretty intense, and remind me of older SEGA and Nintendo bosses where you have to go through many stages or phases of the boss until you finally kill it/him/her. In one situation however, I found the boss fight to be rather frustrating. Some of the boss fights require you to use certain equipment to kill them, such as a special gun; which is no problem. The problem is, it is near impossible to have the boss get distracted by team members, so it always follows you when you are trying to use the autocannon to kill it. The autocannon in this situation is stationary, so you have very little time to get on it and aim it at the fast moving boss. I found using the charged shot from the assault rifle stalled the bot long enough to get a few rounds in to it however.
The game is full of action. You have very minimal pauses in between levels where you are not fighting or in combat readiness. Robots are everywhere and the game makes you feel like they will never stop attacking you. This to me is nice, because it keeps you going. This can also be a problem for some people, because after a while you start wondering "when and where would be a nice spot to quit the game for the night?".. The game is chapter based, and checkpoints are where the saves are at, so you can't really save on your own, which to me is something I don't like. The game makes use of cover, which means you will often use it to recover health and avoid lethal shots from snipers and rockets.

An action third person shooter game that feels like Mass Effect, but definitely operates differently. Is pretty fun and entertaining, and offers some story and interaction with team mates. No really, it almost wants to be Mass Effect; but it somehow manages not to be, which to me is actually worth considering if buying this game.
Pros:
+Good level design.
+Lots of action.
+Weapon variety and upgrading.
+Specialty team members and squad organizing.
+Good boss fights.
+Decent story.
Mix:
=Voice commands are nice when they work.
=Trust system is nice, but vague dialogue choices can lead to accidental loss/gain.
Cons:
-Some situations are rather frustrating to complete.
-Squad members sometimes get in your way.
-Console graphics, some textures are ugly.
Overall, I recommend this game; you won't be bored when you play it.

tl;dr at the bottom
The game's plot tells the tale of a Rust Crew (a team of soldiers formed by the International Robotics Technology Association to uphold the New Geneva Convention) and their operation to find the source of the Hollow-Children (robots which are near indistinguishable to a human) and to shut down it's operations. The characters features Dan Marshall as the main character., and several others as squad members Dan's relationship with the rest of the crew members are affected by the choices that the player makes. For example, replying to Cain with the optimistic banter choice will gain favor with him, where as a sarcastic one will gain you favor with Big Bo. Friendly fire is also taken into consideration, you will loose favor with crew members if you shoot them. The story itself is quite enjoyable, on par with the average hollywood action flick, but with more depth as you try to figure out who is really running the Hollow-Child development.
Gameplay is most easily described as discount Mass Effect. You will lead a squad of three (already including you) and fight wave upon wave of robotic goons, moving through a linear level dotted with chest high walls and barricades that serve as cover for the player to use. The levels are occasionally spiced up with new robot types or unique robots as either a mini-boss or as a boss itself, each neading a (somewhat) different approach to defeat. Combat is like the generic cover shooter, where you are recommended to take cover behind something then you pop out to shoot some rounds, but slightly faster paced and better executed combared to some of it's other competitors. Enemies are a little bit more different than the average cover shooter as their body parts will break and shatter depending on where you shoot. The Squad is easily commanded and will follow orders rather effectively, mind you these orders are very simple.
I doubt multiplayer is still alive, I didn't even touch that part of the game.
tl;dr
Binary domain is a good game if you're looking for an action game with an alright story. The gunplay and the slight banter will keep you mildly entertained while you navigate the sometimes tedious corridors that the game may throw at you occasionally. If you like cover shooters and japanese games, then Binary Domain is a game you should consider getting.

Binary Domain is definitely a game I would recommend. It has a great story which is thrilling and full of surprises at every turn. The gameplay is fast paced and fun. The characters have interesting personalities although I felt they could have been expanded upon more. The game's other pros and cons are listed below along with the previous points which have now been summarised:
+ Great Story
+ Good Gameplay
+ Interesting Characters
+ Variety of different bosses with different move sets.
+ It has Multiple Endings which are based off of a "trust system" (which means there is a reason to replay the single player aside from the great story.)
+ Has a good amount of achievements (which adds further to the replayability of the game)
+ The graphics are pretty good, especially for its age.
- Friendly AI has a tendency to walk in front of you whilst you are shooting (hitting friendly characters lowers their trust of you)
- The game does not work well with most controllers which aren't the Microsoft Xbox 360 Controller (which also has some issues - for me at least anyway).
- The button to use cover is also the same button for sprint/roll which means you may accidentally go into cover whilst trying to sprint/roll.
- The game can only be configured for the most part through an external config program.
Honestly I didn't expect the game to be as good as it is when I first started playing it. It had been sitting in my library for quite a long time so i hadn't given it much thought. When I picked it up recently, which was only due to me looking for a new game to play, I thought it would be some generic shooter that I would blitz through in under a couple of hours. I'm glad I was wrong. The game also has a multiplayer which I haven't tried yet, therefore I'll update my review once I've tried it.
As to rephrase my first point, this game is certainly a hidden gem and I would recommend it to anyone who has some free time, an open mind and probably a controller because I'm not too sure about the Keyboard+Mouse controls (haven't tried using them plus there are some negative reviews surrounding them).
Overall Rating: 8.5/10

Binary Domain is a rather standard third-person cover-based shooter which happens to be fun, well-polished, and highly action-packed. The main premise is about sentient A.I. A group of undercover agents make way through a futuristic Japan in a hope to reach the headquarters of the largest robot manufacturer on the planet. The mission? Find out what is going on and why the forbidden robots who look, talk, and act like humans have been created and set free into the world.
Gameplay mostly consists of futuristic cover-based gun fights against large squads of robotic enemies, although several mini-game sections are present too, such as car chase scenes, defence sections, time-sensitive tasks, and so on. The game also has a lot of boss fights, which usually take form of a giant robot in a shape of some kind of animal. Some of the boss fights were pretty fun and had interesting strategies to them, but a few others were more on the annoying side and at times overstayed their welcome by dragging out.
The game also contains voice recognition and a squad trust mechanic. During many parts of the game, the party members would talk to you and ask you questions, and you have to respond to them in an appropriate manner. There are limited number of commands available, though they tend to cover majority of the situations well enough. This voice recognition is also used to issue commands in battle, such as to instruct your team to advance or retreat for example. Depending on how you act and respond to your squad, you will gain or lose trust with them, which in turn has an effect on the game's ending. Only drawback regarding all this is that the voice recognition is not perfect. At times it fails to pick up the reply you're trying to say, no matter in what tone or accent you say it. Other times it might say a totally different thing that sounds similar to what you've said, and that could affect your trust with a teammate.
The game does a solid effort at storytelling and character development. It mostly attempts to explore what A.I. would be like in the near future and the kind of challenges the society might be facing when that time will come. Of course, there are some parts of the plot that just plain don't make sense or make you really roll your eyes. There are also some cheesy scenes with silly humour present too. Overall it's good enough to keep the player engaged.
Generally a well-executed sci-fi setting with an interesting idea and entertaining combat. Don't expect anything revolutionary, but what you will find is an engaging, action-packed blockbuster that should deliver plenty of fun.

I really like when a game focuses on one core idea and properly execute it.
Aside the fact that we can discuss the gaminess of Layers of Fear, the main experience could be "wandering inside the twisted mind and horrible memories of a painter trying to achieve a masterpiece". And the great visual and mechanical idea is to mess with the mind of the player by changing the layout of the house behind his back.
Once you enter the workshop room with the blank canvas, anything goes. Every room, every object, every note is a piece of a narrative puzzle for you to complete and interpret - and at the same time, your progression seems to influence your final painting.
After completing the game, many questions remains, like who is the character we play ? By leaving these question and many other open to interpretation, the game continues to haunt us in a terrifying but satisfying way.
A good and spooky haunted-house ride of a game.  Plenty of creepiness and tension without over-using cheap scares.

Very good for replayability, has multiple endings and you can continue from your first campaign. Has some nice graphics and sound design. Has some parts with trippy visuals and ever changing environments that makes it stand out somewhat in my opinion. Exploration and obtaining collectables is a must as it factors into the story and influences the ending. It breaks immersion when you know that you can't die, and a run in with that demon only serves as a transition into a new area (although you do have to aviod her). I like the troubled artist take, showing you what happens in the mind of this lunatic, it can be very disturbing at times which adds to the atmosphere. I didn't necessarily find this game scary due to the fact that you can't die and it does take away from the experience, but it does handle "death" in a different way that does set it apart and I do have to give them credit for that, just don't really feel like there's dire consequences for my actions. Overall it's still a good game, beat it around 11 hours and again there is replayability so I think that people should give it a try for a very interesting ride.

This was the very first PopCap game that I've played in my childhood. Despite of having quite some years already I still think it is a game that aged well. It is a fun puzzle game inspired in the dinossaur era with mechanics that are very similar to Puzzle Bobble. There is a classic unlimited mode, a time trial mode (to break a group of eggs the quickest you can), a Stomp Puzzle mode (puzzles to clear areas full of eggs) and a Fossil puzzle, which works as an "adventure" mode where you can collect a fossil part per level of a creature that used to exist in the pre-historical era. All the modes have a difficulty level that you can choose. However, after you complete the Fossil mode, there's nothing much else to do so the game might end up repetitive and boring so do not expect a big longevity. On the other hand, it is a good casual game to play if you have some spare minutes to spend by entertaining yourself with something random. I recommend Dynomite Deluxe to everyone who likes casual puzzle games.

Spore is a very intriguing, fun little game to play. The game is rather short, being able to be completed in a few hours or so- depending on how capable you are at playing it.
However, the game is prone to crashing. There's some irritating bugs. And the graphics are pretty standard.

I'm pretty disappointed in Spore, which really says something since I bought this with a pretty low exception.
The game is broken up into several stages so, let me break it down.
The Cell Stage: This stage is a fun little minigame. Something similar to Osmos. Not bad, but it's a pretty short section of the game.
The Creature Stage: In this stage, you move around the map, allying with other creatures or attacking them. This boils down to a series of button matching events. I had fun with this stage.
The Tribal Stage: This is a RTS stage. You train tribe members into various roles (healer, heavy damage, lite damage) and attack or ally other tribes. This is where the game started to sour for me. The game world felt very scripted for something to could have been more dynamic.
The Civilization Stage: The is another RTS style stage. My problem with this stage was the tech trees were very shallow. It felt like Maxis did the bare minimum and called it a day for this stage. Very disappointing.
The Space Stage: This is the last stage, and clearly Maxis meant for this to be the bread and butter of the game, which makes it all the worse when you realize that it's not fun. You can fly to other planets, make alliances, fight enemies, and take quests. Although your given teraforming tools, their poorly explained, and I never found much use for them. The bulk of this section is taking quests, going to a planet, picking something up, and dropping it off back at the quest giver. This gets monotonous very fast.
All and all, I think you can find better games than this for what your looking for. This wont really scratch your Sim or Sim City itch. If your just curious, pick it up when it's on sale, but be prepared to give up on it when it becomes boring.

“Arcade shooter with online coop” is what made me buy this game. Metal Slug 3 is a 2D-sidecrolling shooter with awesome weapons, cool vehicles, amazing boss fights and now on steam with ONLINE COOP.
You go through six missions. Each having branching paths you can take with different weapons, vehicles and enemies. Some are easier/harder and others are longer/shorter and it’s up to you which path you want to take. I found this very interesting as it made the game much more fun to play through several times to try every different path. The levels, the enemies and sound is superb and sometimes I'd just like to play the game cause of these things alone.When it comes to multiplayer you just create a lobby, invite a friend, start and play. Easy, good and simple. There is also online leaderboards for those who like that sort of thing. Game features controller support which you then can use to get the “authentic arcade experience” if you so desire but a normal controller or keyboard works just as fine. I noticed a few bugs when trying to connect to a friend (or him/she connecting to me) and while pausing the game. It was nothing that ruined the game for me at all though.
In short, it’s just a fun shooter you can play online with a friend, and it gives you plenty of reasons to play the game again.

The world you're thrown into is queer and rather unsettling. You're never really directly told the plot in game, instead you're left to piece it together through notes you find (blue duckies) and scenes during memories (the puzzle/exploration stages to progress the game). I honestly got scared a few times, but I'm an incredibly big wuss so that doesn't say much.
The puzzles range from really simple, to somewhat abstract. I remember one frustrating part I couldn't pass (plane memory) that I looked up because I really just couldn't figure out what I was doing wrong. There are a couple situations that are more "platform" like but generally you're just walking around figuring stuff out/not peeing your pants avoiding Seren.
I really loved the art style. Chunky, blocky shapes and contrasting colors. Vaguely reminded me of Mirror's Edge. The music/sounds really help sell the mood. Watching the main hub get filled up with stuff from the memories was cool too.

This is a great little indie game that takes place mostly in various eerie, surreal, but beautiful environments. There is a strong female protagonist and a good sci-fi story that you slowly piece together as you play. In describing the gameplay, I would say this is a first-person walking simulator with a good mix of puzzles. There are a few areas with some platforming (especially in the unfortunate timed end sequence) and even some shooting, though the shooting is directed at environmental components and not people.
The plot revolves around a computer system called the Soul Cloud where people can download and store their memories before they die (think of like the Lucid Dream set up in the movie
). You find yourself in the Soul Cloud traversing someone's memories which take on a sort of nightmarish quality due to a computer virus and/or some sinister person who is out to get you and who has corrupted the Soul Cloud in order to lash out at you. I am trying to be vague so as not to give away any of the plot. As you "solve" each memory, you uncover more and more of the story of what has come before and what has brought you into the cloud.
I liked the visual representation of the surreal environments but I admit that I didn't like the cartoony art style that was used to portray some of the concrete memories you unlock. The sound design and music in the game was also pretty well done except some of the creepy sounds got repetitive at times. My one big complaint about the game was with the wonkiness I experienced while using my Xbox 360 controller. For some reason, there were times when I used the left stick to strafe left in the game that my character would get stuck strafing left, which would be annoying and downright dangerous in some of the few platforming sections of the game. I don't have any issues like this with my controller with any other games. This was the biggest nuisance but I was able to deal with it and enjoy the game anyway. I am just putting it out there for others to know about if it influences their decision to get this game.
If you like a good sci-fi story with some surreal creepiness and some decent puzzles then you should get this game.

When someone looks at the screenshots, they may think that Master Reboot has very little to offer visually but in reality what it offers is easily some of the most aesthetically varied environments I've come across in most games. Without getting into spoilers it will be hard to explain why Master Reboot is so enjoyable but here is my attempt.
What the developers have achieved isn't a horror game in the normal sense. In fact, I'd go so far as to say that this is not a horror game at all, but it does successfully create an eerie atmosphere through the use of places which are quite unsettling due to how alien they appear. The game itself is set within a virtual world that seems somewhat warped, like a cross between Tron and Alice in Wonderland and that in itself makes it interesting to explore. The puzzles themselves won't tax your mental agility much but there are some really tricky ones that will require some concentration. The decrypting of the code in the graveyard is probably going to have you searching the internet though.
From a narrative point of view, there is a plot behind all these places you explore. But you won't make much sense of it without looking for the Blue ducks scattered around the locations since these provide clues to the plot. While I did take a really good stab at collecting them all it seems that I missed some and didn't get to see the alternative ending, but I suspect I know what it is based upon the plot anyway. I would recommend anyone playing Master Reboot to spend some time collecting the ducks to figure out what is really happening in order to really appreciate what is happening. The plot is not handed to you on a silver platter, so you will need to piece together the information from the clues yourself to grasp the depth of the storyline.
Overall I would say Master Reboot deserves more attention than it received. It's stylised visuals may not be cutting edge but they were perfectly matched to the storyline and setting of the game. The pacing of things was nice and the developers had a good stab at making the player uneasy but really could have avoided repeating the same cheap scares over and over to the point where they just didn't matter any more. There is some platforming sections here but they really aren't very difficult and they are rare compared to the other activities you will do. Much of Master Reboot is focussed on exploring the environments and solving the occasional brainteaser, so while you will see things like guns and axes in the screenshots you need to be aware that these are not used for fighting. This makes for a refreshing change of pace for an industry which insists on making 90% of its games focussed on overcoming challenges by bullet or blade.
What a refreshing change to have games like Master Reboot around who strive to do things differently!

Over twenty years old, but still a great shooter game after all those years. It has everything it needs for this type of game. If you like classical Shoot'Em Up games this is for you. Fun and motivating. Definitely worth a buy. The 2015 Edition adds Steam Achievements. Graphics can be improved with a HQ Filter (then the game looks slightly different than in the screenshots). The game works fine with a gamepad. There are three different zones with nine levels each (27 levels total). The game becomes quite a challenge if you don't find a way to collect money and upgrade your ship (18 items available in the shop). Collecting items and selling them in the shop will help you out (the only time you can't use a controller is for selling, you need the mouse). You can buy up to five shields, there are different weapons available for air and ground targets (or against both). Some of the weapons are always equipped, others you can switch during combat. A little bit annoying are the limited savegame slots (you have to delete old savegames first) and that you can't really distinguish them (no titles, no dates). I owned this game back in the 90s but never really played it (I think it was a shareware version just with Bravo sector levels). When I was buying it for Steam I didn't even think I would play it for hours, really a great classic game that, playing it for several hours now, exceeded my expectations, addicting gameplay. I think you can have up to ten hours of casual fun with this game to play it through and unlock the achievements.

The other things I hate
Unfair enemy spawns.
For example, there is a horde. So they throw a big rat ogre onto your face, so you can't move at all, you either fight the ogre, the horde, or try to manage to fight them both at once, which is doable if you keep back and don't get overrun. But then, on top of that, they spawn the rat, packmaster, right behind you, with no warning, no anything, and he hooks you immediately and drags you away, with no ability to dodge what-so-ever. Apparently you can duck before he hooks you, so he will miss, but it never worked for me. Normal dodging didn't work either. Pushing him doesn't work...
Sometimes, the rat ogre gets spawned in the most unfair of places, literally impossible to dodge, and then on top of that, they decide to throw in that horde, as well as some stormwermin, a packmaster, and maybe a few other special Skaven. So you literally get stuck with no place to move or dodge, you're not even able to make one step, and of course, you die
So combine all of that, the massive horde witht he rat ogre, the unfair spawn of the packmaster, with the stupid AI and how they can't do absolutely anything for themselves, or you, and you get an aggravating situation, which happens a lot.
And the third thing I hate is the hit detection. Nothing special here, but I just get hit while I'm out o the reach for some enemies, Or though walls. In the last game I played, the rat ogre just smashed me though the wall, and the missionw as over.
So yeah, generally, I highly recommend this game. AI is okay on easier difficulties. Hard is easily managable as well, though you can see how the AI is starting to lag behind even there. But on Nightmare... Nah. I managed to complete high majority of missions on nightmare with bots. I only have two to go, and I don't even want to try them. And cataclysm... No thanks.
So if you're going solo... be warned if you're going for high difficulty, because aggravation is sure to ensue, all the time, due to incompetence of the AI mostly, but as well as some unfair enemy spawning. Reflex is based off a Quake 3 mod. It has a lot of Quake 3's gameplay elements, but with some tweaks to weaponry, new mechanics and movement options. So if you're a fan of Quake 3 or similar games, you'll get a gist of what you're getting.
+Smooth, fast paced gameplay with a layer of strategy. One of the best in the genre.
+Simple but elegant graphics that does not hinder gameplay.
+Netcode is amazing. You can play at 80 ping and not have much of an issue.
+Matchmaking, something uncommon in AFPS games (issues addressed later).
+Insane customization, especially with Steam Workshop support. You can change almost everything, from sounds to the
.
+Map-making. You can buy the game just to design maps, it's that good. You can play on user-generated maps, and there are TONS of good ones.
+Small community tournaments and events happen frequently, a few times a month.
-Extremely small playerbase. Main reason I have trouble recommending the game. It takes too long to find a match, and you'll rarely find one for larger modes like Capture The Flag (which is fun as hell). This severely hinders matchmaking, even though I gave it a pro.
-Runs well on modern PCs. However, I occasionally get slight preformance issues on my laptop. It's outdated but should easily run games of this graphical quality. I usually get 80-100fps, but it rarely dips to 40-60fps. Might be a problem exclusive to me.
-I had a issue where my mouse sensitivity was different between fullscreen and windowed, despite the settings being the same. Not a huge issue since fullscreen always has the correct sensitivity, and I always play on fullscreen. It might have been fixed though, and after asking around, no one seems to have this issue except me.
Overall, I LOVE this game. And pleasantly surprised it made it out of early access after 3 years, with constant improvements.
However the playerbase is too small to find proper matches. Matchmaking only works properly under a sizable playerbase, without one you'll have to constantly fight against veterans that will rip you apart. If it were not for my RSI and the small playerbase, I'd play this game everyday. It's such a shame that great games are often left in the dark.
Buy if you're willing to deal with a small playerbase and therefore lose matches constantly (unless you're familiar enought with the genre).
If not, I cannot recommend it, no matter how much I enjoy it and would like it to grow.

I sort of have a mixed opinion on this one, but I find that the pros outweigh the cons slightly.
Spore is a game where you can create your own species, and make them Carnivores, Herbivores, or Omnivores.  It's up to you. You have free will to make it look and do whatever you like, as long as you can gather enough DNA points that is, which is normally collected by just completing simple tasks.  You can befriend other generated species made by the community,  or you can make them your enemy and completely wipe them out off your continent. The choice is yours.
There are five stages (in a nutshell) : Water, Land, Tribal, Economy, and Space.  They are all equally lengthy and manage to keep you in your seat for a while, as a whole new creation mechanic is added to each one.
And then there are the cons of the game.  As always, games are not perfect.  I find that as I get farther down the five stages, each one gets more and more boring after a while.  Sure, it adds new things, but I personally liked the first two stages the best.  The first two gave you the power to move around your creature.  In the last 3 stages, you are stuck using the point and click mechanics.
Overall, the game is quite fun and can kill a few hours. But after a while it just gets a little bit boring, and I don't really see me playing this one again.

Master Reboot looks like the coolest game ever made. A dark, moody cyberpunk game with a really cool concept – after death people can be stored in a “soul cloud”, and their relatives and friends can interact with these AI ghosts. You start plugged into the soul cloud, and it’s obvious that something has gone terribly wrong. Parts of the world are missing, or broken, and you’re being stalked by a roving anti-virus program called Serra.exe, who just so happens to materialise as Sadako from
during her raver years.
From a gameplay angle, Master Reboot is more Gone Home than System Shock 2. If you enjoy these “walking simulators” – storytelling through exploration of environment – you’ll probably find a lot to like about Master Reboot. The puzzles gating off one area to the next could charitably be described as “rudimentary” – most of them are variations of “find yellow, green and red keys and deliver them to the corresponding lock”. While they facilitate environmental exploration, as a gameplay mechanic I found them very tedious. Even the few genuine puzzles tend to be pretty braindead, usually solved in seconds (sometimes by accident).
The game does briefly flirt with other game styles, including stealth, shooting and platforming, but the game was obviously not designed to accommodate these shifts – the single level utilising stealth is laughably easy, with Serra patrolling up the middle of a plane while you push buttons when her back is turned. Unless you walk into her limited field of view, you’re safe – as long as you do not touch her you can jump around inches from her back. Evasion consists of nothing more than crouching by a seat until she’s passed.
The last level suddenly becomes a timed precision first person platformer – something which I believe is now considered a war crime in most civilised countries. The controls are clumsy, and the timing is so tight that any kind of mistake will essentially force you to restart. Completing the game at that point was frankly a relief, and almost managed to sour the goodwill the game had built up.
In spite of these issues the story and atmosphere does just about manage to carry the game – the cold, minimalist cyberpunk environments and creepy sound design are often brilliant with particular mention going to the excellent lighting, though there are a couple of amateurish stages that let the side down. The scares do sort of work, especially early on, but they’re very scripted and it soon becomes clear that there are only a small number of circumstances where Serra can actually harm you. There are also bizarre, cartoonish flash style interludes that are not only poorly drawn and animated, but jar with the aesthetics of the game as a whole. The game would have been stronger as a whole with those story elements woven into the game in a less incongruous manner.
Master Reboot often feels like a student project, scrappy and unfinished but built with obvious enthusiasm and love for the craft. As a result it is a game that is impossible to hate – but 12 quid is proper game money, and that means it must be held up against the standards of its peers. In that cold, harsh light the game just does not stack up. If you can find it in a sale, I might tentatively recommend it, particularly if you are forgiving of clunky mechanics.

Master Reboot is a fantastic little heavily story-driven adventure/puzzle game.
In the near-future, a company named Mysteri has developed software known as the Soul Cloud. The Soul Cloud is a sort of virutal reality which is inhabited by uploaded versions of the real world's deceased, as well as their living guests. You find yourself here and must journey through a number of memories, piecing together recent events.
The puzzles are pretty simplistic. They're enjoyable enough but they're not the draw here. It's entirely story and ambiance, both of which I feel to be well-executed.

Wonderful game, if a bit frustrating at times.

If there was an ingame option screen I could probably just switch to keyboard and mouse (I need to invert the mouse) but no, I have to start the whole level over again.  Anyways:
Scale: 1=despised 2=negative 3=could go either way 4=positive 5=loved
Game design: 4/5 The game itself is pretty simple.  Run round in the dark and find clues to the story.  It mixes elements of survival horror (I wouldn't call this an exclusively survival horror game though, very little can actually hurt you), puzzles, platforming, hidden object.  It's actually a good mix, and despite my beef with the platforming, the game itself doesn't feel broken.  Perhaps a bit dated.  3D navigation is a bit clunky, and some of the puzzles don't make any sense (but are still easy), but none of it actually gets in the way of gameplay.  Maybe you could call this game "casual horror"?
Tone: 3/5   The largest problem with the game is it's selection of advertised screenshots.  It has some cool and haunting imagery, but like the game play, there ir a mix of styles present.  There are weird little cutscenes at the end of each level that look like they were made in Flash.  The impression of the game is a bit different than what is actually there, granted that it is difficult to present a game with this much variety.  It simply might not be the epic horror mystery that you are looking for.  The concept is great, but the story is overly simple and a bit confusing.  I don't know if the game intends to keep you guessing about which girl is which, but I'm still getting them mixed up.  I can nitpick more but ultimately it doesn't interfere with the experience that much.  I really want to enforce that this game is actually quite casual, don't expect anything mindblowing and you should enjoy it.
Personal skew: 2/5 I'm not mad anymore, and might attempt that last level again.  Hardcore gamers will find this game easy and possibly laughable, I don't think that most will feel it to be a waste of time, but some definitely will.  Casual gamers will get the most out of this, especially if you're interested in horror games but don't want to be overwhelmed.

This game is definitely something interesting.
The premise is very interesting, with an online cloud-system where dead people's memories are stored, and the story is also very intriquing, as you uncover more of your memories and figure out not only what is going on, but also who your player-character is.
The art-style during gameplay is very visually pleasing and fits the game well, and while it's quite obvious that the drawn cutscenes aren't very proffesional, they do the job of telling a good story.
The sound design is also really great, as the songs in the background and the various sound effects that appear really make the atmosphere, and as the game is a lot about atmosphere, the art-style and the sound design deliever perfectly.
Not to mention, the ending credits-song is really good. It is a great song to end the game with.
The gameplay is also quite fun, as you do different puzzles, and while there are some puzzles that can be quite frustrating to figure out, most of the puzzles are quite fun to figure out.
Seren.exe, the creepy girl-character that follows you, is at first quite creepy and I definitely got a shock when I first enqountered her, and she definitely fits the creepy atmosphere. However, as the game goes on, her presence can be quickly discovered by the players, and when she isn't killing, but just staring at you creepily, her effectiveness becomes a lot less scary, as I definitely made some jokes in my head about her just standing in the corner not doing anything.
Overall, a worthwhile game that has a interesting premise and some great atmosphere. It is quite short, but if you like this sort of game, you'll probably get your money worth.

A beautiful, freaky first-person puzzle game that takes place in the virtual reality "memory city" of the protagonist, whose identity is obscured at first but ultimately emerges as the player explores various memory fragments.  What begins as garbled and contradictory transforms over time into a pleasing, coherent story.
The only story beat that annoyed was the use of the "scary little girl" cliché, but it's forgivable, largely due to the dynamics of the story itself.  In short, it makes sense.
The game takes place over three acts, the meat of which is the second act, featuring twelve levels over three stages; within a stage, levels can be visited in any order and abandoned temporarily if a puzzle is too difficult at first.
By and large the puzzles are easy to solve with a little persistence; often the trick is to simply find and figure out which objects in the world are puzzle pieces.  I did consult a walkthrough once for a challenge that appeared particularly nonsensical (at the end of the School level) - I sadly stand by that decision as the solution required previous memorization of an image not to be found in the puzzle area itself.  There were a few other puzzles that I didn't "get", but which were quickly solvable by "brute force" combination of available elements.  Also, there is a series in act three that will require the use of Steam's built-in screenshot function ... or fraps if you get the non-Steam version.  This was  irksome, but by contrast the great majority of levels are engaging and fun to figure out.
My entire playthrough took just over five hours.  A short game, but it's all quality time.  If you aren't confronted with a puzzle, you are observing memories and piecing together the story of the central characters or running through the occasional action sequence.  These elements are well mixed with good pacing.  For the completionist, a couple extra hours might be had combing every level for the collectible memories.  I wish I had seen all of them, but I preferred to finish the game rather than essentially "pixel hunt" for every last story clue.  Personally, I dig short games.
Overall, I unreservedly recommend Master Reboot.  It's worth a few hours of your time to find your way through this weird virtual world and resolve a compelling, sympathetic story.

Possibly one of my favorite RPG's of all time, this game is commonly called the best of the Elder Scrolls series for good reason.
First, I'll begin on the soundtrack. The first song you ever hear, my god, it's beautiful, there's no other word I can think of. It's got great balancing between the various instruments and strikes that balance perfectly between being calm and yet, intense and epic, sending chills down your spine likely as the song hits its climax. I will say, in game, you will want to turn down music since it's very loud compared to the rest of the game sounds.
Second, the amount of options on how to build your character. You have tons of skills, each providing good changes to how combat works if you're character is built around using those skills. I will say that magic is not as refined as it was in Oblivion. Magic suffers from having a "Cast Chance" based on skill level, intelligence, and stamina. Even your beginning healing spell and basic fireball spell both only have between 10-20 for characters not built for it from the start, or up to 50-60 for a character designed to use them, which also suffers from nonregenerating magicka, which was added later into Oblivion, making magic very annoying to try to build.
Next, I'll talk a bit about combat. Melee combat is based very much around 3 major stats, Strength, Agility, and the weapon skill for that weapon. Strength, as you might expect, affects damage, though different than how Oblivion did it. Each weapon has a select set of damage amounts based off the type of attack you perform (moving forward/backward does a Stab, side to side does a Slash, standing still or moving at an angle does a Chop) and strenth acts as a multiplier, up to a maximum up to double the base damage at 100 strength (I've found from my experience). Agility affects 3 major aspects to combat, Dodge Chance, Hit Chance, and Knockdown Resistance. Your weapon skill allows you to hit more frequently. As for magic combat, you have Intelligence, Willpower, and the magic skill being used. Intelligence affects the amount of magicka you have and the Cast Chance. The magic skill for the spell you are using affects Cast Chance a lot more than Intelligence. Willpower affects your ability to resist enemy magic. I will say that there are times combat feels a bit unrefined due to there being no Active Block button, Blocking is based on Block skill, which affects the chance to block attacks, though, blocking attacks will completely negate all melee damage dealt.
Finally, overall gameplay, well, I personally find it well designed as well as being immersive. You have a very basic Fast Travel, which is paying NPC's with "Silt Striders" or boats to take you to certain cities within range, and then you walk to you're headed, no highlighting your area with your cursor and clicking and magically teleporting. Questing is immense and you can fail a lot of quests as well as several quests having multiple outcomes. This game does have a difficulty slider, though the game will not hold your hand, if you wander into a dungeon you shouldn't be in yet, the game will let you know with NPC's who will turn you into their new floormat. The next thing this game does rather well, ranking up in Factions. It's not do a quest, instantly rank up, do another quest, and so on and so forth. Instead, you do the quest, and if the next quest is intended for a higher rank, and you aren't that rank, but you've done all the quests before it, you still need to gain the skills that the Faction "Prefers" Like the Morag Tong is a kind of legal assassination Faction and "Prefers" skills like Short Blade, Light Armor, and Acrobatics. The game's world is immense as well, I'd estimate it larger than even Skyrim.
Now, onto my complaints with this game. There are quite a few bugs that can occasionally screw up questing, but you can fix all of them with the use of the Console, which I had to do once so far due to something I did early before I got a quest and it kind of screwed it up since I didn't pick up the required item from the one body, and his body disappeared before I could go back and get it. While it was a minor inconvenience, the Console does allow you to fix a lot of those bugs. Another fairly large complaint I have is how fairly useless some skills are, such as sneak, which is almost useless compared to the future games, or speechcraft or merchanting, similar to the future games. Another complaint is how some skills are approached like Alchemy, if it's below 20, you won't even see the first indgredient effect for example. The other complaint was how magic as a whole was approached with nonregenerating magic and Cast Chance, though I can't deny some magic effects being amazing, such as Levitate, which allows you to basically fly around like a birdie for a little bit.
Overall, I'd say this is probably the best of all the Elder Scrolls despite the individual improvements to magic and smoother flowing combat that the future games had. The DLC is amazing as hell, and Solstheim is possibly one of my favorite areas ever put into a DLC. Mournhold is colorful and has a lot of hidden secrets to explore. I've logged about 45-50 hours into my current character and I've yet to even touch the main storyline of the game, the main storyline of Solstheim, or even to venture into Mournhold. The game is huge and insanely fun. I'd highly recommend getting it for anyone who has ever even remotely liked RPG's.

An underrated and overlooked third person shooter classic from the lead designer of the Yakuza series and it most definitely shows. Despite the occasionally banal and linear level design, the game's story and characters more than make up for it. Which is quite surprising, as I initially went into this expecting another fun, albeit mindless third person shooter to kill a few hours with. But without divulging too many details, I actually found myself quite invested into the story and the plight of our characters, as well as some very fun and interesting plot twists. If you mix the cyberpunk affectations of Ghost in the Shell, pepper in some snarky Yakuza humor and some Gears of War cover based gameplay, this is what you end up with. In terms of player choice, you are given a "trust system" by which you can choose what characters you want to tag along with you for certain amounts of time, thus building up your trust meter and being able to unlock additional dialogue, cutscenes, and even some new narrative points, which makes for a more immersive experience and adds to it's replayability. However, the AI can be quite ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at times, with team mates seemingly WANTING you to shoot them by constantly getting in your way at every given opportunity, which then degrades your trust meter if you shoot them accidentally, not to mention the fact that the AI has to comment EVERY single time you kill an enemy by giving you some positive reinforcement, such as Bo constantly yelling "That was SWEET!" which made me chuckle the first few times, but after repeated comments by the AI it ultimately became very annoying. But despite all this, it was a blast to go through, and the boss battles are insane and as over the top as you would expect from the designer of Yakuza, not to mention the difficulty was very satisfying, and the weapon upgrade system and squad upgrades allowed for a fair, albeit limited amount of customization options as well. However, my absolute biggest gripe with this game was the completely ♥♥♥♥ing annoying and unnecessary "Voice command" system, not only was this nothing more than a useless gimmick, but the game will automatically assume that you have a microphone plugged in to give commands to your squad mates, so after fiddle ♥♥♥♥ing around for about 20 minutes, I finally realized that it needs to be manually disabled in the options menu and from what I've heard in reading other reviews, even if you have a mic, the game does a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor job at detecting the player's voice and is ultimately useless. But after ameliorating this issue, the regular button input squad commands are very simple to use and the AI will actually listen to your commands promptly. So, all in all, if you're looking for some more shooters to play or some more sci-fi goodness for your diet, then look no further.
