Binary Domain is a third person shooter game which sets far in the future where robots have become so smart that it can even imitate humans. This game has 6 chapters in total with 4 ending variations. In this game, you'll play as the main character with up to 5 AI controlled teammates  which will fight with you.
I love how the game uses character voices in almost all of the dialogues and i have to mention the game uses different dialogues (from different person) for different situations (mostly story related issues). The bgms also sounds great with the exciting feel (especially in the cutscenes and some "minigames" in each chapter). All in all, the sounds feels good to hear, except if you listen to it for a long time; you'll get bored with it.
Although this is an old game, the game graphics isn't that bad at all. In fact, it's still on par with some lower tier games at the same price. I also like how the game designed the robots to peel their skins whenever they take enough damage. When the robots have a very low health, you mostly can see their skeletons in an almost fried state.
I'm quite confused at the first part of the story, although it'll be explained later in the chapters. The story turned out great. You'll see cutscenes most of the time (although the cutscenes tend to crash the game), and the story flows really smooth. I don't really want to give much spoiler for the story, so i'll skip that. There isn't much story about the character background's though, although they'll share some of their habits or homeland from the non main story related dialogues.
You'll be able to converse to your AI teammate once a while. Your response can increase or reduce your "trust" with them which will affect the story ending. "Trust" can also be farmed by killing enemies in an awesome way (triple kill, fast kill, etc) although you can also reduce their trust by shooting them. The story branches to four variations although it still has the same conclusion.
The first few hours that i did for this game is to make sure that it'll work on my machine. The game always crash in the first cutscene. I know that i'm running the very minimum spec, but i didn't think it's the only issue since a lot of people in the discussion thread complained about it. I ended up playing in windowed although i have to pause for every minutes or so to adjust my mouse position.
The crash doesn't end at that one cutscene. The game will also crash whenever i stay for too long in an area, and sadly, there is no manual save. I need to farm to get enough money and "trust" for the best ending at an area, but because of the constant crashes, i have to redo it several times after farming for around 2h+ straight. The crash is getting worse when i played in no mercy mode (hardest mode) halfway through the game. It crashes around once for every checkpoint.
Even though i played the game in windowed mode, the control input is still recognized when you alt tab out of the game after you launch it. Thanks to this, my no mercy save was deleted when i was already in chapter 3 out of 6. I have to redo the farming again which is in chapter 2.
There are 4 difficulties in this game (easiest to hardest): cakewalk, rust'em up, survivor, and no mercy. No mercy mode will be unlocked after you clear survivor mode. The only difference in the difficulties are the enemy health,  damage, and AI (which will hit you more accurately).
This game also features voice input, although it doesn't work well in mine; I need to say the word several times slowly to make it work. I ended up turning it off and replied it with a keyboard which cuts my response time (which sometimes leads me to death).
You'll start with a tutorial but sadly, the tutorial doesn't give an accurate info. I hardly can understand what they meant when they asked me to press a button. For example, they asked me to press middle mouse button with "m" button display. Thanks to this, I ended up closing the game and opened the configuration file to figure out what that means.
Apart from the troubles, the game itself is very great. You'll have some teammates and you use an assault rifle as a main weapon. There will be some weapon laying around which can be taken for your secondary (which will be worse than your assault rifle). Your primary weapon will start as a useless weapon until you upgrade it to be the best weapon in the game (second, if not the best). Your main and secondary weapon will have a fixed amount of ammo and you might run out of them when you play no mercy mode. The game also offers bombs and a pistol which has unlimited ammo to help you with that.
You'll also have an access to a "shock burst", an ultimate weapon which will stun your enemies (including bosses) in the range. You'll have a maximum of 8 shots in total which mostly can be charged from a vial which is dropped by enemies. This will be a vital weapon in killing bosses in no mercy mode.
You don't need a headshot in this game. Although headshot will give you an advantage, it'll be easiler to shoot your enemies' legs since it'll give them trouble in shooting.
This game also features the use of "nanomachines", which is basically a buff for you and your teammates. You can buy or take them from certain places and the most important thing is, they are limited. There is this vending machine which sells a lot of things, including "nanomachines", and they have different stock of "nanomachines". You can also have only one of the same kind and you have a fixed slot to place them all.
As i said before, there's also a vending machine in some places. It's not only selling "nanomachines" though. They have health kits, ammos, bombs, "nanomachines", and even upgrades.
There are a lot of boss fights in this game, especially near the end. Every bosses have their own weak points and you'll need different strategies to beat them. The boss fights can be completed in minutes, although some will take longer than that (it's not taking hours though).
Apart from the shooting scenes, this game features a lot of "minigames" like scene. Some of these minigames will be accompanied with QTEs which will harder in later chapters because of the need of fast response time. However, one of this "minigame" tends to bug
which will make you fall off the ground despite the fact that you're standing in a solid ground.
Pros:
- 6 chapters
- Teammates
- Weapon upgrades and buffs
- Minigames
- Tons of challenging boss fights
Cons:
- Weird button information in tutorial
- Constant crashes
- Bugs

A fun love letter to big, dumb action movies with a great story that borrows from Blade Runner and Asimov's robot series. While the narrative is serious in its themes the game never takes itself too seriously and instead pushes the player forward with constant shootouts and action set pieces. Gunplay is satisying and fast with the ability to dodge roll out of the way of enemy fire, and weapon feedback is really satisfying. That sweet 'ding!' sound when you land a heashot is rewarding as hell, as well as seeing enemies crumble in a shower of metal and sparks when you shoot off their armor or blow off some limbs.
Mechanically the game is simple, but this suits the popcorn-action flick feel I got while playing the game. It took me 8.5 hours to complete the main story, but I'm definitely going to go through the levels again to listen to different team member's banter and to use different weapons. I had a blast with this game.

Your jet moves slower than it does in the '94 version and doesn't keep up with the mouse if you are playing with the mouse.

I was first introduced to Layers of Fear two years ago by a friend of mine in Iowa. I had spent a fair amount of time at hers and her husband's place by this point, and she had just received the game. I wasn't much for horror games, but the storyline and art style intrigued me. So I sat and watched, and was pleasantly scared senseless when a window banged shut *JUST* after I had read what was on the other side.
Layers of Fear *learns* as you play. Just when you think you know the path you are on is solid, something grabs your attention and you'll wind up going down an entirely different path.
The soundtrack to this game is amazing. Classic piano music with emotion you can definitely feel. It puts you right in the shoes of the character you are portraying. As you play through the game, more and more of it will make sense, and the music really does help with this.
All this being said, I was promised no jump scares when I played Layers of Fear. There aren't any, per se. There are a few instances where you will turn around and something will jump out of the shadows at you, but I had a prickling feeling on the back of my neck that something was going to happen.
My advice to someone new to the horror and/or psychedelic horror genre? Play this with the lights off in the daytime where you can light from outside. Makes it just dark enough to be scary, but light enough that you won't be scared out of your wits.
And my advice to the veterans of the genre? Grab your Monster, close the blinds and play at night! Grab the headphones and crank that sucker up, because you are in for one HELL of a ride!

It's a known rule for some of the best games to have some of the best absences.
As you take your first look at Reflex, the thought of getting it is because you either fell in love with the idea of a new type of Quake game, or you just wanted to mess around with friends.
My friend, for example, convinced me to buy this game a few years ago, and as the second experience I had in a fast arena shooter (after Quakecraft in Minecraft servers), it's no doubt that this was a great update of the idea for me.
We'd play for hours on end. The graphics are amazing, the models were fun, the framerate was relatively high for my computer (which is still eh), and the community was okay.
The first year I stopped playing it, the community took a step back. Many servers were still running and being sponsored, but it was rare to find someone to fill the blanks. There were still a few games.
The second year they died out to the point where every time I launch the game, there are around five servers with one to three people on it.
(Why? My theory is the 1v1 system, which was updated recently. Two players one duel with eachother in a singular arena for around six minutes, while everyone stood by in a queue. People voiced in the chat that one should leave, desperate to get in. I joined a rather popular game once where four people left because they'd been waiting around thirty minutes for a spot in a six minute game. Rather ridiculous, if you ask me.)
Now. If you're interested in playing with friends, and when you're on, they're on? Give it a shot. It normally sells abnormally cheap on sales, and its a fairly small and to the point game you catch onto in around ten minutes.
But the community is an animal that just got slammed by a car on the highway... It's still got a little bit of life in it, if at all, but it's sure to be dead soon, assuming the developers don't put it out of its misery.
It's difficult for me to not recommend this game. It will always be remembered by me, however.
(If this game ever does get popularity once again, please notify me somehow, such as messaging me on Steam. I'm awaiting the good news.)

This game is well made no doubt and you can feel that DarkGaia is a competent game designer. But this game feels extremely rushed and unpolished. I expected more of this game. I'd like to make this review short and to the point so I'll just dive into it.
STORY
Compared to the first game this game feels more like a spin-off story than a completed sequel. Although  the storytelling and the writing is very good i still feel that alot more story could had been mashed in there. I cleared the final dungeon at around 12 hours at level 19. This was just after picking up my last party member. For obvious reasons this left me with a feeling that the game was not really complete. One bonus is that there is quiet alot of optional content in the game that provides more story. That's all fine and dandy but personaly i would had liked to see the main story expanded instead. Out of the six main characters only two of them have any time at all to see any real king of character development. With that said the characters are still very well written and atleast a couple of them are genuinly likeable.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay is solid but nothing out of the ordinary. The battles are hard at times and can be quiet annoying but the game offers loads of different ways to tackle them. You can for example play a battle slowly with one heavy damage character and three Clerics if that floats your boat. The upside to the difficulty is that i found myself satisfied when i defeated certain bosses. Battles aside the puzzles are mostly frustrating and kinda feel placed in the game to expand the playtime.
GRAPHICS
I like DarkGaias mapping alot. I really feel that he makes the most out of the built in Graphics in every RPG Maker engine. He has a real knack for making all areas feel unique and full of life.
MUSIC
Some really good choises here. I especially like the fantastic battle music from NemesisTheory. There is not much to say about this really. The soundtrack as a whole does it's job well and provides even more atmosphere to the areas and battles of the game.
MINOR POINTS
There are some bugs in the game. It's one of the things that makes the game feel rushed. Overall it's nothing game breaking though and it does not really lower the overall experience that much.
OVERALL
The game is still worth the price in my opinion. You get 10-15 hours of really solid old-school gameplay out of it. But you better be sure that you enjoy the SNES era of JRPGs because this game is not for everyone.

Finally beat the game!  Well, one of several endings.  I have to say that this game is an exceptional turn based RPG.  Here are a few reasons that I personally enjoyed the game:
The class system is way more balanced than Final Fantasy ever achieved.  With the right combination of skills and equipment, you can make every class a useful one.  Every character can be developed however you see fit.  There is a lot of replay value in just trying out differently developed characters.
There are a lot of side quests, but nothing that you have to devote hundreds of hours to complete.
The story line is fantastic.  It's not over saturated with juvenile snark like most modern games in the genre.  Its a story that grabs you, and compells you to keep playing.  Apparently there are several endings, and decisions you make can affect the endings and storyline.  That also adds to the replay value.
The difficulty is hard, but reasonable.  You have to apply thought and strategy to get through it, which means it doesn't get very repetitive (except for later dungeons, where the switching mechanisms can drive you nuts!)  But not so nuts that you throw the controller and give up.  A lot of people complain about the difficulty, but if any of you remember playing final fantasy 1 and getting off your ship at the wrong port, or playing Dragon Warrior 1 and crossing one too many bridges, the difficulty doesn't even come close to those days.
The soundtrack is really good.  I'm not a musical person, but I appreciated the variety of background music.  It set the mood for the different scenes very well.
I'd give this an 8/10, and I personally can't wait to see another Legionwood game.

As a fellow RPGMaker enthusiast I truly wanted to be able to give this game a favorable review. But for every enjoyable part, there seemed to be an unequally annoying part that made me forget it shortly after. I often felt that I was playing a contest entry NOT a published product.
Enjoyed: --------------------------------------------------
- The simple, but well thought class/job choices.
(One of my annoying list was slightly mitigated by the ability to sub-class everyone as a Cleric.)
- The availability of a multitude of items, with actual utility.
(making up for possible bad class choice in battle, and when out of mana.)
- A reasonably believable story line.
(Much less suspension of disbelief is necessary to enjoy it, unlike many JRPG stories.)
- Competent map making.
(A little boxy, but for RPGMakerXVA default tiles, the attention of variety is acceptable.)
- Market pricing.
(It is nice that the price of goods and acquisition of money are relatively painless, but not excessive.)
Annoyed: --------------------------------------------------
- Complete lack of any quest log.
(It's nearly impossible to keep track of side quests without writing them down on paper.)
- Painfully linear game play.
(Everything, including most over land map access is key-to-open, without any reason to return once completed.)
- Long winded and RAMBLING dialogue.
(To each their own, but after the third 500+ word story sequence, with dramatic pauses and area transitions to boot, I had to FORCE MYSELF to push through them without quitting. Your story is NOT bad, a little cliché but not bad. Do yourself a favor and try not to spell out every detail in WORDS. Leave some of it up to the reader to intuit from setting, animation, and music. It reduces the tedium of reading it, and respects their intelligence at the same time.)
- WTF Difficulty curve!?!
(I realize that you added a difficulty slider to the options menu, and it works, but the difficulty goes from laughable on CASUAL, to randomly deadly on NORMAL, to survival? ROFLCOPTER! on PURIST. It seems that you are using a random troop member replacement script for battles, and that results in some battles where you MUST escape, or die. Period. And if you aren't using a random replacement script, you must enjoy♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off your customers. -- While I can accept this in a scenario where battles are visible, and I have at least a chance to 'chose' them, the default random battle mechanic makes it downright infuriating at times. Ex: The difficulty spike, in NORMAL, inside the second dungeon/cave was enough to finely make me rage quit for the day.)
- What? That was a puzzle?!?
(At least a few times, I was left to assume that I was looking for an item to 'pass' an obstacle. Neither the obstacle itself, nor the item I found that allowed me to do so, had any indication, in its description or dialogue, of its actual purpose. I either randomly returned, or hoped I was right in back tracking, to discover how they related.)

Possibly one of my favorite RPG's of all time, this game is commonly called the best of the Elder Scrolls series for good reason.
First, I'll begin on the soundtrack. The first song you ever hear, my god, it's beautiful, there's no other word I can think of. It's got great balancing between the various instruments and strikes that balance perfectly between being calm and yet, intense and epic, sending chills down your spine likely as the song hits its climax. I will say, in game, you will want to turn down music since it's very loud compared to the rest of the game sounds.
Second, the amount of options on how to build your character. You have tons of skills, each providing good changes to how combat works if you're character is built around using those skills. I will say that magic is not as refined as it was in Oblivion. Magic suffers from having a "Cast Chance" based on skill level, intelligence, and stamina. Even your beginning healing spell and basic fireball spell both only have between 10-20 for characters not built for it from the start, or up to 50-60 for a character designed to use them, which also suffers from nonregenerating magicka, which was added later into Oblivion, making magic very annoying to try to build.
Next, I'll talk a bit about combat. Melee combat is based very much around 3 major stats, Strength, Agility, and the weapon skill for that weapon. Strength, as you might expect, affects damage, though different than how Oblivion did it. Each weapon has a select set of damage amounts based off the type of attack you perform (moving forward/backward does a Stab, side to side does a Slash, standing still or moving at an angle does a Chop) and strenth acts as a multiplier, up to a maximum up to double the base damage at 100 strength (I've found from my experience). Agility affects 3 major aspects to combat, Dodge Chance, Hit Chance, and Knockdown Resistance. Your weapon skill allows you to hit more frequently. As for magic combat, you have Intelligence, Willpower, and the magic skill being used. Intelligence affects the amount of magicka you have and the Cast Chance. The magic skill for the spell you are using affects Cast Chance a lot more than Intelligence. Willpower affects your ability to resist enemy magic. I will say that there are times combat feels a bit unrefined due to there being no Active Block button, Blocking is based on Block skill, which affects the chance to block attacks, though, blocking attacks will completely negate all melee damage dealt.
Finally, overall gameplay, well, I personally find it well designed as well as being immersive. You have a very basic Fast Travel, which is paying NPC's with "Silt Striders" or boats to take you to certain cities within range, and then you walk to you're headed, no highlighting your area with your cursor and clicking and magically teleporting. Questing is immense and you can fail a lot of quests as well as several quests having multiple outcomes. This game does have a difficulty slider, though the game will not hold your hand, if you wander into a dungeon you shouldn't be in yet, the game will let you know with NPC's who will turn you into their new floormat. The next thing this game does rather well, ranking up in Factions. It's not do a quest, instantly rank up, do another quest, and so on and so forth. Instead, you do the quest, and if the next quest is intended for a higher rank, and you aren't that rank, but you've done all the quests before it, you still need to gain the skills that the Faction "Prefers" Like the Morag Tong is a kind of legal assassination Faction and "Prefers" skills like Short Blade, Light Armor, and Acrobatics. The game's world is immense as well, I'd estimate it larger than even Skyrim.
Now, onto my complaints with this game. There are quite a few bugs that can occasionally screw up questing, but you can fix all of them with the use of the Console, which I had to do once so far due to something I did early before I got a quest and it kind of screwed it up since I didn't pick up the required item from the one body, and his body disappeared before I could go back and get it. While it was a minor inconvenience, the Console does allow you to fix a lot of those bugs. Another fairly large complaint I have is how fairly useless some skills are, such as sneak, which is almost useless compared to the future games, or speechcraft or merchanting, similar to the future games. Another complaint is how some skills are approached like Alchemy, if it's below 20, you won't even see the first indgredient effect for example. The other complaint was how magic as a whole was approached with nonregenerating magic and Cast Chance, though I can't deny some magic effects being amazing, such as Levitate, which allows you to basically fly around like a birdie for a little bit.
Overall, I'd say this is probably the best of all the Elder Scrolls despite the individual improvements to magic and smoother flowing combat that the future games had. The DLC is amazing as hell, and Solstheim is possibly one of my favorite areas ever put into a DLC. Mournhold is colorful and has a lot of hidden secrets to explore. I've logged about 45-50 hours into my current character and I've yet to even touch the main storyline of the game, the main storyline of Solstheim, or even to venture into Mournhold. The game is huge and insanely fun. I'd highly recommend getting it for anyone who has ever even remotely liked RPG's.

Epic game with tons of freedom. Probably the truest open-world RPG Bethesda has made. If you can get a handle on the somewhat challenging character growth system, enjoy a game with older graphics, and put up with a few odd bugs, it's one of the better entries into the TES series. Main questline good and quite lengthy (30+ hours). With plenty of factions to join and interesting side quests it will keep you busy for weeks or even months. If you can, get the GOTY edition; Tribunal and Bloodmoon are both fantastic and Skyrim's Dragonborn DLC will make a lot more sense. Only minor complaints would have to be 1) shields auto-block which makes combat feel a lot less skillful; 2) it's impossible to retrieve arrows from the environment which makes arrows a scarce commodity. I was afraid to use my good arrows for basically the entire game because of this; 3) fast travel is only from city to city, which means there is a lot of walking involved. Not necessarily a horrible thing, because there are some cool random NPC encounters along roads, but it does slow the game's pace down a bit and it would be nice to be able to fast travel from the map screen like you can in Oblivion and Skyrim. Overall though it's a great game, especially if you're a TES fan.

The characters themselves look the best they've ever looked; when I first began playing I was very disappointed in the way they looked, they were all sort of the same looking. Federation ship (also, any race can play any faction). The weapons have become more and more epic over the years just like everything else in STO. 100% Worth a shot, if you've been uncertain about whether or not to go for it, now would be the time. Especially since it's free!!!!!

The Game is good and very addicting, and pretty much recommended for those fed up with the usual fantasy MMO genre most MMOs nowadays follows. For Trekkies, in can give you the insights of post-Star Trek Nemesis World if the J.J Abrams movies never happens (Though some of you might think this is yet another 'alternate reality' separate from the TV shows and J.J Abrams' reboots).
The downside of this game is, while it is addictive enough, it can be boring after a set period of time, since most of the missions are quite repetitive and recycle the lore established by the TV shows. Also, it's basically a 'Pay for Win' game. I don't blame the developers since it is a common problem in most free-to-play games, but it hinders those who wish to get off the storyline and try the PvP.
Aside from the downside and the repetitive gameplay, the story is quite good, though some might disagree with its war storyline. The story might not make sense in term of continuity, since I think it fits well with the TV shows. For you first timers who is not familiar with the Star Trek universe, it can help you understand some of it, though it may not include some crucial histories, just the outlines introduced in the TV shows and pre-reboot movies.
That's all for the review of this game. Live long and Prosper.

Legionwood 2: Rise of the Eternal's Realm is a classic RPG game set in the expansive world of legionwood. It follows 1000 years after the first game Legionwood 1. Another problem arrises after 1000 years after Lann (Gaia) kills Castoth and it is up to you to save Legionwood once more.
Legionwood 2 is a very difficult game in which requires more planning and quick thinking than traditional RPG games. It offers extensive character customisation, allowing you to choose the class of each character given to you. Legionwood 2 offers non-linear gameplay and gives many optional side quests to explore and conquer as well.
Legionwood 2 has a morality system as well whether you will be hailed as a hero in the end or be dispised by many for your cunning acts. Apart from the morality system, certain actions and decisions and completion of quests would also contribute to the final ending. Simply saying, Legionwood 2 is not a 1 time affair. It has great replay value in that aspect.
It offers around 21+ hours of gameplay if you are to finish the game once through and it is a fully enjoyable 21 hours of gameplay. For those who would like a very challenging traditional RPG game, this is the game for you! (The battles are very difficult if you do not plan, you have been warned)

If like me you're a nostalgic of old snes jrpg era you'll freaking LOVE IT. Beware beginners though, it's challenging don't expect to be able to bash "attack attack attack heal attack attack heal" to win it requires more strategy to best your opponents. And this is GREAT.
The music....oh God the music is so delightful. It's like if Chrono Trigger's soundtrack met Secret of Mana and decided to go HD with real instruments.
The storyline is classic but well put together, characters are well written so far. The mapping is good too, you have much things to find out in every area, you don't have useless items or skills, YES , state inflicting skills for once are useful!
Definetely worth the few bucks required to give it a try. If you loved old Final Fantasy, Chrono Trigger, Breath of Fire etc by any mean, BUY THIS. I sware you won't regret it.

This is touted as an old school Final Fantasy homage, so be prepared to deal with exactly what that means.  This game can be described as "status effects: the game".  Most enemies will bind, blind, sleep, and generally annoy you in every fight.  Your characters will counter with such fiercesome status effects as miss, evade, and no effect, all of which lead you to an untimely grave from the somewhat OP ability for enemies to lay out almost any character in a single turn.  Honestly, this was what the designer intended judging by their other posts, and that is fine, some games aren't for everybody, I get that.  The real reason that I am hanging up the playthrough for this is just that it seems to not generate fun for me.  This game really requires the player to focus on turn order, defense strategies, and many other complex things that just don't seem to fit in to my particular playstyle.  Aside from the mechanics, there are some real positive ideas that went into this design, including the ability to change your class whenever you choose without permanent losses, a dual class system to spice things up, and some sort of moral choice system that I cannot attest to because I'm throwing in the towel early.  The nitpick things about this game are fairly comical from what I've see, they include the sprite possibly changing when you talk to an "idle" character, which another review indicated was a simple missed checkbox in RPGMaker.  A few typos here and there that give a bit of a guffaw.  The biggest detractor aside from the needlessly difficult fights, however, is that these characters suffer from "Dragon Age syndrome" in that they choose to expound the story by murdering your brain with text (says the guy with the long review).  Honestly, after a few minutes into the story, I had no idea what was going on anymore because after my 9-5 I didn't want to read "War and Peace" to start, what is at its core, an RPGMaker game.  To help out potential customers, I will say this: If you love difficult, strategic, thinking mans turn based combat, this should be a good time for you.  If not, I would have to say steer clear.

Legionwood 2:RotER is a solid addition to the RPG maker roster for the cost, but be warned, it is DIFFICULT.
The story and characters are standard RPG fare, with an interesting if somewhat ambiguous class system.  If you play this game and get frustrated I recommend reading some of the class guides and planning ahead.
Pros: Again, has everything an RPG needs to work well enough to be worth the purchase cost if you have the stones to finish it. This game is hard enough to be a challenge to even the most hardcore RPG fan.
Cons: This game is PUNISHING.  Nearly all fights, even the every few second random battles, are quite hard and cannot be plowed through as in most RPG games.  Your characters are extremly weak early in the game, and require some grinding to strengthen yourself each time you progress to new areas/enemies. Most of the random enemies have some combination of brutal evasion rates, damage type immunities, multiple attacks per round, spellcasting, AND status effects linked to those multiple attacks, and in some cases ALL of the above (Im looking at you Dire Wasps!!!)
Honestly most of this wouldnt be all that bad, except that you do not get a truly dedicated healer, and must rely mostly on items and "guarding" to regenerate health and mana in combat.  This will FORCE you to spend alot of your time whittling down enemy groups to the last enemy, and then blinding/silencing it so it cannot damage you while you slowly regen your characters up for the next fight.
Tips: Save every 2-3 battles in most areas, as the end can come unexpectedly with one unlucky ambush by multiattack enemies.
Stock up on status effect cure items at all times.  You will be curing 2-3 times a fight or more against some enemies (Curse you Dire wasps!!!)
Do yourself a favor and read some class guides, the tips therein will save you many tears and much hairpulling.
Keep older weapons around for a while, you never know when that shiney new elemental sword of uberness will be met with a whole area of enemies totally immune to it... sigh.

Master Reboot is one of those games with an interesting idea but a poor execution due to a lack of narrative and context. If you're a completionist and happen to find all the rubber ducks, you'll understand the context, but outside of that, this game will only confuse more with its rather poor excusues.
Basically (and you don't find this out until the end of the game, but I'm also trying to save you money) you play some chick named Madison who invented the "Soul Cloud" with a dude named David or something, I actually already forgot. Anyway, they invent the soul cloud under this company named Mysteri in the year 2026 where technology is supposedly going to be futuristic just like how it was in George Orwell's 1984. Anway, the whole game takes place in the soul cloud where users can place their memories and re-experience them for a limited amount of time. At least that's what I took away from it. This guy David is murdered by someone named Astrid, I never caught the relationship between Astrid and Madison, but I believe they knew each other. Also, Astrid had died four years prior but was brought back to life; don't understand how that works, but alright I'll let it slide. So Madison is in the soul cloud because of some virus that is shown to have been sent to Madison from an anonymous user, the virus basically effed up the cloud, the virus being named a bunch of random letters and numbers.exe. Madison, being so tech smart inventing some crazy idea, opens the virus which infiltrates the clouds servers, deleting people's data. A bunch of stupid people are mad as shown in "tweet" like this one, "i haet teh sole cloude". Yeah, that's right, people in the future are still terrible at spelling.
So that's basically the story, the gameplay involves you, Madison, navigating your own memories just to get to the virus. Basically, the giant library room that becomes this platforming nightmare has the virus which is really just a digital and angry Astrid that you've probably seen throughout the game acting like Alma from the FEAR games. The memories range from your childhood to your romantic feelings with David, rather generic to be honest. Also, the game is supposed to be a sort of horror game, but the jump scares were laughable. I feel like there was supposed to be emotion with the memories, but the emotion was detached due to the lack of narrative mentioned earlier. The Stanley Parable had more emotion.
The graphics were toon shaded without the black edges which were explained in game due to the soul cloud being in the early stages. As George Carlin would say, "Bull-sh!t", the toon shading is a cop out, especially when it doesn't even look good. I mean, at least Gearbox makes Borderlands look awesome. This was rubbish. It doesn't help when the devs make an excuse of in game graphics being toon shaded and then the actual memories are 2D flash animated or puppet pinned from After Effects. You'd think that the memories themselves would be detailed 3D considering that they're taken from the human's mind? Think of the film Final Cut starring the late, great Robin Williams. The memories that he works with are fully realized and completely real, in the flesh. The 2D is such a cop out, what rubbish.
The music and sounds were the only good thing, as they were both evidently creepier than the game itself. And even then, the sounds had some weird mixing.
4.0/10

Now, I got this for five dollars and that is in the end what it feels like it should be priced at. The polish is not there, the ideas are sometimes half-baked, but overall this is a fun game, at the right price. I found it to be a lot like something David Lynch might have done back in the eighties, around the time of Dune. The game does not hold your hand and instead let's you solve most things on your own, there are clues from time to time. Sometimes the path is so obvious it feels rushed and other times it is so obscure it becomes frustrating.
The visual style is something I enjoyed when the textures were not so muddy, it made me wonder why it wasn't polished more. I am not certain how big the team was behind this game, but I have seen a team of four put out something far better looking than this. Now, the lighting is well implemented, but the over all look of the game comes across as rushed. There are levels that seem forced due to how they rendered the environment, it looks like some student project out of Unity from time to time. This really takes away from the real well done segments, that seem to set you up for a great experience, just to let you down again.
The music is fantastic, being the real strongpoint of the game. I'm surprised it was not used more often, especially during the art cut scenes, that turn out to be sloppy due to a lack of music. Over all the animations are good enough to not make you feel ripped off, but I could not expect you to get fifteen dollars worth of gameplay out of this. For the five I paid, I am  very happy with the game and it would be so much greater if he price was less.
All in all, this is a game I enjoyed playing for the most part. The story could have been better, but it works well enough to make you think at bit. There really isn't any voice acting, but when there is it works. There were times when I really wanted to like this game more than I do. It never let me down completely, but it also didn't blow me away. If it is less than ten dollars, pick it up. Otherwise wait it out.

If you aren't familiar with Raptor, this is an old-school shoot em up, one of the the first available for PC in the early 90's. It features the ability to accumulate points, that also act as your cash. You can use the cash to purchase ship upgrades, such as missiles, or auto-attacking guns to make some levels more manageable. True vets to the bullet hell games will find this one a little easier to play, especially compared to japanese games in the same genre, but veteran mode can pose a challenge. Give this game a try if you have an extra $5, but don't you dare pass it up if it's on sale.

Gamers born before 1995 will love this one, but i dont recommend this for younger people, who are used to games holding thier hands. Morrowind might be a bit obsolete, but some features will appeal to a lot of you. Unlike Skyrim and Oblivion, this game wont mark everything on your map, you wont be following unmissable signs. All you have is your annoying, but useful journal, where youll find the advices given by npc-s. Also, there is no fast travel in morrowind. It can be frustrating, but it teaches you to plan your moves, and make perfect use of your supplies and abilities. You can finish Skyrim with no magic, no crafting or sneaking abilities; all you need is heavy armor and a two-handed weapon. And you can even become an arch-mage without magical abilities. Well, good luck with that in Morrowind. Dont be surprised when a foe is immune to physical damage. You do have access to loads of potions and scrolls, but it's a very limited access.   Anyway, morrowind might be an old game, the battle system might be obsolete, but (unlike TES IV and V) this game is not about following that stupid arrow. The GOTY edition contains the 2 expansions, with this addition it took 83 hours for me to finish the story. And it was only 1 character, lots of factions, 100-s of side quests completely missed. So yeah, if you can tolerate the flaws of old games, and you like open world RPG-s, then this one's definitely for you. (All these comparisons with the other TES games made me forget some things: awesome story, beatuiful world-in its own way, and a soundtrack that should be boring after 80 hours, but for some reason it isnt; and also: way more character choices then what you get in modern rpg-s)

I've been playing STO for the last 5 years, but only just recently switched to the steam client, and I gotta say I love this game! The story is very Treky, and fun to experience. Any fan of star trek owes it to themselves to experience it. You can pretty much play through the entire story portion of the game without spending a dime.
Once you have completed the story, there's still plenty to do thanks to the foundry! Star Trek Fans are an extremely creative and passionate lot, and they have crafted some in game missions and story arcs that surpass any of the official stuff. Sure, there's plenty of garbage in there too, but it has a decent rating system to make it easier to find the gems. My only complaint about the foundry is that there isn't anyway to favorite or bookmark an author. This makes it a pain when playing a continuing mission arc that hasn't finished, or you just don't have the time to do 5 or 6 hour long quests.
I have heard the PvP portion of the game isn't too fair for complete free players, but I haven't really done much of that since I am more of a role player. Still, it's excellent and fun and worth trying out for the story alone(Most of which can be done solo or in groups, which means you can do missions with your friends, and if they aren't on you can lone wolf it and you don't have to grab a random PUG unless you want to)
Over the course of the last 5 years, STO has drastically improved. In terms of missions, cinema scenes, environments and graphics. I am confident they will continue to improve for hopefully another 5 years. This is one game, I don't seem to tire of.(Though I think that's largely due to the Foundry keeping me entertained with new stories while I wait for the official releases)

My first review on here.
I played this game since an old friend introduced me to it when it went free to play years ago. Even bought a lifetime supscription for the hell of it. It was on and off. It reintroduced me to Star Trek, and it can be fun to play even with some of the big problems it has
I'm going to revise this review and make it shorter and less bias. It does have some of the original cast members from the shows providing their voices of the original characters like Worf, Nog, Tuvok, etc. And Morn is played by well...Morn. It has an active but small role playing community where one could feel like a real character in the Trek universe. The guild or fleet system is pretty robust with many benefits to fleet members like access to ships and gear that only fleet members can get. The game's crew does regularly add new content almost monthly. And there is plenty to do here like random events, play adventure zones, fight in battlezones(yet few of these are pvp zones), practice your character's crafting or R&D, and play STFs and other more team-based instances with firends or complete strangers.
To top it all off, it is ALL FREE! Almost anything can be bought without using any real money whatsoever. You will have to prioritize what you want if you want to play to earn, but one can just get whatever they want in the game just by grinding it. I wish I discovered this before I bought the lifetime supscription. Biggest DOH moment in my life. LOL!XD. But I still payed some money here and there to support it anyway.
Now for the negatives. This game does get vary buggy. So buggy even old bugs will come back from time to time. Many of these bugs are funny, but some are game breaking like a broken mail system. And there are bugs and borderline exploiting bugs that have never been fixed for years. The community can get a bit too negative or toxic in places. And the gameplay can get unbalanced as its  seems to be about damage and not much else.
Even though I give this game a thumbs down for all those cons, this game can still be vary fun. And this game is vary generous for an MMO as its vary possible to get whatever one wants without paying for it at all if one knows how to budget and set in-game financial priorities. For that sense, I recommend this game 100%. But a fair warning, it will have some serious rough edges that can hurt your experience.

I wrote a review for Legionwood 2 about a week ago based on my experiences in the first 2-3 hours into the game. Although I was able to analyse the battle mechanics and world design to quite some depth, I also pointed out weaknesses in the character development, and how information about the world was conveyed to the player. Thankfully, as I played further into the game I found that these problems were addressed, and I felt it would be necessary to re-write my review, and hopefully help the developer in the process. I will avoid all spoilers beyond the first two hours of this game.
If, like me, you have never played a Legionwood game before, you may wish to brace yourself for the first few hours of the game. The player is assaulted with world information and lore over the first few hours, and I found it very difficult to actually understand what was going on. Naturally it was difficult to become invested in the events of the game at that point. The character development showed similar problems - the main party members were able to supply the player with large quantities of information to keep the story moving, but showed little personality (I was convinced that some characters lacked any personality traits whatsoever - Felix frequently made snide comments or light jokes, and Lionel showed some signs of mourning for Clara, but Aelia and later Marcus showed no detectable emotions or character). Thankfully, as the player progresses further into the story, some of these characters have their background explored, and their personality expanded upon. The story itself becomes easier to follow, too, as characters start to respond to recent events instead of bringing up pieces of lore that the player feels little relation to. The player is able to undertake many side-quests as they progress further in the story, which offer opportunites to improve your party, better pace the events of the main quest, and learn more about specific corners of the world. It's a shame that all of this only picks up after a few (5?) hours of gameplay, but what is present is very well-written, and a definite strength of the game.
The meat of the game, the battles, are both challenging and satisfying. It is rare to find an RPG with such enjoyable battles, and I'm not just talking about RPG Maker titles. Bear in mind that they do have a high level of difficulty from the start, so if you have never completed a Final Fantasy game, you may want to steer clear from this one to avoid frustration. Personally, I really appreciated the difficulty, and it forced me to think tactically whenever I encountered a strong opponent. The battles are viewed from a side-on perspective (a big plus for me!) with a conditional turn-based system similar to that of Final Fantasy X. This lends a lot to the strategy, as you must consider not only strength and weakness, but also timing and order of the moves you execute. Characters may be assigned classes (think of the jobs systems of the earlier Final Fantasies) that roughly describes what functions they may serve in battle. And since you are unlikely to win all your battles by just repeatedly attacking, there is real value in choosing classes that inflict status conditions, or reduce enemy statistics, or have a higher critical hit ratio, etc. Although I may be asking a bit much, it could have been fun to see the characters develop within their chosen classes and not just as a whole, but the system is fine as it is and I would not wish it to become unbalanced.
The graphics and sounds are pleasant but not outstanding. The developer has achieved much using the resources supplied with RPG Maker VX, and this is in no way a criticism. The environments are richly detailed - moss growing on cavern walls, tufts of grass amid the odd flower on bright mountain paths, broken furniture and bones littering grey halls in untouched ruins (but who ever heard of doors rotting shut?) The only criticisms I do have are minor, and refer to graphical elements added by the developer: face portraits generally look a little odd, but such should be expected when using the in-built editor, and some components of the user inferface when in a battle are a little difficult to work with (highlights could be a little difficult to see, and icons in the CTB gauge do not specify which enemy they may represent). I find it easy to overlook such niggles, though, as the rest of the game world is presented very well.
I have yet to complete the game, but I have encountered a few bugs or small mistakes as I have played the game - they are almost always benign, thankfully.
* In certain cut-scenes, if Lionel has the wound status when other party members are removed, the game may cut to the Game Over screen and force the player to load their previous save.
* The CTB gauge occasionally gives incorrect information, in one of two ways: a character's turn might not start when it is stated to on the gauge, and enemies might take their turns earlier than suggested. These may be symptoms of the same problem, which I imagine is due to the way the CTB system is implemented.
* This might not be a bug, but upon learning a new spell when already knowing 8, Marcus forgot one of his previous spells. If this is not a bug, it would be nice to be prompted with a choice upon attempting to learn a move that will cause you to forget an existing one.
* Some skill descriptions differ when comparing the item form and the learned skill form (debilitating shot).
* Some of the metal chests appear to be closed after the player has opened them if they leave the screen and re-enter.
* Some of the sleeping characters change sprite when they are interacted with (they might need to have their direction fixed to prevent this?)
* Some speech contains spelling mistakes.
* Upon meeting one of the kings, he describes the Queen to be on his right. She is actually on his left. (I found it quite amusing to imagine him, with his eyes closed, gesturing to empty space while introducing her, and everyone in the room being too afraid to correct him!)
I stress that these bugs do not irritate me when playing the game - most are harmless, and I list them in the hope that they might aid the developer in identifying and fixing them in future updates.
In summary, I would recommend this game to anyone who has previously completed a Final Fantasy title and is prepared to play through the first few hours before they are able to connect with the world and its characters. Combat is very much enjoyable preciely because it presents a challenge and is well-balanced (when did you last play an RPG where you felt you had to stock up on potions when you left a village?), and there is a large amount of content available between crossing the land as part of the main quest and completing many side-quests along the way, with the occasional well-written cut-scene to break up the action. While I am not humming the tunes outside of the game they are certainly not boring to listen to and overall the world is well-presented. Previously I had criticised the game quite heavily for having so many good features that were not tied together well due to poor character and story development; now I find I am eating my words as I play further into the game. Well done, Dark Gaia.

This game makes me very irate. I'm less than two hours in, and here's what I have to complain about:

I'm a huge fan of the first Legionwood, which has a fantastic story, a memorable cast of characters, and very challenging battles.  The game was so inspiring to me.  If you haven't played Legionwood: Tale of the Two Swords, I highly recommend it!  Plus, if you do, you'll be familiar with the setting in this game.
However, that being said, to enjoy this game, one would not have to play through the First Legionwood.
I really do think it would enhance your experience though!  There are some changes to how you develop your characters this time around, but the overall feeling is still there I think with the new class system.  It's a blast.  The battles are fast & fierce!  Everything is so much smoother!  I grew up playing RPGs and the Final Fantasy games as they were released in the US, and old school RPGs are what I crave these days.  The story is great, and there are many nods to the events in the original.  I find myself never bored at all, and quite honestly, I thought it would be hard to top the first game. But I feel as if Dark Gaia has achieved it! The script is phenomenal, the dialog is fresh, very well written, and the soundtrack for this game is breathtaking.  Now over 13 hours in I can say this game is a masterpiece.  This is such a unique way to continue the story from Legionwood: Tale of the Two Swords, I found myself in awe.  The characters in this game have real personalities, and characterization is a key for good storytelling.  This game has it all.  Do yourself a favor and give it a shot.  Anyone who plays this game for at least a few hours will be completely enthralled.
If you are a fan of RPGs, you will love this.

Legionwood 2 is an outstanding RPG. If this game was released during the 16 bit generation it would of been held up as one of the great classics of that generation. If you like turn based RPG's, then this is a game for you.
The gameplay is classic turn-based battles and over world exploration. Basically everything you would expect from an RPG from the 16 bit generation. The game can be difficult at times and require some grinding, I personally had to do very little. The game allows you to change your job/classes to better suit a situation, a lot of times reclasses will be far more effective than grinding.
I found the music and sound effects to fit the theme of the game nicely. I am no music aficionado but I can say this, both the music and sound effects kept me immersed in the game world.
The graphics in this game look similar to the RTP, but they are modified in various ways. I enjoy this better than most of the original graphics styles that popular RPG Maker games try to put out. The RTP graphics are done in the style of classic RPG's and so our these, which is just perfect. The mapping in this game is spot on just like in the first Legionwood. Everything feels natural like it should, trees look like they are growing where trees would naturally grow. No odd ball out of place map items that I can find.
The story in Legionwood 2 is its strong suit. Dark Gaia is writer first and a game developer second, and it shows. The story is the focus throughout the game and its enjoyable all the way through. They're are lots of surprises and unexpected events that occur. I don't want to spoil anything, but it doesn't dissapoint. The characters are all unique and you form story opinions about them. Personally Felix is my favorite one, he will come of a little douchy at first but that is what makes him so great. If you like characters that redeem them selves, you will also love Felix. The others are also fantastic in their own right. Lionel is more of your traditional RPG character, but he quickly breaks out of that mold with all the interactions he has with the other characters.
Legionwood 2 is glitch free from what I can tell, the game runs very smoothly for me. Don't let my play time fool you, I have played this game via direct download before it was available on Steam. I plan to play this game in its entirety again, thats how good it is. If you are sick of overly hard or overly artsy RPG Maker games give this one a shot. Legionwood 2 is what an RPG Maker game is supposed to be.

I came to that game from Skyborn and Deadly Sin 2 and this game is not even as half as engaging as any of those two. Unlike in Skyborn you can't see the monsters - battles occur at random moment and unlike in Deadly Sin 2, you aren't able to 'turn off' monsters respawns, so any kind of walking and/or exploration is tedious as it is continously interrupted by fights. Combat isn't balanced well, at least not in starting areas (first farmland quest), where some of the enemies seem to have much higher abilities than you are.
Unlike in Skyborn or Deadly Sins 2, fight difficulty isn't adjustable at all, which, considering how unfair fights feel, is a big letdown. I don't care about 'old-school nostalgic hard difficulty', I want to be able to play a game as _I_ want it, so having an option of easy difficulty on fights would be much more fun to me. Alas, it is absent.
As debuffs are expiring so slowly out of combat and as I'm not sure if characters have any sort of health and SP regeneration over time, most of the times I was fighting well under full power and losing over and over again, which was just frustrating. With all battles occuring at random, it is just too much frustration in general with exploration and walking around.
And 300+ of money just to resurrect the character after yet another death, _in the city I've saved_, _on a quest_ on behalf of town? Just ridiculous, like those people don't have any sense of gratitude. And as I didn't notice any items that can help with resurrestion while in travels, every time the character is killed it is a track all way back to church - through random, out of blue battles - and all way back into dungeon.  And there is no visible threat management, so monsters seem to attack party members in random.
The only interesting mechanic thing is a subclass system but it is such a minor detail in a big picture of frustration that I didn't feel it worth my time to shamble through bad unfair-looking combat.
I do appreciate the ability to skip intro, although vanity label with the name of the studio in the beginning of the game can also use some screentime trimming. Also, I don't know if it is a glitch of a feature, but sometimes when you 'talk' to sleeping characters their sprites flip to some other sprites, which would be fun if flipped sprites remained the same - sort of you like peek into their dreams; I found it very amusing. I also liked Aelia portrait (others are ok) but won't it kill developers to maybe make several different emoting portraits so characters won't have same stuck expression all the time?
As it is at first hour of the game, the writing seems to be uninspired at best (why Clara run to The Hero just to die at his arms when _he knows First Aid spell_ by default)? Although I like that barbarians were given some slight depth in Boudica, instead of 'just evil people out to kill us' label.
Considering all of this, personally can't recommend.

Playing this game for roughly 1.5 hours now, and really I think the game is good considering the generation it's trying to capture. Engaging in a battle, and just attacking while paying the minimum amount of attention will likely get you killed more often then not. It takes a little planning and some real thought on how to approach the groups of monsters. More then once have I delved into a cave full of monsters, earned a substantial amount of money, just to lose it all on resurrection costs and inn stays. Think about the fight and utilize your characters' abilities. For a while I was using Lionel primarily to First Aid allies that were getting crushed in battle. After a few levels, they easily best groups of enemies.
A lot of reviews make this game out to be bad and hard, and I just didn't think it was fair. By today's standards, yes it could be considered quite brutal at times, but that doesn't make it bad. The Elder Scrolls III Morrowind is a genre defining game that has been influencial on most modern day RPGs. It helped solidify Bethseda's solid marketplace position as a video game developer. It is considered a classic game and one of the greatest games ever made for the following reasons.
Vvardenfell
Morrowind throws you (the Outlander) into the alien setting of Vvardenfell, an island in the North East of Morrowind. The land itself was to players back in 2003 as alien as it is to players today. The setting is a unique one ; volcanic wastes, giant mushroom trees and coastal mud flats are but a few. The folks at Bethesda truly managed to make a memorable setting that is still special when compared to all the other RPGs released in the 14 years since its launch. Its a joy to explore and the mystery of the entire island is a driving force. There is always more to explore and even more to find. The world is filled with caves, ruins and small settlements. Part of the joy of Morrowind is the exploration of the game ; its a truly open world that doesn't feel like its empty.
The Outlander
When you arrive in Seyda Need in the first five minutes of the game, you're scum. You're filth in the eyes of the citizens. However, as you progress, your impact will be felt by many. NPCs may reference an impact of one of your actions in a quest. You feel like you're actually a part of the world. Your decisions matter as opposed to those of other games. You feel like you're progressing (there is so level scaling so you're actually becoming stronger and not being made to fight enemies at the same level as you). This helps add to the world ;a place might be dangerous for you initially, but 20 levels later you've grown enough to challenge it , adding to the hostile feeling of Morrowind.
Oh and finally, Cliffracers.

Morrowind is a game with one of (if not the absolute best) the best worlds/settings to be seen in an RPG, and a unique, enigmatic atmosphere. Just about anything you can see in Morrowind can be visited at some point, and just about every quest is designed to have natural alternate approaches. It is a world that is not only beautiful, but also fully explorable, with a rich, deep lore and interesting NPCs. Many people criticise Morrowind's combat, and the sometimes vague quest directions, but there is one rule you need to follow to enjoy Morrowind: Respect its advice and systems. There is the infamous idea of missing all your attacks, and failing all your spellcasts, but this only happens at low fatigue, and with the quests, the optimal way to approach them is to play like you're in Morrowind.
Morrowind is often criticised for being antiquated, but honestly I think just about anyone with an open mind and enough patience and time can appreciate it, even today.

There are interesting ideas and in my short time with it nothing seems broken, but this game needs a lot of polish. The controls work fine, but sometimes don't feel great (I played with an Xbox 360 controller). For example, there are occasionally items you have to crouch down before you hit the action button to pick them up/activate/whatever. The problem is you have to HOLD the crouch button while you hit the action button, which means your left hand has to reach over and hit one of the facebuttons. It's awkward. There are things in the audio that bug me, like the small torches that light up an area. They sound like a much bigger fire than they actually are, and the sound zone around them is short and drops off quickly. When I absent-mindedly walked by a torch, I was startled because I suddenly heard a big fire and didn't know where it was from (it didn't register in my mind until a few seconds later that the big fire sound was connected to this small fire). There was also a cut scene that played after the school memory where the the audio seemed way too quiet compared to the rest of the game. The art is competent, but the cutscene art style feels strange juxtaposed to the darker mood of the rest of the game. It's not cohesive.
I've played through three "memories" (think "levels") and I want to like the game, but it just needs more polish. As it stands now, it seems like an awesome student project or a demonstration, but I don't think it's ready for primetime. If there's ever a major update that adds some polish, I'd love to come back to it.

Now before I get started I want to let everyone know, I have nothing against Raptor. I played it as a kid for hours on end and bought the 2015 edition out of nostalgia.
Everything I remember as a kid is there. The one thing I don't remember being in the 1994 release are the bugs, specifically
Buggy Mouse controls - Sometimes there is an invisible forcefield, that prevents your mouse cursor (or your plane) from being able to track across the length of the playing screen and is a problem with all screen resolutions. Now you can navigate the menus with ease with the keyboard, but when your playing the game proper, you don't want to contend with this whilst flying the plane, especially as the playing field can get pretty crowded at times.

I would like to tell you a tale about my dear driver Dan. He is from the wonderful country of Germany. He Joined my race team as soon as it was formed and for the most part, he is an ok driver. Much better than his partner named Fry. Now Fry couldn't drive a shopping cart down the dairy isle at his local grocery store without f**king it up somehow. But, he was cheap and kept the seat warm till I could hire someone that could at least walk in a strait line without crashing.
Back to my dear driver Dan. Now, for the first 7 races of the GT season, our team sucked. We just outright should not even be associated with cars at all. Perhaps professional paper airplane racing was better suited for a team of our caliber. But we kept pressing on.
Then one day in Germany, aparently Dan decided to himself: “you know what? I’m really sick of sucking so bad. I’m gonna give a good race today.”
And my dear friends, he did. While Fry was trying his best not to get lapped for the 2nd time of the day, Dan was up in the top 10, then the top five, then the top three…
Do you know where my dear driver ended up at the finish line? Lol no you silly steam player. He finished third. But, it was like we won the world that day.
Later in the day, a few hours after the race finished, we waited for dumb fry to finally cross the finish line. We loaded up the trailers and headed back home.
I’m still in my first season. We have improved our racing capabilities. Even fry was able to finish 18th one race. We gave him a high five, much like adults giving a participation ribbon to the last place tee ball team for the young dumb snot snorting kids. We act like they did something, but all they did was drive their dads to drink that day.
In summary, this game has occupied my weekend and has gave me much joy. The events both on the track and off the track make this a very realistic and enjoyable game to play.
The learning curve is average. It will be a high learning curve is you’re not familiar with how racing works. However, well worth the effort and time to put in to the game.
It’s a true gem and I recommend it to anyone that is on the fence.

Despite being released in 2008, this game still rivals even new releases. I've been a huge fan of Spore since I first played it in 2010, and am still dumbfounded by the level of creativity of some of the community's creations.

This game has serious replayability, and the exploration aspect is mindblowing. You can explore an entire galaxy full of stars, the vast majority of which have orbiting planets, some of which have moons. Alongside this, the space stage has a number of beautiful features such as binary systems, black holes, protoplanetary systems, a stunning galactic core, cube planets, and the elusive storybook planets. There are also many others including easter eggs (finding Earth, for example).
Each stage is as good as the previous, and the level of customisation is mindblowing. For this price, everyone should be buying this game... Well, I'd be saying that if online worked for everyone.

As a person who's watched Joe Gran's YouTube channel for a long time, one of the characters that has stood out to me the most has been 90's Nick, because I come across his archetype quite often in online circles.
This feels like if that character made a throwback game. It's not a good game by any stretch of the word, but it nails down the feeling and aesthetics of mid-to-late 90's PS1 poly aesthetics (which I can admit are quite likable!). That being said, the combat is boring, there's very little differentiation between enemy types, and the game is super easy as you'll be able to hoard painkillers as you complete mundane task after mundane task. I got a good amount of the achievements in far under an hour, which isn't really appealing since the game itself cost me $11.99. If you're looking for something to itch your Silent Hill scratch, you're probably just better off playing an emulated version of Silent Hill 2 or 3.

Honestly, the game isn't very challenging nor is it very long. You can complete the entire game in about 2 hours. But I'm not here to destroy this game, I actually quite enjoyed it. For what it's worth, 1995 is a very quaint and compelling spin on the old school survival horror games. It is very reminiscent of Silent Hill and does a good job of making you feel the nostalgia and the sense of mystery that the old games did. The notes tell the story and give you a feel for what's going on in this world. A few surprises here and there, along with some basic back tracking and puzzles to get the gears turning. The price is a little steep for the game as-is (DLC is apparently scheduled to come soon), so if you can get this when it's on sale I say it's worth it. If you take your time and really go through and read everything and explore all the areas the game has to offer I feel you mostly get your money's worth. I give it a solid 7.5/10!

I've heard the name Metal Slug for years and I've always heard good things, but this time I finally bit and tried this edition. I am pleasantly surprised and how classic and yet modern this game feels. It has the difficulty of old arcade style machines and classic consoles like the Sega Genesis or Super Nintendo, however, it's not so frustrating that I want to throw my controller through my monitor. It's a fast-paced, button-mashing, everything dodging, Contra-esque game that really brings back what quality is in games - Gameplay.  Even with the pseudo 16bit graphics, the animations are solid. Every sprite frame is fluid and well animated, giving a fresh appearance to a retro game design.
I bought this on this recent Steam Summer Sale, but knowing the game now, I would more than likely have purchased the game at full price. This game definitely gets my recommendation.

A very fun Left 4 Dead style game set in the Warhammer universe using melee, and ranged combat. The combat is visceral and rewarding where the melee is particularly satisfying with the uniqe hit/blood system adding to feeling of carving up the vermintide. There has been considerable post launch support in terms of patches, free content and the DLC has been fair in terms of content to price ratio (I am not commenting on the skin DLC as I have not bought them and don’t care about cosmetics although if you like to play dress up they are available and you get what you pay for as in it is not a game as in no damn loot boxes). They include new stories, maps, weapons, and contracts in each one which is much better than most of the crap DLC for games these days that do not add much; they are each well crafted mini expansions.
If you like a solid 4 player co-op in the style of Left 4 Dead and want that in the Warhammer universe this is most assuredly a solid pick. Worth it at full price and doubly so for the price offered on the many sales and bundles it has been on/in. I have had a lot of fun with this game with my own friends and also with meeting people online as the community is very friendly which is another huge plus. Even if you have no idea what is going on the veterans are very kind and willing to help you with your journey unlike many games where the communities are completely toxic.
The engine is well optimised, runs well, and looks good on almost any setup. It had some problems at launch but there have been so many patches since then that the game is in a superb state mechanically. I have had a lot of fun with this games and barring the final DLC I am looking forward to the second instalment of the game as the first was and still is a super fun game to play.
My only complaint is that if you decide to play on your own (though there is usually enough people online to find a full group) the bots can be utterly stupid even after many AI updates which can get quite infuriating at times. They have come a long way since the initial release and are much better to have at your side than before, but still suffer from some idiotic AI at times. It is good that game did well and you really don't need to play with bots if you either find a game or just open your lobby and wait in the tavern for it to fill up.
Best played with friends but still fun alone and a solid time with others in the community. The base game goes on deep sale all the time and all the DLC is worth it while they all go on sale a lot as well. I recommend picking the base on sale as it just goes on so often and grabbing the DLC on or off sale as they are pretty darn good and worth their price although you could wait and get them all fairly discounted too.
They have also expanded the game with extra quests through the contract system as a free content update which was very nice of them and only the host needs the DLC which means that even if you just bought the base game you can join someone with the DLC and play it all. Very good developers who actively develop for the consumer and not completely for the shareholders as is becoming the norm these days. No loot boxes and no micro-transactions plus being a very competent and fun game with a great community means that this is one you shouldn't pass up if you haven't already picked it up.

This is a horror game unlike any I've ever played. It's more than just "you're in a scaaary house in a scaaaaaary forest, and there's spooky monsters trying to kill you :(". It's a Sci Fi setting of a virtual world built to house memories. You'll see blurred lines between what's real and what's part of the simulation.
The storytelling style reminds me of Bioshock, where you know something really bad happened, but you aren't sure what it is. The game has you going through corrupted versions of the main character's memories. Little clues along the way flesh out the story piece by piece, as you look for patterns among her memories, trying to figure out their chronological order and how they relate to the current situation. The game never comes right out and tells you exactly what's going on.
There's also puzzles in this game, but in my opinion, they were the weakest part of the experience. They typically have a rather illogical solution that's not very fun to figure out. The worst one being the Simon-Says-like puzzle, where (spoilers but trust me you don't want to have to figure this out for yourself) the first 4 patterns shown to you are completely pointless and you only have to remember the last pattern. There's also an area that's literally just a giant maze that's extremely long and boring and seems to be built specifically to screw over people who follow the "Follow the right wall" strategy. Whenever I actually say "Thank god that's over" out loud while playing your game, something's wrong.
Either way, it's a short little game with a detail rich plot that was an overall good experience. I bought it on sale for 3 dollars, and it took me 4 hours to finish it. I would not recommend it at full price, but keep it in your wishlist and wait for a sale.

The Elder Scrolls III Morrowind is a genre defining game that has been influencial on most modern day RPGs. It helped solidify Bethseda's solid marketplace position as a video game developer. It is considered a classic game and one of the greatest games ever made for the following reasons.
Vvardenfell
Morrowind throws you (the Outlander) into the alien setting of Vvardenfell, an island in the North East of Morrowind. The land itself was to players back in 2003 as alien as it is to players today. The setting is a unique one ; volcanic wastes, giant mushroom trees and coastal mud flats are but a few. The folks at Bethesda truly managed to make a memorable setting that is still special when compared to all the other RPGs released in the 14 years since its launch. Its a joy to explore and the mystery of the entire island is a driving force. There is always more to explore and even more to find. The world is filled with caves, ruins and small settlements. Part of the joy of Morrowind is the exploration of the game ; its a truly open world that doesn't feel like its empty.
The Outlander
When you arrive in Seyda Need in the first five minutes of the game, you're scum. You're filth in the eyes of the citizens. However, as you progress, your impact will be felt by many. NPCs may reference an impact of one of your actions in a quest. You feel like you're actually a part of the world. Your decisions matter as opposed to those of other games. You feel like you're progressing (there is so level scaling so you're actually becoming stronger and not being made to fight enemies at the same level as you). This helps add to the world ;a place might be dangerous for you initially, but 20 levels later you've grown enough to challenge it , adding to the hostile feeling of Morrowind.
Oh and finally, Cliffracers.
Get the game..

Morrowind is a game with one of (if not the absolute best) the best worlds/settings to be seen in an RPG, and a unique, enigmatic atmosphere. Just about anything you can see in Morrowind can be visited at some point, and just about every quest is designed to have natural alternate approaches. It is a world that is not only beautiful, but also fully explorable, with a rich, deep lore and interesting NPCs. Many people criticise Morrowind's combat, and the sometimes vague quest directions, but there is one rule you need to follow to enjoy Morrowind: Respect its advice and systems. There is the infamous idea of missing all your attacks, and failing all your spellcasts, but this only happens at low fatigue, and with the quests, the optimal way to approach them is to play like you're in Morrowind.
Morrowind is often criticised for being antiquated, but honestly I think just about anyone with an open mind and enough patience and time can appreciate it, even today.
