There's nothing quite as nostalgic to 90's kids such as myself than retro survival horror games. Resident Evil, Alone in the Dark, Silent Hill, Eternal Darkness, Parasite Eve... they all conjure memories relating back to feelings of tension, suspense, and fright through a newly discovered video game genre. Back then, we weren't so desensitized, and even pixels that we could barely make out horrified us in forgotten ways. Back in 1995 attempts to put the player back in the glory days of horror gaming, all the while telling a complex story.
The plot starts off simple, something that we've heard a hundred times over; you must uncover the mystery surrounding the disappearance of your daughter. The rest of the game is told through a series of notes and dialogue segments with a couple of other characters that you meet along the way, though sadly the story stays perplexing. In the end, there is somewhat of closure, but in all honesty the tale just feels like bits and pieces of a larger story being woven unevenly together. Needless to say, it's neigh impossible to follow unless you focus on just the "true" ending; by the way, there are two endings.
From there, things just go from bad to worse. Yeah, this game does have the clunky tank controls, as it should being that it's emulating old Playstation games, but really that's the only plus side here. The older graphics warp in very strange ways, especially the ground, though it seems to be due to the CRT TV effect emulating the "wrapped" effect of an older television set. If you turn this effect off, the game just looks bad... and not even in an old PSX graphics style kinda bad, just plain bad. You can even walk through things that you shouldn't be able to. The audio is even worse, or lack thereof. A good horror game, whether it be new or old, should have tense music, but this game has a very relaxing "soundtrack".
The first enemy you encounter literally looks like a poop nugget... I can't even make that stuff up, I have no idea what it's actually supposed to be. There are two other bad guys, plus one "boss" monster that appears a couple of times. These foes pose absolutely no threat, since whenever you hit them they're stunned and can't fight back at all. When it comes to the boss monster you can huddle yourself into a narrow confinement and it can't come through, while you pelt it with bullets. This renders the "survival" part of the survival horror tag completely useless, you won't need healing items at all. There aren't even any decent, mysterious puzzles to solve. The people you meet send you on "fetch quests"; go here, do this thing, come back here for further instructions.
I'm actually extremely disheartened to say that Back in 1995 disappointed me tremendously. I've been looking forward to playing this title since it released, but couldn't justify the asking price for such a minimal amount of game time. So I got it on sale for half off, but I've refunded it. The store page claims 2-3 hours of playtime, yet I beat the game (including the "true" ending) in an hour and a half. That's with exploring every area, and killing all monsters. Though that's only the bottom layer of why I refunded this title, the biggest concern is that it has none of the elements that make a decent survival horror experience. Even at half off and an update lingering in the near future (this never came to pass), forego this title and just play an actual survival horror game from the good 'ol days.

I hate being blatantly insulting or contrary but this game is largely a crapper.  In it you play as Kent Crapsworth the 1st, a completely boring snoozefest of a character trying to reach some tower far off in the distance whilst attempting to regain his memory and find his daughter or something.  Literally, I don't need to give you any exposition because the character is mundane and the backstory I just regurgitated is about all you get throughout the whole darn thing.
Back in 1995 is a noble attempt to go back to the days of old school Alone in the Dark, Silent Hill and Resident Evil.  It's heart is in the right place but all of its body parts are stitched together like Frankenstein.  My heart literally sank as I played; the whole affair not even taking a whole two hours to beat...with the secret portion of the game being counted into that playtime as well.
Crapsworth's quest requires you storming through office buildings and rooftops in search of documents, notes, etc. that really don't say a darn thing interesting.  You'll get a whopping three weapons in order to combat and take on a series of brown bomber enemies including renegade Thanksgiving butterballs, stationary worm creatures culled from Tremors II:  Aftershocks, an embryo on stilts and a massive hulking fleshbeast (that looks much more threatening than he is).  In between these fights that offer no challenge you'll meet nondescript characters who push the story along as you collect massive amounts of healing items, an army surplus of bullets and pretty much everything else that negates the aspect of "survival."
Surprisingly enough, the tank controls are quite responsive with even an automatic lock-on system making sure enemies eat every bit of hot lead you throw at them, althrough you can beat the whole game by swinging your pipe wrench a few times and running for the hills.  I chose to kill every single creature in order to get at least half of my money's worth out of this royal flush.  Toilet humor is not my forte but this game inspires it plentifully.
When talking about graphics n' sound, well, let's change the subject!  Even the early AITD's looked far better than this and don't even get me started on the first Silent Hill.  The sound is also horrendous, sporting some of the worst music I've heard in a horror game coupled to tepid sound effects that perfectly match.  Again, I feel bad about walking all over this game but DO NOT buy it unless it's $5 or under (hopefully under).  $11.99 is an absolute travesty of a price to even ask for such a weak "game."  The developer's heart is in the right place, sure, yet this costs money and you can spend it far better elsewhere. Well that was disappointing...
I was somewhat really interested by Back In 1995. I grew up loving the PlayStation and the images from the Tomb Raider 1 to 5, MGS, Resident Evil 1 to 3, Silent Hill, FFVIII or Syphon Filter 1 to 3 are forever stuck in my mind. I love the aesthetic from this era. I think for certain genres, survival/horror in particular, it brings not only nostalgia, but a sense of weirdness and it is forcing you to imagine the details hidden in the pixelated mess that some of the most gruesome games of this time can show. So yeah, I dig the idea of this look. I still enjoy playing SH and RE1,2 and 3 to this day, and I'm still saying "it holds up"...at least for SH and RE3. I say all that, so there is a context for me bashing the game afterward.
I can "pray" the effort put into the technical re-creation of the PlayStation graphical flaws. You have the CRT effect of your old tv. You have the textures that bends when approaching the camera. You have the peculiar type of aliasing. The range of color for the textures and the sound design seems straight from this machine. So yeah, this could have been produced on Sony's first console in 1995. And you know what? It would have been a mediocre if not bad game, even for it's time.
Because even for a 1995's game, it's ugly. There is no effort put into the colors, the lighting, the models and textures. The most common monster looks like a potato with arms and the other three are so messed up and unrefined visually that you can't really tell what it is supposed to be. There is like no attention to detail in the textures.
The semi-fixed camera, inspired by Silent Hill, lets us see through wall, or through the character, and has no purpose whatsoever, neither in terms of framing, nor in terms of gameplay, to show us where to look. And this poor use of the camera is just one example of the absence of art direction. The characters have no personality and the story is not fleshed out and revolves around the oldest trick in the book. For once, I'm going to say that it is far too short, but not for the time/price ratio. Just because the story never has time to really kick in.
TL;DR I get the idea and I am a sucker for the survival/horror of the PS1 era, but this is lazy. This game is to PlayStation aesthetic what RPG Maker is to pixel art. The base is technically there, but the visual artistry and the game-design mastery are nowhere to be seen. Oh and it costs actual money, when it's barelly enough to be on Gamejolt. You know what, don't buy this game, go play Banned Memories: Yamanashi for free on Gamejolt.

I highly recommend this to anyone who prefers a shooter that is more realisticly paced than arcadey chaos.
This is surprisingly one of the best shooters I have played.  The movement and combat is fluid, but not overly arcade-feeling.  There is realism and movement feels natural, but not overly tight or restrictive as with many "realistic shooters". The movement pace is toned down to a realistic level, there is no jerky back and forth all over the place dodgy crap, as inertia seems to have been taken into account.  This is especially evident when exiting a moving vehicle.  You don't just pop to the outside, instantly free to move in some random direction of your choosing.  You actually exit the vehicle, as in open the door and slide out, and then your momentum is still carrying you until you transition to moving under your own power.  If you're moving fast enough, you actually hit the ground and roll!  All very natural looking and feeling.
The scope of the game is pretty wide.  I haven't been able to play in any actual war battles that affect the current war campaign since none of my soldiers are level 5 yet.  From what I see and have read, it seems like the War is what you would get if someone did a mashup of a Total War style army movement on the campaign map with players fighting all the resulting battles as Assault Teams clash.  More on this when I get to experience it first-hand.
Thoughtful, methodical movement and positioning and well aimed shots are key.  The weapons feel natural, and so does weapon switching.  There is no shoot-shoot-shoot-instagrenade-shoot-shoot.  You have to switch to the grenade.  This, along with the grenade arc shown on screen as you pull the pin and hold it, makes grenade use just as natural feeling and realistic as the rest of the movement and gunplay.
Even with the basic kit that you start with, I often end rounds near the top of the scoreboard, so I have no concerns about it being "pay-to-win".  Anyone who says otherwise probably has the "you killed me, therefore you had an unfair advantage" thing going on.

Quick Summary: Third Person Shooter with an interesting campaign story, that plays like it should be co-op, but is only single player. If you’ve played Scourge: Outbreak, Inversion, or the first Mass Effect you will have a decent idea how the combat and graphics are in Binary Domain. Binary Domain also has a unique voice command system where your computer controlled squad mates will recognize orders that you give through your microphone. The orders are limited, so if you don’t have a microphone (or are just too lazy to find it like me) you can just use your keyboard to issue the commands. You usually have between 2 – 4 generic options (charge, regroup, cover me, etc.) so don’t worry about sticking with the keyboard because you’re not missing out on too much.
A century or so into the future, global warming has caused terrible damage to the planet, especially flooding caused by rising oceans. Japan has sealed itself off from the rest of the world with a massive sea wall, and nobody really knows what’s going on in there. At the same time, robotics technology has advanced so far that there are now laws in place preventing people from building robots that are too life-like. You play Dan, a member of an international Rust Crew, whose job it is to investigate violations of these laws. You and your team have your work cut out for you because around the world, people are finding “hollow children,” robots with human skin (like terminators), but they’re so well programed that even they don’t realize they’re robots. Since only a certain Japanese corporation has the tech to do something like this, your Rust Crew is sent to infiltrate Japan and find out what’s going on.
The game plays in Third Person Shooter perspective and since you have the ability to revive teammates who fall in battle using a medkit (and vice versa), the game is generally fast paced. You have regenerating health and can take cover behind objects, with a small assortment of weapons that you can find/buy. Killing enemies gets you credits that you can spend in automated shopping kiosks scattered around the game. The kiosks also allow you to buy upgrades to your primary weapon, but you should definitely focus your spending on “nanomachines” which are upgrades that you can apply to you and your team, such as increased melee damage, damage resistance, hold more grenades, etc.
An interesting system in the game is “trust” where your teammates will occasionally ask you questions, and depending on your answer, their trust in you will go up or down. Just choose the default answer and you’ll get a trust “up” about 90% of the time. You can also increase trust by being awesome in battle, for example scoring one shot kills or multi-kills will cause your team to admire you more. You can drive the trust down by accidentally shooting your ally or mouthing off at them when they ask you a question. Supposedly the trust system affects how well your teammates follow your orders or aid you in combat but honestly I don’t know if it does anything significant. Just like any squad game, you’ll be doing 99% of the killing anyways.
You should try Binary Domain if:
+You like fast paced action (Call of Duty, Gears of War, etc.) but you only have money to buy indie games. The graphics are not up to “modern” standards, but you probably got this game for free or close to it.
+You enjoy sci-fi futuristic stories with killer robots, and questions about the morality of artificial intelligence. The story is very “Japanese” so if you watch a lot of anime you might find it predictable.
You should Not try Binary Domain if:
-You’re looking for a co-op campaign. The only co-op is in the multiplayer Invasion mode, which I couldn’t try since multi-player is dead. As I mentioned earlier, the game “looks” like it was made for co-op play (like Resident Evil 5 where there’s almost always someone with you), but sadly it’s just you and your computer controlled teammates.
-You’re looking for an “easy” game. The robot enemies have a lot of health (you blast pieces off of them and they keep crawling at you) and even on easy difficulty you can very quickly be incapacitated. There’s also the looming threat of friendly fire. Maybe you don’t care about accidently shooting a teammate and lowering trust (sometimes feels like they’re purposely running into your fire line), but they sometimes shoot you too.

It's like the creator wanted to make a Minecraft mod that adds cars, except they decided that Minecraft had way too many options for building so they took everything out except the cars.
Upon opening the game, I was excited to run around collecting parts that I could cobble together to build my own vehicle, except there is no survival mode, no single player storyline, there is no multiplayer option, and the only mode you get to play is Creative. You are thrust into a world that actually looks pretty nice, but in reality is too small to make some of the bigger creations this game could thrive on. I was immediately reminded of Garry's Mod with tools like the welder and connector, but this game is significantly simpler and building my first car only took about 10 minutes. I started browsing the inventory of items to find out that there really isn't very many. There are 2 engines, one driver's chair with a steering wheel (although 4 other chairs without a steering wheel which are useless), a few switches, 2 wheels, and a handful of decorative blocks. The inventory is extremely limiting, and while I see the potential for making a lot of different machines, it seems incredibly lacking. The controls are pretty easy to get the hang of, but it has a bad problem where entering a vehicle seat changes you to 3rd person veiw (unchangable) and you can no longer activate any controls aside from the forward, backward, left, and right controls of the steering wheel. If you have switches or buttons on your vehicle you must activate them before sitting in the chair, which makes a lot of vehicles start up before you even get in. The physics, which are really the most important part of a game like this, are not fantastic. Friction seems very limited and turning in any vehicle is like sliding on ice.
The other part of this game, flying vehicles, can only be achieved through one single thruster unit. There are no airplane parts, no blades, and no wings. Once you make your first flying machine you will quickly notice that the sky limit is so low that it is not nearly as fun as you thought. While it may be easy to blame all of these problems on the fact that it's still in alpha and not a completed game yet, it has been out for quite some time now and you really expect it to have considerably more. I thought maybe it was just a gateway for modders to make the real game, but even the mods seem lame with just adding one pre-made vehicle (who really wants to drive around an empty world in someone elses creation for hours?) or small packs of decorative blocks. This whole game feels like it would be better off as a mod to another crafting game instead of standing on its own.

Erm......So, what's so 2015 about this edition? I can understand that a full-fledged HD remake might be asking a bit much, but I'll take any actual improvements and modernizations I can get. I'd settle for a remastered soundtrack. But really, the only thing we get is an "HQ filter" that marginally improves the visuals. I'll be honest though, I only bought this release because I pirated the 2010 version, and I felt bad about it.
On to the actual game. If you've never played Raptor Call of the Shadows, it's a classic shoot-em-up that existed before today's bullet hells that permeate the genre with the likes of Cave and Treasure's offerings, etc. This means there's actually a reasonable amount of munitions being fired at you at any given time, with exception to some boss fights in the later difficulties.
The game is split up into three zones, each containing 9 levels, for 27 levels total. In between levels you can buy weapons and consumables from a shop with money you earn by shooting down enemies and destroying parts of the environment.  These weapons add variety to your arsenal from your standard air-to-air rockets all the way up to death lasers. These weapons are selectable during the mission, so you can adjust for various situations on the fly. However, having to cycle through all these weapons to use the one you want can be frustrating, so I recommend you only keep weapons you actually need and sell the rest.
A few things the game does well includes a nice, gradual difficulty curve, gameplay is fairly well-balanced, and there's a nice degree of progression. The soundtrack deserves its own mention, because even with dated instruments, it's still pretty sweet. However, the sound rendering is such that lots of action can cause the music to muffle or jitter.
If you're using a gamepad, you'll need to reconfigure the defaults right away. The only button mapped correctly is the shot button. You'll have to use bombs and change weapons using the keyboard until you make corrections. Also, when making these corrections, use the Enter key on the keyboard, then push the button on the gamepad. Otherwise your mapping won't work for some reason.
Here's the breakdown: if you already own Raptor in one incarnation or another, the 2015 release is not worth a purchase. However, for those just now discovering this title, it's a fun game that is completely worth an insta-buy.

This game is a must-have experience for the fans of the horror genre. It's a wild trip that messes with your senses, while you enjoy every single  thrill and uncover an interesting mystery
Pros:
good pacing  for both uncovering of the story, but also setting the mood and then scaring the living hell out of you along the way
well built tension and well placed jump scares
the whole atmosphere was thrilling: imagery (the psychedelic ones especially), sound, environment
great attention to details and lovely architectural setting
Cons:
Too few puzzles and too easy  (yes, the game relies heavily on general atmosphere and choices, but it would've made it more interesting)
Saving system a bit strange; “loads” you in portrait room every time and then you land where you left off. Took me a bit to realize this though so I messed up the “save point” a couple of times and restarted the chapter
A bit too short as game play (probably because I liked it :) )
Some achievements don't trigger properly!! Finishing touch, for example is one that should trigger when you finish the game and it didn't for me. (saw more complaints for this one going around)

My major complaint is that the story leaves a bit too much to the player's imagination. Yes, you can fill in the gaps, but you can't actually be sure about what happened overall which can leave you a bit unsatisfied, no matter what ending you get. (I got the “good” one from the first try and still can't fill in some gaps which I would've like to fill, like the “ingredients” and where they come from)
It's a bit hard to figure out how to get the alternative endings; there is very contradictory information all around. And it is not the kind of hard that relies on logic, a mystery for you to solve, it really seems a bit..random.
Overall I enjoyed every second of it and I am really considering expanding it by buying some DLCs.

I believe this project was primarily intended for a very specific audience: players with fond memories of 32-bit 3D games, who maintained a fondness for those rough, chunky polygon graphics well after the next wave of consoles arrived, and came to regard those limitations as having created a legitimate style all their own, no less valid than NES and SNES-style pixel art. I'm part of that group, though you may not be.
Even if you are, you still may not "get" this game. It's totally a style-over-substance work, but it's somewhat excusable for how well it nails the look of those fully rendered Playstation 3D adventures, such as Silent Hill 1, Echo Night, Clock Tower: Ghost Head and Aconcagua. Even if it isn't comparable to the length or objective quality of those games. The characteristic "texture warping" of the PS1's 3D rendering is faithfully recreated: every surface seems to stretch and pulse with your every step, making the world feel much more dynamic and ominously unstable than it really is. Since its presence in this game is as a deliberate feature rather than an unintentional consequence of the hardware, the environments and camera angles are laid out to take maximum advantage of its effects.
Unless you are playing on an actual CRT monitor, I definitely recommend leaving the noisy CRT filter on to experience the full effect, and it's necessary for one of the game's fourth wall-breaking tricks to work. While so many modern retrogaming throwbacks would obviously never be able to run on the hardware they attempt to pay homage to, practically nothing about this game's visual presentation is out of character with a Playstation, Saturn or 3DO release from 1995, and I find that quite appealing.
Don't expect a great breadth or depth of content. I finished it in about two hours (counting offline play), there's only two "puzzles" that require any degree of thinking, and there's only one room in the game with enemies that might actually kill you. Resident Evil 2, this ain't. The ending is very inconclusive, and mainly serves as a sort of developer's commentary. Despite these huge flaws, I felt that Back in 1995 was a worthwhile jaunt through some attractive and faithfully presented retro-3D environments, with a few clever "gotcha" moments and a palpable foreboding atmosphere. The developer is going to patch in voice acting eventually; if it sounds anything like the accented deadpan narration in the second trailer, it should contribute further to the overall feel and sense of 32-bit-era authenticity.
Cautiously recommended for a certain type of gamer. You probably already know if you'll consider it to have been worth your time and money or not. If nothing else, it's definitely better and less pretentious than most other indie "walking simulators" on Steam. Oh, and there is actually a deeper significance to the title, though like everything else in the story, it's never fully explained.

If you enjoy both (1) the impressionistic look of early, primitive 3D graphics as seen on the PS1/Saturn/3DO; as well as (2) slower-paced, puzzle-sprinkled gameplay that is lighter on action but heavy on atmosphere, I think you'll love this game. If you think a game's price point should be based on how many hours you get out of the game, this game is gonna disappoint you.
I personally value quality over quantity, and I felt like the "heart" the developer put into this game was palpable. This game is more about atmosphere and narrative than mechanics; if that appeals to you, I strongly recommend buying it!

This was an instant buy for me when I saw it being advertised before one of the Grand Prix's last year, and I have not been disappointed.
It's awesome to finally have a management game in a sport I enjoy watching and sim-ing, and Motorsport Manager certainly held me for a long time. In fact, with mods, it still does.
The environments are beautiful, the updated car models are chunkier and more substantial, so those livery changes finally show up as more than the simple two-tone designs we had at release. Playing the staff and driver market is fun, and working your way up the field is rewarding. For the casual gamer who enjoys motorsport, this game is an absolute must have. If you don't do racing, but enjoy management sims, you'll likely enjoy this too.
A couple of big negative points though, which I feel are more a me thing than a game issue:-
As a power gamer, I found after about 50 hours or so, everything got seriously easy. The AI are, unfortunately, too dim to challenge a player who knows what they are doing, and they struggle to keep up with your pace of car development whenever you hit a stat reset. The same goes for qualifying in a session that has a wet and dry period, where the AI don't look ahead in the weather reports, and then set their quali times in the dry on Inters.
The second thing is there are too many ways for a player to abuse a system for their gain - notably the Risk system on car develpment, which makes the game even easier (I didn't even use this method and still found a lack of difficulty).
However, with the game being so easy to mod for beginners (simple editing of databases), and the ability for more advanced users to modify the actual code of the game, difficulty and overhaul mods have been made which can keep even power gamers like myself challenged and engaged. A huge boon to modding is that mods can be grabbed both with or without Workshop, and can be mixed and matched as you see fit.
Without mods - I would only recommend this to casual gamers, regardless of whether you are a motorsport fan or not. If you play an hour here or there and want your progress to not be too slow, then it's a good title for you.
With mods - There is now something for everyone, and if you like your games challenging and you want to be in it for the long haul, you can opt for that experience while still enjoying the visually beautiful game that PlaySport have brought us.

Very unique Tron-like environments.
Most of the game is solving puzzles and searching for key items, with some 3d platform action and spooky stealth.
The game has its share of jumpscare spooky scary moments, but they're done well, adding just the right amount of tension.
There's an overarching plot of death and mayhem and sabotage that gets unraveled by clicking ducks throughout the game.
I could see some people getting annoyed with the exploration and with certain puzzles. I was on the brink of looking up walkthroughs more than once, but each time I wound up finding the next necessary thing soon after.
I could see some people getting annoyed with the 3d platforming. It took me many tries to get past the last room. It wasn't horrible, just takes some practice and skill. If you're a paraplegic wanting puzzles-only, this is not the game for you.
I could see some people getting annoyed by the jumpscares. But as long as you aren't at risk for heart attacks and you can tolerate spooks, don't let them stop you from playing.
The game is very unique, satisfying, and creepy.

I hesitantly recommend this game because of the gaping holes in whatever concept of a storyline it seems to have, but if you are a fan of psychological thrillers, then you'd be a fan of this game.
Personally, I'd favor a more structured background of your situation in the game, but if you appreciate mystery more than I do the pieces of the big puzzle can be a thrill to assemble.
The games succeeds in two points: It's very eerie (a must have for games such as this), and its puzzles vary widely enough to stay interesting throughout the entire game. Whether it's mazes, lasers, shaped puzzles, item hunts, audio matchups, etc, every puzzle was simple yet complex enough to allow for the thrill and the (limited) storytelling in between.
I picked this game up on sale, and if you're looking for a quick thrill, I recommend you do too.

Master Reboot is an abstract puzzle game with some horror elements.  You are basically trapped inside someone's memories that have been stored in a computer while you attempt to escape from and destroy a virus.  Gameplay consists of solving puzzles to explore the memories and some occasional simple combat.  Most of the puzzles are straightforward which is a nice change of pace from some other games I've played recently.
While the game doesn't start well with a rather poor introduction/tutorial level, it gets a lot more interesting later.  You make your way through memories of someone's life, slowly learning about their life as you progress.  Along the way you will find collectibles that give you more information about this person's life related to the memory they are found in.
Graphically, the game is nothing special.  It uses a low detail art style with a dark horror-like atmosphere to emphasize the fact that you are inside someone's memories inhabited by a virus.  It works well, though the way colors are handled leads to some nasty color banding and really poor contrast in places.
Overall I definitely enjoyed Master Reboot.  It's a unique experience unlike any other game I've played.

Usually Western dating sims are pretty bad, but this is interesting. The best part, its hilarious. I like the dialogue, its unique and funny. There are negatives though. It gets repetitive really fast, since there isn't much the characters say and the game is simple, and also due to its simplicity its heavily luck based, it's very easy to get bored of it. And the characters aren't very fleshed out. They have deeper stories implied but you never really get into the details of each character, which is often the best part of a visual novel/dating sim like game, but it just isn't there here. I also find it a bit strange how it differs from a standard game of the genre, as you can and are encouraged woo all the girls at the same time and there's absoliutely no consequences to that, but it's not necessarily a negative, just an oddity.
It's far from perfect, but its mostly enjoyable, overall I'd definitely recommend it.

So I've spent several hundred hours (except that it doesn't show up since I made the mistake of installing the game via Arc at first which wasn't my brightest idea) and a sizeable amount of money on this game and after all of that I can kind of recommend it. Kind of.
As with many things, it depends what you're looking for in a game, so I thought I'd give you an idea what you can expect.
1. Graphics
Not entirely state-of-the-art, but not too bad for a MMO. It looks nice. Lots of nebulae in space, some seriously pretty alien worlds, you get the idea. Earth Space Dock is pretty, too, but unfortunately I'm not too fond of Starfleet ships.
The way some cutscenes are animated are just plain awful, though. Not entirely sure if it gets better with later content or if I just stopped noticing at some point.
2. Controls
There's so many buttons you have to press that you will feel like this game was created for octopodes at one point or another.
The good thing: you can bind anything to everything. There are even sneaky (but completely rule-compliant) ways to bind several things to one key, at the cost of flexibility.
Long story short: Depending on your playstyle, it may not be an easy game to play, but that's one of the fun parts. Patience + training + experimenting = progress, and progress is a pretty fulfilling thing.
3. Technical Stuffs
"Server Not Responding (insert huge number here)" might well be the inofficial motto of STO, at least on some days.
Cryptic does not seem too fond of bug fixes and stability improvements and some mission bugs are pretty damn game-breaking. Like spawning players outside a permanently locked door upon death, five meters away from the mission goal. Gee, thanks, Cryptic.
It's annoying, but I've rarely lost my cool because of that. If the occasional bug and/or server hiccup is your pet peeve however, STO is probably not the game for you.
4. Content, Yay!
4.1 Is STO P2W or not?
Depends on what you plan to win. All regular game content can easily be played without spending a dime.
PvE can be done, too - paywall'd content consists primarily of ships, while most gear is merely grind-y. If you're not planning to climb your way to the top of the DPS ranking, you'll be fine if you take some time to learn.
PvP is definitely P2W as far as I know, but playing PvP isn't exactly mandatory - I personally prefer PvE anyway.
The big drawback concerning paid content is that it is ridiculously expensive. 'Micro'-transaction my butt. We're talking at the very least 25$ for one measly (but admittedly account-wide unlocked) endgame ship.
One the plus side, they are incredibly cool. You don't technically need to throw all your money at PWE, but you might very well find yourself wanting to.
Useful but boring paid stuff like more bank slots and stuff isn't quite as expensive, but still far from cheap. It's the one reason why I only kiiiiind of recommend this game, to be honest.
4.2 Outfits, Customization and stuff.
Do you like half-naked alien space babes? Do you like half-naked alien space dudes? Do you like completely dressed alien space babes? All of the above?
Congratulations, this is the game for you.
There's a huge amount of customization in this game - think "Skyrim", except with very slightly less ugly hair and WAY more body sliders - and you can play with it to your heart's content, since your outfits don't influence your armor rating. And while there is some skimpy stuff in STO, it's not the default, which is nice.
You can change up your ships, too, but there's a lot of paid content involved in that - still, you can always change hull materials and, most amazingly, there's patterns that come in a plethora of colors. Some players do really neat stuff with that.
4.3 Writing
It's not always absolutely top notch, but it does have its moments and it never get's *too* bad - there are just some story missions that I will probably not replay for the writing. For the loot - maybe.
There's also some lazy writing - or maybe coding (or both) - faction-wise: Every KDF characters will continuously spam tlhIngan Hol and talk of honor. In one mission my KDF-aligned Romulan captain got called "Starfleet" thrice.
4.4 Trekkiness
You can visit several classic Trek locations, like DS9 for example - or Vulcan. Now featuring a statue of Spock, even.
In general, while you can fly the original USS Enterprise (for about 5$, that is), the game is a lot more kind to fans of DS9 or Voyager, for timeline reasons - although Scotty and Bones do get cameos in one of the story missions.
With the advent of the Delta Quadrant content, they started hiring some of the ST:VOY actors to reprise their characters, which led to some very nice moments for fans of that show.
One the other side, if you're looking for diplomacy not involving gunboats, this game is probably not the right choice for you. No matter what you do, at the end of the day your captain will have a higher body count than Captain Janeway, as the community likes to quip.
Apart from the 'shooting everything' issue, some people didn't particularly like the toned-down jerkiness of the playable Romulans.
4.5 Community
Very prone to drama and some parts of it are devoid of any sense of humor (please note: SOME parts!), but as long as you know when to keep your flap shut, you're unlikely to get into much trouble - at least judging from my personal experience.
4.6 Conclusion
You know what, I'll just give you some tips instead and let you draw your own conclusions:
-If this game sounds like you might enjoy it, give it a try - it's free.
-If you do want to try it, be warned: It takes a while to dl.
-Don't get too attached to your first character; from my experience it's best to just rush in and do the game first and then work on a proper build and such on your second character, once you have learned the ropes. If you don't mind playing a bit of a mess: Go ahead.
-Don't know what faction to choose? Look up a list of all available ships for each faction.
-Still no idea? If you play a Romulan, you get to choose your allegiance at level 10, so that's a good place to start
-Have fun.

The best 'modern' Elder Scrolls game by a long shot, and a rude awakening for anyone whose introduction to ES was Oblivion or Skyrim. You begin as literally a nobody, born under a certain sign to uncertain parents, released from the Imperial City's prison under questionable circumstances and thrust into a world where nobody likes you and everything will probably try to kill you. There is no magical arrow in the sky showing you where to go, and even the smallest of encounters can be deadly. Fast travel exists only in the form of paid transports, running everywhere will render you too exhausted to fight effectively, untrained spells will fail and unpracticed attacks will miss. But this is what makes Morrowind special; a truly fantastic, alien, landscape, real challenges, complex plotlines requiring real choices and tests of loyalty and skill instead of 'follow the magic arrow to the next cutscene'.

This game takes "classic" to a whole new level. If you didn't grow up in the 90's playing horror games, this one IS NOT for you. On the other hand, if you remember your PS1 days and games like Silent Hill, then you MIGHT want to give this a try.
Tank controls, warping unsightly textures your eyes will never get used to in 2016, static cameras, etc. It's all here. The game is even presented in 4:3 aspect ratio. Don't get me wrong, it's nowhere near the caliber of Silent Hill or Resident Evil of the era, but it's a great throwback nonetheless. The story is pretty straight forward and short. I liked it.
I do recommend this game to the few people that will appreciate what it's trying to do. To all the rest, steer clear. If you even have the slightest doubt that you may not like it, I suggest you don't buy it. If you approach the game with an open mind, and I mean OPEN MIND, and want to revisit the PS1 days for a couple of hours, then go for it.
With a steam controller in hand, I was happy to invest a couple of hours into Back in 1995. Kudos to Takaaki Ichijo for this accomplishment and for having the balls to actually pull off such an ambitious and risky project. I look forward to more of his work.

You can either watch it or read it!
*SPOILERS*
Back In 1995 is a throwback to the survival horror classics of the 1990s - such as Resident Evil, Silent Hill, and Alone in the Dark.
I was really hyped for about a month waiting for it to come out. I didn't realize at the time it was going to be a one-man dev team, literally as I was downloading it, I was reading around on the game itself and came across that bit of information and all my hype basically disintegrated.
Having already, in my mind, dedicated the next two hours to old-school survival horror, I figured I'd give it a whirl.
First, this game supports quite a variety of controllers, which is sweet because this could've completed contradicted the point to the entire game - "an homage to 90's survival horror".
The game then next give your CRT Effect options to simulate the crappy tvs a lot of us in our mid twenties plus grew up with. At first I was going to skip this effect, but ultimately opted for the CRT without noise, as old televisions have given my headaches my entire life.
You start off on the roof of a random building, gazing off in the distance, you play as Kent as he is trying to get to a distant tower for unknown reasons.
As all 90s survival horror titles, health items and ammo are scattered through the entire world and you have unlimited inventory space.
Now I'll admit, the first monsters I called the "Mr. Hankeys" the entire game because they literally look like a giant turd nuggets with arms. Which is pretty weird, but at the same time, I was infinitely relieved they didn't go with zombies. I've always a huge zombie fan in the 90s, but something about them wouldn't sit right in this game.
The first monsters are generally pretty easy to dispose of, three hits with your melee is all it takes.
After unlocking a door or two, you answer a telephone and pass out.
You wake up to a doctor taking care of you. After of which, he sends you on a couple errands where you have to complete puzzles and flex your brain just a little bit to complete. Just a fair warning, this is classic survival horror, so not a lot of things are going to make logical sense.
After a couple puzzles, some items scavenging, and finding your first gun, you find yourself at Central University Hospital.
Heading to the cafeteria, the find the shotgun and when could maybe considered the first and only boss battle.
Which, by the way, the briefcase here can only be opened when your find the note stating how to open it. I found the code first and got♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when it wouldn't work. Make sure you go down the hallway across the hall on the left hand side of the screen, it's a little hidden.
After a little site seeing, you get to the final area of the game. Which appears to be a luxury, rooftop penthouse. This is where things begin to fall in place. After finding a crank to open a drawer - yes, every survival horror game has to have a crank, somehow, somewhere, I don't make the rules, I do however fully except them - you start to find a lot of notes directed at your character Kent regarding his mental condition. Even going so far as to explain why there is no run option in the game. Kent's condition caused him to lose that ability as well as cognitive functions.
His mental condition is so unstable, he believes he is still in the year 1995 - hence the title.
When your reach your final destination, the tower in the distance. Kent decides he's had enough and chooses to end his suffering.
Which not to take away from the seriousness of the story... but he was on rooftops the entire game... he could've just jumped from anywhere and it would've had the same effect.
Some things I want to point out that I liked
-Tank controllers were spot on
-The monsters were original, the big one really reminded me of the final transformation of Berkin from Resident Evil 2.
-The overall feel was definitely 90s survival horror
-The save points were 90s computers
-Glitches were almost nonexistent
-Notes everywhere, just like Silent Hill and Resident Evil
Something I think need work
-some of the rooms were just a little empty
-I found a glitch that gave me unlimited shotgun ammo pickups, in the hospital if you go back to the rooftop and return to the room with the briefcase, the ammo will respawn.
-Also a second glitch that I unlocked the "finish the game" and "get flashlight" achievements, but somehow not "clear the first stage", "clear the opening sequence", "get the pipewrench", "get pistol" that are all completed within the first 10 minutes of playing.
-The enemies should be a little tougher, if you attack first, they'll stop moving and as long as your keep attacking you'll kill them.
-For an oldschool survival horror, there's too many health items and too much ammo.
-If there were to be a sequel, which I really hope there is, I'd recommend more story depth and more boss battles. The story worked just fine for this project.
After the game was over, it did something I did not all expect. After what I thought were the credits, the game started over again without me doing anything. I retained all my weapons and items and figured, "what the hell, lets run through it a little more". Upon entering the room with the telephone, instead I found a flashlight. After thinking "what kind of creepypasta♥♥♥♥♥♥is this?" I turned it on and was met with some text, then the font changed to a modern style.
Intrigued, I continued. I went back to the roof and there was a scaffolding that hadn't been there before. I then made my way rooftop to rooftop, each covering an area I'd already been to.
You find various notes on your way back to the tower, each one seeming to refer more to real life than the situation in the game itself. To me, the entire game is merely a social commentary on retrogaming and those of us who simply can't let it go. Those of us w ho grasp to that nostalgia, that first love we all had. It was new to us, that's why it was so great. We were young and everything seemed to pop so much more. Then we grew up, less and less felt new to us, and that first love became a only a memory.
Making my way to the end, this time taking only 5 minutes or so, you're met with the final text "Am I no different than he, who spent 20 years running away? Aren't we the same? From now on, will I lead a meaningless life. Is there no way to reclaim my own life?"
I feel like this is the developer saying, 20 years ago when we were young, the ones before us were attached to Atari games and Pac-man. They refused to move on no matter how much we tried to   convince them Playstation, Resident Evil and Metal Gear Solid were better. They stopped moving forward, as have we - and if we aren't moving forward, we aren't progressing. We can't change the way nostalgia makes us feel.
Loved the game, hope there is a sequel or the dev makes another survival horror. Hell of an installment for, primarily, just one developer.

Back in 1995 is a retro-styled survival-horror game that takes most of its influence from a 1994 Japan-only 3DO horror game known as Dr. Hauzer and Silent Hill. The game has the sort of things you would expect from such an undertaking, such as fixed camera angles, limited supplies, tank controls. What may be a bit less predictable in the journey itself.
Now, let me first clarify something here and now; this game is not in the same league as the Resident Evil's and Silent Hill's of yesteryear. It doesn't even get in the remote ballpark of that level of quality during the 2-3 hour journey, and reminds me a lot more of the B-Tier horror game from that same era. I also feel I should preface this review with a mention that I am a horror enthusiast; I eat this genre right up. I played every Resident Evil and Silent Hill game through more than once ages ago, and have played more and more of the genre as time as gone on; I have played niche old titles ranging from Hungry Ghosts for the PS2 to Deep Fear on the Saturn, I've played all the Dead Space games and recently Night of the Sacrifice (Ikenie no Yoru) on the Wii, more recent indie horrors such as Left Alone and Dead Secret within the week, along with a ton of others. I have become more aware within the last few months I am beginning to run out of older horror games to play through; I have dug into the niche and the mostly forgotten, and I am almost done playing through every horror game that released before 2004, everything from the more well known Fatal Frame games to niche Korean-only PC releases. I think understanding where I'm coming from will help me explain my thoughts on this game.
Back in 1995 both succeeds and misses at what it is trying to be, and also provides an unexpected element that it also both succeeds and misses in. I'll talk about both elements here.
Firstly, as a retro horror game. The game actually does manage to capture that feel sometimes, particularly the feel of the B-Horror romps from yesteryear. I would put it at maybe the same quality as Chaos Break or Deep Fear, if you've played either of those. Games that have some flawed execution and rough edges, but can capture you with some well deployed curiosity. The game has four main segments, and each segment does manage to be more intriguing than the last and put new twists on the game to avoid becoming repetitive. The combat is super simple and maybe too easy for its own good; most of the enemies can be taken out pretty easily with just the crowbar you start off with, and while enemies attacks hurt, I found myself not very challenged by the game. There were a few puzzles that were a bit medium-easy in their difficulty for me, but were a bit of fun to mess around with.
The graphics look a bit worse than they should. Being able to alter the screen filter is good (I played the game with the CRT filter on but no noise, mostly), but the texture distortion is a bit much (textures distort and twist based on their perspective to the camera, which is an intended effect). It was very exaggerated and in some areas made the game look incredibly messy. The music went between being forgettable and a few nice tracks, but didn't really ever help the atmosphere, I felt. I get the game was going for a pre-PSX horror game sound style more similar to Alone in the Dark, Ecstatica, or the aftermentioned Dr. Hauzer, but I felt they could of easily gotten away with more atmospheric tracks and nobody would of given it any thought. The monsters aren't overused thankfully (there's only a handful of encounters in the game), and while there's only four different kinds they are used sparsely. I actually like most of them (the last two types especially), but the first monster type I could never find remotely scary or creepy, which is unfortunate (they look like fleshy Pacman ghosts to me).
Still, there's some interesting moments sprinkled throughout, some fun twists, a few moments that got me a bit to be startled or panicked, and on a whole I would say it was pretty alright. I think it's above the only other immediate indie comparisons I can give to this game, BlackSoul and Babysitter Bloodbath (some of the only retro-styled fixed camera angle indie horror games out there to this level). It's not just the most true to its roots, but the best executed of the three, in my opinion.
Which gets to a second element that many may not actually see coming about this game, I certainly didn't, which the game both hits the nail well on and doesn't. I'll spoiler tag this part, and would recommend if you plan to play the game and want to best experience it, not to read this, but I think it's important to mention.
.
The story is pretty interesting, but let-down by a rather abrupt ending.
Still, I enjoyed the game actually. It both lived up to what I wanted it to be, didn't live up to it, and surprised me in ways I wasn't expecting. It's not a flawless game, but I do think there will be appeal for the rabid horror enthusiast that are like myself. It's not the truly excellent and complete return to old-school horror I think some want it to be, but if you go in with a bit of an open mind, some appreciation for the older B-Tier horror game, and don't mind a 2-3 hour experience, you might find some things to like here. It could of been executed better in certain areas, but what's there is still a pretty nice game which I feel I'm warming up to more a few hours after completing it. Not everything I wanted from it, but a nice experience that did give me some things I wasn't aware I wanted.

Big survival horror (RE/SH) fan here. Game has a lot of fundamental issues such as enemy AI (easily killed because they are stuck). Setting up the controller is a challenge as the default settings don't appear to work for anything other than possibly the PS4 controller. If you are using an XB1 controller you can start the game with KB/M and then go into the OPTIONS while IN THE GAME. There you can move around your controller settings. I believe I had the layout of the steam contoller and the Dpad layout of the DS4 and it was working alright. Your notes/info section only holds the info for the last item you inspected (which will include a locked door) and you can't view older files found. Ended up writing down puzzles with pen and paper (by my counter, there were only 2-3 puzzles). Using weapons other than the wrench was difficult in the sense that the function buttons didnt work correctly. The gun would randomly shoot when I only used the aim button, and I had to keep hitting aim on/off to shoot additional shots. Unless there is a hidden ending, I clocked 1 1/2 hours to finish the game. Going to hit my save file to check another few portions of the game out as 2 achievements are still "hidden". Really let down so far with this game.

The rest of the negative reviews on this page really explain in far more detail than I'm willing to go into about why this game completely whiffs on what makes older survival horror games fun and interesting, but this game is basically an hour of kinda meandering build-up and an absolute blue-balling mess of an ending sequence with very little substance to its plot or atmosphere.
Nah.

I'll preface this review by saying that I love survival horror games. I've spent several thousands of hours playing and watching many games of the genre, including the Silent Hill, Resident Evil, Alone in the Dark and Fatal Frame series, so it goes without saying I have no problem with dated controls or graphics.
I was really excited for Back in 1995, and I wanted to like it. I was practically waiting down to the hour for it to be out on Steam. I already knew it was going to be a short game, as stated in the info on steam: "Approximate playtime is 2-3 hours".

First to put things straight, that approximation is VERY off. I completely finished everything the game had to offer in about 1.25 hours, this is INCLUDING a section that had no gameplay and was just a set of text commentary. I already expected the game to be short and wouldn't have had a problem with it were it not for my second problem with the game:
Substance. The game lacks any real substance in terms of plot, story devices or a conclusion. Most of the game is spent plodding along following instructions and tidbits of newspaper clippings and notes which establish a hint at some sort of extra layer to the story that is never quite fulfilled. The living characters are basically props, they offer nothing to the story and have no characterisation or personality. Even the unvoiced protagonist has barely anything to offer. It's a shame because after the
the game looked like it was going to take a turn for the interesting, before being cut short and ending the game (which by the way, is basically just developer commentary which while cool doesn't really make up for the lack of conclusion). This game really excels at getting your hopes up for some excitement, then letting you down abruptly.
In terms of audio, I was pretty underwhelmed. There was very little sound in the game, no change of footsteps whatsoever no matter what ground you walk on. The music was, well, I at least enjoyed the opening track? A lot of the music I found to be honestly kinda jarring and not in a good way. Usually a focal point of survival horror games is the use of sound design in order to create tension, fear and a foreboding sense of danger, whereas in this game it was mostly just some noise in the background, bar a few encounters with enemies that triggered music.
So how about as an actual game. Well, the enemies are laughably easy, there was perhaps ONE enemy out of I believe the four that exist in the game that was even slightly threatening, and even then I had no issue taking it down. The game throws ammunition at you, as well as health items (painkillers). I should note here that I used painkillers
in the entire game, when I intentionally allowed an enemy to hurt me to see if they even could attack or were non-hostile. For the rest of the game I stacked up probably around 15 or 16 bottles of painkillers that went unused because I never was even touched by an enemy. This is another key focus in survival horror games, you're supposed to fear enemies, you're supposed to have a need to conserve ammo, fighting is supposed to be difficult and risky, not a cakewalk with no chance of dying. I feel like the game completely misses the point in this aspect. The other side of gameplay is made up by some "puzzles" that either flat out tell you the solution to them by examining notes, or involve just process of elimination. Figuring out how to progress for most of the game was simply a matter of walking around examining everything until you get the solution handed to you on a platter.
I don't really want to comment on the graphics too much because one of the big appeals of this game was the graphic style, the outdated low detail polygonal models and areas. I actually liked this idea, I'm a big fan of lo-fi visuals and I think in horror games it can sometimes contribute to the experience to have limited graphics. What I will say is some of the graphics start to contort and stretch in strange ways some times which honestly looks horrid, I'm not even sure if this is intentional or not but it reminded me more of a weird emulator glitch rather than something on actual hardware of 1995.
So in conclusion, while I see that the creator of this game wanted to make a homage to some of the classics of this era of gaming, I honestly think all they made was a mere collection of references to an era. The style was great, and as I stated before I really, really wanted to like it but it just simply offered very little as a gaming experience. If the aim was to make a small game that reminded people of the games they played in 1995, I feel like it fell flat. It missed the key things that made these games great: atmosphere, plot (good or bad), fear, and most importantly CLIMAX. All of those games had excitement, and genuine endings, conclusions to the gameplay. Back in 1995 offers only a trudging path of ambiguity and build-up. I don't usually judge games on playtime vs price, but more they experience they give, and I don't feel like this game had much to offer for the price to play it.
Short version: Neat idea & style, executed poorly. Not worth the price it's set at.

The name of the game is Back In 1995, however I remember playing Alone in the Dark in 1993 and that didnt even look this bad.
"Back in 1995" promised to be a throwback to PS1-era survival horror.  The very first (and extremely major) gripe I had from the get go was the CRT filter.  It has three filter options, CRT static, CRT standard and no CRT filter.  The static filter option made my head hurt immediately, and the game is unbearably ugly without the filter altogether, so I went with normal CRT filter.
Now, I managed to play it for about a half hour before even the normal CRT filter made my eyes hurt, but by then, just about every other aspect of the game turned me off.
It has old-style tank movement, which is fine, however the camera was awful.  The monsters I encountered just looked like random pixel blobs and weren't menacing at all.  Extremely easy to kill.
The background noise is nails-on-a-chalkboard awful, and model animations are rough even for the era they were trying to capture.  I found that walking backward is actually faster than walking forward, after finding out there is no run option, just "relaxed stroll" speed.
The first couple of objectives were "go here and find this for me and bring it back" type stuff.  Truthfully, there was very little creepiness to it all.  It has all the other survival horror tropes, like unclear story and random notes to read and such.
If I were to find a positive, it would be the menu UI is simplistic and functional.  That's really all I got.
Quite honestly, the effort was just too little for me.  I expected early PS1 era, and I got something that looks visually bad even by Sega Saturn standards.
I really wanted to like this, and I'm sure it will find its audience, but just about every aspect of the game rubbed me the wrong way.

This was an instant buy for me when I saw it being advertised before one of the Grand Prix's last year, and I have not been disappointed.
It's awesome to finally have a management game in a sport I enjoy watching and sim-ing, and Motorsport Manager certainly held me for a long time. In fact, with mods, it still does.
The environments are beautiful, the updated car models are chunkier and more substantial, so those livery changes finally show up as more than the simple two-tone designs we had at release. Playing the staff and driver market is fun, and working your way up the field is rewarding. For the casual gamer who enjoys motorsport, this game is an absolute must have. If you don't do racing, but enjoy management sims, you'll likely enjoy this too.
A couple of big negative points though, which I feel are more a me thing than a game issue:-
As a power gamer, I found after about 50 hours or so, everything got seriously easy. The AI are, unfortunately, too dim to challenge a player who knows what they are doing, and they struggle to keep up with your pace of car development whenever you hit a stat reset. The same goes for qualifying in a session that has a wet and dry period, where the AI don't look ahead in the weather reports, and then set their quali times in the dry on Inters.
The second thing is there are too many ways for a player to abuse a system for their gain - notably the Risk system on car develpment, which makes the game even easier (I didn't even use this method and still found a lack of difficulty).
However, with the game being so easy to mod for beginners (simple editing of databases), and the ability for more advanced users to modify the actual code of the game, difficulty and overhaul mods have been made which can keep even power gamers like myself challenged and engaged. A huge boon to modding is that mods can be grabbed both with or without Workshop, and can be mixed and matched as you see fit.
Without mods - I would only recommend this to casual gamers, regardless of whether you are a motorsport fan or not. If you play an hour here or there and want your progress to not be too slow, then it's a good title for you.
With mods - There is now something for everyone, and if you like your games challenging and you want to be in it for the long haul, you can opt for that experience while still enjoying the visually beautiful game that PlaySport have brought us.

Japanese developer surprisingly make a good shooter game. The gameplay itself isn't that special, but it plays well as a cover-based third person shooter. The game has an interesting mechanic where headshots can make the enemies turn against themselves, and it can be utilized for tactical advantages.
The story of the game sets on a cyberpunk-esque Japan in the near future, where robots permeate our human life. Among the robots, there are some which looked like exacty like humans. The story goes on to touch on an interesting question: what does it make to be human? Does a very smart AI, programmed since its inception to perceive itself as a human, has lived a human life? As a third person shooter, the game doesn't delve too deep with such philosophical question. It acts more lika Hollywood action film with comedic quips. However the dilemmatic answer to the question is presented rather grippingly, sometimes unsettling, through the decisions made and words spoken by the characters.
As for the characters, the characterization starts out with typical stereotypes: loud Americans, swearing British, exquisite French; but it came through and fun. The characters remain memorable, even for minor characters. The game employs a "Trust system", where you can build the trust of your teammates through conversations (you can use voice-chat; I didn't because my spelling sucks) and actions (e.g. doing melee/headshot kills gain trust, friendly fires lose trust). This helps giving the characters a life. The more you interact with them the more you feel attached with them. The system also affects the ending which determines each character's fate.
The noticeable downside of this game is sometimes it has cheesy dialogues and unnecessary, obvious narratives. The romance that developed with one character also seems to happened rather out of nowhere (seems to be justified from the main character's playboy-ish attitude), though it progressed fine when it happened.
Gameplay-wise, some of the bossess are terrible bullet sponge so that it can be tiring to fight (like the giant motorbike and the gorilla). And although the game offer tactical options to control your teammmates I rarely find the situation where I have to take command over my squad, since the AI seems to be smart enough and strong enough to go by their way.
Overall, Binary Domain still has an interesting story and solid gameplay. It's nice game to play and I recommend it.

So I've spent several hundred hours (except that it doesn't show up since I made the mistake of installing the game via Arc at first which wasn't my brightest idea) and a sizeable amount of money on this game and after all of that I can kind of recommend it. Kind of.
As with many things, it depends what you're looking for in a game, so I thought I'd give you an idea what you can expect.
1. Graphics
Not entirely state-of-the-art, but not too bad for a MMO. It looks nice. Lots of nebulae in space, some seriously pretty alien worlds, you get the idea. Earth Space Dock is pretty, too, but unfortunately I'm not too fond of Starfleet ships.
The way some cutscenes are animated are just plain awful, though. Not entirely sure if it gets better with later content or if I just stopped noticing at some point.
2. Controls
There's so many buttons you have to press that you will feel like this game was created for octopodes at one point or another.
The good thing: you can bind anything to everything. There are even sneaky (but completely rule-compliant) ways to bind several things to one key, at the cost of flexibility.
Long story short: Depending on your playstyle, it may not be an easy game to play, but that's one of the fun parts. Patience + training + experimenting = progress, and progress is a pretty fulfilling thing.
3. Technical Stuffs
"Server Not Responding (insert huge number here)" might well be the inofficial motto of STO, at least on some days.
Cryptic does not seem too fond of bug fixes and stability improvements and some mission bugs are pretty damn game-breaking. Like spawning players outside a permanently locked door upon death, five meters away from the mission goal. Gee, thanks, Cryptic.
It's annoying, but I've rarely lost my cool because of that. If the occasional bug and/or server hiccup is your pet peeve however, STO is probably not the game for you.
4. Content, Yay!
4.1 Is STO P2W or not?
Depends on what you plan to win. All regular game content can easily be played without spending a dime.
PvE can be done, too - paywall'd content consists primarily of ships, while most gear is merely grind-y. If you're not planning to climb your way to the top of the DPS ranking, you'll be fine if you take some time to learn.
PvP is definitely P2W as far as I know, but playing PvP isn't exactly mandatory - I personally prefer PvE anyway.
The big drawback concerning paid content is that it is ridiculously expensive. 'Micro'-transaction my butt. We're talking at the very least 25$ for one measly (but admittedly account-wide unlocked) endgame ship.
One the plus side, they are incredibly cool. You don't technically need to throw all your money at PWE, but you might very well find yourself wanting to.
Useful but boring paid stuff like more bank slots and stuff isn't quite as expensive, but still far from cheap. It's the one reason why I only kiiiiind of recommend this game, to be honest.
4.2 Outfits, Customization and stuff.
Do you like half-naked alien space babes? Do you like half-naked alien space dudes? Do you like completely dressed alien space babes? All of the above?
Congratulations, this is the game for you.
There's a huge amount of customization in this game - think "Skyrim", except with very slightly less ugly hair and WAY more body sliders - and you can play with it to your heart's content, since your outfits don't influence your armor rating. And while there is some skimpy stuff in STO, it's not the default, which is nice.
You can change up your ships, too, but there's a lot of paid content involved in that - still, you can always change hull materials and, most amazingly, there's patterns that come in a plethora of colors. Some players do really neat stuff with that.
4.3 Writing
It's not always absolutely top notch, but it does have its moments and it never get's *too* bad - there are just some story missions that I will probably not replay for the writing. For the loot - maybe.
There's also some lazy writing - or maybe coding (or both) - faction-wise: Every KDF characters will continuously spam tlhIngan Hol and talk of honor. In one mission my KDF-aligned Romulan captain got called "Starfleet" thrice.
4.4 Trekkiness
You can visit several classic Trek locations, like DS9 for example - or Vulcan. Now featuring a statue of Spock, even.
In general, while you can fly the original USS Enterprise (for about 5$, that is), the game is a lot more kind to fans of DS9 or Voyager, for timeline reasons - although Scotty and Bones do get cameos in one of the story missions.
With the advent of the Delta Quadrant content, they started hiring some of the ST:VOY actors to reprise their characters, which led to some very nice moments for fans of that show.
One the other side, if you're looking for diplomacy not involving gunboats, this game is probably not the right choice for you. No matter what you do, at the end of the day your captain will have a higher body count than Captain Janeway, as the community likes to quip.
Apart from the 'shooting everything' issue, some people didn't particularly like the toned-down jerkiness of the playable Romulans.
4.5 Community
Very prone to drama and some parts of it are devoid of any sense of humor (please note: SOME parts!), but as long as you know when to keep your flap shut, you're unlikely to get into much trouble - at least judging from my personal experience.
4.6 Conclusion
You know what, I'll just give you some tips instead and let you draw your own conclusions:
-If this game sounds like you might enjoy it, give it a try - it's free.
-If you do want to try it, be warned: It takes a while to dl.
-Don't get too attached to your first character; from my experience it's best to just rush in and do the game first and then work on a proper build and such on your second character, once you have learned the ropes. If you don't mind playing a bit of a mess: Go ahead.
-Don't know what faction to choose? Look up a list of all available ships for each faction.
-Still no idea? If you play a Romulan, you get to choose your allegiance at level 10, so that's a good place to start
-Have fun.

The 1994 gem, Raptor: Call of the Shadows, is a great game! It's classic, vertically-scrolling shoot-em-up fun with a cool arsenal of weapons. It's not particularly difficult, but knowing which weapons to use at what points to rack up maximum damage makes for some fun strategy. And the music was great, too! Still gets me pumped!
This 2015 update of an old gaming staple, though, is lazy and improves absolutely nothing about the game.
Graphically, the game is unchanged. The game is still locked to a low FPS rate, and though the resolution is configurable via the game launcher, there is no option for 1920x1080. There IS an option for a "smoothing filter" though this does nothing more than muddy the whole appearance of the game.
This version also still rocks the classic, midi tunes that made my young boy heart thump in anticipation of my airborne battles. However, the tracks don't loop seamlessly as I recall them doing in the original iteration. There seems to be a brief pause of silence at the end of a track before it picks up again from the beginning and it's quite annoying.
Onto gameplay. At its core, this version of Raptor is excatly as the original. Controller support has been implimented, but it's sub-par. I still have to grab hold of the mouse on menus to know what I'm doing. On that note, though, when I do use the mouse, the on screen cursor will hit these mysterious vertical and/or horizontal "boundaries" past which cannot navigated without first giving the mouse shaking about the mouse pad. This I can't explain, but I've not had any similar issue with any other application on my PC.
Lastly, what has proven to be MOST troublesome about this half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥release is the completely unintuitive management of save profiles. I'm a gamer who saves often, and it wasn't long before I discovered that every time you save in this game, it does NOT overwrite the previous save, but instead creates ANOTHER save affiliated with the same name. Additionally, there's a very limited number of available save states, so if you forget to go back and delete previous saves from the main menu, you could came back to the hangar after having completed a mission only to discover that you CAN'T save your progress, and you can't delete previous saves without navigating back to the main menu, meaning that all progress from the previous save is inherently lost.
It's the sort of thing that makes you wonder if the developers every bothered to play their port before releasing it to the public.
I would NOT recommend this port to any person wishing to experience Raptor: Call of the Shadows. I would instead tell them install DOSBox and run the original version- it's actually a bit better.

In my restless dreams, I see that game.
Silent Hill.
You promised you'd take me there again someday, Konami, you mother♥♥♥♥ingshitkicking♥♥♥♥♥sonsof♥♥♥♥♥es.
But you never did.
Well I'm alone there now...
In our 'special place'...
Waiting for someone to capture that spirit while actually doing something original.
Unfortunately, in spite of a commendable effort, Back in 1995 will not scratch that itch in a meaningful way.
The entire goal of this game is to milk them elusive “nostalgia feels,” and it does that to a shallow point; it manages to get the good, the bad, and the ugly aspects of classic survival horror. You are Kent, a dude just trying to get his daughter back? Or maybe get to a tower in the distance? It isn't clear. But after a near blow for blow Silent Hill 2 monologue you're thrust into the “action,” as it were.
If you've played any classic survivals it nails the look (something between Silent Hill and Alone in the Dark). Heck, if you haven't just check it out on Youtube, then come back.
So it nails that to a tee, right? The aesthetic, anyway. But it lacks the twisted soul. The first few enemies you encounter are like sadder, slower cousins of the fat dragon statues in the original Dark Souls (sans fire breath), and you can kill them with little effort – every strike interrupts their attack. As a matter of fact, with the exception of one behemoth beastie every critter (I counted three, maybe four?) is pretty easy to kill and not in the least intimidating. There are save points at every potential encounter, bullets everywhere, and an obscene amount of healing items... and far as I can tell no enemies ever respawned.
The sound design, where a game like this (SILENT HILL) should shine, falls super flat. Prepare your ears for the same footfalls for two to three hours, regardless of whether you're stepping on marble or rug or steel. It got to be very grating (nearly as grating as my single speed – SUNDAY STROLL).
Between the awkward fixed camera angles and white noise/scan lines I was nursing a mild headache by the end of my playthrough... that's what Back in 1995 is trying to emulate, yes (the look, not the headaches probably), but searching for a key in a cramped office space for thirty minutes when every turn results in a sudden camera change was pretty jarring.
“So they've screwed the pooch with story, horror, atmosphere... what about the puzzles? Silent Hill in particular is known for its (sometimes divisive) puzzles. Does Back in 1995 have any?” If by puzzle you mean searching through notes for a number combination then you are in luck! That is the extent of it.
I appreciate what the folks at Throw the warped code out were trying to do here, but it isn't enough to make a handful of flesh colored turd monsters wandering around a boring, lifeless environment compelling or spooky or good. I didn't care about my player character, I didn't care about getting to the tower or finding my daughter, because I was given no reason to care. I encountered three characters, each one less interesting than the next... I just don't know. Then the story just fizzles out in the lamest way and it's over in just under two hours (that includes 20, 30 minutes of looking for a key or number combination).
It wasn't good. It wallowed in the past and fell victim to the same pitfalls (and then some!) of classic survival horror without applying over 20 years of gaming knowledge and wisdom garnered since then. Back in 1995 feels like a half finished student product: bare bones with some potential, and too referential to have a distinct voice.
