A very enjoyable and addictive game.
I've just come from putting my first 9 hours on the game, so far I'm pretty seriously hooked but here are the pros and cons.
Pros:
Lots of fun and plenty of settings/strategies to mess with.
Several different motorsports (though I've only played the 'f1' series).
Really nice graphics and optimisation in 3d view.
If you're an f1 fan you'll find lots of little references to different characters and personality traits like the ice-man perk or the ex driver with a mighty moustache.
A nice economy model; the parts feel ridiculously expensive, as do the 35,000,000 upgrades for your factory but spending the cash helps make you more (even if my boss is always warning me about cutting it too fine).
Now the cons:
Some rules and strategies that exist in F1 aren't part of the game, having to start on the tyres from Q2, for example, which caught me out terribly after I managed to get my driver into P4 on the hardest compound only to find you could pick at the race start.
Tyre degredation doesn't seem to affect handling, wrong tyre choice also doesn't punish you in any way other than pace, I actually took a race win by switching from inters to softs 3 laps before the track dried up, not seen a crash or spin yet as a result.
The interface can be a little overwhelming at first though the tutorial helps a lot.
Ultimately I think this game is excellent, the cons aren't really cons but just niggles to an avid F1 fan, then again, the absence of some of the super realism does improve the playability of the concept and fits with what the game is aiming for.
If you can get it for sub £25 I think you'll be more than happy, even if you are a through-and-through F1 fan.

Easy to pick up, hard to put down... prepare to lose countless hours of your life!
Just like Football Manager, Motorsport Manager allows you to take full control. Pick a race tier, choose the team or create your own from scratch, the choice is yours.
There is much to consider, hiring staff, building factories, developing car components... the list is extensive, my advice? Build and improve every car component, and in this order: Brakes, Suspension, Gearbox, Engine. Aim for 75% reliability, get your race mechanics on the job!
It is imperative to scout for talented designers, race mechanics and drivers. Hiring the best you can afford will improve your parts and pit stops per race ten fold.
TOP TIP: Towards the middle of the season begin development of risky components. These parts will carry forward into the next season with the risk element being removed. Rinse and repeat this process!
From F1 to virtual... the game features all the drama and politics of the sport. From voting on regulations to signing sponsors and dealing with the press, but the true test begins on the track. Watch a battle unfold in a 47 lap race in 3D, or 2D for less powerful computers. Come rain or shine, each race will challenge you, pause and think ahead... race strategy is crucial!
This is just a brief taste of what to expect... I've logged over 50 hours to date and thankfully no issues to report, smooth as butter. Always save regularly as a precautionary.
Overall no other sim compares, but patience is required. Fans of F1/GT will enjoy this experience. Build the team, master the tech, win the race!

The simple graphics and puzzles fit far better then than to the distorted real world, where your main worry is jumpscares. Once you get desensitized to the jumpscare after jumpscare, you're left with average puzzles and limited game areas, which are cut off by a distracting red fence. The stages vary from peaceful roaming to crap-your-pants panic runs. The 2D animated cut scenes were so drastically different from the rest of the game, it almost gave my brain whiplash.
Was it worth the four euros I bought it for? Yes. Am I glad I played it through? Yes. Will I play it again? No.

This game has a great, but sad, story to tell.  I like how it unfolds as little clips of memory.
The puzzles are good and worth the time and effort.  Some are really simple.  Some are a little trickier, but not quite hard enough to flip a table over them.  It was an enjoyable balance.
Depending on how jumpy you are, Master Reboot might make you want to play with the lights on.  It uses lighting and shadows to great effect.  You're never quite sure if something dangerous is just around that corner, and it happens infrequently enough to surprise you each time.
There are some flaws in the execution of the game.  Sometimes the 3D graphics feel a little dated, but I wasn't sure if that was intended or not given the game's setting and story-telling method.
Over all, this is definitely worth it.  I hope the developer produces more games in the future.

Has the idea of saving an immersive social network with the ability to keep deceased loved ones alive ever appealed to you? Then this might just be the game for you.
First off this game took me by surprise. Although not as polished as a triple-A title it has a unique charm about it that draws you in and keeps you interested. The whole story behind this game is very intriguing and reminds me of very few other titles. And although the storyline was thin it was highly engrossing and kept me hooked right until the end. I just wanted to know more and find out everything I could about the world around me and the people in it.
The level designs are tremendous; they have a charm about them that is just so unique and imaginative. Every single one of them offers something different to all the others, I loved just looking at everything around me and taking it all in each time. The characters are pretty interesting and every titbit of information I gleamed helped me feel immersed in these people’s lives and how you ended up lost in this world. The art style is great, very colourful, striking and a word I keep using unique.
The gameplay is good too, a first person exploration game across a huge variety of stages, each with its own goals and objectives completely different to all those before. The puzzles are not the most difficult but offer enough satisfaction when you manage to figure them out. The enemy in this game takes on the form of a malevolent all powerful AI, as they often do, who will stop at nothing to destroy you. When she chases you it can be a little tense that’s for sure.
The price tag is little high on this one but if you see it on sale it is well worth a play through. It may take a short time to really get into but once it’s sunk its teeth in there is no letting go.
Have fun ^_^

Similar to DOS version except for some VERY IMPORTANT differences!
- Pressing F10 to refil your shields & give you a Deathray has been removed
- Saving your game creates a new save file so you'll end up with multiple copies of your current profile. Saved each level? good luck finding the recent one!
- Mouse speed is dependant on your Windows Cursor speed. Sometimes it's higher. Sometimes it doesn't reach all the menu items; fixed by moving into opposite screen edge for a bit.
Other than those 3, the new stuffs are minor.
- Explosions have more particles, like fireworks.
- Music may be very slightly different but sounds exactly the same. They are .wav files instead of the built-in midi, so you can replace them with some actual remastered ones from Youtube.
- You can choose between 640 x 400 or 960 x 600 resolutions. Again, both look identical. Don't load Fullscreen through the Loader else the game may look stretched. Load it Windowed, then press Alt+Enter.
- Includes a High-Quality filter, which essentially blurs everything.
While Raptor is an excellent game, this 'Enhanced' version doesn't need DOSbox, that's really it, so don't buy it if you can find the DOS version. Maybe pick it up though so you can proudly say that you've bought it.

It's important to understand that Raptor is a 20 year old game-- not a modern pixel-hipster homage. As such, it has issues that a lot of DOS-era games had; most notably, the framerate is just always going to be low, no matter how awesome your computer is. That's how the original was, and that's how it is now.
DotEmu has added a High Quality filter which improves the framerate (to 25~30 fps), but it muddies up the graphics, which were way ahead of their time in 1994.
The game itself is a moderately deep top-down shooter; earn money, buy upgrades between missions, move to the next level once your aircraft is suffuciently armed and armored. The upgrade mechanics are still satisfying, even after all this time.

As of right now, I have 883 hours in and still enjoy this game.  I'm writing this review because there is a lot of hate towards the devs, and sometimes they annoy me, but you have to be realistic when it comes to an MMO.  Lets start here, about the MMO thing.  This is basically a single player game, no it totally is unless you want to do PvP.  So you dont have to rely on anyone, although its a good idea to join a fleet because of the bonuses.  Next is the free to play part, going into this game I was very hesitant because any other F2P game is a money grab it seems.  You can get to endgame by spending $0 and you dont have to grind grind grind grind to get there.  I spent $5 before endgame to increase my in game money cap so I could get better ships, you really dont have to do that though.  That said, I have enjoyed the game so much I felt guilty only spending $5 and have a little more since, and will continue to buy small things here and there.  Spending cash on ships is a lot yes, but look at it like this, if you spend $5 for the money cap, and $30 for a ship, you spent $35 for an amazing game.  Going back to the fleet bonuses, if you save the other kind of money in the game (no cash needed theres 2 systems of money - real and energy credits) you can buy a fleet ship and get a $30 ship for free.  Playing the market with the fake money is fun for me, so I easily obtained great ships for free.  Now to the part about the devs, people complain they dont listen and are greedy.  I assure you they do listen, they shouldnt add all this content everyone wants at once because I would have gotten bored a long time ago.  They release things slowly but surely, and that keeps in interesting.  The devs are also not greedy, this game is a full time job for them and in order to keep it going they have to make money, thats just how it is and thats fair.  Thats why I feel guilty having spent not much on it and will keep buying things.  There are some problems I will report about the game, such as the server.  It seems to getting better but can be annoying when its down, lately its been really good.  We'll see after the new season when the game starts getting heavy traffic again.  Also, the ground combat is kind of meh, I mean its ok, just dont expect Call of Duty.  ANyway, I recommend, get it and enjoy.

This isn't really one cohesive game, but a series of mini-games, so I'll just review each one seperately:
No fun at all, but it's designed as a tutorial to introduce you to the creature-creation and DNA mechanics; swim towards stuff in 2D to get points once your creature auto-eats it - other creatures for 'bad'/'carnivore' points, plants for 'good'/'herbivore' points; a mixture for 'neutral'/'omnivore' points.
Like the cellular stage, but 3D, and to get the 'good' points, you have to sing, dance and pose your way into getting other creatures to like you.  Creature customisation gets real here and you spend most of your time wandering around picking up skeletons to unlock new parts.  This is the most boring stage IMHO due to it's repetition.
Exactly like the creature stage apart from instead of unlocking new parts, you unlock buildings to give you weapons to kill, or instruments to win over other tribes; it's only less boring than the creature stage because it passes much more quickly.
The overall point of this stage is the same as the tribal stage, but you also get to design vehicles (land / sea / air) and buildings - as the modelling is the most fun part of the whole game, this is real fun.  You have a -little- bit of resource management as when you're putting the buildings in your city, there's an optimal pattern. It also introduces the 'diplomacy' mechanic which is basically 'get people to like you by giving them money, and then ask them to give you everything they own'.  This bit goes by in a flash, but that's good because the most fun part is...
This is basically where you apply everything at once - you build spaceships, buildings, vehicles, and even new creatures (once you get the 'creature tweaker' tool for your spaceship).  You can basically take over the whole galaxy by terraforming each planet and putting down colonies...which is fun and satisfying for the first few times, but once you get your first million bucks everything becomes VERY easy and the game stops being fun to play.
It doesn't stop being addictive, however, because you still find yourself saying things like "If I make my main spaceship look like a star destroyer, can I try and befriend every other alien race who's ships are TIE-fighters so I can fly around with an Imperial fleet?" and you spend the next several hours exploring the galaxy finding / uplifting new races; or you set yourself the task of entirely wiping out the 'big bad' Grox...which I think is impossible, but still.
So yeah, I mean...it's a really great casual game, but if you're after any depth at all you will end up disappointed.  It is very cool flying around in an X-Wing though, and painting every planet white...and setting the ground units to imperial walkers and the air-units to Snow Speeders so you can re-enact the battle of Hoth...

Player gets ambushed by a ghost from a closet three times, and all those three times - same fighting animation of same models in same position (yes, 'position', not 'positions'). Sound sample library is quite small, you can hear recurring sound patterns. Despite all those bad things I said about art, game

The strongest aspect of
is
(and, for that, I am ready to forgive all its drawbacks). What starts looking like simple cyberpunk narrative about people losing their personalities in a world of soulless demonic machines, slowly and subtly turns into story about people, whose struggle, hard work and love changed world, and reminds us about simple but important thing - machines can never change who we really are, only we can. It reminds us that tools we create can make our lives easier and happier, but they cannot make us kind, selfless, diligent and rational, as they cannot cure envy, malice or infantility.
It reminds us that greatest threat for any human being is another human being, and that no machine should be feared more.

Space combat is great. Feels like Star Trek space combat should feel. I've never gotten tired of it. Tons of customization of ship abilities via the Bridge Officer system, and any character can fly any ship (as long as you have the currency to buy the ship you want), so you can switch it up if you get bored flying a big slow ship and fly something small and fast (or vice versa). The only problem I have is that flying Escorts (small/fast) seems to be noticably more efficient than flying Cruisers (big/slow). Escorts pump out so much damage so quickly that I finish missions much faster. Cruisers are much more durable, but they kill things so slowly that I get a bit frustrated sometimes. Maybe I'm just doing something wrong, but flying Escorts seems like the way to go most of the time.
Ground combat is awful. Overly simple, buggy, just poorly designed. I've never liked it and it hasn't gotten much better since the game's closed beta that I participated in. Your Away Team AI is inept, regularly not following my commands or falling through the world or getting stuck on objects/terrain. They never get out of the way of AoE effects in a timely manner and regularly die due to their own incompetence. I rush through ground missions so I can get back to the fun space combat.
The story is pretty good. Plenty of cameos by Star Trek actors doing voiceovers. Missions are treated somewhat like episodes from the TV shows, with title cards and cinematic warp-in entrances, and that helps the universe feel a bit more Trek-like. Missions are usually part of an over-arcing story that takes many missions to complete. This is much better than other MMOs and their standard 'Kill X Bears' for no particularly interesting reason. STO is galactic warfare between large empires and (sometimes) diplomacy.
Endgame isn't very good, and never has been, imo. Too much repeating of the same content over and over again to get badges to turn in for reputation points to unlock the next tier which requires even more badge turn-ins than the last tier. It could be worse, but it wore me down pretty quickly and I take long breaks from this game pretty often because I burn out on this repetitive content. It's probably much easier to put up with if you have a few friends to play with, as you won't have to deal with the randomness of queueing for a group through the game's group finder.
If you're a Trek fan, you should play this game. It's free, after all, and the cash shop isn't that bad. Yes, many of the game's best ships are behind paywalls, but you can earn the cash shop currency in-game without ever spending a cent. That's what I do, and while it's slow, it's much better than shelling out $25 for a ship I'm not even sure if I'll like.

Over 200 hours played and I still can't find the words to properly describe how awesome this game is.
If you're into strategy/management sims then you'll like this game.
If you're into motor racing then you'll like this game.
If you're into both, like I am - then you'll absolutely love this game.
This game is just a pure out and out extremely detailed, multi-faceted, challenging and realistic motor racing management sim. Period.
Struggling to think of any negatives, because, really, I can't, but the only slight snags are:
1.) Real life teams, drivers and sponsors are not licensed, but this is not a big issue as you can quickly download MODS which provide all three very easily.
2.) Long-term, the game does become repetitive and once you reach the top echelons it's very easy.
Again, this isn't really a big issue, as you can always start over again, or quit your team and join a new one.
If you're still bored, there are challenges to complete and obviously plenty of pretty challenging achievements to unlock.
3.) The AI is pretty dumb on race day/quali at adapting to different weather conditions.
I personally don't find this a big issue as if you are starting out with an uncompetitive team, you can exploit this to your advantage for some sneaky points.
Besides, if you wanted to, you could always edit the game config to change the AI difficulty.
Overall, this gets a 10/10.  Best game I've played all year.

I've been playing about a week and a half, and can't stop.  This is a nicely designed game.  It has a few quirks, mostly to do with the company's servers having glitches, and going offline.  However, the game itself, is stellar.  The space combat is better than Eve, because you don't just set an orbit, and then wait.  You're forced to utilize tactics, both on the ground, and in space.  There are some camera, auto-attack, and other settings which can be tweaked, and I recommend using them to set the game up how you like to play, because there can be some annoyances.  However, the game is incredibly deep, and includes so many different side things that you can be doing while you battle.  The different officers, skills, and abilities offer an immense level of customization.  The graphics and sound effects are amazing.  There are some truely epics places, and moments.  Because combat requires aiming, and dodging, even in space, it rarely gets repetitive.  There's a vast solar system to explore, and always plenty of things which need doing.  Once you get to level 50, and can start answering distress calls, it sometimes feels like there's too many people to save, and not enough time for all of it, and which is a good thing.  There are plenty of places where you can go and show off your customized appearance.  So far, I haven't seen any two players who look alike.  There are fleets, which can be factioned into armadas, and which can be factioned into alliances.  Or, you can just create a small, temporary team.  The storyline missions are all soloable.  So, you can get however as social, or antisocial, as you'd like.  Friendly to both casual, and hardcore alike.  You don't need to be a trekkie to enjoy it.  It's actually just a bonus to those who are.  To those who aren't, it's just a good MMO.
All that said, the server issues are a thing to consider.  I truely wish they could fix that.  It can be annoying to get disconnected from the server in the midst of an epic battle.  Although, it's just a game.  So, long as you don't take it too seriously, it doesn't have to be that much of a bother.
It's F2P, but there are certain items which do require real money.  There's no pay wall, because you don't really need any of those items to be able to play, and enjoy the game.  However, there comes a point where they stop giving you free stuff, and you have to either grind for months, or pay to get it.  Fortunately, it's not necessary, because you can always fly your beat up old freebie hulk, and still find plenty of fun things to do.
This game is more about storyline driven quests, than go fetch.  Although, I've found a few fetch quests which offer nice rewards, and are worth doing.  You never feel like you're stuck in one place, fighting the same monsters, for very long.  It's more of a gorilla-style, shoot and scoot, combat scenerio.  But, there's a few areas to farm, if that's your fancy.
There are player create, storyline driven quests to complete, some of which are very interesting, and well crafted.
Definitely give it a try.  It's one of the best MMOs I've ever played, before.  It's really easy to feel like you're a part of this universe, and that it's development depends on your contribution.  It engages with you, instead of forcing you to go and find missions. There are plenty to find, but the main ones come to you.  There's very little doubling back over empty territory to go and turn in a mission, most of the time.  In the places which do require that, it's just a short sprint, and you're back, again.  No long journeys.  No creep respawns to avoid.  You can even warp, or beam back, if you don't feel like walking.  There's plenty of loot drops.  You can sell most items on the exchange to other plyers.  You don't have to go find people.  You just list your items, and let them buy it.  But, you can also sell to NPCs.  I recommend doing that over using the recycler, because you get 50% from NPC merchants, as opposed to 40% from recycling.  There's very little need to buy anything, though, because you either earn it from completely a quest, or from a drop.
I haven't found much to complain about, other than the server bugs.  Well... And, the crafting system.  Which is practically worthless, unless you're willing to spend real money, or fly from system to system searching for a little scrap here, and a little scrap there.  Cost of materials on the exchange is ridiculous.  Just forget about it.  However, it's also the least important aspect of the game.  You can easily play this game without ever crafting a single thing, as many players do.
So, there's no reason to not give it a try, except for server bugs.

great CoOp FPS with focus on melee combat in a fantasy setting.
It's like
, but better, because you have hero classes, crafting, loot, unlockables and the enemy hordes are better balanced. The missions cover different and ellaborate environments (medieval style town streets, cemetary, dungeons, harbor side, forest, farm, cave tunnels etc.) and objectives include withstanding attacks, destroying objects, protecting locations and gathering supplies. You can play any mission on any difficulty, so this game is for players of any skill level. There's a decent chance to find other people to play with, but, if you don't, the bot team members are good enough on easy, too. The more you play, the more things you unlock (e.g., forge for crafting weapons, shrine for changing weapon traits or getting new weapons, a contract board, lore entries).
After finishing all 3 acts of the main game (which took me 7 hours), you can continue with the DLCs or just continue playing the same missions for better loot on the same or harder difficulty.
The enemies are the same all the time: (1) regular rats (skavenslaves, clanrats, sack rats) with melee attacks; (2) armored rats (stormvermins) with powerful melee attacks (harder to kill, require aiming for the head or armor penetrating/poisoned weapons); (3) assassins (gutter runners) (agile, try to attack you by surprise, knock down and slash you until someone saves you); (4) gas rats (poison wind globadiers) (use poison gas bombs, have larger healthbars); (5) ratling gunners (similar to gas rats, but have a devastating gattling guns instead of gas bombs); (6) pack masters (put a loop around your neck by surprise and try to take you away from the rest of your team to enslave you - but actually you just slowly expire, until someone saves you); (7) giant rats (ogre rats) (large, bulky and strong rats, which show up once in a while and are hard to kill, require team effort).
And that's what's this game is about: getting better at killing rats and acquiring better weapons + teamplay. It's fun and for 7 EUR (75% discount price of the standard edition) it's a fair deal. But, unfortunately, there's no complete or GOTY edition, so you have to buy the additional DLCs (Drachenfels, Karak Azgaraz, Stromdorf) separately and they are quite costly. Since, it's pretty much the same experience, just in a different setting, I don't think that the price is justified.
- For some reason this game requires 40 GB of space, although there's not that much content in it.
- Although, in general, the game looks beautiful, the objects and characters look more like something from 2012 than from 2016.
- Frame rate jumping, despite my 8 GB RAM, 4 GB AMD Radeon R9 380, SSD, and 4 GHz 8-core AMD FX-8350
Nevertheless, I enjoyed this game quite a bit.

This game is the father of classic shoot'em ups, a must-have for the lovers of the genre; I remember playing this when I was 10 years old and struggling to survive against the horde of battleships from the outer regions and their deadly lasers, man those were the days.
It perfectly holds up to today's standards, the graphics which were ahead of it's time are still more than decent, it has lots of weapons to buy along the way each of which are most effective against different type of enemies (missiles that can only hit ground targets and inflict great damage upon them), homing turrets that can quickly destroy enemies without having to get close to them (but in exchange they don't target ground enemies), and many more.
The soundtrack is varied, consisting of more than 10 tracks which play depending on the level of each sector you're on, and all of them convey that die-hard feeling; you're going to blow everything up and nothing can stop you.
As for the cons, I will say that even though this is a supposed "2015 edition" it isn't any different to the 2010 edition, or any different to the original game for that matter; I can even go as far as to say the original 94 game was even better since this port have a couple issues which I'll quickly list below:
- Save feature bug, when you save your pilot after each mission, it doesn't overwrite your previous save, instead creates another one, and with time you can't save anymore until you erase some of the files which becomes tedious soon.
- Mouse controls are weird, it's hard to dodge bullets and position when moving the Raptor feels like skating on ice for the first time; prepare your keyboard.
Overall the game still feels like the same classic game from the 90's and I would 100% recommend it for lovers of the genre or for the people who want to check shoot-em-ups for the first time alike.

It's an old 2D vertical scroller shooter style game. The best that ever was. You're a mercenary pilot, sent on missions to other worlds in order destroy your employer's competition. You take other pilots' planes away with bullets, missiles, and/or plasma fire, then you buy more ways of taking your bullets, missiles and/or plasma bolts and putting them into enemy craft, and then you take their planes away again.
I'm not really sure what it is that makes this game so special, but I've been coming back to it over and over again since the mid 90s.
It's got a very rudimentary character creation, several constantly active (when equipped) weapons and many more selectable ones that, fairly obviously, only fire when selected, and some really fun gameplay. There's definitely some nostalgia in there too.
Two slight annoyances:
1) The mouse is really sticky for some reason. It never used to be in this game, but now the pointer will refuse to move past an apparently random point from time to time, only passing it when you swing back and forward again, as if to take a run up and break through an invisible mouse-barrier. Odd.
2) The launcher lets you pick the resolution and run in full screen, but then sticks the image in the top right corner of the screen. I can't help but think there's not much point in having a full screen option if all you're doing is giving us black space.

Spore tends to get some mixed reviews, but between the yea and nae side, I'm definitely with the "yea"s.
Despite some rather nasty bugs I've seen reported (yet have never experienced myself across 3 different PC builds with 3 different versions of windows of the games era) and a few un-fulfilled promises about the amount and variety of gameplay Spore would have, it's still a wonderful game and fits into my collection quite nicely between SimLife, Civilization, and EscapeVelocity. I'm kinda dating myself a little with those references, but if you enjoyed those games or the genres they came from, then collectively you'll likely enjoy Spore
You start in a cellular / molecular stage which is...well...Sparkle2Evo..."thats all I got to say 'bout that."
Next, you're on land and as a walking, talking, biting creature have more of a "squad leader & servants" role to play in eating, killing, mating, and exploring your way through new body parts that offer bigger and better bonuses to gameplay.
Then you move to a rudimentary Age of Empires tribal stage where you manage a small flock of your spawn and interract with (and ultimately ravage if ya play like me and always go the hostile route over the cuddly, fuzzy, social route which IS offered I might mention) other tribes of creatures.
Then you hit the global "Civilization" stage where you're moving ground, air, and sea units to claim, control, and harvest resources while you devise the downfall or annexing of your neighboring nations.
And last but certainly far from least, the space stage. This part of the game could have (and in the past, regularly was, and with great success; see EV:Nova) been its own full-production game. Exploring space, planet-scaping newly discovered worlds for colonization, a (rather awkward and sometimes uncooperative) combat system with various upgrades and features all coat this area of the game with a thick layer of nerdy OCD. Here you meet other species, conduct trade routes, colonize planets, establish automated trade routes, improve your ship, explore further and further and with more and more efficiency and profit making more and more homeworlds as you go for your species until...well....honestly I haven't gotten past this part. I enjoy it too much and haven't wanted it to end any of the half a dozen or so times I've played to this point and coasted along in place for a while before setting it down only to start over again later to replay it all.
There have been many frustrations with this game for me, partly because I enjoyed it so much I didn't want anything to go wrong ever, most often it was due to a program crash that would hit me unexpectedly when I hadn't saved my game in a particularly productive couple of hours. But it was easily more a problem with my computers than it was the software itself.
But that being said...I know the integrity of the program has been in question multiple times so...for some notable ratings...actually I suppose I'll put them at the top.

It’s compelling. There are some quite good novel ideas I liked. The interface is well done, only in few contexts not enough info is available or shown. The game lifted a couple good things from Grand Prix Manager 2 (and a couple not as good ones) but… no sale. There are too many issues for me. A few examples follow.
Rules issues:
– Yellow flags are only cosmetic and not implemented (drivers can overtake in yellow flagged sectors without penalties).
– The Safety car rules were not implemented correctly. Positions are unfreezed too early: it’s possible to overtake as soon as the SC enters the pits, while in reallity overtakes are allowed only after the beginning of the following lap.
Realism issues:
– Slick tyres on a fully soaked track never lead to aquaplaning, the car is simply slower but I’ve never seen accidents increase. Think of Brazil 2003, Malaysia 2009 or Brazil 2016: drivers can get aquaplaning even on wets in reality, here not even running on a soaked track with slicks.
– The car’s setup is the same for wet and dry conditions, which is not relistic.
– It’s too easy to make money and find sponsors. Try telling McLaren, which has been without a main sponsor for a few years.
Gameplay issues:
– Achievments don’t always trigger correctly. For example: “start last and win” was never given to me, even though my drivers did it about 20 times. Other achievements were triggered incorrectly, like “win 3 in a row”, which was awarded to me with p1 p2+fl p1 p1 (so 3 wins in 4).
– The final standings report incorrectly drive-through penalties: most drivers who had a collision will be marked as having a drive-through penalty, even when none was given and they simply pit to repair broken components.
– 16 year-old drivers can get “just divorced”.
– Female drivers are often described as male, for example: “the man”; but the game makes use of the driver’s gender in other pieces of text, so it’s inconsistent.
– It’s possible to become a rival (in which case the driver refuses to renew as long as the rival is in the team) of an unemployed driver (definitely a bug since you can get the effect only on teammates).
– Teammates can be dating while both consider the other a rival and refuse to renew the contract as long as the other is in the team.
– The championship title can be attributed by journalists during interview even though it’s not mathematically certain (I think this bug is caused by neglecting to count bonus points).
– You’ll receive in-game e-mails with glaring factual mistakes like: “30 pts difference in the standings” when there are 10; or “18 pts differencein the standings” which actually are 56; or “4 races to go” when actually there are 5 left on the calendar).
– Occasional spelling mistakes (“occassionally”).
A couple suggestions: make intro videos and all other videos or the camera pan on the circuit skippable. Let players simulate the races; it’s enough to decide the pitstop strategy (with aggression and fuel usage in the stints in between) before the race. It should be possible to save setups or compare them with past races on the same circuit.

This game is great.
It's one-of-a-kind with its play style that combines suspense and tactics with a first person shooter. Well, I say 'shooter' - you'll probably spend more time rooting through cabinets and suitcases or clubbing people in the face than you will actually shooting.
If you've got this far, you'll probably understand the basic idea of the game; you have to hunt someone whilst being hunted. But it's not just that. You also have to stay out of jail, keep on top of money and look after yourself by going to the toilet, having a bite to eat or taking a nap every now and then, and all of this takes place in a maze of similar-looking corridoors filled with falling lifeboats and lunatics who want to kill you with a letter opener. If it weren't for the viewable map, the game would simply be filled with passengers constantly dying of thirt whilst searching for a bar at which you can buy some life-saving beer. And all of this is outside the main purpose, which is to stay on top of the leaderboard.
To do that, you've got to search for a weapon that'll give you a good amount of money for your kill, before hunting down and slaughtering your quarry within the time limit - whichever deck they happen to be on. Whilst all of that's happening, you're trying to work out which of the random people you bump into is going to brutally murder you, which will undoubtedly lead to you carefully backing away from, or pulling a gun on, any person who looks remotely suspicious, despite their totally innocent intentions (murdering somebody who isn't you).
tl;dr
I impaled a man with a set of knitting needles because he looked at my funny, and you will, too.

'Disorienting' is an excellent word to describe Master Reboot. It's kind of sci-fi and kind of horror with lots of walking around and a little puzzle solving. But the story comes from finding ducks. Yes, little blue squeaky ducks. Ducks give little bits of story details in each level. Nothing is particularly explicit in Master Reboot, except the animated cutscenes at the end of each level, with each level being someone's memory. Who that someone is, who you are, and who's trying to stop you is all part of the story you'll have to piece together from animated cutscenes and ducks.
But it still mostly works. The pacing is a bit off, but if you play the levels "in order" (there is no numbered order, but levels unlock in groups and you can play them in a sequential order) you'll probably get the story by the time you get to the end. It's short, less than 3 hours beginning to end, but interesting enough. It's clearly a student effort but it's neat and weird.
If you want to play a game where you're being stalked by a glowy eyed waifu monster in really pretty and extremely creepy places, this is for you.

Highly stylized puzzle / platformer game where you play through memories to uncover the story. The trailer makes the game seem like constant super-intense action, but it's actually really well paced, and feels more like exploration than anything.
The story really has to be pieced together through scraps of details to get the most out of it, which I'm not really good at while playing... so the details of the story didn't really influence my enjoyment of the game any, but the basics of the story really added to the experience of the memories I think, given how they tended to be unnerving in nature.
The art style in this game is really beautiful. Simple texture work and geometry, along with lots of bloom effects, shadows, and saturated lighting create really atmospheric dream-like levels. In some places the textures seem low-quality and ugly, but for the most part everything fits together better than most indie games manage to pull off. There are a bunch of cartoony vector art / cut-scenes which feel a bit out of place, but they're not bad. They remind me of Mirror's Edge's cut-scenes, and how they were a vastly different style from the actual game itself. There's also a lot of REALLY well done painted-style art, which was great to find.
The sound design is extremely well done in this game... lots of stereo sound effects that add to the creepiness of the memories. The music itself is really great, and adds tension in all the appropriate places, and doesn't stick out while playing. It's really easy to slip into the experience they were trying to provide in this game.
There really isn't a tutorial in this game... pretty much just action icons that appear when you can interact with something. You start off knowing absolutely nothing about your character or where you are.. so you wander around and discover things on your own. Even so, it's pretty straight forward, and you can't really do much other than progress forward, but it still feels more open than it actually is, which is pretty good.
The majority of the puzzles in this game offer absolutely no explanation, so you have to really be observant, or resort to trial and error methods to solve them. At the beginning of the game discovering the solutions to the obscure puzzles felt super rewarding but later on just felt frustrating because they were so obscure. The puzzles aren't particularly difficult, and you can often find the solution in a couple of minutes. There are many clues to how to solve the puzzles in the design themselves, just through the use of things like color-coding. Some puzzles do have blatant hints, and some puzzles are based purely on memory or being able to repeat a pattern. I only really had an issue with a couple puzzles, and had to resort to trial and error simply because they weren't clear enough... so even though I was still able to solve them, I didn't necessarily know WHY it was the answer.
The puzzles are really just a way to complete each memory sequence, to reveal the explanation of that memory. Within each memory there are things you can interact with in order to get more snippets of the story. Along the way there are occasional platforming scenarios, and even some time-based action sequences. I didn't really like the platforming, as I would tend to misstep and fall to my death constantly... but the action sequences were much better as they really added tension and creepiness to the game.
The game took me around 4-5 hours to complete, which includes trying to find as many hidden things as possible, and lots of restarts due to platforming fails. There are a few wonky bits in the game (where you just wonder why the hell it was included), but way more memorable bits to offset them. The game most reminds me of Among Sleep, but similarish games include The Path, Kairo, and Antichamber.
This might also be the first duck-based video-game I've ever seen...

This game takes place inside a virtual storage of memories, a place where you can relive parts of your or someone else's life, and even keep living after your physical body dies. Playing as a certain someone who may or may be not alive, you delve through corrupted memories of a group of friends who have shared triumph and tragedy. Putting pieces of past together, you find out what happened, what is broken and whether or not you can still fix it.
While graphics are substandart and puzzles are dull, the game is an immersive travel through a beautiful void of surreal landscapes and abandoned places. The story is simple, but well presented, and the overall experience is deeply touching. If you liked like Myst, Dear Esther and Gone Home, this less known game would certainly please you.

Master Reboot is a strange little game, but in a good sense. The art style is very pretty and well suited to the game, and although it's fairly basic geometry, it doesn't take anything away from the game. It in fact adds a lovely stylized look. The mechanics are very basic, but that also works very well for the game, as it's not overcomplicated and it allows more focus on the exploration and puzzle elements. The audio design is fantastic as well, adding a lot to the sometimes quite creepy atmosphere.
All in all, a fantastic little game, and definitely worth grabbing, especially while it's on sale!

Master Reboot is a mixture of exploration, puzzle solving and survival.  The basic premise of the game is that in the future, people can upload their dead relatives' memories to an interactive computer system, "the Cloud" where they can access them through a computer and share treasured moments etc. When things inevitably go wrong the creators of the Cloud send the game's Heroine to investigate.
Much about the setting can be learned along the way and if you pick up all the source information scattered around the game the truth about the Cloud and its conception in the "real world" becomes chillingly clear.
Puzzles are fairly simple for the most part, more than a distraction but by no means the defining feature of the game, as you also have to deal with occasionally quite terrifying manifestations of the Cloud/Memories all the while trying to make sense of what you find along the way.
Visually Master Reboot has a slightly Manga-esque vibe; the design has an atmospheric, dream-like quality that draws the player in, slowly at first but after about a half-hours worth of play I was totally hooked.  If I were forced to compare this to anything I would say it is like the written fiction of William Gibson and Philip K♥♥♥♥♥♥ but with a distictly Anime, Ghost in the Shell style visual aesthetic.
Overall Master Reboot is an excellent piece of interactive storytelling.  It is relatively short, so I wouldn't recommend paying full price for the game this long after release; however if it's on offer snap it up, it's well worth your time.

DON’T JUDGE THIS GAME BY ITS DEMO
Having played the Demo, I didn’t really expect much from Binary Domain, and only bought it on a whim years later when I moved over to PC.  Imagine my surprise then, when it turned out to be a really good game, which nonetheless managed to make a terrible first impression on myself and many other people.
To summarize, the Demo was very badly put together.  The first level of the Demo goes over well enough, even though your main gun feels a bit inaccurate and the giant robot, who I assumed was a boss (turns out he’s only a mini-boss at best), is fairly anticlimactic.  The second level, however, is what kills the demo.  While the first one is taken from chapter 2, fairly early on; the second is taken from chapter 4, about midway through the story, and is among the hardest fights in the entire game.  To exasperate things further, Binary Domain has an RPG mechanic where you can upgrade your (and your teammate’s) primary weapon, so it’s natural that your main gun starts out a bit weak and inaccurate.  While this isn’t a problem in the early level, when the demo drops you in the middle of the campaign with un-upgraded guns, things become controller-shatteringly frustrating.   Even the first few levels of the full game left a bad taste in my mouth, with the PC (Dan Marshall) and his partner (Big Bo) acting like obnoxious frat boys.  Chapter 1 comes to a close with a cut scene that is incredibly cringe-inducing, and doesn’t set hopes high for the game.  Luckily, the story gets better in chapter 2, and only continues to impress from then on.
Without wishing to give too much away, the narrative is well-done, with characters that are written and voiced with a fair degree of competency.  A lot of the action is a little over-the-top in an anime-esq. way, which I found fairly enjoyable, and what seems like a very straightforward plot, takes some unexpected twists and detours and manages to bring out our protagonist’s best traits.  As for the gameplay, it’s kind of like Gears of War, with a dose of Dead Space’s dismemberment system.  All of the enemies are robots, and most can be divested of limbs in useful ways.  Blow legs off to slow them down, shoot their gun-arms off, or score a headshot to make them fight amongst themselves.  The Giant Robot boss fights are also an absolute joy, even if one or two seem kind of spongy.  Dan’s assault rifle is actually pretty satisfying to use too, once you put a point or two in accuracy.  The rpg elements, as half-baked as they are, still manage to be enjoyable.
There are definitely flaws, but they’re manageable.  The game has a voice command system, which is very progressive in the fact that it doesn’t matter what your age, gender, or country of origin is, the game doesn’t understand what everyone is saying equally.  Thankfully, you can turn off this system and still issue all the voice commands that actually matter with a voice menu.  I’ve done several playthroughs with this and never felt like I was missing out.  It probably helps that it’s mostly useful for issuing specific commands to your squad (you can still issue general commands without it), but like every shooter with squad mechanics that isn’t Republic Commando, it’s probably better to not bother. Just focus on shooting the baddies yourself.   There is a ‘trust’ system too, which can be a little annoying as there are rewards for building trust (by talking to squad mates or doing well in combat with them in party) but it’s easy to lose trust to friendly fire (the AI does walk in front of you sometimes).  Lastly, the game is definitely better with a controller, because the binds for a keyboard are a bit awkward.
TL;DR Binary Domain is a very fun third person shooter with characters that I ended up liking, and a plot that genuinely surprised me.  Don’t be turned off by the awful demo, the game is definitely worth a buy.  (Not the map pack though, Multiplayer is dead).

The "I got more jump scares from my vacuum robot while writing this" long version:
Wow.  Layers of Fear: What a disappointment. I am so glad that it was one of those "free for 24 hours" games from Humble Bundle and that I didn't pay for this.
The soundtrack was nice, and atmospheric, something I can listen to again.  The game, however, was almost anything but.  For some reason, I was reminded of the game The 7th Guest, where it tried to be scary, tried to be disturbing, and failed on a few levels.  There were two points in the game where I actually jumped, but that was it.
This game feels like "Oh hey, we have the Unity Engine, let's see what we can do with it!" rather than a polished game.  It was very generic in the levels, and re-used a lot of areas, just re-skinned.  I hated it when I was trying to look at something, and the room just started turning, telling me to get on with the game.  It was interesting how they managed to get the walking gait into the motion, but boy did it make my head hurt and my stomach queasy...
Story-wise, it was hardly original, and has been (over) done before.  Honestly, it really does feel like a first attempt at a game, or a university/college project than anything else.  All I had to do was open doors and cupboards, and when I got stuck, look up at the ceiling or just turn around and go back the way I came.  More of a Big Fish Games point-and-click timewaster than an action game.  It was also contradictory, but I guess that has to do with the three endings; the artist couldn't decide if he was insane, a loving father and husband or a talentless hack who did some weird stuff.
My verdict? I'm uninstalling it.  For me, it was a waste of time.  The Humble Bundle site promised that this game was full of puzzles, and there were none to be found. I wanted puzzles, darnit!

Layers of Fear is a first-person psychedelic horror game. Players take control of a painter whose sole purpose is to finish his Magnum Opus. The player must navigate through both a constantly changing Victorian-era mansion and ghastly visions.
LoF is not as much a horror game as a jump scare opening things walking sim. There is little dread really and most of the "horror" comes from jump scares. There are some eerie moments, but definitely few and far between. Almost 100% of the gameplay is walking in a straight line and opening cupboards, lockers, doors, everything. That doesn't mean that the game is bad, but it's also not good as I expected after reading all the stellar comments.
It's basically Gone Home with jump scares. Interesting experience, sometimes, but mostly rather meh. It's also rather short at 2-3h. There are three endings though, so there is a bit of replayability, but game loses almost all of its fun factor on subsequent playthroughs as there is nothing new that would surprise you. If you like jump scare horror then feel free to jump right in, otherwise I'd avoid.

Do you think Skyrim is the best game ever? Good on ya. Have you played Morrowind? No? THINE FOOL.
Morrowind is arguably one of the best of the Elder Scrolls series. Although I prefer Skyrim's leveling system, Morrowind's leveling system works fine.

If you like Skyrim/Oblivion, and haven't played Morrowind, play it. It's aged, yeah. But you can pick up mod packs that soup up the graphics and make it, visually, rival Skyrim. The combat is the biggest thing that has aged, but it still is functional.

If I had to describe this game in one word... I wouldn't be able to. It's literally amazing, fun and addicting all at the same time. Originally when I found that game, I was looking for a motorsport game that's chilled back and relaxed. I saw the game and was like "Yeah, that's the perfect game I am looking for!". Welp I have not been more wrong in my entire life... This game is all but chilled back and relaxed, especially during races. You have to make split second decision, which can not only determine the outcome of the race, but the outcome of the whole season. Insane right? And it's right here at the click of your fingers!
Overall it's decently optimised, since there's a 2D mode, for slower PCs, and a 3D, over the top, mode with fancy environmental graphics, of the track and all the stuff around it, as well as cool car models.
Everything in the game is not licensed so track names, team names and driver names will be different but they represent their real life version clearly. That's not a problem though, since Motorsport Manager also has a great community! Since the implementation of the Steam Workshop, a tone of people have started making mods, which even change the cars used and update the info of teams etc. so that it is like the real life one.
However, a big disclaimer is that the game requires you to have some understanding of Motorsports and particualrly open-wheel racing, since the base game is focused around the formula series, and the main thing in the game is strategy and car development. Of course the people at Playsport introduced a DLC, which you can buy for 7.99€, that adds the GT side of things to the Motorsport world.
Playsport Games haven't stayed in the shadow and not done anything, they've added 2 more DLCs: a car livery pack, which allows you to change the looks of your car in-game, and a "Build your own team" DLC, which to be honest who doesn't like to imagine that they've created a brand and run it themselves and see their brand succeed. And that's not even the good part, those 2 DLCs are entirely free and you can get them when you buy the game!
All in all the game is great, you should 100% get it if you are motorsports fan, if you are not, you might have trouble at the start but with the instructions and experince you should be able to pick up the game easily since the machanics aren't    unnecessarily overcomplicated.

If you love Formula One and Motorsports, you are going to love this game, as it gives you a simulated environment where so many familiar things (which you usually hear from commentators) are under your direct control and management. Lovingly stressful, especially if you take your favorite team under your management and screw up basic stuff like tire strategies. In the end though, the game will be a lot fun as it combines turn by turn strategic decisions and a real-time "from-the-pit-wall" management of live race action and decisionmaking.

There are some bugs that need ironing out. But nothing gamebreaking for the first 100-200 hours. And boy are the races fun.
Getting yourself from the lowest league with the ♥♥♥♥♥iest car to the WMC Champion is worth every minute of the time you put in there. And it might take quite a while (which, by the way, is a good thing!)

Master Reboot is a story driven adventure game.  It has some interesting puzzles, the art style is beautiful, and at the same time the game has a nice creepy vibe to it.
*The Story*
This game has one of the more interesting stories that I have seen for an adventure game.  Depending on how closely you follow it, it can take two or more playthroughs to fully understand what is going on.  At first you might seemed confused, but given time you will grasp the story.
*The graphics/sound*
The art style of this game is very impressive in my opinion.  Each level or area gives off its own vibe, whether it be vibrant, gloomy, or any of the other designs of the levels.  You get sucked in with the atmosphere.  The sound is also very good.  You can get a little panicked as you feel you are being followed by rustling behind you, screams or other odd sounds coming from who knows where, and other sounds that make you wonder what is going on.
*Overall*
I highly recommend this game.  As I said, it has a great vibe, nice engaging story, and can scare you at times.  The length isn't overly long, at a playtime of 3 hours if you don't rush it.  If you want something different then definitely check this game out.

Master Reboot had been in my backlog for several months but I finally took the time over the past few days to play through and even 100% the achievements.
The game was not flawless by any means but to my mind the warts are just about what one should expect from such an ambitious indie project. Missing things like a key/controller config, multiple save slots (or a persistent way to view ducky and animated memories), borderless window, etc. are all minor quibbles that at worst I'd appreciate seeing in future projects.
But the game so masterfully tells its story that the technical deficiencies don't really diminish my opinion of it, in the end. While there are no major plot twists or unexpected turns, the revelation of the plot as well as exposition on the settings and characters are all slowly dripped to the player in an epistolary style, primarily via documents and photos unlocked by finding the blue duckies in each level. The bits and pieces found reveal just enough to the player that unlocking a new one feels like satisfying detective work.
Further, the setting and plot serve one another well and like all good sci-fi, they form a sort of feedback loop to make a greater whole than either aspect alone. The concept of the Soul Cloud and all of its implications are borne from the mundane human stories, and the regular lives of the characters are made extraordinary by the cyberpunk setup. Yes, cyberpunk. The game is set in a much nearer future than most cyberpunk sf but the concept of the Soul Cloud would be right at home in Ghost in the Shell - it's essentially one big shell for many many ghosts. The near-future setting helped rather than hindered my disbelief and I could believe that this sort of tech would exist in "tomorrow's tomorrow".
The only criticism I might lodge at the plot and setting is that there's absolutely no falling action or an epilogue of any sorts, so the end feels just a bit abrupt. This very well could have been intentional as it leaves the player to consider what might happen next, and the ultimate outcome of a "happy" or "sad" ending depends on their own perspective and conclusions drawn. I understand a sequel is also in the works, which at this juncture I am quite looking forward to.
A quick note about the audio/visual aspects, since I feel a review is incomplete without SOME words on that front. The flat-shaded, low-poly look was very effective in cooridination with the shader and lighting effects. I don't have much more to say on this front, but I mean- I took a couple of dozen screenshots
. The game looks good! As far as audio, I have even less to say here. The soundtrack is largely ambient and the sound effects did their job - I ran into no technical issues or points of aural annoyance.
All told, Master Reboot is a diamond in the rough. I would heartily recommend it to anyone who can look around a few technical and gameplay frustrations to find an exceptional story. Games like Master Reboot are why I carry a torch for indies.

I didn't play much during early access, but decided to get give it a go now that it is officially released. For someone who has put an insane amount of hours into Quake 3/Quake Live, it was very easy to adjust to this game after setting up my binds (nearly identical to q3) and sensitivity. The gameplay and game modes are basically the same as Quake and all the weapons are near duplicates as well, but the movement is a bit different if you've only played vanilla Quake 3. But it's easy to catch on and soon enough you'll be blazing through the maps learning jumps and shortcuts. While the community is pretty small, if you don't see an active server with your preferable game mode you can easily jump into matchmaking with your selected game mode choices and you'll usually  find an opponent within a couple minutes. You'll also be placed into a game lobby to mess around in with other players who are also queued up if you so choose. However, this is not ideal to support the community and it would be better suited to have active servers that populated with larger amounts of people, as three player FFA/instagib games are not as fun and there is a break between the action after each game while it finds you a new game. It would be nice if there would be an option after the game ends to stay on the server so other people can join in and populate the server. There is also a character customization, item drops, and a XP/lvl up progression system. However currently the level system seems to serve no purpose other than locking people out from competitive matchmaking below level 15. Game is a lot of fun and the combat is very responsive/engine feels great, but needs more people playing.

The point I want to make however, is that the game's real beauty comes out in it's gameplay which is both extremely fun and wildly addictive.

This is a surprisingly good game. A game I haven't heard of until I got it. I don't even remember how, so it must have been a giveaway. This is, as every other person is saying, a hidden gem. Basically this is a "console" shooter with covers, regeneration and auto-aim. But just saying this, I feel like I'm doing this game a disserving. Behind the bland and generic-looking grafics, was the most of intense and immerseful action games I have ever played. Introduction was a bit weak, I have to say. The swimming part felt awkward and unneeded, but other than that - first big robot got me on board. Speaking of robots. They are all you will shoot in this game. But they are all different in all kinds of way. And peeling their armor to actually kill them feels weirdly satisfying. Not to mention the giant transformers and tentacle robot bosses - this is a Japanese game after all. The story feels much like a manga or anime would too. Or even like a character-driven novella. They can be goofy and cheesy, but they show detail when needed. The main plot revolves around androids, that believe they are actually human. So the actual story contains philosophical drama about artificial life. Characters even mention Mary Shelley's Frankenstein by name somewhere. But game doesn't hold itself too seriously to be a turn-off for the people who just want to have fun. I say this is a must play. Words can't do it justice.

Fun Co-Op, will easily last you and up to 3 friends along with you a good 100-150 hours of content. The character chemistry, banter and contextual dialogues is also a big, nay, HUGE aspect of making the game really feel alive.
Downside is that it's a bit buggy, has a few glitches, also sometimes connectivity can be quite ♥♥♥♥♥♥ since it has no dedicated servers. Peer to peer, however let me say it's one of the BETTER p2p systems out there, *cough* For Honor *cough* . Graphics are absolutely gorgeous, but sometimes it can make levels a bit confusing if you don't look at your map often, and even then, I have gotten lost a few times but after the 60h mark you'll be familiar with most maps. It's also a haven for loot hoarders - different tiers of weapons with different stats and even varying "traits" (number of traits depends on weapon level, type, and different tiers have different traits, said traits being either bonus passive abilities or conditional abilities).
5 characters (not classes), each with their own weapon types, some unique to them alone, some shared with other characters. Each one can equip a melee and ranged weapon.
Enemies are truly diverse - you have  your standard cannon fodder small rats, then come the armored and big as men Stormvermin, the quick and extremely dangerous to lone targets Gutter Runners (assassin rats basically), the devastating Rattling Gunners, the devious poisoned wind globadiers who hurl balls of gas at you, packmasters who can catch and drag you with a hook if he gets close enough, enabling other rats to swarm and quickly kill you. And, of course, last but not least - the Rat Ogre. You've probably already gotten a general idea from the name only, a big mass of muscle that charges you head on and throws you around, chunking huge bits of your health if you let him land hits on you. It can get really tense dealing with a multitude of these enemies at the same time, luckily they can also hit their own with their AoE attacks, and the rat ogre doesn't care a whole much about his "comrades", often charging through and stomping his smaller kin.
Now in this game, you can dodge, and this is the most important part. It's no breeze through the park on the highest difficulties, you NEED to stick together and play to each other's strengths. Spasmy reactions and a good aim will only get you so far, you CANNOT fight alone, and although you luckily can play without other people as the game gives you bots who are stupid af unless you download the Quality of Life mod which improves and lets you customize bots from the options to make them chase healing items and other useless stuff less, especially if you want them carrying tomes, which improve your rolls at the end of a mission to acquire items, and you will almost always be pursuing them, and I recommend reading guides on which maps have them and where they are(it's the same spot every time).
For me, 10/10. Now, is it a perfect game? No, of course not, there is no such a thing. But it's incredibly fun, especially with friends on the mics. It has a lot of action, a lot of tension as well on higher difficulty as characters die from 3-4 hits and getting hit can be extremely easy when you get surrounded, thankfully blocking works in all directions so at least you don't have to worry about the ones behind you as much. A lot of lore related stuff as well, the game has an in-game lorebook that you can collect pages for, for those lore-nerds out there.
The game was done with respect and with understanding of the franchise and the relations between these different races and organisations within said races. A fantastic game, and the sequel coming in around a year which is going to feature CHAOS seems like an even bigger treat and serious GoTY potential just on sheer content and atmosphere.

This game should be called Layers of Horror Tripe
Good things first.
Paintings are interesting and creepy (too bad they are repetitive). Graphics are also well made, especially for a Unity game.
The bad now.
Well, the most important thing: gameplay. It is just a room walking simulator with typical stupid jump-not-scares (scary only if you're a pansy). During your walking you will encounter majority of known horror cliches: creepy (more like crappy) dolls, babies crying, phones ringing, people whispering, doors suddenly opening or closing, and Silent Hills PT (pity it didn't come out) waifu attacking the main character rip-off.
Maybe at least the story is good? Nope it is not. It's another insane person cliché. At least the developers capture the insane part pretty well (for an indie game of course) stuff like rooms transforming, paintings changing places, etc.
I was so irritated by "playing" (more like walking it to be honest) that I thinks it's actually good that the game is rather short, because if it were any longer I would go insane just as the main character.
Honestly I have no idea, why this game has such a good rating on steam, maybe because most of the people didn't play it long enough, but only watched YouTubers' fake reactions to the jump-not-scares. Maybe it's good for people who don't watch or play a lot of horrors, or specifically for them because the will know what to expect, and they don't like originality (the thing that this game lacks the most).
At least the game was free on humble store. In my it is not worth more than 5$. I had low expectations of this game but it still disappointed me.

Morrowind really sucked when I first played it... then I played it again and again and again and not because I didn't have any other games, but because I told a friend about my character, and he told me about his and they were completely different. I was then interested in exploring all of the possible paths that one could follow while playing morrowind. It became my cult-favorite/alltime-favorite game.
Then came along Oblivion which was promised to be morrowind with nice graphics and I played that and hated it. Then DLC came out and I played it again and again and again you get the picture. Soon, I found myself lost in the massive world of tamerial and it became my cult-favorite/second-most-favorite game of all time.
Along comes the big bad Skyrim and I was prepared. I expected the game to be dumbed down, and I expected it to be the last ES game that would I ever play. Because, I figured that I'd like the story and dlc but it would lose it's replay value in the dumbing down process. I played it and I hated it then the DLC came out and I hated that too. I managed to put a hundred or so hours into it and felt as though it was wasted time. Then came along 200 hours, and I said that was enough, I'm way over powered, and the game is not much fun anymore. Along comes the modding community to save the day, and that is what they did. I became addicted to modding my skyrim and playing a few levels and modding it more till I broke the game, fresh install, rinse and repeat.Then I used the memory patcher and everything just worked and I decieded that I'd play the game one more time to see if I could tolerate it as an ES title. Now, three different characters later I can say that Skyrim has become my cult-favorite/third/second-all-time-favorite game. I enjoy this more now than oblivion, but chronologically it is third :p
Now I've decided to give Morrowind another play-through, right now I'm on the road on my way to balmora and loving it but not for any of the reasons stated above, but because there is a level of nostalgia that is present. I worry that the cliff racers and the terrible combat mechanics will force me to abandon my task.
