I have to admit, I had no idea what to expect from this game and I was pleasantly surprised about it. The whole idea of being in the future where something like Soul Cloud which is storing dead people's memories and souls exists is very interesting. So what happened? Well, the Soul Cloud had crash which corrupted some data. And you have to restore some of them by looking into memories of somebody with said corrupted data. The whole game is split-up into a lot of levels, each one is representing some memory. So you can expect child memories, memories from school, flying, being on beach, everything you can imagine.
But it's not a hippie game like you would expect from what I just wrote. I mean, few memories are nice and pleasant, but you will be surprised how scary some of them will turn. And I mean it when I say scary. This is what is this game good at. Atmosphere. Absolutely amazing atmosphere that will suck you into the game. Second good thing is its own art and design style. Music is well placed and everything fits together. The only thing I could reproach is that sometimes you can see that some objects are made pretty poorly. There are just few of them, it doesn't disrupt the game, but let's not pretend they aren't there. Overall the game looks just great. Oh, and I almost forgot! There are puzzles in some levels, but don't worry, if you're not into them. There aren't a lot of them and although they aren't extremely easy, you won't get stuck, I promise!
So what is the summary? 9/10. I recommend this game to anybody who likes atmospheric games and horror ones even tho it's more chilly than scary - don't worry that you couldn't sleep at night. So that's it, stop reading this and go play it!

Master Reboot is a Sci-Fi First Person Exploration game, set in a virtual world dedicated to store dead people's memories and personalities, so that they're able to relieve their life, and also contact their family and friends, even after their unfortunate death.
As you play, you'll uncover more about your past self and a bit about the world by visiting different memories.
Sounds promising, right? Well, it certainly did!
So, let's start with presentation.
For me, the
were a mixed bag, to be honest.
In the first level, you're greeted with amazing colors and lightning effects and just really polished graphics overall. While there are sparks of that throughout the rest of the game, it unfortunately falls a bit short of what it showed at the start.
Texture work is almost inexistent at times, with a lot of the game beings mostly shaders and lights/shadows, and not a lot of details on textures, it's mostly just blurred colors.
This makes the game look cheaper than it needed at times, specially since we had already seen a better work overall.
On the other hand, the lighting effects are still awesome, and it's clearly a focus of the game's artstyle, specially inside the Hub World, with a very Neon feel to it.
Besides, a really huge problem I had was with the brightness balance. This game is way too dark. Seriously, I wasn't able to see, at times (at the Hospital level, experimenting with the achievements). It was literally pitch black. I could change the brightness, BUT, you can't change the settings as you play, and the brightness meter isn't well calibrated, meaning that you can't really know when to stop.
That's a bummer. I'll talk more about technical issues further.
As I said, a mixed bag. Sometimes it looks awesome, other times it just feels rushed and cheap.
Regarding
, though, I mostly enjoyed it. It has an eerie feel to it, but it's also beautiful, not just there to make you feel uncomfortable. Besides, it helps create an atmosphere in the several places you visit (i.e.: a circus).
SoundEffects, on the other hand, felt a bit unbalanced (some of them genuinely bad), sometimes being too loud to the point of distorting the sounds. But, overall, they helped the atmosphere of the game.
I think it has done its purpose, but overall, it could have been better.
So, how's gameplay, one might ask?
Well, this is where the game falls a bit too short. The game is mostly comprised of several areas (essentially 3 tiers that you unlock as you complete them), each with a certain memory. While there are bits of the game outside of memories, that's where most of the gameplay and exploration is set, so I'll focus on that.
There's a hub area, in the virtual world, from which you can choose any of the areas of the available tier. These include place such as an Hospital, a Fairground, a Library, a Flight, and so on. You visit several places from your past life, trying to uncover exactly who you were, and who you were with.
So far so good, I actually liked the structure of the game.
In each area, it's more like a puzzle game. You'll have to explore the areas, and try to find out exactly what needs to be done.
While you do that, there are little blue ducks, that give you pictures of a certain memory, a little piece of the puzzle of your past, if you will. These are usually fairly well hidden, and they're basically their reward for exploration.
These areas, however, have two main problems. The first one, is that they're fairly small, rendering exploration a bit of a relative term, as there's not much to explore. Instead of exploring a big area, you're just looking under benches and the sort. Not very interesting.
The second problem, is that most of the puzzles are fairly counter-intuitive, and have barely anything to do with your own purpose or memory. They're just... there. Acting as a hinderance more than a vehicle for the story. And that's unfortunate.
They vary from too easy to random, for the most part.
On their side though, is that they were certainly varied and SOME of them were pretty well thought and design. Unfortunately, the exception doesn't really make the rule.
Most of the puzzles feel out of place and with solutions that aren't in any way tied to the memory.
However, the areas weren't all just puzzles. They were actually very varied. The Hospital was more of a Horror-themed area, while the Flight was a stealthy mission. It certainly had more to it than I expected, but, the developers didn't seem either experienced or resourceful enough to do it all. The Stealth level was just frustrating at the beginning, but laughable once you figure out what to do. And the Horror level, somehow, managed to be less scary than other levels that were far more oppressive in a subtle way.
In general, Master Reboot tried to hard to make a game out of the concept, and feeling a bit to shallow in that regard.
I can understand why they've done it, but I think they only got sidestracked from the initial concept and ended up not doing either very well.
One important aspect (for me, at least) is how they've done the achievements. Most of them are only there as an additional bit of challenge to the levels, but, once again, it doesn't add anything to the game. On the contrary, the way you're "encouraged" to play is actually less fun.
On the Hospital level, for example, the achievements was to play without the Flashlight. "Well, bring it on, then!"... Boy, did I regret it. It didn't make it scarier. It simply made it frustrating. In many corridors there was literally no light. It was pitch black. I didn't know where to go, and there weren't really any distant visual or audio cues. It was just a case of pressing WASD and hoping I wasn't going against the wall. It was... not a good experience, from a gameplay standpoint.
The other achievements seem to follow the same rule, being more of a problem than a cool incentive to play the game in interesting ways.
Alright,
is out of the way. Now comes the really disappointing part for me.
You know, as this was an Exploration game in such a promising world, I didn't care about gameplay too much. I was just expecting great encounters and insight into this future society. Maybe even questioning Death. But... it barely happened, unfortunately.
This game seemed the perfect way of throwing some ideas at the player through the world itself, but it did none of that. It simply turned into a dramatic story about 2 random people who created the Soul Cloud... just because. No philosophy behind it was explained or even refered throughout the game. It was created in the same way as Facebook, which is disappointing, to say the least.
The world was there, and you were in it, but you didn't really feel a part of it in any way.
In the end of each area you get a cutscene about your previous life, but it's just a story about love and friendship with a murder thrown' in the middle to make it seem dark. It's just... shallow, forgeting the initial premise.
Maybe I was expecting too much. Or just something different. And this game wasn't aiming for it.
Well, maybe. But even in that case, looking back at the game, there's no reason for it to standout, aside from the pretty lighting. Gameplay is just there just to call it a game, as it wasn't the focus at all. The story was far more generic than it could have been with the endless possibilities of the Soul Cloud. The world was far too empty as well, with more focus on real world memories than the virtual world of the undead.
All in all, this game is just a missed opportunity. It was set in a great world, full of very interesting concepts. But, it does nothing with it, trying to be too much at once, ending up missing most of its points.
It has impressive lightning effects and great audio design, but as a game... there's nothing I can't think of to justify a recommendation.

My synopsis, Toukiden 2 is a great monster hunting game for fans of solo play, but I'd avoid this if you're into multiplayer.
Story:  7/10
Surprisingly good story for a game of its type, despite being somewhat cheesy and "typical."  It can be quite sad at times, so be warned.  The game is all in Japanese (only) audio too.  Fortunately, there is no cringe-worthy English voiceover to ruin this game's story.  The dialogue translation, from what I can tell, is mostly fine with a few spelling/grammar errors here and there.
Character Customization:  8/10
This is a pretty nice feature about the game.  It has better character customization than many comparative games, including 20 different voices and many hairstyles and facial features to choose from.  However, the body customization is quite lacking sadly.  You also cannot change your character's body appearance later in the game, although you can still change your hairstyle.
Gameplay:  8.5/10
A lot of depth here, more than I could feasibly write in this review.  I'll do my best to paint a basic picture for you.  Basically, fight oni (monsters in this game), get materials from them, craft better armor/weapons, fight more oni for more materials for better gear.  This is largely what the endgame is, and there is so much more to it.  I still haven't done everything technical yet, such as the best endgame weapons.
If I recall, there are 2000 different weapons and 800 different armor pieces.  Those numbers are deceiving because many of the pieces have both Low and High Rank variants, effectively decreasing that variety by at least half.  If you add in color variations of several many more pieces, reduce that total even further.  However, there is still a high variety of weapons and armor to choose from for your needs.  Speaking of weapons/classes, there are many.  Sword, Twin Knives, Spear, Naginata, Bow, Rifle, Chain and Sickle, Sword and Shield, Whip, Club, and Gauntlets.  May have missed one or two, but that's already quite a variety, each offering their own playstyle.  Each of these weapons and armors you get have different parameters.  Let me save you trouble by defining the Aegis stat on armor early: that's what affects your HP regen.  I never knew that for dozens of hours.
There is also a mitama (spirit) kind of system that you can tune to fit your playstyle.  For example, you might use a full speed build to unleash blindingly fast combos of death with a sword, or you might play it safe with a defense build and use a sword and shield to "tank" your enemy.  Plenty of different builds out there, for sure.
You get some "magical green hand" that lets you break parts on monsters and cancel dangerous attacks they use which is kind of neat.  Aiming it is wonky sometimes.  You can also use it to climb walls and pull yourself to enemies.
The world map is "mostly" open, barring some areas till you reach certain segments of the story.  However, at a certain point, you "can" forge far ahead of where you should be in story which is pretty fun.  Until you beat the story, your time spent in the open world is limited.  There's an "exposure limit" which acts as the timer; if you max it out, you die.  However, you can use a shrine to reset the timer and keep exploring.  I like this system because it really adds to the atmosphere of the game, or at least it did while it was still a thing to worry about.
After clearing the game, you get access to "High Rank" mode which basically buffs the enemies quite a bit.  More HP, attack power, and some new attack patterns to watch for.  This applies to the open world monsters and also changes the drops on the map.  You can also upgrade your older "Low Rank" gear into their respective "High Rank" versions.  It's pretty expensive in late game, but it's manageable if you sell stuff you don't need.
Regarding variety of monsters, like most games of its type, it sadly falls prone to "recycled monster syndrome."  That is, let's make this one a different color and change the element and maybe a few attacks, keeping everything else the same.  It seems you can't escape this no matter what game you play, so it's not really a big deal given that the base variety of monsters to kill is respectable anyway.
A few of the monsters seem just a "bit" unfair in that they may never stop moving, constantly seem to be attacking with wide AOEs and backsweep attacks that are nigh impossible to dodge, are so huge that you can't reliably hit them (a dancing pair of giant legs is a nightmare to hit, I promise), or they get knocked back so far away from your allies that you can't reliably hit them.  Which brings me to the AI allies.
The AI is very good for a game of its type.  Some call it "too" good; however, later in the game you really do start to notice the difference you make in the group.  Sadly, some monsters get comboed "so hard" that they fly all over the place, no joke.  Try chasing a monster that keeps getting knocked back 25+ meters right as you get to it, over and over.  Not very fun when you waste your "burn time" chasing down the monster, but it is manageable.
Audio:  9/10
Firstly, I will say that I love this game's soundtrack.  It's one of the better ones I've heard, beautifully orchestrated.  After doing some research, I found that the composer also did work on Pokemon Mystery Dungeon: Explorer's of Time for the Nintendo DS.  If you enjoyed that soundtrack, you'll love this one too for sure.
Regarding sound effects, they aren't necessarily bad.  However, I recommend turning them "down."  For some reason, these types of games like to aurally assault your ears with a cacophony of very loud and annoying sound effects.  As a result, my sound effects volume is now at "half."
The character voices are in Japanese, as I noted.  I don't mind the quality of the voices, but some characters just have "that voice" if you know what I mean.  "The whole gang's here" kind of deal.  There is a small problem where the voices will not have subtitles while running around the overworld, resulting in English players having no idea what is being discussed.  Fortunately, this only seems to be for common roaming and does not affect the story dialogue.
Multiplayer:  1/10
Dead as a doorknob in the servers.  Every time I've checked, I couldn't find a group.  This may offer some opportunity if you have a friend to play with, but even that isn't anything exciting.  The world isn't open and is instead instanced in servers, requiring missions to be taken.  If you want a multiplayer game, look elsewhere.
Overall:  8/10
Toukiden 2 is a game I mostly recommend to solo players that are fans of this type of genre of gaming.  The story can be somewhat interesting, despite being typical.  Gameplay wise, it offers quite a lot to do at endgame, and even after playing this for over 140 hours at the time of me writing this review, I still keep coming back to play it for a short bit every now and then.  Is it worth $60?  Only if you feel it will be a game you don't mind playing alone and plan to invest lots of time in endgame towards.
I hope this persuades you to purchase (or stay far away from) this game.

If I had reviewed this game a few months ago, it would have definitely gotten a thumbs up... but now that I have over 700 hours into the game, I've started to see cracks in the facade. To start with the positives, the game plays like a single player game. I myself do not really care for MMOs in general as I generally don't like being forced to deal with the toxic communities of games, but STO is much different. Sure there are jerks, but by in large the community is willing to help you if you have a question. The game plays just like a single player game, just incase you really don't want to deal with other players.
Also, the ships are pretty well modeled, and space combat (especially with a lot of ships) really gives you that big battle feeling of the Star Trek TV shows.
Unfortunately those are the only positive I can say without adding negatives, so lets dive into the rest.
The story lines for the Romulans and Klingons are especially strong (the Federation is rather generic), unfortunately very early in those two races stories, you end up having to do the same exact missions you had to do as a Federation character. To me it seems to be a huge cop-out by the developer. If you play at an average pace, you will be done with all of the story missions up to current day. When you consider that this game debuted almost 6 years ago, that is quite disappointing. In my opinion, rather than getting any wash-up actor who made a guest appearence, or had a supporting role on any of the Trek shows, they should forget about that and focus on more frequent releases of storyline missions.
Speaking of missions, there are a few gems that are well written, creative, and fun to play, but by in large every missions consists of an opening space phase where you fight to reach a planet, you then beam down and have to fight on the ground and accomplish an objective, and then you beam back to your ship and have to battle in order to leave. Those types of missions make up a good 85-95% of the game.
Also, the major story arc the game has been leading up to for years (fighting the Iconians), has been a complete disappointment since it has debuted. Almost as if the developers didn't know what to do with it now that it has finally arrived, and now they are in a big rush to end it and debut their new story arc for the game.
Thankfully the new story arc seems to involve more exploration and less shooting, which is what Star Trek is really supposed to be about (in theory). Everyone loves space battles, but after the five hundreth time of doing them, it is nice to have something different.
There is a system in the game where people can create their own stories and missions, and make them available for everyone else in game to play. It is a good idea in theory, but even the top rated ones I have sampled are amateurish and dialogue heavy. After 5 minutes of playing one you will just want to get on with it and start skipping dialogue.
One of the biggest universal complaints about this game are the microtransactions. Yes, this is a "free to play" game, and they need to make their money somehow. I don't have a problem with it, but I do have a problem for the ridiculous prices they charge you for the smallest stuff. Want to rename your character? That will be $5. Want to respec your skills? Another $5. Want a cool ship instead of the neutered free ones they give you? That will be $20 AT LEAST. The norm is $25-30. Anything cool, from ships to uniforms, that you may want will no doubt cost you money. Yes you can get the TNG Enterprise D or the Enterprise E from the later movies for free, but they are the much weaker versions. Fortunately you CAN get through all of the storyline missions with the free ships. You may have a bit of trouble in the later stages of the game, but it can be done. I will give the developer credit for how masterfully they've made the game to convince players to pay money. The longer you play the game you can really see how things like daily dilithium refining caps, lack of inventory space, bank space, etc is all crafted to steer you to spend money. It's very sad that the serious players have to have one main character and then several other characters that all essentially farm and supply the main character with enough resources/in game currency to accomplish things in a reasonable amount of time.
Also, it is worth mentioning that the Klingon faction is essentially dead in the game. The majority of players either play Federation, or Federation aligned Romulans in the game.
Also, doesn't anyone think it is odd that this game which is mainly about the Federation, who are essentially space communists, is centered around an in game item selling system? In order to make any decent amount of money in the game, you will have to work "The Exchange" and sell items to other players.
Which brings me to the end of this long review. Once you finish the story missions, have joined a fleet (this game's equivalent of a guild) and have gotten decent gear, you will be able to handle anything in PVE (PVP in this game is essentially non-existant, not that it isn't there, people just don't really play it). It is at this time that all there really is left to do is to grind for every so slightly better, and more time consuming to get, gear. When you stop and think about it, and consider that PVP in this game is almost a non-entity and you can already beat most things in PVE when you are in the "end game" with ease , what is the point of grinding? If you continue to grind for better gear, and drop lots of money getting the top tier gear, you're only essentially doing it for bragging rights.
So anyways, to sum all of this up, if you really love Star Trek and want to try this, go for it, play through the storyline missions, but don't spend a dime on it. Also expect to run out of things to do, other than grinding, within a couple months (depending on how often you play). It's not so much that STO is a bad game, I do think they have gotten a lot right and did fairly right by Star Trek, but that it has fallen victim to the micro-transaction model of making games and is very clearly a cash grab at this point in its life.
One final thing, if you do think you want to spend money on this game, consider that someday the game's servers will be taken down permanently (like all old MMOs) and you will be left with nothing to show for your money spent.

Reflex is a well-done arena first-person shooter. To put it diplomatically, Reflex clearly borrows very heavily from Quake 3 (and the CPMA mod which I didn’t play, but see that one of the Reflex creators was involved in its development). So, putting aside the choice to lean and build on Quake 3, if you’ve played Quake, you can jump into Reflex and find a familiar game, with weapons that you know how to use and movement that you’ve probably wasted many hours mastering. That said, it’s also different. It’s like playing chess on a different planet with pieces that are customized on an elongated, crisp, colorful board. The movement has its difference from say standard Quake Live gameplay and provides for some interesting and fun elements to learn. Ditto, but less so for the weapons (they’re fairly similar to QL, with timing one’s shots seeming to be the new component).
There are, however, several nice features in the game. You can create a party (like in Rocket League) to play with friends, the map making looks great, and the training map is useful for adapting to Reflex and improving one’s movement. The capture the flag is especially fun and think it has great potential in this game, given it is so fast-paced. Lastly, the graphics have a clean, minimalistic appeal with the components of the game (sounds, visuals, etc.) adding up to a unique, fresh gaming experience.
Bottom line: The developers put together a well-crafted fps geared towards gamers who appreciate attention to detail and high (or non-existent?) skill ceilings. I hope it has a future.

The graphics and color pallet are simplistic and bright to keep concentration on the match at hand. It keeps target acquisition to a fine point, no losing your target in all the pretty graphics. And the UI is almost entirely customizable. Fully customizable keybinds as a good PC game should have, completely tweakable HUD that lets you remove any fluff you don't like, move and resize, and even snag some mods on the market that add brand new HUD elements such as the enemy player's current health weapon and ammo during 1v1s, or an animated speedometer bar.
This game is everything you will ever want in an Arena FPS. Pick this up, and you will only be dissapointed that more people didn't pick this up sooner. Get on the trend so this baby can get mainstream!

Last race of the season at Phoenix. My two drivers - let's call them Dave and Emma - are at the top of the championship, with Dave 9 points ahead.. They're enough points ahead of everyone else that the title is just between them now. They've grown to hate each other, and Dave's ontract is up for renewal at the end of the season - but won't renew while Emma is with the team.
I decide to let them race for it, as we're far enough ahead in the team championship that we should still win it unless there's a freak result. The only team that can beat us is Ferrari (well, a legally safe knockoff of Ferrari), but it's a long shot. My drivers are starting at the back, because of the reversed grid rule.
At the start, Dave and Emma immediately begin scything through the field, with Emma slightly ahead. The Ferrari drivers are first and second, but nothing to worry about yet - until Dave crashes on lap 3. ♥♥♥♥. Emma now just needs to finish in the top 8 to win the title. I check the team standings - and then remember it's a double points race. Ferrari are going to win the title.
Welp.
Emma gives it her best shot and gets up to 8th, enough to win the title. I tell her to keep pushing, as we've got a team championship to win. With 2 laps to go, she's running third, behind the Ferraris. At this point, we're just three points short. Just when I had accepted losing, the second Ferrari starts pouring black smoke.
I couldn't believe it. As the Ferrari slows to a crawl, Emma swoops past for second place. The broken Ferrari eventually finishes fifth, giving Emma the driver's title and my team the championship. Fantastic.
It's been a long time since I got this invested in a game. A must-have for any motorsport fans. Oh, and Dave was fired at the end of the season.

At full price, Master Reboot is not worth it. One problem is that it's rather short (less than four hours to finish it).
While the simplicity of the graphics could be excused by the theme, they do not just *appear* simple but *are* simple. That's the difference to Tron 2.0 from 2003: Master Reboot wouldn't have looked good even back then. Had they been more stylized, the game might've looked better.
The game is never about fighting enemies but running away from them, a bit similar to Silent Hill: Shattered Memories. The weapons the player on occasion have are not used for shooting enemies.
Beside hiding from the (scripted) enemy behaviour, the game has a number of puzzles. Unfortunately, a number of them felt nonsensical.
And why include first-person platforming? Tron 2.0 should've already taught that it's a bad idea.
Bottom line:
+ interesting plot
+ interesting setting
- platforming
- some poorly designed puzzles (e.g., the beach)
- overly simple and poor graphics.
Worth trying, but not at the full price.

This is... likely the weirdest game I've ever played. Entertaining? Not so much. What Master Reboot does is make your brain work - along with creepy and suggestive imagery. Very ambient, some jump scares... I could wax eternal in some pretentious rant about parables between the narrative and our growing dependence on social media and "the cloud", but meh... Yes, there is a story, but it's presented in a somewhat heady way - as with Myst, you need to piece the various bits and bobs together on your own; nothing is presented with absolute clarity and a thorough explanation.
In a nutshell: Everything's colourful. Then everything's weird. Then you go all over looking for little blue rubber ducks. Then there are creepy little girls and teddy bears all around, then things get REALLY weird, weirder still (!), then there's an epic boss fight, and then it ends - and you just sit there wondering what the smurf just happened. On the whole, though, I actually recommend taking a look. You don't get games like this every day. Or every year. Or even every decade.
(I personally didn't really care for the music or the artwork, but to each their own.)

SPORE has smooth animation and a science-backed gameplay; you start off as a cell, then continue to evolve and adapt to everyday life on the road to sentience and space-travel. Strong humor and sarcasm is evident, and some elements of the game leave you wanting to advance farther and experiment with ways to make the game easier. Much like the game Fallout, it is a massive single-player role playing game. Again, the animation and programming were smooth--but not flawless--for its time.
Endless combinations of parts can lead to hours of mixing and matching creature types.
However, there are a number of bugs and glitches in this game. The game's developer, Maxis, is not fixing these bugs anymore due to the game now being old and finished. Also, the add-on packs such as Galactic Adventures are too costly now that it is 6 years old.
Overall, the gameplay is unique, though a few glitches have possibly been overlooked.

As a fan of the GW lore, and Mordheim the tabletop, I wasn't expecting much from another virtual GW game, as they can be abit hit or miss.  This does hit however. And its nearly center mass...
So, you are basically doing raids(from an mmo) or missions in your four person team, using a safehouse (the Inn) to upgrade your gear or change character.  It takes a few levels to unlock the 'bounty' missions and crafting stations, which adds some depth and customisation to the game, especially when you are playing the same missions again and again in the multiplayer.(if you dont host/have mates expect to jump between hosts when they leave etc.)
Game play is mixed between 'move along here killing these rats' to 'move along here defend this' with abit of 'surivive this  bit while this happens' thrown in for good measure.  Have not run into any bugs, but i havent played any dlc yet, so maybe there are some hiding in there...
The different characters play differently enough to mix up gamplay, and at the higher levels you can unlock different setups so you dont have to swap in and out different characters to balance up for a multiplayer team all playing ranged characters.  I'd say the characters do fall into a 'trinity' sort of arrangement, just sawp out the healer with a greif taker/enemy attention grabber.  Like I said though, you can mix up your kit enough to change the play style somewhat, and cross the triangle.
Graphically Id say this game is great, like the table top enlarged with more gorey gore to it. (You can turn the blood off if you want.) The only thing is it leaves me wishing they made a 40K version.  Honestly , that would be a dream game. (HINT HINT)

I wish there was a third recommendation option. I guess I "recommend*" the game with some reservations. Considering this game overall, I can honestly only recommend this game for fans of Star Trek. The game has a significant amount of references and fleshes out the lore from the original timeline. The game mostly takes place after the events Voyager and the last TNG film.
It is a decent Star Trek game and a mediocre MMORPG.
The space battles are great, but the away missions and land battles aren't all that great. The character and ship customization is pretty decent, but to a point. More options open up as you increase in rank, but even then the options are fairly limited. The extra options cost money, unless you patiently and strategically work with the game's different currencies and economy.
The game looks and sounds great with fairly easy to use mechanics and controls. If your machine can run it and you tweak with the settings enough, the game flows pretty well and can be engaging (pun intended) and fun. There isn't really any PvP elements to the game, most of the missions are arguably singer player, and they seem to come out with new story missions and updated versions of existing missions every few months. Even still, after a while it can lose what charm it has and become a rather tedious grind fest if your only objective is to acquire dillithium to trade for zen to use to buy a ship or character item.
The biggest flaws in the game are much like any other MMORPG. Anytime there is an update, be prepared to download and install a big patch file. The server status is hit or miss. One day the game plays great, the next day you'll lose connection with the servers every five seconds, if you can even log in at all. Sometimes you can log in alright, but then once you actually get into the game, there can be an intense amount of lag in the battles and even the UI. There are certainly remedies and quick fixes such as not using on demand patching, running force verifications of game files, lowering settings, changing instances, etc. But at the end of the day, there is only so much you can do from your end if the host servers are out of commision.
When it works, STO is a fun time suck and distraction. When it doesn't work, the game is a frustrating nightmare.

Reflex Arena is a adrenaline-inducing competitive arena shooter in the likes of Quake. It boasts 10 unique weapons which all handle exceptionally well, and a large variety of maps to play in. This game is full of crazy fast paced action and requires utmost speed and precision.
- The visuals are sleek and stylish. They're both beautiful and simple at the same time, minimising environmental distractions. All the effects and weapon projectiles/particles look stunning in the heat of the action. The character customisation has a fair bit of depth, but unfortunately all cosmetics must be bought (real money) or rarely randomly dropped. I think the visuals of Reflex Arena make this a very competent sidegrade to Quake.
- The audio is fairly good but nothing special. All guns sound unique and have a good feel to them, but they don't sound very exciting. The gameplay can be quiet at times with a lack of music. Overall, Reflex Arena's weakest area is the audio, although it's still alright.
- Reflex Arena is a twitch based arena PVP FPS. Turn your FOV up to max and get ready for one of the most intense games on Steam. This is a very speed orientated game, and offers unique jump mechanics that further increase speed and jump height. I loved the large selection of weapons. Before a match starts, you play in a practice match to get yourself prepared. This is a great time to try out all the cool weapons and get your mind in the game. All guns are powerful in their own right, but some more than others. To prevent weapon abuse, every gun has limited ammo, but during the arena you can pick up more. With old school gameplay and a multitude of gamemodes and mutators, Reflex Arena is tremendous fun and more people should play it. The only reason I'm not playing it is the lack of local servers, as outer-regional servers are too laggy. Overall, Reflex Arena has awesome gameplay, if you find a good server.
- With this being a competitive multiplayer game, you'd expect bugs and performance issues to be at a minimum. Luckily during my time, I encountered no technical issues. Reflex Arena overall is a very well polished game.
If you're looking for a new modern game just like Quake, then you'll certainly love Reflex Arena.

You know what. This game is just... I don't know where to place it.
Do I like it? Do I dislike it? Love it? Hate it?
I honestly do not know.
It's such a mystery to me, it's such a rollercoaster of a game, a sort of love-hate relationship if you will.
On one hand, holy smokes, more Hotline Miami! Hotline Miami is my favourite game, and seeing a sequel, I of course had to have it.
On the other, sequels are notorious for screwing up what originals did really damn well. So, which one does Hotline Miami 2 fall under?
Well, it has a great story. God damn, there's been spots in the dialogue that made my
. The delivery on some of it's lines are absolutely GENIUS. Chills were definitely recieved.
Then there's the playthrough. Let me just say that I'm so glad that the story was so enticing for a long time Hotline Miami fan like me, because the gameplay has some serious downsides at times.
Map design falls flat at times, it can have really absurdly large maps where the enemies will snipe you out and kill you, and then it can have really fun, old Hotline Miami 1 levels, including high combos, high kill counts etc. (Thank you, Richter levels)
Also, not a fan that they've sorta focused on guns way more than melee weapons (The aforementioned large map designs come in play here - melee weapons are just not favourable if you're going to get sniped across the map)
The masks are a cool twist though, and the user made levels also utilise the Hotline Miami 1 masks - more on that later!
The soundtrack, I don't know.
It's got some really good ones. It's also got some really painfully mediocre, borderline unfitting ones. It barely scratches my need for a Hotline Miami soundtrack itch, and if I were to grade it, it'd be a B -
The achievements, of course, I've done them all. Like I did for Hotline MIami 1, I did for Hotline Miami 2. I had to. I just love them so much.
Most of them are kinda okay, some quite clever actually, referencing easter eggs, showing you an alternate story (Bar of Broken Heroes), some utilise you getting a kill with all the weapons (Trust me, the weapon you haven't gotten is always the one you least expect. I actually did this one with pen and paper, and googling all the weapons in the game - and crossing them out).
And then there's the worst achievement I've ever seen get made.
The genocide achievement. 50'000 kills in your save file. Whichever person thought this would be a good idea deserves a slap right across the face hole, and let me tell you why -
Alright, so, let me preface this by saying I've finished the game twice, and then once more in hardmode. I think I've gotten 20'000 kills from that. Just twenty thousand kills. Know how many kills the original game asked you for, before giving you an achievement? 1989. Know why that's a cool achievement count?
Because
50'000 is such a dumb number and you can't do it legitimately without getting bored to death.
Enough about that though.
Where the game really shines is, the character creator. Annoyed at the poor level design at some levels? User created maps.
Want to use Hotline Miami 1 masks? User created maps.
Want to get some additional, non-canon story, but "it'll suffice your fix"? User created maps.
All in all, on sale, pretty good. In full price, 15€ is pretty acceptable if you're really eager to play it.
The soundtrack DLC is pretty good itself too, you get all of the songs in FLAC. Just weed out the bad ones. You'll know the ones.
You will need thick skin for this game.

It's all about the story. The game has a very potent and compelling story, that drops inklings along the way, unfolding in clues and in your mind as you piece it all together. If one thing sold me on this game, it was that story.
The artstyle is interesting - while not the most polished, it is still very alluring and beautiful, landscapes and scenery feel sprawling and endless, and you feel like you could walk forever in a memory (game-sense literally) till you hit the digital perimeter that reminds you that you are in a digital world. It does an excellent job conveying a sense of the surreal, and while not perfect, is more than sufficient.
I could see where elements within the game (as well as moments) tie it to horror, though I would define horror as much more, this game certainly had it's moments that startled me, which I did not forsee being a thing, and to be surprised in that way is always a good thing, feels refreshing and not a rehash of "seen-it-coming"s, though towards the last quarter of the game these moments become more of an annoyance than a genuine disturbance. I would have liked to have seen more of the type of scares you get in the early game, around the late game.
Very little choice, so to call this an exploration game would be inaccurate. The game probably closest fits "Adventure" and "Puzzle-solving" in the Myst-type (showing my age) sense, I suppose but I feel that it doesn't exactly take away from what the game is aiming to offer.
And what it is offering is a story. Hands down the #1 reason to play this game. I'm sure you've seen variations of this story elsewhere in other media, but that's likely because it is such an intriguing concept and one that I feel cannot be explored enough so I welcome this game and anything else that shares in the theme.
I vote you play it. Screen shot it, film a "Let's Play!", discuss the ideas the game broaches with others and build on them and expand your mind to something almost otherworldly that is yet still a possibility someday for us.
Lastly, just get it because you'll enjoy it and you'll be supporting the Devs and also I love you.

It manages to pull off creepy (well some of the time). It has collectible ducks. It has a goddess of destruction. It has a storyline you gradually piece together. What more could you want?
All in all it's essentially an exploring and puzzle game, As you solve the various puzzles and explore memories you uncover what's been going on and begin to see how you ended up where you are now. It's not too difficult (although some of the puzzles towards the end I found annoying rather than hard).
There's also no way to go back and find any collectibles you've missed once you've finished the game, a free play would have been nice (and there was easily enough room in the hub and it would have worked with the story). Over exploring also detracts from the creepiness since a lot of it is cued - walk here - sound effect here - graphic over there, and triggering the same response repeatedly pretty much nukes any sense of threat. It is nicely put together though and well worth a play through. The interactivity with equippable items is also a little clunky but entirely forgivable.
Oh and you can play the entire game in Welsh. Full audio, all materials in game, everything. In Welsh. Can't see that appealing to a huge number of people to be honest, but it is unusual.

I used to love Grand Prix Manager 2 when I was a kid and even installed it a couple of times in the last few years.. but playing a game that is by now 20 years old has its obvious drawbacks and I was happy when this finally came out. After initial release I wasn't in love straight away, but after a few months I think I feel that old feeling coming back to me!
If you used to love GPM2 or GPW like I did you I think this will be worth your money, especially when you combine this with the GT DLC and the excellent ICE Mod 2017.
I don't think I would use the word 'realistic' to describe this game but the game mechanics feel like they are actually portraying real world aspects of racing. For instance: having to buy HQ component X to upgrade car component Y might be a simplified mechanic, but it is actually a good way to bring across that the team that makes the right investments might have the upperhand at some point. The promotion/relegation system ofcourse is not realistic, but it adds reward to the game.
One of my favorite things in the game is designing the new seasons livery. These are the small things that really add immersion to this sort of game.
Something that needs work in my opinion is the staff and driver (contract) management. It seems I can not sign a driver for next season and I have to wait until a contract has expired until I can offer someone a contract without having to pay off my current driver. Also I can't change my driver order so if a driver is injured or ill I can't temporarily replace him.
During the race itself I really hope the way blue flags work will get a good look at some point. If you're racing for position and about to be lapped you are basically screwed.
I am currently in my second season as Mclaren (with the 2017 ICE mod) and I am enjoying it more than my first season. I love the driver switches and the teams that drop and rise in perfomance compaired to the first season. Hopefully when contract management is given more attention there will actually be a silly season which will add a lot of immersion in my opinion.

I played a bit.
Recommendations for improvement:
Spawn triggers for certain events. (Garden of Moor: near grim 1, once you drop, it seems to want to spawn a patrol. There is zero chance to avoid it, and will wipe most attempts.)
The darkness mechanic: I dislike it. Requiring a torch, prevents quick reactions to events, and hurts a player's ability to do the mission with bots.
Better animations for the different phases of an attack. Example: Bright mage's bolt staff has three stages for the charge, and it is fairly tricky to known when you are in stage two or three.
The overheat mechanic seems to prevent a bright mage from utilizing the alt fire quite often. With the bolt staff, unless with the appropriate traits or with perfect timing, you will overheat, and you will take damage. Just make it so you have a better buffer with a few of the alt fires with the staves.
Likes:
The high learning curve. Easy and normal have a definite change in difficulty, same with hard and above. You really feel the difference in play. However, even with white tier weapons, if you master the mechanics of blocking, pushing, and dodging, then you can complete higher difficulties.
The better weapons open up different play styles to the player. If you have a weapon with excellent pushing and blocking, then you can crowd control better, while a weapon with backstabbery or high dps can drop ogres (tanks) quickly.
The sound effects for each special and the patrols are distinct and easily heard if you have headphones in. Once you learn each of the queues, the player can prepare for the specials.
Recommendations for newbies:
Go to last stand, pick a class, and start learning how to utlize the push, block, and dodge mechanics.
(Reminder: Keyboard
Block is alt fire or mouse 2. Most hits take half a stamina shield. Stormvermin and Ogre's take more.
While blocking, pressing primary fire or mouse 1 will push at the cost of one stamina shield
Dodge can be preformed either with the jump button or space bar. You can only dodge left, right, and backwards. If moving forward, you will jump straight up.)
Once mastered, the regular portion of the game becomes much easier.
Crowd control can be done with each class and each weapon, but has different requirements on how you can do it.
Shields are the best, while daggers are the worst, straight up. But there is a technique, where you utlizing dodging, pushing, and multi-targeted attacks to control large crowds of scaven.
(It's a dance.
Once the hoard gets within striking distance, move forward and hit if able or push, the dodge back. Afterwards, you want to use a multi-target attack, then dodge left or right. Either push or use another multi-target attack. Rinse and repeat.
With staves, it's a bit different, because each staff does better depending on targets. Bolt can insta-gib stormvermin and most specials, while fireball and flameriver do better at crowd control. But the dance is simple.
Use the attack, dodge, or press r to vent, and dodge back.)
On lower difficulties, being in gray health, doesn't mean you will die next time, but it's best that you save healing items for this time period. On nightmare and higher, gray means death on next down, so it's best not to form bad habits on the lower difficulties.
I would not worry about the trinkets. Yes group heal trinket (you heal yourself, and everyone close to you is healed as well), grim trinket (decreases the amount of health lost due to grims), and gernade trinket (this one effects the range of the explosion and prevents friendly fire on nightmare and above) tend to be valued higher than other trinkets. As long as you play, you will get them. Sometimes, you get lucky and get them through a contract or a roll of the bones, but they are not necessary for completing higher levels of difficulty.
Skill > Items
Conserve amo unless you can regain it through a trait (scavenger), otherwise the specials can and will over run you.
For ogre, there is a dance that will enable you to kite ogres for days. Step one, learn the ogre's attack animations. Step two, dodge backwards will escape most of them. Step 3, attack when able. A critical blow to the head, or certain items or weapon's attacks will stun an ogre briefly.
Gernades are best served for crowd control. They deal flat damage to all enemies within range. While one hundred damage to an ogre may be nice, but on nightmare and higher, the ogre's hp > one thousand.

There isn't another game like it on the market, especially if you dive into some of the mods (like Prophecy of Pendor or A Clash of Kings). You build an army from scratch, loot and plunder, do quests, run errands to improve relations, trade goods, and enter tournaments untill eventually you're fighting hundreds of troops in a Lord's army and trying to conquer your first castle. With enough time and effort, you can can conquer the entire world and become King. You're not just witnessing the battles, you're fighting right alongside your men. And there are mods for just about anything you can think of. Want to fight for the North in Game of Thrones? Mods. American Civil War? Mods. Sword battles in feudal japan? Mods. There's something for everyone. Once you start playing, you can't stop. I'd easily have paid a full $60 to play the base game but with all of the mods, it's worth so much more. It's the most bang I've ever got for my buck.
Also, if you're into Nordic lore and vikings, buy the Viking Conquest DLC. Not only does it fix all of the original game's shortcomings, but it has a surprisingly fascinating (and historically accurate) storyline that follows the Viking invasion of England by Ragnar Lodbrok's many sons (like Bjorn Ironside and Sigurd Snake-In-The-Eye). Plus, it's wicked fun to sail the oceans with your men and fight on ships.

When you stop to dwell on those familiar words, it becomes evident that they apply not just to those we meet at the altar, but to our friends, family; all our relationships in life, that at some point must inevitably come to an end. But what if they didn't have to? What if there was a way to live on forever; to visit those who's bodies have long since fallen away, indefinitely, even after passing away ourselves. Thus is the idea behind the Soul Cloud, a device capable of recreating someone's personality, their likes and dislikes, and all of their memories in digital form where they can be visited by loved ones, and continue their life without the fear of death hanging over them...that is, until the server itself begins to die, and all those inhabiting it.
Here lies the basic premise to Master Reboot, a wildly ambitious project from the small team at Wales Interactive, which places you inside the Soul Cloud at the point of its downfall as an unknown protagonist just as lost as you are admist its bizarre architecture and endless hallways. It's a game that is hard to categorize because from each moment to the next you are found doing something entirely different, though all in the attempt to discover who you are and what has happened to an invention hailed as one of the most important in recent memory.
The narrative unfolds in a nonlinear, but structure format, with each memory you revisit giving you but a small piece of the overarching plot, until it finally falls into place and you're clued in on what all of it has been for. Unfortunately, that revelation falls a bit flat, switching gears at the last moment and leaving you with an empty sort of nothingness that doesn't sufficiently wrap up the myriad of lose ends that have been scattered before you during the course of the game. As the credits began to roll, I couldn't help but feel the developers had forgotten I was still expecting an ending, and had decided to simply go with the last minute plot device to close things off.
Up until that point though the game is an entirely different beast, one that reinvents itself with each level giving you a new mechanic or puzzle to work with. The variety is great, and certainly welcome, but it also creates Master Reboot's biggest problem, its terrible inconsistency. Moment to moment it manages to reach both impressive heights and dreadful lows, fluctuating between the things that work and mechanics that never should have been in the game at all.
This is most apparent when the developers attempt to juxtapose in horror elements which create aggravating instant kill scenarios that both break immersion, and are completely off from the emphasis on atmosphere and exploration that is found in most of the game. Along with these come arbitrary time limits that force you to continually replay segments, one off action sequences that aren't properly explained, and an abundance of odd elements that don't have time to be expanded upon into anything meaningful. I can appreciate all the ideas at play here, but find it hard to ignore how only about half of them actually work and fit within then game.
Similarly, the ascetic is one of the game's biggest assets, with a creative and engaging art direction and some stunning lighting effects. It's a huge shame then that so much of the game is inside cramped, dark environments, with blurry textures and some truly horrific pop-in (even for a game running Unreal Engine 3). When you're taken out of the buildings and hallways, it's truly a sight to behold, but these moments are fleeting to the point I purposely stayed longer in them to appreciate how beautiful they are.
Perhaps more aggravating than the discrepancies in the art design is the constant awkward cuts away from your perspective. Games like Bioshock and Half-Life proved that you can tell a great first-person story without the need to continually take control and the camera away from the player, so the fact Wales Interactive opted for such a graceless method of showcasing  important moments is frustrating, and greatly impacted my enjoyment. The off putting animated cutscenes that cap each memory were also an odd choice, feeling completely disconnected from the rest of the game even after you learn of the reason for them being there. Poor sound design is also disappointing, as the actual music and effects are quite good at immersing you in the experience, but were not even given a proper stereo directing to where everything sounds as if it's coming from the everywhere.
It might sound as if I abhorred Master Reboot, but in truth I actually enjoyed it to give a cautious recommendation despite its flaws. It's a surreal adventure with big ideas, many of which it disappointingly can't pull off, but when it does is truly fantastic. Wales Interactive has the definite makings of a great indie developer, with a uniquely imaginative vision that could lead to something great down the road. It is certainly disappointing that they also inhabit the other end of the indie spectrum, with a significant lack of polish and numerous amateurish design choices. Master Reboot has some great moments, and some truly terrible ones, but in the end I was still happy to have played it and look forward to what will come out of the newly christened developer. Hopefully they will be able to learn from their mistakes, and build off the strong foundation here.

After such a long time playing this game and trying to get into it, I think I've finally given up. Visually, it's pretty impressive for an RPG Maker game - at least I think it's RPG Maker since those resources (artwork and audio) come from RPG Maker XP. But the game just feels so very tedious, even for an open world kind of game, and there's no real rhyme or reason to anything you need to do or accomplish.
The combat felt okay at best, although the hit detection seemed off at times. It was also easy to fall into a pond or lake and then get stuck. In most cases, you fall into a pond or lake you'd lose some health and respawn on the land where you dropped in. But quite often the game would not remember where to respawn you at, and instead just keep respawning you right back in the pond or lake you fell into, and you're helpless to do anything but either reset the game or watch as your health slowly depletes away.
Constantly having to navigate back and forth across a large landmass without any means of fast travel was another time waster for me. NPC's dropped meaningless clues or would send you on a large fetch quest that often times had you going back and forth across various regions far too often to be any sort of fun.
The biggest challenge in the game is trying to locate all the correct cracks in the floor and walls that will actually do anything of value. You spend so much time straining your eyes for any sort of cracks in the earth you can hit with a pitchfork. And then you get an explosion spell that can open up entrances in the walls. Except half the time one crack in the wall that will reveal an entry way looks no different than the cracks in the walls that do not lead anywhere, and you spend so much time wasting spell power trying to blow everything up, only to then have to leave the dungeon or cave or whatever to recharge your MP.
Some might find it fun to spend aimless hours on a game like this, and that's fine. Maybe this is what all the hype surrounding open world games is all about. If it is, it's not for me.
If you're looking for something a bit more streamlined, and perhaps a bit more story and character driven, you might want to find a different game to play.

但是一旦拉到动作系统上和怪物设计上的话，我说句实话，和怪猎的差距不是一星半点
这系列的判定非常蛋疼，怪猎很多攻击判定是一次判定，而这游戏是整个动作内都有判定，这点非常重要，因为这几乎是个人认为设计得最蛋疼的地方，比如说风切的360攻击类比金狮子的360攻击，金狮子这招是可以通过翻滚和走位躲的，但是风切这招范围大，判定大不说，整个技能内都有判定，而且一旦发怒的风切，使用这招的频率不算低！躲起来十分要命，更比如说咒诅的甩尾，范围简直是大得惊人，而且角度和判定也是极其地令人摸不着头脑，说句实在话，在下级任务的时候，我大多数时候，压根连躲技能的欲望都很少，因为很多攻击的范围简直是令人摸不着头脑的大，在咒诅的甩尾之类的面前，水龙的异次元铁山靠，烬灭刃的二连大甩尾恐怕也就这回事了，我拿近战讨鬼，简直是打得一脸黑线
而更烦人的是这游戏动作特别慢，动作流畅感特别不好，尤其是太刀，对比隔壁怪猎的防性无限牙签太刀，我第一时间上手太刀的时候，我拿的真的不是大剑？？？？
最最重要的一点，这游戏的怪物血量，真的有点太厚了吧？成型以后还好，你御魂没成型的时候去刷上位怪，某些高级上位怪血量真是厚得简直令你说不出话来……对，我说的就是各种壮壮还有咒诅这些
说句实在话，这游戏我玩着体验其实并不算特别好，怪猎x我也算玩了几百个小时了，这游戏我现在玩了60个小时，我就没有我当初玩怪猎x的那种拿到手上就不愿意放下的感觉
如果真要给我评分，讨鬼2我最多只能给到80，但你要说我给不给好评，我还是要给的

If you want a game similar to Monster Hunter, look elsewhere. I cannot understand how this game is rated so positively by the community.
The graphics are clearly not a selling point.
The story is asinine, bland, stupidly catering to japanese anime tropes all the while lacking making the player a part of it. You have the illusion of choice with once in a while two ways to "respond" (ie, your souless husk of a character just nods) that has NO impact on anything happening. Even the "guards vs samurai" plot hook is a big illusion that you'll have any impact on the story. It's just abysmal.
But the worst offender IMO, is the GAMEPLAY. Utterly bad, monsters are HP punching bags with very limited and predictable movesets, and terrible AI. You litteraly stand there mashing your buttons until you charge enough to instantly cut parts, then repeat. The game is EXTREMELY easy, AI companions could finish it on their own without you touching the controller. Seems like you can be revived an inifite number of times too. The weapons are varied, but there is no weight behind any hits you make, and there is nothing to reward controls mastery.
I'll just stop there, honestly I find this game complete crap.

Repulsanoid is a casual atmospheric puzzle game that delivers something new in what I call, "meditative puzzle games".
Gameplay:
This is kind of tricky to describe. You basically control the rotation of a shape (first one is a cube) and you launch a ball inside it which starts bouncing inside the shape.
There are small blocks that you need to "hit" (and light up) with your ball, manipulating and planning its bouncing by rotating your shape and utilizing a few "special" abilities like moving the ball along with the shape while you have a button pressed.
Things get even more tricky as you clear the levels. For example you get a new type of block, which you need to hit, that switches back off if it gets hit a second time, then on again on third etc etc.
The point of the game is to light up all the blocks to clear the level.
I have not encountered this game concept before and it gets extra points for that. Originality is always good! The game encourages you to think in 3 dimensions and physics. I suggest watching a gameplay video to grasp exactly how it plays out.
Graphics:
The game looks very good. Amazingly more so than what you would expect for such a type of game. You don't play an abstract atmospheric puzzle game for the graphics but this one delivers on that department as well.
Music/Sound Design:
The sound is absolutely beatiful and relaxing. I've come to expect this kind of soundtrack on such games and it's part of why I call them "meditative". The soundtrack encourages you to relax and enjoy solving the level.
Pros:
-Pretty original concept.
-Looks much better than what games of this type typically do.
-Music soundtrack is perfect for this type of game.
Neutral:
-Some players may not enjoy this type of gameplay. It is rather hard to master. And I am pretty sure it could get easily annoying if not for the very relaxing soundtrack!
Cons:
I am always happy when I try a game and I can not find any cons when I squeeze my brain for anything worth mentioning.
This is one of those rare games.
Conclusion:
It is a must have if you enjoy these types of games.
Score:
Gameplay: 		9/10
Graphics: 		8/10
Music/Sound:          9/10
Concept/Story:	9/10

I have been debating whether or not this game deserves a positive or negative review for what really is a down the middle purchase right now and decided to be generous for once. The game is relatively short and I do not recommend it at the full price right now, but for a couple of dollars it is somewhat reasonable.
Currently there are 25 levels with varying difficulty and it took me about an hour to get through it. The only major issues I noticed did have an impact on gameplay, so it is worth noting. Texture issues can cause part of the screen to become blocked and obstruct the view of the puzzle. It happened a few times on different levels (as seen in the footage) and made solving one puzzle in particular annoying.
Fundamentally, the mechanics work and it can be challenging. There are currently three colored nodes that include blue (always on), yellow (triggered on or off if hit multiple times), and red (timed deactivation). Some powers are available to help aid in hitting the nodes, but you can complete the puzzles without them.
There is a disjointed story involved as well, which I hope gets fleshed out and organized better so it feels more coherent. Music is decent. Sound effects are minimal, but appropriate. UI is passable.
It isn't terrible, but it might not be enough content to warrant the price right now. Discounted, it is reasonable, but with puzzle games skill is a big factor.

If you come here only searching for the story - you won't be disappointed.
Just for shootouts? Well, you'll be satisfied.
But this game truly shines if you can just forget about it and revel in athmosphere of manslaughter and euphoria of synthwave beats.
Overall, if you didn't play the first game - It's still a solid game, except you won't understand a few callbacks and probably have just a bit harder time getting used to the gameplay. Hotline Miami 2 offers to you: A roster of unique characters with special personalities and abilities each(which also gives you story-gameplay integration in certain ways). When I say personalities, I should mention that the story, while broken down and mixed up, is surprisingly well-written, and accompanied by one of the best soundtracks in 2015's games. Yeah, the story. It's trying to get tracks for each level to follow overall mood not for the map you're playing, but rather for the story you're experiencing, which worked rather nicely for me. The gameplay itself depends on what you're trying to achieve. First time player? Entered a hardmode just for the achievement, not the challenge? You won't have too much fun. Grab a gun, shoot a few times, hope you hit, grab another, rinse, repeat, with certain layer of strategy when there are black fatties involved. If you do try to get the best score, though... It changes, oh boy it changes a lot. Taking risks, daring moves, booming synth bass in your ears, finding a perfect plan and executing it takes time, feels enraging AND satisfying when you finally get that A+(or S even).
Overall: Great story, living and breathing characters, One of best OSTs of 2015, smooth gameplay, one of examples of game being a form of art.
But there may be some minor bugs, plus the game can be somewhat enraging or confusing.
Worth your money, especially on sale. Don't forget to grab the soundtrack DLC.

The plot is basically retreading some of the same territory as Vexille, Appleseed, and other japanese anime movies (seriously, if the boom Boom Satellites or Paul Oakenfold were in the game you'd suspect there was just a group of movie maker buddies bouncing around from studio to studio out there). I don't even make the comparison lightly, Dan (main character) is even voiced by the same voice actor as a main character for Vexille, and another character is voiced by Laura Bailey (of many anime, Nier, Saint's Row, and Ingress fame), though she's more Helena from RE6 than The Boss from SR here.
Again, it's not perfect, but you can easily dump 9 hours or so into it in a playthrough without even getting into multiplayer or a new game. That being said, there are some mildly annoying port elements that haven't been worked out, either -- keyboard and mouse layout didn't impress me so I used the 360 controller, only there doesn't appear to have been the forethought to include 360 keyboard controls displayed, so I had to learn what on the controller corresponded to keyboard inputs on the screen. Made for a REALLY annoying QTE at the end of the game.
That being said, I still thoroughly enjoyed it. If you're wary of the praises being sung for this game, wait for a sale -- I certainly did, and it was absolutely worth it. As someone else said, it has some Buddy Cop elements to it with Dan and Bo, as well as themes similar to Appleseed or Vexille. I wouldn't necessarily say it does some of those themes as well as Ghost in the Shell, but it's a fun game that addresses its points, wraps things up, and makes for a fun cover-based and often spectacle shooter (think SR crazy moments, CoD scripted moments, etc -- some on-rails events to change pace from simply moving forward and shooting everything). And did I mention that since all of the enemies are Terminator-style robots, the game really lets things get chunky with bullet damage? It's pretty enjoyable all around, I would argue, blemishes included. Just make sure you have a controller handy in case you felt the way I did about the K&M controls.

What do I think of
? Well, I'm not sure what the best words to describe it are. This is an action-adventure game, reminiscent of
and its many clones. You're the young man destined to save the land from evil, and so on and so forth. This makes for a story that's deeply rooted in tradition. But hey, tradition is good. As for the game itself... eh... I guess I would describe it as "in-offensive" and "oddly compelling". That doesn't exactly sound like a thrilling or even confident description for this game, but it's the best that I can muster.
As expected of an action-adventure, you'll wander the world and seek enormously-powerful objects, while fighting monsters and solving puzzles. How The fall of gods goes about this is pretty interesting. The world of Ergia isn't massive, but it is very dense. There are a lot of houses and caves to explore, each serving some sort of purpose. As you progress, the tools you obtain will open up previously unavailable areas, which lead to optional yet welcome rewards. This satisfying game-play loop is bolstered by a thoroughly pleasant soundtrack.
The dangers you'll face are almost entirely ineffective. As you explore, you'll earn experience, which can be used to improve your stats. Even early on, you'll find yourself grossly overpowered, and monsters never pose a threat. Keeping your HP and MP up is simple, due to the large number of restoration items, you'll recieve from fresh monster corpses. Most of the bosses are dealt with by figuring out their weakness. It's an extension of the puzzle-solving you employ to get through the dungeons, and it works well enough. Altogether, the combat mechanics are really poor, but you learn to ignore them after awhile.
has a ton of spells, too many in my opinion. Most of these spells are only used a few times over the course of the entire game. There are even a couple that are so useless; you were probably better off never finding them in the first place. The same could be said for the weapons and items. Your inventory will become bloated with quite a bit of junk. The density of this game works against itself, especially towards the end. When you find a spell and it only serves its purpose in one or two instances, then it might as well have been a key with fancy special effects.
The likelihood you'll persevere is exactly why I use words like "oddly-compelling" and "in-offensive" to describe this game. Its combat isn't particularly great, and the constant barrage of collectibles erodes its charming qualities. Still, I found myself entranced by this adventure. The lack of difficulty works in the game's favor, since I could put it down and revisit it whenever I had a few minutes to spare. Sometimes good game design is knowing your limitations. I know I would have dropped this game much earlier; if monsters were capable of killing the hero in a few hits, falling in a hole resulted in instant death, or that progress couldn't be saved at almost any time.
Do I recommend
? Honestly, I wish that there was something in-between the thumbs-up and the thumbs-down. I stuck with this game to see it to the end, and I didn't hate it, but is that really enough for a recommendation? On the other hand, while the game suffers from a number of issues, the adventure elements are pretty solid. Rather than torment myself further, I'm going to break it down. if you're looking for a game that is as good as Zelda, let alone better, then this isn't it, not by a long-shot. If your expectations are low, and you don't mind dealing with some jank, then you could be in for a pleasant surprise.
No guarantees though.

The Fall of Gods is a small indie action RPG game, very similar to the old Zelda titles: your view is from above, all in 2D sprites. The action is also very similar: swing your sword to kill the foes, cut bushes, break jars, collect hearts and coins. The new thing is the skills: sort of spells you can assign to the trigger buttons, the mana points you use slowly replenish.
The good:
The store page says that it's not a full support for the controller, but it's because it doesn't work in the main menu. During the game the controls are perfect.
You can save anytime, and in 4 slots.
A lot of places where you can heal in the beginning: the game doesn't try to murder you as soon as you press 'New game'.
The map system is awesome and very well thought. The caves that you've already looted are marked as 'Done'. Plus it's basically the real screens zoomed out so it's not a theorical map leading you 'somewhere on the North East, behind the big rock'.
When you pass behind a tree or something, your character have an outline. Very handy.
Day and night cycle, yup I kid you not.
The bad:
The foes seem to have telepathic powers and constantly agroo you, even through the walls.
The sound options are very bare: no way to change the volume of music, it's either on or off.
Some actions could have had a bit more animations and sounds, like casting a spell or breaking a jar.
The graphics look a bit blurred, because of the zoom I guess. It does get a bit tiring to the eyes.
The game hooked me up from the beginning, I went exploring the map, finding some small hidden caves - which got marked as done - so nifty! The night fell and some ghosts appeared, and they weren't OP! Then had my first dungeon, under the water where you have to take a breath at some oxygen chimneys and you go around solving small puzzles and killing enraged mermaids; how cool is that?
I totally recommend this game, fun with a lot of original details. Definetly a keeper in my huge library!

Master Reboot is a bit of an odd game. In both an obvious way and a non-obvious way. Essentially, the idea behind Master Reboot is that you are in a future where people can upload their memories, personality, and other traits into a cloud service, and then family and friends can visit these memories or download and install these peoples personalities into robotic shells to continue living with them if they desire. However, there was a crash in the system that caused the whole cloud service to have a reboot, which lost and corrupted some data. And now you play someone delving into the memories of someone with said corrupted data looking for something.
It's basically a walking simulator experience game, except not in a typical sense. The game is split-up into memories, with each memory being a stage. They're called memories, but they're more like surreal dreams, with a lot of odd and abstract imagery and logic. Each memory also is different, and not just in themes, but with what you do. Some are literal walking simulators, but others have elements like puzzles, or things you have to avoid or sneak past or else you'll die.
The stages have some good variety. Some are more relaxing, like this beach stage where you look for items with a metal detector. Others are a bit obtuse with what you must do, like this one amusement park stage you attend too. Some take on a horror tone, with creepy atmosphere and things trying to kill you.
On that note, my favorite stage, and something that was legitimately scary, was the plane memory. With memories in the game like a hospital and school and graveyard, you'd think one of those would be the scariest stage (and they do have some creepy factor, to be sure), but the actual scariest stage was definitely the plane one. It scared me pretty bad a few times, and this is coming from someone who plays a lot of horror games.
That's the thing I think this game does best. Atmosphere. I think the people who will enjoy this game the most are those who like atmosphere and maybe some oddities in their games. It was a bit longer than I was anticipating, but I did like it. Not the best thing I've ever played, but I liked the variety of tasks and settings, even if the basic concept of the game's story was more interesting than the story that develops in the game. But I'd say worth checking out if you're into this kind of thing.
