First I would like to start by saying that this game can be a lot of fun (when it works).  If the game is on sale for 75% or more and you have some money laying around this game is one to consider.  However this is not to say that the game is perfect, in all actuality the game is FULL of glitches and has some very frustrating AI problems.
Pros
~You can create and modify your own creatures, buildings, and vehicles.
~The idea for the game/what they tried to make is a cool idea.
Cons
Cell Stage
~Currents will bring you down to a snails pace, while having no effect on other cells.
~If you play as an herbivore, when you find plants to eat the game auto spawns a swarm of herbivores to come strip it of edible parts.
Creature Stage
~Once you have made a few worlds all the creatures you made in those worlds (and every single step of their evolutionary line) will appear in any new worlds you create.  So if you max out your creatures stats in order to survive, in the next world you will find the maxed out creatures you previously made are there and make completing the creature stage much more difficult.
~In the end most of the creatures end up looking about the same if you go for maxed stats.
~Companion AI are constantly running in front of you blocking you from getting to where you're trying to go
~Companion AI will go sit in front of hostile creatures until they are attacked
~Companion AI will push you out of range during a fight and attack random non targeted creatures
~Epic Creatures spawn near/on your final nesting site and auto target YOU.  (I have personally had 5 epics spawn within close range of my nest and kill me as soon as my creature was controllable, this went on a good 10 minutes and was only solved by changing out parts for a higher level sneak ability)
~Epic creatures tend to also spawn and target anything you show interest in at the end of Creature stage.
~Part way through Creature Stage a UFO appears that follows you around abducting any creature you try to interact with.
Tribal Stage
~Even if you set your stance to friendly so you won't attack other tribes, if the other tribes do something your tribe members don't like they will attack and pursue them.
~Constant traffic jams at your food storage.
~The "clothing" you can put on your creatures rarely fits or looks good on them.
~Same as in the Creature stage, a UFO appears and follows the Tribal Chief, abducting your domesticated animals if the Chief is near your village.
Civilization Stage
~Vehicles sent on missions have a terrible tendency to go through areas that have Epic Creatures in them, I have personally seen them go the long way ardor mountains so that they would go by an Epic.
~Epic Creatures tend to move toward highly trafficked areas, following vehicles to your cities.
Space Stage
~Other races are hell bent on setting up colonies on all the stars around yours.
~Other races are constantly demanding that you pay tribute to them when you are just starting out.
Galactic Adventures
~The game rely on you and the community to make objects, props, worlds, and everything else to make these adventures
~The game only comes with a couple pre made Adventures and you only get points for doing the adventure once.
~Almost all of the available Adventures online are incomplete and unplayable, meaning you can't get any points for them and you fail the mission that you were sent on.
~Most of the adventures made by Players are only worth 3-5 points, where as leveling up your Captain costs hundreds and hundreds of points, more with every level up.
~Props are made with ships and buildings which means that the ugly pie you made for your adventure can show up as a building in Civilization and Space Stage.
~ There is no way to stop these props from showing up as buildings or vehicles in your game without banning them, but if you ban them then you can no longer play the Adventure the part was in.
Building Mode
~The tutorials are lacking in how to descriptions for moving/changing parts.  Unless you read the entire manual you won't find how to do this stuff, and when you do find it it's a single tiny note.  For those who get the game you use (ctrl + A) for asymmetrical parts and press and hold (tab) to open up the expanded movement/placement menu.
~Creatures won't stop moving and that makes it hard to pull back and look over the creature your working on.
The Game itself
~Crashes/Freezing is common, if you don't save often you will lose all your work and have to start over from scratch.
~Saving just before the game crashes will make the planet/save file freeze/crash when you try to reload it meaning you once again have to delete the planet/ save file and start from scratch.
~You are constantly loosing your connection to your EA account and have to restart the game to get back on.
I feel like I am just ranting here and apologize.  I do enjoy the game as anyone who looks at the hours I have put into it can tell you (259.0 Hours when I wrote this, and easily double that on Galactic Adventure and the Creepy Cute pack, 730 hours of gameplay all together)  That's all I can think to say, I hope it was helpful to someone.

On the plus side, it fills a weekend extremely easily, and there is some sense of satisfaction about taking a low level driver and bringing him (and the team) up through the ranks.
I would recommend the game if you enjoy being slightly repetitive, and not having full control over everything. I will keep playing it, but it will never be one of my 'will always go back to, time after time' games as Tropico/Theme Hospital are.

I have mixed feelings about this port. On one hand, it's still Metal Slug 3, which is good and bad. It's good because Metal Slug 3 is still (for the most part) a fun experience that can be enjoyed with friends. It's bad because The boss fight for Mission 4 is still as cheap as a can of tuna. Overall, though, unless you absolutely do NOT enjoy very difficult arcade games, MS3 is a blast.
On the other hand, the framerate drops in this port really killed the experience for me. It runs perfectly fine on consoles and handhelds, so why is it a computer aimed to run video games with much higher graphical fidelity is having problems running MS3 smoothly? This should not be the case for Metal Slug 3.
It's difficult for me to recommend this at full price. Unless you are a die-hard Metal Slug fan that really wants to play it on PC, I'd say wait for a sale or wait for an update that addresses the framerate drops. For now, I would say wait on it.

This game certainly has its charms. Even though I often tend to stay away from RPGMaker games, I bought this one precisely because it chooses another approach than so many other of its kind. Instead of boring me to death with the gazillionth implementation of your typical run of the mill JRPG it chooses to utilize a combat system that brings the player back to the times where "Secret of Mana", "Terranigma" and "Illusion of Time" created some of your fondest gaming memories.
Sure, it does have its quirks (the on occasions rather strange grammar for example), and the bossfights (as far as I played so far) are rather simple (choose the right weapon/magic and smash/shoot/blast it to smithereens), but all in all I feel pleasantly reminded of the games I mentioned above.
In a nutshell: I can recommend this game to everyone who liked classics like "Secret of Mana", "Terranigma" and "Illusion of Time" and who needs a well earned break from all the typical JRPG like games out there in favor of a refreshing (albeit in no way new) combat system, where you beat your enemies yourself instead of waiting for your character to do it for you.

With a style resembling something like Tron mixxed with classic 90's low-poly VR worlds, the graphics of Master Reboot do well to immerse you in the game environment. Minimalistic, but consistant.
Without spoiling anything, the game throws you, the player, into the 'soul cloud' where peoples conciousness can be uploaded. Chased by a rogue AI through the levels, you're tasked with exploring fragments of your past to uncover memories that piece your life back together.

It's a thumbs up and I've had lots of fun playing with it, but there is a significant downside in that there just isn't much game in the actual race. And you spend a lot of time in the races. Your in race decisions basically boil down to tire choice and when to pit. 90% of your in race performance is the car and driver. You can screw up things with poor pit choices, but after a while it's pretty clear what to do and you're just watching the game play itself out.
The meta game is interesting. Lots of choices on who to hire, managing contracts, etc. It's well done. To some extent, it's just a matter of grinding races for money and watching your team inexorably rise as you buy better, well, better everything. But it's a fun grind.
Not sure I'd pay the full $35, I got it on a 50% sale, but then again I look at the hours played and I couldn't complain if I had.

Both frustrating and entertaining at the same time, this is a game that needs a good solid few hours put into it to really explore the finer details of running a successful team. The fact that if you have a good pit strategy then you can be well placed at the end of the race even if you don't have the best/fastest car, makes it all the more entertaining.
I put in a good number of the hours when the free play weekend was on and, when it finished, decided to purchase it only to discover the 50% off deal had ended when the free weekend had and, to be brutally honest, it's not a £24.99 game. For that kind of money I'd be expecting to drive the cars myself rather than just the 'overview control' of managing general driving style and pit stops.
That being said, I still would recommend it, just get it when it's on sale!

This is the best racing management game to come out in many, many years.  That doesn't actually tell you much because the last good one came out sometime around the time that Windows 98 was considered an upgrade...
GOOD:
Accurate representation of how difficult it is to maintain a profitable racing team
Variety of driver quirks that add depth to the drivers
Race strategy and the ability to properly calculate changes to it are very rewarding when you get it right
Building up a terrible team into a championship winning team is also very rewarding
There was a mobile game with the same title but this game is a completely different experience and feels nothing like it in a very, very good way.
NOT SO GOOD:
Visuals - It's not really very pretty and feels like it should run better than it does relative to said graphics
Sometimes cars will all fall into a long conga line to go through a corner and it looks really weird (think safety car bunching while green flagged)
OTHER:
Some reviews talk about crashes.  I have experienced only one in a hundred hours of playing.  I emailed the developer about it and got an actual human response that they were working on a fix.  There was a patch within a week and I have not crashed since.  Maybe I was just lucky, but I've been following the development of this game for over a year and they do seem to genuinely care about their customers and their product.
Some reviews talk about the game being boring.  It's a racing management game.  You run the team and make strategic decisions about developing your headquarters and car as well as tactical decisions during the race.  Some races are really exciting nail biters, some are just fast forwarding until you need to make a pit stop.  That's the nature of racing.  When building up a last place team, though, the ability to simulate a race without running it would be nice, especially since you know you're going to come in last place anyway.
Some reviews complain about lack of multiplayer.  I totally agree.  For as much as I like this game, I'd have twice the hours played if it could be played with others.  I'd have at least two friends who would have bought it by now if it had that feature.  Perhaps this will be in a future DLC or a sequel...
IN SHORT:
I really like what this game offers.  If you enjoy race strategy, this game will keep you entertained for many hours.  Yes, it's the only real option in the genre, and it isn't perfect, but it's good.  I also paid full price and think it was well worth the money.
NOTE:
I haven't played the GT Series stuff at all even though I own it.  I can't tell you how good it is, but some of the options it adds to the game are really nice.  Also, I haven't even looked at the workshop for this game.  I'll do that after I get bored with what the developers have to offer in the game (probably at least a hundred hours of play from now).
FURTHER EDIT:
This game has been out for nearly a year and I'm still putting more time into it.  The challenge of getting to the top and staying there is still as thrilling as when the game was released.

This game ia absolutely gripping, and I've been binging on it for a week now.  I'm dimly aware of an expansion I was really looking forward to, and a Humble Monthly that has unlocked, but I don't care - Predator Racing needs me, and I need them.
Following the advice from another review, I chose to manage Predator Racing, the bottom team in the bottom league.  It's been quite a ride, and aspects of the game have only just started to make sense to me, 58 hours in.  It SEEMS innocent enough - recruit and appoint drivers, fit out cars, decide on a pit strategy and use it.
But things keep happening.  Safety cars come out and destroy the lead you worked to build - or fail to.  Rain looks like it's clearing up, but sometimes it's a pause in the downpour, not an end to it. And then there's the fact that (unlike most games with 'manager' in the title) this game is simulating a managerial career.  So decisions that might annoy the owner might also get me fired.
After 3 seasons, I've promised the chairman that we'll finish 7th this year.  (How anyone gets the achievement for a season 2 championship with Predator is beyond me at the moment.)  Most of our long-term investments have paid off, and there's one or two races in the coming year that we might actually win.  Wish me luck :)

It can be a bit daunting at first, but it soon reveals itself to be more of a simcade as opposed to a hardcore management sim, which is both a pro and a con, I suppose.
There are quite a few areas it could be improved (a review probably isn't the place to go into that, though), and so if an MM2 is on the cards, then I expect it could go on to be one of the must-have titles for fans of management sims.
Motorsport Manager, though, is a great foundation to work from and, if I didn't know it, I wouldn't have been able to tell it had originated on the mobile-gaming platform. In fact, I didn't, and I couldn't.
Check out some vids online of it being played if you're unsure (there are a few of them), but if you're on this page then there's a chance you're already somewhat interested in something like this anyway.

The game is very decent, a replacement to Monster Hunter on PC. Such key feature is the Mitama system, especially in the 2nd game, which allows player to develops their own style and improve on their gears, to me, this is the best part of the game, there are no meta build, just unique ones, which is a boost to the multiplayer experience.

To sum up, i see a bright future to the series if they manage to keeps up with they designs and add some more contents into the game.

Long story short, the bugs and tedious nature of parts of the game are more than thoroughly mitigated by having one of the best character building systems I've ever played. Monster hunter with flashier combat and a magical flair.
Pros: Everyone else can talk about everything else, the biggest reason I'd reccomend this game is the character building.
You equip mitama (spirits of dead heroes) to one of three slots: weapon, defense, and demon hand. There are roughly 10 types, and the type you equip determines the skills you have in combat. Your weapon determines your basic attack abilities/buffs, your defense gives you a utility/defensive skill to activate, and the demon hand gives you an ultimate of sorts.
So that's about 1000 combinations right there. The real meat of character building in Toukiden 2 is that you pick up to 3 boosts from each mitama you have equipped. These boosts change the way you play significantly. As an example, one of my early builds was an elemental archer that used an ability called homing arrow. It used the SPT (spirit) mitamas primarilly and equipped a handful of buffs to elemental damage, homing arrow damage, and others. Pretty simple.
Now that I have well over 100 mitama's unlocked, I spend most of my time in this game trying to find the most absurd way to kill demons. Poison builds, near-death builds, and a particularly fun one that involves almost completely nullifying the cooldowns of all the casted abilities. If you've liked the character building in games such as Dragon Quest, you'll love the deep multiclass ability.
Cons: This game is buggy. There's no hiding its a port of a game optimized for consoles. I skipped the first game because it was a god-awful port and almost did the same on this one. No support for the more rare screen resolutions, NO MOUSE SUPPORT, and multiplayer bugs out on me a lot and I often have to restart to get the game going.
Let me say one of those again. NO MOUSE SUPPORT. Nada. Do not buy this game if you don't have a gamepad. I use an xbox controller and it works fine, I imagine a steam controller would work too but I haven't tested it out, check other reviews for that.
The fun of this game outweighed the flaws. I love deep character building and this game has one of the better styles of character building I've seen. The DLC missions are a bit pricey but add some new oni and more importantly some missions that are a lot better for farming materials than some of the base games.
Buy it, try it, if you can get it working within the 2 hour trial period then I highly reccomend continuing to play until you've acquired a substantial collection of weapons and mitama to try out.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

TLDR:
Neat game if you can stand a few minor issues.
Let me first say that this game has come a long way from when I first played it a year or so ago, and I feel it is at the very least worth a try. This is one of the few F2P games that I feel has consistently improved over the course of it's lifetime.
There are still a few glaring problems that i'm sure you've noticed other people pointing out in their reviews, such as 1hko laser-accurate snipers (which can be sort of countered with the reduced damage perk). Tanks and Planes are genuinely scary as they should be, however you will occasionally get one of those matches where you can't even spawn without a High-Explosive shell rammed up your♥♥♥♥♥or a bomb dropped right into your pants. Some weapons are very clearly imbalanced as all hell. And by far the biggest issue is starting out, you will be fodder, a mear meat dummy to distract said tanks and planes so the real commandos can move in. Your guns will have the effectiveness of a squirt gun in hell, with the accuracy of a stormtrooper (quite literally if you play as the germans).
All that being said I have had a ton of fun with this game, and will most likely continue to so long as good updates, while sparse, keep coming. If you can get over the fact that you are fodder, learn to advance carefuly, learn to actually line up your shots, and stick with it, you'll eventually unlock better weapons and the game will drastically change once you get your first automatic or bolt action weapon.
The game turned upside down when I eventually unlocked an LMG, ♥♥♥♥ being a sniper, I sprayed down planes with that thing and hot damn it felt good. Upgrading my bolt action to a 1hko was difficult, but again the game changed now that I could counter-snipe. Play to the strengths of your current gear, don't be like one my dumbass friend who tries to fight in close quarters with an unmodded bolt action then complains the game sucks when he gets sprayed down by smgs. The best advice I can think to give to someone starting fresh, is to fight on the control points as much as possible, actually use cover, and don't forget to crouch when firing or you won't hit♥♥♥♥♥♥ Hide in a corner like a little sissy if you must, this is war, you do what you have to. Add in the fact that everything you do on a control point multiplies your score by almost 5x, and you will quickly unlock better stuff. Also don't forget to mod your weapons, especially for damage since your semi-auto rifle you start with can go from a 4 hit kill to a 2 hit with like 2 mods.
As far as "pay 2 win" goes, I would say this game is on the lower spectrum, yeah you can progress faster, get an extra perk slot, and an extra equip slot, but only the perk slot really makes a difference and even then you still need to earn the perks, and good luck using that extra equip slot without going over your equip load, you could probably at most fit binoculars or a knife with that extra slot, so yeah not worth it imo when you already have a rifle, anti-tank grenades, and a pistol. Pretty much everything, even skins and acadamy trained soldiers can be bought with in game currency, so there's no need to buy gold unless you want the boosts.
Damn this review was longer than I thought it was going to be. I like this game, give it a shot, if it isn't your thing then it isn't your thing. It's that kind of game.

The most important feedback: I am having a lot of fun playing this game.
Since some time the biggest problem that I have is not to find games with a lot of realism, but games with a lot of fun. I have to say that MM lacks sometime of realism, but maybe is exactly for that reason that I can play it for hours and still wanting to go on for "just another race".
The atmosphere is great and the usage of appropriate mods helps you to feel competing in real life championships. The translations are wonderful; I am playing in italian and I feel that they didn't just translated the texts, but used slangs that are typical in my language.
I find the mechanism to improve the car during the season challenging and clear, but also in this case not that much realistic. I don't know if this is a conscius decision to make the game more enjoyable, but I have to say that it works and that I guess I am enjoying it more than a full realistic  process.
There are still some possible improvements that should be considered also at this not realistic simulation status:
- maybe is a small thing, but during the free pratice there are no ways to know how many laps will last the race! Since during the free pratice you can gain experience with the typres type, it would make sense to have know how long will be the race, in order to plan which tyres you want to test.
- I played two season now and basically it never happened that one of my drivers did during the qualifying a better time in the second run than in the first one. That makes still less sense if you consider that normally at the end of the session the grip is higher!
- it would be great if it would be possible to copy the balance of a car to the other one and above all to copy the balance from the previous year! After finding the right setting in 2016 I don't have the will to start from scratch for the 2017... I would prefere to use the set of the previous year as basis (I am pretty sure that it is how it works in real race as well :) ). You could also consider how much time a driver raced in a specific circuit to improve his/her level of experience.
- the contract negotations are horrible! I understand that you have to pay a penalty if you take a driver/engineer from another team while the older contract is still running, but you should be able to close a contract for the future. And also I think that it would be better to have more staff than just an engineer and two mechanics: it would make more challenging having a five star team.
- I would like to have more transparency to understand how the car for the next year will be influenced by the development of the car for the current one.

The horror in Layers of Fear is the many cliches the hack developers crammed into the game. There isn't a single original thought that went into this —you've seen it all before: dolls, door slams, flying objects, endless corridors, an insane protaganist. Attempts to break realism are trite: you'll encounter large objects floating through a void —I can't recall any other surreal moments. And with the entire game taking place inside an old house, each room looking like the last, the game's visuals will bore you.
Gameplay consists of walking from one room into the next. Sometimes you have to interact with a lever. There aren't any puzzles, no challenge. After completing the game I learned that there are three endings. I found the easiest one, but the two others both require you to autistically search for specific collectibles —retrieving some while leaving others— and interacting with or ignoring other aspects of the game world (such as pushing a wheelchair from one side of the room to the other).
If you want horror, watch a film like Jacob's Ladder, or Rosemary's Baby (which this game has more in common with stylistically than, say, The Texas Chainsaw Massacre). Or, better yet, get into gothic and dark romantic literature. F.E.A.R. is a masterpiece first-person shooter, but it also functions better as horror — ironically, many of its segments surpass anything in Layers of Fear in ambition and visual design. I also recommend playing the first-person shooter horror and puzzle game Realms of the Haunting.

This game is a really good game, it is however, very directed towards thinkers. The story is one you have to be thinking about the whole time, as it's given to you in pieces, and the details at first are very confusing because of how general they are, later though, they get more detailed and as you start actively piecing them together, the core of the story starts becoming known.
A fair bit of warning is that the story requires a decent amount of interpretation on your own part. As well as this is a puzzle game, it is very well done, and some of them you really have to think for. This also goes to say that it's got horror in the mix, and I'm glad to say there are some parts where generally I felt pretty scared, and the environment and audio does a decent job of adding to the horror (not to mention the game does some pretty scary things too, however it's something to be experienced, so I'll just leave it at that.)
At first I thought it was going to be something like Amnesia, where you're gonna have to run and hide from the spooky scary peoples... Glad to tell you that's not the case, maybe there is one instance where it feels like that, but thankfully it's not painful to get past. Don't let that make you think that this game isn't scary though, it was at least to me, generally a decent horror game where I felt anxiety at parts to continue, however the story is what kept me moving, I wanted it to finish, and I feel that this was the best way to tell the story for the style of game that it is.
It meant sitting down after playing it, and having to think about all the pieces and put them together piece by piece to get to the point where I could comprehend the plot in its entierty, like a book. It was more then likely in my opinion the best way to tell the story, not only that but the mental workout of piecing things together while solving puzzles really gave me this feeling of satisfaction and giddiness. I haven't had to sit down and piece together a story in a long time, as well as I haven't played a good puzzle game that didn't involve trying to break space and time, in a very very long time. So it was a very nice refreshing change from the usuall games I have been playing.
I would most certainly recommend this game if you like thinking, especially when it comes to story, and enjoy puzzles.

TL;DR: This is a bad port of Metal Slug 3, overall. Be warned that the replayability the series boasts depends greatly on how much you enjoy trying to get into the top of the leaderboards for score.
If you're into emulation, you've probably come across the Metal Slug series before. If not, you may still know these if you're from an older generation: the time when people would gladly use high-denomination coins to play masterpiece games on huge machines. If you're younger than that and/or don't really care about emulation, then this is probably the crappiest starting point if you want to discover the universe of Metal Slug. If you want the bottom line, scroll to it.
If you want to know some of the finer points of why this is a bad port, Steam user Aulbath has made an incredibly accurate review of Metal Slug 3 for Steam (before many updates were made to the game) on the following address
. You should read his review if you want some of the finer points of what was really wrong with the port at its Steam launch, even if some of it may be outdated.
Before I begin, I'd like you to scroll to see some of the other reviews and see not what they say, but only if they recommend and how long they played the game. Metal Slug games may be rather short, but take into account its theoretical replay value and consider how long the upvoters have clocked into it knowing many of the reviews have been made significantly close to the date the game was released on Steam (that is to say, people aren't enjoying its replay value that much).
Not only can anyone with half a brain detect that this is a bad port which, as far as I know, was ported into phones before being ported into PCs, but it's an annoying port at that. The biggest gripe I have is the lack of options to let you play at a good resolution full-screened, and until some time recently the way the game handled credits (continues) was in my opinion nonsensical for this day and age.
Metal Slug 3 is also one of the weakest in the Metal Slug series, from my memories. True, lots of vehicles were added in comparison to the first two games, and it's fun being an almost-immortal zombie that can't handle being puked upon, and it probably does boast the most branching of level segments of the series, and you probably will have an enjoyable time playing it... but honestly, the game is somewhat less interesting overall comparing to the classic Metal Slug 2; this is particularly true if you've played some of the latter games in the series as well.
I'm glad that I got this through a game bundle, where I got 5 more games along with it for just 5$. I'm going to simply say this: the game isn't worth the money, maybe only on a 80% discount. Why? Yes, it does have online multiplayer. But at the same time, people have to be on your friends list to play with you; this makes sense, in a way, since you probably don't usually want to team up with people that die each time a boss even budges, but they could have that and an option to partner up with randoms. I haven't tried multiplayer yet because of it, since I'd have to pester someone into buying a game that I'm already telling you should be bought at 80% of Steam's listed price.
If you really want a decent Metal Slug experience without using emulation, try getting hold of a GameBoy Advance or PlayStation Portable and their respective versions of Metal Slug: hitpoints based system with persistent upgrades is much better than the continues deal, somewhat. If you really really want to play Metal Slug online, I'd go with Mercenary Kings instead; it's a good homage game, and you'll feel that there's a point going on (albeit sometimes poorly conveyed) instead of trying to get a high score that gets thrown down the gutter every time you need a continue. Mercenary Kings also allows for 4-player co-op and you don't usually feel like you're hammering the "fire" key into needing a new keyboard to chew at a tank/building/whatever. And hey, if you do try emulation, just skip Metal Slug 3 unless you really need to play through the events of the game (which you might feel tempted to if you play the more recent titles).
For the diehard fans, you probably didn't need my review and you'll buy it anyway since you also probably already know the game, better than myself even.
For achivement hunters, this game still has some fairly hard achievments that might hurt your 100%, including passing the game without spending 1 continue (3 lives).
For everyone else, avoid Metal Slug 3; final mission, start.
Edit reason: With updates to the game, it became somewhat less annoying and the review's tone reflects it. However, I still consider you should skip this game for being one of the weaker titles of Metal Slug.

Is this game perfect? No, by all means it could do with a little more features.  But is it a playable claymation shooter with 25 areas, 5 bosses, 4 different ships (each with it's own set of powerups), and local coop that supports gamepads/joysticks? Well yes, yes it is.
There isn't a storyline but arcade shooters don't really require one.  The music and sound effects aren't great but the loops on each stage sort of grow on you as you albeit slowly fly your way through each stage.  The claymation is nostalgic and at least well done - even with a lot of repeating enemies there were new hazards sprinkled in even up to the last area.
Each stage is split into 5 areas, with each area taking up 3~5 minutes of time and the boss at the final area taking up another 5 minutes on average.  The total gametime is only about 2-3 hours if the entire game is finished in one run.
I didn't have any issues with the game that others are mentioning (my sound comes out from both speakers) and adjusting it using my volume mixer worked just fine - Windows 8 64-bit, 3.3 ghz Quad Core, 8GB RAM (though the specs might be higher than needed I think the issue for many people are compatibility issues of some sort as this isn't very taxing).  I never crashed with this game yet and the controls ingame work just fine for my mouse and even the keyboard control scheme worked without any errors (I didn't test the joypad).
I wouldn't mind having a few more options in the settings outside of Music On and Off but it's ultimately passable and very simple to just jump right into the game.  This arcade shooter has just enough to keep you entertained even if the difficulty is fairly low - if you're expecting a bullet hell then this isn't the game for you.
The stages are varied backdrops from the Artic snowlands, deserts to greenier pastures, while the hazards in each stage are a bit on the blander side.
The enemy AI is nothing new for players who tried shooters before with predictable flying patterns and the bosses that provide weapon powerups periodically to speed them along if you don't miss the fodder provided that drop them.  Overall there isn't much challenge here but just enough for the average gamer to finish the game if they are willing.

What can I say? The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind is one of the greatest RPGs ever made, from arguably the greatest RPG series ever made. It's vast, and it feels like it never ends. The many hours you spend playing weave together an incredibly detailed and enriching story that is part of a much larger cosmology that connects and encompasses the entire Elder Scrolls series. You can spend hours just reading the in-game books alone. If you are even remotely interested in role-playing or adventure games, then this is a must-have, as well as its descendents, Oblivion and Skyrim (as of 2013).
For those who are more familiar with Oblivion or Skyrim, this is a more difficult game with a much steeper learning curve. Your character will move slowly at first, will run out of fatigue very quickly (unlike in Skyrim, fatigue is depleted by running and is much more of a factor in how successful all your actions will be), and you will be unable to carry or store much loot. It will take a while to level up and increase your skills at first, but be patient, and you will soon notice that things really do get easier.
Morrowind also seems considerably longer than either Oblivion or Skyrim, because there are many more factions you can join, and each has several questgivers (assuming you want more than just the main quest, which is also lengthy). The other thing you need to know is that there is NO fast-travel in this game. Be prepared to spend a lot of time traveling on foot. But these things just add to the challenge and depth of this classic game. When given a dungeon to explore, you won't get a convenient arrow pointing you to the exact location; often, you'll just be told "it's southwest from X" and it's up to you to find it. This adds to the realism and the immersion.
As if the vanilla game weren't enough, there are two expansion packs included in the GOTY edition that are bound to add many enjoyable hours to your experience, as well as tons of free mods out there to spice things up. The price you pay for this game is nothing compared to the months or years of solid, fun role-playing it provides.
If you like RPGs, give it a chance. It grew on me, and if you're open to the ideas it presents, I'm certain it'll grow on you too.

What does it matter that you can take more damage when Borg cubes in STF's will hit you for 800k damage with their invisible torpedos? Or when tactical people can hit a button and make their weapons do 200% more damage than yours so they destroy everything fast, do the most damage, and as a result, get all the best loot.
Loot. Any and all of the good loot is trapped in the "upper class". You can only get it if you have other high-value items to trade/sell, but first you need high-value items to trade/ sell that you can only get if you have, that's right. To "break in", you're going to need $$$, and that is the curx of the problem of this game (besides the bugs): Play to win. This game is probably by far the worst paramount example of it ever. It's a choice of either pay pr grind, especially with reputations, but at least that gives everyone a somewhat fairer chance to obtain half-decent gear. Upgrading your gear seemed like a good idea at the time, but like with many things in this game, it was implemented poorly, kind of like Obamacare. That brings me to the second big disappointment of this game: great ideas, poor implementation. If every new feature/release stopped being more about cash grab than it was about new content, then maybe this game could be more enjoyable. You know, what games are supposed to be like, instead of feeling like it's your second (or third) job. And GOd forbid you can't "keep up" and make a good dent in the previous grind before the next one comes out.
Coming back to the concept of classes, which in my opinion are sadly obsolete, there was a time when each had a role to play and you needed a balance to successfully finish a mission. Now, there is very little true quality group play, unless you're in a fleet on teamspeak or some other voice chat like I was. There is very little strategy, planning, communication, teamwork, the list goes on. There's trolls galore in matches, or more often "noobs" that people just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at and then leave leaving you and the noob alone unable to finish the mission so you have to leave and take a 1 hour penalty all because people are too impatient and too rude and can't be bothered to communicate and show some of the newer players the ropes. The same goes for chat. On ESD or any other major hub, youask a question, and nobody answers or people just start flaming you for their enjoyment. The forums are practically worthless too, just a feeding ground for those with nothing better to do than rant about how bad Cryptic is rather than actually be constructive. It's like the old saying of giving a man a fish vs teaching him how to fish. Right now, people are just slapping people with the metaphorical fish. And that is the third and final sad face for me about this game: the lack of group play/teamwork/cooperation.
I guess the real reason I kept coming back to this game was the hope that the next thing would make the game alright. As some others have said, "the miracle that was never going to happen". That, or because sometimes teaming up with the people from my fleet on the voice chat and doing runs could be a lot of fun and funny too. Finding a quality fleet can really make a huge difference. I was in the Phoenix Vanguard, and although I've been kicked since I haven't played this game in over 6 months, the people in that fleet are quality people who might be enough to get you to stay around despite all the bad this game has.
People really seem to enjoy flaming Cryptic, but like current events, they do so without knowing all the facts. Here are some facts:
STO was originally developed by Perpetual Entertainment from 2004 to 2008 till they went bankrupt. Even when the liscense went to Cryptic, they had to start from scratch with the code. They started in 2008 and finished in 2010. That is unprecedented to say the least to create not just a game, but an MMORPG in that amount of time. (Just for comparison, one of my favorite games Space Engineers has been in Alpha for over 2 years) Granted, it was buggy as hell and they immediately patch the heck out of it initially once it launched they just had to get it out the door. Since then, Cryptic went from Atari to "Perfect" World (get my drift) and the originaly people who were on the team have since been replaced more than once. The new people don't know how to fix the existing bugs cuase the code is proabaly such a mess it's near inmpossible. (as a side note, how many games do you know of that support 3 different versions of DirectX) But, as they have shown, they can create very good new content, especially once you get to the New Romulus story arc that continues on the Iconians got me hooked and I hope they keep it up. It seems to me that they are slowly trying to re-write the game over with code they do understand and hopefully that will come out on top, but that's not going to happen overnight...
All in all, this game has (had?) the potential to be great. Maybe if someone else had made the game/takes over the game it can become what so many of us want it to be. Who knows, I'm going to college for Computer Science - Game Development and maybe someday in the future I'll have my own studio and be able to boldly go where no man has gone before and create the REAL Star Trek Online...
Kirk out.

After putting so much time into this game and it's 2 DLC I think its about time I return the favor to this game and write a review on it. (Sidenote: Its on my steam version I have 100 so hours. I have spent around 40 times that, just to give you my qualifications).
I'll start with the base game of Mount&Blade:Warband.
Warband is a brilliant Medieval era RPG with brilliant gameplay and while outdated still beatiful graphics. The Gameplay itself is very simple with a 3rd person-esq gameplay map where you move aroun your party and interact with other things and people on the overmap. Their are 3 catagories of things to interact with: Hostile Units, Neutral/Friendly Units, and Villages/Towns/Castles/Caves/etc.
When you interact with a hostile unit you engage in a bit of dialoge before running away, paying them off (depending) or battling them. Battling is a first person form where you control your character and can order your men to do stuff (or just kind of let them run around). These battles can range from Seiging Praven to minor skirmeshes vs 2-3 bandits.
When interacting with Neutral/Friendly Units you simply exchange words that let you acomplish a variety of things as you would expect from talking.
Interactions with (non-hostile) places are simple and you go into a "click on where you want to go" screen.
To Shorten this up my ratings go as follow:
Gameplay: 10/10. Historcally acurate units and troops, weapons, and cattle (Bloody cattle). Overall the gameplay is great and, while technically simple, it's fun and difficult in all the right ways.
Graphics: 7/10. The game is a bit old though is still beatiful and well presented.
Bugs: 8/10. While their are a few bugs, they are not really game breaking and are often funny rather than bad.
Music/Sound: 9/10. All it's missing is "Ride of the Rohirim" by Howard Shore.
Replay Value: 10/10. If you manage to "beat" it after 400 hours, why not do it again. Oh the joy of starting over and dying to one looter...
Now as for the DLC Napoleonic Wars, it can only be summed up as such: Machivelli riding a horse off a cliff while playing "Flight of the Valkyries" on a french horn. ......... The only real drawback to this game is the lack of a singleplayer, but to be honest, multiplayer might as well be singleplayer and you really play this mode to laugh.
As for the Viking Conquest DLC, oh lord where do I begin. While I have not fully explored every feature in the reforge update I can suffice to say that its brilliant on every level you can think of. You play in The forming England during the time of King Alfred the Great, the danish invasions, oh, and the French (Friese) are there to. This might as well be Medieval Simulator and is one of the best games i've ever played. Plus, it has a storymode to introduce you to everything, so props to the dev team for that. I simply do not have words for this game other than buy it now so i'll give you numbers now.
Gameplay: 10/10. Ever wanted to Go Viking? You can. Ever wanted to be an Irish Druid? You can. Ever wanted to subconsuiclly get the greatest history lesson ever about the forming of England (Engaland) ever? Well you better believe you do.
Graphics: 9/10. Still similar to Warbands Graphics, but largly and upgrade.
Bugs: 8/10. Bare in mind its still in development, but really, there aren't many.
Music/Sounds: 11/10. It breaks the scoreboard. Words cannot describe.
Replay Value: 10/10. If you don't downright die (something you can do in this mode), and don't succumb to useless injury (also new), and actually manage to (through miracles) conquer everyone (you cheater), then yes, feel free to replay.
Also, with both Warband and VC, especailly VC, the Character Creation is more in-depth than D&D, so, yeah. Always fun.

The game is divided into 5 stages, and each stage features a somewhat different style of gameplay. Most are like real-time strategy, but they are different and diverse. So it's basically 5 games in one pack. Not only that, the whole game is about your very own creature evolving from one single cell to the biggest race that controls the whole universe. It feels EPIC. It feels like you are the god.
The space stage, being the last stage, is immense with content, and endless. Everyone talks about this epic journey into the heart of galaxy, because it's fantastic. It can get very hard, with the Grox attacking you in laaaarge numbers. You have to tear out a way the hard way, planet by planet, among heavily occupied star systems. But when you do reach the center, you get this feeling again that after billions of years of evolving and fighting and growing you finally become the emperor of the universe. It is moving, trust me. And aside from this main quest (it may not even be main - the game doesn't require you to do this), there are tons of things to do. You can collect artifacts from around the galaxy, ally or fight with other equally advanced races, work toward various badges and unlock the very best equipment, play the financial way by trading spices, and so much more.
At the end of each stage, you get an ability based on your behavior in this stage to help you with the next stage. If you are violent you get an ability that attacks. If you are social you get an ability that helps making friends. And if you play from the very first cell stage all the way to space, you get an ultimate ability for the space stage. There are a good number of different abilities you can get this way, and they create a good number of various playstyles. Conclusion, what you do as a cell at day 1 will affect what you do outside of your home planet.
And of course there's this famed creature creator. You can create EVERYTHING with it. And not only creatures, but also houses, factories, turrets, vehicles, ships, planes, spaceships, and more. WIth Internet connection you can share your creations with other players. In fact these guys at EA are so proud of this creator that they make it one option at the main menu. Yes you can go to the creator and start creating without launching the main game at all.
So is there any complaint at all? Well there is. At whatever stage, if you make a lot of allies, you will be annoyed at how they keep attacking one another and seeking help from you all the time. Makes me think back to Civilization. Can't they just learn to live in peace, like me?! And when I first installed the game it says my key wasn't valid. But just contact EA and they can solve this quickly.
All in all, this game is marvelous, and is recommended for everyone.
Edit: well seems like online action has been dead for some time. Sorry for the inaccuracy. And here I thought there's this magical guy named Maxis who created a lot and lot and lot of things. Other than that this game still rocks.

tl;dr Ace of Spades is fun, for about the first 20 hours or so, but it fails to deliver on it's promises and leaves you unsatisfied and wishing you stuck with Minecraft and TF2 instead.
This game is unique, don't get me wrong, with teabagging actually earning points, exploding graves and fully destructible environments and a great 1 min to go music score making the end of a game frantic and fun. The editor is really great too and some of the less played game-modes (destruction, VIP, Diamond Mine) are actually more fun than TDM and Zombies.
There are only 4 classes, and that isn't a bad thing, but 2 of those classes are basically useless. The engineer for example, moves so slowly and because of their jetpack, snipers can easily bag a headshot on them, plus their submachine gun sucks and takes 1 clip to kill someone to the face. And this class, meant to be the engineer and primary base maker, only begins with 1000 blocks, which is roughly enough to build 2 large walls. And this class is meant to be balanced because it is the fastest. Yeah, no. The engineer is so slow, and in a deathmatch is only useful at the start of a large map when trying to get to the enemies base to camp there.
In fact, let me skip why the other classes are bad at the moment and talk about camping and level design:
From the first map you play, you realise that most maps are balanced in favour of the the Green team, leaving them high up positions with the Blue down on low positions. This is heavily shown on the Arctic Base map, where the Greens literally shoot on top of the Blues spawnpoint, leaving them only a few seconds of invincibility to sprint to some cover or to attempt a flanking manoveur, which is really the only way to beat the Greens in that map. Other maps do the same sort of thing as well.
Not only are the map designs fairly bad but the base-camping is horrendous, not only is base-camping one of the main ways to let your team win but the exploding graves and environments literally dig a hole for the team having their base camped, making sure that it takes too long to dig yourself out and leaving yourself as easy pickings.
Let me get back to the classes now:
The miner, is also pretty useless, as not only is it's most powerful weapon/tool horribly nerfed and the shotgun useless unless sneaking up behind people but it's shovel takes too long to mine and the timebombs do jack to the environment and take up to 10 seconds to explode, not to mention the level design leaves most maps at the bottom of the world height.
The commando and the sniper are really the only classes to choose from, with the commando being rediculously overpowered with a rocket launcher and minigun, but the sniper's 1 kill headshot leave you ducking and weaving all the time.
Also with the classes, the choose your own weapon has so little use it may as well not be there, with only literally 2 things to pick from from each sub-category (primary weapon, secondary weapon, melee, grenade and blocks) and normally the ones you begin with are the best anyways.
There is also a level-up system which is more competitive statistics building, but doesn't work on most servers and all Australian servers.
And while there are many game-types, the only ones that are populated are TDM and Zombies, with Zombies being overpowered and generally not fun because of their insane speed, health and power, plus the limited ammo, health and block building limit of the main survivors.

Ever wondered what would happen if the Yakuza team tried something new? Ever wondered if they could make something else, other than the Yakuza (Ryū ga Gotoku) series? Well, here's our first taste at that - and its tone is very different from the games that they usually make.
If you're expecting innovation, then this isn't the game for you. The gameplay is the same as every other cover shooter in the last decade. The only thing going for it is that every enemy is a robot, and that their covering flies away into bits and pieces when you're shooting them. There's also the trust system which affects your team's view about you, and their performance in battle. Other than that, you'll just plow through enemies like you did in Gears of War's casual mode. Mini games? Not here. Cooky and weird moments? You'll have to play Yakuza for that.
This game is all about story - and it's one heck of a wild ride; a lot different from Kazuma Kiryu's adventures in the Japanese underground. The game doesn't throw a lot of exposition around, and the player is treated as a foreigner to this world that the dev team created. Binary Domain is mature, emotional, and adrenaline-fueled; somehow balanced by smart comedic timing. Though it dashes through the themes and philosophical questions that it asks itself, it's great to see a game try and tread topics like the evolution of AI, and climate change.
And there you have it.

This being said, it also shares the Monster Hunter formula of killing♥♥♥♥♥♥and wearing its carcass so other stuff has a harder time killing you, so you can kill them and wear THEIR carcass. Gathering up materials is massively less tedious as compared to Monster Hunter, so there's a plus.
However, there's something this game doesn't share with Monster Hunter; it's difficulty. If you came expecting a game to kick you in the sternum so hard your ribcage and pelvis switch places, this isn't the game. The CLOSEST you'll get to anything mirroring the difficulity of even the latest Monster Hunter game doesn't rear its head until VERY late in the online portion of the game.
But that doesn't mean there's no fun to be had. This game has it's fair share of content, and provides interesting theory crafting through it's use of Ability granting, skill-boosting spirits called Mitama which you affix to your person. Explaining them would take too long for the sake of this review, honestly.
Overall a fun experience (bring friends) and a nice little story that's a bit more fleshed out than Monster Hunter's "x monster is causing y problem, go kill, hunt-man."

Toukiden 2 is a fantastic feel-good open world (not hub-locked!) demon slaughtering simulator. They've actually managed to make a competent story mode to act as a gateway tutorial to the "main" game, though the game leaves a distinct single-player focus aftertaste.
Play this as a single-player RPG and you'll get more than you expect. Go into this expecting constant multiplayer action and prepare to wait or do some organizing. There's a huge variety of ways to kill demons, too-- boss rush instances, open-world exploration for collectables and secrets, little one-off quests that just (usually) happen to need demons killed. If you're unable to find a multiplayer match, the game does not lock out out of that content: you are free to simulate multiplayer with your single-player "party" members.
Game does not support resolution modes above 1080p, though the resolution is "enough" for what the game tries to pull off. Don't expect a technical lightshow, even though the artstyle is absolutely pleasant.
Gamepad is absolutely required.

The game is a bit pricy compared to the first one -and unjustly so-. However, it does something I haven't seen since years : it improves the original. Most sequel are basically more of the same. Toukiden 2 rekted pretty much every problem I found to the first one.
-Too much loading time and small environnment => Big open world.
-No control over the camera in the village => Can move the camera freely anytime.
-Secondary mitama being a lot less important than the main one => They now have a special ability each.
-Need to lvl up a mitama to the max to change the boosts => You can change them anytime, nearly anywhere.
-No jumping => ...Still no jumping, but a hook instead, to follow flying onis and jump gaps.
-Oni running everywhere => You can stop them in their charge with the hook.
But sadly, it also adds one new problem : Recycling comes with DLCs. What I mean is, instead of putting EVERY content from Toukiden Kiwami, then adding their own, they take half of the content, add another half, then proposes you as DLC the onis and weapons from Kiwami...
If you liked Kiwami, this one is even better, though shorter. If it had all the DLC baseline, I would litteraly recommend it to all, but it's such a waste. Because of how much content went into the DLC, I can't recommend it blindly. If you are into trying a lot of builds, experimenting, exploring and fighting giant thingy, you can give it a go, otherwise, I would suggest to try something else. Maybe Toukiden Kiwami, wich is way more affordable and has a comparable content.

In the mid-1990s Microprose released Grand Prix Manager 2. It was a great game, but it was overly frustrating with all of its bugs. I have wanted a good racing management game ever since. Motorsport Manager is that game. It’s easy to get into, but still gives the player countless decisions to make that impact everything from finances to the race itself.
It is thoroughly addicting, building a team, setting up the cars in practice, and then trying to determine the perfect plan for the race. What advantages to use, which tires, how many laps of fuel, and how long is that rain going to last? Then in the off season, trying to decide on the best people and infrastructure, while still saving money for parts and next year’s car? It is a constant struggle. The game is choice after choice where everything seems important. It’s maddening and addicting trying to figure out why I am still struggling in my 4th season of the lowest division.
It looks great, the tilt-shifted races are beautiful, and the atmosphere sounds are also good. My complaints are that much of the interface retains the tablet born simplicity with a lack of information. Everything is easy to read and get to, but I would rather have had more information on the screen instead of the huge interface boxes. I want to see lap histories, sector info, fuel breakdowns, etc. They could include a lot more stats and put them in the data window where new players could ignore them, but veterans could dig into. The game is great because it is so easy, but it also leaves me wanting more.
Also, why can’t I save car designs or see both cars set-ups at once on the set-up screen? Little things like that make me wish for more.
My biggest complaint comes from overly predictable game events and the complete lack of a manual. The game is very predictable. How many pace cars will I get on lap 2 in a season? In one season 8 out of 11 races had a pace car on lap 2. Always lap 2. More than likely, if a car is going to crash, it will be on lap 2. I have seen a pace car on a lap other than lap 2 once (which came after a pace car on lap 2). It would also be nice if the game was a bit more realistic. A team wants to send their cars out on a soaked track on super softs? There should be spins and accidents, but usually it just means slower lap times. Car retirements, even from being stupid, are rare.
But the lack of a manual for a game like this is just horrible. I have almost 50 hours in the game and I still don’t understand everything. There are so many factors to everything it is often hard to determine what exactly is going wrong. Are my tires worthless this race because of improper management, the outside temperature, the tracks wear level, or because this new chassis is horrible on tires? A lot of the help bubbles are good, but they provide basic information which is rarely enough. Often, I have no idea what a car or driver’s stats actually do, or how the system works. There are numerous guides and forums posts to help, but I often feel like they aren’t much more than what I already know. I find myself searching for dev’s forum posts just so I can get a bit of a glimpse of the how game works.
Still, I love the game, it is a lot of fun if you like management games. I am just hoping for a Motorsport Manger 2 with an in-depth interface and a proper manual.

I've clocked a fair few hours on this game now, and figured I would give it a review..
First of all, as a racing fan, this is hands down one of the most engaging games I've ever played. I will play it for a long time to come and I'm already thinking about the Monza (Milan) race I'm set up to play tomorrow. Nothing like some racing on a sunday!
Have I got new ideas for the setup and strategy? I didn't have a good time out there earlier in the season, I misjudged the weather and paid badly for it. I'm in my pre-season target position in the standings, but it's close, each race is a battle to hold that position and just when I think I've got my car development right where I want it, all performance and reliability neatly full and organized between my 1st and 2nd driver, my opponents just keep developing.. it becomes another race - against time and money - to get that new engine out and reliable enough for the upcoming race.
I also took a risk in pre-season in my allocation for this years car, it didn't pay off though I'll know next time, which put me on the back foot from the jump, to say the season has been a challenge is an understatement. I went into it thinking aha, I've clocked it! I'll set my expectations high and let the money and fame flow. The game brought me back to earth with a bang.
Going into the last 2 races, the pressure's on.
It's experiences like this that draw you into the game, that give you that 'one more race' feeling and that trick of the mind that makes you think like you're a real team principal. That's the hook for this game, and it's backed up by stunning graphics and race simulation.
Having seen the races in all different angles at this point, I think my favourite is top down 3D, it makes the circuits feel more alive to me, and the circuits are packed with detail. Everything you'd expect really, crowds with many littering the fencing around the track, tents, coaches, ambulances, cranes, all manner of buildings, helicopters, planes and on and on.. when the cars are flying round in this view, you could almost swear all the people are moving, walking, cheering.. and not just still in place. Suffice to say.. What they have managed to achieve with the simulation, and that's before you get to the generally superb actual simulation of high level motorsport on track, is truly incredible. Water on track, racing lines developing over time, and then washed away by the rain - the effects of which are excellent - safety cars, virtual and real, all types of rules and regulations all presented and processed accurately.
Big thanks to the developers for delivering such a great core to the game.
There could be more depth to the wider world, I don't find all that much interest in scouting as it currently stands, it feels more like an obligation than a vast world of racing to explore, perhaps after 10+ seasons the world will take more shape but I'd definitely appreciate more detail given to drivers and staff, more history, more.. seriousness. The people and their personalities can feel a little cartoony, in ways that have made me laugh out loud once or twice (my driver getting a crush on his teammate..) but for me, takes you out of the immersion of a real serious sporting world and I feel more balance can be achieved here with some thought put into the next installment down the road, you know.. in a way SI never bothered to do with the FM series.
The HQ is a real cool feature, but I don't have that many reasons to keep going back, and all teams look the same and build the same (dependant on it's needs, but it's choices are fairly linear). With some different country or region variations, team colours and logos, and even specific buildings available for each team, you could easily see this becoming one of the shining parts of a future game. However, I wouldn't like to see it become the interface (click this building to go to scouting etc.), the interface as it stands is bright, clean, easy to understand and nice to use and look at.
The car and car development screen is good, easy to use, some nice additions would be different background screens for the different areas, perhaps different parts of a garage/factory for backgrounds, and more individual staff to hire and interact with here would give this section more depth.
There are a handful of random little things, like being able to save and copy setups, that I could mention as 'wants' here but I know others have covered these in more detail in reviews and posts, and I don't want to go looking for small negatives when I genuinely adore this game, it's absolutely brilliant and if you have even a passing interest in racing or sports management you NEED to check this out. If you've got this far then you're probably someone who already knows that create your own team has been added, which is a great addition along with liveries and a GT pack (should have come with more liveries surely?) so I'll just give a passing mention to those as an example of the great work devs are still putting into it.
It's not perfect but it's damn close, and I can't wait to play it again tomorrow.

What can I say? The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind is one of the greatest RPGs ever made, from arguably the greatest RPG series ever made. It's vast, and it feels like it never ends. The many hours you spend playing weave together an incredibly detailed and enriching story that is part of a much larger cosmology that connects and encompasses the entire Elder Scrolls series. You can spend hours just reading the in-game books alone. If you are even remotely interested in role-playing or adventure games, then this is a must-have, as well as its descendents, Oblivion and Skyrim (as of 2013).
For those who are more familiar with Oblivion or Skyrim, this is a more difficult game with a much steeper learning curve. Your character will move slowly at first, will run out of fatigue very quickly (unlike in Skyrim, fatigue is depleted by running and is much more of a factor in how successful all your actions will be), and you will be unable to carry or store much loot. It will take a while to level up and increase your skills at first, but be patient, and you will soon notice that things really do get easier.
Morrowind also seems considerably longer than either Oblivion or Skyrim, because there are many more factions you can join, and each has several questgivers (assuming you want more than just the main quest, which is also lengthy). The other thing you need to know is that there is NO fast-travel in this game. Be prepared to spend a lot of time traveling on foot. But these things just add to the challenge and depth of this classic game. When given a dungeon to explore, you won't get a convenient arrow pointing you to the exact location; often, you'll just be told "it's southwest from X" and it's up to you to find it. This adds to the realism and the immersion.
As if the vanilla game weren't enough, there are two expansion packs included in the GOTY edition that are bound to add many enjoyable hours to your experience, as well as tons of free mods out there to spice things up. The price you pay for this game is nothing compared to the months or years of solid, fun role-playing it provides.
If you like RPGs, give it a chance. It grew on me, and if you're open to the ideas it presents, I'm certain it'll grow on you too.

An asteroid hurdles through space, speeding past alien spacecraft who follow it, attempting to scan it for any life. Within seconds, the asteroid is out of sight, and enters the orbit of a planet. Catching fire, it slams into the ground, creating a crater from the impact. Hundreds of small fragments explode from the asteroid, scattering themselves around the planet. Some land by cities of sophisticated, lizard-like beigns, others by curious tribes who begin worshipping the fiery rocks, and by clueless creatures who poke and lick them. One particular fragment lands in a small pool of water, and you crawl out - a small, slithery cell who's main goal is to survive.
This is Spore, the tale of how your microscopic race can go from scavengers getting enough food to barely survive, to a thriving empire that controls the entire galaxy. The game is based on five stages: Cell, Creature, Tribe, Civilization, and Space. Cell station is where your journey begins. There is little customization in this stage, except for the basic shape of your cell and organelles. Once you become the top of the food chain, you evolve legs. Stumbling onto land, you enter the Creature Stage.
Here is where the true customization takes place. You can collect various parts from skeletons scattered around the planet and add them to your creature. You can make a huge, strong behemoth who crushes his enemies with his gigantic claws, or a small, nimble beign that flies and steals food from his enemies before they notice he is there. You can create your creature based on your species' diet: omnivore, carnivore, or herbivore. Besides the customization, Creature Stage introduces a huge skill in the game that is incredibly useful - friends and foes.
You can choose whether to impress other races and become friends, or attempt to destroy and annhilate them. You have to be wise as to who you attack and who you ally; making enemies with all the weak creatures could end up with them evolving into way stronger creatures and destroying YOU. Once your brain has increased, your species can begin laying out the foundations for a tribe. Here is where the friends and foes system comes into major effect. To complete the Tribal Stage and become a civilization, you must complete your Tribe Totem Pole. For every tribe you defeat or ally, a new totem is added. This stage goes by rather fast, and prepares you for Civilizational Stage.
Civilization Stage takes inspiration from Sid Meier's Civilization series. Your goal is to control every city on the planet, whether through religious, economic, or military means. Religious races can convert the race into believing your civilization is their leader, and is considered the easiest way to complete the stage. Military is just brute force; when it comes to the guns in this, size DOES matter. Economic is peaceful; you start a trade route with a friendly city and eventually buy their city from them. This takes longer than the other two ways but can be very helpful in the long run.
Once you control the planet, you can launch a space project, starting the Space Stage, which is endless. All the choices you've made in the previous stages add up to decide what class you are in the Space Stage - perhaps a battle-crazed tyrant, or a religious zealot out to convert everyone to the teachings of Spode. During the stage, your goal is to go from the Captain of your Space Project to the Omnipotent Beign of the Universe. On the way, you'll encounter the Grox - a cyborg race who hate all and arguably are the antagonists of the game. (If hours of work are put into it, you could make them your ally- if you ever do, I commend you for your bravery.) Between space pirates, colonizing other planets, upgrading your fleet, and stabalizing your funds, this is by far my favorite stage. Overall, this is a great game for creative people and truly lets your imagination soar.

Having played Monster Hunter for thousands of hours at an end, and currently playing Monster Hunter Generations, I must say that Toukiden 2 is a nice addition to the genre. Now, I have yet to finish the storyline but there is a lot to do and I've been too focused on that. In other words, the game is that intrestesting enough if you give it a chance. So far I can tell that the story is really good when compared to let's say the new Zelda - Breath of the Wild game and of course all of the Monster Hunter games that truly really lack a proper story.
Gameplay wise, the combat is really fun and there are quite a few weapons to try. They are suited for different things and there should be something that suits you there. You can go for slow but heavy hitting weapons with short and long reach. Faster but weaker weapons, and those with more emphasis on Area of Effect in the two categories. There is also bow and gun. You can also form your build around raw damage, critical damage and elemental damage.
Mitama is a very nice addition to the combat with buffs and what not. Think of them as perks. You can have three of them at a time, one main and two secondaries. There are many Mitamas and they provide their own boost depending on in which of three slots you put them. There are many of them and equally many combinations for you to try. Combined with weapons and the companions you can build your character and your team in a way that you prefer.
What about companions? There are quite a few of them with their very own personalities, weapon styles and Mitamas of their own. They add to the combat even more and provide an additional range of variety for how you can set up your team. Do you want them to provide long range support, 1 vs 1 support or AOE support? You can!
As for voice acting, some people might be put off by there only being Japanese. However, I think it suits the characters well and I personally understand Japanese to a degree. It's a nice change compared to the many Zelda and Monster Hunter games where the characters don't speak any language at all to convey their emotions. Even if you do not understand Japanese you can read their emotions through the inflections and tone of their voices. And that is better than nothing at all. Of course, English might have been preferred but let's give it the benefit of the doubt.
Technically the game is not very impressive but if you have played, let's say Monster Hunter 3 Ultimare on Wii U, you will understand that a game like this can still be exceptionally good despite the "outdated" graphics. I think Toukiden 2 is one of those games. It may be a rough diamond in that respect, but this game may turn out to be a bigger gem than you initially thought, should you ever give it a try. The game supports 1080p and 60 Hz.
A fair warning though! You do need a hand controller of some kind if you wish to play this game.
