Reflex used to be my favourite game. It was a promising title and the community had real hope.
I conceived, administrated and broadcast the greatest competitive event for the game, the
over a period of a month and a half.
I'm mentioning this to show my fresh perspective, outlook and passion came from a different place than Quake veterans.
This review aims to look at the game in a variety of areas - as a player, as a spectator, and as a map maker being the core.
Firstly, some history and praise. Reflex was advertised as the spiritual successor to CPMA, a mod for Quake 3 with air-control, rebalanced weapons, instant weapon switching and additional jumping techniques compared to the vanilla game.
Reflex took these concepts and attempted to preserve them in a transition to an original engine, free of the limitations of an engine from 1999. Reflex is easy to install, has a modern visual style and possesses unique features in map editing and workshop integration. Examples of these features are:
•	a modernized, functional and readable scoreboard
•	dynamic colour overrides on map geometry (i.e. not only can you change CTF teams from Red/Blue, the geometry in flag base areas can also be that colour)
•	various mouse input related improvements - sub frame input, integration of povohat's mouse accel driver
•	netcode improvements (sort of - collision is a mess).
I'm now going to attempt to distill individual elements of PLAYING the game, in order to construct a picture of Reflex today.
A fair assumption with Reflex's weapon design was that you'd start with the base that CPMA had and make tweaks, sweeping changes or other design decisions from there, right? Kek.
Paraphrasing one of the top in the scene - weapons feel worse than any equivalents in any other arena fps.
The advantage of weapons in some scenarios and disadvantage in others are not very pronounced - grenades are usable for far more than area denial, plasma gun is substitutable for the lightning gun etc. etc.
The typical counter to a lot of Reflex's strong movement should be the LG, and it lacks damage and knockback. Players can drop on items, come up jump pads nigh unpunished.
They are not in an enjoyable or useful place.
Fighting another player is not satisfying - the high ground acceleration contributes to a perpetual feeling of ice skating & many engagements feel like a gamble with the horrible player collision - fighting in close range is plain awful, and the rocket launcher is affected by this to a significant extent.
Moving in Reflex is an "alright" experience - as above, the high ground accel is a key detractor to the game. Triple jumps are a new addition but are very gimmicky in how they have been implemented by mapmakers. Wall clipping has not been implemented in a sane way - what should make movement a lot more fluid has turned into a zany speed boost. Plasma jumping has been made much easier with the comparatively high knockback - it makes doing PJ's easier for bad players and allows for a greater exploitation from most skilled, again using the word gimmicky to describe the outcome.
The community made original maps are visually cluttered - excess usage of bright colours and prefabs make for an environment where it is difficult to distinguish player models and have poor performance on some systems - even modern ones. I'd like to reference dp4's jungle art as being the absolute worst example of the 'difficult to distinguish' category, and maps like the dp4 art pass with many prefabs, as well as 421's prefab pass as the latter.
Matchmaking has more issues with maps - If it looks pretty, it doesn't matter about gameplay, it can be in the pool. This was showed when Sanctum, by Promeus, was in the pool. While removed now, the addition of an Aerowalk that doesn't play as good as in Quake Live, CPMA, Quake World in any regard is hardly better. The weakness with a lot of these maps is that Reflex has fixed weapon respawn timers - an Aerowalk with 10s instead of 5 is a slow ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥isation of how Aerowalk should be - regardless if it has an art pass or not.
Whether maps would play better with a good weapon system is debatable - the continual addition of Static Discharge with the joke mechanic of a forcefield is testament to this. Breaking the rules of map design CAN be done - but by and large exist for a reason. Static Discharge is not one of those that excel.
Furthermore, while the core Reflex maps are at best "passable" and at worst "abhorrent", the community has already settled into trends with these and it has been very difficult to have a good playing map introduced or tested.
TLDR of this entire segment - as a player, the game is justifiably directly inferior to a modification of a game that came out in 1999. There's a reason everyone in AUS is playing CPMA again, and it's because the GAMEPLAY is just poor. All the other externalities and niceties are a lower priority.
As in the introduction, I ran the best tournament/competition Reflex will ever see. I've observed more games in an intense and consistent period than anybody in the game. Reflex has actually regressed on spectator features.
Props need to be given to Lua wizard and community member QualX. He created a nameplates widget - allowing a name and stack to be displayed above players. The default spectator experience lacks both player stacks on one POV.
Other than that, my broadcast came down to other hud elements, camera control, and visuals.
I needed to utilise different hud widgets to convey over twitch's limited bandwidth stack in a clean and easy to view manner to illustrate near essential information.
Camera control was easy for me broadcasting 1v1. In team modes, however, there is no follow pickup/follow killer designation like every game before it. Quad runs are cool and should be shown. Hectic swapping of POV to find it isn't cool. In the earliest KS trailers, multiview spectator was advertised and is a key CPMA feature that is totally absent. This is something I’d expect from a launched CPM successor
An update removed the functionality of forcing player colours in spectate. This is bad. This is really bad. You force spec colours to a harsh colour like bright green as it 1. matches the player’s setup, so a viewer is familiar & 2. shows decently through questionably decorated maps AND fights twitch's compression to provide something to focus on.
In all honestly the worst part of running my cup was forcing every player to select bright green. Some would use the darkest of blue and it was a nightmare to view. This is a no brainer, has been brought up with the devs repeatedly and ignored.
I'd like to highlight this issue in another scenario. Just yesterday, in the 2v2 cup, you had the broadcast POV force team colours to white and green. Silhouettes were enabled, so that you could see the green team's green highlight through walls. When they jump out into clear view, the player models are red and blue. It's an issue – Reflex is already a chaotic team experience, having confusion heightened is ridiculous.
This extends into mapmaking as well. An easy to use in game editor is good for greyboxing, and not much more.
A well-seasoned mapper considers Reflex devs to have sacrificed standards in order to force an in-game editor. No clipping tool, minimal entities and a lack of control with those entities makes editing a time consuming, minimally functional editor. There are few item pickups for CTF, the lack of access to entities means you can’t change weapon and armour respawn times (e.g. actually having a functioning Aerowalk or having a RA where it should be on q2wcp9).
To completely sum up, Reflex is lacking in almost every aspect, with gimped or nonexistent features. Underneath the surface is a game unable to meet the aspirations or legacy of its predecessors.

Man oh man, where to start?
This game knows what it is, tells you what it is, loves what it is, and playfully mocks you for playing it. ( "Seduce me with your puzzle solving skills!" )
You are a loser.  Oh, sorry, I meant in the game, though maybe in real life too??  Who am I to judge!  Anyway, you're a loser in a dating sim game, a precept that the game knows is a super cheesy dating sim precept, and so instantly sets you up with a super outrageous, over-sexed Love Fairy named Kyu whose job is to make you DatingSimsville new Erotic Deity and she won't take your lame excuses for a "no".  Also she wants your porno mags, but she's mostly there to help you.  She shows you the ropes with an introductory puzzle of the Match-3 variety, but this ain't no Bejeweled or Candy Crush.
You can only move pieces in a straight line with pieces swapping positions with the piece in the previous position.  So if you move a piece all the way across the board for a match, you have to watch out for what else you might match by making that match, something that screwed me over several times when I thought I was about to win.  When you make a match with one of the 4 primary types (Romance, Talent, Sexuality, Flirtation) your "Date Gague" fills up (Not entirely disimilar to the date gague from The Sims 2: Night Life.  Don't lie, I know you played it!).  There are 4 other types of tokens on the grid as well (Joy, Passion, Sensitivity, and Heartbreak) that have different effects.  Joy, shaped like a bell, gives you additional moves and is easily the most crucial piece to keep track of on the playing field.  Sensitivity, shaped like a tear drop, is also incredibly important as it powers different "Presents" you can give the girl while on the date and give yourself special bonuses.  Passion, shaped like a heart, acts as a multiplier for the points received from the four primary tokens.  Heartbreak will ruin your dates day and, by association, YOUR day.  If you match a heartbreak, generally by accident (Though there can be strategy in making one bad match for a REALLY good match), it ain't the end of the world, but more than that can be hard to come back from.  As long as you aren't too impulsive, it shouldn't be problem.  In short:  Match stuff in the right number of turns enough times to make the girl happy!
After the tutorial, Kyu starts introducing you to women.  You get to choose your first conquest-to-be, but after that the game leads you along an eerie line of association that doesn't seem to be referenced for the rest of the game for some reason (Like the mother and daughter that never mention they know each other??), but it's a fantasy in which you seduce women through solving puzzles, so...  Anyway, this is where you start talking and quickly realize you need a pen and paper or a twitchy Alt-Tab finger because you get bonus "Hunie" (Used to buy trait upgrades to improve your performance on dates) when they ask you about the answers they've given you and you answer right (Like how a real girl likes it when actually listen to her, I suppose?  Though maybe in real life they'd rather you forget how much they weigh.)  I ended up with the front of my desktop covered in post-it notes full of their info (Aiko Yumi, 11/9, Age: 28, Weight: 109 lbs., Heigh: 5'4", Cup size: D, Favorite Season: Autumn.  BTW, Scorpios are bad news.  Just sayin'.) so this aspect of the game is like a legit dating sim.  Also, these chicks get hungry.  Fortunately, thanks to Kyu's magic gizmo that she gives you, you know EXACTLY what each of them likes to eat and drink.  Buying them alcohol (Only at night.  If you offer it during the day they'll act like you have "A Problem") will give you a boost to various factors before and during the date.  Buying them food increases the number of times you can talk to them, but make sure they have at least one square left in their hunger gague or they won't go on a date with you or accept additional gifts.  Speaking of gifts, you can buy them with "Munie" (Which you earn from dates, successful and unsuccessful) and they will increase your Hunie, unlock Date Girfts (The ones you use while on the date with sensitivity) and also unlock different outfit options.  That's right, you want all the women to walk around in bikinis all the times?  Even in a cafe?  You can do that.  I found it awkward personally, but I did enjoy the decent variety of outfit and hairstyle options available.
So what about the women?  Utterly fantastic..  for the most part.  They definitely played up every type of personality, so every preference is represented, but I think their popularity can be pretty clearly told by the price each trading card goes for in the Steam Marketplace. (Nikki is, unsuprisingly, high on the list)  They each have a unique, and well performed voice.  I didn't find any of them annoying, though I definitely had my preferences (Let's just say I'd be hot for teacher ;) )  They also don't come across as vapid, subservient moe dating sim girls (Well, except for the one who is purposefully portrayed that way to a creepy extent)  The art work is great too.  Too often I look through the dating sim market and see art that looks like the artist just finished reading Christopher Hart's "Manga for Beginners", and here I was definitely not disappointed.  Oh, and if you're wondering about sexy scenes, you WILL get your sexy scenes.  Apparently the Steam version has some censorship, but if you go to the community page the developers supply a link with a quick fix that gives players a look at the whole picture, so to speak.  But yeah, all the ladies are great!
What else....  Oh, I dig the music!  It's really nice and catchy for some of the stages.  And the sound effects for the puzzles are solid.  OH, and there's a fair amount of secret stuff.  Let's just say you'll reach the end of the main story line and say to yourself "Huh?  Why isn't my photo album full??"  And then there's something called "Alpha Mode" which I haven't fully explored, but it certainly adds on to the playability of the game.  Though I'm not sure you'll get more than 20 hours out of it, unless you just really LIKE it...  Y'know, box of kleenex Like it.
In the end, if you like dating sims you should pick up this game for its humor and solid dialogue/voice acting (Yes, they lend their best porn♥♥♥♥♥♥ic moans to the game).  If you like Match-3 games, then you should get this game because the puzzle aspect is super well developed and not just some tacked on thing like so many of the anime puzzle games that you play through to just unlock images.  If you like both of those things then you NEED this game.  It's amazing.  It'll hit a G-Spot in your brain you didn't know needed stroking.  If it weren't so pervy I'd recommend it to tons of people, but as it is it's definitely a guilty pleasure.
Buy it now!

I recieved this for free in the Humble giveaway...
I have almost bought this game multiple times this year - it was in my wishlist and the only things that ever stopped me from purchasing it were:
1 - the length... reading that it was 2-3 hours long and linear
2 - it is a walking simulator
Now that I have played it - I still feel I made the right choice in not purchasing it (though I will likely purchase the DLC at some point to finish out the story).
Essentially this game consists of 6 levels - each a fairly linear forward moving path that has you collecting an object. Each level gets progressively more twisted than the last - and the trippy visuals and jump scares are done very well. That said there does not seem to be any sort of risk attached to the game - you are not chased, and I think I may have died once but the way it restarted me I am unsure if it was intentional or not.
There are a few puzzles - some which are actually very cool, none of which are particularly challenging (you won't need a walkthrough, at least in my experience).
Do I recommend this game - yes and no. I enjoyed it very much for what it is - but I think I made the right call in saving my money, as at 3.1 hours of play time I am likely to not play this again due to it being very linear and once you know the twist it is kind of pointless to go back and collect anything I may have missed.
I am giving it a thumbs up because the level design, graphics and trippy visual sequences are all top notch. But I do wish there were more of a traditional game here - even if it was just a few chase sequences like the Outlast series.
As it stands - it is a very well put together walking simulator with an interesting hook.
Also - the jump scares are fantastic, lots of startling moments.

I love this game. If they could take the combat from the later games and put it in here, I would give this game a 100000/10. I got the game when it first came out, and played it up until I got a 360 which was a year or two ago. I spent many, many, many hours on this game, and loved it. The only fault I could find was the combat. I would never play as anything but a mage, simply because the physical combat was so unreliable. You could be a foot away from a person, stabbing at them, and miss 9/10 times in the beginning. You almost had to train with trainers in the beginning, which cost a lot of money.
I loved finding little bugs that changed the game (it is a huge game, so bugs were expected). Like how you could skip the second building at the beginning and never get arrested by jumping through a wall, or using the soul trap glitch to make spells permanant (Note: if you do that, keep your speed low. If you go too high above 100 speed, you will litterally run out of the game world).
I highly recomend this game, and I will leave you with a few tips.
1) Don't do ranged items. They also have the unreliable hit chance, you have your own possibility to miss as have to "hit" them to have the possibility of hitting them, and you have to keep buying new items as you miss or break the ones you were using.
2) Sleep a lot. You can sleep anywhere outside of a settlement, and sleeping restores your health and mana.
3) Invest in the unarmored skill. You will eventually be able to take more dammage than with armor on, there is no weight penalty to your running or encumbrabce, and you don't need to repair or buy more.
4) When outside of a settlement, take the time to walk around. Running lowers stamina, which makes it harder to cast spells and hit enemies (Unsure about this, but it may make you easier to hit too).

What can I say about Morrowind that hasn't already been said? This game right here is my number 1 most favorite RPG of all time, and with good reasons. Personally, Oblivion and Skyrim are both great games, but Morrowind just blows them both out the water! Now of course, the graphics are a bit dated and the combat system may be flawed, but this game is still seriously fun! To put it frankly, I had a lot more fun playing Morrowind and exploring this vast world that any other TES game. This game is charming at best and has something about it that just "sticks".
Anyways, you play as, of course, a prisoner who has been convicted of an unknown crime (Geez, this plot never gets old does it Bethesda?), and the emperor apparently notices something about you and wants you to pretty much save the world and blah, blah, blah and don't die. Now of course, this is just the whole setup for the plot as the story is AMAZINGLY enriching and has you play anyway you want. There are tons of sidequests, NPC's to talk too, Shops to steal, dungeons to loot, places to discover, and even more! For a game this old, I still find the graphics amazing because there are so pretty to me! As you explore this vast world (No fast travel mode so you must travel by either foot or a number of services), you come across many remarkable sites that for some reason has more awe for me than Skyrim or Oblivion. Immersion is always in this game every time I play it! Seriously, everytime I play this game, I get so lost in the world of Morrowind that when I finally get off my laptop, and walk around my house, outside, everywhere in the real world, it feels like I'm in a Morrowind setting. To understand what I mean by this, simply play the game :3...
My problem with the Oblivion and Skyrim is that it felt as if the game was holding your hand all the way through while Morrowind is brutally hard from start to finish. This game really does a good job and making you not feel like a hero as even the weakest looking enemies will take you out in a heart beat. Bandits are seriously dangerous in this, any hostile enemy is and you will die A LOT. I like this because it follows the brutal difficulty of the previous games which I also enjoyed, Arena and Daggerfall. And with the GOTY edition, your looking at nearly 200 hours of gameplay as the expansions really add a lot more to the games story.

An asteroid hurdles through space, speeding past alien spacecraft who follow it, attempting to scan it for any life. Within seconds, the asteroid is out of sight, and enters the orbit of a planet. Catching fire, it slams into the ground, creating a crater from the impact. Hundreds of small fragments explode from the asteroid, scattering themselves around the planet. Some land by cities of sophisticated, lizard-like beigns, others by curious tribes who begin worshipping the fiery rocks, and by clueless creatures who poke and lick them. One particular fragment lands in a small pool of water, and you crawl out - a small, slithery cell who's main goal is to survive.
This is Spore, the tale of how your microscopic race can go from scavengers getting enough food to barely survive, to a thriving empire that controls the entire galaxy. The game is based on five stages: Cell, Creature, Tribe, Civilization, and Space. Cell station is where your journey begins. There is little customization in this stage, except for the basic shape of your cell and organelles. Once you become the top of the food chain, you evolve legs. Stumbling onto land, you enter the Creature Stage.
Here is where the true customization takes place. You can collect various parts from skeletons scattered around the planet and add them to your creature. You can make a huge, strong behemoth who crushes his enemies with his gigantic claws, or a small, nimble beign that flies and steals food from his enemies before they notice he is there. You can create your creature based on your species' diet: omnivore, carnivore, or herbivore. Besides the customization, Creature Stage introduces a huge skill in the game that is incredibly useful - friends and foes.
You can choose whether to impress other races and become friends, or attempt to destroy and annhilate them. You have to be wise as to who you attack and who you ally; making enemies with all the weak creatures could end up with them evolving into way stronger creatures and destroying YOU. Once your brain has increased, your species can begin laying out the foundations for a tribe. Here is where the friends and foes system comes into major effect. To complete the Tribal Stage and become a civilization, you must complete your Tribe Totem Pole. For every tribe you defeat or ally, a new totem is added. This stage goes by rather fast, and prepares you for Civilizational Stage.
Civilization Stage takes inspiration from Sid Meier's Civilization series. Your goal is to control every city on the planet, whether through religious, economic, or military means. Religious races can convert the race into believing your civilization is their leader, and is considered the easiest way to complete the stage. Military is just brute force; when it comes to the guns in this, size DOES matter. Economic is peaceful; you start a trade route with a friendly city and eventually buy their city from them. This takes longer than the other two ways but can be very helpful in the long run.
Once you control the planet, you can launch a space project, starting the Space Stage, which is endless. All the choices you've made in the previous stages add up to decide what class you are in the Space Stage - perhaps a battle-crazed tyrant, or a religious zealot out to convert everyone to the teachings of Spode. During the stage, your goal is to go from the Captain of your Space Project to the Omnipotent Beign of the Universe. On the way, you'll encounter the Grox - a cyborg race who hate all and arguably are the antagonists of the game. (If hours of work are put into it, you could make them your ally- if you ever do, I commend you for your bravery.) Between space pirates, colonizing other planets, upgrading your fleet, and stabalizing your funds, this is by far my favorite stage. Overall, this is a great game for creative people and truly lets your imagination soar.

There isn't a whole lot about this game I can say that hasn't been said already. I got this game back in 2010 by retail, and I immediately fell in love with it. The level of creativity in it is amazing, it's funny at times, and has decent replayability. It really allows your mind to wander, and create your own little world. Not to mention it can be difficult at times on the hardest difficulty. The expansion pack Galactic Adventures really added some much needed flavor to the gameplay. I could continue to regurgitate praise for the game (And trust me, it is a great game worthy of the praise it gets) but I felt some things needed to be changed. First off, if they ever created a second spore, they need to add an aquatic/fish stage. That would really lengthen the game and please a lot of fans. While this was on my mind, it was never a big problem for me personally. The big gripe I have with this game is the Space Stage. When I first got to space stage, I was incredibly excited. You are instantly allowed (except for the boring intro tutorial) to wander around and explore this vast universe filled with alien life. You got to find wormholes, explore planets, find aliens, kill aliens, etc... For someone who is really in love with space, I explored every solar system I could get to. However, after exploring for a bit, I noticed that every one of the solar systems is almost the same. I'm not talking about the way they look. Cosmetically, each system can vary from cookie-cutter to extremely unique, as do the planets. But gameplay wise, there wasn't a whole lot of new stuff. Again, Galactic Adventures changed this a little bit, but not entirely. Being the last stage of the game, I felt like it kinda gave up at the end. They could have done so much more with space stage! Now, I know trying to create 100,000 different solar systems is near impossible and time consuming, but I feel like a little more flavor would have been nice. The other thing I saw wrong with space stage was the Grox. The Grox can first show up all the way in creature stage, and the intro into space stage sets them up as a terrifying advanced race bent on destroying all. And that's exactly what they are. When I went to war with these things, I was determined to obliterate them. But no. Their empire is HUGE. About 2400 systems. Again, I know they are supposed to be this invincible empire, which they almost are, but this makes fighting them fun and challenging to just boring... Same thing. Bomb the planet while avoiding space crafts. Move to next planet. Do the same thing over. Even if you cheat, it takes forever. Not to mention it's almost impossible to remain neutral with them. Even if you don't bother them, your allies get attacked, requiring you to fight them off. It's such a hassel. And the worst part is that when you finally take over all 2400 systems, what are you rewarded with? A new weapon? Access to a planet creator? Boosted relations with all alien empires? No. You get an in game medal, and bragging rights. It's just not enough. However, despite all this criticizm, this game is amazing. If you are a person who loves sci-fi, or just loves to make things, give this game a look. It's definately worth the price. 8/10

The building aspect of Ace of Spades: Battle Builder is the best it has going for it. You'll be able to build most structures your creativity allows and you'll also be able to destroy anything you want on the map, including what your teammates and what your enemies have built. Even if this may sound like an open invitation to "griefing" behavior, it really doesn't happen all that often and for too long. Another building mechanic exclusive to this game is that while anything could be built or destroyed, it must all be done within a relatively short amount of time. Players must get ideas and place them into action quickly, as you will not have an unlimited amount of time to implement your creative thoughts into the game's world. This means that the shooter action, the building, the digging, and the destroying all occur in a hectic, funny, and fast paced environment.
In nearly eighteen hours of gameplay, I don't think I came across anyone cheating. All of the game modes play surprisingly differently from each other, and they each offer their own version of fun. Even though I found the Classic Capture the Flag mode to be the most balanced and the most interesting, the other modes also kept me entertained, albeit in shorter spurts. My only real complaint about the game comes from its small player base and lack of patches/updates from the developers. The only populated servers are in Europe, and although you will be able to find matches available at various hours of the day, if you are not playing from Europe, high ping and lag will be an issue that actually hinders the gameplay experience. Concerning development, as I understand, Ace of Spades: Battle Builder has been abandoned and the developers have focused all their time on their next game. Overall, I had a surprising amount of fun with Ace of Spades: Battle Builder. It's just too bad that there aren't many people playing, and the servers that are still alive are only in Europe.

Allies can pick your stupid♥♥♥♥♥up if you fall too often, so you're free to go full HAM on everything you see. There are a ton of different enemies, and an♥♥♥♥♥load of unique bosses. Now that I have finished the game, for me it has an overall fun gameplay and poor character/story development. So:
I didn't expect a very thoughful story from a shooter like this, but I did expect at least the couple of interesting ideas presented in the trailer being developed a bit. Instead, they went rather deep in the plot while combining it with a huge amount of clichés: character stereotypes, sexism, character realationships, race clichés... so the whole thing didn't work for me. You can't take a serious plot and drive it with this kind of script.
The dialogues and reactions are unnatural and the relationships progress (good or bad) escalate too quickly. The trust meter mechanic is useless for me and the options to choose too vague so I ended up choosing always the one on the bottom of the list. Every time I wanted to answer in a more "real" way, I always messed up. The squad management also useless. Can't imagine how could it be if I use voice orders...

This is my first time playing the Toukiden series so i'm new to the lore, ect. However, I did not feel like I got lost and I was able to understand what was going on within the world of Toukiden. That said the quality of the narritive did not "Wow" me. It felt pretty standard fare. The little addition of Arc Records did help give backstory, but it would have been nice to have it referenced in the main narrative as a quest line or something which gave even more backstory. Which is fine for this type of game as i'm mainly here for the gameplay and to fight giant Oni. Speaking of which...
Here is where the game really shines. In this OPEN WORLD game you have 11 weapons to choose from: The sword, knives, spear, guantlets, chain & sickle, bow, club, naginata, rifle, sword and shield, or chain whip. All of which have their own distinct moves and flavor. Nothing feels the same and which weapon you choose will dictate your playstyle. My personal favorites are The Rifle, Chain Whip, and Sword & Shield out of the ones I've played with. I've still yet to touch the Chain & Sickle and Knives at all as i'm still gathering the Mitama - which are the souls of dead heroes who grant you additional skills/power - required for making a decent build. There is a lot of depth hidding in the combat system because of the Mitama and the countless ways you can combine them to come up with cool new builds. Speaking of Mitama... there are a LOT of them hiding around just waiting to be unlocked either through the story, side quests, or defeating powerful Oni and freeing them. You will spend a lot of time unlocking these and creating new and creative builds.
The only real complaint I have is the companion AI in later phases of diffculty when fighting mutliple Oni at once. Your AI companions will seem to alternate between Oni(the one you're NOT attacking currently) instead of just focusing on burning down one THEN moving onto the next one. Its fairly annoying, but i'm not going to dock any points for it. However, there is MULTIPLAYER! Yes you can play co-op with your friends that also enjoy this game! So if you're into that kind of thing that is a plus.
Sound is fine to me. I noticed no issues with the sound on any of the phases or in the open world. I personally like the music, however, it can get a bit repetative but most of the time you won't notice because your too busy fighting Oni.
I'm running the game at a smooth 60FPS 1080p with no slowdown or issues with tearing on screen. I've seen a few complaints about graphics in the discussions, but I think the game looks fine the way it is IMO. I value gameplay over shiny stuffs.
After beating the story you will spend a LOT of time in multiplayer in single player or a lobby with other people unlocking the other gears and goodies for phase 8 - 12 since it can only be unlocked and played in mutliplayer. Once that is done, however, there doesn't appear to be a lot to do as there is no New Game+ which is a real shame because it would have added another layer to the game for those of us who want to keep playing even longer.

The last date you remember is some time during the year 2522.  The end times are here, you’ve been struggling for a while.  Another moon sets, and you get up for another day of slaughter.  There is no happy ending, there is no chance of success, you are not going to be a hero.  Your only desire is to simply see another day, any chance of you living out your life in a cottage next to a river, all gone.  This is not a nightmare, this is Grim Dark.  This is Warhammer: End Times; welcome to the Vermintide.  Hopefully that helps set the mood.
Warhammer: End Times – Vermintide is a grim dark tale told in the Warhammer universe by Fatshark Entertainment.  With a raggedy group of previously mortal enemies banded together just to make it through the night, on the off chance they could complete their quests before their impending death catches up to them.  You’re five great warriors destined to live out your final days slaughtering horde after horde of ratmen clamoring to the surface who desire nothing but death and destruction.
If I were to give as short of summary as possible, it would be “Left4Dead with a melee focus set in Warhammer.”  The gameplay experience is a co-operative survival for 4 players, with 5 unique heroes to choose from, each getting their own vast arsenal of weapons to divvying playstyles even more.  Your pick between swords, great swords, daggers, axes, hammers, shields, bows, crossbows, handguns, repeaters, magic, and everything in between.  The game chronicles an Epic Quest across 13 levels with a story fit for its world, taking you across a massive array of maps and environments, from the peaks of stone walls, to the Magnus Tower, to the trenches in fields, all the way to the gutters and the prisons.  Variety is never something I desired more of during my play throughs.  And that’s not even touching the story DLC.  Don’t have friends?  The AI is suitable to carry through as well, for the singleplayer fans.
Skaven bring a unique new platform to fight endless hordes of, with their impressive mobility and constant, unrelenting threat.  These aren’t just everyday zombies for your endless horde brawler, these are a serious liability.  With staple co-op monsters making an appearance and other “hard to kill” mobs, the Dynamic Spawn System makes a wonderful appearance, or rather, a great job pulling the strings behind the scenes.  Between the gutter runners and the packmasters, you’ll need someone to watch your back.  The Poison Wind Globadiers and the Rat Ogres will give your entire team something to look out for too, requiring solid teamwork to take them down – Along with a few dozen hits from a hefty hammer.  With Skaven, nowhere is safe, there is no hiding.
The levels bring variety in your objectives, from finding relics, to setting back the Skaven camps by destroying their siege, to just trying to get a little food.  My favorite has been the Wizards Tower, during which you hunt down a wizard to earn protection for the Red Moon Inn, the home base for the Ubersreik resistance; the force you lead.  During which, you trudge through a now defunct potion shop, wander through some halls, and come to the Chamber of Gnignol, something impressive that changes based on which character you play through it with.  Your screen won’t match your friends.  You then march through a twisted and warped library, with stairs and chests climbing the walls and ceiling, and fire burning upside-down.  That’s where I’ll leave that, even if it isn’t the end.  It’s one of the first three missions, and it’s all uphill from here.
In addition to the story based content, there is a free endless-wave Survival mode DLC in which you protect an arena and last as long as you can, for glory, loot, and leaderboard.  With no hope of rescue, the heroes are making a last desperate stand, fighting increasingly difficult hordes of Skaven.  The longer you last, the better your loot and the more impressive your trophy.
Progress is delivered in the form of better weapons, trinkets, and cosmetic headgear.  Weapons are not a stat race, they simply get mildly better damage and access to more traits for you to unlock.  Weapon traits are handled through the Forge, requiring you to burn up excess loot to earn upgrade components and unlock them.  Traits can be anything from double damage from behind, to more ammunition, to healing you when you get a hit, to improving stagger from bashes.  A very wide variety of loot to choose from and grind for, if you’re into it.  If not, you can work your way through the entire game perfectly fine with the standard loot if you so desire.  Trinkets offer enhancements to item pickups, to raw buffs, to protection against certain elements, and even purely cosmetic flair for those who don’t need any help.
Now lets leave the gameplay a minute and talk about graphics and sound.  The graphics are wonderful, albeit not top of the line.  They don’t leave you lusting for a generational leap, but they also won’t make you look back on it in nostalgia for its era.  There are plenty of extremely impressive vistas and awe factor moments that are truly well-done locations worth stopping a moment to stare, and none of the assets in the game stand out as poor quality.  The engine handles well enough and scores a respectable framerate on my aged rig, however it is an aged engine and will see occasional dips and a few unreasonably demanding settings.
Next up: Sound.  The sound in this game is wonderful, however it does leave a small bit to be desired.  The meaty sounds of a blade thunking into the flesh of a clanrat is a satisfying sound of metal separating flesh, and the bashes of shields against their skulls is a suitable thud that fits the action as well as giving much needed feedback and heft to the player to confirm the hit.  Fire and cinder sound effects are engaging and feel like you’re there, and are handled wonderfully in surround.  Passive sound effects like footsteps and skittering are subtle but noticeable, a perfect balance for immersion.  Voice lines are well written, crystal clear, with proper ambience applied to make you feel like you’re there.  But that’s where the desire for more comes in.  Voice lines are few, and repeated frequently enough that they all become a joke.  But then again, how many voice lines would you really need for your few hundred playthroughs of the same content?
Overall, the game is a wonderful slaughtering ground for those of us who just need to get a little rat-bashing out of our systems.  A decent story paired with iconic heroes and meaty melee combat, with incentive to play through again and again.  Easily a dozen hours of content even for a one-time pass, and a few dozen more for a repeat co-op experience.  For those desiring more content, there’s a handful of new missions available through DLC to sate your thirst, bringing with them new zones, trinkets and weapons to discover.  With more DLC yet to come this November, giving us even more rats to exterminate.  Definitely worth it’s $30 asking price, and well worth picking up for the price of lunch, the game has been in many bundles and continues to see steep sales on many storefronts.  In addition, it has a Sequel coming out next year, so if you thrust through all the content it has on offer and just can’t get enough, there’s more yet to come.

"Left 4 Dead, but with rats"~People who barely touched the game
I'll get the negative out of the way first. The loot system: upon release, it was unbearable and I quit playing before I even hit level 40. That's not even talking about the myriad of bugs and other problems the game had at release. However, that was years ago now. The grind is still there; now, though, it's good. I might even call it satisfying.
Now for the game itself. I consider the visuals and setting top-notch. Performance-wise, you should have no problem getting the game to look good if you have newer hardware. Beware though, if you want to run the game on ultra-settings and still maintain 60fps, you will need a powerful PC.
Last, but probably most important, the gameplay. On the surface it looks like Left 4 Dead but with rats, and that feeling will only deepen if it's all you expect from the game. The classes all have a unique feel and at least a couple unique melee and ranged weapons each. Some classes share a weapon type, and the only difference between them (most of the time) is the look of them. The longer you play, the more you will feel the differences.
This last bit is part of the gameplay, but very important in my opinion. The skill ceiling in this game is amazingly high. I've put 500 hours into the game, and unlike Left 4 Dead I still feel I can improve my playing. I've heard many players complain that Cataclysm, the highest difficulty in this game, is too difficult; if you have a team of players that is good at the game, it becomes easy. More skilled players can even solo-play on Cataclysm, and i've tried it and can usually get about 1 in 4 games playing solo. To clarify, when I say solo I mean you play alone, not even the bots to help you. This is possible because of the wonderful mechanics in this game, which the community has picked appart and figured out the best ways to manipulate everything.
TL;DR is the game looks like Left 4 Dead on the surface, but leaving it at that is a huge disservice to the game. The skill ceiling and the ever-increasing challenge is enough to keep me and many other players coming back to the game.

Really fun game with quite interesting mechanics. You are trapped on a Ship along with other Players, having to murder each other to win the competition. Each player is assigned to the other in a pair. A Hunter and the Hunted. A Hunter is trying to find and kill the Hunted one, while the Hunted one is most likely a Hunter to someone else and tries to find them and kill them.
So basically you really need to watch your back, as anyone might try to plot to kill you, perhaps waiting for the moment when you go to sleep... Yes, sleep. In the game you have to sustain your character's needs via sleep, eating, drinking, talking and reading books/entertaining. Think of it as The Sims with a twisted plot where characters must kill each other off.
Also... Killing people won't win you the game. Killing them in the most paying way will earn you the victory. Each kill is awarding amount of money based on the weapon you use to kill someone (unless you use environment, like the Freezer/Life-Boats.)

I hear a lot of people claim that this is the best entry in the series, and while it did set the formula and tone for the next two games it has not aged well.
If you're thinking about trying this after playing Oblivion or Skyrim, you'll find a lot of mechanics are more finely-grained, meaning that you don't just have 1 skill for maces, longswords, and axes but rather 1 for each.  It does not make it inherently better or worse but it does increase the learning curve a tad.
For the paranoid save-scummers who worry about glitches or bugs in games, I can guarentee you that you can break quests in this if you are not careful.  It comes from a simpler time when closing off all possible mistakes was not entirely possible.  Companions and quest-essential people CAN DIE.
Overall the best I could say about it is that it retains its charm and broad scope, but it shows its age quite clearly.  It is a very immersive experience that thrusts you into the position of an outcast on the quest to greatness, and pits you against the Dark Elf version of Satan.  If you like Skyrim or Oblivion you'll find it hard to adjust but I can easily say that anyone can get sucked into this.

We'll see how Quake Champions will do - I expect QC to be the biggest, simply because of the sheer marketing power Bethesda and the name "Quake" has, but that does not necessarily mean it will also be the best.
EDIT: Well, QC is here, with terrible netcode and hit detection, it is actually doing no better than Reflex. Hell, in Reflex it's even easier to find a game. I don't have to wait to find, I can just look up a dedicated server with players in it and instantly join.
When you look at gameplay footage from Quake Champions you can pretty much tell that visibility is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, players meld with the background and wish it just had bright skins - as far as I'm concerned, if your game needs bright skins, it has sh!t design. Not that brght skins are a good solution - that's also sh!t design. Then there's the new Unreal Tournament, which jumped the shark by over-using the teamcolors. Most characters got bodypaint and it almost looks like it's glowing. Reflex has by far the most elegant solution. Also runs well on potato computers at like 100+ fps!
It helps that the dev creating this game actually knows how to play it well. Like really well. It's thanks to this, that pretty much every weapon is viable and fulfill it's purpose nicely. Maybe the plasma is a bit too weak (15 dmg/shot), but it still works very well in corridors and has a lot of utility with plasma climbing.
that's right, you've just read Plasma climb! Most weapons can somehow be used for extra movement abilities. There was a time when the Ion (railgun) was leaving a stake in the wall on which you could jump, not sure what happened to that. A lot of weapons have strong knockback too. I will say this though, it's difficult to master the extra movement options with these guns and just spontaneously combine and use it during a regular match as you're B-hopping through the map.
You know how afps are notoriously famous for enabling snowballing too much? Yeah, that won't happen here much. You always get to pick up at least something right away after respawning - weapon or armor in Duel/team based matches. You will always get a chance. It's only the Free-For-All deathmatch game mode that lacks pick-ups - obviously. It could use some kill-based rewards to keep you in the fight (like how in Toxikk enemies drop healthpacks on death).
You'll meet the friendliest players ever here. Even when I was streaming they helped me out with learning some of the trickjumps and how certain mechanics work, down to the very detail, patiently. Obviously, since while the game has a healthy playerbase and is being played they still want more and more to join. They know that many people get intimidated by difficult shooters like this.
Remember when sometimes you would just casually start up the game while you're eating and join your favorite server just to talk to the regulars there, which you already know, played and developed a friendship with? Yeah, me neither. In an age where every game has matchmaking, you don't really get friendly with people any more. You just drop into the next match, and call the guy at the top of the leaderboard a cheater, instead of remembering his name and declaring him your rival, who you must absolutely beat one day.
: Want to watch how the game is played at high rank/in tournaments? Boom, it's right there in the main page/menu. It takes literally just 1 click and you can gaze at how much better the people with 1-2k hours on this game are than you.
You can literally create your own map in a multiplayer match, along with other players. As a result, there's many maps that "made the cut" for being good maps and have been included in many servers. There's already thousands of them. Just before the writing of this review I played on a Sonic themed bunny-track/race map. So if you're wondering why the game download is only 400MB, don't worry there's several gigabytes of custom maps already.
Don't get me wrong, it's nice that there are so many movement options, but it's unnecessarily complex and just scares new players. I'm used to it by now and I love it, but I'm a veteran. I especially like how double/triple jumping works in this game, because
. But just think about how strafejumping works for a second:
. Oh that makes TOTALLY sense and is absolutely intuitive (/sarcasm)... There's another afps called warsow, which at least tried to make bunny-hopping
like it makes sense (your character makes bigger and bigger "steps" with each jump, still looking like he's running, but keeping up the speed).
Another such special move is Circle Jump:
... Just.... what? Sure, not everything has to make sense in a videogame, but c'mon, this is ridiculous!
This movement system also makes it too easy to get stuck in doorways (though that's partly the map designers fault for having small doors) or mistime a jump or fall down. Too fast? You'll miss the jump. Too slow? You won't reach the ledge. You're off course? You can choose to either air-control or air-strafe for speed. If you air-control, you won't be fast enough to reach the other side. If you choose speed, you stay of course and get stuck in the corner. Just... too little margin for error. You're either on point or dead. A good movement system should let you go where you want to go easily and lets you evade shots if you're good enough.
Regardless, flying through bunny-track/race maps at Mach 3 is still fun, but it's okay in that gamemode because it is specifically about mastering movement, much like how you master a track with a specific car in racing simlators.

Even now, i'm not quite sure HOW this game showed up in my Steam Library. I don't ever remember putting it on my Wishlist and i'd never even heard of it prior.
And having played it now, I am so glad I gave this game a chance.
I am usually not that big a fan of cover based shooters as a lot of them tend to feel samey and have this overly serious grim tone to them, but Binary Domain makes itself distinct from other such shooters with some nice little additions that can change how you play. Having a secondary weapon you can change up giving more options for shooting and planning for future encounters, using teammates to initiate tactical moves, blowing off an enemy robot's head or its legs to hamper its movements or destroy its recognition systems, add these to a bunch of different enemy types the game sprinkled in generous quantities and I was having an absoloute blast.
The trust system was something I didn't really pay attention to at first, but toward the end of the game I wish i'd taken more notice of. It's nice to be able to pick your party members for mission sections, for the most part, admittedly the game does sort of drop that toward the end and sticks you with certain people. But even so, it was nice to be able to pick and have teammates suggest actions based on what they good at, Cain's resillience, Bo's distractions, Faye's sniping and so on, it adds just enough variety along with the various different levels and setups that it kept me wanting to play along.
The story reminds me of Metal Gear Solid in a few ways, mostly the absoloute love letter to advanced technology and building up this nice developed cast of characters you really start to appreciate the deeper into Tokyo you go. Especially the main character, it's so nice to be able to play someone who has a decent sense of humour and isn't just serious all the time, it gave the game some much needed levity at the right times.
I'm going to make special mention of the boss fights because, I didn't think shooters had it in them to do boss fights anymore. But this one sure does and a lot of them really know how to make things exciting, be it with incredible resillience, massive size or wicked designs. The final boss is a bit of a let down in the designs regard, but that's not to say it isn't a ridiculously tough final opponent. Big thumbs up on the bosses in this game, I just wish there could've been more.
This game isn't perect and I think it does have it's share of flaws. The music gets repetetive quickly, especially considering they tend to repeat the battle music over and over again. It's not bad music, it just needed more variety. AI partners can be difficult to deal with too, especially when they'll move in front of you when shooting and get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at you for it. The voice controls, I couldn't deal with either. I just turned them off and used tab, made things a bit easier. That being said, mouse and keyboard support probably won't be much good to most people. I was able to adapt to it in due time, but it will probably throw some people for a loop, and even then it can be annoying trying to get into cover and watching Dan leap over it and skirt around it instead of getting behind it.
Overall, Binary Domain is a surprisingly good cover based third person FPS, with good visuals, good characters, good story, amazing boss fights and mild to annoying controls. If you want to see cover based shooting done right and like killing robots, this is an absoloute reccomendation for you. Hell there's even a demo, so you've got no excuse not to try it at least.

Let's get to the short answer to the question "should I buy Toukiden 2?"
If you're a fan of monster hunter games then it's a good match.  If you're just curious about it, you'd better think twice.
It's almost impossible to describe this game without mentioning Monster Hunter, but you should not go in expecting a similar experience.  Here are a bunch of bullet point considerations in no particular order:
-The game community is tiny and therefore the amount of data available is miniscule, even compared to God Eater.  If you can't make your way around Japanese websites, you're going to have a hard time figuring out how gear and weapons work.
-The game has a story campaign that is actually quite decent, and you unlock a large number of important perks by completing it.  The characters are generally quite likable despite each individual character having short screen time, and the plot may not be a work of art but it make the world work.
-The endgame has a boss-rush system instead of a "super-strong-monster-kills-you-in-two-hits" system.  Personally, the apex system in monster hunter killed my motivation.  The ruins boss rush in this game is more fun, because you have to ration your resources over the course of multiple monster kills, and optimizing damage with different weapons and roles can really come together for a satisfying experience.
-The mitama system scratches a particular itch many gamers (including myself) may have: the exploration of build possibilities.  Depending on what weapon you choose, you'll have a lot of satisfying moments where you find interesting synergies between the equippable mitama, and most of the time you'll be able to come up with interesting and unique builds that are still viable.  In many other games, going with a sub-optimal build might invite mockery from other players, but in this game, you can make most builds work.
-The difficulty is lower when compared with Monster Hunter.  That's not to say that this game is easy, but my multiplayer experience had a lot fewer quest failures than when I played Monster Hunter.
-The graphics are nice, but still lacking, especially compared to current-generation games.  This is a vita port, and despite being a very stable one, it is still disappointing that the resources were not spent to make the game look particularly nice.
-The armor selection is somewhat lacking.  This is primarily in comparison to Monster Hunter, which had a noticeably larger variety of armors.  However, you are free to mix and match armors for whatever fashion you pursue, because there are no skills attached to armor in this game.  This leads me to believe that you are meant to choose your armors for the sake of looks, which also makes me confused because you cannot dye armors at all.
Final note:  The monster hunting genre is experiencing a serious drought right now, and Capcom does not want to spend resources on their product, and the next God Eater game is probably not happening too soon.  This game will sate your thirst if you're hungry for that kind of experience.  However, this game does not stand well next to current generation titles, and I only feel so positively about it because the competition is just so scarce.  The game also feels slightly incomplete, when considering the amount of actual content in the game.
I bought this game at full price and played it for a month with my friends, so I do not regret this purchase.  However, I am reluctant to invest any more money into this game or its DLC, because it could be so much more than it is, if only the competition in this genre were a little more fierce.

TL;DR: Wait for the expansion that will actually be a complete game rather than buying this half-completed budget game that is priced as an AAA game.
Toukiden 2 improved on the predecessors (Toukiden and Toukiden Kiwami) in several ways by adding many cool features and mechanisms, such as the open-world map, the oni hand, and several new styles of mitamas. However, Koei Tecmo clearly intends to charge you the price of two AAA game (120$) for 1 complete budget game. Here's why.
Toukiden 2’s gameplay is fun, I won’t deny that. But there is no doubt that it’s a budget game, as pretty much everything except the few new weapons and mechanisms are old and recycled stuffs from the previous games. The graphics, animations, and overall quality are all that of a budget game. There is nothing wrong with this per se, even if it charges you the same price as The Witcher 3, as long as Toukiden 2 is actually a complete game which I would recommend even at 60$. So what's making me unrecommend this one is purely out of morality since KT is completely without morals as you don't even get a complete game for 60$.
Toukiden 2 has far less contents than its predecessor, Toukiden Kiwami, despite the fact people would generally expect each new installment to add upon the predecessors in a game like this. For example, if the previous game had 20 bosses, you would expect more in this new one right? Well, tough luck, we have the exact same number of boss monsters (20) as Kiwami despite Koei has added a few new monsters to Toukiden 2. So how is this possible??
Koei intentionally cut a dozen old monsters from previous games when the number of boss variety is already pathetic in this game to begin with (forcing you to fight the same monsters over and over to progress through the game as a result). Some old bosses are shamelessly sold as 5$ DLCs (imagine if Tigrex is sold as a DLC in a MH game), and keeping away a few others -some of them very iconic (like Kiwami’s poster-monster, the twin-tail wolf that’s extremely fun to fight) – for the inevitable expansion that Koei will once again charge you full price for. There is absolutely no doubt that Koei intends to do this, since all weapons and equipment are purposefully kept weak, with their rank maxed out at 6, whereas the predecessor ones went up to rank 9. A big portion of the open world map is also unused, presumably kept for the expansion. The missions are also limited compared to Kiwami, with 7 phases offline and 12 online, whereas Kiwami had 12 and 19 or 20 respectively.
So basically to get the full game, you will need to spend 120$ plus whatever you decide to spend on the numerous DLCs featuring purposefully-cut contents from old games rather than newly designed ones. If you are really interested in this game, take my advice and wait for the release of Toukiden 2 Kiwami.
Finally, the online is already pretty much dead given than only 300 players are actively playing it (out of a total of 20k players, which is beyond pathetic). You don't care? Well you should even if you plan on soloing the entire game. The fact that Koei doesn't care about getting a lot of sales, has no intention whatsoever to expand their player base and attract new comers with good business practices, and is instead content with the ability to grab some quick cash off the existing tiny niche of players, means that they don't care about you as a customer. So don’t expect ANY technical support or having your complaints heard. With big greedy companies such as EA and Ubisoft, at least they still care about money and players' protests can often have some effect. But when a dev is so lazy and doesn't give a damn about making a complete and quality product, and is only interested in making quick profits, there is NOTHING players can do to make things right. Shortsightedness is worse than pure greed, and Koei Tecmo possesses BOTH traits.
Last words on the port, the PC port also lacks basic features you would expect from a game priced as an “AAA” with ZERO mouse support, atrocious keyboard controls (a controller is an absolute MUST), and no resolution support above 1080P and 60FPS.

It's a sandbox game similar to Minecraft, but allows you to build much more complex machines or structures. Definitely worth playing.
Pros:
-Small blocks, so you can build more detailed structures
-Blocks are scalable
-You can share your creations, or bring someone else's into your world
-Mods are extremely easy to install, and can add a lot to the game
-Multiplayer
-Unlike other games, you can build almost anything- not just houses, but cars, planes, trains, etc- it's really up to your imagination.
-Super addicting. You can spend hours building, painting, and tweaking something.
Cons:
-While the game will run on most computers, it still isn't very well optimized. Expect lag to occur, especially if you're building complex items and your computer isn't the best out there. Playing on flat worlds does help with this, though.
-You can't modify the terrain yet (of course, you could just build over it with painted blocks, effectively making your own terrain- but still).
-Survival mode still hasn't come out, yet, despite being shown in the earlier versions.
-This game can and will be glitchy. You'll probably have your creations spaz out at some point.
-The controls are a little weird, especially if you're like me and have spent lots of time playing games like Minecraft. However, you can just change them in the settings.
-The community is still relatively small, but most people are nice.
-The world is pretty small. You have plenty of space to build and explore, but it's still not very big.
Overall, this is a great game if you enjoy sandbox/building games. I'd highly recommend it.

I hear a lot of people claim that this is the best entry in the series, and while it did set the formula and tone for the next two games it has not aged well.
If you're thinking about trying this after playing Oblivion or Skyrim, you'll find a lot of mechanics are more finely-grained, meaning that you don't just have 1 skill for maces, longswords, and axes but rather 1 for each.  It does not make it inherently better or worse but it does increase the learning curve a tad.
For the paranoid save-scummers who worry about glitches or bugs in games, I can guarentee you that you can break quests in this if you are not careful.  It comes from a simpler time when closing off all possible mistakes was not entirely possible.  Companions and quest-essential people CAN DIE.
Overall the best I could say about it is that it retains its charm and broad scope, but it shows its age quite clearly.  It is a very immersive experience that thrusts you into the position of an outcast on the quest to greatness, and pits you against the Dark Elf version of Satan.  If you like Skyrim or Oblivion you'll find it hard to adjust but I can easily say that anyone can get sucked into this.

This is truly the best RPG I have ever played. I played all of Skyrim, Fallout 3 & New Vegas, and Oblivion. Though it is a much older game, Morrowind has the best world to explore. The armour customizations are much more in dept than any of the previous games, the game is much more challenging, and the guilds are much more worth it. Skyrim doesn't even have guilds, just groups of boring people all looking to you to save them. Oblivion has great guilds but it makes no sense that you can become an arch mage despite having absolutlely no talent for magic.
Firstly, the world you will inhabit is absolutely hateful towards outsiders, which makes sense giving the state of colonialization they are going through. The world of the Dark Elves, also known as Dunmer, is run by the three main Houses. These political factions each specialize in different skills and each compete for power over Morrowind. Morrowind also houses a living God named Vivec, and allows you to join the Imperial Legion, which for some reason is not a joinable faction in either of the newer games. You can also join any one of the three Houses, the Mages Guild, Thieves Guild, Fighters Guild, and the Mora Tong (assassin's guild). You can also join the Temple of Morrowind or the Church of the Imperials. The unique missions from so many different organizations make this game very immersive as you rarely wonder why they don't just tell one of their other oh so capable members to undertake the quest. Unlike in any of it's successors, you must perform missions and develop your related skills in order to advance in a guild.
This game is hard. Creatures do not level up with you so going into the wrong cave too early can be fatal. Magic points only restore with rest as does health and if you're exhausted you will be obsolete in combat. Combat itself is fun though not nearly as polished as it successors are. You can't go looting a bunch of caves in one sitting to say the least. Another challenging aspect of the game is it's map. There are no way points. In order to locate your objectives, you must actually read and follow your directions closely. It makes the game very difficult but intriguiing.
Perhaps a favorite part of the game for me is THERE IS NO FAST TRAVEL!!! This makes the game much more challenging and you appreciate finishing every single quest. There are still ways to access major cities and certain places via magic, teleportation, and giant bugs that will traverse the lands for you for a small fee. This game has a lot of reading since it is as old as it is, but it is truly the best RPG out there. If you can get past the reading, old graphics,  and shaky combat, you will find a game that offers a sense of accomplishment unlike any other and a great story to boot. Will you make the journey?

Spore is a game that combines games. It does so while keeping the same element that binds together all these playstyles. You create your own- WOAH. To understand Spore's key element, you need to take a look at EVERYTHING it has to offer. You begin emerging from a meteor as a cell, where you swim around the Tidepool searching for food. Depending on what you are (carnivore or herbivore) you eat different creatures, food, and other things. eating gives you DNA, the currency that lets you change up your cell in a way that gives it protection, speed, and tricks. These tricks can then be used during the creature stage, which is where youwalk around the surface of the planet (you get to name it, too!) finding food. Other creatures inhabit the land too, though. You have two options: Friend, or food. You unlock HUNDREDS of new partss to use on your creature, including pincers, cooler eyes and mouths, arms, legs, and the list goes on. afterwards you are trested to the Tribal Stages. Here you select units (which are your own creature army) and tell them where to go. Now you can't change the look of your creature, or even RENAME them. All you can do now is give him some odd looking tribal clothes. Other tribes steal your food (new currency), and it gets pretty hectic. Tribal isn't as good, but its short and brings you to Civilization stage. Here your creature has built towns, trade routes, tanks and fighter jets, designed by YOU. Once again, selected unit-based gameplay, but its more fun than Tribal. i just find it fun to send my army to a small town ready to be conquered. As for the Space Stage, you now control your designed spaceship to conquer or ally other planets. Spore gets a 10/10.

I started playing STO  during beta and, like many others, after release soon maxed out a toon and started to wonder what the end-game was, PvP turned out un-balanced and dissapointing, and exploration was repetative, although the episodes (missions) were always rewarding. Being a trekkie I stuck with it as long as I could but managed to get pulled away by friends onto other games and MMO's easily  (yes including SWTOR...) but returned occasionally to see what had changed.
Recently I rejoined after about a year's break and am really enjoing it.  The various game play changes and additions, season expansions, and the defocus of PvP, have made this into a great game delivering the online Star Trek experience I was expecting originally. The new seasons (to me everything from Solane Dyson Sphere onwards) are great and embody the Star Trek experience with the exception that I'm in the captains chair.
Well turned around devs, can't wait for the New Dawn expansion now, but at least I have some time to catch-up.
For those considering the game:
- It's free to play, and playable as free to play, although I have sub'ed for the extra's...
- Feels like Star Trek, Looks like Star Trek, Sounds like Star Trek,
- Great official storyline (seasons and episodes) and player added content with lots of great episodes,
- Extensive customisation (player, ship, bridge officers, duty officers),
- Space combat and Ground combat, but you still feel you are in the same game and plying the same mission,
- Lots of extended and end game content now, so much so you can easily get distracted from the storyline,
- More PvE than PvP,
- PvE - can go it alone and get a full experience, joining a fleet adds to this experience,
- A lot to get your head around now though, but you should expect some technical depth in a Star Trek universe,
- and it's Free-to-Play...
Still a few things I'd like to see added/changed (I still want to explore the various ships internally rather than the same layout on each other than the bridge), but definately worth a re-installing and spending the effort getting familiar with the changes if you gave it up a while ago.

STO has... come a long way from when I first started this.
At this moment, 5 years on, lots of changes, and I gotta say at least its moving in the right direction and worth it at least for that.
I dunno, whenever it first went free to play, that's when I started this first. Long before I had Steam, back when it was vastly different than what I have seen now.
Finding myself getting back to this gem was a nice refreshing taste of nostalgia - and a bit of dissapointment. Some of what I saw as the more fun and Trek-like gameplay is gone. Random missions is replaced with sporatic patrols that shift daily that you need to find. But despite the loss, there is so much more added I can really start to appreciate this game, and willing to admit I'm a lifer now. I've come back to this game time and time again - and it does hold an aspect that I see worth visiting.
Many of the old, glitchy, unwanted parts (and I bet many of the negative reviews here are based on those) are long since gone. New elements have been added to help encourage a wider and more varried feel to the game. Many aspects have been added or changed to encourage development of really impressive improvements.
R&D got an overhaul with the Duty Officers you gain, making it easier to earn good stuff - and add the possibility of making your own unique and impressive equipment.
Bridge Officers have the ability to learn multiple skills, so you can have just a few favorites for the ideal team mix but still have the ability to shift what powers they use to simplify things in certain situations.
Player Traits have been vastly overhauled. Parts of it I regret missing, you can't have an overpowered selection of a dozen or more Reputation traits powering you up - but you can now shift between selections in certain areas not in combat zones. And the mixing is balanced out well so far.
You can make your captain and crew into what you dream here, in many surprising ways.
But comes the only glaring problem I see - its an MMO. Its a kill or be killed area where damage is king. Grinding is a must and you gotta mow down mobs en masse. RP'ers will find some loss in certain builds and styles just not up to par - and if you want the top gear, you'll need to grind. And some grinds can't be done without a certain level of killing strength, so some things - just can't cut it. Doesn't feel very Trek at times. But I can't really call that a truly negative part at the moment.
STO is Trek, just not the TV or Movie Trek. Its another Trek, in another galaxy. Another mirrored universe almost where you need to adapt to new enemies and threats. And face a hard truth. Kill or be killed.
Outside of that, the game itself is showing an unbelieveable ammount of improvements over time. Focusing more on gameplay mechanics to help make enjoying the game easier. You just need to learn that over time.
The Trek part? Well, its there. Cameoes, nods, and a great deal of effort in stories. But some of the later aspects really don't fit like I wish they did. But this isn't really the same Trek I would want it to be. Its not bad, just different. Can't honestly fault that anymore.
Its a good MMO, with good merits and definetly something I could reccomend as you could find what you want in here somewhere - it certainly does have its size to go for it. That and the Foundry. Player-created content is a huge aspect of the game and if you got the time, you'll find a whole slew of additions to content and story that makes this game well worth the visit. The hard part is just finding it.
But that's a bit of the charm. There is so much here, so much possibility. There is good, and bad - but overall, its trying a respectable rate to be better. I gotta admit that's worth it itself.
Now the somewhat dated graphics and cartain core elements - well, that's just cause its an older game. But don't let that dissuade you here. You'll find something worth visiting, and even more worth coming back for. I know I have.

After putting so much time into this game and it's 2 DLC I think its about time I return the favor to this game and write a review on it. (Sidenote: Its on my steam version I have 100 so hours. I have spent around 40 times that, just to give you my qualifications).
I'll start with the base game of Mount&Blade:Warband.
Warband is a brilliant Medieval era RPG with brilliant gameplay and while outdated still beatiful graphics. The Gameplay itself is very simple with a 3rd person-esq gameplay map where you move aroun your party and interact with other things and people on the overmap. Their are 3 catagories of things to interact with: Hostile Units, Neutral/Friendly Units, and Villages/Towns/Castles/Caves/etc.
When you interact with a hostile unit you engage in a bit of dialoge before running away, paying them off (depending) or battling them. Battling is a first person form where you control your character and can order your men to do stuff (or just kind of let them run around). These battles can range from Seiging Praven to minor skirmeshes vs 2-3 bandits.
When interacting with Neutral/Friendly Units you simply exchange words that let you acomplish a variety of things as you would expect from talking.
Interactions with (non-hostile) places are simple and you go into a "click on where you want to go" screen.
To Shorten this up my ratings go as follow:
Gameplay: 10/10. Historcally acurate units and troops, weapons, and cattle (Bloody cattle). Overall the gameplay is great and, while technically simple, it's fun and difficult in all the right ways.
Graphics: 7/10. The game is a bit old though is still beatiful and well presented.
Bugs: 8/10. While their are a few bugs, they are not really game breaking and are often funny rather than bad.
Music/Sound: 9/10. All it's missing is "Ride of the Rohirim" by Howard Shore.
Replay Value: 10/10. If you manage to "beat" it after 400 hours, why not do it again. Oh the joy of starting over and dying to one looter...
Now as for the DLC Napoleonic Wars, it can only be summed up as such: Machivelli riding a horse off a cliff while playing "Flight of the Valkyries" on a french horn. ......... The only real drawback to this game is the lack of a singleplayer, but to be honest, multiplayer might as well be singleplayer and you really play this mode to laugh.
As for the Viking Conquest DLC, oh lord where do I begin. While I have not fully explored every feature in the reforge update I can suffice to say that its brilliant on every level you can think of. You play in The forming England during the time of King Alfred the Great, the danish invasions, oh, and the French (Friese) are there to. This might as well be Medieval Simulator and is one of the best games i've ever played. Plus, it has a storymode to introduce you to everything, so props to the dev team for that. I simply do not have words for this game other than buy it now so i'll give you numbers now.
Gameplay: 10/10. Ever wanted to Go Viking? You can. Ever wanted to be an Irish Druid? You can. Ever wanted to subconsuiclly get the greatest history lesson ever about the forming of England (Engaland) ever? Well you better believe you do.
Graphics: 9/10. Still similar to Warbands Graphics, but largly and upgrade.
Bugs: 8/10. Bare in mind its still in development, but really, there aren't many.
Music/Sounds: 11/10. It breaks the scoreboard. Words cannot describe.
Replay Value: 10/10. If you don't downright die (something you can do in this mode), and don't succumb to useless injury (also new), and actually manage to (through miracles) conquer everyone (you cheater), then yes, feel free to replay.
Also, with both Warband and VC, especailly VC, the Character Creation is more in-depth than D&D, so, yeah. Always fun.
