. (Kinda NSFW, obviously.)
The first thing that I like is that you can play as male or female. Yessss. This is a huge dating sim plus for me. (Okay... This is actually my first dating sim, except for the brief romance in a few visual novels that I play. But, it's still a plus!)

Kyu's a Love Fairy, and she's gonna help me get all the HuniePop girls, or at least she'll try.
I love every game genre, and I love a good puzzle, so the puzzle aspect of HuniePop is so much fun, and the most challenging part.
The puzzle is basically like any other, and luckily it's not timed. Kyu lets you have one gift that'll help you in the future, and when you give a girl a gift she ♥'s, you get one in return. Basically, these are like boosts, and they don't disappear when you use them, thank Gods.
Each date, even if you fail, rewards you with Munie, which can be used to buy the girls gift!
Finally, you get this chic device called the HunieBee, which let's you see each girl's profile, as well as track their location, so you can easily go from one girl to the next. The first time I played through HuniePop, the first girl I met was a pretty Japanese teacher named Aiko, who I reallyyyy reallyyyy liked, and I made sure I romanced her first.
Each girl has a menu: 'talk with her', 'ask on date', 'view inventory', 'girl finder', 'check profile' and 'purchase gifts'.
Also, you can check the HunieBee for each girl, and find out information for each girl, like what their preferred token is on the puzzle, what they like to do (equaling what kind of gifts to get them), etc. The next page is deets, like name, age, even cup size! ^_-
Even after playing for a week, I haven't completed even one girl's collection. I don't know if there's an achievement for this, (oh yeah, there's achievements and I am a total achievement ♥♥♥♥♥) but my OCD demands I complete each one!
The style page is for the playa as it's just eye candy depending on your personal favorite style for each girl!
The photo section is where the NSFW part really comes in. You get four pics from each girl, one after each SUCCESSFUL date.
Oh, and, there are three hidden characters!
The longer you play, the more information you get, the more the girl's quiz you on what they like and do, the more they ask about you, and the harder each date gets.
On the fourth date, if your date is successful, you bring the girl home and HuniePop her. image After this, you get her panties, and once you have the whole collection... Well, that's a secret!
Lemme give some shout-outs, to my four favorite HuniePop girls. Aiko! She is my ABSOLUTE favorite. Followed by, Tiffany, Jessie, and Audrey!
So, that is the amazingness of HuniePop. It's addictive, so addictive. There are some sexy comments and nudity in the game, so it's 18+ for a reason. I just wanna make that clear for anyone interested in playing.

This game seems like it has been a huge undertaking for its developers, the fact that it is F2P I found was also commendable. It almost made me understand the ever increasing pay to win elements that started to appear the more game time I put in. Almost.
I had been waiting for another WW2 shooter, as much as I adore Red Orchestra 2 I was hoping for something else in the genre, because lets face it, there hasn't been a great deal of quailty in that market lately (I'm looking at you Enemy Front!) At first I thought I had found it, but those thoughts waned the more I played.  Don't get me wrong, this game isn't garbage; graphically it's impressive, not to mention that for an early access game, I found it surprisingly bug free, and for a little while I had great fun playing it.
That was until I finally reached the holy grail. After a fair bit of time it took to progress to level 5 (that's how long it takes to unlock the rest of the game. It might not seem like much, but progression is very slow, unless you pay money to skip through it of course), I almost felt like I had achieved something. But this ascendency had proved to be a bitter pill, for this was when I had realised my arduous journey was wasted and I began to instantly regret my trek. The game is already quite tough on beginners, so after several hours in you could be forgiven for thinking you might just be getting the hang of this game. Hell you may on occasion single-handledly save your team, wreaking havoc and feeling like the hero in the title. Then you reach level 5, those man hours you spent learning and progressing as well as that SMG you'd spent hours trying to unlock and perfect, because you didn't want to pay for it, all becomes worthless. You get lumped in the guys who paid through the nose for a tank or unlocked the tougher to earn weaponary that makes your PPD look like a pea-shooter, and you find yourself completely helpless. Tanks pick you off from miles away and snipers who threw their cash in to fully upgrade it, pick you off from even further. Those hours spent having a fun, learning the ropes at the are worthless.... Don't fret though you can always throw your money away and join the darkside with your new-found foes. If you were encouraged to donate instead of paying to win, this game could have been something special.
I can understand the need to throw a few coins for the developers sake, a seemingly big project like this should earn some kind of support from its player base,unfortunately though it gets steadily thrown in your face after a while. You make in game credits but not much, and weapons need to be repaired and ammo replenished and if you were saving up those credits for that K98 or whatever you'd been hoping for, you're going have to hang around for sometime... unless you pay for those gold coins and just buy it, buy it all, buy everything! Everybody else is.

If you've never seen Star Trek before you'll be confused at first, because of the fact that you don't know $#!T about anything going on, and you won't understand almost anything in the game. However, the game does an excellent job of introducing all of the storylines and basically everything in the Star Trek universive to you, so basically, if you play this game long enough, you'll become a Trekkie, without even having watched any of the shows.
STO also has great missions, which are very immersive and interactive. Once you're done with one storyline, there'll always be many more to complete, as the STO team uploads new ones almost every 2-3 months. (Don't quote me.)
This game is absolutely free to play, which is of course, awesome. Every single weapon and ship can be aquired through a great system. Time and effort. Of course, it'll take much less time to aquire certain ships by purchasing them with Zen Points (Currency that is bought with real money), but it all depends on how you'd like to approach the game. I personally have not made a single ship purchase with Zen Points, and I still have a very strong ship that is capable of taking on any foe.
The game also has two im-game currency systems, Energy Credits and Dilithium. You'll be using these two currencies to buy most of your ships and equipment. Both of these currencies are easy to earn and the prices for items are never too high.
It has a great ranking-up and skill-tree system, and also has great PvP missions and PvE missions as well. And in PvP, your'e paired up with people of the same level, so you won't get obliterated by people who are much higher ranked than you.
There are many many things that I haven't mentioned in this review. The devs have put a great amount of time and effort into this amazing game and I think that they deserve praise for it.       But to sum it all up, you get to run around, shoot lasers at people, shoot bigger lasers at ships, get in game credits, buy really cool things, shoot at people more, and play Dabo. Yes, dabo. This game has gambling. What more do you want? Now download the dang game.

Run and gun game released in 2000 on Neo Geo. But... it didn't age a bit and is still more than up to par to today's standards. The screen is filled with enemies, explosions and projectiles. Everything is nicely animated and the cartoonish pixel art graphics are gorgeous.
The gameplay is frenetic, and very responsive. It doesn't feel stiff like a lot of old games, this game is very smooth to play. A good point is that it can be played with mouse & keyboard, or gamepads. And it recognizes different brands of gamepads, unlike a lot of recent games that only lazily recognize the traitorous Xbox360 pad.
Metal Slug 3 is the pinnacle of the series. Tons of weapons, different branching paths, tons of different enemies and creatures to fight (soldiers, zombies, extra-terrestrials, snails, wasps, submarines, planes, yeti men, and so on and so on). Moreover, the gameplay sequences undergo a lot of variation: different vehicles, space invaders/shoot-em-up phases, aquatic fight, and so on and so on. The boss fights are very well done (can be very very tough though). Once a mission has been unlocked in the main campaign mode, it is possible to start from it at any time.
There is an online leaderboard for all the difficulty settings,  but the best thing is that there is an online Co-op mode. ONLINE CO-OP MODE ON METAL SLUG!!!!!!!!!!!!!! This is awesome.
On the negative side, despite the quite good port, some bugs can appear at times to times, such as the sound disappearing. There aren't many graphical filters, but it is possible to add them if you follow this guide (I recommend HQ4X)
Overall, this game is tons of fun, is reasonably challenging and feels great to play. Online Co-op is much appreciated.
I wish Metal Slug X (Metal Slug 2 revamped) will also be ported to Steam by the same team.

Definitely addictive and fairly deep. Unfortunately, many facets of the game could be improved, and currently not worth the price tag.
- Business aspect of the game isn't very deep. 'Marketability' is included in the game and is effected by actions, but there aren't enough actions to tinker with it significantly. What if I built a racing team that makes a TON of money but performs averagely? I'm talking about merchandising, advertising, PR, etc... Not an option. If you don't do well, you're not marketable.
- Racing aspect, while deep, can be a bit frustrating at times. Qualifying is almost a nightmare... it's a completely different method of controlling the racer without a tutorial, and is inconsistent. Simulating qualifying will burn through all your tyres [sic].
- Tinkering with the car setup during practice is fun and rewarding. Only a limited amount of time is given, and there isn't a good way to compare both of your drivers' setups and match them up. Also, a team manager is not likely to be making decisions on what gear ratio to choose for a particular track. Or maybe he/she is?
- During one of my first races, my #1 was bumped by an opponent on the way to the pit stop, and the collision caused damaged the vehicle. However, during the 15-20 seconds it took for my racer to get back to the pit, there was no way for me to adjust what would happen in the pit stop. So my guy with a broken front wing just rolled up to the pit stop and got his tires changed. That's it. There was no way for me to do anything about it, so I just watched it in misery. (it may have been possible to cancel the pit stop altogether, but since it was an early race, that wasn't an easy option to choose)
- I like not always being the winner. A game like this is great for that. Actually makes a good result more rewarding. You'll find yourself rooting for your drivers and team, and will become saddened when they are passed by a superior driver and vehicle almost every time.
Overall a good game, but unfortunately not great. I'll be waiting for Motosport Manager 2, or for the sale to drop to 75%

The only thing missing, is the lack of official licensed racing cars, tracks and championships content but Steam workshop do fill in some of the gaps.
My best moment of Motorsport Manager came at an unexpected mid-season race, while running in the long (50-60laps) vanilla race tier3 European Series league. I was struggling to maintain my 4th championship position, the team boss was unhappy with the performance of the team and was one race from getting the boot. So having gambled on a mixed strategy of 2-stops and 3-stops for my drivers, with questionable quality of engines and brakes, I pushed them all through 49-laps of the race, ignoring their complains, to have them end up on the podium with cars finishing literally on fumes (0.00 laps of fuel left with 1/2 lap remaining). I lost the top spot on the line due to an engine failure but the boss was over the moon afterwards nevertheless. That screaming and nail biting finish of the last lap of the race, made in my opinion Motorsport Manager worth every penny. Highly recommended!

PS: Also my thanks to Playsport Games that gave us a free week of playtime of this excellent game (20-27/03/17). Can't wait to finish all the core leagues and then try my hands on some of the custom workshop content.

It is a game where you play as a manager of a racing team. You scout and recruit members. Improve your car and build buildings that improve development. A nice feature of this game is that the game experience changes over time because new rules are voted upon by you and other managers which will be active next racing season. There are a fair amount of these rules so each season is different. To get money, get sponsors.
I think a good ammount of work went in to this game. It works pretty stable and has many features.
It still has some bugs i hope they intend to solve:
- When there is thunder/lightning the game crashes, happened once.
- Finishes are not correct. Sometimes i finish a few rounds to soon because i am a few rounds behind. Also the game waits for cars that should already have finished.
- At the start of a season you can buy engine parts. But if the rule is engine is fixed you should not be able to choose one.
- Before you race you can choose what type of tyres you bring. But what i want is depending on the size of the fuel tank. This i can not see  at this moment.
- The weather report does not show your place in reference to the weather but the pole position it seems. It would be better so show the positions of the racers there.
- Scrolling trough the car parts in a car is choppy.
- Its not clear to me if the weight of the fuel has any impact on the race.
- After ending a race in fourth place the stats of my driver went down 200% and i don't know why.
I don't like the part of the game where you have to tune the car before a race or test or quallification. I hope they make an option or rule to do it automatically.
All in all i think its a great game but it needs a little but more work.

Some things to note about my review are that I got the game for free, I haven't played the first game, I was unable to try out the multiplayer, I only used one ship type, and I only played through on the easy difficulty.
Platypus II is a side scrolling space shoot 'em up that's supposedly a sequel to Platypus. You fly around in a space ship and shoot all kinds of enemies, ranging from other ships to... well... er... weird things. With seemingly no story, it's basically about defeating the enemies and getting a high score, which will save once you're done. You can pick one of four different types of projectiles when you start. This will determine your normal shots as well as your powered up shots. To get the different variations of your chosen projectile type, you have to kill certain mobs of enemies that will drop a star. You will see a color and letter on the star to denote the types. It seems that there's generally a power shot that will go through enemies and destroy enemy shots but shoot slowly, a wide shot to give you better coverage, an auto shot that lets you hold down the fire button to shoot continually at max speed, and rockets which seem to be the same regardless of your ship choice. You can shoot the star to make it spin around and change to the next in the cycle of set powerups. You can also find a lightning one that will always be lightning. And sometimes stars will drop that are only one type no matter how many times you shoot them, but all of them are on a timer. You can also find crates being carried up by ballons that will drop things like coins, score multipliers, and orbiting cannons that will shoot your current projectiles alongside you. By killing specific groupings of enemies you can get bonus points. Some larger enemies will give lots of points for being killed and will also drop fruit. You can collect the fruit for more bonus points, but if you shoot them they will break apart and leave you scrambling to pick up the pieces before they call off screen. So many points will get you an extra life. There are also bosses at the end of each level. There are five levels with five areas in each. By beating a level you will get a bonus credit.
I like the art of this game a lot. The claymation look is cool with lots of vibrant colors an interesting designs in the backgrounds and enemies. The music is pretty nice too. It contols fine and it pretty simple to control. Being able to choose between different ships is cool for variety, strategy, and just some replay value. The mechnics of bonus points for killing enemy groups makes you want to kill everything rather than avoid it all. And the fruit gathering requiring you to be careful not to just keep blasting constantly is a nice touch. Also, the ability to swith what the powerup you pick up will be on the fly is fun because you have to decide if you want to switch its type and risk waiting longer to grab it or go in early while it's still safe and deal with whatever you get. Plus it introduced new enemies and hazards while staying visually appealing.
There are some problems though. Yeah, it looks pretty, but sometimes all the effects of exploding enemies can get in the way of seeing projectiles, not to mention the scenery getting into the foreground and blocking your view at times. There's also a weird choppiness to the visuals. That's probably somehow my machine, but it seems to meet the requirements so I'm not sure what the problem could be. The music is cool but can get a bit annoying if you don't like the song as stages are a bit long. Steam overlay would be a nice feature to include... or online scoreboards and such, but those are all minor things. I think the biggest problem is the pacing. The game is a bit too long to necessarily do in one sitting unless you generally have longer sittings like myself. Even if you do play it all at once, your trigger finger is bound to get tired. I mean, you CAN hold down the button to auto fire but unless you have that auto fire powerup then you can press the fire button much faster than that standard auto rate. I could use a bit of shortening up or perhaps some more variety in your gameplay to go along with the new enemies and backgrounds that you get.
So what does this add up to? Well, Platypus II is a fun little game, and it's worth playing if you like colorful space shooters. However... 7 bucks is a bit much for the short title. You'd have to really want to get those high scores and try out all the ships to want to keep playing, and it can be a bit tiresome to the fingers. For 3 bucks or less, I'd say it'd be worth getting for the general public. Overall, Platypus II gets a 6 out of 10 for being a pleasing space shoot 'em up experience.

Caught this game for free with a SEGA promotion a while ago. Have to say its a pretty standard fare shooter that has surprisingly crisp graphics and somewhat wonky controls (maybe rectified with a controller?) and a hit-and-miss cover system (not as cleanly done as GOW or Uncharted maybe). The enemies are standard shooter enemies just robotified and the 'Team Members' are exactly what you'd expect in combat, more or less useless.
What makes me review this game positively is its plot, art-direction and graphics, voice talent, and level/boss design. Without the proper mix of these elements this could easily have been a Ho-hum generic shooter. Instead we are treated to an actiony sci-fi plot set in a slightly dystopic future Japan but with a cast of characters that spread a good mix of ethnicities. Your team is made of Americans, British, Chinese, and French members and you routinely meet up with the native population.
Between your team, the Japanese Freedom fighters, the Japanese Government, the evil soulless robots, and the weird class of being called 'Hollow Children' (human like robots) plot relevant variety abounds. Locales are also pretty varied as well and the game has a somewhat contained-but-still-sorta-epic feel to it.
It lasted me about 15 hours and I played on the games 'Hard' mode (which is routinely nowadays the old normal mode).
Right now I see it up on Steam for $15. If you are looking to have a fun 3rd person shooter with a pretty well done plot you certainly can't go wrong with this one. Doubly so if it goes on sale.
If you don't want to lose the cash but do enjoy a good sci-fi story I'd suggest looking around for the collection of cutscenes. Again, this game's draw is its plot and story and most of it unfolds in beautifully rendered and animated cutscenes.
(One last note: the game has a pretty shoddy configuration method, i.e. you have to tweak sound and graphical settings BEFORE you run the game. I think this even goes for controls which are a little bit different than normal since the reload button is defaulted to middle mouse.)

IMMERSION: Star Trek Online tries to tick all of the immersion boxes. It has a story loosely holding it together. It has player agency, allowing players to customise their characters (within limits), although dialog choices are absent for the most part. The game also has a strong license behind it, with established lore, and a fanbase. The game  also has combat, on foot and in vehicles as well. The game even has inventory management, so there's immersion by statistics. Of these, the one method most likely to inspire immersion are vehicle combat, and statistics. If those fail to inspire immersion, there is always the franchise to immerse the player. (8.5/15)
DIFFICULTY: It is possible to adjust the difficulty, this is explained later. Inventory management can impact difficulty by putting players into situations they are ill equipped to handle. Occasionally the control scheme does contribute to difficulty. (7.5/15)
LASTING APPEAL: This is where Star Trek as a franchise comes into play. The game does not maintain the pace of action, and missions become very similar. It is Star Trek fandom that keeps players involved, that and money contributed to the game (6/15)

TL;DR: Extremely immersive, much more difficult with less hand-holding than more modern titles. Slightly broken combat but very mod friendly.
Elder Scolls V: Skyrim is practically pop culture by now, and Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind has unfortunately fallen out of the spotlight in favour of it's newer, more modern brother. Morrowind is an old game, so many people have unfortunately never heard of it. Morrowind is an incredible experience, and is still a fantastic title to this day.
For those in doubt about blowing the dust off such an old and seemingly dead title, I can reassure you that you will be met with a pleasant surprise if you do. This game still has a living and breathing world that is so much fun to explore in.
Another pleasant surprise that you will find is the ramped up difficulty compared to it's newer brothers. If you have ever played Skyrim and wished there was less hand-holding, this will satisfy. You are expected to remember locations, names, and be able to follow directions via text. There is no magical guiding compass to follow. You are promptly kicked out into the world after completing your character creation with the message: "You're on your own now, good luck!"
The game may have "bad" graphics and plenty of bugs, but luckily there are mods that can make this game look a whole lot prettier and fix some of the broken mechanics. ("Morrowind Overhaul" is a great start.) Even with dated graphics, this game has some of the most atmospheric areas I've seen in any game, they are all beautifully designed, unique, and immersive.
My only gripe about the game is the combat, where it sometimes seems impossible to land a hit. Perhaps I'm playing the game wrong, but when I'm hacking away at an enemy, it sometimes just doesn't hit, even with the cursor dead-on the target. Including a miss chance mechanic doesn't help the game much, it just turns out to be infuriating.
Overall, I highly recommend this game, as it's easily one of the most thoughtful and immersive games I've ever played, despite the bugs and miss chance mechanic. Brushing the dust off of Morrowind is one of the best decisions I've ever made, even if I haven't experienced it to it's fullest. (Yet!)

Really hard to stop playing this!
...and now for a more in depth review.  But you have to forgive me.  When I wrote the previous sentence as my review (albeit a very short review) I had been playing this game nonstop since buying it until 4 in the morning.  Good thing it was Saturday night when I bought it!
So what is this game?  It is a cross between a physics-based racing game where the player NEVER gets to drive a car, and an economics sim where sponsors just want to see their name out on the track somewhere - anywhere, but preferably on the winning car, and a personality simulator where your boss and the mechanics and the drivers love you or hate you based on the decisions you make.
Is it worth well over $20?  Well yes.  The graphics, even on my crappy laptop, are quite nice, and the UIs are laid out well.  The game sort of "flows" - you don't have to think too much what you were supposed to do because it brings everything into the forground in a very intuitive way.
But who cares?  I mean if you have a great UI and game flow but the gameplay isn't compelling, why bother?  And here is where the game is wildly addictive - because the game is a CLIFFHANGER.  There's no better word for it.  You're 26 laps into a 28 lap race, the finish line is oh so close and the tires are just about worn out and fuel tank almost empty, and the car's driver pipes up over the microphone "hey my oil change light just came on!  This car needs Jiffy-Lube right now!  Do you want me to quit the race and come in and eat an ice cream cone while I wait for an oil change?"
God are you daft - NO!!!  Then for the next 2 laps he squawks that the engine could BLOW UP at any second, and he has a good point, but that's just the risk we have to take when trying to finish - let alone win.
Races are time consuming - preparing for them just as time consuming.  It's a hard uphill climb, tweaking every little parameter.  And the drivers don't know how to explain themselves beyond "I don't like how it handles."  Well duh.  Could you be more descriptive?  Does it need more toe in or more toe out?  "Na - just don't feel right to me."  Yes well thank you Mr. Neanderthal.  I'll get on that pronto!  It's just like... like... REAL LIFE!
The drivers' inability to help troubleshoot tuning the vehicle makes it just that more satisfying when all the tweaking finally results in a happy driver and all those smiley faces.  Because we somehow managed to change driver's diapers and they be happy driving tringaling down the race track.  Yes you are such a good driver!
Then there's tire wear management and fuel and sponsors and the freaking grounds construction.  Yes we need a wind tunnel but we can't quite afford it right now and an on-grounds race track would be nice but we'll have to make due with tuning the car just once before quailfying and my boss doesn't want me spending money on better car parts and one of the drivers is jealous I gave better brakes to the other driver's car!
The core game is the race itself - but there is so much more going on that this game becomes a very grand and satisfying experience.  I haven't even got 10 hours of play in!
Really the only thing to worry about is not "will I get my money's worth" - no the only thing to worry about is "will I lose all my friends because I really don't want to do anything than play just one more race on Motorsport Manager."  Yes.  Tough decision.  :)
----------------------
--- Update ---
Con:
The worst part of the game is that it drags on too long.  Some people have complained that they would like to be able to compress the real races into a simulation (which practice and qualifying races offer - so it's already in the game engine).  I have to agree.  Spending 20 minutes watching a race I'm already not interested in because the whole setup is still in the ramping up phase is annoying, and it happens at the beginning of the game, so that's pretty frustrating.
Because the game is so time consuming, starting over at a different difficulty because tedious, though the challenge is compelling.  Still - the amount of time this game takes up is unnecessary and detracts from the fun.  It's like the developers intentially added a time sink (somewhat compensated by the ability to reduce laps, but even at the minimum this is not enough).
Pro:
Conversely, the food for thought this game provides for management, team building, budgetting and tactics is an experience I would recommend for anyone.  There are concepts for team management which I have never seen brought into play in any other game before I played this, and it is a mind-openning experience.

What a pleasant surprise.
I am a fan of management games; sim-something, as long as it is engaging and not drifting from the usual. I have a long story with Football Manager, and related sport games; so when I heard that there was a new simulation made for autosports; I had to check it out, and glad to see that Steam had a promo on it, and a free weekend.
The game feels "right"; it is not too complex to scare away people; has a nice UI and overall, you have a clue about what is going on, even if you never played other management games. It reminds me a lot of an old EA game made as F1 simulation from the perspective of the management and not of the pilots. Fundamentally the game is very similar to this one; where you get a team, race, and try to win the chanpionship.
here you don't drive, but you direct. You start giving directions to the R&D to improve one or more areas of your car; sign pilots, sign mechanic, designers and technicians, and then begin to test your car on the various tracks, while the season goes on. I had the chance to try only the "F1" equivalent; and I was sucked in the game mechanic, which is brutal but very clear: you need to balance things and check what your pilots and engineers suggest, if you want to have a chance.
The game:
You have mostly a static screen with various options; no fancy stuff here; you go in the various sections and decide where to allocate money. You can expand your base of operation with new and expensive equipment, or invest in research to improve the car (or both, if you are in a big  wealty team). The whole season is a rinse and repeat of the same: practice, where the pilots tell you how they feel about the setup; and you change 6 parameters that are reflecting in the "handling" "speed" and "downforce" categories. You start with bars where the engineers give you the min and max suggested for that track; then start to experiment, getting feedback from the pilots, and changing things accordingly.
Practice and 3 qualification stages are fundamentally the same; you run few laps, change settings based on feedback (and time on track of course), few laps and so on. Keep in mind that practice is the only time where pilots are more vocal, and you can gain XP to let them improve on that particular track. During qualification you mostly do minor tweaks, so get the setup as polished as possible during the practice.
The race is a bit different, since you have to manage fuel, wheel consumption and overall car efficiency. Push too hard and the engine blow up; too aggressive and the pilot will crash or will eat up too much fuel and wheel will degrade to the point where they will end up last.
It is a game of chess, where you observe the situation, take some risks and hope that you did the right thing. No 2 races are the same, and even the fastest car could end up loosing, if your strategy is poor.
So far the game has been harsh but any fault was because of me not doing things right; not because I had no clue of what was I doing (or not doing). If you fail, it is because you are not careful or listen enough. Although going for a stronger team makes everything easier; so it si not exactly like with football manager games, where you have a certain degree of outcomes.
Graphic is fine; nothing fancy but the game doesn't need it; the UI is clean and straightforward. The music is a bit repetitive, but you can use yours. The sound effects are nice; I just wish that they would put some audio clips, instead everything is text based. This is 2017, you would expect voiced acting at least.
I would suggest to give it a try, if you are looking for a good simulation of auto sports.

I am absolutely loving it.  I don't generally like dropping full price down on a game; so when I did for Toukiden 2, I was already prepared to go for a refund at the slightest inkling of dissatisfaction. However, after about 1 hour, I had determined to keep the game beyond all doubt. The combat is fun and quite fluid (though fluidity does somewhat depend on the skill of the player). Do you like the "hit it till it dies" genre of games?

On a side note, this game is a pretty great non-monhun monster hunter game.
Explore the surprisingly large open world of Edo styled Japananese fantasy and battle mysterious Youkai and Oni as you journey through the world.
Equipt yourself with one of eleven different weapons and master the ways of hitting things till they die. You'll be so overwhelmed by the variety of weapons that you'll pick one and completely ignore the rest because it's hard learning a weapon and upgrading stuff is expensive.
Craft interesting sets of armour styled in that iconic samurai style, or don't because you have no idea where half the parts required to make that set come from.
Swing from tree to tree using the new gimmick of this game and then stop using it after you learn that there's a faster method of travel.
Fight large and awesome monsters as you traverse the world, and then realise that you have to kill them because the game locks you into a tiny arena with each encounter.
Explore the dungeons of the game in an interesting boss rush style of gameplay... And then become depressed because you decided to venture further down but the difficulty ramps up like a staircase for godzilla.
In all honesty, this game is really fun. It's a monster hunter for the casuals really. There's a lot more attack variety, and you eat damage like a hunter eats well done steaks, ie you really don't feel much with level appropriate gear... I say this because it's easy to get behind with gear upgrades.
If you're interested in the hunting genre of games, it's a worthy purchase. Just make sure that you have a controller with working bumpers... which I don't... You'll know why if you buy it...

Don't even compare this game to L4D2. L4D2 is clunky and is rightfully so for an old game...lacks content too.
Now, onto the review. Vermintide is a hero shooter/chopper. There are 5 different heroes. Each hero has a different set of weapons availiable in both melee and ranged combat. Different weapons hit different number of targets, deal different damage and specialize in situations.
Every weapon can also have up to three traits. Traits keep the game fresh and you can obtain fun combos. However in end game your trait combos are pretty much fixated or required. However, the devs have taken measures to make sure traits are balanced and fun to use. You don't use to use the best and most optimal trait combo to win. Hell, you can take on the hardest difficulty with default weapons.
The game is highly focused on melee combat and its very well polished. You can dodge, block and push rats away. Learning how to dance around rats and use walls to your advantage is highly crucial to your survival. This game has a rather steep learning curve especially in the hardest difficulty (Cataclysm). Content wise there are a variety of special rats you need to kill and it takes time to learn how to play around them.
The only negative thing about the game is its huge grind. To obtain a weapon with a specific trait combination in mind can take a very long time or just 1 try. Everything is RNG so it can be very frustrating to get what you want. HOWEVER, mods exist to change that problem.
The devs gives the community a lot of freedom over mods. That comes with a price as well (hackiing/cheating). Overall 9/10.

This game started Waifu War 3.
More thoughts:

The puzzle system is great.  You can slide a gem across the entire column or row to make a match, moving each piece you drag it across too.  This allows for thoughtful combos.  You also unlock special moves that do various things to the board that you can use to build a unique strategy.  The puzzles never really feel unfair;  The game never really feels cheap like some other games do (puzzle quest, anyone?)
While date puzzles give you 20 turns to fill the score, the sex puzzles require you to match gems to fill a depleting meter.  This makes the sex puzzles a change of pace from the careful strategy of the date puzzles to a twitchy match-them-quickly type of play.  It's a different type of challenge entirely and it's great.
The RPG element of leveling up your stats for the puzzles adds a growth element that allows you to overcome the increasing difficulty of the puzzles.  You can raise your stats in any order as well.
I liked the dialogue.  Some people hate it, but I thought it was good.
It has a pretty basic story that I won't get into but it is serviceable to what's going on in the game.  Everything seems to make sense and I guess that means that it's good.
Overall, I'd say the game is worth playing if you're into puzzle games and don't hate the idea of dating women in a video game.

Picked the game up on an offer and played it start to finish in 10 hours.
The scenes and dialog are tacky as hell and take great care not to miss out on any B-movie trope and cliché, catch phrases and similiar writing. If you expect some high-level prose than you are probably not going to enjoy this. The overarching story progression is a different thing, but still very much over the top.
But if you can find a fun side to this, have a laugh about it and also enjoy high-paced, non-stop bullet action with a great enemy disabling system and lots of boss fighting, than by all means pick the game up. The overall production value is rather great and I thought the controversial microphone implementation doesn't make too much of a difference. You can get by very well without a microphone, as you can give simple orders and answer questions with the keyboard.
The combat is at the same time formulaic in a way that it throws masses of enemies at you every few seconds, divided by cut scenes, but also stands out a bit through the disabling system: As part of a so-called "rust crew", your enemies are robots. If you shoot them in the leg they will crawl around for a bit and continue to fight. Shoot them in the head and they will walk around confused, shooting their allies. If you excel in a skirmish, your crew will give positive feedback (although I never figured out what crew relations are good for, guess they might influence cut scenes).
What I liked the most about the game was the atmosphere and setting. Sadly there aren't that many games set in a Cyberpunk setting, and this game does a good job at approaching it. The action usually overtones the noir, but the classic themes of high-tech/low-life are present, you will find yourself wandering between futuristic slums as well as clean and rich upper-class areas, although all of those only in a tube-ish manner.
I would say it's definitely worth around 10 euros if you can put up with Binary Domain's flaws and quirks, and endure being reminded of classic buddy movies and Action flicks from past times.

I know next to nothing about racing. I don't watch it, I don't know anyone that watches it... My knowlege of racing extends as far as PS2 NASCAR games I played as a kid, and an interest in engineering theory. Single-seater Formula 1 type racing? I know NOTHING about.
Coming from this perspective, I want to say that Motorsport Manager is an EXCEPTIONAL game. There's a lot to do. There's a learning curve, no doubt about it. But I've longed since the days of the flop that was EA Sport's football coach sim for a game that really lets me "role play" the position of a sports team's manager, and NO game has done it as well as this one does.
Get past the daunting amount of numbers and options you see on the front end initially (and granted, I went in without a tutorial on that part for reasons of wanting to test the waters on the management aspect right away), and you'll find an extremely robust manager's experience. Hiring and firing, scouting drivers, fostering trust between drivers and mechanics, modding your vehicles, building up your facilities, doing interviews for news publications... This game has EVERYTHING. And even as someone who knows little about racing, with the basics explained in the tutorial (the racing part I DID finish), I've already found a great deal of tense, tactical fun in the core racing aspect.
I don't like racing. But this game's gonna MAKE me like it. Absolutely recommend (just be ready for a bit of a learning curve).

First off this game has been developed by some of the team that created Left for Dead, and it shows, in a good way. The core game is the same, but Vermintide has its own feel, loadouts set prior to mission start, in game loot system, and 5 different classes; Soldier, Dwarf, Witch Hunter, Elf & the Bright Wizard.
The content may be/seem limited with 12 maps/missions in the base game, and the DLC’s only adding 3 each, but the quality of the base game is second only to the design on the DLC maps.
Each mission lasts around 20-30min depending on the specific mission, random encounters & player skill, or lack of.
There are two main types of missions.
1)	A liner map with 1 or more main objective somewhere along the route. These often have other objective along the way that will have to be completed before further progress can be achieved.
2)	An enclosed map where the objective is to collect items or defend/destroy specific locations.
Each have groups of enemy scattered around and hoards waiting in the wings that will attack on mass at the sound of a battle horn.
There is a story, but it's not at the forefront, it feels like more of a collection of mission and can be completed on easy rather quickly (free weekend), but this game is designed more to push you, up the difficulty, collect the tomes & grimlores, earn better loot and push the hardest difficulties.
This is where the game excels. On the easy difficulties (easy, normal & hard) you can hack and slash your way through almost spamming the attack, whilst Nightmare will ask more of you, dodging, blocking and attack time become critical if you want to survive. Then there’s Cataclysm, every swing, block & dodge counts, mistakes here can have you down for the count, and every enemy is lethal. Once you start playing this is what you will find yourself aiming for, completing every mission on cata.
With a lot of the combat being focused around melee the enemy reacts to where you hit them.
Take the 2 handed sword (a favourite swarm killer for me) for example. On Nightmare this will kill most normal enemy on 2 hits, but swing it right and you can make heads roll on mass.
Melee weapons are varied; duel swords & daggers, mace, two handed sword & hammers, axe and shield, rapier & more)
Ranged weapons are also varied; duel muskets, repeater handguns and rifles, crossbows, bows with poised tipped arrows, staff that hurl bolts & fireballs & more.
Loadouts; every class has a loadout with 1 melee, 1 ranged, 1 hat (cosmetic) and 3 trinket slots available. Melee and ranged weapons are restricted to class, whilst any trinket combinations can be used giving bonuses like healing nearby allies when you using meds, faster movement speed, chance to duplicate picked up items, chance to not consume items on use & more.
The enemy or “Scaven” are rats, most are weak and only a threat en-mass but mixed in are other varieties that can course chaos if not dealt with swiftly or brought down with a coordinated team assault. I will leave you to discover this yourself, only tip I will give you is all event like hordes or special spawns can usually be heard before seen.
The enemy also react differently if on their own or in small groups, being less likely to attack unless engaged and even cowering or running away until they find backup. They feel more like a living thing that a generic computer AI enemy.
There is a random loot system to this game, whilst you can up the odds by collecting Tomes and Grims through most of the missions it can still be annoying getting specific items, & with the Tomes and Grim locations not changing it can take some grinding for the best loot, but it's still a load of fun doing so.

This game does not respect the time you invest into it.
Everything is random, except the levels themselves. And let me tell you THOSE LEVELS ARE LONG.
Be prepared to spend a good 20-30 minutes in one effing level just to be rewarded with a low quality item for a character you don't want to play as.
Want to increase your chances? There are a couple of ways of doing that. OF COURSE there is! You can use an item in one of your trinket slots (you start with 1 slot and at level 30 you have 3). What this does? It increases the chances that the random roll at the end of the level will have an item for you (INCREASES not GUARANTEES it). So, you waste a slot for a CHANCE to get an item for you.
Is there another way, you ask. OF COURSE THERE IS! You can get tomes and grimoires that further increase a chance to get a good quality item. The problem is: You have to find them on the level (their places are always the same) and carry them to the end of the mission with you. The problem? They take inventory space. The tomes ocupy the healing item slot on your inventory and grimoires not only occupy the potion slot but decreases your health (and your team's health) by 33% (total health). So... If you want to have a good (good HAH!) chance of getting better items, you need to cap yourself heavily AND complete the mission.
So... Let's say you got lucky and received that juicy orange item (the second highest tier you can get (don't get me started on red items.)). Ok, now you have your item. Awesome! Except it's not. All items have perks. Those perks are random (Ugh!) and come DISABLED by default on every single item you acquire. You need to unlock them. Great. So how you do that. Well, on the forge of course. You'll need tokens to unlock those perks. Every item tier uses a different kind of token to upgrade them. And how do you acquire tokens? By smelting items of that tier or completing missions that reward them. The problem (problems?)?:
1) Perks not only are random but most of them have a range percentage of activating the effect. For example: 1-6% of increasing your attack speed by 40% for 5 seconds after killing an enemy. So, you have to PAY to activate the perk and PRAY that you get on the high end of that range. (i.e 6% not 1%)
2) If your item comes with a perk you don't want. You can change the perk. Awesome, isn't it? Except it isn't. You need to use the Shrine to change the perks. And what does that do? Well, you have to pay tokens to change it and you cannot even tell which perk you want to change and which perk you want... If an orange item has two good perks and one bad you pay the tokens and the game rolls 3 new perks for you. Yep. 3. So, you have a chance of getting an even worse set of perks.
Is there another way of getting items. OF COURSE THERE IS: Quests and Contracts. (I hope you have all the DLC because you are going to need it.) Every day the game rolls another set of quest and contracts for you at the Bounty Board. Contracts give you bonuses (like 2 hours of increased damage) or tokens to spend on the slot machine (i.e: Forge and Shrine). Quests give you items... Except they are random and some are cosmetic items. Plus, to get the item you need keys. Those keys you acquire by completing contracts. Some quests need 8-10 keys to complete. You can only acquire a max of 2 keys per day (only 2 contracts per day have them as a reward (that means you'll spend 5 (at best) real life days to get a 10 key (red)item as a quest reward). Plus if the contract happen to be on a DLC map... well... you can't get it unless you or a friend have the DLC. Plus there's always one on an easy difficulty map and another on a nightmare difficulty map.
Closing thoughts:

So, the game expects you to grind and grind and grind some more on the same maps over and over and over until you get what you want, all based on luck alone.
Unless you are a masochist and/or want to just waste time, give it a pass, for your own sake.

The puzzle system is great.  You can slide a gem across the entire column or row to make a match, moving each piece you drag it across too.  This allows for thoughtful combos.  You also unlock special moves that do various things to the board that you can use to build a unique strategy.  The puzzles never really feel unfair;  The game never really feels cheap like some other games do (puzzle quest, anyone?)
While date puzzles give you 20 turns to fill the score, the sex puzzles require you to match gems to fill a depleting meter.  This makes the sex puzzles a change of pace from the careful strategy of the date puzzles to a twitchy match-them-quickly type of play.  It's a different type of challenge entirely and it's great.
The RPG element of leveling up your stats for the puzzles adds a growth element that allows you to overcome the increasing difficulty of the puzzles.  You can raise your stats in any order as well.
I liked the dialogue.  Some people hate it, but I thought it was good.
It has a pretty basic story that I won't get into but it is serviceable to what's going on in the game.  Everything seems to make sense and I guess that means that it's good.
Overall, I'd say the game is worth playing if you're into puzzle games and don't hate the idea of dating women in a video game.

Devil's Details was known for their..."Japanese" games. However, they wanted to get out of their comfort zone and go for something they'd never tried: A 3rd person Shooter.
Binary Domain is a homage to the late 90s/early 2000 action movies. With cheesy dialogue, ludicrous action scenes, american bada$$ heroes and robots. Lots and lots of robots.
Those robots are the only enemy type you'll face against, but they manage to be varied in their own way. When shooting at them, you can blow their limbs off, tear their armor appart and even make them go nuts and attack their allies. They respond impresively at this things. For example, blowing the arm where they were holding their gun will make them crouch and pick it up with the other, while kneecaping them makes them crawl and shoot from the ground. And they don't flinch in the slightest. They really feel like mindless killing machines.
The story is quite interesting with a few plot twists, and the characters are very well done and charming.
If you liked Gears Of War, Resident Evil 6 or the likes, you're going to love this game. It's the simplicity and over-the-topness that really sells it

I like this game, it's alright. There's not much to say with it, but there are obviously pros and cons with this game. A pro would be the "create your own animal" aspect, they really give you the parts to do this. I own the Creepy and Cute pack and robot parts, so that adds another 80-100 parts to the already decent selection, disregarding mods.
A con that should rather be addressed would be, in my personal opinion, the lack of replayability. Sure, its fun for a couple of hours, evolving your creature, making a tribe and going to space, but this DOES NOT CHANGE. You just take your creature through the same levels again and again and again. There's also a lack of inspiration to move past the creature stage, but that's just me. Spore changes itself from 2D all-you-can-eat buffet with combat plastered on to thirdperson survival game with creature combat to something like a real time strategy game with masks and hats or whatever. I haven't even gone to space yet, but I'm going to assume its entirely different as well. If I wanted to play minigames, I would've booted up ♥♥♥♥ing Mario Party.
This next issue doesn't really matter any more, but the DRM was just shoddily integrated and really said "We're EA and we don't really give a flying♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;. When your "most anticipated game" gets spotlight as the most pirated game ever, you know you did something horribly wrong. Also, you were only allowed to install 3 times once upon a time and the DRM was the largest reason why the game got 1 star on Amazon. Anyway, I'm beating a dead horse that was festering for about 6 years or so, but it was a noticeable point in Spore's history, and I don't put that term in a good way.
Spore is, overall, a decently aged game. I wouldn't recommend it at 20$ right now, but its worth a good 10-15$.

Spore is a unique game. It lets you create your own species and evolve them from microscopic cells, to a space-fairing empire. As you go along each stage, you get to use a powerful editor that lets you create virtualy anything you want. You could create something out of Mass Effect or Halo, or whatever you want. Imagination is the limit! When not in the editors, you will be spending time in Spore's 5 different stages. Each stage has its own kind of gameplay, giving you different genres of playstyle. I enjoyed all of the stages, but thre were a few problems I had. The lack of an auto save feature can be annoying at times. The gme sometimes crashes and  when I forget to save, I lose alot or all progress. (So remember to save) Another problem I had was in tribal stage were my tribe's men wouldn't harvest meat from hunting. (This wasn't too big a deal, I just restarted the game and it was fixed) There are a few bugs here and there, but they shouldn't be gamebreaking. Overall, this is one of my favorite games. (If you like this game, be sure to heck out it's other awesome dlcs.)

While I only have a few minutes on this version, I have logged several hundred hours on the xbox version. Morrowind is by far the best of the recent Elder Scrolls games.  The world seems much more open from the start due to the limited hand holding compared to Oblivion and Skyrim.  It is the most challenging and also the game that requires the most planning.  If you don't know what you are doing during character creation you can limit your endgame potential drastically.
Leveling requires careful planning in regards to which skills you are going to use in order to maximize your stat point bonuses.  There is also an insane amount of customization compared to the newer games, especially with respect to enchanting.  Instead of having specific spells and effects available for each item slot like Skyrim, you are able to enchant any spell you know in very interesting ways.  For example, you can enchant levitation as a constant effect onto an article of clothing, allowing you to fly indefinitely.  The same for invisibility, health and mana regeneration, or stats like strength.  Also you can
adjust the strength of the spell based on the quality of the soul used and the quality of the garment.
The entire atmosphere of the game and the features that were available in Morrowind make it superior to the "prettier" games that came after.

I bought this game in an effort to quell my need to hit things with a japanese sword, and I was surprised when I got that and way more. tl;dr, buy this game if you want a great 20 hour experience. Here's why:
Characters - Unconventially, I'd like to start with the characters, because I feel that they are the greatest strength of this game, hands down. Complex designs make each character unique and their personalities are differentiated but not cliche. Furthermore, each one's backstory is developed throughout the main story campaign, which is a great feat due to the amount of characters. I'd say the number one way this game will stay with me is its characters.
Gameplay - its a pretty normal hack and slash game, but the depth surprised me. With a ridiculous amount of weapons that each have their own skills, I think anyone can find a niche that's comfortable for them.
Customization - This is one aspect where the game shines a lot. There's a ton of weapons and armor to choose from, but the main thing that creates ridiculous build diversity is the mitama, character cards that give special abilities to the character. Each one has 4 actives, 9 passives, a support skill, and an offense skill. And you can equip three. I think I've spent over an hour already picking my mitama for my build...
Story - Maybe I'm just a sucker for anime writing, but I felt like the story fulfilled its most important role: driving the gameplay. Its interesting, maybe a bit predictable, but definitely rewarding and keeps you playing. And, as I mentioned before, it develops the characters and gives them significance within the world.
All in all, 10/10 experience, this is the most pleasant surprise I've had in a long time.

The most dissatisfying loot system known to mankind. I mean, all games have RNG to a degree, but if you have a specific item you'd like to try in mind, good luck getting it. Even with the addition of items that supposedly increase the "chance" for an item drop for a specific character, you'll still end up with tons of other items/duplicates thanks to the completely random reward system. How random you ask? Well, first the system selects 8 items from all the items in the game. Hah. Then, you roll dice, and depending on how "good" you roll, you receive 1 randomly selected item of those. No, you can't "downgrade" your roll in order to get that pistol you wanted since launch. Take your bloody 20th axe and move on to the next 30 minute mission to repeat this experience.
You know what is more dissatisfying than spending 30 minutes in a mission to receive another single hand axe duplicate? Spending 29 and dying in the last minute to receive diddly squat. Long levels and no reward if you fail really go hand in hand with the sheer impossebility to actually gear up your character and no checkpoints.
The game can be fun. If you get lucky and actually get an item you enjoy using. I'd suggest rolling some die, flipping some coin or hitting las vegas before buying this game. If you're exceptionally lucky, you'll like this game. If your luck is however about average, you can enjoy some pretty decent gameplay until you get bored because you can't change up your playstyle or reach higher difficulties.
As a closing statement: This is a rare example of a game that actually made me not regret the money, but the time I spent on it. I keep thinking "next mission will be the one where it drops. It has to be.". I guess that is how gambleing works. Only you are not gambleing money, but your life's time. Keep that in mind.

Spore appealed to me because of it's concept, you can literally create life and guide your species through their vast journey that is life.  I had it on my wishlist, and I saw it was on sale for about $5 so I gave it a shot.
I encounter my first problem as I start up the game.  EA not surprisngly is forcing you to create an EA account to play online, I do so to get the full game experience, silently cursing EA in my mind.  After creating my account, I restart Spore and see if my account works, nope.  I thought it might be my internet or Steam/Origin conflict, so I decided to go to Google to see what was wrong.  Turns out, Spore online hasn't been working since June, 2013 (release of Origin) and EA still hasn't fixed their problem.  Everyone that bought the game after June 2013 can't play online.  They claim they're "working on it" but I'm not buying it.
I then decided to start up a game of Spore anyway because I knew EA wasn't going to fix it anytime soon.
The game has 5 seperate sections for your Spore: Micro-organism, Animal, Tribe, Civilization, and Space.  The following gamemode correspond to the respecting game sections: Arcade, Free Roam Adventure, Small scale RPG, Large Scale RPG, and a MMO/RPG.  Each of these gamemodes are very basic, but they play fine and are still fun.
Throughout your species' journey you will have the chance to customize or "evolve" your creature.  The customization is quite extensive, you could spend hours just creating your creature.  Everything you add or remove will influence your species' behavior in the game, your creature's actions could also influence this.  Not only can you customize your species, but their buildings, vehicles, cloathes etc.
Graphics wise the game isn't impressive.  Yes I know it's supossed to look like a cartoon, but regardless some textures are blurry and blended together too much.  Texture pop-ins are a bit frequent, but forgiving.
I think I've covered everything but the multiplayer.  Now what is the multiplayer?  Well, when you get into space you gave the whole galaxy to explore, and you meet new species along the way.  There is a chance that you will visit a player's species, and you could interact with said species.  You don't get to interact with an actual player, but it is interesting to see what other player have created.  So why am I complaining about not being able to play it?  Because EA gets away with♥♥♥♥♥♥like this all the time and doesn't give a crap on fixing it.  Yes the multiplayer is simple, but I want the full game when I buy it, and I shouldn't be penalized for buying the game later than everyone else did.

While I only have a few minutes on this version, I have logged several hundred hours on the xbox version. Morrowind is by far the best of the recent Elder Scrolls games.  The world seems much more open from the start due to the limited hand holding compared to Oblivion and Skyrim.  It is the most challenging and also the game that requires the most planning.  If you don't know what you are doing during character creation you can limit your endgame potential drastically.
Leveling requires careful planning in regards to which skills you are going to use in order to maximize your stat point bonuses.  There is also an insane amount of customization compared to the newer games, especially with respect to enchanting.  Instead of having specific spells and effects available for each item slot like Skyrim, you are able to enchant any spell you know in very interesting ways.  For example, you can enchant levitation as a constant effect onto an article of clothing, allowing you to fly indefinitely.  The same for invisibility, health and mana regeneration, or stats like strength.  Also you can
adjust the strength of the spell based on the quality of the soul used and the quality of the garment.
The entire atmosphere of the game and the features that were available in Morrowind make it superior to the "prettier" games that came after.

First and foremost, my time playing is actually longer than the 8 hours shown because I'm playing Toukiden 2 on PSVita also. My total playtime is more along the lines of 15 or 16 hours. I'll use Monster Hunter as a reference since Toukiden wouldn't exist if it weren't for the Monster Hunter series.
Toukiden 2 is the best version of the series and one of if not THE best alternative to Monster Hunter yet. I could actually play this instead of Monster Hunter because of the better visuals, better controls and key points that Toukiden does differently than Capcom's series. Toukiden 2 the equivalent of the transition from Monster Hunter Unite, which is an excellent version of MH to Monster Hunter 3 Ultimate, which is just better in every way. That's what Toukiden 2 is to Kiwami.
In Toukiden 2, the animations are better and there are more of them, sound and presentation are still excellent with heavy Japanese themes, the combos are similar at first glance but deeper than they were in Kiwami. Enemy AI is more aggressive than it is in Kiwami, elemental attributes in armor and weapons actually makes a difference here whereas it didn't make much of a difference in Kiwami. The town is massive in Toukiden 2 as the town was tiny in Kiwami. The open world is actually an open world and access to the different ages ties into that world as opposed to how Kiwami handled the ages. Similar to Monster Hunter, ages being nothing more than a different stage you're transported to. In other words,  In Toukiden 2 you can actually run out of the village, across the plains and to the Age of Peace without the game visibly loading.  The graphics are better but that's probably a minor upgrade considering Kiwami is a good looking game. Toukiden 2 runs at 60FPS  which makes a huge difference as Kiwami is locked at 30. Character creation is deeper as well as I was able to make Jim Kelly complete with an afro, whereas Kiwami wouldn't allow any non Japanese characters to be created.
Of the new weapons, I've only used the Sword and Shield but it's really awesome and clearly inspired by the Switch Axe and Charge Blade in Monster Hunter.  It's basic combo set is good enough but a bit slow. Activating the secondary move set turns the Sword and Shield into a bully weapon as a second blade comes out of the shield allowing the player to dual wield in a way complete with a dodge move and increase in speed. The Demon Hand is also a great addition and is inspired by the grappling hook in Freedom Wars on PSVita which I loved. It can be used to grab monsters and trip them up, grab monsters to pull the player towards them attacking in the process and grapple trees, cliff edges and bridges to get to areas that normally wouldn't be possible. Since the open world is large there is also a new quick run ability that looks like something out of Ninja Scroll or Yotoden.
The story is a bit of a prequel as it starts at the beginning of the Awakening which is referred to many times in Toukiden and Toukiden Kiwami. Just having a story is a blessing instead of. ..kill monster...make stuff...kill more monsters....make more stuff...
One of my favorite additions that had me laughing to the point of tears is the limb destruction. Permanent limb destruction. There's a technique you can activate with the Demon Hand to permanently destroy limbs on monsters. This is new to the series as Toukiden and Kiwami had limb destruction, but a ghost image of the limb would appear and the monster would still behave as if the limb was never destroyed. This is still the case until the player attacks with the Demon Hand powered up. It destroys limbs completely and initially, I couldn't figure out why the Wind Shredder was hunch over like a rabbit and moving weird like he was trying to scoot away on his backside. When I rotated the camera and looked at him, I noticed his front legs were permanently destroyed. He couldn't run anymore, he couldn't even walk effectively. I was laughing so hard seeing that.
So...what are the negatives? If new comers are trying Toukiden for the first time with this version of the game, the learning curve is steep.
Mouse and keyboard support is broken.
Some monsters will tower over you to the extent that they block the camera.
Some characters will speak while on missions from time to time but no translation is provided (all dialogue is in Japanese).
Aiming with the Demon Hand while grappling is done faster but less accurately with the left analog stick. Aiming can be done with the right analog (or in my case, the right touchpad on the Steam controller) but it's slower. Not good.
That's it. Seriously. The game runs great, 1080p/60 without breaking a sweat, full screen (I;m playing on a Surface Studio) and other than the right analog issue I mentioned above, it controls great provided you're using a controller (Xbox 1 controller or Steam controller. I haven't tried a DS4 yet). If you're a Monster Hunter fan that's sick of Capcom screwing around with PC support or the lack thereof, the Toukiden 2 is a great alternative that plays faster, open world, has a good story and is more brutal in its combat.

Wow. One of the best words to describe this game. If your looking for an easy game this is not it. It has quite the easy learning curve and it can last you hours. I will now go over certain aspects of the game and tell you what I like and what I don't.
Gameplay:
Mount and Blade has quite the different form of combat. It also has a pretty odd map and movement mode. However its fairly easy to figure out. As an example of the complicated weapon system, I shall now go through the spear:
So spears in this game work in two different ways, with mount and without. Without a mount, spears/lances can still be pretty good weapons, using a spear on the ground allows you to swing the spear, while on a mount you can couch the lance for massive amounts of damage.
Mount and Blade has a vast amount of weapons and armor types giving you the ability to really make your character how you want it. You could make a steppe warrior on horseback or a big burly nord with a huge axe. The choice is really yours with this game.
The game also has a troop system. Instead of lone gunning it, the game allows you to create large armies of troops including infantry, cavalry, and archers. Each faction has its own form of each and (mostly) large, varying, troop trees. While some factions have better archers, and others have great cavalry, you arent limited to any specific faction. The game features companions as well. Companions are characters that level up the same way you do and can be equiped with things of your choosing
Now onto the map mode. The map for this game is realitivly easy to understand, certain terrains make you go slower and other faster. The game has a set map instead a randomly generated one, and includes many towns, castles, and villages. All of which are capturable, either by your own faction or already set factions. The game features 6 factions to choose and also allows you to make your own faction.
Now since the game is amazing they also decided to let you have character levels. Character levels allow you to get certain bonuses towards aspects of the game by utilizing skills, traits, and weapon skills. Skills include intelligence and strength (much like fallout) and provide bonuses to your traits and allow you to make your traits go higher depending on which skill they rely on. Traits include things like prisoner management, horse riding, and ironflesh. Weapon skills make you more accurate, do more damage, and increase critical strike chance. Weapon skills can also go up just by using the weapon.
All in all Mount and Blade's gameplay is pretty smooth and easy to enjoy.
Graphics:
So graphics in this game aren't the best. But that's mainly because of how old it is, and while they arent the best persay, you can optimize them pretty well. Sadly the game dosen't feature many options for character's hair or color, it has a very advanced character creation menu.
The graphics aren't the greatest but it really dosen't matter when your not focusing on that
Workshop:
This game recently added in steam workshop support and even before the update many mods existed. The modding community for this game is very active and always coming up with amazing ideas for new maps and time settings.
Not only that but it also has active communtiy overall. Many people looking to help others and share stories about playing.
Overall:
I think Mount and Blade is a fantastic game, and can lead to endless no-lifeing of its limitless world
9/10 would definitely play again

I think it's safe to say that Arena FPS is dead.
However, that doesn't mean it's forgotten.
Reflex is a modern revamp of the Quake 3 Arena mod Challenge Promode Arena, or CPMA. This mod aimed to break the original game's limitations to create an even higher skill ceiling.
Reflex itself has come a long way since it's release, with numerous major patches improving the game in every way. The communication between the devs and players is amazing as a result of the game's own forum board and discord server. The community of players is excellent as well, with almost all of them being veterans at the game, there is always something to be learned.
However, there is a downside to all the experienced players. New players have an extremely tough time with this game, losing every duel they play and getting crushed in every server they enter. To put it frankly, this game isn't meant for everyone. As a result, the playerbase is small. This does make it tight-knit, and in some cases friendly, but it's generally a negative aspect for a game to have such a small playerbase.
The one personal issue I had with the game was that it requires a lot of time to be put into practice to enjoy the game on your own. You could avoid that by getting your friends into the game, but you might have so difficulty with that because the game is so extreme and punishes casual players.
If you're all about Arena FPS, this game is most def for you.
If you're willing to put in 100 hours just to stand a chance against half the players, this game is for you.
If not, don't bother buying.

The Good:
Binary Domain is basically the love child between a fun summer blockbuster and Isaac Asimov. It's capable of being both emotionally enthralling and utterly ridiculous in every good way. It has all the action movie set pieces you could want but it also has genuinely good story with likable characters and interesting themes. One of the most unique parts of Binary Domain is the trust system which can effect the ending of the game. By selecting characters to be in your squad you are able to build up trust with them by performing well in combat and interacting with them. These moments where you do get to talk to the characters for unique dialog are great and flesh them out past their deceptive stereotype shells and the first time you hear their repeat dialog during combat are nice too. Gameplay wise Binary Domain is a bog standard third person shooter with one caveat. It's the only game I've played where robots are the primary enemy and they're actually fun to shoot. The feel of shredding a robots armor off and sound the sound of shooting their limbs off and watching them crawl to you is great. Not to mention that nice ping when you get a headshot which has the added bonus of causing the robot to malfunction and target its allies. And while the gunplay overall is average, the shotguns stand out with lots of range and a tight spread. Your squad are also pretty competent even with minimal use of the order system which allows you to bark orders through a mic or pressing Tab. I never once felt like I had to baby them and in one case I had my own sniper take out enemy snipers when I didn't have my own sniper rifle equipped. It was a great moment during gameplay that helped make that character more likable. Enemy types, including bosses, are varied and fun to fight. There are also some light RPG mechanics with a six slot mini-Tetris system or passive upgrades. The English dubbing is also top notch for the most part and only helped the story.
The Bad:
The most annoying part of this game is the repetitive combat dialog. Your squad has a limited vocabulary during combat and they love repeating themselves often. The level design would be my second complaint. Sometimes the game has shades of Final Fantasy 7's Midgar, but too often the game takes place in generic industrial zone or office space. Lastly, the port has some minor inconveniences with how it handles mouse sensitivity and FOV, but with a little finagling within the menus it's not an issue.
Verdict:
Binary Domain is a gem. It certainly has issues and may appear generic on the surface, but it's a fun ride and has depth to its story. I give it a recommendation to all third person shooter and sci-fi story fans. If value is a concern, my playthrough of the 2nd hardest setting clocked in at just over 11 hours.
Note:
Without spoiling, I highly recommended getting the character named Cain to very high trust.

Rating: 8/10
Overview: Third Person Shooter
The Good:
+ Great graphics without needing high specs. Game seems to be optimized fairly well (post patches)
+ A surprisingly decent story that offers a lot of interesting characters.
+ The shooting mechanics are fantastic. Shooting robots causes bits and pieces to fly everywhere, shooting robots in different body parts effects movement, aiming, shooting a robot's head off allows the robot to fight for you etc. All of this leads to a very satisfying feeling of killing enemies.
+ Killing enemies rewards you with money which is used to buy/upgrade perks and weapon upgrades for you and your teammates.
+ Within every chapter you can select up to one or two teammates. Depending on who you choose changes the dialogue in certain parts. There is also a 'trust' system, say the right things and perform well in combat and you will build trust among team mates. Higher trust means they are more likely to follow orders in combat in addition to changing the outcome at the end of the game. The trust system doesn't drastically change the game and I would have liked it put to better use but its always nice to see new gameplay mechanics.
+ The game does a great job with pacing. You never feel bored and the game constantly changes things up so every battle feels fresh and unique.
+ The story is sparingly good, presenting a moral and ethical dilemma and gives you something to think about.
+ Cain, a robot with a French accent.
+ Soundtrack
The Average:
On a technical level the game could use a bit more polish. Lowering the sound does nothing for cinematics, you can only change graphics, sound, controller outside of the game.
Certain bosses feel like bullet sponges, especially at the higher difficulties.
The Bad:
- Multiplayer is dead making it impossible to collect achievements.
Conclusion:
This is one of the better third person shooters that came out of the PS3/360 generation. Sadly, due to timing and bad marketing the game never really found the success it deserved. Overall This is a great third person shooter that needs a sequel.
