With more than 4.5K hours played... gods where did my life go?!  I have to say I've seen some good and some bad in this game.
The Bad:
The minimum requirements aer something of a joke, you need much more RAM than they list (I've got double that and can still get lag-stormed).  You can buy the lifetime membership, but a little math showed me that it won't reach the break even point for around 5 years.  While being a lifer is supposed to offer some perks like priority log in, I'm still bumped pretty often.  There's also a LOT of divergance from Star Trek canon.  RPG elements are close to non-existant.  Can be pretty grindy too.
The Good:
Fairly easy to pick up, can be enjoyable to play.  You can get access to the Foundry to create Fan Content, though the quality and ease of these missions is all over the place.  There is some pretty good tie ins to Star Trek as we all know and love (even some easter eggs on the Constitution Class).
Sure, get it and play, but be careful if you decide to join a Fleet... there are some really really bad ones out there and some good ones.  Ask questions and if the person will answer, then chances are they're in a fleet that would be a good match.

First time ever making a review and it's for an unassuming, obscure little Early-Access game called Drunk on Nectar. I feel it's fitting; I love insects and arachnids ever since I was a kid and I've always wanted a game like this to come into fruition. Now that it's finally here....
I LOVE it. A lot.
At this current point in time, the game has three modes to choose from.
issues challenges for the player to complete in as quick a time as possible for a spot on the leaderboard.
allows the play to either survive as their chosen critter through the first day of spring (foraging/hunting for food whilst avoiding predators), or allows the player to freely explore the map without the pressing need for food.
allows you to build your own ecosystem, choosing the plants and animals you put in. It also allows you to take control of any of the animals in said ecosystem. This is also a great platform with which to practice the controls and get the hang of your chosen bug.
As for the bugs you can choose from, the game currently allows players to control from the following:
Dragonfly
Jumping Spider
Ladybird/Ladybug
Bee
Monarch Butterfly (both caterpillar and adult are available to choose from)
Viceroy Butterfly
Also available to play on Nature Sandbox are Ants and Mealybugs. The roster will grow to include more (the Lacewing and Praying Mantis are currently being developed), as well as include the life-cycle of each creature. The developers are very open to community suggestions and I have my fingers crossed for my favorite insect, the Assassin Bug.
On the topic of the developers, they are clearly very passionate about this project and very interactive with the community. You can tell they love insects and arachnids; the knowledge that they have for each individual species is very apparent in the gameplay. For me, this kind of devotion and friendliness towards the community is a plus, especially in an early-access game like this. What more, they take constructive criticism for this game very well, and are quick to add fixes and features that allow their players a better experience.
Such criticisms included the camera, which did make playing certain creatures like the Jumping Spider more difficult and frustrating than it needed to be. In response to this, the developers gave the option to allow the camera to move independently from the creature. A very helpful change.
Another con is replay value. While I can play this game for hours, I can see the novelty wearing off for other people and, once they've played all the modes and creatures, there's little to keep them coming back until another major update happens. I feel the future plan of multi-player will solve this issue, allowing modes like Creature Quest to be even more fun and competitive. Imagine a mode much like The Isle, where the prey you hunt and the predators you avoid are other players. That will certainly bring lots of replayability to this game.
I can also see the controls may be overwhelming to some new players, but the game is very helpful in this department (regularly dropping instructions on which button does what) and once you get the hang of it, it comes natural.
Overall, this game is fun, educational, and unique. If you love animals, particularly the creepy crawlies, then I highly recommend this game.

Binary Domain is SEGA's foray into the 3rd Person Cover Shooter genre.  It is a roughly 10 hours long game with an enjoyable action movie writing and presentation.  As Sgt Dan Marshall, part of a multinational elite anti-robot team, you will battle hordes of military robots and crazy mecha bosses while attemptint to stop a rogue corporation building illegal AI robots.  The game is a thoroughly enjoyable affair that I would strongly recommend to gamers who enjoy the shooter genre in general.  It basically takes the Gears of War formula, and improves on it with more gadgets, weapons, weapon upgrades, voice commands and a squad trust mechanic that ultimately alters the game's ending depending on which squad members trust you to what degree.  This would also be a good point to note its shortcomings, I guess: The voice command system is rather problematic (but thankfully totally optional), the cover mechanics obviously needed a lot more polish (running into cover does not automatically lean you against it like Gears of War, and I found myself desperately trying to get in or out of cover more times than I would have liked), the enemies are bullet sponges (but that usually is not much of a worry because it has been handled well; they are armored and as you shoot you peel off armor plates, concentrated fire on specific limbs can result in dismemberment) and the campaign is a bit short.  All in all, it's a great experience, a totally underrated game and a solid recommendation from me.  Two thumbs up.

Morrowind is the swan song of an era. Built in the fleeting early 2000s window of opportunity where there was already enough money sloshing around the industry to support a lavish open world first person CRPG but before the pressure of needing it to sell to literally every last person on earth in order to recoup costs and having to water it down accordingly.
The first time you swing a knife that thing's gonna slash down, give every indication of colliding with whatever you were trying to hit, and do no damage whatsoever. Because despite looking very much 2002 (the graphics slightly hokey but redeemed by unheard of draw distances and consistently on-point audiovisual design (yes even the faces dammit)) it's running old testament dice rolls under the hood. There are skill trees for shockingly useless weapon types and the game won't lift a finger to stop you from murdering and/or♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off essential NPCs, offering only a little dialog box after the fact asking whether you want to reload a save or continue on your doomed quest. It's not a particularly unforgiving game but it asks that you engage it on its own terms and learn the systems in order to succeed instead of waltzing in like an obnoxious tourist on an all-in package trip to the final boss. If you can manage this, you'll find few videogame locales are as immersive (there's this almost Minecraft-ish internal concistency to the way every object and actor works in exactly the same way and a lot of emergent fun to be had exploiting this) and memorable as Morrowind's Vvardenfell.
Oh right and then they ported it to the fledgling Xbox where it proceeded to sell a trillion copies and in one of the great tragic misunderstandings of our era instead of going 'hey looks like console gamers have a taste for complex, immersive CRPGs too' Bethesda went 'oh there's money in open world console RPGs? better make Oblivion simple enough for elementary school kids because all console owners are idiots!'
(note: my playtime on the steam version isn't indicative of how long I've actually spent playing as I also own the original CD-ROM release, the Xbox version, the DVD-ROM GOTY PC rerelease plus its Xbox counterpart and I must've logged 300ish hours over the years.)

Gameplay (Commentary)

This title will take quite a bit to explain and talk to you what I think its all about.
It's a reimagining of Quake 3 arena with the CPMA mode, which was a mod created for the base game of Q3 that helps balance things out for a competitive nature, so strafe jumping is alot better to perform, rockets tend to deal better damage overall, better maps, ect.   Reflex builds upon that and also re-introduces the long lost arena shooter genre that has been literally gone since 1999 when Counter Strike first came out that pretty much pussified the fps market as a whole.
And what I mean by that is the infinte skill cieling this game has and that's gonna be more noticeable once you start playing against other players.  there's no loadouts, there is no perks, no demon runes,(Looking at DOOM 2016 mp) nothing here that grants you a one-shot kill or a 100 percent win factor like in most mainstream games, every step of the way.  There's only you, yourself, and the set of skills you know that determines whether your match is successful or will end in failure, which failure is more likely to happen if it's your first time playing an arena fps or if you're just not playing enougu.
There are strategically placed weapon/item/powerup spawn locations in each carefully crafted map that you immerse yourself as soon as you spawn, but you gotta get to them first and score and kill the other guy before he/she does the same to you.  all the weapons are situational, so keep that in mind.
Many of the weapons behave the same way from Quake 3 arena, so long time fans of the classic Id Software games should feel right at home, and those that haven't?  well, you're gonna struggle, just like me.  I was always a fan of the old Doom/Quake games but I was never a quake/unreal professioal or god at these aggressive multiplayer games, so I tend to ♥♥♥♥ up alot of the time, which will set me back and all the sudden, the wrong move and I'm pretty much ♥♥♥♥ed for the entire game unless I can get to another weapon and hopefully a green or yellow armor because chances are red armor is already taken.  Otherwise the game's already over by the the time the other person is already 5 points ahead so why bother continuing.
It may also take time to get used to the movement here, which also plays a big role in the gameplay.  I'll put it simple straight:  You camp, you die.  you need to stay mobile and control the map as much as you can, deny weapon, health, powerup, and armor spawns by collecting and also fighting your opponent.  your health does not regenerate.  patch yourself up with health and armor laying around.
there are lots of maps.   lots of them.   And there's even a map editor that you can create maps yourself and submit them to the workshop for others to see and rate them.  the whole HUD display is also customizable, to the health and armor bars (that's right, no health regen, kids!!)  you can even download several widget addons, so you could have the original quake 3 weapon sounds playing on the weapons, or even hitmarkers if you're into that modern stuff even though sounds will play if you hit someone with a weapon.   your bot is also customizable!
The thing is, The game is tailored for high level degree of competitive enviromnent, and the main game mode is 1 versus 1, and with a lot of Quake vets in mind, they already know what they're doing so don't be suprised if you lose the game by 0-32 on your first couple of games.   The high skill wall is enough to turn the average gamer away because we're so used to the trendss of modern military shooters that have ran king for almost 2 decades now.  No, Reflex says skill is king here and that's that.
I get that the game favors skill over anything else, but at the same time, It doesn't sound or feel fun getting annihilated by a more experienced player, which also turn lots of players away as well who also want to experience what Reflex has to offer, but that's all theory from me and don't actually take that literal.  Games nowadays rely on that luck factor to determine whether you'll have a successful game or it'll all end in failure.
This game will not resonate with a modern gaming audience today, which is one thing that will set this title back leagues behind alot of the most popular titles out there right now.  it's a niche thing.
I think some of the other problems with this game is with low player count, the long wait times to get your turn to play in a match, since there's a heavy concetration on duel mode where two players are duking it out.  many people just want to start fragging as soon as they buy the game, and unfortunately there's not that many people online that play other game modes besides duel.
Reflex has everything it needs to be extremely fun, competitive, fast-paced, consistent with everything so far, damage with weapons are respectable with zero modifiers unlike something you'd find in Team Fortress 2 or any inconsistencies in CSGO.   However, it's missing the most important aspect of any multiplayer video game:  The players.
This isn't a game for everyone as it seems.
*Extremely fast paced Arena combat.   Kill or be killed.
*Competition ensures zero ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.   There are season plays similar to Overwatch and some other games like Rocket League does as well!  win gold weapon prizes if you can.
*Built-in level editor helps create more future maps for the game!
*You can collect cosmetic items and weapon skins!
*some tutorial modes are available to try out immediately.
*infinite skill wall.  Quake veterans.  not a good combination.  Not a Quake vet with 15+ years of experience?   You're gonna get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you, especially if you're not dedicated to the game.  This isn't something like PUBG where you'll rack up kills with no effort, because that's not gonna happen.  you won't have any perks,demon power ups or loadouts like in DOOM 2016 to help either.   No practice in this game?   no wins for you.
*because the game is focused on 1v1 games, you'll be waiting atleast 6 to 10 minutes or less depending when you joined a server.  this is also another setback for this title----new players getting into this game are going to wonder why is it taking so long to play or waiting in the lobby for god knows how much longer--they just want to get in and start fragging like they do in other shooters and see how this game works all round, not wait 10 minutes to play because in that time frame, they could boot up another game like CSGO or even Overwatch in so much less and start fragging and enjoying their game.
I get it's 1 versus 1, but even it can get a little...boring while watching 2 players.  They need to have more popular game modes open so that people can try this game out, sort of the same thing Quake Champions is doing..except that title has Overwatch abilities now.  no one would want to pay 9 dollars to just sit and watch a match the whole time and then get absolutely destroyed.  It must be really off-putting for new players to experience what Reflex has to offer and never get it because the skill ceiling is out of reach for them.
With all that said, This is a game I would have a hard time recommending to anyone

Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is a fantastic game, the graphics are gorgeous, the gameplay is super satisfying and the co-op is fantastic. Yet the content is where it lacks, my friends and I bought the edition where we had one of the DLC's and still we finished this way too soon. What seemed like the starting campaign was the full game, we were honestly suprised that it was over so quick. And yes, yes, you can obviously replay many missions to grind for more loot and try to get more of all those fancy weapons but with these limited missions, it's not worth that.
So besides this games many great aspects (and it's usually low framerates on even a decent rig) it didn't really left me any choice. The game is short, too short, and I'm not going to grind the same missions over and over on harder difficulties to keep myself occupied.
My verdict is, if you can get this game for cheap (lower than 10 bucks) get it with some friends and you'll surely get around 10 hours fun out of this, if you're looking for a good co-op game to invest a lot of time in, don't get it, this'll not be what you're looking for.

This game is very similar to the Left 4 Dead series, but I would say it's in the same genre rather than a clone. Vermintide does a ton differently and in an effective manner, mostly the focus on melee combat and items as progression.
I really like the melee combat in this game. Each melee weapon has a set of attacks with an arc and damage type. Sweeping strikes are good for clearing mobs of rats but tend not to do much damage. Precision strikes are murderous if you hit the head and can pierce the armor of Stormvermin, a specialist enemy.
Since each weapon has a different move set, there is a lot of variety even within an individual character class.
The bad:
The game has an unpredictable difficulty curve. Green Items help to beat Normal missions, while Blue are generally required to beat Hard missions. Grinding the gear is also heavily randomized so that throws a wrench in the flow of the game.
The game REQUIRES teamwork, full stop. I only recommend this game if you have a group of friends that are into it and will play it with you - there is no single player content, and the AI bots will let you down if you play solo.
Sometimes the rats make no noise and surprise you. It can get frustrating.
Ragdoll physics bug out regularly with rubber necks and limbs bouncing around. I find it funny, but it is not a 'feature'.
Bottom line;
If you want brutally satisfying multiplayer adventures, grab this on sale.

Got this for free from the Humble Bundle store. Here's my thoughts.
I don't really do a lot of horror games. But for free, it's hard to say no. So I fired it up and gave it a shot. Maybe spoilers ahead.
The story unfolds that you're some sort of painter who's also done some truly horrific things to his family. It's a trip through madness as his mind unravels as he comes to grips with what he did. The bad thing is that he's not really sorry about it. Instead he rationalizes it. It's all been done for the sake of creating his "masterpiece" painting.
In the beginning, I was genuinely scared at times. But then something odd happened. Something unexpected. I came to realize that no matter what I encountered, none of it was more scary than me. I was the true monster in the house. By the end I was in the mindset that all these jump scares were just there to distract me from my good work of finishing my gory masterpiece, and I felt ginuine drive to push past them, rather than be scared by them. In wasn't so much a conquoring of fear as much as it was an assertion of dominance over it.
In retrospect, I'm not sure if I would have played this game at $20. $10 or less seems like a fair price. It's relitively short. (I finished it in around 4 - 5 hours.. maybe less.) But it does say future playthroughs can be different based on choices. If you have the opportunity to pick this up on sale or free, I'd recommend it.

Astral Traveler is an intergalactic space racing game requiring speedy reflexes and unfaltering coordination. There's 47 sectors, each one a breakneck track with obstacles and sometimes enemies. Retaining your speed is vital so crashing can have devastating consequences. You can boost your speed to ludicrous levels by phasing through pulsars, which are little blue orbs. The phase window is extremely small, and the closer your are to the pulsar the bigger the speed boost. Phase too late and you crash into it, damaging your ship and halting your speed. Accompanying each of the 5 Nebulas (a group of sectors) is an energetic and suitably high tempo electro song, which gives another dose of adrenaline amidst the insanely speedy gameplay.
- The game looks quite beautiful despite not having the best graphical quality. Each Nebula hosts a distinct biome, such as the forest area featuring trees and wooden track, and desert area with a cracked dirt path. The visual variety is decent and helps diminish monotony. When travelling at immense speed, visual effects are employed to induce a feeling of speed. The background detail is minimal, but helps give a sense of depth and scope. When travelling at such insane speeds, great graphical detail would be superfluous and squandered anyway. Overall, Astral Traveler has nice and varied visuals.
- The music of Astral Traveler is suitably intense and the electro sounds coincide with the space nature of the game. While each song is good, there are far too few with there being only a single song per Nebula. With only 5 songs for the whole game, eventually the music loses its appeal and the audio of Astral Traveler falters in consequence. The sound effects are sharp and crisp, but not particularly interesting.
- In this game you have to reach the warp gate in the smallest time possible. To do so requires exploiting pulsars to gain speed while avoiding obstacles. There's a few interesting gameplay mechanics in this game. You manoeuvre a space ship possessing the abilities of jumping, phasing and shooting. Yes, not only does this game involve maintaining high speed and avoiding obstacles, but it also throws combat into the mix. With the combination of phasing through pulsars, jumping over gaps, and gunning down enemies it gets really intense at times. But that's not all, you'll also encounter full 360 degree tracks, translucent platforms, platforming segments requiring insane spin-jumping manoeuvring, and parts where you where you fly through space and squeeze through obstacles.
Progression is handled really well in this game. The difficulty curve and gradual introduction of new unique obstacles is very well done. The next level will always test your skills in a new way, with clever level design or maybe a new enemy like the one that can only be killed by phasing through it's projectiles and thus deflecting it back.
The controls were responsive but felt best on a controller. And while most games punish dying with a long loading screen, Astral Traveler will warp you back into the level before you can blink. You can also restart instantaneously with a single button press which is very convenient. The ship's turning speed does feel too slow at times, especially when there's platforms that only appear at close proximity thus giving very little time to react. Occasionally I felt I just couldn't turn in time to reach a platform at a large angle away from me, but practice and memory serves to overcome it.
With 47 levels with ranks and leaderboards, the game lasts a good deal of time. The insane breakneck racing mixed with space shooting remains fun throughout the entirety of Astral Traveler thanks to its visual variety and new interesting obstacles encountered along the way.
- Despite no tutorial, a quick glance at the keybindings is sufficient. The game is quite easy to pick up and play, but the skill ceiling is high.
- For me, the big appeal of this game is replaying each stage to achieve an A rank (or hopefully an S rank). The game itself is easy enough to complete, but the real fun and satisfaction comes from perfecting each stage. With 47 increasingly difficult stages, it's no easy task to achieve A rank in all of them, but it's worth replaying them until you do.
- Unfortunately not; though a track editor (and Steam workshop) would be pretty cool.
At this price, it's definitely worth it. There's enough exhilarating gameplay to last you a while and for only $4.99 it's worth it even if you're not typically a fan of such a game.
Overall, Astral Traveler is good bang for the buck. The decent longevity and replayability potential ensures many hours of enjoyment.

Morrowind isn't for casuals.  Don't expect to make a new character, walk into the first dungeon you see, and kick♥♥♥♥♥  Unlike Skyrim, this game does not scale with your level.  As a level 1 you might encounter a cave with level 10 enemies.  If dying a lot upsets you then don't buy this game.
I've often heard people complain that there is no fast travel in this game.  Wrong.  Let's see... there are silt striders (giant flee looking things), mage guild travel services that teleport you, scrolls that teleport you to a nearby temple, items that give you levitation, boots that make you run with "blinding" speed, etc.
A lot of people don't like how much melee attacks miss.  Here is the equation for landing a melee attack:  (Weapon Skill + (Agility / 5) + (Luck / 10)) * (0.75 + 0.5 * Current Fatigue / Maximum Fatigue) + Fortify Attack Magnitude - Blind Magnitude.  If you have high agility, weapon skill, luck, and fatigue then you won't have to worry about missing a lot.
MAGES listen up.  Magicka does not regenerate in this game.  You have to rely on potions and leveling up to regain magicka.  I never played as an archer in this game so I don't have anything to say about that.  Sneaking is difficult from what I've noticed, as in you will be deteced a lot.
I am sounding really negative right now but really, this game is challenging.  You don't find this level of difficulty in RPGs now a days.  When you start a quest you don't have a marker to tell you where to go.  You have to READ your journal to know where to go.  Even then the details given by the quest giver can be very vague.  There is no voice acting in this game other than brief chatter before you initiate a conversation.
If you are into detailed RPG elements, open-world exploration, and are up for a challenge then this game is for you.
TL;DR:  Don't buy this game expecting it to be a cake-walk like Skyrim, buy it if you want to apply yourself to a challenging, in depth RPG.

This is one of the first games that made my jaw drop (minor spoilers may follow).
Yeah, its pretty dated in terms of graphics and mechanics now, but in my opinion it still holds up as the best TES game yet.
Does the game have issues? Hell yes it does - from kind of static, stat based combat, through a cluttered inventory system, quest breaking bugs, terrible character animations, and sometimes unintuitive navigation and progression. The thing is, that even those things, in my opinion, don't detract from the overall game.
It still has probably the most interesting setting out of all TES games, with deep lore and inter-faction intrigue. All this set against a main plot about, in now typical TES fashion, being the messiah. The difference, compared to Skyrim, for example, is that Morrowind makes you work for it. You don't get to be the savior after a couple of hours of gameplay - you'll have to prove yourself in front of several faction leaders, and deal with religious persecution along the way.
You can join and rank up in any faction, some of which prevent you from joining other competing ones, and take part in quests which range from common item fetching, assassinations and monster hunts, to some actual problem solving and investigation - something that later games in the series rarely provide. What, again, differentiates Morrowind from the 4th and 5th installments is the lack of handholding. The quest arrow you probably got used to is nowhere to be found and the game will actually require you to find places, items and people on your own, providing, sometimes vague, directions from NPCs. You may find this annoying and tedious, but, in my opinion, the final result is that the game doesn't treat you like an idiot who can't find his or her way around and actually believes, that you can make it on your own. The world has enough distinct landmarks and locations to make the directions given by NPCs sufficient to get you where you need to go.
Mechanically, apart from the stat based fighting, it's the most complex TES game next to Daggerfall, but it gets rid of a lot of pointless passive skills while still providing a lot of variety in terms of possible builds. Typical of the series, you level up by actually using the skills and with enough effort you can max out everything. Can't be bothered to develop a particular attribute or skill? You can probably either make a potion for it or charm an item. And because the game distinguishes between between left and right for things like gloves and shoulder pads and includes belts, armored pants, regular pants and shirts as separate wearable items - the possibilities of customisation are probably larger than in most other games.
The magic system is really flexible, allowing you to choose between ready-made spells, making your own crazy spell effect combinations (provided you have the gold, skill and mana pool to pull it off), or simply charming a piece of your armor to let you cast any spell available ingame with the item's separate, rechargeable charge. Additionally, the game doesn't restrict particular spells to specific items - if an item can handle the power of the spell, you can charm it.
Want to cast fireballs with the rate of a machine gun? You can. Want to make a ring that lets you perform quarter mile long jumps while slowing your fall? You can. If you get your head around the mechanics of the game, you can do anything.
So, how does the game hold up after over 11 years? Surprisingly good. Sure, textures can get pretty blurry up close, and animations aren't anything to brag about, but at the same time the whole explorable area has a very unique and varied style and atmosphere to it. You get your typical medieval towns, castles, forts, tribal camps, cities within large pyramid-like structures (including the capital, Vivec, made out of several such sections), run down swamp and coast towns, and - probably my favorite - cities with buildings made out of giant crab shells.
And if you're still put off by the visuals, the game can be modded to a state that gives Skyrim a run for its money. By now you can get mods for anything, from textures, models, lighting and sound effects, to animations, as well as additional factions, quests, locations, items, and - under continued development - a recreation of the rest of the province of Morrowind based on lore and developer notes with its own towns, quests, and new, harder monsters. Additionally, the community managed to fix most of the bugs that Bethesda managed to miss over the years.
Morrowind, unlike the most recent installment in the TES series, is not a game for everyone - especially, if you're a fan of the recently omnipresent streamlining of everything. You'll probably have to get over several hurdles along the way, and the game has its problems, sometimes major ones, but for someone who wants to go really deep into mechanics, exploration and customization, this one is highly recommended.
Get it, if you havent done so yet.

An absolute failure of a sequel that dumbs down the formula and completely misses what made the original great. While the first game was also difficult, it at least provided you with a multitude of different play styles. The first Hotline Miami was NOT difficult just for the sake of being difficult, it was rewarding to progress through a level in your own way. In the sequel, you're often only given the illusion of choice: it's very clear that the developers intended for you to play through each level in a certain way. The amount of bait and hide tactics required to clear some of these missions are absolutely infuriating. The most offensive thing about this game, however- is the off-screen enemies killing you, a tactic that feels cheap, and given the slight randomization in enemy spawn locations, purely difficult for the sake of being difficult.
And probably the most disappointing thing is the story. Gone is the "bad acid trip" feeling of the first game, with its unreliable narration and cryptic dialog. Instead we're greeted with unimaginative one dimensional characters and a truly ham-fisted and half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt at a narrative in the same style, with none of the substance.
One of the most disappointing games I've ever played. And that's saying a lot. At least the music was okay- although still inferior to the first game's soundtrack by a long shot. If you're a fan of the first game, save yourself the disappointment.

Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number takes the player to a neon and cocaine filled fictional 1989 Miami Florida, with a vast cast of characters all from different strokes of life. As you play through the story the characters will begin to spiral down into the dark recesses of their own psyche just like in true Hotline Miami fashion, however this game lacks the wide variety of mask like in the first installment . Instead of having a slew of mask to choose from you are given different characters or weapons that will change the way you approach the level to leave a wake of blood and guts in your path.
When you first start up the game the thing that will grab your attention first is the phenomenal soundtrack, like the first game the developers have gone above and beyond finding songs that match the fast pace, skull bashing, shotgun toting gameplay. It doesn't stop there tho, they also made the audio effects aesthetically pleasing. The guns boom with the force of their caliber, skulls pop crack like firewood in a campfire, necks snap with the crunch of bone, and the thud of flesh to fist all depicts the force and pain that follows your gruesome actions.
Visually Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number sticks true to its colors by staying in the pixel art style of its predecessor, the color pallet of this series is beautiful with bright fluorescent colors giving the feeling of each level being a building somewhere in the neon void that is the mean streets of Miami. On the other hand the lack of detailed graphics on characters allows for the Hitchcock effect to take part in the player's mind, furthermore the environmental elements are detailed just enough that there is never a moment of questioning what an object on any given mission was.
When looking into how the game plays it's a bit hard to put a pin in it, Hotline at its core is a puzzle game where timing and speed is the key to a high score. players will find themselves charging at enemies again and again, dying and restarting over and over, just to shave two seconds off a run and find a new way to clear a room of multiple enemies in one swing of a knife or spray of an assault rifle. But don't let the fast pace style of gameplay discourage gamers who like to take their time and think through the next move, you can still take a slow almost stealthy approach to each level and get a score bonus for doing so in a covert fashion. The combo system is very well done to where as you execute and score kills it adds to your combo but non-lethal ways of removing a foe (unless playing as the journalist) will not add to the combo meter. This keeps the player going flat out as they race for the blood soaked first place position on the leaderboards.
Unlike the original Hotline Miami title this one has a more Pulp Fiction like structure to the story. In place of following the bloody acts of one person as he remembers his past. Wrong Number follows the gradual fall of people caught up in the turmoil of a collapsing world and not in chronological order. One moment you will be playing as a soldier fighting against Russians on the Hawaiian front in the early eighties, to playing as a Russian mob boss in the late eighties retaking turf lost in the forming  of the Russo-American Coalition in the first game. The Fans, a group of friends mimicking the acts of the first game, bring an interesting view to the development of the story. As they go on their self righteous killing sprees of gangs,  drug dealers, and russian mob members they almost seem to get lost in what they are truly trying to accomplish with these acts of violence.
In the end Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is an outstanding game, through a vast array of characters fast gameplay and beautiful 8-bit graphics, it plunges the player into the lives of it's cast and puts the blood on your hands letting you determine how to purge the dark underbelly that is Miami Florida.

TL:DR - Left 4 Dead, but way better.  Buy it.
I'll keep this simple; this game has the same core mechanic as Left 4 Dead.  It's a four-player co-op horde survival game.  Except; this game is WAY better than L4D or L4D2:

It has a much richer universe, first off, i.e. Warhammer.
It has a loot mechanic, and I find myself striving to acquire higher tiers of loot with different item modifiers that can push me a little further.  (A chance for shots to penetrate the target and hit the next, a chance to gain increased attack speed for a duration, everytime a healing item is used on an ally 80% of your health is restored, and MANY more modifiers exist.)
It has melee, variable speeds with different weapons, power attacks, and blocking.
It has interesting missions, a story to tell, and GREAT voice acting.  There is banter between the characters as they fight for their lives.
It's polished, the matchmaking WORKS, it has flawless servers, in-game friends lists for joining/inviting to games.
The graphics are gorgeous.
I highly recommend this game for anyone who enjoyed Left 4 Dead.

I've just finished this game today, after being interested for years and having owned it for some time. Binary Domain is an excellent third-person shooter, with a thought provoking story and fun gameplay. In short, you should pick this up, especially if it is on sale. I actually got it for free during a give-away.
With that said, I finished the game on Normal in 7 hours, so it is a fairly short game. However, I would list that as a strength because the gameplay itself isn't anything special, and a longer campaign would have made the game less enjoyable, I think. Bossfights could be a pain, becuase most of them love spamming homing missles agaisnt you, but while this is annoying, it never made any of them impossible--at least on normal. I haven't played on higher difficulties, but I imagine that this mechanic will make higher difficulties very frustrating.
I really enjoyed the story. If you are a fan of Sci-Fi, you will find a lot to like here. The plot is basically all about whether or not synthetic life is actually life, which is nothing new, but it does introduce a unique, interesting, and unexpected plot twist towards the end. This twist makes the question even more interesting. However, this was also my main source of frustration. The game teases a choice to be made, but in reality, there isn't one. It's unfortunate, especially because I found myself disagreeing with the side our character seemed to take. The game also has alternate endings, but they are sadly just small variations of the same ending--and as you might expect, they ARE based on your squad trust levels.
It's a real shame that this game isn't getting a sequal, because honestly, Binary Domain is a great game overall, and Binary Domain 2 could have potentially been one of the best third-person shooters ever with the right improvements. Pick this game up if you can, and who knows, maybe Sega will change their minds...

For those more used to Skyrim, Morrowind might seem like a wholly different experience. But, I guarantee it is just as epic, if not more so. While still an RPG, this adventure plays more like a tabletop game - stats and skills are king. You will find it to be far more invested in details and micro-managing, and this may make the beginning of your quest VERY difficult - this game does little to no hand-holding, and pulls no punches with difficulty and length - you want to get somewhere? Sorry, no fast-travel, you either hire a carriage, use magic, or rough it through the woods like a grown-up. You want to get money? You do work for people, because you'll find next to no coins in your dungeon raids (but lots of other loot).
However, if you start off small and work your way up gradually, the experience will stack on and you'll be fine.
Unlike the adventures in the Nordic lands, the home of the Dunmer is a exceptionally unique place for a fantasy game - this is no medieval countryside, but a volcanic island home to giant insects, dinosaurs, and mushroom trees.
One last note - Morrowind is LONG. I highly recommend playing when you have an excess of free time, as the sheer number of things to do will eat it ALL up in short while. Under moon and star, may your quest sail smoothly...

Same resolution and aspect ratio issue that existed in DQH, OPPW3 and Berserk (may go back further, but I have not touched any prior games), where image is stretched to your native monitor resolution regardless of in-game resolution settings and any sort of hardware/software aspect ratio scaling settings you may have on your PC. With my 1920x1200 monitor, I had to modify my monitor driver to change the native resolution to a 16:9 resolution to get the games display at the correct aspect ratio.
Considering this and the many other technical issues with the above-mentioned games, none of them got any sort of fix released by Koei Tecmo. Which speaks to me that these ports are basically quick cash grabs and they have little or no intention from the onset to provide any sort of support for these games.
I lived with the issues on DQH and used community-released fixes for OPPW3. Refunded Berserk because I knew it would likely not receive the same amount of support from the community as OPPW3 and tried (and subsequently refunded) Toukiden 2 because I was naive to hope that KT would have upped their game and fixed this issue by now.
In summary, is it a bad game? Based on reviews I'd say no, but this, however, is definitely a bad port, so I recommend that everyone skip this and go for the Vita version because based on the limited time I had with the game, the game models, textures, lighting and physics are very much Vita level of quality.

After finishing the main story, I think I can confidently give my opinion of this game. Think of it as "Bite sized monster hunter" the game itself plays very similarly to monster hunter, find a large creature and kill it, simple enough. The large creatures arent exactly difficult, and theyre killed relativly fast (Maybe thats why they're easier.) The longest fight I had was about 12 minutes, and I was very undergeared. The creatures are also kind of easy beacuse they have trouble with tracking. If youre at a lower elevation then them, and they use a range attack, it will go right over your head. They also have very projected attacks, and most of the time you can just walk out of the way, no sprinting or dodging required if youre paying attention. All of this said, its a very fun game. Slaying large monster is always fun, and even though I said the game was kinda easy, theres a lot of attacks that require dodging and punish you if you arent familiar with the attacks. Online is a little borked right now, but they game becomes more difficult online, and much more fun by extension. Overall, I'd give it a 7.5/10, I'd raise it if the online wasnt so weirded up since multiplayer is such a big aspect. As port quality is concerned, I'm very suprised Koei actually made a good port. I have played many video games. I have played FPS, RPG, ect. And no game I have ever played has captured a universe as well as Star Trek Online does. The absolute accuracy of the Star Trek universe is captured in this game, along with many fun quests, space battles, and (despite what people say about them,) the amazing ground missions. There is truly a massive open world to explore, with vast planets, space stations, and actual galaxies. And you know what else? IT'S COMPLETELY FREE. It doesn't have that pay to win feel that other free games have, but you do have the option to spend money on ZEN tokens, which can be used to buy weapons, ships, and cosmetic items, but it's not needed. I admit, I've spent about $15 on ZEN, with which I bought a new science vessel. Overall, it just makes you feel joyful, cruising through space and discovering new planets. I would definetely reccomend it. I would honestly give it a 9.8/10.

The idea for this game is great and this game could be incredible, but I just don't see any progress being made, even after a year. Most updates are small, meaningless, and add nothing to the game, thanks for that toilet we all wanted. Problems that have existed since the game's release still plague it, such as huge lag spikes when colliding objects, Multi-player extreme rubber banding, and poor optimization on large machines. However the most disappointing thing about this game is the constant promise of "survival mode". I'm just gonna say it. I don't believe they’re working on it and it will never be finished. There is simply no evidence that any of their time has ever been spent on it. No inventory system, no crafting system, No hunger/survival aspects, no monetary systems, no combat systems. There's nothing here and there's no proof that they have ever done anything for survival mode what so ever. One scrap of evidence and I'll change my review. Until then, I cannot recommend it.
EDIT 06/24/2017, After reaching 1st place in the steam reviews and gaining some negative attention this review was set to hidden to improve the sales of the game during the summer sale. This was intended to be an honest review and I won’t be silenced. I've lost respect for this game and they've proven to me this game and the developers cannot be trusted.
EDIT 06/25/2017, Hidden from the front page again. Updating this post seems to bring it back up. I will not be silenced.
EDIT 07/05/2017, This review has gotten way more attention than I ever intended, even from a developer. I'm glad the developers are at least willing to listen to criticism about a valid point. In my previous edits I've mentioned my review being hidden from the front page and this did happen, despite my review have having hundreds of ratings more than any other. I find it unlikely my review was rotated out, because it was the top review and none of the other top reviews were ever hidden. For the haters out there, I’d like you to know I really do love the idea of Scrap Mechanic.  The possibilities are truly endless and I’ve even posted a couple of my own creations to the Steam Workshop. The purpose of this review was never meant to sabotage Axolot Game, but rather to push them. This game has shown clear signs of abandon-ware and the public deserves to know. Almost no progress has been made in the last year and anyone can check this. At the end of the day I would prefer to be wrong and have to change this review. However, my doubts remain and until then, I do not recommend this game.

I really enjoy this game.  It is not pay to win as all players have access to the same weapons.  You can pay to get the weapons earlier but by the time they become available to you, you no longer will be playing in tier 0, or with beginners.
They have something for everyone: infantry, recon (sniper), tanker, pilot or paratrooper.
Pros: Developers are active on the forums!  Gunplay is very good. It will take you a while to master your weapon, but when you do it's very rewarding.   You get rewarded more for capping and defending points vs. just trying to have a good kdr (infantry obviously).  The game is updated frequently with new mechanics, balancing tweaks and new toys.
Cons: Sound effects are very low quality.  You need at least a mid range pc from 4 or 5 years ago to play at 60 fps.  It takes a very long time for them to implement new maps and new armies to fight for (japanese, british and italians are not yet in the game, currently you can choose between the U.S., Russia and Germany).
TLDR:  It is a well made game from a group of talented and passionate people who work very hard on the game.  It is NOT p2w.

Now that I have managed to survive for a day in the game, I will write this review. I haven't played all modes or all bugs yet but I think I've seen enough to say the following:
SURVIVAL:
So far I am enjoying this game. I spent about an hour in survival mode just trying to learn the game. I managed to actually survive a day as a bee on easy difficulty. I think it's better to wait to play as the spider or dragonfly, as it's much harder to feed yourself by hunting than by foraging nectar. Even on easy it seemed like the survival was a little too... grindy? If you focus on anything other than eating nectar the entire time, you are going to die. It wasn't until after I had already survived a day that I tried the other mode - Nature Sandbox.
>>>>NATURE SANDBOX: START HERE!<<<<
At least in my opinion, I think it would have been better to start in the sandbox. You can jump between playing as any of the bugs already in the world. Much better for exploring and learning the game than jumping straight into survival. As I type this I realize how obvious that sounds, but at first I had assumed that the sandbox was just a spectator-only mode.
WISHLIST:
Better tutorial - The tutorial pages are a little overwhelming at first. It was hard to retain most of the info, I found myself having to constantly reread it after dying in various ways in order to find out how I could have prevented my death. It's not that the controls are difficult or unintuitive, it's just a lot to learn and there will be much trial and error.
More levels - Only one map so far. I'm confident that there will end up being more than one level based on the dev notes, but I am mentioning it anyway.
Multiplayer - Devs say this is low priority, but I think it could bring A LOT of fun and replay value to this game. Team deathmatch and Racing are two multiplayer modes that I think would be quite fun.
Pretty stoked on this game.

At first, you would think from playing BD that this was inspired by Mass Effect. The stylised art approach, the full voice acting, the squad-based commands and use of a cover system are all similiar to everyones favourite space-opera. But as it turns out, they were both released during the same year and could rightly be called cousins both in mechanics and in quality but does not have the same depth as Mass Effect.
The voice acting is consistantly great throughout and the characters are interesting even if they are largely stereotypes. There is a well-developed rapport built between them which makes this a distinctly character driven storyline with an overarching plot that is seemingly very simple but actually turns out to be very thought provoking. What I was genuinely impressed with was how it threw up a story-line twist which was similiar to what I expected but at the same time was so original that it genuinely brought a smile to my face at how refreshingly different the plot became as a result. That is a rare thing these days.
If there was one critisism I could level at BD it would be the lack of balance to the difficulty. It is almost sciztsophenic in how challenging it wants to be, varying from insaney easy to unfair. It feels like the devs intentionally threw medi-kits at you in order to get you through certain boss battles because it can be almost impossible to avoid getting hit and not to mention that the game has an absolutely ton of them! All bosses were also very memorable except for one which felt very lacklustre. SEGA have also done a wonderful job by varying what you do which puts it head and shoulders over the original Mass Effect when it comes to variety of content. Smart use of mini-games which function as cut-scenes and some impressive set-peices make you genuinely want to see what the game is going to have you doing next.
All in all, BD is an unsung classic. Somehow it slipped into obscurity over the years which is why a much-deserved sequel never appeared and is well worth purchasing. It isn't the longest of games but it is undenyably entertaining from start to finish.

TL;DR:  Great gameplay and really cool gear and skill customization, but the game is bogged down by some glaring technical / interface issues.  Get it on console if you can, as many of the issues are largely PC specific (practically unusable voicechat, no mouse support, not-great controller support, hackers, poor text chat.)  Get it on PC only if the game is really appealing to you and you have no other way to play it.  And if you've played Kiwami, you may want to skip this, because it's $60 for what is basically a reskin of Kiwami with a few new weapons and abilities (and a bunch of Kiwami's stuff actually taken AWAY, for that matter.)
PROS:
-Fun, straightforward hack-and-slash gameplay.  A little grindy in places, but ultimately I had a lot of fun trying out all the different weapons and combinations.
-No shortage of gear customization options, but nothing insanely complicated either.  Crafting new armor is satisfying and the armor is visually appealing.
-Solid story.  Nothing groundbreaking, but it kept me interested.  Did take a little while to GET interesting, though.
-Straightforward, relaxing, multiplayer co-op.  The game's gear system and the technical aspects of some weapons are attractive to serious players, but the multiplayer is still playable for casual players.  It's been great fun and a very non-toxic multiplayer experience, which is a pleasant break from other games I've been playing lately.
CONS:
-Voicechat has virtually no options--good luck if you want to use anything other than your default device.  EDIT:  A recent patch has allowed it so you can at least toggle voicechat on and off before starting the game (not even in-game.)  We're still missing basic stuff like push-to-talk, volume control, muting, etc.
-Character chatter is not translated.  There is no English voiceover, so that means if you don't speak Japanese, you're going to miss the idle chatter between your party members, all the stuff your Mitama say during and after fights, etc.
-Can't customize controller inputs.  This is a problem because the existing control scheme is not great for some weapons.
-In-game chat exists in multiplayer, but for whatever rediculous reason you are restricted to chatting a few words at a time.  So if you want to string together a sentence or two you'll have to break it apart into several entries--it's like trying to write a book on twitter.
-Server interface is, again, restricted to just a few characters for the title and such.  There's really no reason for this--can your modern 2017 game not handle the servers being a few letters longer?
-Lots of cheaters in multiplayer, just to warn you.  It's cooperative, so that might not bother some of you, but the game lacks even the most basic of protection against cheaters.  Let's leave it at that.
-NO MOUSE SUPPORT.  This is honestly bad enough with normal weapons, but with weapons like the rifle requiring you to aim, this basically means you'd better be on pad.  If you don't have a pad for your PC, don't buy this game.
-No way to kick players in multiplayer.  There aren't a lot of reasons to kick people, but there are still little kids running around named "Adolf Hitler" and trolling your chat, and it would damned sure be nice to kick them.
I honestly struggled with whether to go with "no" or "yes."  There is an amazing game here if you're able to get past the technical issues, but they're so basic, numerous, and ultimately inexcusable that it's hard to recommend the game.  My best advice is that you read through the technical issues and see if any of them will affect you, and if none of them do, then go for it.
Or you can just get butthurt that I gave the game you like a red thumb and mark this review as unhelpful, y'know.  Whatever feeds your Tenku.

I wanted to play a good amount of hours into this game first before doing a review on it. Let me say this first, I played the first Toukiden a lot on my Vita so I already have a general idea of what I am getting into.
Q: How is the port?
A: For the most part, the port is far better than the Toukiden Kiwami port. 1080p and 30/60 FPS lock is a better improvement than the previous game's options. This is a PS4 port if you are wondering so the graphics are decent but they get the job done. I only noticed a few really ugly textures. The biggest downside to this port is the completely lousy keyboard controls. I have an xbox controller so I don't have this problem but I tried keyboard to test. It is absolutely impossible to play because the keybinds are all over the place and you can't change the controls to certain keys like ENTER. Koei has a track record for putting out awful PC controls. They definitely need to fix or get better at this, no  exception even if this was ported from console.
Q: Do I recommend or not?
A: I highly recommend this game if you love Monster Hunter and JRPG. This games has Open world for single player and a lobby system for multiplayer. What I don't highly recommend you play this if you dont like the genre and you don't have a controller.
Q: What improved?
A: Almost everything has been improved from the first game except maybe the overall story pacing. The characters are distinct and quite memorable but I found the story pacing all over the place. Sometimes moves along too fast or too slow and sometimes too convenient or resolved too fast. Otherwise the gameplay has been improved with two new weapons. I love the Demon Arm addition and the open world helps give more lore to the world that the previous game lacked.
Overall score: 8/10

I wanted to like this game. I really did. But browser games are so bad.
In, and of itself, it's a pretty solid shooter. You aim, you fire, you hit somebody, they die. It's basic.
The User Interface is a little daunting at first. And it takes some time to get used to.
Until you grind for a few days to level six, or buy a premade soldier (with real money), you can only play in instanced death matches, not the actual war. And it's the same repetitive combat over and over again of capture the point.
At this point, I feel like the game is basically finished. They just continue to remain in early access so they can make huge changes without warning and avoid negative feed back.
The clipping issues are terrible, you can often drive through trees and even buildings or fall through the ground.
The animations are juggy, they stutter a bit and sometimes don't completely follow through. (Like when reloading or switching weapons.)
The latency can be an issue. And that's not even from having good or bad internet. The input latency from your keyboard and mouse is incredibly noticeable. (To me, at least.) And it feels unresponsive.
If they had moved to a standalone client instead of trying to be a browser game it would have been a great success.
The cash shops aren't that bad, and they aren't required to enjoy the game until you get to high levels.
All in all, if you're really itching for a World War II Themed shooter, there are other options.....

I can't reccomend this game enough, personally. You have 5 characters to choose from that all have different roles and a very large arsenal of weapons to choose from. BUT you have to unlock them in game by playing. Playing on a more difficult difficulty gives you a better chance to get better loot with the best of the items (red and orange tier) not even showing up on normal and hard difficulties.
Okay now about the loot system that people seem to have a huge problem with. Assuming you complete the mission there's a screen at the end of the game that consists of 7 dice. each dice has 6 sides and a 2/6 chance to land heads up. If you pick a up a tome of which there are 3 in a mission, you get those 2/6 dice replaced with 4/6 dice. Getting a grimoire which gives a massive down side of everyone in the party losing 1/3 of their maximum health. BUT if you make it to the end of the mission, then you get a guaranteed face up dice. Some people really hate it, but personally I think it feels like good progression.
Of the 5 characters, the Empire soldier, the dwarf, and the viktor saltzpyre are all mostly melee based. But Sienna and the elf are both ranged focused. However, what i like about Vermintide is that while this is while that is typically correct, you aren't forced to play it that way. You can pick up melee focused staffs (staves?) for sienna and melee focused bows for the elf. You can also choose to be more ranged as the dwarf or viktor. If you can use the weapons well, then you can do whatever you want.
As a side note, try to play online. Solo is fine but you really start to feel the drag once you get to hard and nightmare difficulty.

Considering how mixed the reviews are and how I feel about the game, I felt like I'd throw my input into the mix. For me, this really was the GOTY for 2015, this seems like a sorely overlooked gem honestly. you see the obvious description of "L4D with ratmen," though how I've always felt inclined to describe it is as L4D with gameplay, trying to make a point of how this game really takes a step forward in gameplay depth and replayability in the genre archetype L4D brought forth.
I really never did enjoy L4D very much, and between 1 and 2 probably never hit 80 hours back on xbox, and I think to sell Vermintide as simply a L4D reskin does it terrible injustice. While I won't of course say this is the perfection of the style (looking forward to Vermintide 2 and projects from other developers inspired by Fatshark's ideas), to the best of my awareness, it really is the best that's come yet. Vermintide is a game I can call beautiful.
There is so much about Vermintide I found myself really satisfied with that I didn't expect as I purchased it. The skill ceilling, weapon variety and playstyle nuance between classes all stand out as areas of excellence acheived by the developers. one of the things that really makes the game great is just how different playing the different weapons and classes is, with different hitboxes, frame data, on-hit behavior, dodge lengths and speeds for all of them, all with great flavor and feel to weilding, an A+ no doubt on weapon design, both in the mundane swords, axes and hammers and creative instruments like the different magical staves and bows.
And the end-game difficulty, that's something that really won me over and along with the replayability provided by the detail put into class and weapon design ensures me over 1,000 hours in time, I'm still at sub-150 at the time of this review, but this is pretty much set.
Vermintide has a skill ceilling well beyond that of most PvE games, one high enough to satisfy someone who appreciates the challenge present in Monster Hunter and Souls-likes, even with a more easily surmounted initial learning curve. it's easy to jump in on a low difficulty and work your way through the mechanics, especially with the help of the great community, then once you've developed your skills and familarity there's a host of different ways to notch up the difficulty and restrictions of your run up to where you're grinding your face into true-soloing maps with non-upgraded weapons.
For any of you out there that have put 1,000 or more hours into Monster Hunter and are familiar with that feeling of just tossing your body infront of an end-game elder dragon for weeks at a time until you *finally* succeed, that's a feeling Vermintide offers to bring you in it's endgame. There is legitimate challenge to be had here and consequently legitimate feelings of accomplishment and self-improvement. For Example I've must have spent probably 10 hours so far trying to run the very first level solo on the second to last difficulty with pretty decent equipment yet to no avail, and I know that when I finally do clear it on my own, it will feel just the same as overcoming a difficult roadbloack in Monster Hunter, and even after that reward there will be many more opportunities to feel it with still more improvement to make and skill to build.
This has been the first review I've written for steam, I'm sorry it hasn't been very mechanical, technical or formal, frankly I've been one-sided and imbalanced, but I've done the best to convey how I really feel about this game. I highly recommend this game to anybody who thought that L4D may have been a nice idea, but that the game itself was too simple and repetitive, or to anybody who appreciates a challenging and deep PvE experience. I honestly think this Game stands beside Monster Hunter and Souls as pinnacles of PvE gameplay.

Yep, it's good.
Pros:
1.  You feel like you're in charge.  Good or bad, millions of dollars and your season could depend on when or if you build that Telemetry building.
2.  Drivers are like spoiled children.  Just like real life.
3.  Budgets, budgets, budgets.
4.  Not too gnitty gritty, but when I sweat .1 degrees of a wing angle in practice, that's enough for me.
5.  Build it and they will come.  A Test Track, that is.  Drivers love a winner.
6.  Eeerrraaaaaaammmm!
Cons:
1.  Your mechanics are idiots at setups.  Especially the new ones, in ERS, which is when you really need their help.
2.  Couple little bugs.  One driver got sick, and dropped to 0 lbs. weight for the rest of his life.  So, he's faster now?
3.  Could have used an extra zoom or a In-Car Cam graphics level.  Instead, it's decent, but not super pretty.
4.  On the graphics note, cars take slow corners with a jerky turning radius.  Could have been smoothed out a little.
5.  And cars sometimes collide or even pass through each other.  Moreso in practice than races.
6.  Tire wear can be dramatic, especially if you can't afford super nice compounds on hot tracks... which probably makes sense.
7.  Budget, budget, budget.
8.  Drivers could have more specific feedback on the radio, or have more varied responses to overtakes, etc.
This game doesn't give you much help in the beginning.   Learning that you should pit each lap in the beginning of a practice session, for example, may seem intuitive to some... but others have to learn the hard way.
Also, the game shouldn't allow you to build a part for a car once the season is over until after the new chassis is designed.  It's a tough way to learn a lesson about throwing away money.
All in all, though, it's an excellent game.  There's flaws that can be easily avoided, and it delivers a lot of atmosphere.  Well done.

The protagonist can carry 4 types of weapon: handgun with infinite ammo, assault rifle with energy blast, grenades (including holographic decoy) and one weapon of choice (sniper rifle, shotgun, RPG, etc.). Companions have 1-2 types (unchangable), with the main being upgradable as well as protagonist's assault rifle.
Tactical part includes squad based combat with 4 commands (can be activated with
or hotkeys). AI is mostly adequate, except when companions jump at the line of fire and ignore
a friendly and completely optional request to get back to safety. Also the game features
- the better you fight and talk, the more companions trust you and the better their chances to survive (affects the ending).
There are quite interesting and challenging boss battles (bosses are giant non-anthropomorphic robots) and partial enemy destruction (again, because robots). Graphics (especially facial animations), sound (VA and soundtrack) and controls are good. Rare QTEs (4-5 in the whole campaign) were difficult for me, but there was a checkpoint in 10-30 seconds before each one.
The negative part of the game is the city combat - you don't turn living cities with civilians into battlefields. Or it might be related to the general satirical tone of the plot - lack of empathy from the military (the only person who mentions it is a cop).

The game is somewhat like COD and Mass Effect mashed together, but in a japanese style gameplay.  A linear story shooter that makes you feel more and more powerful as you upgrade your weapons and your teammates, and gives a false illusion that the interaction you have with NPC will effect later in the game like Mass Effect. Gives bosses for challenge, w/ different game mechanic to keep the game fresh. For $3.75 it gave me around 12hr of fun which many other game gives me less game time and would cost more. If your looking for some singleplayer fun shooter to kill time, I would recommend. Although the multiplayer side of the game is dead.

Giving the PC version a thumbs down because it does NOT support anything over 1080p/60. The 60fps cap is annoying but acceptable if the physics are locked to it or something, but admittedly we should strive for 60fps as a minimum, these days, not a maximum. 144hz monitors are becoming very cheap. The main issue is that anybody with a 1440p monitor can only play this at 1080, which does not scale very well to 1440, leading to a somewhat frustrating experience. Also because of that, the weird desktop scaling that has to happen when the game goes fullscreen causes a lot of issues with GSync monitors as well.

A vast improvement over the first Toukiden which was a nightmare to run on PC. A surprisingly stellar port that hasn't crashed or bugged out on me yet.
All that aside, Toukiden 2 feels a little less like Monster Hunter now and more like Dragon's Dogma. What I mean is no more hopping from zone to zone in small maps and not everything is a hunting mission. The world is open for you to explore and it's packed with things to do in it. It's not uncommon to discover huge oni and help out other slayers on the field on your way to a quest. I don't find myself grinding the same missions over and over to get materials. They even made the story in this one a lot more interesting.
All in all, if you like the first Toukiden or if you're a fan of Monster Hunter or even Dragon's Dogma then you should definitely give this a shot.
Oh and you'll need a controller. Damn near every controller released since the Xbox 360 works on PC so there's really no excuse not to have one.

I saw the game being streamed and saw gameplay of it on Youtube and intantly got interested in it. I loved Left For Dead but stopped playing due to that no one plays that anymore so i thought why not, let's relive Left For Dead set in a theme i love as well.
Instantly loved the game, loved the banter between the characters and how well the voice actors pictured the characters and their beliefs. Also love the loot system, yes it's rage inducing at times but once you get that 7 roll it makes your entire day and all the hard work worth it.
The combat? It's just as Left For Dead and more, there's light attack, heavy attack, block, pushing and dodging all three which are all viable in different situation and what weapon you're currently using. And unlike Left For Dead each character has their unique playstyle with their own weapons and cosmetic gear.
Now the game is not without flaws, sometimes you run into bugged ai pathing which yes is annoying when it's a Stormvermin patrol stuck in a corridor you need to pass but otherwise at this moment there's not too many bugs that i can say that's noticeable, not that i've seen at least.
Another down side is that as fun as the game is, it's best enjoyed with friends on voice. Public Matchmaker is fine but you will perform best with people you know and how their playstyle is.
The NET code is also surprisingly good, it's peer to peer but anything you kill dies instantly on anyone elses client. Otherwise it's the standard ping issues where you see a rat a meter away that should miss you but hits you anyway and a delayed strike before it hits the enemy.
I'd recommend this game if you have a few friends to play it with.

Yep, it's good.
Pros:
1.  You feel like you're in charge.  Good or bad, millions of dollars and your season could depend on when or if you build that Telemetry building.
2.  Drivers are like spoiled children.  Just like real life.
3.  Budgets, budgets, budgets.
4.  Not too gnitty gritty, but when I sweat .1 degrees of a wing angle in practice, that's enough for me.
5.  Build it and they will come.  A Test Track, that is.  Drivers love a winner.
6.  Eeerrraaaaaaammmm!
Cons:
1.  Your mechanics are idiots at setups.  Especially the new ones, in ERS, which is when you really need their help.
2.  Couple little bugs.  One driver got sick, and dropped to 0 lbs. weight for the rest of his life.  So, he's faster now?
3.  Could have used an extra zoom or a In-Car Cam graphics level.  Instead, it's decent, but not super pretty.
4.  On the graphics note, cars take slow corners with a jerky turning radius.  Could have been smoothed out a little.
5.  And cars sometimes collide or even pass through each other.  Moreso in practice than races.
6.  Tire wear can be dramatic, especially if you can't afford super nice compounds on hot tracks... which probably makes sense.
7.  Budget, budget, budget.
8.  Drivers could have more specific feedback on the radio, or have more varied responses to overtakes, etc.
This game doesn't give you much help in the beginning.   Learning that you should pit each lap in the beginning of a practice session, for example, may seem intuitive to some... but others have to learn the hard way.
Also, the game shouldn't allow you to build a part for a car once the season is over until after the new chassis is designed.  It's a tough way to learn a lesson about throwing away money.
All in all, though, it's an excellent game.  There's flaws that can be easily avoided, and it delivers a lot of atmosphere.  Well done.

Panzer Elite Action is basically leveraging the existing assets and engine, but making an action game out of it, and while Panzer Elite is an anthentic WW2 tank sim, PEA is an action title that had you blasting dozens and dozens of tanks during a single mission, not to mention infantry, antitank guns, and more.
As this is action title, you get a third-person view, and you drive with the keyboard while aim with the mouse. Unfortunately, dualstick is not possible, as this is an older title. (If you have Xpadder, use it to emulate keystrokes)  And you get bases on the screen that can refill your ammo or repair your damages. If you get killed, you can respawn at the last checkpoint, which is pretty frequent so you don't need to repeat a lot of the kills.
You get both German, Russian, and American action, with the tanks, and there are even AI teammates to help you, and generally AI teammates are very good in assessing threats and eliminating them, but they have several weaknesses: they don't do anti-air (and you need to use your coax MG for anti air in several missions) , they don't do long distance shooting (whereas you can), they don't know how to use a repair depot (you can order them to if you're close), and they cannot do destruction (i.e. take down a windmill as per objective).  Try not to let them die, as playing alone is sometimes rather painful. There are some missions where you suddenly lose control of your AI team mates and you need to go at it all alone, which can be a bit scary at first.
Beyond that, squad controls are simplistic: forward sweep, or group formation. Pressing each command repeatedly will toggle through some options such as pincer, scout, attack, and wedge, line, column and so on.
As this is a tank, you can choose to do EASY DRIVING, which lets you steer toward the turret aim (but only if you are moving forward or backward), and left/right still means turn / strafe, or use the WASD keys to maneuver the tank independent of the turret.
The mini-map will warn you of approaching forces,  and/ or defenders if you are attacking, but just general vicinity, not exact position. You do have binoculars for scouting and if available, call in air support for some bombardment.
So while the action is still fast and exciting, there is some tactical component to it, such as taking the high terrain, flanking the enemy, engage at range, and so on.
The AI isn't so bright, as they rely on rush and ambush, but they can be a challenge on higher difficulty levels and on tight levels such as Stalingrad, where you get ambushed left and right.  Fortunately, the depots are available quite frequently and you can always backtrack a long ways to repair and rearm if needed.
All in all, the game is rather fun to play, if you can get it working. It seems the bink libraries included doesn't work right on Windows 10. Disabling the BIK files seems to allow the game to run properly.  If it's for a few dollars, it is worth a couple hours of your time.

I'm going to open with pointing out my bias, because I played and loved this game endlessly on XBox back when it came out.
Objectively, the graphics are very dated, and the gameplay does feel a little clunky. However if you're any fan of more classic RPG's, you need to give this game a look. Before Oblivion's more medieval landscape (Shivering Isles exheunt) and before Skyrim's Canada, Morrowind built a beautiful fantasy landscape, filled with spectacular creatures, varied characters, dwarven mechanations, and original quests.Technically speaking, the sound and graphics aren't much to speak of (though the music is adventurous, and really ups the experience). There is not much voice acting to speak of in most of this game, instead Bethesda opted for text boxes to save space. However, this opens the door for so much lore, and flavor text (which is important, damnit!) that this feels like the best crafted version of the Elder Scrolls universe.
The game isn't levelled like it's predecessors, the world stays as it is, and you start out pretty weak. But it pushes you to be strong, and if you put the time in, you can overcome every challenge. There isn't a lot of emphasis on balance, because like a classic RPG, this game doesn't hold your hand. There isn't a compass to help you find quest points, instead you have a journal which subjectively directs you to your quest goal. For example, "The cave is north of Seyda Neen, a bit past the bridge on the river." It feels like a real adventure, going through it.
If I were to price it: 30-Full price due to the age. But the game now can be found for incredibly cheap, I recommend it to anyone who enjoys a hard RPG experience.
