Back in 2002-06 or something, I remember BARELY being able to play this game on my PC for longer than 30 minutes without having the damn game crash.  But it was so addicting and immersive, I would reload the game and wait through the 2 minutes of loading just to progress another 30 minutes!  That says a lot coming from someone in the Call of Duty, roll your face on the keyboard, and needs instant gratification generation.
If you are familiar with Oblivion and Skyrim but never had the chance to play Morrowind in its prime, I regret to inform you, that you missed out on one of THEE greatest love hate relationships in the video game world.  (Also if you loved Morrowind but played Skyrim and Oblivion, I feel your pain)
But I write this game as freshly played in my mind, as almost a decade past, but recently I bought the game in its entirety for under $4 and then prompted to install the overhaul mod which updates the graphics, gameplay issues, but sadly not the combat.
What did Morrowind have that the following Elder Scroll games had missing?
Punishing the player for making stupid characters!
Any character you make in Skyrim can essentially kill right off the bat, ehh Oblivion more or less so.
But Morrowind?
*Oh you want to make a armored-mage?  Well goodluck moving two feet out of town without running out of stamina.
*Merchant/Bard? LOL I hope you like hitting the quick save button every ten seconds to avoid rats from killing you!
*Bad♥♥♥♥♥orc w/ excellent two-handed axe skills?  20 Cliffracers are waiting for you on the way to Balmora!
No class is stupid, but I'm just saying, the player had to find creative ways to overcome simple obstacles, there existed a learning curve in playing the character you made.  It could be the fact that you needed to load up on enchantments and potions, use your tradeskills to acquire gold in order to purchase gear to compensate for your bad combat skills, or rest 16 hours between every "major" fight so you can use your bezerker racial and become the Reaper.
Also for the old school Pen and RPG player, this was just a wet dream from customizable ANYTHING (spells, armor, enchanted armor, durability on said items, SO MANY ARMOR SLOTS, stat point allocation, min-maxing skills or stats) the only thing that was missing was a way to show off to other people you did 40 hitpoints of damage on a crit, but you could just scream at your buddy Chris over the telephone that you rolled 2 crits in a row!
Its complication is what gave the game its flavor, because in the end, the character you made was unique.  That's the best part of the game, when your creating your own custom class and your thinking to yourself....I should take a minor skill in alchemy because my orc Hagor will need to eat shrooms he found on the ground, and by god I want to know what its effects are!
Or my wood elf mage was trained with a dagger in her youth, so you choose a competency in short-blades over mysticism (who heals anyways!)
Allowing the player to handi-cap himself/herself with odd and most of the time ineffective-skillsets; helped create this immersive environment of danger and excitement.  After all, what fun is a game if you know your going to win 100% of the time (even if you have to reload your quick save a dozen times).

The good, the bad and the ugly for Morrowind.
I've been following TES series for a while now, but since I was born too young to appreciate arena, daggerfall or anything pre-morrowind I basically was exposed for the first time to this game with a fresh perspective. I couldn't tell you what esentially motivated me, maybe it was the early exposure to doom and hexen and just looking at the screenshots thinking "YES! THIS IS A GAME I NEED TO PLAY!" but I ended up picking it up and playing it over and over again. I started out playing around, having fun, killing everything that moved and generally causing havok (problem was I treated it too much like a FPS back in those early formative years). Yet as time went on and I found myself going back to play old classic games I started taking the story, the gameplay, and generally everything all the more serious. Granted I'd sometime shank a mutha-♥♥♥♥er out of petty spite even to this day, but generally I enjoyed the finer story functions about this game.
The good:
The choices! Good god the choices! No NPC or item is sacred in this game. If you want it (and you got the skills to take it) you can make it yours. Don't like the attitude of a story-criticle npc? Kill 'em! Just... you know... auto-save first... You never know if you're actually going to want to I dunno... beat the game at some point. From a serrious standpoint though the story is solid. Every detail is outlined (if not through long-winded dialog then through flash text narritives), even when completeing story/side missions the progression which you gather information is IMHO just the right ammount of difficulty. You have to know where to look, who to ask, and actually think before you do or say something. While JRPGs like ff7 may have broke me early on into the world of RPG-style games it's actual RPGs like this that gave me a healthy appreciation.
The bad:
So many bugs, glitches and game-breaking ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t instances that have tested my patience far too many times... I couldn't tell you how many times I've made pain-stakeing advances into the game just to have something ♥♥♥♥ up in the mechanics for me to be able to progress further and forcing me to load a MUCH ealier save (I know my bad, breaking the cardinal rule of SAVE OFTEN, sue me). It's this kind of nonsense that actually seeded the orginal thoughts that Bethesda maybe doesn't play-test their games or debug them as extensively as they should. Blessing or curse, it at least prepaired me for future games in this and the fallout series.
The ugly:
Travel time. Look I know this has been a thing for a while in Bethesda's open-exploration worlds and often times its part of it's charm but Jesus H Christo... Sometimes getting from point A to point B is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ Thakfully they gave you the option of fast-travel in oblivion and beyond if you've been to the town or map-point in question previously. Yet here in Morrowind, there's none of that fast-travel ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t here. Man up and march on and watch out for them cliff-racers...
Story:9/10
Debugging:3/10
Nostalgic tingle: 8/10 (fyi, to those that may follow my reviews, the nostalgic value of these old games is my over-all score of them)

The expansions are challenging and offer dozens of different critters, weapon and armor styles, and add to the already titanic map. Combat can be a bit basic, as all one really does is hammer their mouse, but this game runs on the story line. This game is one that I return to over and over despite the fact that it's over a decade old because it is simply that outrageously good.

A game which hinges on it's multiplayer community. It's basically the Assassin live-action game rule set. It's a silly game to have some fun with, but doesn't have a well balanced sense of play.
Everyone is huntering another person on the ship, and your goal is to kill your target with the most valuable item at the time to earn the most cash before the round is over. If you die by another person hunting you, your hunt is over for that turn. But, if anyone else that kills you during that match, you can still hunt down your quarry.
The game tries to discourage camping, but the negative effects doesn't rise fast enough before any single match is over to prevent camping a safe spot. Additionally, there isn't too much to discourage people from out right murdering everyone they see. If they are already behind in the game, the deduction on killing someone not as your quarry will remove some cash.
If you're looking to have some laughs, this is a good game to grab and play with your friends. But you might struggle to find a sense of balanced play if anyone decides to play cheesy.

Binary Domain is a halfway decent 3rd person shooter with a LOT of rough edges and weird bits.  I got it for free from a Sega promotion, and I would have been♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥if I'd paid any actual money for it.
The shooter aspects of the game are fine, nothing spectacular but competently executed.  I shot a lot of robots in the junk; can't complain about that.  The boss fights are pretty fun, although they have a tendency to stunlock you in weird ways.  The main character's assault rifle is upgradeable, and I was shredding robot limbs like leafy greens on a Food Network show by the end.  There were one or two "puzzle moments" where I had to use the gun's "bosonic charge" or whatever to break barrels that weren't having any of this "bullet" business.
There's some squad tactics and such, but this is a mess.  There's a voice command feature that is a neat gimmick for about thirty seconds, as those things are wont to be.  My squadmates rarely did anything useful, and at LEAST once per encounter they decided that standing between me and the enemy was a smart thing to do.  If I get good kills, they compliment me, with the same phrase ad nauseum.  All of them are just-this-side-of-racist caricatures of stereotypical nationalities.  The French robot in particular stopped just short of going "oh hoh hoh" at the end of every phrase.  The dialog is pretty bad, and it's delivered pretty poorly to boot.   The audio in cutscenes is poorly balanced, with the dialog being drowned out by the music.
The plot is... convoluted, full of holes, and becomes utter garbage in the last act.  I caught bits and pieces of it, at one point they were talking about having sex with robots, there was a cutscene where I swear a dude was feeling up a rack of servers, and in another part there was a literal triple cross.  A character changed sides and then changed sides again within the span of about 2 minutes.
Binary Domain is also a pretty awful console port.  The mouse and keyboard controls are okay for the most part, but they're totally busted in several sequences involving fixed guns and a "tank" sequence I hit at one point.  I was throwing my mouse across the pad 5-10 times to get my character to turn 90 degrees in any direction.   The gamepad controls might be better, but it didn't work with my Xbox One controller at all.  Trying to move the camera just made it spin in circles.  Often times, the button prompts were maddeningly nonspecific, telling me to press a mouse button but not which one, or just showing a "[_]" icon instead of a key.
So it's a halfway decent shooter with a lot of worthless experimental elements, terrible AI, an overly convoluted story, and it's a bad port of a console game.  Metal Gear Solid fans will love it!

A hidden gem from a previous generation.
Binary Domain is set in a pretty "standard" futuristic setting, where robots and AI in all sorts of applications have become the norm.
You play the role of Dan Marshall, a wise-cracking ex-marine who is part of something known as a "Rust Crew", an international black-ops task force sent to deal with violations of the geneva convention (in the case of this story, "making robots that look like humans"). The job this time
The story is not particularly stand-out. It's not bad though. The premise it pokes at is pretty interesting: "What is it to be human", essentially.
The characters are pretty fun and the game clearly doesn't want you to take it seriously. A lot of banter floats around during and between missions.
The gameplay is where this game REALLY shines though. It's pretty much just another cover shooter, but it has an INSANELY satisfying limb-based destruction system. Nearly every enemy you can fight will have their armor and limbs stripped away by weapons fire.
You can shoot off their arms (individually) and reduce their offensive capibilities.
You can shoot off their heads and mess up their IFF tracker, causing them to attack enemies instead of you.
You can shoot off their legs and have them crawl on the ground.
It really never gets old. Such a simple system, but so very satisfying.
Something also worth noting is something the game calls the "trust" system. Characters have a fluctuating level of "trust" in you that dictates if they will respond to orders you give. High levels of trust means they have little reason to deny your orders, low levels means they'll often ignore them.
Trust can be increased in a few ways:
>Responding in a manner they like to prompts (i.e., if somebody asks you "can you keep it up" and you say "yes", their trust will probably rise)
>Killing enemies in a fast and efficent manner
Conversely, trust drops when you do things characters dislike, such as shooting them, or responding inappropriately.
You can also answer prompts and give orders through voice commands. Though I see little need for this outside of "immersion" as holding tab and pressing a button during a fight sufficed for me.

As a game based on art and horror, Layers of Fear excellently plays with visuals in a way few other games can. The way the environment changes is thrilling and adds a sense of uncertainty to every step you take. It even plays with what can't be seen, offering audio cues that something beyond your scope of vision is occuring. If you have any appreciation for art, even if it's as simple as being able to admire the periodic painting, then this game is for you. It's an emotional journey as well, offering bits and pieces of your life at a time so that you can piece it all together. Some things yet are only hinted at. The way the blood was extracted is detailed, but who did it come from? Maybe you'll find different clues than me. I certainly missed some, so maybe there's a piece or two of this puzzle I'm missing. Finish it for yourself. You won't regret it.
P.S. The basement in the first area houses the Halloween special addition, consisting of a room with a Ouiji Board and a short story book, only some pages appear to be missing. Piece together the entire book. The only way out is to Exit.

I'm having a difficult time reviewing this game.
On one hand, it's a fairly interesting experience that you may enjoy if you're a horror fan, especially if you enjoy psychological, Silent Hill-esque type horror like myself. You play as a painter who's very clearly having some mental issues, and you explore his mansion looking for the items needed to complete your painting. Along the way you experience psychosis and uncover notes that slowly reveal the tragedy of your family. Sounds pretty neat, right?
Unfortunately, the actual gameplay is where this game suffers, greatly. There's not much to actually, well, do-you basically just progress from one random room to the next, looking for notes along the way. Although the rooms are random, the path is extremely linear, as every door is locked except for the one you need to advance through. There really isn't much "exploration", per se, it's honestly like a spooky walking simulator. Even finding the key items is very linear and simple. The amount of actual scares are also very slim, which was disappointing. You pretty much just keep walking through everything and eventually stumble across the key items, there's no rhyme or reason, or challenge behind it. It became a bit of a tedious bore after awhile, even though I was enjoying the game for the first hour or so. The puzzles are also super simple, or just plain uninspired.
Since there was such a lack of baddies in this game, some intense, well thought out puzzles would've helped the gameplay a lot.
The plot, while interesting enough, never gets fleshed out properly and ultimately feels lacking. I'm still not sure what
. The voice acting is also pretty bad, imo.
All in all, this game fell just short of me being able to recommend it. The premise itself is interesting, the graphics are gorgeous, but it's just too lackluster in too many areas, and at the end of the day I regret spending the 20 bucks. If you're a horror fan and you manage to snag it on sale it might be worth your time-otherwise don't sweat passing this one up.

Let me make something abundantly clear. I'm not a fanboy of Toukiden franchise. I detested the first Toukiden. No memorable monsters, zero difficulty, boring grind for cash and exp for Mitama ( just like armor skills in Monster Hunter ) but you actually had to level them up to unlock certain skills. It was a bad port and boring game.
So why did I even buy Toukiden 2 you say?
Well I like the hunting "genre" too much so I had to at least give it a try. I could have always refund the game right? Yet I didn't...
Is the game a bad port? Yes... yes it is. No mouse support at all ( I was going to play this game with friends but since they are pure PC players they do not use gamepads and won't buy them, so I guess Koei lost some money ) The game freezes at random moments and uses too much CPU... One time crashed after a long battle so my save was lost. Its frustrating.
GFX in Toukiden are almost laughable by the current standards. It certainly does not look like a next gen game but polished PS3 game with a sharper resolution. Blurry textures everywhere just look at the character creator and you will disappointed. First time I downloaded the game it wouldn't even launch LOL... had to re-download.
Since you have lasted this far let me quickly point out what I don't like in the game and then why I still recommend it ( albeit not at the current price point ) :
-  weapons didn't really get much new moves ( apart from katana, dual blades and i think that's it... everything feels the same ) That means that I have limited arsenal of weapons that I like and can use. In Monster Hunter I liked almost every weapon. It had weight behind the attacks and It felt like I'm actually helping my team by stunning monsters etc. THAT being said I hated Hbowguns in MH. Toukiden feels a bit easier with ranged weapons which is good.
- Monsters... yeah still don't like them and still are not memorable at all. Unlike Monster Hunter where most players have their favorites monsters that they LIKE to fight. You learn their moveset and anticipate what they will do. I cannot get the same thrill of the hunt in Toukiden...
- Special Effects could have been toned down because I can't sometimes see what the monster is doing with all the nonsesne going on especially with 4 players/NPC...
- Still can't find online players :(
- No items no strategy. Again this is the the Monster Hunter thing ( it really felt good to use flash bomb at the right time or to trap a monster to help out a team ) That element is missing from Toukiden HOWEVER this isn't entirely true. Stay until i point out the positives.
- Armor design / grind for materials ( Monster Hunter was also Grindy as F,,, could kill monster 14 times to get 1 GEM... while others could have gotten 3... so yeah I had bad luck )
THE POSITIVES :
- new Mitama abilities add depth to the combat! You can have attack speed boost, shadow clone of yourself etc. Makes the game far more interesting and fast paced. However that depth is also a curse because it takes LOOONG time to figure out what works and what does not... Seriously I spent A LONG time in Tutorials which is kinda annoying ( unlike Monster Hunter where I felt at home from the beginning it was easier yet challenging, It was about mastery of your weapon and learning Monster patterns ).
- I like the new running and grappling hook moves ( which can help your team by smashing monster to the ground for free hits ) Also there are different Mitamas that can help out your friends... ( still prefer items from MH though ).
- so far I'm impressed with how the story is presented ( voice acting and jokes of the characters ) I like the character build up and the events.. something that was a bit missing from MH ( but in all honestly I don't care about the story but the gameplay itself ) Regardless it was a nice suprise.
- open world... they managed to keep it interesting ( at least in the beginning ) by adding events, treasure and some hidden stuff ) *EDIT* After spending quite a few hours and finishing main story line I have to say that this "open world" is a joke... Goblins everywhere you will end up just running past them, treasures are lackluster and "open" is not so open at all. See that hill ? You can't climb it. How about that lake over there well you can't go there either. Its a collection of tunnels and bigger / smaller areas. Imagine Monster Hunter map didn't have loading screen when you go to next area... feels cramped and gets boring quickly... although initially it gave you "illusion" of stuff to do but wears REALLY quickly.
I have to say that this game is at best average but can be fun ( 5/10 ). If I only had friends to play it with. Also its way more complicated in some ways so it will take time to learn the basics and move on to advanced stuff.

I can only hope toukiden doesn't do what almost every worthwhile vita game does by offering a much better version to sell full price down the road. I'm saying this because if they offer nintendo a product they may do that.
In toukiden, you play as a demon slayer hunting down oni and sending them off Monster hunter style. Mitama, fallen soldiers slain by oni, accompany you, offering special active and passive abilities that assist you in battle. Same general idea with equipment, you need the power of your enemies to stand a chance. Nothing new here. Though the grapple arm has special attack and defense attributes that offer some more versatility. The combat is smooth, but to be honest, I am nowhere near being able to take down anything significant in a reasonable amount of time.
The main difference between this and the other hunters, including the first toukiden, is that instead of short bursts of quests and intense battles, it's a much smoother slow burn of exploration and combat, that doesn't make you feel weird for having a big PC just to play a bunch of 10-15 minute missions, and watch cutscenes. Granted some are longer, but the point still stands.
Toukiden 2 should be what we want, a feature filled open world hunter rpg that actually uses a healthy combination of open areas, movement and action mechanics, as well as augmentations that anyone would think about while playing, like mid attack evasion, invincibility, critical attacks, stamina recovery, attack buffs defence buffs, and recovering your magic use through sending demons. A combination of spirits that slightly or drastically alter the gameplay through skills and magic. Light heavy and signature attacks that offer more expansive types of combat. Everything is there.
Is it worth 60 or so dollars? I would almost always say no. But to be honest, if this is what people want, they need to show for it in sales, This is one less game we need to buy a different console for or wait a decade or so to be able to play it. And because the vita is on its way out, that's one less platform holding the game back down the line. And I'd like to think that koei is not going to let a series die once they started it up. I will admit that depending on your taste in hunter games you may be better off holding out, and I will also admit that if capcom took a look outside and decided that they want to make a PC monster hunter or another dragons dogma that gets finished, I will have a few regrets. The concept they decided to push is worth the money. But I can't help wondering why no one else was doing it. Because upon a closer look, it does look like they're reusuing assets.

Hack and slash and fighting games just feel natural on a controller. The game doesn't feel as monotonous or grindy as God Eater. I am about 5 hours in so far and can say that I'm liking it.
+Graphics are decent. IMO I don't really care much
+Feels crisp and natural on a controller (Playing on xbox 360 controller)
+Good performance (Constant 60 FPS, No glitches)
+Characters seem fleshed out. They aren't walking bots. The japanese VA's really nailed the targeted personality traits.
+Good Soundtrack
? I've yet to try out the multiplayer coop but hopefully plan to later.

Its nothing really but just something that kinda bugs me for a bit.
If you are solely not buying the game just because theres no KB/Mouse support, I feel bad for you. You are missing out. I know that its stupid for KOEI TECHMO to not include it in the PC version but it should be expected if you've ever bought a PC ported game from them. KOEI TECHMO really outdid themselves with this PC port. The FPS cap is actually 60 and not 30 like most of their games and I haven't come across any launch or game breaking errors. Pick the right setup, deal with the weather, choose the right strategy, repair, design, manage staff and sponsors — in the eyes of a fan, it's quite similar to the real world racing team's concerns.
My advice, if you plan to buy it. Set the longest race length in the settings, then pick the weakest team in the lowest tier (because this is not mandatory, you can choose whoever you want), and lead them to success. Mechanics work differently, you'll have to use your wit to overcome challenging situations. Some mechanics may seem broken at first, but there are often techniques which you must master in order to get anywhere which is part of solving the wondrous mystery which is Morrowind. An adventure huge in scale; it may not be perfect (what game is), the adventures you will go on and mysteries you will solve will leave you in awe if you can overcome some of the technical limitations Morrowind has to date. Do not be put off though if you are looking for an alien yet timeless journey which you can stick your teeth into for hundreds of countless hours! BattleRush is a neat little WWII-themed FPS, often likened to a first-person version of Foxhole. It involves platoon-level combat between players who work together to destroy the enemy's base while simultaneously gathering resources to build vehicles, fortifications and emplacements. However, this game is still in very, very early development and suffers from a multitude of issues- but once they are overlooked, BattleRush shines as a pretty decent multiplayer FPS filled with potential.
-Decent gameplay, controls are easy enough and the actual firefights, when they happen, can get quite intense.
-Mostly destructible environment, buildings will fall down, trees will topple.
-A large variety of vehicles and structures to build.
-A massive and very pretty map allowing for very unpredictable (and audacious) manoeuvres.
-Poor optimization, but option menu gives you only three graphics settings (low, medium & high) that just change the vegetation as far as I can tell
-Confusing and unnecessarily flashy UI written in broken English, looks like it was made for a mobile game (should be solved in future)
-Lack of variety, (gamemodes, sides etc.) but again, this should be solved in the future
-Several powerful classes (machinegunner and bazooka dude among others) are purchasable DLCs, adding an unfortunate P2W aspect to the game.
-Strange realism choices (map is realistic, but the soldier models look super-cartoony, grenades are laughably ineffective, no optics etc.)
However, given how early in development this game is, these issues should hopefully be sorted out soon.
Something important to note about BattleRush is that the huge map makes games super slow-paced, much like a simulator (only a lot less realistic and tactical). If you want to charge into enemy lines proudly shouting 'URRAAAAA' with guns blazing while a bass boosted version of the Soviet National Anthem plays in the background, this game might not be the best choice for you. Otherwise, if you're a WWII enthusiast, an FPS fan or just looking for something free to pick up and play through the weekend, BattleRush might do just the trick!

: As you can guess this one carries around a Minigun or a Rocket Launcher, used correctly this class can be a game changer.
: It can choose a Block Gun (Mostly used to build defenses or paths  given that it doesn´t do a lot of damage) or an MP5, always carries around a Jetpack, but don´t get your hopes up cause it only lasts a couple seconds and it takes time to recharge.
Also theres melee weapons like picks or knives for all classes and specific class items like Mines (Sniper), Grenades (Heavy) or TNT (Miner).
What makes this game diferent from other Arena Shooters is that the entire map can be used for destruction or construction. Don´t expect much from the physics, if you destroy the structure´s base (all of it, even a single block can hold a 100x100 building) the entire thing will crumble and fall
(but blocks that formed part of it will clip trough the floor and never be seen again...).
In regards of construction every class has can place blocks (although the builder does it much, much faster) and make cover or builds like a simple but fortified sniper nest to bridges, small buildings, towers,etc. So you can try to make a bridge in the sky and attack your enemy from above or grab a shovel (miner only, other classes have a pick axe) and a make tunnel to the enemy base.
Regarding Gamemodes you have:
Team Deathmatch: 1st team to reach a certain amount of kills wins.
Inteligence: Gotta get to the enemy base, take their case and bring it to your base.
Zombie Mode
: Make defenses, stay alive, or eat the tasty humans (and dig fast as f***!!!).
Classic Mode: If you ever played the 1st game and feel nostalgic or just wanna try something simple, no classes, only one weapon which is the M1 Garand and 3 very simple maps.
The game doesnt have many maps to play in (like 12 or so) but it doesn´t matter much given that players change it all the time, you´ll find more holes in the ground or simple 1-block walls here and there than you think.

Now, I haven't played this in a while, and not for too long, but I just have a few things to say.
First of all, I played the old version of this game, and was not half bad at it, I hope. I loved the simplicity, and everything seemed pretty balanced. The digging and building aspect was extremely useful. In fear of getting gunned down by a SMG wielding maniac? Build a small fortification. Got a short ranged weapon? Tunnel behind them. Want to protect your base? Build some fortifications to slow the enemy down. Lots of good stuff that kept everyone guessing and generally having a good time.
Then jetpacks happened.
So now, building defences is practically usless when some guy can just use a class with a in-built fly hack. As much as I love some of the new features, and gamemodes like classic CTF, which brings back all that was good about the original, and more, this game just lacks the smoothness of generic shooters and the quirkyness of lesser known titles such as the old voxel shooter this game emerged from. It makes me feel like it has no idea what it wants to be.
TL;DR: I'm afraid I can't reccomend this product at full price, seeing as the old version still exists under a different name and still has a fairly active community. However, I wouldn't totally rule it out if it's on sale and you have a few spare bucks. It can be fun, but it's got quite a few problems.
I hope this review is helpful to any looking at buying this title.

Layers of Fear is a solid psychological horror game, with endlessly-imaginative visuals, terrific sound design, and a tragic story that keeps you coming back for more. Games like Layers of Fear are often disparingly dubbed as "walking simulators" because said games place far more emphasis on storytelling than gameplay, but LoF uses that lack of gameplay to its advantage; rather than having you bother with complex game mechanics to progress, LoF provides you with an experience that could be likened to a roller-coaster ride or visual novel, and it is best to go into the game expecting such an experience. You can tell that Bloober Team spent a huge amount of time thinking about how to scare the player in as many ways as possible, constantly bringing your character's sanity into question. Attempting to separate truth from fiction in such a bizarre, amorphous setting is certainly part of LoF's appeal.
I do have a few criticisms with the game. however. For a $19.99 pricetag, the game takes approximately three to four hours to complete, and while there are indeed multiple endings that warrant multiple playthroughs, the game at large is quite similar no matter what ending you're attempting to get. For this reason, I would advocate waiting for a sale to purchase LoF. Also, the story itself could have used a bit more imagination and detail; while the game provides a definite  storyline for you to follow, I wish the main character and his family received further development so I could be more invested in their lives and fates. These things being said, LoF is a very good game overall and certainly worth a try, whether you're a horror aficionado or dipping your toes in terror for the first time.

I have a hard time recommending this game. It was not bad, but it is rather short and although you are supposed to do multiple playthroughs I was not interested in replays, simply because there is not much you can guess as to which of the endings you'd be getting or what to do to alter the story (even though it boasts that in the beginning). Getting one of the endings requires you to find collectibles and that is definitely not something I want to spend time with (although there are less than 20, missing one means you did not find all and I don't see a point of playing it with a walkthrough).
It could have been more subtle with how you are introduced to the level switching and the camera/frustrum trickery. As in, if it would be introducing the 'glitches' slower, you would not be sure about what's going on. As is, you know it in 10 minutes of gameplay. This was definitely my favourite thing about the game and I have not seen it done this way before in a horror game (and nowhere else besides Antichamber, possibly). I also liked the impossible space in which you are moving.
I liked the atmosphere but overall the horror parts did not quite work for me. The jumpscare galore is fine but it did not manage to build tension for the constant fright the first Amnesia games invoked. There is nothing to fear, if you don't lose progress.
The puzzle elements exist just so the game would not be a haunted house on rails and writing a number you see on a wall to a lock is a puzzle probably only in video games. That is my biggest complaint, actually. There is not much mechanics wise - you walk and look at things.
My favourite (and definitely memorable) level was the tall library and if the whole thing would be as surreal or more geared towards it, I think I'd recommend it.
Overall, if you are a horror game fan, this one is definitely one of the best ones. It's well produced (sound, video, story) and so on but for me, it was just OK. I would not recommend it to someone who is not a massive horror game fan.

Toukiden 2 is also a much, much better game than the original Toukiden or Kiwami. These are monster hunter-esque games but with a Japanese-fantastical setting to it. The graphics have been improved, 2 new weapons have been added, the story is told in a more immersive way, The world is huge and it is open with just some instancing when doing specific missions and in Co-op mode, but with no transitions between areas at all. I have only played for 4 hours and the game actually feels amazingly well done and immersive. They improved a lot of things, it actually feels like a start of a new franchise.
I would have recommended this game exclusively on a sale but, after playing a bit, not anymore! This game deserves to be bought at full price. I bought this game because it reminded me of an F1 racing management sim my mother bought for me as one of my first non NES games. I'm not really a fan of racing, but this doesn't require that of me. I don't need to be a mechanic to understand and operate my racing team.
So after 17 hours of time, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone interested in management sims. The in-race decision making will bring with it a learning curve if you aren't already knowledgeable about motorsports, but it's something that can certainly be learned. Constant winning won't be easy, but what good would the game be if it was?
The game isn't perfect of course. I was hoping more of the drivers might be procedurally generated rather than being the same career to career (while learning I started over a few times). I also would have more liked to start my own company, but that is DLC coming out in just a few days from my writing this. The voting system on rule-changes is an interesting mini-game, but how it tells you if it would benefit you isn't always clear. That may be more my failing than the game's, however.
Another thing was the adjustment of your driving team after you signed them to a contract. The contract will denote if they should be the #1, the #2, equal with each other, or in reserve. It took a bit to figure out that the only way it actually manifests is in how they feel the car they are driving is outfitted compared to the other driver. That might be okay, but a more immediate visual representation of driver status is something I would like to see.
All in all I'm having fun with this game. For me part of that is nostalgia, but I wouldn't have even considered trying it without that factoring in.

I was immediately suprised to hear that MS3 was being released on Steam. A classic from my years of practically living in an arcade, I've sunk numerous hours of my youth in front of machines playing these games. Imagine my suprise playing it on my laptop 14 years later.
And unfortunately, my time with it on this platform was barely passable.
The main selling point for this port of MS3 was online co-op with a friend. I honestly feel that the netcode for this game is poor as I both me and my pal have low ping counts towards each other, and started to play a game to see each  other teleporting and not responding to controls until 3 seconds later. Very disappointing.
Another issue with the game i have is the limitations of credits. I find this to be a puzzling restriction, as the 20 credits are not change able, and keep only but the good players of the game from reaching the end with a handful of credits left. Perhaps I've been spoiled with emulators and their key to add credits, but even yet, this restriction is puzzling.
Finally, a good chunk of sounds in this port have Very noticible changes in they way they sound, compared to their arcade counterparts. the sub-boss in Mission 2,and the main boss of Mission 4 have a high pitched whining noise that replace the original sounds of some of their attacks. I suspect that this is a result from the game being ported and not an emulation, but as an audophile, these changes are very noticible, and not subtle at all. It may seem like a nitpick, and I would agree if their replacement wasn't an annoying high pitched whine. A real nitpick would be "OKAY!" playing after each selection from their menus.
Other than those issues, the main game is a complete port, no issues.  I can't completely reccommend this game from my standpoint, as the above has left me a tad disappointed, but If you've never played MS3 before, and you don't know how to MAME or other emulators, you could do much worse than playing this port.

One of the best classic role-playing games to date. There is so much to do and explore; you may die a lot but you’ll learn a ton throughout your enormous adventure. You’ll barely be able to kill a rat, but you'll feel powerful once you find that magical weapon or skill which puts you at uncanny odds against your enemies. You'll feel lonely at times until you find a naked barbarian looking for his magical Axe.
Morrowind may not be for everyone, it is an entirely different beast from other mammoths in the franchise such as TES IV: Oblivion and TES V: Skyrim but being different doesn't mean the game is bad in any way. Mechanics work differently, you'll have to use your wit to overcome challenging situations. Some mechanics may seem broken at first, but there are often techniques which you must master in order to get anywhere which is part of solving the wondrous mystery which is Morrowind. It’s not a mindless RPG like many modern games, it’s a true RPG, one which you’ll remember for a very long time.
An adventure huge in scale; it may not be perfect (what game is), the adventures you will go on and mysteries you will solve will leave you in awe if you can overcome some of the technical limitations Morrowind has to date. Do not be put off though if you are looking for an alien yet timeless journey which you can stick your teeth into for hundreds of countless hours! To top it off, this is coming from somebody who hated Morrowind to begin with. Don’t give up, take your time and most of all enjoy yourself, you’ll overcome many of the problem’s you encounter.

I want to make this clear that this is a pretty painful review to write. I ♥♥♥♥ing loved this game. But it'd be a disservice to anyone buying the game to not tell them what they're in for.
I've played this game on and off for its entire lifespan on Steam and got my friends to buy it (and even bought it for them in some cases), but I regret to say that its time has come and gone. Since launch, there have been a few minor patches ending in April, there has been no promotion, and the playerbase has nosedived to the lowest point it has ever been at. I had so much fun with this game. I wanted it to go far and prove that AFPS was still a thing. But it doesn't matter how polished it is, this thing has no playerbase momentum and no developer support. I know a negative review isn't exactly going to help things, but now that the playerbase is failing to rise above thirty players at any given time, I can't recommend this to anyone. You're not going to get what you want out of the game at this point.
To every AFPS developer out there right now, either market your product better or give up. This game had about as many advantages as an AFPS could have and it's dead. Rest in peace Reflex, it was fun while it lasted.

Good game, but needs an acceleration button.
Really enjoyable, and in some ways quite theraputic, but the 3x speed is just not quite fast enough at times.  If you lose both cars in a race on the first lap (v unlikely btw) you'd be "forced" to watch the entire race to be able to progress, and there's something wrong in that being even possible.  Or, if you're comfortably leading then a faster setting would allow to move the game towards the next pitstop window.
Have enjoyed some epic races with cars qualifying 13th and squeezing the last few % of life out of the components and holding off the faster cars with a one-stop strategy.  Perfect mid-tier stuff, in my opening WMC race, so the excitement is there when needed (and no need to speed up at that point).
Suggestions (to speed up race e.g. 5x - 10x speed):
* unless red line on component reached on a driver
* unless car < 3 laps fuel
* unless car < 30% tyre
* or both cars out of race
In those scenarios you would (as a user have to) accept that you are able to slow the race down should any qualitive decisions be required (e.g. faster car approaching you or you approaching another).  It reduces the effectiveness of the orders changing rapidly, but moves the game on.
Definitely worth playing, but don't feel it's worth the premium price.  Bought on a 50% deal and I don't think it's worth more than that.

I was baffled the first time I saw what Q2 and Q3 pro players used to do. For the purpose of seeing their opponents more clearly, they were stripping textures of the walls and models in the game, leaving the game with solid color objects which helped them aim better, reduce lag and so on. The same kind of 'design' is what attracted me to Ratz Instagib, beside that Instagib word in the title.
For those unaware, Instagib is popular FPS mode that originated in Quake 2 and was popularized by Unreal Tournament. It has only one rule - one shot, one kill. It means there are no additional powerups, shields, health pickups. If you miss your shot, good opponent will make you die instantly. Instagib is basically mode-for-all - you can snipe or rush, whatever you find suiting, with weapon that's reminiscent of Quake's Railgun and UT's Plasma Rifle.
Ratz Instagib is gaming title completely dedicated to Instagib where you take on a role of cute little rat you can customize with random items that drop after the game in various well known modes such as duel (one on one), deathmatch (free for all), team deathmatch (you probably get it), CTF (capture the flag) and freezetag (the same game we've used to play as kids, but in the streets).
Game consists of 13 official maps and heck a lot of unofficial maps. Official maps are very well designed, although there should be some pointer about number of players because some maps are way too cramped for 5+ players. Unofficial maps are... well, it's hit or miss really. Some that I've played are pretty good, while others are seriously horrible. There's really handy and easy to understand map editor available in the game which you can use to create your own maps. I think Ratz Editor is probably the easiest map editor I've come across in all my years of gaming.
An important aspect of every FPS is movement. In Ratz, it's really fluid, and you can change direction at any point suprising your enemies and delivering vengeance after their miss. I had immense fun bunny hopping and circle jumping properly for the first time. I never did it properly in Quake and that made me dead meat in every single match. Ratz is really simplified and works wonders even for the first time players. Additional way to control your player is quasi rocket jump you can use to boost yourself to higher ground in the game.
This is a game of skill - it means you will probably meet a bunch of veterans in the game already, but don't be discouraged - after two hours of play your eyes will already register the movement of Ratz stars and your fingers will try to emulate. All of a sudden, you will be climbing the ladder and ending your matches fourth, third, second and even as a winner. Ratz Instagib succeds where most FPS multiplayer games fail: you can have fun both winning and losing in this game. One of my matches, a two on two team deathmatch ended with my team winning 80-79. Those were ten most intense moments of my day.
There really isn't anything negative to be said about Ratz Instagib, but two fair warnings must be given out. First, game is using color scheme which will make your eyes bleed at one point, so taking a break is something you should do every match or two. Good thing is you can easily change color of enemy models, even in the middle of the match so you can see them better. Secondly, player base is really not that big, that's why I am afraid to recommend Ratz Instagib at its full price, although it's completely worth it. However, at current discount price (the first and lowest I've ever seen) of 0.79 €/$, it's a steal, and people should be beaten for not purchasing it right now. Currently, on European server that I use to play, I had full TDM and DM matches and you can always arrange a duel with players via online chat. Unfortunately, matches like Capture The Flag are harder to organize, it's probably wise to ask for people to play in community forums and add them to your friends list.
Ratz Instagib is intense, completely skill-based simplified shooter that brings back the glorious days of solid color textures aiming to drain your eyes dry and present you with Carpal tunnel syndrome. Damn good time, I have to say.
I can't remember when I had more fun with the game I've purchased after selling few Steam trading cards on the market.

TL;DR Review:
Morrowind is a unique entry in the Elder Scrolls series that is just as fun, engaging and addictive as its big brothers Oblivion and Skyrim, but you will have to work a bit harder to get to the rich nougaty center.
Long Review:
Morrowind was the first Elder Scrolls game to be released for the Windows platform, and it's clear that Bethesda rewrote the engine from the ground up.  Gone were the problematic, randomly-generated dungeons of Daggerfall.  Now all content would be hand-created, using specialized tools to still allow the massive amounts of content that hallmark an Elder Scrolls game.
The setting deserves a special mention - it's as far away from your standard generic fantasy setting as possible.  Green gives way to volcanic grey, red and purple.  You fight giant insects, dinosaur-like creatures and steampunk constructs.  Trees give way to cities built under huge mushrooms and massive stone formations.  You travel between cities tucked inside the hollowed-out shell of a giant bug.  It's almost like adventuring in an alien world instead of a fantasy one.
There is a lot to do.  Over ninety dungeons to raid, four cities and thirteen towns to explore, three noble houses and four guilds to join - each of which has their own questline.  And that's not even touching the main plot, which is arguably the best one ever written for an Elder Scrolls game.
Downsides?  Of course.  There's no fast travel, so you'll initially be doing a lot of walking around.  But between the silt striders (the giant bugs mentioned above), teleportation between mage's guilds, scrolls of intervention and the Mark and Recall spells, you'll eventually be jumping around Morrowind with ease, and it feels more realistic.
The leveling system isn't quite as broken as the one in Oblivion but it's not as good as Skyrim.  And the progression isn't balanced well - you'll spend a long time feeling like a shmuck and then suddenly you'll be a godling.
Also, because this version includes both expansion packs, early on in the game you'll be attacked by a fairly difficult enemy.  This fight can be hard for new players, but if you persevere your reward will be an excellent set of light armor that will make the rest of the early game much easier.
I'm not big on mods for Morrowind, but I'd recommend the Morrowind Code Patch, especially if you play a stealthy character because it enables sneak-toggle (by default you have to hold down the sneak button for as long as you're sneaking).  It also does other silly, inconsequential things like fix a ton of crashes and savegame corruptions.  You can learn more about it and get it here:
If you've never played an Elder Scrolls game, I would strongly suggest you start here.  If you played Oblivion or Skyrim and want more, Morrowind will pay off for you in spades.  I highly recommend it.

It's a very difficult game to get into; I was thoroughly assured I'd wasted my money on this game because my first TES game was Skyrim, and this game just felt so different. There's no fast travel except for Mark/Recall spells, intervention spells, Silstriders (Basically the Morrowind equivalent of horse carriages) and boats. The combat is also difficult to get used to and I at first thought the hit detection was broken.
However, as I persevered and brought myself to keep playing it, the game became more and more enjoyable; I began to level up and I started to actually be able to fight enemies I'd never dreamed I could kill. Pretty soon, I was running around with no armor on fist-fighting everything just because I could.
Because Morrowind gives you the freedom to do that.
Once you get used to how the game plays (and the graphics :p) It turns into a whole new immersive world.
Indeed, once you master the art of Morrowind, you'll never want to return to Skyrim. Ever. The game will suck you in even now all the same as it did 10 years ago to the first people who played it. The story is enthralling and amazing; though it does take a while to pick up, the legend of the Nerevarine puts the Dragonborn to shame. The story is also far deeper than Skyrim's "Look, some dragons! They want to kill us for pretty much no reason so kill them instead!". The primary antoganist is an outcasted Dark Elf named "Dagoth Ur"  who's entire wish is to free the Dark Elves from the Empire and make them one of the most powerful races in all of Tamriel. He even extends an offer to you for you to join him.
A shining point of this game is that you have near complete freedom. Don't like someone? Taunt them into attacking you. See someone with expensive loot? Steal it and sell it, no BS "fence" required. Want to wipe out an entire faction? You can certainly do that.
Speaking of freedom, you can even make your own spells and a wide assortment of enchantments. Want a sword that turns into a powerful Bound Dagger when you stab someone? Go right ahead. Want a ring that makes you completely invisible? You can certainly do that. Want to be the strongest person in the world? You can go catch Corprus and sleep for an entire year.
With this immersive freedom comes immersive consequences as well. Someone doesn't like you? You won't be able to buy there wares and they'll give you the cold shoulder with anything you ask them. Want to go on a killing spree? A 5000 bounty will earn you a death warrant. Forever. Want to try your hand with a spear when your character is only specialized in swords? Sorry, you're gonna miss every hit because your character has no idea how to use a spear.
Overall, this is an amazing game with a great story and very fun gameplay. The downside is that it takes a LLLOOONNNGG time to get settled in;
My verdict is this:
If you're coming from Skyrim or Oblivion or even Fallout, expect a bumpy ride at first. Hell, expect the first ten hours or so to be riddled with "What? That's BS, there's no way I died there!" And "How does this work?" and "This is dumb" and "these graphics are terrible". If you're looking for immediate gratification without any level of experience, look elsewhere. This isn't the type of game where you can become an unstoppable badass within the first three hours. This game actually requires patience and skill.
If you're willing to be patient, and learn the game, then you're in for more than Skyrim or Oblivion could ever offer you. You're in
For the greatest game
Of your life.
PS: This game has mods! If there's something you're unhappy with in this game (Like the atrocious graphics) look into modding! It's simple and significantly increases replay value.
TL;DR version
Best game you'll ever play if you're willing to be patient and endure how painful it will be to actually get used to it and really get absorbed and immersed in the story and overall game.

In comparison to the more recent Oblivion and Skyrim Elder Scrolls games, Morrowind can be a love/hate relationship for many reasons. You have more skills, spell types, creature/enemy types, more dungeons/places, more quests and NPC's... Think about Skyrim, then combine it with Oblivion, and you still won't meet the scale of Morrowind. Unfortunately in an un-modded Morrowind, many people, especially those that started their Elder Scrolls experience with Skyrim,  will dislike the combat and graphics. For those of you that can't stand dated graphics, there are many mods that can enhance the graphics to match that of Skyrim. There are also mods that make combat play like it does in Oblivion and Skyrim, allow you to smith items, do every day jobs, etc.
All in all, Morrowind (with mods in tow) can give you an even greater experience than that of even Skyrim, if only because of the massive amounts of capabilities and options available to you that they removed in the newer games. I highly recommend this game. It is well worth the money, even at full price, and will give you nearly countless hours of enjoyment.

A.  It's a hunting game.  And all this implies (seeing same enemies a lot, using body parts to craft gear, and so on).  If you enjoyed God Eater you will probably like it.
B.  Use a controller.  Extremely minimal mouse support, more importantly this type of game feels 10x better with a controller.  Sounds like you need to download the ps4 drivers yourself if you have a DS4 fyi.
C.  If you want the game to be harder, don't bring AI companions.  They are insanely good, can rez you, don't die themselves, and can kill most things without your help.  Just bring your waifu/husbando if you must.  Makes farming random parts a lot easier with a full party honestly.
D.  All the dialogue is in Japanese.  I consider this a plus mostly, but it is a bit off putting when you never know what their random comments in the game world mean.  So far the translation has been pretty good though.
E.  Max is 60 fps with 1080p resolution.  No freaking idea when this became a "letdown".

If you are a Star Trek fan, this game is a must. The storyline is fun and engaging (if Star Trek is your thing) and as a whole this game is probably the best Star Trek execution in a game ever. If you aren't into MMORPGs, you can treat it as a nice, long singleplayer campaign with the possiblity for coop-play.
If you're not fuzzed about Star Trek either way, then this is just another MMORPG. Like WoW and others like it, there is a relatively long leveling process and then an endgame grind that can take as long as you want it to with regular updates to the content. Like WoW and other MMORPGs, the endgame dungeons become 1 part skill and 2 parts finding the glitches (aka weaknesses) of that particular boss (yes, I don't like that kind of gameplay). Also, this game has added some endgame content that would have to be considered pay-to-win if you are playing competitively (like essentially all the F2P MMORPGs do).
If you really dislike Star Trek (or sci-fi in general), you probably won't like this game either

I've played this game for 700 hours, and have played this game to win. I've played this game to max out my level, achieve the highest score, get the most out of my characters.
Before I explain why I dont like this game,
I would recommend this game if you are looking to have a fun time, if you are a casual gamer and a star trek nerd, you should definately give this game a shot. You can play through the campaign and have fun with your friends easily without spending a dime. Anything beyond that, I am not so sure, unless you like grinding your organs to mush. So, if you are in it for fun, and not to win it, then absolutely go on and download this game, skip the rest of what I have to say.
Now, if the above does not apply to you, I would not recommend this game if you are looking to do what I did in this game, play to win. Before I start my review of the game as a whole, which might turn into a rant, let me say one major turnoff to all non-casual gamers, and that is that this game is SUPER DUPER POOPER SCOOPER Pay 2 Win, it's really pay 2 win, and every update that the devs stick into the disgrace of a game that it is right now, make it more and more pay 2 win.
Originally created in a sort of rock paper scissors manner where you needed different classes of ships and types of captains to win in pvp or pve, (which mainly become the game after the storyline, and becomes a repetitive grind anyhow), the developers are slowly getting rid of this concept. It is common knowledge among all veteran players of this game that all that matters if you really want to win, is DPS. The usefulness of players that run ships like cruisers and science ships is so miniscule compared to those of escorts (the tactical officers main ship), and high dps cruisers, a more recent addition, (disgusting imo), that at high levels, after long hours of grinding, you will find yourself obsolete as anything but an escort player or tactical officer. This problem is so large that you will find that when you enter PvP especially, that players will exploit the broken game mechanics enormously, pairing different equipments, bonuses, and abilities, (there are so damn many), in ways that they are not intended, but allowed by the developers, that they are impossible to beat. The exploitation of everything at high ranks, the balancing of statistics to get the most out of escorts and such, really retracts from the star trek atmosphere. There are so many flaws I can go on and on about in the game, and before I run out of breath talking about this one flaw, exploitation, ill just lay them all out for you:
1. Players exploit the game at high levels
2. The game is unbalanced for different playstyles at higher levels
3. Most players are at max level so you cant do anything in pvp
4. After you finish a set of missions, you will find yourself grinding the same PvE events for countless hours for just a few pieces of borg tech for example, unless you deem yourself a wallet warrior.
5. The in-game economy is very limited and boring.
6. The actual storyline is repetitive and sparse.
7. Broken game mechanics brings little variety to ships (if they want to win and be useful)
8. They are always adding new ways to spend money or grind your organs to mush, they add plenty of new ships, plenty of new equipment, and new missions to get equipment, they hardly work on REALLY fixing the game and polishing it's mechanics. Instead of revisiting problems, they will simply expand. For example, if cruisers are underpowered because tanking and drawing fire is useless in PvE, they simply increase the damage of cruisers)
9. Besides the main storyline, side missions or personal missions are just as boring and typical, almost 100% of them are just rinse and repeat. Go shoot some ships, shoot some people on the ground, and run around pressing F to do some scan sci-fi stuff.
10. Did I mention scans and the F key? Yes, everything besides shooting♥♥♥♥♥♥up, (which is easy because your character and ship locks onto everything automatically, making every enemy encounter just repeated buttons to press over and over, even with autofire on you are simply using your simple and boring abilities over and over to kill your enemy, waiting for abilities to recharge, rinse and repeat, rinse and repeat, grind GRIND GRIND!!!!
Sorry, went on a bit of a tangent. Anyway back to the F key. Anything besides shooting♥♥♥♥♥♥up is basically going around, pressing the F key, whether you are healing wounded patients or scanning asteroids, you simply press the F key and wait for the bar to reach 100% and yay thats all. This isn't completely true, there are a few things in the campaign and side missions and stuff in the game that require a bit of skill, but 90% of these tasks have the same mechanics, and the way they are set up (easy as hell and boring to tears), you can probably set up a couple of macros to solve them anyway if you really cared. There are only a few instances in the newer campaigns that aren't the same damn easy puzzle, repeated over and over. The only useful mini-game is the one that you use to go dilithium mining, and that one is... Ok. :)
Back on course, I think the #1 problem is the broken mechanics at higher levels:
You will encounter players using dyson ships (completely STO-unique ships), firing romulan weapons (disruptors), using only beam weapons, (because multi-weapon ships are useless besides the occasional special weapon, and torpedoes are largely useless too thank you game mechanics), using borg ship modules, while using tholian engines and shields.

You will find starfleet ships using antiproton weapons, and only antiproton cannons, or only antiproton beams, because adding a torpedo to a weapons slot would be useless, as torpedoes are quite useless without wasting plenty of skill points on them anyway and you need those skill points for beam weapons becuase torpedoes do nothing against enemy shields. In comparison to the more recent Oblivion and Skyrim Elder Scrolls games, Morrowind can be a love/hate relationship for many reasons. You have more skills, spell types, creature/enemy types, more dungeons/places, more quests and NPC's... Think about Skyrim, then combine it with Oblivion, and you still won't meet the scale of Morrowind. Unfortunately in an un-modded Morrowind, many people, especially those that started their Elder Scrolls experience with Skyrim,  will dislike the combat and graphics. For those of you that can't stand dated graphics, there are many mods that can enhance the graphics to match that of Skyrim. There are also mods that make combat play like it does in Oblivion and Skyrim, allow you to smith items, do every day jobs, etc.
All in all, Morrowind (with mods in tow) can give you an even greater experience than that of even Skyrim, if only because of the massive amounts of capabilities and options available to you that they removed in the newer games. I highly recommend this game. It is well worth the money, even at full price, and will give you nearly countless hours of enjoyment.

I played Morrowind for 2 years straight before I got into any MMOs and it felt as big as any MMO out there today. Thanks to today's addons for this game it helps replayablility. I do not use any mods that alter gameplay too much mind you, because the game itself is fantastic, I basically use addons to update the graphics.
Morrowind has it's pro's and con's just like any other game. For me the pro's far outweigh the con's though.
My Pro's:
- Massive gameplay area, although not as big as Skyrim.
- Tons of factions. 10+ all with their own quest chain.
- Great houses. Choose between three great houses and complete quests. Ultimately you end up with a home, the location depending on the house you chose to join.
- Lengendary items. Sure Oblivion and Skyrim have them also, but it seem that you get those from quest rewards. Morrowind rewards you with many of these by surprise.
- Soundtrack is fantastic.
Con's:
- Slow start. Literally you start off so slow. You walk and run sooo slooow.
- Attacking is difficult. With your low stats, you can be standing directly in front of a bad guy swinging like crazy but missing him. Of course all this goes away once you level up your skills.
- Switching from magic to weapon is cumberson. There is no doubt Skyrim's dual hand abilities is leaps and bounds over Morrowinds combat system.
- Quests are hard to follow. With so much exploration you come across a lot of quests, all kept in a journal. As well as any notable conversation. After hours of game play, quests are hard to follow and the journal interface is somewhat confusing to find things that may be important.
Of course there are more minor ones, but these are the ones that stand out the most in my mind. Even though there are issues that impact the game, I can easily say that Morrowind is in the top 5 of my favorite games. A game that is truely epic. If you go off doing as many faction quests lines as you can, exploring as much as you can before completing the main story line, once you finish the game you will feel like you have been on an amazing journey.

Unfortunately that means that if you have a low skill then you can just swing your weapon at the enemy and continually miss.

An open world RPG? A modding community that is still alive? An engaging story, with well-written characters and a dark atmosphere? Cliff Racers?

WARNING: When I downloaded this game, I had to go into registry files to change and add some data to make it work with the help of a YouTube video:
Now to the game.  To quickly sum up the game, there are 5 stages to go through with your creations: Cell, Creature, Tribal, Civilisation and Space.
In the Cell Stage, you start as a very simple life form that you develop through either eating meat and other life forms or plants (you decide which before starting).  You can become an omnivore by unlocking the mouth that can eat the other kind of food and therefore eat anything and even an omnivore mouth that can eat both.  This stage is essentially a 2D game as you can only move up, down, left and right.  To summarise this stage, it's "every man for himself" in that you try and eat while not being killed by any other life forms that are either trying to eat you or are just covered in spikes.
In the Creature Stage, your creature leaves the sea and begins to live on the land.  In this stage you have to concentrate on communication with other creatures.  This means either by wiping out certain creatures of befriending them.  This is the stage where you finish developing your creature and it stays in the same form until the end of the game.  Your last chance to edit your creature is when you tell it to move onto the next stage.
In the Tribal Stage, your creature has become the dominant species on the planet.  This stage is similar to the Creature Stage in that you have to either destroy or befriend the other tribes that appear around the map.  The only difference is that to wipe out another tribe, you have to destroy its hut which can be found as the main building in what is essentially their base.
In the Civilisation Stage, your base changes from a camp-like area to a city.  In this city you can build houses, factories and entertainment buildings as well as turrets around the edge.  To defeat the other cities that pop up around the entire planet (yes, this is a fight to own the planet now) you can either attack their city by military means using tanks, ships and aircraft or use the alternative methods of trade routes and religion (I'm not entirely sure how the trade routes and religious means work because I always go military because killing them is more fun).
In the Space Stage, you initially start by expanding your empire to other star systems by placing colonies on planets in other star systems.  You will meet other species who will usually be neutral or weirdly favourable to your presence among them.  These is 1 species that will always start hating you, know as "The Grox," who have a massive empire in the middle of the galaxy.  Speaking of the galaxy, this stage is pretty cool in that you can zoom out fully and see the entire galaxy and where you are within it.  After doing a load of set missions for your empire, the game essentially becomes a free-roam game where you can wage war or be peaceful and make alliances with other species.  The only real bad thing about this stage is that at first, acquiring money becomes a bit of a grind when going between the planets you own collecting spces to sell.
Overall I'd rate this game very well.  The only downfall is that it is near enough guaranteed that there will be a stage that you don't like.  It's a brilliant game though, especially for those who like to design things: Not only do you just design your creature in the Creature Stage, you also design your buildings and vehicles in the Civilisation Stage and your space ship in the Space Stage.  To be honest, the only thing I hated about this game was getting it to work, but as I said at the beginning, it's pretty simple to do with the help of the YouTube video I provided a link to.

This is a bargain-bin game in full game costume. Get it on sale only. I'm a longtime sim game player, as well as an avid race fan. I know all angles here. This game is deceptively shallow.
Player choice- Or not? The game ensures you have things to do during most races, but these things are pretty arbitrary. Maybe you have a driver whose tire temps are too low for no real reason at all so you have to order them to "push" or even "attack" to get the tire temps up- why? Shouldn't they just be maintaining the tire temps I ordered in the first place?
The game throws a lot of little bits at you like this. Every time you want to add fuel to a car you have to click the plus for every single gallon- the game won't default to a full tank or anything. So when your car comes into the pits you HAVE to click plus for every single gallon to add, or your car would run out of gas. If your brain gets in gear for half a second you realize this is mindless busywork they added- any other game defaults to some reasonable value you can tweak to your preference. To compare this to a real race, in every race series in the real world, teams agree to an ideal schedule before every race just in case the radios go out or who knows what. Maybe we plan on stopping at lap 11 for tires and fuel, then again on lap 22, and on to the finish at lap 33. This game doesn't have that feature, because then you could finish some races without ever having to click any buttons. They had to specifically choose to put some clicks in, just to keep you busy. Once you realize these tricks, the veneer washes away, and you see this is just bargain-bin time-wasting game. Not a bad one, just a cheap one. If they wanted to add in fake clicks, why not have people negotiating sponsor deals in the middle of the race or some other arbitrary stuff? It could be anything.
Same goes for the start of every new season. I saved up the absolute maximum budget you can possibly put in for the next season, and my staff are rated #1 in the league. So at the end of the first race of the second season my cars are... in the mid to back of the field, of course. What was the point of struggling all last season to barely get above the middle of the pack on my limited budget, if I'm just going to end up where I started? Yeesh.
So this is a fun time wasting game, I'll probably put a solid 50 hours into it before I get totally bored, but it's really just not worth more than sale price.
Oh and the graphics? Ha. It has a 2d mode with a pixellated background that look like it could run on a 1990s computer, and a 3d mode that zooms way out on the race to make it seem like there's more going on but in reality this could probably be rendered on a computer from the 2000s. Again, it's all veneer designed to trick you into thinking you're getting more, but if you brain works at all you start to see the holes.

I decided to write this review only for myself to point out what is actually wrong with this game. You don't have to read it because I'm ♥♥♥♥ing terrible at writing and formatting. This is more like a note than an argumentative article.
This game plays like a mediocre action based MMO game rather than a Monster Hunter game due to various designs of monsters and player's options.
The monsters have 2 life bars. The shield bar and the HP bar. You have to attack the shield bar before you can damage the HP bar (the bar that makes monsters die). The problem is that the shield bar ♥♥♥♥ing regenerate after an amount of time.  In order to damage monster while the shield bar is up, you have to break the parts of the monster. The purple limb will replace the broken part and the broken part will be lying on the ground. If you attack the purple limb you can directly damage the HP bar. But after a while the monster will regenerate the limb back. To prevent that you have to spend 1 min of your life standing still holding a right shoulder button near the broken part to get rid of it before the monster can regen.
So instead of just learning the monster's movesets and having fun killing the monster, you have to do these tedious chores in order to make the fight less tedious. This makes the fights almost impossible to do alone. Your basic attacks deal insignificant damage and your strong attacks consume stamina like a starving deviljho. The game solved this by giving you NPCs which do all the work for you, including playing the freaking game. This makes the game too easy in the beginning. But once you got to higher difficulty, the game starts to slap in your face because you didn't bother to learn the movesets of the monsters for 2 reasons:
1. Monsters die quickly anyway with the help of NPCs or
2. The movesets of the monsters are full of ♥♥♥♥ing loads of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, like cheap MMO boss monsters with the hitboxes of plesioth's hip.

You love high skill cap games

You will suck at first and lose to everyone, then you win one in ten duels, then half your duels and then most your duels - you might even think that you're good. Reflex has an insanely high skill cap and you can constantly improve on something - better movement, aiming, positioning, timing etc.
Community wise the people here are no different from any other game despite how much they will harp on about how reflex is superior. Alright, 50 hours in and I feel ready to write a reasonably well-informed review of this. So let's give it a crack, shall we?
Vermintide is a game in which a team of 4 players (with AI filling in whatever slots are vacant) go through instanced missions. The missions have five difficulty levels ranging from 'Easy' to 'Cataclysm'.
Each of those players (or AI) selects one of five heroes, with no duplicate heroes being allowed (players who wish to play a hero already selected have the choice of not joining that game, or playing a different hero).
Each hero has their strengths and weaknesses, and their own set of equipment. Each hero also has several types of equipment for each of their weapons - for example, the Witch has a sword, a fire sword and a mace for her melee weapons.
Unfortunately, those are not always balanced, and (for example) many players agree that the fire sword (that applies a damage over time effect) is underpowered due to the players mainly mowing down endless hoards of Skaven, or using ranged weapons against the 'Special' Skaven.
In addition to their weapons, each hero may equip up to 3 trinkets (depending on account level, the slots are unlocked at 1/15/30).
Those trinkets can offer a wide range of benefits, from increasing the probability of a Loot Die spawning to granting a chance at duplicating any supply item picked by the player and more.
Item rarity directly effects it's power, with white (plentiful) being the weakest, green (common) being the next, blue (rare) being the second best and orange (exotic) being the best. There is an additional rarity tier, which is red (masterwork), but those are oftentimes inferior to a perfect crafted exotic due to having locked-in trait sets.
Players who wish to crush some Skaven on higher difficulty early on might find their weapons aren't quite up for the job
During the missions they gather consumables (buff potions, healing items and bombs) to use to overcome the various challenges, and items to keep until the end of the mission to improve it's rewards (tomes, grimoires and loot dice).
At the end of each mission, if the players were victorious they roll seven dice of varying types (depending on what items were gathered), with more dice rolling positive results improving the reward obtained.
Theoretically.
Of course, that is not always the case, and many times players will find themselves wishing they actually rolled less than they did ("By Sigmar, why did I roll 5 instead of 4? I could've had an exotic trinket instead of this duplicate!").
Also, not all loot boosting items are present in every mission; shorter and easier missions typically do not include Grimoires or Tomes, and Loot Dice may or may not appear by random chance.
Despite this, players often find the reliability of winning those missions and the speed and ease of the runs to be more enticing than the more difficult runs.
Still, with a bit of time and dedication - and a few Nightmare Rampart runs - any player will find themselves sufficiently skilled and geared to take on the game's challenges and have a good time.
Thus, my conclusion is: 'Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide' is an excellent game. 8/10.
